Day of the Tentacle is my favourite game of all time, so I guess ever since this remaster was announced I've had something of a positivity bias towards it. Why do I love the game so much? Wow... where do I start? The game is set in a cartoon world with fitting art and music, where slapstick humour is abundant. It is one of the few games that truly makes me feel like I am "playing" a cartoon. Mix that with everything you can expect from a LucasArts adventure game (y'know, stealing various items, getting creative with how you use items together, doing terrible things to NPCs just to get closer to your goal), and you are in for a treat.
Despite its Saturday Morning Cartoon setting, the puzzles are actually logical and very well thought out. What really makes the puzzles special in this game is its time travel element; most of the game deals with the three protagonists separated from each other in different time periods. Hoagie is stranded way back in colonial times, Laverne has ended up in a tentacle-ruled future, and Bernard is back in the present (well, the '90s). Naturally, your actions in one time period could have a direct effect on a later one. For example, Hoagie can change a significant part of American history in order to make Laverne's life (four hundred years later) much easier. See where I'm going with this?
Like I've already said, the graphics and music fit the game's cartoon atmosphere wonderfully. Even the original version of the game is fully voice acted (well, the CD-ROM version... those voiceover files wouldn't fit on the floppy disk version!) and that was a big deal back in 1993. The voice acting is done to a professional standard, and stars Richard Sanders (from WKRP in Cincinnati) as Bernard. Sound effects are typically cartoony, dialogue is well written, it's great fun exploring the mansion in three different moments in time (which is very well designed), and the characters are just amazing. I love them all.
Oh, and get this... the original Maniac Mansion (DOTT's prequel) is included and fully playable. So you're basically getting two awesome adventure games for the price of one.
Those pixelly graphics from the '90s have all been redrawn - but not redesigned - so they look exactly as you remember them, except much cleaner! This has allowed artists to pay certain attention to detail that couldn't be done back when working with so few pixels; signs and other items have additional text on them now. One of my personal favourites is what the sign above the lobby door says. Also, smoother panning when the screen scrolls. Music has been digitally remastered too, for a more modern sound. Higher quality sound effects are in place, and the original, uncompressed voice over recordings have been used. The interface has been remastered too, and you can now play the game with a verb dial that has excluded the verbs considered "useless" on the item you are interacting with.
However, if you want to see the old graphics, hear the old music, or use the old interface, all of those options are there too! Unlike other remasters and special editions I've played, this one has a much more customizable experience. You don't have to use all the original settings at once or all the remastered settings; instead you can mix and match. You might want to see the new graphics, but hear the old music. Or perhaps you want pixel graphics while using the new verb dial. You can select each setting separately, letting you play exactly how you want.
When playing for your first time, you will unlock concept art as you progress further into the game and enter more and more scenes. Developer commentary is available; when starting a new game, you will be asked whether you want commentary on or off, but you can toggle it at any time in the main menu too. The Steam version also includes a great set of achievements, as well as trading cards and all the perks that come with those. Also, as can be expected in any modern computer game...
.
The first Maniac Mansion is playable like it's always been, but instead of the C64 version included with the original release of DOTT, the remaster includes the Amiga version, so the graphics and audio are notably better quality.
For newcomers, controls are displayed at the start of the game, and can also be found on the options screen (something the original didn't really have). Back when the game was first released, you were expected to read the manual. Or not. Whichever came first.
Am I recommending this game? Of
I am! The biggest complaint I can come up with is that some of the remastered sound effects aren't as funny as the original ones (especially that new Hoagie belch sound... I'm sorry but that's nowhere
as hilarious as the old one). So if that's the best I can come up with... I must be really impressed with this game overall! Remastered graphics that make the game more appealing to a contemporary audience without losing the original's charm, concept art and developer commentary for the hardcore fans, and perhaps most importantly, an accessible way for new customers to get their hands on the awesomeness that is Day of the Tentacle.

Imagine your VERY favourite cake. Something large and chocolately with huge chocolate shards on top. Ok, then. Imagine you go to the your favourite cake store, cos they've made brilliant cakes for you on previous occasions. You ask for that cake. It takes them ages to  finish it, but whatever you'll enjoy it when you get it. Finally they bring the cake out. It's only a half a cake, and it doesn't have the icing on top or the shards. 'Hey, what gives?' you complain. The baker tells you he has decided to ration the cake: you only get half the cake, for the same amount of money and you can't buy the other half for at least 2 years. There is a message written on the cake, 'Hap Birth To Maxi'.... but you can only read half of it. Who is Maxi? Why do you have his cake? Again, the baker tells you in 2 yrs time you can order the other half to read the entire message and figure out the mystery. Well, that sucks, but nevermind.. Hey, why doesn't it have the chocolate shards? Baker says, you can have some chocolate shards, not as many as before, but it will cost you extra. You love this cake. So you grumble and pay for the shards . Also the end of the box seems flimsier than before and you feel like the whole bottom of it could fall out at any sec.
So you take the cake home. It's still an excellent cake. Even if you only got half of it, had to pay extra for the shards and you may never find out who Maxi is.
That my friends, is what Mankind Divided is. An excellent game, from a series you remember fondly,.with most of what you liked before, but cleaved in two and sold back to to you in random DLC chunks and no promise of ever getting the other half and finding out what happened in all those unfinished plot threads. It's not a bad game, but it has been gutted & trimmed leaving you feeling unsatisfied. With the game's shaky sales, there's no guarantee we'll ever get the other half and find out what happened in all those unresolved plot lines. Such as shame, as it's still one of the tastiest cakes in the shop., skimpy as your portion is.
I will solve one mystery for you though. The name on the cake of the guy whose special day has come? His name is Maxi. Maximum Profits.

I played this game fresh off of Deadlight, another side-scrolling 2D platformer type game. Coincidentally they also share the trait of each being one of my favorite genres: Deadlight is set in a zombie post-apocalypse and Mark of the Ninja is a stealth sneaking game.
Mark of the Ninja is a better game all around. Controls feel smooth, responsive. None of the puzzles really gave me a hard time but that was true for Deadlight as well.
Speaking of stealth games: major plus points for the Metal Gear Solid reference and the Thief video game franchise references.
On the other hand, major minus points for the middle-school English caliber "haikus". Extra minus points for being *BAD* middle-school English caliber haikus. English teachers continue to tell people that all a haiku consists of is to fit three lines together in a 5-7-5 syllabic structure, nothing more. This leads to that stupid "refrigerator" nonsense. Most people don't even know what a real haiku is but I'm not here to educate you about it in a review for a videogame. What's worse is that the writers for this game couldn't even do a bad job correctly. They couldn't even write three lines that fit into the 5-7-5, they instead wrote one 17 syllable line and cut it up into three separate lines of 5-7-5 to make it fit. They did a crappy job making crap. That's an achievement.

I want to be fair here and review the most hot topics, what it does well, and how it really falters without too many comparisons to other games.
To address some common concerns off the bat-
I have no issues getting into games/waiting due to player base. It's been relatively fast for me. It's not dead- relax.
Second, haven't encountered any real problems with the graphics either- been a smooth ride there performance wise.
My main problem boils down to it's just not that fun the majority of the time. It has its moments I won't deny it that- there is some cool action during portions of the zero gravity zones that I haven't quite experienced before (the jet packing in the old Tribes games is sort of similar but it's more fleshed out here) and some of the characters have unique play-styles that can be fun once you've invested a considerable amount of time.
Let's do a rundown of why you MAY not want to play this game in it's current state:
1) It's reallllly lacking in personality. The map design is serviceable for the most part but many times just feels like bland corridors pieced together. It's not abysmal but not exactly thrilling either.
2)Half the time the game modes are legitimately interchangeable (I didn't know you could reskin a game mode but here we are).
3) Doesn't appear to be a way to search for servers to play a certain map or mode yet. Quickplay and making your own match is it. That may change eventually but I'm reviewing current build not a potential future.
4)There is no way to practice aside from a map you can bounce around in solo and shoot dummies that don't move. Most of the tutorials are links to youtube clips, which seems like a cop-out. Lack of practice mode and it's inability to ease you into the mechanics is particularly an issue in Lawbrakers because most of the characters require a decent investment to really be able to hold your own. The game bills itself as tough (to quote- "FPS with no easy mode!") so it's unfortunate the only way you can get better is to suck/under perform in public matches while you listen to guys complain because you didn't sink 40 hours into the beta. Obviously that won't be your experience 100% of the time but when you make a game with a medium to high skill cap, it's probably a solid idea to create a user friendly way to get decent. I'm not totally giving up on Lawbreakers because I can't return it at this point but to be frank, there are more enjoyable free experiences to keep in mind before purchasing. Just food for thought from a new player perspective.'
8/14 Edit: Keep in mind my critiques start with "why you MAY not want to play this game in it's current state" (which is what people will get at time of review) not "why you SHOULDNT play ever." I have no personal interest in taking the game down- only want new players to make the most informed choice as to if this is for you or not : )

There's an extra mode to replay with all your gear which is supposed to be more challenging, so there is some replay value. I want to start by saying that in its current state one should consider this game to be in "early access" even though on the software and mechanical polish level it's a complete experience it still needs a lot of the growth in terms of content that an EA title would require. Think of PUBG- insanely fun and an all around great time but it only has 1 map and 2 game modes.
Probably the most fun I've had playing an FPS in a long, long time. It's kinetic, fluid, and just plain exciting. Every role plays differently and demands a different set of skills to play effectively, making it fun to learn how each of them plays and satisfying when you figure them out. The game modes are all unique twists on familiar formulas and lend themselves to intense fights over what could be just a second more for victory or defeat. I highly recommend watching some gameplay videos if you're interested but not quite ready to commit. The game feels just as good to play as it looks. The controls are incredibly tight, (most) everything works the way it seems like it should and you rarely run into those "what happened?" moments you get with a lot of other shooters- If you die or lose you know exactly why and exactly how it's your fault. Conversely when you do well you feel like you earned it. My biggest gripes have to be the variety and progression. The roles are sufficient for now, but there are only so many maps and game modes. BKP has promised that all updates will be free for the life of the game and that they're currently in late-stage development on new roles, maps, and game modes so there's a lot to look forward to but the $30 ($40 if you got the deluxe edition like I did) price tag shows in this area. Since there's no ranked mode and there are no character upgrades/perks it doesn't feel like leveling really earns you anything- not even the right to call yourself the best. The simple addition of an Elo rating system would go a long way towards rewarding players for good performance as well as improving matchmaking so that you only play with opponents who will provide an adequate challenge to you.
In summary: If you like fun, if you like speed, if you want a challenge/high levels of competition, and you don't mind being in on the ground floor of an already incredibly polished (though somewhat sparse) experience then I would highly recommend this game. If you're looking for something that will hold your hands or require a more complete experience then I would wait and see how they improve the new player experience. That said, buy your copy now so you can shape the way the game grows.

Mark of the Ninja is a perfect example of 2D stealth platforming at its finest. It's obvious from the very beginning of the game that the creators put a lot of thought into how the game's mechanics work, and it shows that the developers really care about the game.
This is not your average stealth game. Everything about it has been tweaked to perfection, and it shows. One thing I really like about this game is the optional commentary, which adds a lot by showing you how the game was created. Of course you can turn the commentary off in the options menu, but I've left it on for my first playthrough and I'm really enjoying it so far.
The music in Mark of the Ninja is very well done, and really contributes to the overall atmosphere of the game. When you're just sneaking around, it's a soothing zen-like experience, but when you're detected by an enemy, it switches to a pulse-pounding combat theme that gets me on edge every time.
The gameplay mechanics are extremely well done. As you progress through the story, you pick up new tools and skills along the way, which adds new depth to the strategy of the game. For example, in the second level you pick up noisemakers which can be thrown to distract a guard, allowing you to sneak up on him for a kill. There are hidden levels, too, that present an entirely new challenge by making you seriously think out your actions before doing anything, as one false step can spell your doom. Fortunately, you're not limited to just a few lives, so if you die a few times it's not going to matter that much.
I'm playing this game with an XBox controller, and I suggest you do the same if you want the best experience. I tried the keyboard/mouse controls for a few minutes, and there's just too much going on so it's really hard to keep track of which key does what, especially when you need precision. And there are a lot of times in this game where you'll need to be very precise. I'm only a few levels into it so far, but I've already encounted quite a few areas where I had to throw a dart to take out a light, then run like hell to hide before the guards noticed, and things like that just don't work as well on a keyboard/mouse control scheme.
For players who care more about the story than the gameplay, Mark of the Ninja won't disappoint you either. The writing is top-notch, and I really enjoy the fact that there are hidden scrolls that give background information to supplement what the NPCs tell you. The cutscenes are beautifully animated in a cartoonish, almost anime-like style that really fits the game perfectly.
If you want a hack-n-slash ninja game, I suggest you look elsewhere. But if you want a true stealth game that will really make you plan out your actions as you jump from one hiding spot to the next, you should be playing Mark of the Ninja right now. I can't remember the last time I had this much fun in a stealth game.

Went into this wanting to like it, but it is hard to recommend for a few reasons.
I'll start with what I do like. It's cute, pretty looking, and there does seem to be a good variety of creatures, some rarer than others. I think I enjoy it -just- enough to see my story playthrough to completion. It's "interesting" to mess with for a little while.
And that is about it on the positives.
In the game, you mold terrain and use special powers to affect the ecology of a plot of land.
Depending on what you do, you can lead creatures and plants down different evolutionary branches.
This seems like it would be very engaging, but when you realize that most of what happens in this game is very cosmetic, it'll begin to wear thin. You will spend a disappointing amount of time just watching the map spin around as the game counts up the years in fast-forward mode while giving you a readout of what species are thriving or struggling. The creatures do literally nothing except wander around and pull food out of thin air to chew on. There's no real emergent systems or interaction to be enjoyed. You are forced to float over to new creatures to "capture" them or else they don't "count", which logs them in your library and grants you XP.
Leveling up gives you a higher capacity of points with which to edit terrain (which is pointless because you can easily regenerate them for free) and eventually larger-and-larger square cursors (there's no circle tool, ugh) to edit more terrain at once.
The controls are strange and a bit awkward. You'll probably want to use a gamepad, and even then it's a struggle. The music is ambient and reptitive to a fault.
The story is... well it might as well not be there. It's nonsense. Just an excuse to guide you as you travel down the evolutionary path.
And this is a bit of a personal gripe, but the game plays way too fast and loose with actual science. You can probably get some nice info from the creature descriptions, but its hard to tell how much of it is legitimate fact, when the Australopithecus is described as a primate that has eaten the "Fruit of Knowledge" (an in-game item). I feel there is a wasted opportunity to teach people about evolutionary science, as that is SORELY needed in these days of fundamentalist religion attacking science. Though I can understand that this is not so much of an issue in Japan, where this was made.
I think what could have saved this game for me is a more robust evolution model that is able to produce non-existing animals, perhaps by mixing and matching parts and colors. Creatures do not adapt to their environment, they simply appear when specific conditions are met to give rise to them. At least with dynamic evolution I would feel like a specific playthrough was unique. However, traversing down the tree is not going to give you many different results. The vast majority of creatures are pallette swaps of the same 30 or so models. And they sort of rely on eachother to progress in a linear fashion. If your playthrough is different from someone else's, it's only due to the way you shaped the land and the creatures you may have neglected to evolve, rather than any you have uniquely come up with.
I can't recommend spending $30 on this game, which will apparently go up after the release sale is over.
If it was something you could get for 5-10 dollars, it's a neat little toy, but not much more.
Due to a lack of meaningful content or interaction, I'd have to tell you to skip this birthday, cause the cake is only half-baked.

All the negative reviews for this game are simply because of performance issues, and with regarding that the developers have already released a temporary solution. Im not saying that its ok for developers to release unfinished or buggy games, however I would suggest leaving your review to when u can actually play the game so that you can critisize it for its mechanics, not for its bugs. Also with regards to the price, yes...this game is marginally overpriced, so my suggestion is to wait for the price to drop to about 20-25 euro before you get it as it simply doesnt have enough content to justify 40euro.
Having said all that, I would like to say that the game worked fairly well for me with only a few simple glitches here and there. With regards to controls, the game is clearly intended to be played with a controller so I would highly suggest you use this over K+M controls, as they dont feel very flowing and comfortable. Another thing to note is that the tutorial seems to be a very long and handheld experience and it wasnt at all to my liking, so dont let it put you off from the actual game.
As for the gameplay, I would highly suggest moving to free mode if you would like to create a world of your own desire. Once you have done this you can choose whatever path along the evolution line you want and it really is satisfying seeing your world grow into a marvelous masterpiece. For those of you interested in the science of evolution, this game is a very realistic simulation of how many complex life forms evolved from tiny plankton in the depths of the ocean. If you like this type of simulation/creation gameplay, this is the game for you. Although the game seems simple from the surface, once you delve deeper into the game you realise how in depth the game really is.
To conclude, this isnt a game for everyone, but if you enjoy these types of games, this is a fun and relaxing evolution game that you simply cannot resist (still wait a few weeks and let the price drop).

I can tell that this is a great game, because I marathon'd it in one or two sits.
It made being sneaky feel rewarding, which is so important for a game about a ninja. A single dude with a sword can't just slash his way through a crowd of armed gunmen, no matter how many tattoos he has, unless he also has a few tricks up his sleeve and it's dark. Get shot a few times and he's done.
Even though it's a sidescroller, and you pretty much just go left to right, or up, or to some point on the map, the way to get there is suprisingly not that linear most of the time. You have choices for which paths to take, whether that's across rooftops, through the streets, or somewhere in between.
It has lots of secrets and unlockables, which I've meant to get back to but haven't for some reason.
The environment is very responsive, and it's easy to climb on walls, some ceilings, enter and crawl through vents, grapple on branches and light posts, and hide in dumpsters. Somewhat related to that is one thing I didn't like too much, and that's the controls. I just wanted to feel more, you know, in control with the controls, but jumping almost always feels too bouncy and slidey, more vertical than horizontal really, and running never felt fast enough, at least in exchange for its penalty to stealth (too noisy). Getting close enough to an enemy to stealth kill them during short windows where they aren't looking towards where you're coming from could be really difficult sometimes.
I appreciated that it had a learning curve instead of it being the same thing throughout the game. It gradually introduces traps and puzzles, and, of course, beefs up the enemies to make them harder to kill; but not without giving the player new abilities and better stats too.
The ending was great. I won't spoil anything, but I THINK I made the wrong choice at the end the first time I played it. I dunno. Everyone is going to die because of me, I'm pretty sure.

Let's review this game on two levels: the game itself, and then its Oculus Rift support.
First off, the game in general is okay. It is frankly gorgeous, for what that's worth, but it turns out that working puzzles by pointing the camera just leads to frustrating puzzles, and spending a lot of time staring at your nonexistent shoes to avoid setting things off. The puzzles aren't bad enough for me to warn people against the game—but they aren't good enough for me to recommend it either, and that's coming from someone who loves this type of game. If you're looking for a first-person puzzle game, you could do worse, but you could do a lot better too.
As for the Oculus Rift support: it's terrible. The frame rate is NOT vr-friendly even on a GTX 970. Several effects (including the near-omnipresent water) don't behave sensibly in RIft mode, which is disappointing and distracting. And on a much more fundamental level, puzzles that require you to crane your field of vision up and down are just uncomfortable on your neck. I can see how the "your gaze is a form of input" idea might sound like a good fit for virtual reality, but in this case it's just not—if you're tempted to get this as something to do with your Rift, it's really not worth it.

Pneuma: Breath of Life is a wonderful puzzle game. The puzzles are all clever and creative, and they're all set within a pretty world that's a joy to explore. I really don't know what else I can truly say about it. It looks good, it plays well, the puzzles are rewarding and clever -- and what more do you want out of a puzzle game? I feel like I can recommend it to anyone that loves a good puzzler. It's not quite perfect though, but even the downside isn't much to write about.
The biggest problem with the game is the narrator, the protagonist, who talks endlessly. The things he says rarely interesting and they do little more than make you dislike him more and more, little by little. There's an arch to it, surely, but the moment I just put the voice volume down to 0 and turned off the subtitles, suddenly I was exploring a truly wonderful world, without this stream-of-consciousness semi-philosophical blabbering. The game just got better. The other thing is a pretty blatant mistake, which raises pretty big alarms.
In the very tutorial, at the very start of the game, you're asked to interact with a lever. Click and hold, then use W/D to move it --- wait, what? D does nothing. A does nothing. W does nothing. No, it's supposed to be W/S. Backwards and forwards. Easy to figure out, but how does something like this make it through playtesting? Seriously! Anyone testing the game should've found this from the start and it should've been fixed instantly. So really my first impression with the game was "oh dear, did anybody actually test this before release?".
Thankfully it was the only real problem I had. A couple of finicky puzzles, sure, but all doable. The one time I actually managed to just 'break' the game was by locking myself in a room by undoing the puzzle I had solved to open the door. I slipped inside, the door closed behind me, and then the puzzle within the room was solved -- but I had to go back. But I couldn't. The door was closed. Oops. Not a big deal since I could just quit to main menu and resume again, which saved me having to backtrack to the little puzzle hub.
All in all, I liked it.

This game is amzing. Classic 2D game model with stealth based combat that punishes you realistically for being spotted. Every time a guard sees you they hose you down with bullets on the spot and, even if you somehow manage to get away, you lose a huge chunk of your score at the end of the level. The game really gives you the feeling that you're an outdated weapon surviving in the modern world only by being the best, and so the best is what you must be. Also something about a magic plant your clan turned into ink which they used to inexpertly and very painfully burn pretty pictures into your skin. The story is predictable and cheesey so I didn't pay too much attention to it, but don't let that stop you from getting this game. The gameplay is so wonderful and the design so simple that the story doesn't really matter too much. The satisfaction of wrapping a chain around a guard's neck, hanging him from a lamp post, and then waiting for his friends to walk by and see his hanging corps is all I need to keep playing this game over and over again.

10/10 Would kee-yah a guard again.

Only sixteen hours in, I beat the game and was halfway through my New Game+ when I realized that I had been slaving over this game for hours on end and from the looks of it, I wasn't bored. I must say, the graphics compliment the theme nicely. The gameplay is incredible, and I enjoy the tedious and careful approach you sometimes have to take during certain levels. Nearly everything you do makes a sound. The guards are alert, and they do their job well. I miss that in stealth games. The sound fits the gameplay quite snug as well and all in all, it's a wonderful game, and I can proudly stick it in my favorites list and recommend it to you.

For the 1 1/2 free trial of the game recently all I have to say is "good god is does this game feel unfinished". Not only are the visuals only impressive on the surface but character animation during cinematics and conversation seem inhuman and overly twitchy, with characters sometimes even reacting slowly and sometimes interrupting their own actions. The sound design is an absolute mess with every weapon sounding like a rapid fire stapler with no impact at all while character and background noise is incredibly inconsitent. One momoent I can clearly hear some random NPC having a convo 10 feet away while those that I am passing right next to sound muted or muffled, thank goodness the important story characters are boosted enough that you can never miss what they are saying. Besides all that "unimportant" story stuff, some of us are just here to be Badass Jensen takin down the baddies so as long as the gameplay is alright a lot can be ignored. Sadly the gameplay is hampered in a dozen small ways from UI interaction to gameplay clarity. Buttons that bring up a menu aspect should easily be able to bring it back down instead of pressing Esc all the time or having to manually close it with the mouse pointer. If you think that using a controller would solve the issue then I hope you love controller schemes designed by lizard men. WTH is with sprint being "Y"(Triangle) not L3 while aug menu is L3, which means that during combat the "quick Augments" is mapped to your MOVEMENT stick and is not even brought up QUICKLY. BE CAREFUL THOUGH it seems unresponsive is the name of the game for mankind divided as interacting with anything too quickly or pressing to much at one time will EASILY cause a storm of bugs to occur, everything from becoming unable to jump to objects floating in mid air. OH and object physics is a whole can of worms on its own, fair guess as what something may do if you move anything to within the same city block as another object, also why does no object appear to have any actual weight OR PERHAPS EARTH HAS STARTED TO LOSE ITS GRAVITATIONAL PULL so objects are so easily moved if they have not been coded to be unmoveable. Even though my steam library says I only played for perhaps 3-4 hours it was more like 7-8 and who knows perhaps after a LONG time suddenly everything is fixed and looks/sounds/plays awesome but I can only suggest this game for people who REALLY REALLY MUST HAVE more Deus EX.

After spending a couple hours with this game I have to say...wow.  This is exactly what I wanted from an arena shooter.  Thanks to CliffyB, it feels just like the old days of Unreal Tournament, but with some new tricks up it's sleeve.  The game feels like a mixture of Unreal Tournament's fast paced and bloody play style deftly fused with Overwatch's personality and objective, role-based game play.
So far no class I have played feels particularly unbalanced, and the amount of damage it takes to kill someone feels just right.  If you haven't played an old school arena shooter and have been playing nothing but twitch shooters like COD this is going to throw you off at first.  It takes a fair amount of damage to kill you and your enemy.
The weapons and abilities each character has are so varied that each character feels unique in his or her own right.  Every character has a special movement ability which can be something as simple as fast movement or as stylish as the Vanguard's jet mode.  Usually when the character doesn't have one of the more fancy ones, the game bolsters that character with the ability to double, triple or even quadruple jump.  The characters each have a grenade type ability and an ultimate ability.  These ultimate abilities aren't always just damage based.  For example the Vanguard's special does damage and created a zero-g pocket that everyone instead can fly around in.  The characters also carry 1-2 different weapons and each weapon; much like Overwatch, can sometimes have secondary firing abilities.  Just about every weapon type you can imagine is presented here, including some neat new ones like the Harrier's rocket boots that you can weaponize by flying backwards.
The game modes presents are all variations on old classics like CTF, King of the Hill, and Ball based games, but the variations keep them from getting stale.  For example, the CTF style game here (called Overcharge) has the teams competing for control of a battery.  But once you get the battery back to your base you have to protect it while it charges.  If the enemy team takes it from you, it retains it's charge...so you might end up doing some of their work for them.
Lastly, the game does have some real money items you can buy, but much like Overwatch they are all cosmetic.  Honestly, I'm not crazy about the skins I have seen, but it's just a nice touch.  And assuming that the game ends up surviving (which I hope it does), I imagine we will get more skins.
In short, if you have been looking for an arena shooter with modern trappings that make it feel relevant and cool...this is the game for you.  If you'll excuse me, I have some faces I need to melt.

The Way of life is truly inspirational and accurately depicts the struggles between solemnly isolated elderly in under developed locations and spoiled kids in first world societies.
Reminds me of that amazing and not depressing Apple "lemmings" ad, but a twist happens, and you quickly end up in donut and dragon paradise over life-threatening lava which turns out to be orange juice.
You start off as a business man who has to make his way through the crowd of mindless slaves of the all powerful Gaben. You make it into his office, and you realize something. You just got old.
You realize that the skin on your face starts drooping and you need to get to the plastic surgeon clinic to fix this problem. But the traffic is equivalent to that of a highway, and you cannot rely on stoplights or crossing guards to help yourself, the poor man, get across this highway. But you feel exhausted, and need to sit down to take a sniff of your hallucination inducing wrinkle cream. As you get up and start walking across the street, you see all your retirement home friends and then BAM, you are out cold.
You begin to hallucinate about your childhood experiences in Sierra Leone, and how you wished you could eat the biggest donut in the world. But there was a catch. The dragons which you always wished you could have came back to haunt you, and the orange juice which you never finished for breakfast was mixed into a giant pool of liquid death. You slowly and carefully make your way up the stairs, and as you realize that you got to the top, the game ends.
93/10, could have been a bit worse but sadly it made the gaming industry look like those sad souls walking off of cliffs in the once again amazing "lemmings" ad.

I bought this game and tried to play it on my brand new Alienware 17 R4 laptop and the performance was horrible. It was literally unplayable. I don't feel like trying to tweak settings to get such a non-graphics-intensive game to work, so I went ahead and asked for a refund. It's like the port to PC was 100% an after thought. The dev studio failed hard on this one. Too bad, since the concept looks really great.

As ever when there are technical issues I feel required to point out that there are issues (ones that I don't personally have) so there is an element of buyer beware - that said, my computer handles it fine (as it should, seeing as my computer is still top of the line).
So onto the actual game. It starts off a little slow; but as you continue the actual complexity of what you're having to do to get creatures to 'birth' quickly starts to ramp up until you're changing the entire ecosystem to get a T-rex to spawn. The actual game itself is well designed, and for a console port it plays fairly smoothly for me. Overal I've had a considerable amount of fun in the time I've played. It plays somewhat like Viva Pinata, which is awesome, though with more big stompy dinosaurs and less candy filled paper.
The graphics are a bit cheesy (and dated) and the audio is a little repetitive, however the former has never been a good reason to put me off a game, and the latter is very easily solved, equally whilst the graphics aren't exactly the best, they 'feel' right somehow - possibly for the above mentioned Viva Pinata similarities
There is a fairly sizeable downside - the keyboard and mouse controls are.... counter intuitive. Not the worst I've encountered over the years, and I did manage to get used to them. That said, if you're not someone who plays ports very often you may find yourself struggling to adapt to controls being entirely different to 'normal' keybinds.

This is still today one of the best games i have ever played. This game proved that a comic book based videogame can be great, instead of a lot of movie tied videogames that tend to suck. It has a mix of classic and modern gameplay, that blends together well. You start the game by bringing Joker again to Arkham Asylum, but soon he breaks free and takes control of the entire island. The story in this game is superbly written, and the villains fantastic, like Scarecrow with fear gas, Poison Ivy with plants, and of course Joker, the main villain star. The gameplay is breaked into 3 types: exploration, where you progress through the asylum, discover new places, enjoy the graphics, relax, and find collectibles and solves riddles, with plenty of easter eggs. But not everything can be collected right away, you'll need to obtain new gadgets and come back later. The combat is simple and fluid, using a button to attack and another to counter mainly, with a few more tricks. But the enemies aren't varied, with only 2 or 3 that will require another tactic, and a mini-boss that's very recicled. Lastly there's the the stealth sections, where you must plan and take down Joker goons in a room without being detected. It sounds cool, but it's more random than i would like. It's still enjoyable though. In the end, this isn't exactly an open world game, but more of a linear, focused story that works very well here, although it's a bit short. But after finishing the story and collecting everything, there's still the challenge mode, where you will face some combat challenges where you need to keep a combo to earn a high score, or face some stealth sections where you must take down Joker goons with some extra requirements. This challenges are harder than the story mode, but still doable. This game is a must buy on sale, but the game have crashed 2 times and there's a bug where the game exits if you internet connection gets cut off. This last one is annoying, because you will lose progress, and get frustrated. While this game no longer have DRM other than Steam, it seems that some code is still unintendedly present. But despite that it's still a great game, and while the core mechanics are much improved in Batman Arkham City, this one has the best story and villains, because it's more focused.

Let me start by saying that I fully understand what The Way Of Life is TRYING to accomplish, and I respect it for the most part. You play the part of a person, basically, who has to accomplish menial tasks. The game comes from the fact that each of these tasks are experienced at a different age. For example (and I use this example because it's as far as I got in the stupid game), when the game starts, you must cross the road first as an adult, then as a senior, and finally the road is re-imagined through the eyes of a child.
Starting up the game, anyone would be skeptical. The minimalist opening screen, and complete lack of any options (including controls, graphics, etc.) kind of describes what kind of game this is going to be, and leads me to believe that this isn't a stylistic choice, but a limitation. You click the dude from the bathroom sign, and you're prompted to cross a street. Simple enough as an adult. Avoid the cars, cross, and go to your office. Then you play as a senior, and here's where the game starts to♥♥♥♥♥♥the bed. You have to be the quickest old guy in the world, and cross the street, but now there's a twist where your camera is extra slow, and you have the walking pace of a parapalegic tortoise.
Finally, the concept crescendos with the same sequence, but as a small child. The roads and cars and pale greys of the previous worlds are gone, and replaced with a huge bridge, flaming dragons, and a vast lava pit, all leading up to "Sugar Land" or some♥♥♥♥♥♥ I don't remember. Here is where I will give the game the only compliment I have for it; It looks pretty cool. The hexagonal trees and impossible architecture is jarring at first, but the lava looks really cool. Almost like one of those 3d scramble pictures, but I digress.
Having to figure out the controls isn't that bad. Seasoned gamers know which buttons will likely be mapped, and it's pretty easy to deconstruct from there. Having multiple controls depending on what age your character is isn't that bad either. Where it all falls apart is the level design itself. I feel like this game wasn't even tested beyond making sure the scripts ran. I must have tried that bridge level as a small child around 50 times, and each time, found myself falling into the pit of lava below. I would've given up around 10 times, but I refused to (and still refuse to) let a game this stupid beat me.
It's bad. I hope it gets better, but that doesn't seem likely. The story is abstract, if not absent entirely. The controls are clunky and frustrating, and the level design shoddy at best. The visuals... well, it looks pretty cool. Certainly weird, but cool. I don't even remember installing this, but it was in my library, so I checked it out. As I said in the beginning of this review, I really like the concept, and really respect what the creators were, I'm sure, TRYING to accomplish. The execution, however, was godawful, and I feel dumber for having not been able to cross that stupid bridge to Sugar Mountain or whatever the ♥♥♥♥ it's called.

Lawbreakers is rough around the edges and is not as polshed as some other shooters on the market (character models aren't as sharp, ragdolls corpses look unfinished and your corpse will frequently fall through the map), but after a few matches the diamond in the rough starts to shine.  Probably the biggest learning curve for FPS players is going to be movement around the map and in zero G areas.  Plus, its different depending on your class.   If you've played Tribes, you'll be right at home.
Game mode variety at least for now is very refreshing.  No two matches feel the same.  All are variations of CTF and holding zones but the strengths and weakness of the classes determine how you will play offense or defense.
Role variety is good for now.  It's early, so balancing tweaks and reworks are sure to happen.  There's a good combination of classes that do well in close quarters and those that do good at distances.  You can't expect to be able to take on any class in any situation.  Juggernaught vs. Gunslinger at a distance, Jugg is most likely going to lose.  Battle Medic vs. Battle Medic in close quarters, bye bye medic.  The key is to recognize those imbalanced situations and know when to retreat or wait for help.
Graphics are good.  I wouldn't say amazing.  Boss Key went for more realistic models instead of cartoony and that probably makes me more critical of them.  But in the heat of a match, its not really a factor.
There's a good variety of maps already available.  The best thing about the maps is how well the movement systems works with them.  All areas are accessible by all the classes, but the means to get there are different.  For example, Harrier can use boost to move vertically, while Vanguard flies like a jet, Juggernaunt needs to sprint and leap, and Battle Medic can levitate.  As a result the multilayed with interconnecting passages on maps feel very fresh depending on your role.
I've only got 10 hrs into it, but already feel like I got my money's worth.  The lack of polish (cosmetic stuff) gives it a F2P first impression.  But after a few matches its something that you would put your cash on the table to have access to all the classes without hesitation.

Finally beat this game today. There are loads of reviews that go in depth about this game, so there's really only a few things I want to talk about.
The first topic is choice. Each enemy, each room, is a puzzle. Only, the game doesn't hold your hand, or explain how you -should- solve it. It simply gives you tools (some of which you can choose via loadout) and presents a challenge. Ultimately, you craft the way you solve these puzzles. I really felt like I was coming up with unique solutions, and that even if I played again I couldn't replicate what I did 100%. And if you want a harder/easier experience, how you decide to play the game can cater to a more casual/hardcore experience. In a stealth game, it's all about letting the player choose, and Mark of the Ninja nails it.
I was originally going to explain in a bit of detail about how I felt about the story/ending, but on second thought I won't. Ever played a stealth game, or a game with stealth, get caught, and predictably yell "How did they see me!?". I know I have, but I promise you that you will not find yourself yelling that when you play Mark of the Ninja. Why? No, it's not because there's no stealth in the game. It's because Mark of the Ninja finally cracks the secret code to make stealth enjoyable and easy to execute.
The vibrant and colorful art style of Mark of the Ninja is, in great part, to thank for the great stealth system. Whenever you are visible, the main character is colorful; however, when you are stealthed and invisible, the character is completely black.  This, in combination with the easy-to-see vision cones coming from the enemies, makes it super easy to know whether or not you're going to be seen in a situation.
Additionally, the game boasts a line of sight mechanics that creates some interesting situations.  Again, the art style helps in this.  While you lack the power to see through walls and obstacles, the main character's keen hearing is represented in footfall animations that let you know where that guard on the other side of the door is walking.  Keep in mind though, if you don't walk quietly, the guards will hear you as well.
While the game has great stealth mechanics, the game gives you options as to how to approach a challenge.  The game has many tools to choose from, ranging from spike traps to smoke bombs.  You also have a handful of shurikens you can throw simultaneously to knock out lights and distract guards.  You can choose whether you want to slay all your enemies in a given level, or whether you prefer going the ghost route, as if you were never there.
As you progress through the game, you will gain experience which will allow you to acquire different techniques.  These techniques vary from tool upgrades to situational stealth kill maneuvers.  If you go that route, though, be prepared to hide those bodies!

Lawbreakers is the skill based shooter I've been dying for. This is the first game that's compelled me to actually write a review for it.
OVERALL
----------
I am in love with this game and if they get the competitive mode right then I predict this game will develop a thriving hardcore fanbase. This is the game to capture the disillusioned DPS mains from Overwatch who are tired of having to flex onto a boring tank or healer. It's a competitive hero based shooter where the shooting skills actually come first.
GAME MODES
--------------
The game modes manage to blend the complex "round based strategy" (like you find in counterstrike) with the chaos and instant gratification of a respawning deathmatch. The dedicated spawn rooms keep the chaos fair and predictable though so you don't just randomly get shot in the back. Additionally, the snowball potential is limited to getting into better position for the next "round" so this keeps a comeback within reach while still rewarding good play. Overall I think the game modes are a work of genius.
CHARACTER DESIGN
---------------------
The aesthetics and personalities of the characters is probably the lowpoint of the game. Some of the designs are plain ugly and unattractive, and the personalities as a whole are forgettable. Almost wish they just let the characters be faceless bots because when compared to something like Overwatch it's kind of cringe at times. Skins will mitigate this to an extent & overall doesn't matter to me much at all.
CHARACTER GAMEPLAY
-------------------------
On the gameplay end of things the characters are absolutely wonderful with only the vanguard seems somewhat shallow and boring (though some people love her). Each role is unique and incredibly powerful within their niche without feeling helpless outside it. I've gotten plenty of MVP's with every class which is a great sign for balance. When you play in a coordinated fashion, the different movesets combine in ways that allows teamwork to be incredibly satisfying.
Of special note, the medic class is actually fun and capable of kicking some♥♥♥♥♥if you can rock her high skill cieling guns. This is awesome since their this kit is likely going to be the backbone of the competitive meta. Hopefully they have another heal class in the works (Harrier doesn't quite do enough healing to count).
SKILL
-----
Overall though my favorite part is that the game is absolutely skill based with serious individual carry potential. 5 people per team is the perfect number to allow real teamwork as well as stand out performance. Obviously at the high levels teamwork will be necessary, but due to the high number of engagements you will have per match, one person popping off can have significant impact on the outcome. I think this makes both your wins AND your losses feel more deserved which ultimately makes BOTH more enjoyable.
DEVS
--------
Boss Key just realeased their first dev update where they said they were addressing most of the issues that exist at this time while also confirming a competitive mode and two more heroes. If they keep being as awesome as they seem, the game is likely to keep growing.

Ever played a stealth game, or a game with stealth, get caught, and predictably yell "How did they see me!?". I know I have, but I promise you that you will not find yourself yelling that when you play Mark of the Ninja. Why? No, it's not because there's no stealth in the game. It's because Mark of the Ninja finally cracks the secret code to make stealth enjoyable and easy to execute.
The vibrant and colorful art style of Mark of the Ninja is, in great part, to thank for the great stealth system. Whenever you are visible, the main character is colorful; however, when you are stealthed and invisible, the character is completely black.  This, in combination with the easy-to-see vision cones coming from the enemies, makes it super easy to know whether or not you're going to be seen in a situation.
Additionally, the game boasts a line of sight mechanics that creates some interesting situations.  Again, the art style helps in this.  While you lack the power to see through walls and obstacles, the main character's keen hearing is represented in footfall animations that let you know where that guard on the other side of the door is walking.  Keep in mind though, if you don't walk quietly, the guards will hear you as well.
While the game has great stealth mechanics, the game gives you options as to how to approach a challenge.  The game has many tools to choose from, ranging from spike traps to smoke bombs.  You also have a handful of shurikens you can throw simultaneously to knock out lights and distract guards.  You can choose whether you want to slay all your enemies in a given level, or whether you prefer going the ghost route, as if you were never there.
As you progress through the game, you will gain experience which will allow you to acquire different techniques.  These techniques vary from tool upgrades to situational stealth kill maneuvers.  If you go that route, though, be prepared to hide those bodies!

Pneuma: Breath of Life is a puzzle game with philosophical overtones.  Screenshots make it look like a Myst-like experience, but it's much more similar to the recently released Talos Principle. Levels are vibrant in color, though mostly narrow and linear.
The puzzles themselves are often clever, based around perspective.  A few stand out, however, for being obtuse and poorly communicated to the player.  Ultimately, however, the puzzles never really rose above being decent; I had no massive feeling of accomplishment, owing to their generally small scope and the limited number of interactions needed to solve them.
What I most disliked was the story.  The voiced narrator that frequently plays throughout the game annoyed me greatly. His jejune ramblings and initially arrogant tone clashed with the otherwise serene setting of the game.  He goes down a rabbit hole of metaphysics, sounding more like an idiot every time.  As the story progressed, it became so extremely self-referential that I couldn't help but roll my eyes.
Finally, the game is quite short.  Nearly half of my 4 hours playtime was spent idling, and I only really got stuck on one puzzle.  I'd imagine that most gamers could beat the game in under three hours. I feel the game is priced appropriately for that length of time. Having a limited time in the world, whose narrow levels never let me explore it, and with a protagonist that I hated, made me not want to return.  Pneuma is not a bad game, but after completing it, my reaction is more of a shrug.

Where to begin with this game...
This is another short, free, arthouse style indie game I came across while looking into the new releases from the past few weeks, and honestly, I find this game incredibly hard to describe. Not from a gameplay or presentation aspect, as it's actually a fairly straight forward platformer/walking simulator, but more so from my views as the player. Much like "The Plan", another short indie game I previously reviewed from Krillbite studios, The story behind The Way of Life is simple and told with barely any written or spoken word of dialogue beyond the title screen. In fact, I could draw many comparisons to The Plan and this game, as they both share very similar gameplay traits and premises. Where as The Plan's story focused on the short life of a fly and how it viewed the world around itself, The Way of Life centers around a single, average person for each section of the game and focuses on the way they each view the world around them while crossing the same, short stretch of road.
(Warning, the next 3 paragraphs essentially cover the entire story of this game as of it's initial steam launch. If you do not wish to spoil this short but interesting tale before playing the game first-hand, please skip to the final 3 paragraphs)
You begin by playing as a businessman who crosses a busy and crowded crosswalk on his way to the office building where he works. The world around him is dim and dank, the many people who get in his way and push him back as he tries to move forward appearing to be nothing more than angular shadows and blotches in the shapes of people. Dark and hopeless, you push your way through and enter the building at the end of the path, going down a hallway and into your office.
Immediately following this, you play as a much older man, presumably retired and going across the same stretch of road. You're vision, while still very gloomy, has become blurry and your motions have become harder to control. As you make it to the middle of the street, the only presumable dialog that comes from any character in the entirety of the game appears before you in gray text, barely visible against the background of the foggy buildings clouded behind your slowly degenerating vision, reading "I'm feeling weak... I need to rest a little..." After this point, you make your way to the other side of the street, being greeted by a group of other elderly people, though still blotted out as little more than blackened husks in your eyes.
Finally, you'll take on the roll of a young boy, seeing the world in wondrous hues and colors that couldn't even be imagined in the worlds of the other characters. As he approaches what is presumably the middle of the road, the white lines that used to make up the crosswalk have formed into an ascending staircase looming over a river of fire and lava, leading to an enormous sweets shop that is clearly visible in the distance. Tactically, you must hop from step to step to avoid stepping between them and falling into the flames. As you climb higher and higher, you'll notice that the people and cars that once blocked the paths for the older characters have been replaced with small, colorful, wyvern-esque dragons who fly across the higher steps and lightly push you closer to the edge. As you overcome them and reach the top, you enter the open entrance to the sweets shop, and are rewarded with a giant doughnut.
The bleak and uncaring view the businessman faces on his way to work, the blurred and jarring speediness of the world around the old man as he crosses the street, and the vibrant imaginative landscapes seen through the eyes of the hopeful child on his way to the candy store all serve as wonderful and true to life allegories of the human condition. Simply put, this unspoken story is a short, cut and dry look into the perspectives we have of our every day lives, and how they change with age, the passing of time, and the changes of the world around us. What's more, this game is masterfully crafted with all of its design choices and gameplay mechanics. Even when they feel odd or out of place, like the old man's hard to control camera view or the child's weirdly touch and go jumping mechanics, they honestly feel intentionally implemented and help to add another layer of relatable realism and depth to this simple game.
My only complaint, much like with "The Plan", is it's length (it will only take you roughly 7-10 minutes to complete). However, I feel that complaint is honestly justified with this game, as it's premise allows for an endless multitude of different situations that could be explored, like a teenager crossing the road on his way to school, a toddler going to the store across the way with his mother, darker situations like a homeless man crossing the street to go and sleep in an alleyway or buy drugs from a dealer, and so on. Thankfully, this is truly only a portion of the game which was developed for a 2 day game jam, and as such, the developers have already assured us that they will be releasing more "episodes" to the game over time. Whether those portions of the game will be free or not though has yet to be determined.
So, in closing, do I recommend this game? I'm happy to say, yes, I do. It's a short, minimalist passion project with a motif and style reminiscent of an art piece by Picasso or Dali, and, again, much like "The Plan", its simplicity highlights the deeper meaning behind its gameplay flawlessly. I'm sorry for all the comparisons I've made to The Plan in this review, as I want this and all of my reviews to be as objective as possible, but honestly, despite their differences in style and presentation, I recommend this game for the exact same reasons as The Plan, and I stand by my initial statements that short, beautifully crafted games like these truly deserve more recognition than they usually receive. In short, I look forward to seeing what else the developer adds to this game in the long run even if it isn't free, and for what's already here, I highly suggest you take a look.

Pneuma: Breath of Life is a first person narrated puzzle adventure game where you play as god in a way, but is it interesting to play as god in this game? It's a fifty fifty split.
The game is beautiful, there's no doubt about that, with all the great structural designs and the shiny colors painted on it, it's a fitting look for what the game is and the story it's telling, but unfortunately it doesn't bother paying attention to little details in its design for a player to make sense of it, and so because of the lack of detailed quality in its design, you are reminded that you're playing a game rather than being immersed in it, in the experience it's trying to give you.
The story, being god / figuring out what's in the mind of god, is interesting, accompanied with the narration of the person you play as being witty and funny, but it was presented kind of awkwardly and abruptly in the begging, but the ending was amazing and it left an impression on me, but sadly that was the only part that threw me away. It's worth noting though, that the whole game from begging to end, in a sense, is forth wall-breaking, which is kind of nice.
The puzzles are simple and fun, with most of the puzzles rely on your perspective/vision on certain parts of them, and some of them in some way puts you in a nice little ride. They're beautiful when solving it, and when solved. With puzzles, it's different from person to person, but for me, all of them were easy to figure out and solve. To put in up for comparison, it was a lot less difficult that Portal (1 or 2), and less so than The Talos Principle. I'm not seeing it's bad that it's easy, I'm just saying they are, I don't mind it, because I had fun solving them.
Pneuma: Breath of Life is not a bad game, it's a great fun game with good looks and great narration, but it, this will sound cheesy, failed to capture my love for it, with there being little to no charm to it, feeling empty with not much sense of life, and not much fine tuning in quality control to help immersion in its world. I can see how great this game is, but it lacked better execution in all departments, with all of these departments being decent but creative.
For the 'nice' but not 'great' experience I had with the game, with my two hour completion of it, I'd recommend it at half price. I'm kind of sad that the my experience with it wasn't amazing, as I could see how amazing it could have been, but I'm hoping the next game, with the same topic of being god and the structure of it, has more of an impact with better execution and more charm.

There may be some who say this game is not pay to win (or complete) but they are only telling the truth in that you can complete it without money so long as you log in twice a day every day for the next 348 or so years assuming no new content is added.
I am not joking about the 348 years bit... I did the math and while you could tweak things, the estimate should be accurate to within +/- 72 years.
The main issue is that the reset bonus caps out at 2048x and since you can only get 169 diamonds before reaching halfway through Sutra, the best enchancement you can get is the 64x time booster. Even if you do "finish" the game you only get a total of 187 diamonds. So even then you are stuck at the 64x booster assuming you saved all your diamonds and never spent them except on the booster.
Now 64x2048=131,072 time multiplier
...but even with this high a multiplier, it still takes 69 days to go from skill level 60 to 61. Note that the cap is Lv 70 for skills and the cost doubles each level. This is 17,664 days (not including all the days to get from 60 to 69) to go from 69 to 70 which you have to do at least 3 times in order to get the "Sacrificed yourself 3 times" achievement.
Note that if you fuly participate in all the events, you can win extra diamonds, but not a lot. The last event required you to log in 16 days in a row AND have Sutra unlocked at dateable stage in order to earn you 10 diamonds. With Karma on day 9, unless you were already at end game stage (reached 2048 reset bonus), you could earn 3 diamonds. So arguably with this reward system you could crawl to 240 diamonds in maybe 2 years thus allowing you to buy another 64x booster. Note that from the wording this will increasy your multiplier from 64x to 128x, which basically cuts the time required to complete the game in half to 174 years...
....hopefully things get better.

Crush Crush is an idle dating simulator which is also a simple time waster that's not just addictive but also includes pretty attractive girls ranging from a tsundere to a tomboy.
As I mentioned before, this game is a simple time waster featuring some kawaii girls. You first meet a girl, usually in a bad scenario and you become her crush. Overtime, you try to flirt with her to become her lover through rapid, endless clicking, taking her out on a date, buying her gifts and so on and so fourth. There's a somewhat of a story involved in the game, but's usually completely irrelevant for this type of genre. Overtime, as you increase your personality traits and level up in your job, you'll meet more girls and you'll do the same thing you did with the first over and over again.
There're also microtransactions in the game. The "p2w" currency in this game is diamond. You can get them through achieving your status with your girl of desired and achievements. I did "p2w" in quotation marks because the game is pretty much playable without purchasing diamonds. Unless you don't want to reset your game to get the bonus. Yes, there's a prostiege mode in the game but it's not as bad as you may think. As you play, the game you get bonuses that make the game easier as you soft reset your game. I've apparently heard there's a limit on how long you can hold your bonus but I didn't notice it myself.
Also, you don't even need to play the game to progress, if you're really that lazy. At least for 7 days, then your progress will be stuck until you play again. It's a nice addition, but I can understand the balance they need to do. Apparently, in a later patch (at the time of this review), they'll be adding voice actors for the girls, which I hope they'll do a great job on.Overall, the game might be a mixed bag for you. You'll need to play for yourself if you want to understand for yourself.
The girls are pretty interesting but not too story driven. You're  just introduced to them in a particular scenario. Depending on your tastes, the girls can be quite attractive to you.They have their own stats and personality Overall, despite them not too great, storywise, they're pretty nice and definetely attractive.
Music is nice but it can get annoying pretty easily and quickly. There's not a lot to say for music to be honest...

So right off the bat I love this game. It has a great sense of style with a simple story that I found myself surprisingly engaged with by the time I reached the end.
The stealth genre is one that sometimes feels very restrictive and punishing if you don't follow the set paths and hide behind the boxes the game wants you to but Mark of the Ninja feels more open and lets you approach areas in different ways and complete them in a way that suits your own style of play. If you choose to be sneaky you're given non-intrusive visual cues to help let you know when you're covered in darkness or if you're making too much noise to attract nearby guards which made me feel that if I ever sounded an alarm or tipped off a soldier that it wasn't the fault of the game but rather my own. If you're into the bloodshed the game gradually rolls out a variety of items to distract and hamstring enemies as well as different abilities to finish the job whether you're hanging from the ceiling or hiding behind doors.
Also worth noting is how this game feels; there's a certain weight to your ninja that comes into play when jumping from wall to wall or breaking into a run that once you get going makes movement flow very well. Your ninja can climb, grapple, glide, and more to get around troops and solve simple puzzles.
There are many abilities to use, items/costumes to unlock, secret collectables to find and all that fun stuff but ultimately it's the freedom you get of how to proceed that puts Mark of the Ninja above other stealth games for me. If a sequel happens I would be hard pressed to think of what could be improved but right now I cannot recommend this game enough.

Grand Theft Auto V is the definition of a love-hate relationship. It's one of those games that would greatly benefit from a "neutral" recommendation. This game does a lot of things right, and a lot of things wrong. I'll be discussing the single player portion and the online portion in seperate sections, as at this point they are nowhere near the same game anymore.
TL;DR at bottom!
General
The attention to detail throughout the game is absolutely stunning. Puddles are dynamic, people comment on your car as you drive by, cars will have their tires turned into the curb when downhill parking. It's mad. It's clear that significant amounts of effort when into creating a living, breathing environment for Los Santos.
The game is gorgeous. Everywhere you turn there is a beautiful sunset, impressive reflections, and eye-catching, vibrant colors. It's such a breath of fresh air compared to the generic brown/grey colour palette.
Luckily, optimization allows GTA V to run as smooth as butter. I've been running the game on a GTX 1060 6GB on ultra high settings, and have been consistently getting a 60-70+ FPS with very few frame drops. Friends with lower end GPUs have reported the same thing to me. This game is widely playable across a lot of systems in my experience.
First Person is a welcomed edition from the last gen edition of the game (if anyone still plays those...). Nearly the entire game can be played through in first person, which offers an interesting (and often times challenging) perspective for races, firefights, and roaming the city.
Single Player
The single player is, and always has been, an amazingly enjoyable experience. It's a lovely blend of gritty, twisted, dark plotlines and absurd, entertaining fun. There are some scenes that were a bit too much for me, () but this all ultimately comes down to personal preference. The character dynamic between Franklin, Micheal, and Trevor is fun to watch unfold throughout your time playing, which could be a while. It took me about 50+ hours to finish the main story, and 90+ hours to 100% it. However, content is limited thanks to Rockstars inability to hear the community's cry for solo content. A lot of people wouldn't mind spending $10, $20 on an expansion for the single player, but Rockstar continues to ignore half of it's game to continue to work on it's cash cow.
Grand Theft Auto Online
GTA Online sings a tune very different from that of the single player. Online is at best, a hugely entertaining passtime, and at worst, a horrible nightmare to play. The game essentially revolves around completing missions, jobs, heists, etc. in order to acquire large sums of money. You then use this money to buy vehicles, weapons, and property (which often times unlocks new missions, jobs, and heists to play at your disposal). The main problem with this model is that unless you're willing to grind your♥♥♥♥♥off, you're not getting anything quick. As more and more updates come out, the prices of things go up and up, all in a desperate attempt to push Shark Cards (In game currency for real money). What's even worse is that the value of Shark Cards has not kept up with the insane inflation that GTA Online has had over the years. On launch, $1,000,000 was an insane amount of money. Now it's chump change. With every new update comes millions upon millions of dollars you need to spend in order to get anything. The most expensive Shark Card in the game ($99.99 USD) gives you $8,000,000 in game. You will burn through that quick. So unless you're ready to spend a LOT of money to get everything you want, you'll be grinding. What adds insult to injury is all of the hackers spawning themselves infinite amounts of money, and all the bans that don't get applied. You'd be lucky not to have some sort of hacker in your lobby. They run rampant, with free rain to kill everyone and everything, and spawn themselves (and you) money. Don't worry, Rockstar will just ban them, right? That'd be nice. Most of the time they do ban waves, they catch thousands of innocent players who have worked hard for their money, and will either take their money or ban them completely from Online. It's entirely innapropriate and Rockstar really needs to work on it. So say you've acquired your money, you've bought some nice things, and now you're enjoying free roam. Prepare to be blasted to hell by one of the most toxic communities I've ever experienced. This game breeds toxicity. People will blow up you, your car, your plane, and your will to live. Low leveled players have little to no chance of fighting back, as they don't have sticky bombs, miniguns, or any other of the strong anti-grief weapons. Your only option after that is passive mode, which is no fun whatsoever. Basically, what I'm getting at is Online is a complete nightmare to play alone. However, if you and a couple buddies pick up the game and play together, you're in for some of the most fun you'll ever have. Playing races and missions together, away from public lobbies, is the most entertaining thing I've ever played. The most recent update, the Doomsday Heist, reintroduced new PvE content instead of the ♥♥♥♥♥♥, hollow PvP content they've been pushing lately. It's a huge step in the right direction for the future of this game, and if they continue on the path of PvE and co-op I can see this game lasting a lot longer into the future. I cannot stress it enough: If you plan on getting this game for Online, get it with friends!
TL;DR
Pros:
Amazing single player experience
Extremely detailed world
Beautiful scenery and environments
Impressive optimizations
Stupid fun
Recent updates for online are a step in the right direction
Cons:
Rest in Peace single player content
Stupid hard push on Shark Cards
One of the most toxic communities I've ever seen
Hackers run rampant
24/7 Grind to get anywhere
I want to be able to fully recommend this game 100%, but I simply can't. While I do fully recommend it if you plan on playing it with friends, the downsides of playing Online by yourself are staggering. I repeat, if you plan on playing the Online, play it with a couple of friends. You will enjoy your experience exponentially more.

This is one of those rare games that hits you right in the heart and haunts you well after you finish it. For people who say a game can't be art because it can't emotionally effect you' I submit Always Sometimes Monsters as a game that qualifies as art. There are few games that cause you to question the decisions you make when playing and to even question your own humanity like Always Sometimes Monsters. Be warned every decision will have a consequence and sometimes it feels like you just can't make the right call. This is the beauty of Always Sometimes Monsters. In a market flooded by games where you heroically save the day and are always the good guy this game stands out.
Most of the limitations of this game aren't necessarily its own faults; but more the limitations of RPG Maker. Ignore the reviews saying the ending seemed forced and the plot silly or forced. I suspect that they truly wanted a completely good ending that made all the characters happy. Not every game needs to  It truly is a wonderful game but I warn you it is not a happy ride yet you would be remiss not to play it.
