Should've beaten this game since a long time ago, very good stealth platformer.
This game can be compared as Metal Gear in 2D. You stay under enemy's feet, you climb on the shadow, you walk behind enemies, you hide behind vases/doors. Fighting enemies head on is not recommended and normally would result in lower overall scores after a level ends. To achieve that, you're given various tools like Caltrops or skills like Mark of Serenity or you can even use environmental hazards like spike traps to kill enemies indirectly. Granted, you need some plans ahead to do that, but it's fun when you can pull the strings. There's another option.... to stay quiet and move stealthily, or run like no tomorrow to the checkpoints/objectives ignoring everything. Your call, as the game allows multiple approaches to finish the game.
Game mechanic has some RPG style where you're given talent points and you can assign it to skills (new stealth kill style) and  items (upgrade armor) to be unlocked. This offers some flexibility to suit your playing style.
Graphic is very good and polished. A bit gore here and there but all cartoon-ish so it's ok. The levels are drawn well and the characters do animations when dying (not disappear into thin air), running or terrorized. The game even uses lightning system to calculate detection for AIs. While the AIs are still predictable, it's a good mechanic already. Overall, the game maintains dark appearance throughout and it's suitable with the stealth theme of the game.
As for the sound, it's a quiet game. Only when you alert the guard and trigger the alarm will  the game suddenly play real upbeat sound. Most of the times you'll only hear your footsteps or ambient background sound. The last level music is good, though - and it seems like they put more effort into making it as written in the documentary (DLC).
Story is just classic, not a big invention since sliced bread but the plot is well written. You're a ninja, you're sent on a missions and gotten a tattooed seal that helps but has major drawback on your mind and so on but it keeps me interested in the game - can't tell no spoiler. Most of the times it's told to players via cinematics in-between a level with voice acting included (which is a job well-done as the artists know how to portray the chars they play).
For replayability it lies on New Game Plus+ mode, where enemies basically will one hit KO you and the AI's hearing and eyesight capabilities won't be displayed in screen like in normal mode. In normal mode you're still given a radar in-level for AI's hearing and eyesight capabilities.
Overall difficulty it's sustainable, not too hard not too easy - there are checkpoints in each level so you won't get frustrated. Well, except New Game Plus as it thinks you've beaten the game at least once and have knowledge already.
For playing this game I recommend you to use controller. So far, I find no problem playing with either dinput or xinput based controller. I've tested with Rumblepad 2 and xinput mode F310.
Overall, this is a very polished game saves for occasional glitches as reported here:
Well worth it and recommended.

I liked Deus Ex: HR a lot, but overall the gameplay in MD feels better and more polished. There are no difficulty progression hurdles anymore like the boss fights in HR. In MD the difficulty progresses smoothly thoughout the game which I personally like a lot more.
The hacking works about the same as in HR, but I rather use the new 'auto-hack tool' to get into computers and open locks. Unless hacking is directly missions related you can skip most of the 'loot' hacking. There is plenty of loot everywhere (normal difficulty) so the hacking is really just for players that wants to max upgrade all their weapons and stuff (which is not needed).
The maps are all well designed and there is enough of lore in the game to keep you interested and curious when you explore the map. Graphically the game looks really crispy, lots of high-res textures everywhere and good graphics effects. Only the cutscenes look much lower relolution than the ingame graphics (same deal as with HR). I do see some inconsistencies in the graphic design here and there (such as a story character that has pens and pencils in his breast pocket while it is the future and everyone uses a pad/computer, or characters wearing '80s glasses and assecories, etc.
One slight annoyance in the game I have is the over-twitchy mouse movement. Aiming weapons can be a pain in the behind sometimes, because you can't get a steady(ish) aim. The mouse keeps twitching with minimal movement. during the game I have to set my mouse to low dpi setting just for the gun related combat. There are no mouse options in the game so you can only adjust it with your (gaming) mouse dpi settings. Oh and I can't change the FOV. It is okay, but a 90% FOV would have been better.
As for the story it okay as far as I've played, but there is less drama and emotional connections compared to the HR story. I feel less engaged and interested in the story and the background of the characters than I was in HR.
Some people disliked the game because of micro-trnasactions, but I have not even noticed them and I did not need them as far as ive played. I have my inventory completely filled as it is so there is absolutely no need to do any micro-transactions!
Overall I really like this game and you notice that there are many talented people behind this artistic project to make the game a reality. It is a polished tripple A artwork that belongs in your Steam library!

WARNING. This game is not optimized for the PC as of posting this, but a Hot Fix is to be expected. It's a shame to see that it is taking some time to get it fixed, but is priority TOPIC... They are working primarily fixing performance issues, but the other main issues are at least being discussed on how to resolve them.
As a Launch title the 25% discount makes sense as the Keyboard binds are extremely janky with no real way to change them, no way to legitimatly Exit the game and the Keyboard tutorial including Joystick comands. It just screams shotty Console Port.
There are of course some work arounds like Shift+Tab Exit Game option or Alt+F4, and manually remaping using other means.
After putting in a few hours into the game it has really been enjoyable. It can be fickle at times to figure out what the best way to get requirements for new life to be met along the way of terraforming, but tempertare change takes time and once something is born their Adaptation Tempetures help creatures stay alive. While you may encounter creatures being created than going extinct repeatably over a short period of time, I found that some other hidden criterea have yet to be fully met like food source or just poping into the wrong location of the map.
As the game progresses things get easier I really do like how they did the story mode, starting with a small cube with a limited objective requireing less to worry about during the growth of the world. As you change chapters you keep your old cube and simply expand upon it so that you don't have to completely start over. They also added some achievements for you to get during story mode like don't use any Evolution Seeds, or Finish by 5million cycles.
Expanding the the gameplay there are items that make the game EASIER and are not really necessary to be used. There are a few items that are required like River Source or Broth of life, which I wish they did something else with the how to use some of the items. Some items are well balanced in my opinion like Stones that change the temperature. I personally haven't used them as I enjoy terraforming, but from what I understand you can only use one of each type at a time and it effects a certain area around the stone. This is cool for different ecosystems around the cube. Theretically you could have one part of a cube colder  while the other side is much hotter. I will definetly play around with this in the future as different parts of the Evolution Tree requires tempertures ranging from 20*C to 45*C.
To expand upon the Evolution tree, it turely is expansive. You really get a feel of creating your own world and eco-system. There are 5 seperate trees to expand upon with sub-branches of each creature at the least 3 times including dead end branches. The Evolution tree really does show they spent a lot of time researching and planing on how to best lay it out for quality gameplay development and diversity. Each creature gives a little bit of a discription and the details of requirements to be birthed and survive alond with a Rarity of up to 9 Stars, they enterestingly chose to give different colors for the stars ever 3 Stars. A bit odd and can be confused at first glance, but it does make it a lot easier to view how many stars it is.
All in all this is a quality game that is worth the price that will easily fill 20 hours of gameplay. This game has great replayability and expansion options that they do wish to expand upon the game. Whether that is a sequel or a DLC that is yet to be known, but I would look forward to whatever they choose to add to the game.
TL;DR if you are looking for a quality peaceful game to just relax and play and really enjoy God Games or City Builders or just simply fascinated with Creatures of old and the development of the world I would strongly suggest this game.

Harvester: A deeply entertaining ghost of the FMV Craze
Whenever a new technology comes out into the mainstream, you bound to get some experimental stuff. Movies that used color and sound to express new feelings and ideas, music that used synthesizers to push boundries. When games get new technology they don't know what to do with, you get Harvester. Harvester is half Point-and-click FMV Madness and half side scrolling beat-em-up with even more madness. It's what happens when you write a game story after marathoning the entire first season of the Twilight Zone while high on ketamine.
The story is probably the most entertaining part of the game, as it does attempt to gently ease you in to the mania of Harvester. Your name is Steve, you've awoken in the town of Harvest, you have one week to join the mysterious Lodge. The whole town of Harvest is like if you let William S. Burroughs write the scripts to Leave It To Beaver, it's 50's America with a bag of dark twists thrown on it for good measure. The town has a missile base run by a batshit Air Force General who rigged the launch control to a literal big red button, there's a mysteriously large amount of random hobo deaths and of course, the Lodge that you have to get into.
Gameplay is a 50/50 split between the story's main arcs. The first half is a stock standard point-and-click game where you can either do the story missions or google all the weird conversation trees you can start. And that's not even counting how weird some of the actual trees you use to get items are. I highly reccomend you get a basic walkthrough for the early half because the puzzles the game throws at you are some of the most obtuse I've seen in a game. The other half is a broken and yet still entertaining beat-em-up as Steve navigates the Lodge. How entertaining? It's where you fight bellhops, walking pieces of ancient art, chess pieces and yourself. Also there are more puzzles, so do keep that walkthrough on standby.
Harvester is like a really entertaining B movie and I have no idea if that's what the devs intended it to be or not. Regardless, I can't help but reccomend this game just because it's entertaining in the depths of its madness. One can't help but laugh as you watch Steve just act so normally in a town that is definitely not in the realm of normal. It's a game where you electrocute a random Italian barber and his pet demonic sheep so you can steal his prized barber's pole, you can inadvertantly cause World War III and global annihalation for accidently talking about llamas, and where you solve a puzzle by beating a guy at chess so an axe falls on his head and reveals a key hidden in his head. Utter madness, but enjoyable madness.

After growing up on more traditional arena shooters, (Quake, UT, etc.) I've been waiting a long time to fine a game that recaptures the pace, skill and unapologetic chaos of the genre.
This game often gets compared to Overwatch but it really isn't a good comparison. Overwatch is a Hero shooter where matchups and classes are as important, if not more, than pure gunplay. While LawBreakers has different heroes with different abilities, classes and roles are nowhere to be found - everyone has to be able to get kills, everyone has to be able to play the objective - there are no support roles, and no tanking.
The gameplay in LawBreakers is as fast and satisfying as you would expect from a game build in the Unreal Engine by Cliff Bleszinski  and other ex Unreal devs, and produces a game that wouldn't feel out of place in the Unreal franchise, bombastic trash talking included.
What differentiates the game from Unreal and brings it into the modern era is the set of variet characters with their own weapons, combos and gameplay styles. No more rushing around to pick up the best weapons, what you have is what you get - and because of the diversity of the characters and playstyles, it works - there is something for basically any play style. Consequently, expect a steep learning curve to master any of the characters - there is a lot to learn.
Matchmaking works well - in my experience it usually takes a few seconds to get into a game lobby and then a minute or two to get into the match, although at times the team balancing is a little suspect at present.
Graphically the game looks good and runs well, although it won't win any design awards - stylistically and artistically it looks very much like Unreal Tournament, which is fine. Similarly, the characters themselves are all much of a likeness - 110% rage and swagger at all times. That's not going to win you any awards, but honestly, this is an arena shooter, so who cares?
The customisation is pretty good, and Twitch integration works well, although for me this is secondary to the gameplay.
The number of game modes and maps at launch is adequate, if a little limited, but fun nonetheless. Because you can play multiple game modes on each map things are kept relatively varied. I expect this to be remedied as more content is released over time.
Overall, other than the relatively limited map rotation, my only real complaints with LawBreakers have been aesthetic and personality based, which as I have said, I don't consider to be major issues. I am just really pleased to finally get a true arena shooter in 2017, after waiting for so long it's a real joy, (especially after being disappointed with the Quake Champions Beta). Beware though, as with any arena shooter, there are major skill gaps, and you will find yourself in matches where your team is getting absolutely crushed - just remember to return the favour in another match.

Batman: Arkham Asylum is a 2009 action-adventure video game based on the DC Comics superhero Batman. It was developed by Rocksteady Studios and published by Eidos Interactive in conjunction with Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment for the PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 video game consoles, and Microsoft Windows. It was released worldwide for consoles, beginning in North America on August 25, 2009, with a Microsoft Windows version following on September 15.
Written by veteran Batman writer Paul Dini, Arkham Asylum is based on the long-running comic book mythos. In the game's main storyline, Batman's archenemy, the Joker, instigates an elaborate plot to seize control of Arkham Asylum and trap Batman inside with many of his incarcerated foes. With Joker threatening to detonate hidden bombs around fictional Gotham City, Batman is forced to fight his way through the asylum's inmates and put an end to the Joker's plans. Most of the game's leading characters are voiced by actors who have appeared in other media based on the DC Animated Universe; Kevin Conroy, Mark Hamill, and Arleen Sorkin reprised their roles as Batman, the Joker, and his sidekick Harley Quinn respectively. The game is presented from the third-person perspective with a primary focus on Batman's combat and stealth abilities, detective skills, and gadgets that can be used in combat and exploration.
The game received critical acclaim—particularly for its narrative—and won several awards, including Best Action Adventure game, Best Game, and Game of the Year from different media outlets. It held the Guinness World Record for "Most Critically Acclaimed Superhero Game Ever". A Game of the Year edition was released on March 26, 2010, and an OS X version was released in November 2011. Arkham Asylum '​s success launched a series of Batman: Arkham sequels, beginning in October 2011 with Batman: Arkham City.

Mark of the Ninja is one of the great stealth games.  It is a 2D game, utilizing Klei's signature art style to tell a surprisingly good story with solid voice acting.  Thankfully it isn't punishingly difficult like Klei's previous Shank games.
Gameplay manages a perfect balance between a fast and fluid action game, and a slow and methodical stealth game.  It's fast enough to please action game lovers, but still offers satisfying stealth mechanics.  You utilize shadows and vents to make your way through levels, with access to a variety of ninja equipment to help you distract and kill enemies.  Klei came up with a very nice vision system, where you can only clearly see what your character can see, with the rest of the screen intelligently blurred out so you not only have to think about your position in relation to lights, but also how well you can see.  Loud enough sounds such as footsteps are visible on the screen thanks to your ninja training.  The game also offers a focus mode which pauses time to allow you to aim and multi-target equipment.  The controls are intuitive and very responsive, at least when using a gamepad.  I have not tested the game with kb/m.
As you progress you can unlock new ninja styles, abilities and killing moves to help you progress through the levels more easily.  Ninja styles have their own strengths and weaknesses and can alter what equipment you are allowed to carry.  I found myself using the standard style for the most part, but it's nice to have options.
The Special Edition DLC includes a new level, a distraction item, and a thrown weapon, as well as a new non-lethal ninja style for those who don't like to kill enemies in stealth games.  All of this equipment can be utilized in the main campaign once the DLC level is completed and does make the game a bit easier since the new items allow you to do some previously impossible actions.  The DLC also adds commentary nodes scattered throughout the game which you can read.  They are unobtrusive for the most part though there are a couple that pop up automatically.  Overall it's a worthwhile DLC but doesn't contain a whole lot of content.
Mark of the Ninja is possibly the best stealth game I have ever played and one of very few games I can find nothing negative to say about.  It is a must play.

105 miles west of Ireland, your crew spots a British destroyer 8 miles off starboard, you begin to manouvre and give the order to descend to periscope depth. As the watch crew begin to climb back into the U-Boat, it suddenly becomes evident that the destroyer has also seen you, and this is confirmed with a shell that lands no more than 200m astern. The watch officer is the last man still on deck, and just as he starts to decend the ladder a shell lands a direct hit on the conning tower. The watch officer is dead.
You set the engines to flank speed and order crash dive. Bells ring out as all men take up action stations and the conning tower is secured as the boat starts to tilt nose first into the depths of the Atlantic. The destroyer has closed distance and unleashes volley after volley towards the U-boat as it slowly starts to descend. More hits, the deck gun is damaged, one of the rear torpedo tubes is destoyed and several pipes burst with seawater flooding into the boat.
At a depth of 85m you order dive planes set to 0 degrees and the boat starts to level out. The leaks have been plugged and you have the diesel engines shutdown and a startup of the electric motors and the crew resorts to 'silent running'. Now at just 1/3 speed, the Hydrophone operator whispers that the warship has closed to less than 1000m, then the dreaded ping is heard. Ricocheting through the metalwork is gradually gets faster until it suddenly stops and the whole crew can hear the engines quickly passing overhead.
The hydrophone operator whispers that he hears splashes, and immediately you order flank speed and hard to port. Seconds later explosions rock the boat, more water bursts from the seams of pipes and gauges. The lights go out temporarily and the boats is listing to port. Silent running is abandoned and the crew get to work plugging holes and repairing equipment. The pumps are all switched on to try to empty the rapidly flooding compatments of water and the boat continues to descend uncontrollably into the abyss.
More depths charges are dropped as the crew wrestles to bring the boat back under control, the depth gauge shows you have dropped to 180m and the limits of the boat are starting to be reached. The whole boat creaks and groans as the pressure builds up outside. The crew has managed to fix the leaks, the pumps are still doing their work and the water level is starting to subside.
Another update form the hydrophone operator, the enemy ship has slowed down and is doing a sweep with their own hydrophone. Silent running is once again ordered and the boat slowly ascends at 3 knots towards periscope depth. More splashes are heard, but far away now.
Reaching 15m you take a peek through the periscope and spot the destroyer no more than 800m away passing across the bow from port to starboard. The ship is identified from the ships identification manual and calculations are made on speed and distance. The order is given to flood all forward torpedo tubes, and the dull scraping of metal on metal can be heard as the doors open.
The pings start again and you give the order to fire. You can hear the whoosh as each fish sets on its way, and behind you the hydropohone operator confirms all torpedos are on course. All that can be heard now is the tick, tick, tick, of the stopwatch, and the breathing of the crew.
Through the periscope you see a flash and a round lands no further than a few feet away from the viewfinder. Dive, dive, dive. The periscope is lowered just as the stopwatch stops ticking. More seconds go past and the weapons officer whispers "i think they all missed...", just as the navigation officer calls out a depth of 50m.
Then there is an almighty explosion, and the crew cheers. "direct hit" calls out the hydrophone opererator and you give the order to ascend to periscope depth. Taking a peek you see for the first time the carnage. A torpedo hit almost directly in the centre of the ship, breaking the ship clean in half. Bodies and wreckage lay strewn hundreds of metres around the remains, the sea ablaze with escaping diesel and oil.
The boat surfaces and a message is send to HQ. '1 warship destroyed = 1200 tons, 12 torpedos remaining. Light damage'
"Get those tubes reloaded, then get some rest comrades, soon we will reach the convoy lanes, and that is where the real fun begins..."

I have very fond memories about Day of the Tentacle (DotT), back in the DOS days, Lucasarts was my favourite games company, their adventures were the best and their Star Wars games are pretty legendary in their own right. DotT is one of those games that was released when PC gained its status as superiour gaming platform. All previous adventures games still got released on multiple platforms (think Amiga etc), but not this one. It was also released on CDROM and the whole game features voice acting, pretty big deal back in the day.
And so, with rose tinted glasses I started playing this game, would it still be as good as I remembered it? Or would it turn out to be one of those classics that didn't age well, like a fine wine turning into vinegar. Well I can assure you, that none of the magic is lost. The game is still very much fun today, everything still stands, it only lost some of its freshness, but that was to be expected as it's a remaster that stays 100% faithfull to the original.
I'm also very happy that they did not change any of the graphics. When I learned that the Monkey Island series were rereleased, I was excited. Until I saw it at a friend of mine, that is when disappointment set in. They changed the graphics and the new graphics just didn't do it for me, in fact they were a big turn-off. If you never played the game before, you probably would have no issue with it, but the problem for me was that they changed too much. You could still play the original graphics, but what is the point of that? You could just as easily use ScummVM then.
This is not the case with DotT, the graphics have been retained. To be honest, the graphics had been retained as how I remembered them. There is a big difference, how we remember things is not how they really were, it's just our minds that make the memory more beautiful than it really is. In this case the remastered graphics just look like the originals with 100x Anti-Aliasing applied on them.
I was able to quickly finish the game as I still remembered a lot and the things i forgot were quickly figured out. You should not read any guides, as this will increase the enjoyment of an adventure game, the whole point is to figure these things out after all.
This game had a big impact on me as a youngster, I forgot how many things in the game I picked up in my vocabulairy and still use, though i completely forgot where they came from - this game!
Take this as you will, some guy has fond memories of an old game, the remastered version of said game is also liked by him. Does this mean it's a great game or that the guy is senile? That's up for you to decide when you're GOING BACK TO THE MANSION!
The game works flawlessly on SteamOS/Linux, the default Steam Controller setup is a bit weird, but ofcourse you can change it to your liking. Streams to the Steam Link without problems (great way to play the game btw).

I played this game in the 90s when I was budding gamer, and I have fond memories. I grabbed this game for $8.99 the other day basically for nostalgia. I wasn't sure if I'd actually like the game again - would I find it too silly? too easy? plain boring? BUT, it is actually a fun little puzzle game. I was cruising along for a while, half playing the game and half strolling down memory lane, and then I actually got stuck. I'll admit I've had to use google a couple times. Some of the puzzles actually make you think. My advice: click on EVERYTHING. Pick up ALL objects. Listen to what the people are saying - they often drop hints. Go back and re-explore areas - it's easy to overlook something that you thought was meaningless. As for the remaster side of things - it's perfect. The new graphics are how I remember the game looking back when graphics weren't superduperHD. The new controls are simple and easy, and the new sound is good.
All in all, this is a good remaster of a classic game. If you played this game in the 90s, I *definitely* recommend getting this.

In the two hours I played this game while it was free, it crashed to desktop once during the opening mission because I had the audacity to try and open the customize weapon menu before it had given me a reason to, and then froze me in place when I opened the safe in my home after the post opening mission cut scene.
I initially did not buy this game due to bad reviews, and I can't honestly say I am interested in purchasing it due to the experience I just had.

The game struggles to deliver a rich story, which is shallow - that you'll realize actually playing the game, aside from cool-looking trailers.
The characters are kinda "weak", you won't remember who they are, nor what they do, after you complete the game (or even during it).
The combat is... Sigh. The combat tries to mimic the Metal Gear Solid with its "enemy's field of vision" and Hitman with its "hide the body before it's spotted by other enemies". And looks like it's a perfect blend. But, actually, it's not.
The combat (the fun part of it) relies on energy, which is constantly drained when you're using augments (cyborg super-powers), and it goes out very quickly. For example, you see a bunch of enemies, turn on the stealth augment, also the "silent walk" one, and *boom* your energy has depleted before you even killed/disabled a single one. It's limited turns in XCOM 2 all over again. =)
Graphically it isn't that appealing, as it should be. It even crashed (with a memory leak, e.g. "eating" all available RAM) during a stream. After that I decided to happily drop that game, and post a review. =)
And about the input lag. Yes, as the majority of the fellas in the reviews are saying - the game has an enormous (taking in mind it's 2017 after all) input lag. Like you have the v/sync on, and framebuffer is set to, like, 3-4 frames (even though the v/sync was turned off in the options (I use nVidia's "fast sync") and the framebuffer was manually set to 1 frame in the GPU driver settings).
And those "filler" cutscenes... The videos are supposed to be interesting, not uninspiring and blunt. Take a look at the cutscenes in first Spyro games, MGS's, Deadpool, Dying Light, ect. - the vids there make you wanna watch them, not skip them, they pour a perfectly dosed mixture of suspense, humour and action onto player, makes him "believe" the story.
To sum it up, it's a "simple" "shootah", which pretends to be a mix of MGS and Hitman, but loses that "cover" pretty quick, but once you find that out - two hours are already spent, and you can't do a refund. =)

Overall, this is a great game. I won't waste time on single player, because it's great and you get what you pay for. Anyway, what I wanted to talk about is Online. It's a great experience, but beware, because you're bound to meet your fair share of hackers who will go out of their way to make it impossible for you to enjoy the game. Talking from experience here. The other major issue is Rockstar's anti-cheat system. There are players who have legitimately earned a lot of money (like double RP and cash weeks, heists and whatnot) and still got banned, so there's that.
Last but not least, the things that are being added in the DLCs are expensive and require either grinding or buying shark cards. Your decision.
A tip that I use sometimes: If you're interested in doing the CEO/gunrunning/import/export stuff by yourself and/or with friends, you can try unplugging your Ethernet cable for a spilt second (if you're using a wired connection, that is) and quickly putting it back in. This will throw you into a public session all by yourself and it usually takes some time for it to fill (at times it will remain empty all the time, if you're lucky).
All in all, I do recommend the game, but only if you will be able to deal with the aforementioned issues.

Mark of the Ninja is a ninja simulator, plain and simple. Stealth is as much a part of it as action is, and the strongest point of the game is the way it plays with the balance between the two in order to represent a variety of different ninja tropes. The stealth works so well due to how explicit the game is. The effects of light and sound are clearly marked, leaving no guess to the consequences of your actions. This allows for complex strategies without the sudden surprise of a detection. The game's finer points are explained by a companion, Orai. This keeps tutorials and backstory in the game's context while allowing the protagonist to remain silently stoic, both avoiding an assigned protagonist personality and playing towards another ninja trope. The game's weakest areas seem to be those that weren't developed simultaneously; the cartoony art style, the same one used in the studio's previous game, doesn't quite jive with Mark of the Ninja's more serious tone and the PC control scheme leaves something to be desired. Several actions are tied to single keys based on exacting and constantly changing contexts. Despite clearly marking the outcome, this makes complicated maneuvers almost impossible to execute swiftly. As far as the DLC, the only strong point of it seems to be the commentary. It does add a new ninja path and two new weapons which do add a new set of options and restrictions, but that doesn't totally change the game. Which begs the question of whether commentary is worth the extra expense.

Wow. That’s all I have to say after playing this game. Despite being colorful, simple, and having a tacky soundtrack, this game really made me weep. It’s just so beautiful, and dark at the same time.
The story is about a group of wild animals going through hard times during the Cold War. They are all close, so they decide to unite together to make enough income to support their families by joining an international racing competition. Their friendship, compassion, and familial relationships all are affected by the glory, the fortune, and the fame of becoming a Wild Animal Racer. What started as a straightforward method to make extra money for the other wild animals in the savannah, started going down in a spiral of competitiveness, drugs, backstabbing, and money. The choices you have to make in this game really impact the story, and often I couldn’t control myself: I would start weeping at the computer, experiencing the hardship the characters are going through. The gameplay is truly immersive. I really don’t know what to feel after finishing it, it was almost as if I lost a child. That’s how emotionally scarring it was. Despite all the pain this game put me through, it is beautiful, and really showcases how human (or in this case animal) relationship works, and pushes these characters to the limit.
This game is definitely worth the price tag for the impact it creates. After playing Wild Animal Racing, you will become a different person..

Gameplay it is very fun and enjoyable. Yes there is many bugs where you teleport around but it happened when i screwed up already, but i see how it could be a huge problem. Music i really did enjoy and liked listening to, it fit the action of the scene and always nice to have some heartpumping action music while you slow down time and kill 5 people in a room. You can see this as a bad thing but to me the music was one of the best parts of the game in my mind.

Basically i had fun and found it enjoyable. I feel like gunpoint is better then this, but i had more heartpumping moments in this. Cons:
Map Design - Every map boils down to a big circle in the middle with multiple pathways directly to spawn. Right out of spawn areas will then have barriers and walls making them easy to camp, complete with health drops, and cause a blowout.
Blow outs - The game has no player skill balancing,  resulting in nearly every match being a blow out where two lvl. 40s camping enemy spawn destroy the team of lvl. 2s. There is also no ranked playlist for these better players to go.
Balance - The community has willed that about 3 of the 7 classes are the only viable ones so you are often playing against and with teams of only snipers, assassins, and grenadeirs. Whether or not these classes are overpowered isn't really the problem, it's just that the community will overwhelmingly pick these classes.
Servers - You will often take damage from places that you were standing a while ago, could be a hitbox or latency issue.
Pros:
There are plenty of pros, but none of them are really all their own. This game doesn't really have any originality to it, but it picks quite a few elements from other games that I enjoy. Just not enough to make a good game.

A fun shooter with interesting, refreshing mechanics and a worrisome player count.
With a better marketing scheme it could have easily carried itself on its strengths, which are (a) its complete emphasis on momentum and aggression; and (b) the low-gravity mechanics.  The characters and maps lack anything interesting to say about the game or its world, however, and their voice lines are at best cringey and at worst downright stupid.  They're edgelords made even edgier by the moon exploding(?) or something.  Who knows?  But it's a blast to play.
So why a negative review?
I wanted this game to succeed, don't get me wrong.  I played in almost all of the alpha and beta tests, gave feedback in Discord, bought the deluxe edition on preorder; did all the things that someone who was bored of Overwatch and wanted something more than another "Q of the Game" shooter should do.  But it seems the game is dead on arrival.
I'll be straight - there's no playerbase.  Three days in and I can barely fill out matches.  I've had numerous maps where people leave and slots can't be filled, or 4v4 games because they literally can't match two players into the game to make it a 5v5.  At the end of the day, Overwatch has better characters and art style to draw people in, and this game's strongest suit, its mechanics, aren't so much better that they'll draw too many people away from its competitors in the genre.
I hope this game grows over time as more people become disillusioned with OW and its other Character Shooter brethren, but I worry that it was simply released at the wrong time, a game that offered something polished but not shiny enough to lure people away from the sleek goliath of Overwatch.  If you don't mind a game with a small community, dive right in, by all means - it's only $30, which was a smart move and could prove to be the thing that keeps the game alive long-term.  But I can't in good conscience recommend that someone with a passing interest spend even that much at this point.
(But honestly, I had to make this a negative review anyway because of that horrendous "Spirit in the Sky" cover in the trailer.  It's an abomination.  It genuinely might be the worst cover I have ever heard of any song.  When the aliens come, it will be the reason they murder us all.)

Just played Always Sometimes Monsters.  I thought “a story-driven RPG, I love those, it’s probably great.”  I started playing, the story intrigued me, and I was excited to explore the world and the characters.
The actual controls and mechanics were lackluster, but that can be expected from an RPG Maker game.  I ignored those annoyances.
The game forced me to slog through tedious tasks at points, probably for some sort of profound statement about labor.  I was bored out of my mind but said “hey, maybe the story will be worth it, I know it is for other games.”
The story, world, and characters started off interesting.  But when I got to the third city of the game it seemed like the developers had gotten lazy and decided to only put what was absolutely necessary in the location.  There was little to do outside of story events, which was different from the first cities with plenty of little side-stories to look into.
After that point there was almost no gameplay and almost nothing to do outside of just take in the story and make choices.  That’s because the game’s about making choices; in fact, it rubs the choice-making part of the game in your face.
At this point the story fell flat because it didn’t flesh the backstory out any more, and it left a few major details about the past up to the player (which the player had no prior information about and no clues as to how it would influence the rest of the game.)  After a bad plot twist I was left with a less-than-believable scenario which would end up seeming like complete fantasy once a cliche bad guy was added to the mix.  Finally, in the last moments of the game you’re left with very little agency because the ending has been decided almost completely by the choices you made earlier in the game (not even the most meaningful choices, but the seemingly arbitrary ones near the end.)  No matter what you try to do, you’re most likely going to end up with an extremely depressing ending.
By the end of the game I was unsatisfied, disenchanted with the world and characters, and feeling cheated out of 10 hours of my life.  Always Sometimes Monsters has a story like an emo teenager’s pessimistic fantasy land, which is a shame because the premise was good and if the devs had made the whole game feel like the first hour, they could have made a real work of art.
tl;dr - If you're looking for a game with a good story, keep looking, because this one makes you think it's what you're looking for until you have invested too much time into it to quit.

Mark of the ninja is 2D stealth action side scroller game, where direct action is not often key to success. You must use deception and hiding in the shadows, if you want to success on this game.
Game can be very frustrated time to time when you get constantly killed, but when you finally success to avoid or kill your enemies s can be very rewarding experience afterall.
Game can be hard/tricky. but thanks for many checkpoints you don't forced to begin too far from where you died last time. So this is is not a so big dead that it first sounds.
[u[ Graphics and presentation [/u]
More than graphics, i was impressed by how visuals are done in this game. Game shows what your character sees and what your enemies see or where they are going.
Good example is when you try to distract your enemies by creating some noise, like throwing your knife to gong.
You can see how far it will sounds and does your enemy hear it at all. There is nothing more annoying than when you try to hide from your enemies and you aren't sure if they can or cannot see you. Or they spot you even you are sure that you are hiding.
I am not huge fan of platforming or stealth games in general, but i had much fun to play it.
Game can be quite hard, but it is still very rewarding and i was enjoying this game a lot.
I died many times in this game, but due many checkpoints it wasn't so big deal and when you finally managed to get out of that situation, you feel satisfaction. But most of time i was to blame for dying not that game is too hard.
Visual indication for what your enemies see and hear was one of the main point that i liked in this game. Also when you outsmarted your enemies or killed them from shadows without being detected was very fun.
So my final opinion is. I highly recommend it.

Lets get some quick points out first:
This game is not dead in any sense.
This game takes elements from Overwatch, Batttleborn, TF2 and Quake whilst making it feel original and refreshing.
Fast paced, skill based and balanced. Never thought you'd hear that, huh? I've seen healers get more kills than primary DPS characters.
My first few matches in LawBreakers were a sobering experience where I was demolished. Coming from popular FPS/Ability games such as Overwatch I felt it would be the same. OH, HOW WRONG I WAS. You automatically realize that this game is quick, as you're swinging around all over the battlefield  trying to keep your reticle at a target, or trying to close in a kill as some of the assassin classes. This game doesn't show mercy for new players, and I love it. Its git gud, or die trying every match.
Objective is king. You can get points for killing enemy players, but not nearly as much as pushing objective. They made it in a way that your game relies on how well you work as a team. I've MVP'd so many games just by capturing point, or running the ball.
The game is beautiful. Everything from the UI to the Character movement seems to be so smooth. Servers are great. The match queues are short, and the waiting room is a battle royale. THE SOUNDTRACK IS FIERCE AS WELL.

TL;DR version: As a very confusing PSA once said, "This is your brain on drugs." The same quote can be applied here, only if your brain was on drugs and you had a very traumatic childhood. Cheesy FMV graphics, very basic point-and-click controls; what really makes it a great play is the story, characters, and environment. Solid 8/10. Kids, stay in school, eat your vegetables, and save this game for when you're a little aged up, mmkay?
Now for the full review, let us first address the elephant in the room: this game probably no longer possesses the title of "the most violent adventure game of all time." So if you're like me, a jaded 3dg3l0rd looking to push yourself to disturbing new boundaries and discover just how far you're willing to go, this game probably won't satisfy that perverse itch much. However, I don't consider myself disappointed since the game offers up more than only people bursting like gore-filled balloons when you stab them. (Yeah, just as a heads-up: while this may no longer be the most violent adventure game of all time, it's definitely still not for the kiddies. Unless you were brought up by Charles Manson, in which case: charge forth, young psychopath; this will probably feel right at home to you.)
"What could possibly be in this game that would cause a reviewer to compare it to the thoughts you have while on questionable substances combined with the acts of a murderous cult leader?" the 25% of you who wandered onto this Steam page fully blind may ask. Well, I'll do my best to break it down for ye wee few without giving away any spoilers.
For starters, what's this game about? You play as a man named Steve who wakes up one morning to find that not only has he lost his memory, but home and the people in it are all a little "off." And by "off," I mean that the entire town of Harvest is inhabited by exaggerated 1950's charicatures, each with a rather psychotic and sociopathic edge. As it turns out, Steve only has six days to uncover the mysteries of this surreal little town and find a way to escape back to normal society, all with an ominous-sounding blood drive looming on the seventh day.
This game is bizarre, to say the least. It does a good job of making sure nothing feels right from the second you enter the world, though I think the lovably outdated FMV style graphics and slightly off-kilter soundtrack do a lot to build the weird atmosphere. It keeps you on your toes and questioning everything, since nothing about this game is predictable if you're a first-time player. It's rather like being in an excessively dark, twisted version of Alice in Wonderland: nothing is logical or makes sense, and the world and its inhabitants follow their own set of senseless rules that endlessly baffle, annoy, and even horrify your main character. Yet, much like Alice in Wonderland it manages to find its own strange balance in that the world is surprisingly well fleshed-out (no pun intended, har har): there are no inconsistencies to the world's logic, or lack thereof, and nobody acts out of character. This, combined with the everyman protagonist, make the kooky environment just grounded enough that you can follow along, while also being wild enough to keep you intrigued.
Like with most FMV games, the performances given by the actors range from patchy to perfect. However, if anything I feel like the uncanny blend of mediocre and semi-professional acting works in this game's favor. These characters are supposed to be strange, sometimes to the point where you begin to question whether or not they're even people, so the unusual behavior is only fitting and helps add to the purposeful unease the game works so hard to instill in you, the player. A lot of the dialogue and cutscenes will make your skin crawl and send a deep discomfort twisting in your belly.
Unfortunately, the playthrough does get a little marred by its dated, simplistic mechanics, particularly in the last third which is oddly combat heavy. Sorry, DigiFX Interactive, but it's just not all that interesting to walk back and forth click-spamming literally two-dimensional baddies. What makes the game so fun, interesting, and unique is interacting with the wacky characters and seeing the effects your actions have on Harvest. Take that away and a little of its charm is simply lost. However, it doesn't render the game unplayable by any means and doesn't serve to dampen much of the experience, so this is more of a nitpick than anything else.
Believe it or not, this game is actually far smarter than you would expect. Granted, the commentary and message it's trying to get across are somewhat jumbled and hard to interpret, but when you play you can tell that a lot of effort and attention went into making each detail precise and perfect. It's obvious that the people who made it did so with a great deal of loving care, which is something that I feel is rare and precious, particularly in a medium that can make modern Hollywood's oversaturation seem tame by comparison. It's impressive what they managed to accomplish with limited technology and a budget that one imagines was probably less than overly generous.
The only thing I really have left to say is that this is not for the PC at heart. Seriously, if this game was released today, Tumblrarians and hysterical mothers would be out in full-force boycotting any store selling it, burning every copy they could lay their hands on, and marching in neat little circles outside the developers' houses, screaming lynch mob-style threats. In my opinion, this game is broadly offensive to all and doesn't really focus on targeting any one group in particular, so no demographic comes across as hated or particularly contemptuous; rather all are worthy of disgust in their own ways. Speaking as an LGBT+ Tumblrarian who's quite fond of keeping things fairly PC, I honestly admire this balls-to-the-wall, "0 f***s given about your sensitivities" attitude, and rejoice that this game came out in the 90's when it was more acceptable to call out the flaws in both minority and majority groups alike.
Overall, an intriguing experience, and one that I would highly recommend for the brave, weird-seeking, and strong-stomached among you.

EA's Need for Speed franchise has been in an odd position the last couple years. While the franchise often worked to mix up the formula from year to year a decent bit, the release of EA's own Burnout Paradise posed a bit of a conundrum for the publisher. With Burnout switching to an open world setting, it meant that it competed directly with Need for Speed in that space. Last year's Need for Speed ProStreet was a diversion for the series from recent years, going to track-based racing, plenty of tuning options and focusing entirely on the events than exploring the city or running from the cops.
ProStreet didn't turn out too well, so Black Box went back to the drawing board and returned to an open world setting with this year's Need for Speed Undercover, but that wasn't the only design change. Undercover also seems to be directed right at the casual market, both in terms of presentation and its extremely relaxed learning curve.

Its a shame you can only give one review per game, as this really does need two.
Firstly - Single player. There is not much to say about it that hasnt already been said. It is one of the best I have ever played. I am not new to the GTA franchise, and have always held San Andreas on a ridiculously high pedastal, but I would say that this game has exceeded everything San Andreas held for me. The story is immersive, the characters are unique, insane and well built. There is plenty to do and more than enough to keep you coming back way after the final heist is complete. It is one of the best games of all time and every gamer should have this in their library (I somehow own it over 2 consoles plus PC).
However - I also have to include a review of online play in here too. Which is where I become torn. I have spent many hours online, doing various heists with friends, completed CM, grinding CEO, MC, bunkers, hangers ... grinding - endlessly.
The problem is that everything in the game is now so expensive that its becoming obvious Rockstar are trying to push people into buying Shark Cards to be able to afford everything the game has to offer without spending days/weeks/months killing your soul with grinds - or cheat.
Leading me on to issue number two with online play - other people. Hackers, cheaters, trolls, idiots. EVERYWHERE. And with the introduction of the new prep missions for the new heists, involving running around in free mode fully visable to all of the above, you have to luck out and find yourself in a session with some reasonable and quiet people - if not, some idiot with a tank/hydra/other form of destruction, will float in and mess up your day - or cost you all the supplies youve spent hours grinding (did i mention grinding?). Oh, or hit you with the unavoidable death ray from his/her facility.
I love playing the heists with my friends, I enjoy the odd supply run to kill time, and dont get me wrong online play is ok. But .... *sigh*
I want to both thumbs up and down this game. For different reason. However, in the end I do think there is enjoyment to online, if youre lucky. But the overall near perfection of the single player mode means I cant not recommend GTA V.

But i digress. The Arkham series has the best combat system of any action game.. Free flow system.. Timing, combos, and power moves, make you feel like Batman.. Utilizing all his tools, moves, and gadgets while throwing devastating kicks, punchs, and body slams!
You will solve little puzzles,  enter detective mode for crime scenes, collect dozens of Riddler trohpies, and combat some epic names from the Batman franchise.. Its really tough to explain without ruining too much of the story, so ill leave that up to you..
Cant get enough of this extremely rewarding, and fulfilling combat?  No problem.. Change styles, with many different era batman costumes.. Play as Joker, Robin, Catwoman, etc.
I could go on, and on about the Arkham series, but bottom line is, the combat.. The combat is impactful, thumping, and extremely satisfying.. It is the crux of the series!  And, ya know.. BATMAN!  Up until now, Batman games have been pure garbage.. I was born in the early 80's, and game after game were extreme disappointments, until i found this title!

The way of life
I don’t know why this hasn’t received an award for best game of the year because I tell you right now: it deserves it 100%. I’ve honestly played this game for so long now and have not regretted one minute of it. Every minute felt like a complete emotional roller coaster; had my ups and downs with it as it brought a complete emotional experience.
Gameplay
Right, I want to make this completely clear. The graphics in this game are not ‘mind boggling’ in any way. They are just perfect with the whole game genre. This made me personally think about my life. What have I done to contribute to society like this game has? But that’s one side of the story. Now to the actual gameplay; at first it’s anxious and very slow. As time went on I started to get the feel (both physical and mental). The music really makes the game that bit more emotional. When listening to the soundtrack and ambience of the atmosphere you are almost bound to sprout a tear in your eyes. The soundtrack was playing with the string of my heart.
Level 1: You’re a middle aged guy/woman or whatever you want to classify yourself as (That’s what makes this game so good, You are who you are in the game. You make your own character up and you make those around you up as well). The whole objective is to cross a road; by doing so you start to evaluate your surroundings (as you would in real life) and start to gather information about everything. Now by this you might be thinking this is really easy but it’s not! There are people obstructing your path: People almost holding you back from achieving your main goal and this relates to real life; No matter who you are. There will always be someone in your way trying to make you not achieve your goal. After you have crossed the road you will be faced with a building. What makes this building so special is the fact the building is an ordinary building. It has an entrance point (A door obviously) Now when you go through that door. The objective is right in front of you. A few feet away lays another door. What this taught me is that you go through so much to open a door. Close that and you may be closer to opening a new door. In this corridor there are about 5 doors each left and right. The door we want is straight ahead (no options to pick other doors) which is rather good because this is now teaching us that not only do we other options in our faces but we are almost forced to go with an option
Level 2: You’re an old woman/man. Your vision has went statically like an 1990 television not connected to anything. Now this is what really got me. The music has changed to kind of classical. Which really does bring the atmosphere more alive, as of the last level there where a lot of people crossing that road obstructing your path to your main objective. What really makes this emotional is the fact that there is no more people. There are literally 5 or so people at the other end of the road. This teaches us how some people die younger than other. That few people rarely make it to being that old of an age. Now the movement speed the old entity presents to us is very slow. This made me think he has a walking stick because we are the ultimate creators to this creation. Slowly we make it too the zebra. What really broke me is the true fact that 6/9 cars will not stop for old people crossing the road because the sole fact that they’re really slow at crossing the road and some people need to get places. Now we can accept the fact if someone is in a real rush to get somewhere that they can take a sneaky 50mph sprint through a zebra crossing not waiting on an elderly person crossing acceptable. But not 2 thirds of people. So we make the chance after 6 cars have just sprinted their way past. Slowly and steadily I placed the feet of an elderly man onto the zebra crossing and was walking ever so slowly. I just gapped it when the other 3 cars started driving (What also amazes me is this is set in the future as the cars have no acceleration and they can break in a split second. Technology grows on us every day.) By this point we are in the middle of the road which is in fact split by an island of pavements. Enough to have a bench placed in the middle. Now as an old man we have to accept the fact that we will get tired and exhausted pretty quickly. So that is why the bench is placed there. We go and take a nap on the bench for a good 1 minute and can raise up again and go to the next zebra crossing. And again the passive cars theory (which I explained just a bit up) is applied. The futuristic cars theory is also applied (Explained a little bit above). So the 6 cars pass and we take a sprint of faith to make it to that same old building we opened the door up. Which too us is a huge achievement with the length of time it actually took us to make it there. That’s the level complete. What really does get me is the whole truth behind this.
Level 3: You are a little boy/girl. This brings back memories of when I was young and I was full of creativity and imagination. You’re set on an island isolated and surrounded by which seems to be lava. Now to the left of you is another island that is higher above lava level than your island. There is a bridge connecting between the two islands is a bridge. A well build bridge (Brings back the memories of your younger construction days living out in the middle of nowhere. Had to find something to do so building a bridge was a fairly common exercise where I lived). The whole objective was to cross that bridge into into the next island which had a house with the door concealing this huge pink donut. Now this teaches us that basically when you go through so much at the end of it you’re rewarded. Rewarded with a sweet. You may be thinking this will be easy but stop thinking this way: There’s something obstructing our path and almost knocking us off target to eternal oblivion. If we are not careful we will feel pain. Like those bad mistakes you made. Not being patient enough and receiving punishment but with another chance. This really broke me and I almost burst out in tears about this fact but anyway. As we pass the main objective and make it to the new island we are faced with a building and a huge door and as we approach it there is a big spinning donut. At this point we are so happy in life to achieve this goal of getting candy. Then we walk and the game is over.
Conclusion:
The best game ever. 10/10 for me. Thanks

Crush Crush seems like it should be a game I don't like. Yet somehow I'm still putting time into it.
Let's be fair here though, this isn't your typical "boot up and spend a few hours at a time" type of game. It's an idle game that relies on resource allocation (in this case, time) in order to raise affection levels and earn money to progress through multiple relationship levels of the girls. Earning achievements unlocks more time slots that can allow for more activities active at once. Hobbies increase your attractiveness to the girls and also unlock jobs, which can be worked at to earn money and promotions to higher tiered jobs.
Each girl has a set of conditions at each relationship level. This starts off simple like needing some affection and money to unlock the next level. As you progress you can go on dates or give gifts to meet more criteria. Earning affection is done through clicking, but once you start getting the hobbies levelled up the affection levels will also increase automatically depending on hobby level. This is largely where the idle part comes in, as you assign time to tasks and then let the game take care of them itself, logging back in to alter tasks as needed. Daily events are also a thing, using up time slots to earn bonuses like money or a time skip. Some daily events also offer unique rewards if you participate enough like special costumes or poster images, although needing to log in at least twice in a day for them (once to start the timer, once to claim the reward before events change) is annoying.
Admittedly, I probably wouldn't be that interested if not for the girls themselves. There are quite a few girls to meet with brief backgrounds showing how you met (often in disastrous ways). What shines is your interactions with them, like Mio who is a walking goldmine of video game references, Quill who lives the life of a cat and we can't forget BEARVERLY WHO IS LITERALLY A BEAR.
While it is a recommendation, the game does have one major flaw currently. Mark of the Ninja, developed by the critically acclaimed studio Klei Entertainment, with their successful Shank series, Don't Starve and now Invisible Inc.
Mark of the Ninja is like Dishononered mixed in with Thief: The Dark Project and produced into a 2D stealth action platformer, with great stealth, great bloody action and challenging yet not too difficult puzzles. Mark of the Ninja really shines as a 2D stealth game and Klei Entertainment have actually done a very good port from is original XBOX360 port to the PC. Controls are easy and quick to use. The music is brilliant and reminds me of some of the great Ninja films I have seen.
The cutscenes and their animation truly shine as a Klei Entertainment game, as Pixar has its own animation techniques with its masterpieces, so does Klei Entertainment with its games and also Mark of the Ninja. The cutscenes' animations remind me of Disney/Pixar films, only more gory than the family friendly Disney we all know and love.
The only thing that put me off was the voice acting. Its not terrible nor is it the best voice acting performance. Certainly it won't win any awards from me for best voice acting, but it gets the job done. Another thing which kind of bugged me was the puzzles, sometimes they were too easy, sometimes too hard, and sometimes damn frustrating!
The story, very well written and has a good plot twist in the end. However, about midway into the story, it kind of lacks in storytelling and I got really bored in playing that specific bit. It was the same guards and dogs, etc... just re-textured to fit in the environment your in.
I did notice some minor bugs here and there like guards not noticing me when I am fully visible in light and sometimes guards getting stuck in an area, however not game breaking.
Plus once you complete the game, there is a new game plus mode which removes all the things that helped you and make it even more challenging. Overall, this is a great Klei Entertainment game and should be definitely be played be people who either like 2D games, stealth games or want to play something a little different...

is a self-described, "..horror shooter with elements of quest." That doesn't seem like too great of a sign.
The game doesn't particularly excel in horror, shooter, or elements of quest. The scares are pretty easy to see coming and usually just involve a loud distorted noise to catch you off guard. I mean, the same could be said to describe most modern "horror" games, but whatever. I'm not fond of it in other games, and I'm not fond of it here. The shooting is mind-numbingly basic. You only get a pistol, which, if used at too long of a range, does literally nothing to enemies. The zoom is smooth going in with right-click, but when released it instantly snaps out. If you die before completing a level, you don't get the ammo back that you used before you died. This makes things a bit difficult when enemies always require X amount of bullets to kill.
The story is the most confusing thing about this game. You start with a scene of a car driving toward the Red Lake (it kind of just clips through the road and slides forward, which is actually pretty funny) and a voice actor (the English voice acting was surprisingly decent for what I expected) telling you about how you have to investigate the lake. It's basic, but it works. What doesn't work is the transition between levels. In the beginning it's not so bad, but at later levels you're randomly thrown into some sort of dream world and then back out and then you're falling out of a helicopter..? I don't really get if something was supposed to be a hallucination or a dream or something. Who knows. From my understanding, the enemies are all the different things that have emerged from the lake. You have dogs, ghost cats, orb things, weird zombie guy, solid black guy that only moves when you don't look at him, and big zombie guy. I don't know how these all fit together and I didn't really want to play long enough to figure it out.
Graphically speaking, it's not bad. No complaints for the price. The sounds are passable, but sometimes have errors with suddenly stopping or playing incorrectly. I mentioned the big zombie guy a bit ago. He actually had a half decent song for when you're fighting him. I mean, it's completely unfitting and made me burst out laughing because the scene was so unexpected, but still.
If a bit of polish was added to the game, it wouldn't be so bad. There are a lot of translation errors that could be easily fixed by simply having a fluent English speaker proof-read and submit replacement text that makes more sense (hmu, devs, I'll be your editor). There's no way to know how much health you have left, so that's kind of a big thing to fix.
It's really difficult to recommend games like this even when they're only a dollar. On one hand, it's only a dollar; on the other hand, it's an entire dollar. If you really want to experience this game: wait for a sale, gift it to your friend, and listen to them groan about it. That's how I got this game.

Instead it is a jumble of buttons that need mashing several times to finally operate (because this game lags a LOT despite having more than double the recommended specs) and when they do work they overcompensate themselves. The movement, buttons and mouse combined in this way result in a pointless learning curve which rapidly progresses into a headache - especially if you're left handed. There are 14 keys for movement where the scroll on the mouse would have been adequate for zoom and arrows and/or WASD for movement. The movement itself is not smooth.
The tutorial waffles, drags out and is not clear, concise or engaging at all; in fact rather rude when you quickly get bored and try to experiment with controls to learn what you can and cannot do.
Recommend sticking to the version on PS4.

Birthday the Beginning is a lighthearted game, with a soft look, and very casual gameplay. You can go at your own pace, building your world, creating every last detail, adding items to your world, and making small tweaks to encourage the next evolution you are looking for. You can move time forward at your leisure, and take as much time as you want exploring the world you have created, observing the lives of each creature living in it.
The controls, at times, are a bit against the player. Sometimes, you’ll want to move the camera forward, only to move it into a wall or the floor, and the movement animations sometimes don’t line up with what you are inputting on your keyboard or controller. While this isn’t a big problem, it does sometimes take away from this authentic world the developers have created.
The graphics are simplistic, but instead of this being a drawback, this is a big gain. It allows us to focus on your creations. The simple look fits well with the mechanics, as well as make the game feel less catastrophic with too many detailed things moving at once. The animal and plant animations are also smooth, and flow. There are some things, like how when an animal eats, the food appears in front of them, with no real transition.
The world sizes are rather constrained, and I would like it if there were bigger world options. Once you really start building separate regions, you realize how small the world is. This might just be a problem on my side, though, as I tend to like huge worlds to slowly develop. However, this does allow you to focus only on a small section, and trying to develop the world in which only your most favorite creatures live in. You have a choice on what animals and plants you want in your very limited space, so this could be a purposeful choice.
The sound design is fantastic. Sound effects are good, and give a real sense of “You did it!” when you level up etc., and the sound when you go from macro to micro is so satisfying. The music is very melancholy and laid back, adding to the atmosphere of the game as a whole. Each animal (and plant?) has their own set of sound effects to go along with their animations, and they are pleasant, but at some times, stereotypical (?). I really don’t have anything else to say about sound, as overall, it’s quite solid.
Overall, this game is a joy to play, and hard to put down. The game is simple, yet offers much depth in the way you build your world, and manage things like temperature etc. This game is good for anyone who wants to have a relaxing time, with no stress, and also has a fascination with evolution or geography.

There isn't often an occasion to utter the following words, so I take great joy in being able to say them: Ronin is a GOOD, UNIQUE game! I wanted to start by saying that, because at least for me, that's all I need to hear.
Ronin is about a heroine seeking justice for atrocities a criminal syndicate comitted against her. You don't see much story for the interesting puzzle-esque combat system, which for some may be a detriment, but for me, it's more of a "Hey, you go ahead and play. The story will be here if you're interested. The graphics are simple but fun, and well executed.
The gameplay is an interesting offspring of platforming and stealth, but Ronin is no stealth game. Nor is it particularly a platformer, either. You run around in active time, until enemies engage you in combat. You then take turns moving and jumping to knock down and eventually kill your enemies with samurai movie esque violence. The puzzle is in planning your moves to keep the enemies off their feet, and avoiding their convenient laser reticules indicating impending violence.
There are a few cons. The game's menu could use a usability pass... It's difficult to realize, especially with their color scheme, that there's a whole skill and menu system with perks to add to your character. That being said, the level up perks are really fun and interesting! The only other mild flaw I found was if you're working on an extremely high resolution, the menu doesn't function properly. I assume this bug will be fixed, though.
Good:
Bad:
Ugly:
Over all, well worth the money and a chunk of your time.

In the view of a worker, you struggle to pass everyone as others push you back and keep you behind your goals. What you have to realize is, all the other workers beat you and were already leaving, nobody is a winner. In the childs view, everything is full of life! you are proud to be and see the world full of color and joyous views. The concrete/asphalt is lava and the steps(crosswalk lines) are your only way across to the SWEET vitctory that lies ahead. The final questions however, for all three perspectives, what is the commonality of the one location across this small distance? what is the goal to be? Why do they all head to one destination, and see it soo different? These are questions for us to answer on our own.

TL;DR:

Absolutely beautiful. Though it is personal preference if you like the comicbook style Mark of Ninja comes along, you can't deny that it looks stunning. Animations are fluent, and killing scenes are well put together. It fits the theme and I really love that art style. Only thing I didn't like is the fact that you don't get any options at all to change anything. Only resolutions and some small little things. But  therefore it should run on any pc.
Overall it gets its job done. Chases are covered by tempting music and there's no point where it gets annoying. Some tracks are really awesome. Could have been a little more music after all, but it was okay. Have to admit here that I'm not a big fan of eastern music. Voice-acting was suitable, but there isn't that much talking anyways.
You see, where the dog is buried. It absolutely has no story. And what is presented to you is a pure shame. There is so much potential but none of it was used. Instead you get this forced filler, which doesn't explain anything. You get no backstory of your character or any protagonist / antagonist. And on top of it all: The ending. Very poor. I call it "Mass Effect 3 Syndrome". In the end it doesn't matter which ending you choose since it only changes one cutscene. Lots of potential wasted here. The game could have gotten even better if it had a well told story. Or at least any story that isn't cliché-filled.
Do you like stealth games? Do you like challenging games? Then here you have it. MOT has it all. As a true fan of stealthing games I now have found my new favourite one. It's even better than Dishonored. You have so many options to go through one stage. May it be thorugh the shafts or through underground tunnels. The choice is yours. You get a few options to get pass enemies by blinding them, killing them with little insects (yup. You heard it right.) and so on. And it is so much fun! I always reloaded after I screwed up to get the perfect way through the level. Even if that took me half an hour for just one stage. I couldn't resist. And you won't either. I don't want to spoil too much of how you get through the levels or what you can do, since that's part of the fun to figure it all out yourself.
It wasn't that hard, but it was challenging. Especially those small riddles you get, where you're teleported in another room and figure out which lever is the right one and how you freaking get there in the first place. Lots of fun there. Featuring New Game Plus you have the option to play through it once more if you felt it was too easy. I myself was pleased and sometimes I even raged. Gonna be honest here: I skipped one riddle since it frustrated me so much that I was too dumb to find the solution. Good luck for you! ;)
- I haven't come along one single bug.
- Lack of options
- Runs smoothly
- I completed it in roughly 8 hours which is quite okay for such games. If the story would have been better I'd crave for more, but since it has none it would have gotten repetetive quite fast, so 8 hours is a good deal.
- You'll get it on Sale for 3 bucks.
- It has New Game Plus, which is even harder since it takes away your advantages of your hud that shows you how much noise you're doing.
Buy it if you love stealth games. If you're looking more for a story-based game you'll be quite disappointed.

This is where it all began - most likely the coolest superhero game series ever, even with the problems it suffered later (the not exactly innovative Origins, and the buggy launch of AK). And what a start it was!
Even today, the game looks really dang good, and the atmosphere rocks still! Don't be misled by my low number of hours... I did buy this game when it came out (back then, still with the horrible Windows Live system), and played it like crazy, and just was given AA and AC for free because I bought AK a while ago, and just started replaying this one AGAIN. And it still is one of the best entries in the series.
AC might be bigger, AK more technically advanced, the other games have more gadgets and stuff, but this still has such a great vibe to it, and a cool story.
The intro (even though it gets a bit long on your 2nd, 3rd, ... playthrough) is a great start, and off you go, exploring the huge Asylum, which is split up into different segments.
You can focus on the story and go for that mostly, or you can try to find all the Riddler secrets and interrogation tapes, which will tell you more about the villains.
If you have played any of the more recent ACs, Shadow Of Mordor or any of the newer Batman games, the gameplay will be fun, and you will be familiar with the controls. Hitting, combos, blocking, etc.
The game runs perfectly well on my system, and I think that you really SHOULD get it if you haven't tried it yet, especially when it is on sale. One of the coolest games of the recent years, a totally great entry to the Batman-franchise (the game really does justice to the Batman we all love... the cool, enigmatic, torn, threatening one), it still looks great and is fun, and there are some very cool moments in there, especially those that are related to the fear toxin.
The boss fights might be more varied and interesting in later games, but still, they are fun in this one (and less "waaayy too long" than they were in Origins), and I think it's decently challenging...and a ton of fun.
If you love Batman, or the games I mentioned above, if you wanna see how the Arkham-franchise began with a killer game, get this game! Right now, during the xmas sale, its five Euros, so GET IT!
