The game is essentionally a beat-em-up game with (what it likes to call) strategy (really you just figure out where something is or what gadget to use, and that totally works anyway). In the game you are stranded in the grounds of Arkham Asylum and it's buildings. There is an overworld which is the open grounds itself, and then there are the buildings which you only really go in for story or to get riddler trophies you couldn't get before (that being said you will spend most your time in the buildings which are designed amazingly incase you're worried about a closterphobic indoor game). You get a whole load of gadgets as you go through the story and you solve mini story related puzzles and riddler trophy related puzzles. The combat is fast and simple, and the best kind. You simply punch people until you get the chance to counter (much like Assassin's Creed). I should probably also say just for anyone wondering; there's no multiplayer mode, which is good in this case.
The game is a great Batman story. It does everything a Batman thing should. It's dark, creepy, makes you feel uneasy and is enjoyable (mainly because from time to time you get a break from the usual gameplay to keep things interesting). As for plot twists there aren't really any except for near the end, but meh.
As for outside the campaign (but really you buy this game for the campaign) there isn't much. There are challanges which give a few houres of fun, character models you can unlock - and thats about it. There are some fun side quests like collecting interview tapes which provide character backstory that are interesting to listen to, and there are riddler trophies which I had no interest in but were fun to find none the less. Extra costumes would have been nice. The upgrade system is something you'd expect - and it works. You simply get XP by doing things then choose what you want to upgrade - combat, armour, stealth, gadgets or batarangs (there are multiple types of upgrades for each of those).
I also want to note how good the joker is! He is probably the best portrayal of the joker in anything (tied with Heath Ledger from the Dark Knight) and it's because of Mark Hammil (Luke Skywalker)'s voice, absoloutley brilliant!
And on the subject of characters you really do feel like batman, he's a bit of a bland main character but that's because the game doesn't delve into his physcology, which is unfortunate and seems lacking now that I think about it, but I didn't seem to care whilst I was playing so thats good.
All the other villains are also great for the in-game time they are given.
I don't know why I like this so much. Perhaps it's just cos its a solid game that gives a high quality 20 houres of fun at the least. Worth the money, definatley. I got the Game of the Year Edition in the winter sale, so thats fine, but if you're buying it at the normal price, get the normal version, as the GOTY Edition simply gives you DLC that is just some challanges unrelated to the story, which isnt why you buy the game.

A Throwback to the Unreal Tournament games, LawBreakers is a game about movement and twitch shooting. It features numerous classes that are pretty distinct from each other, and usually, a good combination of these is reuqired for a good match. There are several game modes, but it basically boils down to some form of "King of the Hill" or "Capture the Flag"
Pros:
Great Movement
Solid weapon variety
Maps. While only 8 at launch I don't have one that I particularly hate.
Score System - Even if you play as a support (Battle Medic) You get rewarded if are actually healing teammates.
Cons:
Match Length - some games just drag out too long, even if one side is blowing out the other.
Modes - Again basically only comes down to CTF or KotH
Balance - Now I'm not sure that this is truly a "con" as I don't think anything is currently "gamebreaking" balance wise, but I feel like the "tank" classes are a bit too squishy, and I don't often play as them. Also I feel like some DPS classes secondary weapons or alt fire modes do a bit too much damage at certain distances. Again, though nothing currently gamebreaking to me in the least.
Overall I am enjoying this game quite a bit and would definitely recommend this game to people who like shooters, but want to try something different to most current popular shooters like CoD, Overwatch, Battlefield and PUBG.

When this game came out i really loved it from the beginning and when online came out i jumped straight in. In the first few years online was amazing (besides the griefer issue which has always been there) but in the last few years gta online has been getting worse and worse while also getting better at the same time. The thing is that the continuous updates to gta online have brought in some amazing and enjoyable content but also have been reinforcing the aforementioned griefer issue. The increasing "trend" of going into online lobbies and specifically going out of your way to ruin the experiences of other players is negatively affecting the enjoyment of many players. With the latest dlcs adding loads of new weaponized vehicles into the game, it has become way too easy to harass players and there is a high chance that the other player cannot do anything to stop the harassment aside from changing lobbies. With the new dlc the prices of items and vehicles have gone up dramatically, forming this huge paywall that can only be passed with either modding your account, grinding for days or even weeks to get enough in-game money or rockstar's preferred option to purchase in-game money with real-life money via micro-transactions. In the new doomsday heist dlc this has become just unacceptable in my opinion. To host the new heist you need to buy a facility to do so and facilities cost anywhere from 2 million to even 6 million and compare that to the 200k apartment needed to start the "original" heists. Also the latest dlc has brought the griefing to an all time high by introducing any griefer's wet dream into the game: the orbital cannon a.k.a  the "pay 500k to instantly kill anyone in the lobby-gun" So in conclusion the game's singleplayer mode is amazing but the online mode in which i was focusing here is great if you have the time or money to get the "cool new toys" but if like most people, you dont then i would recommend you to pass on this one. I still have hope that rockstar will see their mistakes and make the paywall of new content more reasonable, but only time will tell.

INTRODUCTION:
-Mark of the Ninja was released in mid 2012 originally for the Xbox Live Arcade and eventually released on Steam. It is a 2D side scrolling Stealth game which delivers gameplay which heavily emphasizes stealth combat (either Lethal or Non-Lethal). It has then received several critical acclaim from both players and critics alike.
-The player takes on the role of "The Marked One", an unnamed Ninja from the Hisomu Clan during the modern (relatively futuristic) world. After a massive attack by a heavily armed and technologically superior mercenary group on your home Dojo, the Marked One awakens to find himself tagged by mysterious tattoos which grant him unrivaled skills and ability. Use this new found powers to drive away the invaders and uncover their plans.
PROS:
+ Nice quality graphics specially for a 2D Game
+ Very Well Made Stealth mechanic
+The Soundtracks are very asian style and that´s pretty cool.
+ Good character progression that accomodate different playstylesm like you can use playstyle like killing with sword,bare hand knockout or just sneak pass them.
+Nice Puzzles plus there is Challenge Rooms hidden in each levels.
+ High replay value
+ Mission objectives can be approached and completed in multiple ways plus the map level is very big.
CONS:
- The Controls are a little messy but when you get to the third level you get used to it .
- Some puzzles are repetitive and frustrating
-No Level Editor
-No non-lethal option for Bosses
-No Workshop
-No Multiplayer
Conclusion:
-The Game is awesome and you should pick it with the dlc ,this game delievers one of the best ninja stealth experiences in 2D Version plus the soundtracks ,animations and graphics are pretty cool.
If you like stealth games like this one you should really pick it at sale or even in full price 100% worth it buying .

Must play for:
- people who are sick with RPG Maker games in fantasy setting,
- people who thinks every RPG Maker game is bad.
Personally I don't care how game was made - if it's engine written from begin to end by devs or any version of RPG Maker, all of this is not important. What really matter is content and Always Sometimes Monsters doesn't fail in that matter. What is this game about? In short: it's about player, which means you. Every choice brings consequences. How the story will go and how will it end - it depend only on you and what you would do in some situations. It's not some kind of epic story, it's not also some masterpiece that will leave you speechless while playing or ending it - it's just a nice game full of things that might give you some thoughts, or not, and you will think it's trying to be something more than it is. There is a demo version of game, so give it a try and decide for yourself if you want to continue this story or not. I don't regret time spending playing Always Sometimes Monsters. In fact, I would gladly play more story-driven games.

It's a decent game, worth the first, and maybe second playthrough. Yeah, the game throws out a lot of "decisions" for the player to make but a lot of them in retrospect really don't seem matter a lot. Even the "multiple endings" really just seem like multiple
of the one or two same endings. But it's nice to play through at least once.

Always Sometimes Monsters is the sort of retro-styled game I can get behind, mostly because the gameplay and narrative is pretty ingenious.  This isn't a story about saving the world, rescuing a princess, or beating a giant baddy.  it's a game about trying to win someone back, about lost love and time.  It's never quite as cleverly written as it could be, but it's engaging in a way very few other game narratives are simply by the nature of the day-to-day choices I was given.  Should I spend my time mowing the yard or playing video games?  Should I steal from an old woman or help her out?  Both?
Also fascinating too are the frequent hints of some overarching plot lines that are delightfully ambiguos in nature.  This is a world where big plots are happening around the fringes of this little love story, and I cannot stress enough how cool of a notion that is.  Instead of focusing on the mysteries of the aurora borealis problems, the nefarious organizations and politics surrounding a quiet little city, or the like, these are given just enough little winking moments to get me intrigued into the world without actually pulling me into a trite "save the world" story.  It's kind of brilliant.
My only real problem with the game stems from a sometimes annoying fatigue system.  You have to eat food on occasion to survive, but often times, just walking from a restaurant to your bed will fatigue you enough that you can't sleep.  The meter drains just a little too fast, and I can't help but think that it should be eliminated entirely in favor of a "eat twice per day" simpler system.  At the very least, it needs tinkering.
That very minor quibble aside, I think the game's fantastic.  I'm not usually one for retro-styling, but the graphics are a complete non-issue and the 16-bit-esque music is pretty fantastic.  I love that theme song.  It's a terrific little gem, and I cannot recommend it enough to anyone looking for a clever slice-of-life type game with big aspirations.

I remember the most tense moment I have ever had playing this game , the first time I shot a torpedo to sink a boat.
Now you can just go shooting these little ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s willy nilly; the torepdos are limited. They are a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥to reload. If they hit at the wrong angle, they can just bounce of the ship. If they malfunction, you can give your position away. So many things can go wrong. Sometimes the boats are too fast, they speed away past you before you can set up. They may ping you, and may be inclined to ram your sub or drop depth charges. They may call for air support to strafe and destroy your sub.

Very rarely do I feel inclined to write any review for any game, and definently not serious ones. But oh man you guys, this game.
I got this game as a gift, a cheap one that me and my friends could hope to just play some multiplayer. With that pack, all the games didnt really have any multiplayer so that fell through the roof. But I decided to give this one a shot. And I am so glad I did.
This game is a fantastic arcade take on a Sim. It can be super serious, it can be relaxing and fun. It can be brutal, terrifying, hilarious, stressful, all of those things at once. Nothing like this games campaign have I ever played anywhere else.
You start off as a submarine captain, and take on the role really of destroying shipping and enemy ships. You are the hunter. Rarely do you find anything that can challenge you. You sink tonnage like no tommorrow and the numbers add up. Germany pushes and more and more, it looks like you will win the war.
Then the game changes.
So slowly over time, more noticably with every patrol you are assigned, the game gets scarier. The destroyers pop up en mass. Convoys move together, and develop tactics. Friendly subs get destroyed every day. It becomes less about sinking ships on your patrol route and more about surviving the war. I spent time just praying that the months would zoom by between each patrol. You buy as many upgrades as you can, hoping that you can survive just a little longer; that your crew has a chance to live. Nothing quite like it.
It was a summer day, on my first patrol, and I hadnt seen anything for the entirety of the patrol. On the way back to base, I finally get hit with one of those markers; a ship not far away. I set up in the perfect postion, just off the coast where he would pass in front of me not 400 meters away. The water was soft, peaceful and calm with no heavy waves. Out of the crisp water stuck my little periscope, scanning the horizon, until finally she appeared. She came chugging along, a little french shipping vessel. You cant help but think of the people on this poor little ship. Closer and closer she sailed until she finally was just to my left. Timing it just correctly, I fired the first torpedo. The anticipation and andrenaline of shooting a torpedo, that time you have to wait tensely just hoping and praying that it will hit correctly, or at all... I dont think I have felt a feeling quite like it since.
Finally a glorius explosion.
This game is worth so much guys, give it a change and you will love it.

The best submarine game sim to date. Having played it many yearse previous on a physical copy I had to repurchase it for a digital version. It's an oldie, and a game which others should have inspired from, yet game developers being too lazy or fearful of doing so for some insane reason. The whole awesome idea of free-roaming, being led to a general area to do as you desire, and to chose what target you want to hunt enroute & in your patrol area. The whole awesome bit of tending to the crew, weapon choices, the customization, and the whole freedom of it all. Everything about this freedom of choice & the way you tackle it is what makes this game so special. It boggles my mind as to why no game developer since wants to make something like Silent Hunter 3 with 2016 game mechanics & resources. Yes, we do have World of Warships, yet that doesn't count because it won't last as Silent Hunter 3. Once WoWS is gone, so are the ships. The beauty of Silent Hunter 3 is that its singleplayer, something you can mod, and something you can have fun with.
I love how the atmosphere, the mood, and the grittiness stick in this game. Same with how awesome the models, the visuals, and everything holds up to 2016 standards. It all appears glorious that this game stays as my favourite, even as time goes by. I have to also hold this game highly because it's a Romanian Ubisoft gaming studio, something North Americans struggle with when making war games. Europeans tends to add in variety while North Americans blindly stick to North American point of view. The beauty of this game also lies with how there's variety in nations, and even some ship types. The music itself also holds itself up strongly, even in 2016. It still has that nice gritty mood to it with no comical sound-effects, just pure German warfare thoughts & pride.
Even though I never managed to live long enough to pass the first year (my saves used to get messy), I still love this game lots. I miss my trusty VIIB that I'm wanting it back again, and to eventually surpass 10 patrols while relearning & learning new things about this game, missing it many years previous. Relearned how to make my torpedoes swim faster, getting nicer kills in the process.
I love how you can roam around the submarine, peak from the periscope, peak from the bridge, or even manually man the deck gun. There's so many visually pleasing & complex parts to this game that everything is satisfying and rewarding. No matter what you do, it's all fun. Even with how you can add decals to your subs, or how the way you can map out ship directions. You have to plot your actions accordingly that the in game map is powerful enough to allow you to do what you need to do. The rest? Up to you and the mods for added fun.
to this game lies with the whole multiplayer & variety of things. For multiplayer you're given no freedom by being dumped into scenarios. It's not fun. I'm still recalling an unfun session I had by being dumped next to a convoy while shouting at an old friend whom couldn't do anything. I was a kid then & my temper was fierce & spoiled. I regret shouting at him after being forced to dive fairly deep while being unable to do anything. I was hoping more for free-roaming co-op with a comrade to randomly sail the seas to then hunt freely, something I"m wishing the new 'UBOOT' kickstarter game to do. As for the 'variety of things', that basically means more ship types could have been added to SH3 to add in more war boats, more convoy related ships, more 'forgotten' vessels, among others. That, and Ubisoft is blind to what makes Silent Hunter 3 fun, and as to not 'remastering' this game to 2016 standards. It's a real shame. It's an odlie, but the best sub sim & open world game around with no equal.
Give it a try to see why Silent Hunter 3 is the best, and as to why I keep shaming game studios for being lazy idiots for not inspiring & building off of the success & strong points of Silent Hunter 3. There's still a market for these games, and there's still a giant void to be filled. World of Warships scratches the itch, just doesn't heal it. It feels good when you scratch it, just doesn't help anything in any way. Uboot is a Kickstarter game inspiring from this, yet it may end up doing the same thing in a more complex & punishing manner. I'm hoping for someone to make a modern 2016 Silent Hunter 3 (more so with full range of surface ships) because the naval genre is still quite empty & forgotten. You can agrue as much as you want, yet you can't deny there's no open world war games.

Just gonna get something out there. This is not a clone of Super Smash Brothers. I repeat: This is NOT a clone of Super Smash Bros. The mechanics are quite different compared to each of the four games, and it's on an entirely different platform. Let me give you the rundown on why this game is not a clone.
*The base mechanics: Character stats, moves, and how to use them.*
Without using your brain, you can notice similarities to Super Smash Brothers. However, if you use your brain, you will notice (Like myself) that the mechanics are in their own world. For instance, character stats. Now, in Smash, each character had attributes (Like launching power, weight influencing their defence, and movement speed.) that made them unique. Brawlhalla, however, visually displays character stats (Strength, Defense, Dexterity, and Speed.), allowing new players to know how a character basely operates before playing them.
Let's move on to the next part, which talks about attacks and how characters do them. In Smash, each character has three smash attacks, three tilt attacks, four special moves, a jab, a double jump, a grab that can extend into a combo by throwing them in one of four directions, a roll and a shield. They also have an airdodge, which changed as the games went on. What does Brawlhalla have? Five special moves, no tilt attacks, a jab, a triple jump, and an airdodge. Now, let's address why there aren't any "smash" attacks.
In Brawlhalla, most of your moves are mapped to the heavy/special key (Debatable what it's called). Each character has their own unique special moves while on the ground, whereas in the air, they share the same recovery animations and attacks. I can't exactly remember how many individual characters there are, but there are at least twenty-something. How do these characters use those special moves? By picking up their weapons. Yes. "Their" weapons. Each character has two movesets. That's right. Two! Only a few smash characters can manipulate their abilities on the fly (Shulk), so that puts Brawlhalla in it's own world.
Let's also talk about some other mechanics. Beware: Advanced tech skill incoming! You have been warned.
In the Smash games, there are a few key forms of input that can help you win or at the very least, survive. One of these is D.I. (Directional influence). D.I. is a technique that allows you to live longer. Here's how it works: When you get launched in a direction, hold the opposite direction with the control stick, allowing your character to survive a fatal attack. Brawlhalla doesn't have this mechanic, which makes the game far less competitive than Smash. That leads me into my next point.
Brawlhalla is a casual game. Shocked? Well, if you can't tell the difference between a pepper and a piece of meat, you should be surprised. Smash (For the most part) is a competitive game. The community has twisted the "party game" series into a balls busting competitive experience. Brawlhalla on the other hand has simple mechanics, ranking system, and by being a free game, it's attracting a lot of gamers, which is what casual games do by default (Cough Every mp game these days Cough). Smash on the other hand has far deeper mechanics, a more lively (And less toxic) community. Another thing: Smash didn't have it's hand held to make it's way into the competitive scene. It had to WORK for that esports attention and recognition. Brawlhalla on the other hand came out in a time where organizations were craving more competitive games to grab and make money off of.
God, went on for a while. Look, the morale of the story was to address the half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥comparisons to Super Smash Brothers, and to also say that this game is just good. Plain good. If it was a full priced game, I wouldn't recommend it. But since it's a free game, I can easily say that it's worth your time, not money (Ha). Also, no microtransactions in the way of progression! Holy♥♥♥♥♥♥ A FREE GAME without progression halting microtransactions! Who knew?

This is one of the very best games in video game history.
I played it in my childhood and now played it again after 20 years or so. Still remembered all the the things and managed to get from start to end in under 5 houres. Usually - if you are new to this game - you probably need more than 40 houres playtime to get to the end.
Btw. there are also possibilities of playing the old 1993 version of the game via Dosbox or ScummVM. But: those few Euros it costs on steam are completely worth this new version of the game. It has very pretty reworked graphics not giving up the original style.

Getting this remastered version of Day of the Tentacle is worth it. Not only have the backgrounds and sprites been redrawn to more closely resemble Peter Chan's original drawings and paintings, but the nutjobs working on this actually dug up all the audio tapes containing the voicework, re-digitalized them in higher quality, and then sliced and re-organized them and put them back into the game. Crazy. As in most of these Remastered game editions, you can switch to the old pixely graphics by pressing F1, which also switches you to more classical midi tunes instead of the slightly smoother music you get now.
My favorite addition, though, are the commentaries by the original team working on Day of the Tentacle. You'll get insight in how the game was made, and especially how they had to wrestle with the limitations forced on them by PC technology of the era.
It's a very lovingly done project, and while Day of the Tentacle isn't even my favorite Lucasarts adventure, I really enjoyed revisiting it like this. And if you're wondering, you can still play the entirety of Maniac Mansion inside this game!

Even though I "beat the game" if there is a way to beat it, this has several "spoilers," I geuss you could say.
You start off as a man pushing his way through a crowd of people with limited places to walk to. After passing the sugar candy boothe on the street not caring, he is immediately directed to his office, and the story ends. Then you play as an old man. You notice that the music is slower, in a more depressing fashion, as well as you can notice that your vision is really low sensitivity, and when you're done moving the mouse, carrys on for a second, as though you don't have enough muscle to stop. You have to rest on a bench instead of crossing the road first. Then you make your way slowly over to the other side where the other elders are. Then, your final journey, a child. He sees everything with color, always moving frantically. He can jump and sprint. You run along and jump across a staircase that leads to sugar land. If you fall you will fall into the lava and swarm of hot dragons around you.
I simply love the idea that this game proceeds to give me.
I'm somewhat of a philosipher, which indicates I have, of course, thought of this view on age several times before. Do different aged people, figuratively speaking, see simple events and challenges differently? I mean, the elder didn't even see the sugar boothe, he had to rest on the bench! The man saw it but couldn't walk towards it! The child had to go through different challenges to get there! It's brilliant! The child was seeing colorful things, with a great imagination, the man saw only the things he had to do to keep his rent, and blanked everything else out, and the elder, finally, was just attempting to make it across the street in the first place! Seriously, if you didn't see this while playing the game, you probably thought it was a stupid waste of time. Though it only took me three minutes to win, it really opened my eyes. Plus, this is a free game, with interesting graphics, neat AI, and a terrific idea that many people go by! 8.5/10

I'm not sure how I missed this priceless little gem! I am an avid fan of stealth games, and somehow this amazing stealth title managed to escape my notice! You play as a ninja(obviously) who is making his way across some massive platformer levels. Like most stealth games there are various routes you can take to achieve your goals.
You can slip past your enemies undetected or  you can strike from the shadows. If you decide to kill a foe, remember to hide the body so it doesn't get discovered by guards. Yea, it has all of this including tools, environmental kills, light breaking, hiding spots all like the big boy stealth games, but stuffed into a gorgeous cartoony side scroller.
The game is nearly flawless. Almost. I encountered a few occasions during a couple cutscenes where there was no speech audio, even though characters were clearly talking. Still, that's a small bug, and while slightly annoying it shouldn't be something to discourage true stealth fans from owning this game.

I've played this game durning early access and let me say I throughly enjoyed with only a few hiccups. Now that it's officially launched, I do have a few complaints.
First and foremost, the net code is horrible. The game will play fine if you have a ping under 100 which is possible if you live in Europe, Central US or West Coast but if you live in the East Coast or Australia, you will have problems either because the internet connection is bad or there are no nearby servers. This game doesn't handle lag like most other games. Instead, it appears the game just tries to stay synced rather than skip and stutter. This causes problems because of how hitboxes will misalign with the model.
Second, the balance in the game is pretty horrendous at times. Or it used to be. The balance has gotten MUCH better since launch with a certain class getting a much needed nerf and a few classes getting a nice little buff. However, there still exists a few problems. Many pistols act more like SMGs yet have a much higher headshot multiplier and not as much recoil. Dual wield weapons reign supreme in this game as well because they are incredibly easy to spam and get kills. This problem becomes worse when applied to a class like Shadow who is only needs to hit an enemy with 5 or 6 bullets to kill a tank with his dual wield SMGs/pistols.
However, looking past these outstanding issues, you have a pretty polished game and is really good at feeling like a class based arena shooter. The gunplay is very nice however, many guns don't feel they have the kick that they should but I digress. Sound design is incredibly, except for some of the voice actors. The Tank, Wraith, and Grenadier all have pretty good voice actors. Then you have the female Shadow, Berserker, and Marksman who sound as if they are trying a little to hard to sound cool. The music is fantastic. The ambient music that plays in most maps is really soothing and has a nice contrast to the fast paced action and the title screen/main menu music has a nice futuristic tone and is just a great way to open the game. I partically love the future aesthetic that the game tries to capture with the map design.
Ballistic Overkill is a really good game with huge glaring issues that would most likely be fixed in due time with future patches and updates. As much as I would say it is a great game though, it's just above the bar of average and fixing these issues would make it a good game.

Incredibly disappointed in RONIN -- I very badly wanted to like this game.
It tries to play like a mix of Gunpoint and Hotline Miami, a combination of precision movement and precise, brutal combat.
Unfortunately both the combat and the movement are at best unresponsive and clumsy, and at worst buggy. The movement between real-time and turn-based is inconsistent (can't pull up ledges in turn-based? why?), the jumping arc is a suggestion at best, with many deaths being more the result of the jump not going where it claims it will than a miscalculation. Sometimes running into an enemy near a wall will make you clip through the wall, forcing you to restart the checkpoint
If the combat abilities are consistent at all then the issue is that the rules are never explained -- sometimes you can use your abilities with enough points accumulated and sometimes you can't. Enemy sightline raycasts are only visible outside of combat (and even then only sometimes?), so sometimes an enemy halfway across the map will target you, sometimes they won't.
All in all, the game would be fantastic for anyone who loved Gunpoint, Hotline Miami, or Mark of the Ninja, if it wasn't an unpolished mess. As-is, the difficulty of RONIN feels more like the product of bad design, rather than of player mistakes or imprecision like in the aformentioned games.

While I do have some complaints about this game mostly around lack of polish for a released title, the mechanics and raw gameplay are amazing, and definitely worth the $30 price. Don't worry about player counts. Its a 5v5 arena-style FPS. Concurrent player counts will not give you the whole story, and 1000+ concurrent players will be plenty to find matches fast. Rounds are quick and fun. This is no MOBA where things take 45+ minutes. Players cycle in and out of matches quickly, so matchmaking should rarely be a problem for any major regions.
The gameplay itself:
- Fast
- Fun
- Frantic
- Tactical
- Interesting weapon and ability variety
- Decent map design (mostly)
- Cool movement options
My cons are mostly related to quality-of-life and missing features that really should be standard in a multiplayer FPS by now:
- 110 degree FOV limit (technically you can override via console command to go higher, but it resets after every map)
- Mouse sensitivity artificially won't go lower than 0.10, which on a high DPI mouse is not ideal. (Lowering DPI on the mouse side lowers in-game precision but is a temp workaround)
- No HUD customization
- Can't choose your crosshairs (the defaults are pretty awful)
- Weird console-driven HUD/UI decisions (mostly fonts and graphical elements are way too big, like you're supposed to be looking at them from 10-15 ft away, but we're PC gamers who are 2 ft from our monitors.)
- Visual variety in maps is lacking. Most seem to use a similar setting / texture palette. Hopefully as they release the (free) map packs this will improve
I'm pretty sure most of the cons will be addressed by patches, and they aren't THAT bad so the game is still very much enjoyable. If you want to play a new arena-style FPS with a lot of interesting ideas (and they are pretty well implemented), get this game!

I never played the original LEGO Star Wars games when they first came out. Coming from having played some of the more recent LEGO games (LoTR, Marvel Superheroes), I can definitely see that the games have improved over the years.
Compared to the newer games, the easiest way to describe this game is annoying. There's a lot of endlessly respawning enemies in almost every level and not much you can do about them until you get to freeplay.
The hub world is cramped with no way to open the character roster to try out the characters you've unlocked without actually freeplaying a mission. Sometimes you can find the character you want wandering around the cantina if you get lucky. In freeplay, you have a tiny subset of your unlocked characters you can bring, of which all but 2 are chosen randomly so you probably won't get to play with your favorite characters.
Your AI controlled teammate does ZERO damage to enemies and is at best a distraction since the enemies focus almost exclusively on the player anyways. You're effectively punished for playing solo.
The difficulty (until you unlock cheats) is firmly on the side of annoying. The penalty for dying is minimal so it's not really difficult, but it's still not fun to be getting shot at by a dozen different enemies focused exclusively on you, interrupting you left and right and killing you frequently until you do whatever is needed to stop the respawns or move to the next area. On the other hand, the auto deflect cheat with exploding blaster bolts is immensely satisfying once unlocked.
Vehicle missions are awful. Controls are terrible, and there's way too much running back and forth through endlessly respawning swarms of enemies to pick up torpedoes or (even worse) tow a bomb to a target.
There's a lot more content reuse (game time is padded with an extra challenge mode for each level where you can't use extras) but it still counts towards 100% completion.
There's a very annoying bug where the game effectively freezes for a few seconds every once in awhile. This is on a modern PC with dedicated graphics and a SSD.
Much of this is forgiveable (except for the bugs) since this is simply a remastered version of the games that started this (mostly) wonderful collection of TellTale LEGO games. The newer games have improved upon these issues, and the newer games with the huge overworlds are surprisingly fun open world games.
I can recommend this game based on the humor and for anyone who wants to complete their LEGO game collection, but unless you've got some seriously strong rose colored glasses on the gameplay falls short compared to the newer games.

I don't usually play lots of AAA games, but I grabbed Divided for the free weekend.
I put the game in a very harsh environment. It was running off a network mounted drive, which is inherently slow compared to a normal install.
The first thing I noticed that my dual-screen setup was detected correctly, to the point of the relative position of the screens. This is not common across Linux as a gaming platform, so it was a nice surprise, and a great demonstration that it can indeed be done. The Linux experience in general doesn't feel like a port from Windows, or a hack job. I even saw two audio streams added to Pulseaudio, so if I wanted, I could have adjusted the effects and music volume separately right from the system tray, but the defaults had a nice balance.
A big annoyance with the game was a constant minimizing. Any time I switched out of the game, it would minimize itself, plus at seemingly random times, it would mute itself, which I had to manually unmute, because it stayed that way even after switching back to the game. Maybe this was Pulseaudio itself, but Divided is the only game this happens to.
The first, initial load took about 20 minutes, however, further load times were all below 30 seconds. After that first start, I had to adjust everything down to the lowest setting, so that my poor, four-five year old system could handle the game and the menu with about 15-20 FPS (I decided to not put any blame on the game performance wise, because it complained about my specs before even starting, and said that performance may suffer, even though my PC just about meets minimum requirements). It's worth mentioning though, that the intro video ran worse than the actual game. Go figure.
Controls don't have a lot of feel to them, to which problem the abundance of weaponry and tactical options just added a bit.
The tutorials were rather confusing, and they don't require you to complete them, you just have to get to a certain point. They are restartable and skippable, which are all good decisions and let me choose to skip them when I felt I was getting it just fine.
There are an overwhelming amount of systems in play, and you get to use all of them nearly right off the bat. This adds to the confusion at the beginning. I would have much rather preferred if they were introduced one at a time. If you played the previous games, these mechanics may or may not be clear. For me however, whom this is the first Deus Ex game, it was a bit too much at once.
I could clearly feel the microtransaction system come into effect right from when I first found a curious little card in one of the bodies I looted - reminding me that it's going to be presented at some point as a currency. I didn't get to said point before leaving the game, just to be clear. From that point, it was always lurking in most of the loot as a constant reminder. (Even bigger, if you paid for the game)
From what little I experienced of the game, it looks to be a decent FPS with tactics you select at the beginning. It's still going to ask for more money after you bought the game.
I decided to not buy Divided after the free weekend period, due to microtransactions, the performance and the rather dumb looking AI.

The conversation method can be rather odd, in that options you initially had, but never follow, will mysteriously disappear. Some characters will also stop speaking to you out of the blue. That being said however, It's all part of the nature and charm of the game, and it doesn't put me off in the least.

Ah the classic AA. WHile there's clearly some issues, this game was pretty groundbreaking for a few good reasons. Even now as dated as it kind of feels in comparison to the newer games, it still has a lot to offer.
Let's face it, comic book based games don't really do terribly well.  It's pretty rare to see a Comic book based game shine as much as AA did. Alot of it had to do with the casting, getting most of the BAS actors together for this game was a very smart choice by Rocksteady. But it's really the gameplay that makes the game as good as it is. The combat flows really well, and AA's ability to mix Stealth and action gameplay in a way that just worked, was amazing.
Now it's not without flaws. The "Boss" system in the game gets really repetitive.  I read someone say it has a "Legend of Zelda three hit to win" style of boss fights. and it's pretty spot on. TL;DR Good minimalist puzzle game with countless community levels, reflexes are important, get it on discount.
There are two rules to Ichi to start:
1. Direct the bouncing yellow ball over all dots to win
2. Tap to rotate the red triangles (which direct the ball to bounce in various directions)
As you progress through levels, other puzzle elements are added. But the core remains the same. Each level takes a few minutes to solve, and there are many levels including an active community level system. The graphics are pleasantly minimalist, like a doodle in a bored student's notebook. You can replay levels and try to get to the optimal solution. However the price of $5 is a bit much for what you get, and there a few flaws which keep this from being a great game.
The reflex part is an issue, since the ball moves at a reasonable clip and you need to time your taps to direct it properly. Although most video game players shouldn't have too much trouble with it, there seems to be no way to slow the ball down. It would be nice to adjust the speed, say for those who aren't used to button mashing. Which brings me to my next quibble with the game. Although tapping the touchscreen should be easy, I had to resort to a usb mouse since my taps were sometimes not registering. A very minor issue is that it's not immediately obvious before the level starts which direction the ball will go.
Those issues (and maybe the price) keep this from being a top-notch game. But for the sale price, it should be enjoyable by people who liked laser ray tracing games and Prelogate.

I love clicker games, and a clicker game based on a dating sim seemed like a good idea.  There is definitely a lot of waiting, but that's what the resets are for.
Originally, I was going to recommend this game but there were a few problems that stopped me in my tracks.
The first problem, is the diamonds; there is not enough to earn them.  You earn one for each stage you progress with each girl until you reach the final stage in which you get three hearts.  That seems fair at first, but there's one catch: you can only get those diamonds once.  The only other way to earn diamonds is to buy them.  Since there are a lot of ways to spend the diamonds and not enough ways to earn them, it feels a tad unfair.  Even one of the women in game, Pamu, mentions how silly spending money on this game is, and she takes away your diamonds the further you progress with her.
The second and third problems are Karma & Sutra.  These characters require you to reset your game in order to advance their stages.  The reason being is because you their requirements for progression involves specific number of reset boosts, which only waste your time.  Everytime you reset the game, depending on how much progress you made with the women in each "gameplay", assuming you get to all of them, you get a certain boost that adds up everytime you reset.  This can take forever unless you chose to cheat the game, but then it's not fun anymore.  That isn't to say that constantly resetting is fun either.
The biggest problem with this game is how it runs.  This game, simple as it is, takes up most, if not all, of my computer's processing power.  I can set the settings to fastest, take away the particles, and keep it windowed in order to make it run at its most efficient.  But as soon as I wanna open any other program, it causes my computer to overheat and crash.  My computer has never crashed up until this point.  I wasn't even playing the game, and my computer crashed from overheating.  That was the final nail in the coffin.
TL:DR
Until the devs find a way to optimize the game and offer more ways to earn diamonds, stay away from this game.  Play Cookie Clicker or one of the Honey games instead.

Runes is a casual puzzle game with a simple mechanic.
The objective is to match the image shown by sliding the marbles along the grid in the directions that are shown on them to swap position with another marble.
The difficulty progressively get harder across the 120 levels and completing them in the least amount of moves becomes a challenge so completing them all with a gold star can give you many hours of game play, well worth of the low price.
There's a clean and easy to use interface to play on and has a nice sound track plus a level select screen to continue from where you left off or go back to retry previous levels and get a better turn rating.

MARK OF THE NINJA is a 2D side-scroller stealth game, with gobs of replayability.
Premise:  you're a ninja.  Specifically, a ninja with magical insanity-inducing tattoos.  You sneak through levels on behalf of your clan, dispatching enemies quietly- or noisily - or just letting them live.  Up to you, really.
The real fun of this game is how many different ways you can play it.  With each level, you can equip different tools (for attack or distraction), and a different costume.  The costumes and equipment unlock as you progress.  Each costume and item has strengths and weaknesses, and each will change how you play.  The Nightmare mask, for example (my current favorite) is built on terrorizing your enemies into murdering each other.
Heh heh heh.
If that's not your cuppa tea, that's okay.  There are six (seven, if you got the DLC) costumes to choose from.
The achievements are very well done - they're challenging, but not impossible.  Two playthroughs can get you all of them, though you may be tempted to keep going even after getting 100%
Highly recommended.

The TL;DR is that the game is good if you like the LEGO game style, but it's going to take you a long time to 100% the game.  Controls aren't perfect.  All in all, it's what you'd expect - this is the first major "franchise" LEGO game that was released.
I played this when it came out on PS2 in two separate iterations, and if I remember correctly, this is ported off one of the other console versions, so there are some minor differences, especially if you get stuck and try to find a walkthrough.  If you're familiar with the LEGO game formula and like it, you'll like this.  The controls aren't tight, but as I recall, they weren't all that tight on the console in the first place.
Nothing is exceedingly difficult, but it can take some time to 100% the game.  You do need to do the blue canister challenges to get 100%; otherwise you end up at 88.8%.  The AI can do strange things, but that also seems to be a LEGO quirk - I don't think I've played one game yet in the series where the AI second player doesn't get stuck or killed repeatedly at one point.
The gameplay is fun, but it can get tedious trying to 100% - it requires playing 36 levels twice *at minimum*, and you'll need to grind studs at some point, so I'd recommend playing the levels that wil let you unlock the stud multiplier red bricks first (all in the "Original Trilogy" levels - SW, ESB, RotJ).  Once you activate all of them, your multiplier is something like 4860x, and ity makes that particular aspect of the game much easier.
I'm pretty sure the 40 hours of playtime I have is from one playthrough.  Once you've completed it, there's almost no replay value - my playthrough here was pretty much because I wanted to take a shot at it because I hadn't played the console version in years, and as I mentioned, there were some differences, so there was some "new" stuff for me.
The story is good, unless you're a Star Wars purist and can't take a joke; it's not original to the game or true to the films, and it isn't supposed to be.

Let me give a quick synopsis of the game without spoiling too much of the plot.
The stories revolves around a starving artist, an author who has had a bad mental block and can't seem to get their life together. During this block their publisher has been pushing them and in the process has lost their boyfriend/girlfriend who they were madly in love with. Months after the events transpired the protagonist recieves a letter in the mail inviting them to their exes wedding that is comming up (Rough am I right?) and spend the rest of the game trying to get there to stop it. Now as the story continues you find out more the protagonists backstory and how it shaped the person they are today, along the way you learn their troubles, triumphs, and that we all may be always sometimes monsters.
Now that it's been 3 weeks since I finished the game I came to realise just how much this game has made an impact on my life. I've been battling my own dealings along with drifting apart from everyone I care about. This game taught me that you need to love those around you while they are still there because one day you may wake up to find that friends turn to foes and you may be left with nothing but the clothes on your back. This game taught me to love and care and I thank it for that. The devs made a masterpiece with this one and I hope you all will see that. It's definitely worth the $10 and don't let the fact that it was made in RPG maker fool you, because it's definitely one of my favorite indie gems.

I'm going to try a new thing and not hit the recommend or don't recommend buttons until I'm done writing this because this is, at least to me, a complicated game to process. So I'll just talk through my impressions and decide at the end.
I've played it out of my obsession to play games that are "different" and can can say at least this much: It's ambitious.
The game aims to tell a story about low-income living, poverty and other current social issues contained within the main character's journey to find some closure with his or her ex. The game runs much like a dating sim with it having essentially several turns over a number of days that you have available. You usually need to grind enough money to move to the next stop along your journey and occasionally use your turns to get involved with some plot points, such as swinging an election, breaking a strike, helping either a megacorporation to demolish the projects to build a cinema complex, or the residents in exposing the company's nefarious plot to...uh...make money, I guess.
Where the game excels is in portraying some of the chilling aspects of poverty and low-income jobs. It will not be uncommon, at least during your first few days, to be forced to sleep on a trash matress on account of having been evicted from your apartment, and the jobs you take to make money are just soul-crushingly boring and repetitive mini games. Just like in real life.
The biggest failure of the game, however, is sadly its biggest ambition. It fails to be anything but transparent and heavy handed in its delivery. I love seeing games having a mature attitude towards sexuality, gender and social status, but when the game just stops dead in its tracks to essentially look at the screen and say "PREJUDICE IS BAD", some of the impact is lost. It also has a bit of an agenda when giving you two day jobs in each location one clearly meant to be "good"and one clearly meant to be "evil". The meat processing factory pays decently and you have to slaughter them piggies for a shorter span of time than you have to spend at the tofu factory doing the same thing but hey, if you power through it, the reward will be far greater. In cash. Nice job being subtle, game.
The story and dialogue are fine, thematically, and the way you tailor the story by playing is satisfying, but the actual writing leaves a bit to be desired.
The game lacks a proper full screen mode and the menus can be a ♥♥♥♥♥ to navigate, especially with little to no tutorial telling you which the three or four keys you'll be using are. Sound and music are minimalistic, ok, but nothing to write home about.
At the end of the day, however, I did play it through to the end. It's interesting if nothing more, and I am going to give it a reluctant thumbs up, with the mention that you should wait for it to go on sale.

FOR THE SHORT REVIEW CHECK THE BOTTOM!
Mark of the Ninja is a stealth/action game brought to you by the same guy who made Shank 1&2. The game itself is fully 2D, however it doesn't take away from the gameplay. The graphic design is a bit cartoonish/comics bookish, which fits to the game. Sounds, and voices are quite good aswell. The game has a story mode, a new game plus. The story is not a big deal, it takes you on 12 levels, and three longer missions (one of these missions around 3-4 levels long). The levels have collectable stuffs, which gives you extra points at the end of the map, challenge rooms, and additional background information for the story. Also every map has 3 challenges (for example: terrify a guard by killing an other guard., or let 3 dogs smell you). Also the game has multiple ending, but sadly that simple at the last level you can choose to kill this guy, or the other one.
Your main gear is a sword, a distraction item, an attacking item, non-lethal darts and the ability to freeze time to aim with your items. Before you start a level, you have to choose 1 out of 6 mask (7 if you have the DLC), which will highly affect your gameplay. One gives you 2 attack items, and 0 distraction item, you regenerate health by killing (instead of reaching the checkpoints) but, you can't freeze time, another one gives you 2 distraction items, takes away your sword, but the enemies can't hear you (this is my personal favourite). A little RPG aspect of the game: if you complete a maps challenge, you get 1 skillpoint to spend, on abilities (Slidekick, more armor, hanging down like Batman/Spiderman, ect...) or, to unlock new attack/distraction items, and to upgrade them.
About the gameplay: certanly the strongest part of the game, the fact, you can play multiple ways. You can either go as a silent predator, and kill everyone, or go silent and try to be invisible, without killing anybody. The game rewards the silent way more. You get much more points at the end of the levels, if you do not alarm the guards, and leave everybody alive. Killing people is a QTE kinda thing. You press the attack when the enemy doesn't see you and and shows a direction, and a button to press. If you screw it up, you'll get less points. If you try to kill an enemy face-to-face, it's not gonna happen. You have to take him down to the ground, then execute him. Since it's hard to beat the game without killing anyone there are always multiple (at least 2) ways to go to the objective. Sometimes even the main objective have multiple ways to deal with. For example you have to prevent a helicopter to take off. You can go straight and kill the pilot, OR you could sabotage the helicopter some way. That's the beauty of MotN, it's all up to You.
Stealth: The game uses a nice idea: if you run, you make noise, and the guards gonna investigate, if they hear something, like your footsteps, birds flying away, or distraction items. Via the various tools you have you can knock them out without killing them, or use a distraction item, to get pass. If you move very fast and they see you they might get terrified, start shooting randomly and alarm everybody, and they actively start to search for you. Also if you screw something up (you alarm the guards accidentaly) don't worry, there are plenty checkpoints, so it doesn't get fustrating. (I mean you don't have to basicly start the entire level from the beginning.
Now what do i miss from this game? First of all more gamemodes would be nice, for example a kind of horde mode, where you must stop the enemies arming and exploding some bombs (like in Shank 2). Co-op mode. Even if the two players are helping each other, or try to kill the other one, both would be interesting. And the final: Custom maps, which you can download from the Steam Workshop.
IN SHORT:
Definitely one of the best 2D stealth game, the story is OK, but nothing spectacular. If you like stealth games, where you have choice of how you want to play, this is highly recommended for you. (Also i recommend to use an xbox 360 controller to play this game)
pros:
- good stealth mechanics
- okay story
- nice graphic design, and voices/sounds
- good RPG elements
- challenges
- more ways to play the game
- cheap
cons:
- no custom maps
- only 2 gamemodes (story mode + new game plus)

This game does everything it wants to do the right way.
Every problem you encounter can be solved in different ways, either silent and sneaky or deadly or by efficient distraction. Also because you have a lot of freedom in movement (climbing walls, grappling hook, vents, ...)
It is not an action game! Action is even less prominent than in Splinter Cell. In my eyes it is more like a puzzle game, where it is crucial to find the right solution for a problem or situation by analyzing the environment and your opponents.
And if you want to, you can try to find the solution which provides the most points, which can also be very fun, if you're into it.
The game provides points for every action you do and
, the more silent and inconspicious you act, the more points you get, though some sophisticated ways to kill also give a lot of points (e.g. scaring a guard so much it shoots another one or even jumps off a cliff into death).
The story-line of this game is pretty nice, and a bit twisted, and has a nice ending (no spoilers here). Although I think, there would have been (or still is) a lot of potential for more Levels/Campaigns, just because the mechanics are so awesome.
After going through the campaign once a new difficulty is unlocked (New Game Plus), which gives the whole game a much more realistic character and contains real new qualititative difficulties. E.g. your vision is limited to the direction you actually face, you don't see enemies' sight range anymore, you do not see sound ranges and enemies generally recognize you faster. It makes it awesome to replay the whole game again because in some situations these changes have a real impact and needs you to think more to get past it.
An awesome and diverse stealth-puzzle-game with awesome mechanics, nice story-line and very high replayability (at least once), but a little bit short.
Had to be one of the if not the best free game on steam.

So harvester is an interesting game that is different from anything else I played. Not because of the gameplay, but the subject matter. This is an adventure game for the first 2/3rd's of it. The game uses FMV videos so you will see very campy acting from human characters, however I think this fits perfectly with the games unsettling tone. The sound is fine, nothing stands out, but nothing bad does either, it's perfectly fine.
The gameplay starts as a point and click game and a good one. You click to navigate and to pick up and use objects. It has nice puzzles and although it can be hard to know where to go next, the town is small enough that it won't be for long. The last 1/3rd of the game is the stumbling block though, as it focuses on action. It's really bad. It felt too random, like I wasn't in control of the outcome. To be fair some of the best puzzles are in the last parts of the game, I just wish it wasn't bogged down by awful combat.
The story is the real star here. It was so interesting that I kept going even in the worst parts of the game. Everyone was weird in their own way and I really wanted to know why, as the town gives a weird vibe from the moment you step out of your room. And without spoiling anything the game dives into subject matter that can get...uncomfortable. While the game isn't the goriest ever, it was still hard to get through some of it. But it wasn't for tacky shock value. It's trying to make a point. And that point is probably more relevent now than it was when the game first came out.
Overall this game is worth playing for the story. Just know that this game will test your will power because of the content and your patience because of the last 1/3rd of the gameplay

Mark of the Ninja is a side-scrolling stealth game that actually lives up to the idea that levels have more than one way of going through them. The player is given a few tools and tricks and is challenged with making their way through any guards, traps, or other hazards in a given level. It's a really good and simple system that doesn't hold the player's hand. The objective is simply to make it through the level, and it's up to the player how they want to accomplish that.
You can't last long if you break stealth. You're a ninja running around with a sword, and enemies are guards packing guns that will kill quickly if you're caught. Level design is really great, and you're given plenty of freedom to get through any situation your way instead of being pigeonholed into a set strategy. Every level has a series of challenges and if you complete enough, you unlock new costumes that change the way you play (each costume comes with bonuses and penalties). Along the way you'll also unlock new tools and techniques that expand the way that you can take enemies down (or sneak by them).
The stealth mechanics are simple and easy to understand, but are good enough to carry the game. You can see how much noise everything is making with sound indicators that expand from whatever is causing the noise (tools, enemies, gunshots, the player, etc) and enemies have cones of vision that you can take advantage of. It's not a long game, but it's consistently good. And once you've finished, you can start new game+, which makes the game more challenging by giving the player a cone of vision like the enemies have, as well as removing sound indicators.
All-in-all, it's a fun little downloadable title that's worth going through if you like stealth games, It's got a lot of variety, a lot of unlockables, and a new game+ mode which is always welcome. Recommended.

Ah, the good old '90s! Full Motion Videos were a new thing: the first time I saw them was when playing Command & Conquer. They gave you a movie-like experience (at the time these videos had an extremely low resolution, though). The way it affected the point-and-click adventure game genre was the inclusion of a lot of cutscenes in between stages and regardless of how serious the characters looked they were ultimately acting in a very cheesy way. It was as if you were taking part in a B movie.
Harvester is on par with games such as Phantasmagoria 1-2 or Dark Seed 1-2. These were all games that tried to look like an interactive movie experience. And while Dark Seed introduced the unique vision of H.R. Giger into the gaming world Phantasmagoria and Harvester showed you something violent, something brutal that nobody had ever seen before. Your protagonist could die in many ways depending on the trap or enemy it faced. These cutscenes always depicted something horrible, something extremely gory.
Our protagonist, Steve, wakes up one day only to find himself in the '50s. He does not recognise the town of Harvest; in fact, he has no idea who the people are in his house. As much as they claim to be his parents or younger brother he has no recollection of them. Amnesia or not, Steve has a big day ahead of him: he is soon to marry Stephanie and just as the future in-laws Steve's parents, too, expect him to join the Lodge. The Lodge is where the Order of the Harvest Moon is found and in order to join them Steve must complete the process of initiation. This consists of several tasks that are, unfortunately, violent things. These initially seem to be just pranks but will soon get out of control.
Once we leave an establishment the game shows us the map of Harvest. We are free to move anywhere we please. As certain activities are completed the game switches the day-night cycle. It's always worth returning to the same spot to speak with the same people. We can find out how they feel about the things happening in town and each day brings us closer to the Lodge and a truly horrifying, long sequence of gore-fest. During my playthrough the Lodge always reminded me of Twin Peaks' Black Lodge as some of the dialogues were similarly cryptic, nonsense mumbo-jumbo.
Beside picking up items, using them, solving puzzles, interacting with people we also fight others ranging from people to the supernatural. A handful of melee weapons as well as guns are available for us to do so - these sequences can easily make us lose the game. Our health indicator should be checked manually by opening up our inventory. Remember: this was the '90s so no checkpoint system existed; a lost battle means game over once and for all. Make sure you save regularly especially in the last half an hour or so.
Although it received mixed reviews 20 years ago Harvester managed to become a cult classic. Frankly, I don't know if I should recommend this to kids from the new millennium. This is a must if you were born in the '80s and played many games in the '90s. You can give this one a try if you love point-and-click games and would like to get to know some of the gory ones from the '90s.

To me, Ichi strikes a good balance with regards to difficulty and length. I usually end up quitting pure puzzle games like this for one of two reasons:
1. I come across a puzzle that just feels impossible no matter how long I look at it, resulting in loss of motivation to pick it back up again.
2. The sheer number of puzzles is giant. More is not always equal to better, and I find myself getting bored if there's no more new mechanics to be thrown in.
Thankfully, Ichi exhibits neither of these. Not once did I feel hopelessly stuck on a puzzle. A few minutes of thinking was always enough to get over any hurdle. Also, the amount of developer-made puzzles is enough to satisfyingly explore the mechanics the game has to offer. There's also a level editor with online sharing, but I think the game is fulfilling enough with the base levels.
Speaking of mechanics, the game play is very simple being a mobile game. This is not a bad thing, as this set of mechanics is very tight and even employs a bit of reaction time. One thing I love is when games reveal to you an ability that you had all along. Ichi has one of those (I'm talking about the action that doesn't count as a "tap"). When the game showed it, I definitely had an "oooohhhhhh... I see" moment.
It's usually pretty cheap on sale, so I recommend giving it a look if you haven't already.

An options menu driven gnome town management game with an isometric pixel art style and groovy chiptunes music.
As long as you enjoy the management genre, in all of its menu based gameplay glory, you can get many hours of enjoyment for such a small price.
Your task as manager is to designate areas for specific functions, create jobs that carry out the functions, assign those jobs to gnomes, and then tweak and refine everything until maximum efficiency is achieved. Your goal is to create a stable, functional colony. The gnomes must be organized to harvest, grow, produce, or trade for food to survive winters. Walls must be built to keep out wild animals, decorative living spaces built to enhance the quality of life and moods, and armies raised to protect against ever increasing goblin invasions. Mines must be dug to support the construction of these structures, and the precious ores and minerals must be processed by skilled gnomes at their various crafting stations, before finally being turned into weapons and armor by your assigned armor smiths and weapon smiths.
The game simulates the actions that each gnome does: moving, attacking, mining, crafting, hauling, etc. But, you, as the manager, get to decide what needs to be mined, what trees are designated for harvesting, what items need to be crafted, where the crafting stations go. It is up to you where the milk goes, what a milkman is called, what a milkman does, and which gnomes get to be milkmen. But you cannot simply tell a gnome to go get a specific bucket of milk and move it to where you want. You are the boss who designs the perfect job systems that ensure everyone always has something to do and knows what they should be doing it. You are not the kind of boss who can waste his time telling each individual what to do. Watching the colony play out the consequences of the systems that you have designed for them can be both rewarding and frustrating (as colony management should be).

I love this game for two reasons: its incredibly cute aesthetic, and the difficulty of the puzzles.
The snakebirds are abolsutely adorable! The game's motion, sounds, environments, and background music all go really well together.
I also love the depth of the puzzles. They are pretty tough, and often require you to really plan ahead. Indeed, don't let your guard down just becaue of the cutesy aesthetic - this is a difficult puzzle game. Children might find it a bit tough and frustrating. (I found it frustrating at times!)
I also like the 'quality of life' features, like not having a strict progression of puzzles, so even if you are stuck you can keep playing other adjacent levels. Also, within each level you have the ability to easily and quickly undo any number of moves or reset the level, which really helps you as you ponder what the solution might be and avoids having to repeat yourself too much.
One criticism I have is that one of the key controls might not be very well tutorialised. Maybe I just missed it, but I didn't know how to switch which bird I was controlling the first time I was confronted with a multi-bird puzzle, and I had to look it up.
Still, its a great game, and I really enjoyed it.
I got it as part of a Humble Bundle product a while ago, and it certainly contributed to making that purchase worthwhile.

At its best, RONIN is like playing a tightly choreographed fight scene. The controls are fairly unforgiving (you'll accidentally jump into power lines or directly into the path of a bullet more than once), and it takes a while to get used to them, but when the game clicks it is one of the most satisfying melee systems I've ever used. The flow of the game is very much reliant on trying, dying and repeating, but intentionally so. While it may sometimes get frustrating tackling the same room of enemies for the fifth time in a row, trying to kill them all without setting off an alarm, when you finally do it is immensely satisfying. The game isn't perfect, but it's a fantastic experience.

Because of its visual style, it’s extremely easy to get the wrong idea about Ronin. Take a look at one screenshot and you’ll think it’s similar to Gunpoint. Take a look at another and it will remind you of Mark of the Ninja. Don’t judge a book by its cover, goes the old saying, and in Ronin’s case, it’s certainly true. Ronin doesn’t actually play anything like either of those games. Ronin is an odd beast filled with contradictions. It’s an action game, but its combat system is turn-based. It’s a 2D side-scrolling platformer and yet it doesn’t really compare to any platformer you’ve ever played. It has stealth elements, but it bluntly states that it is not a stealth game and advises the player to simply kill everyone.
Ronin has a razor-sharp focus on the gameplay which is reflected in the fact that the story is extremely simple. Its most obvious inspiration is Kill Bill as Ronin tells the tale of a katana-wielding heroine on a bloody revenge path. The entire story is delivered through approximately 20 short lines of text and there’s no mucking about. They killed your father. Now you kill them. The end.
So how does it play? At first glance, it really does come off as your regular side-scrolling platformer. Until you encounter your first enemy, that is. Once an enemy spots you, the turn-based system kicks in. Seeing as how Ronin’s protagonist only wields a katana, the goal is to get close to the enemy and cut him down. During your turn, you can plan your next jump using a dynamic jump arc, attack an enemy or use certain abilities or gadgets that may be at your disposal depending on the situation. During this planning phase, you will be able to see the next move your enemies will make as well. If they’re aiming at the location you are currently occupying, you will have to move as the game employs a one shot, one kill rule. You can jump on enemies to knock them out for a couple of turns and you can also jump into them which will send them flying either into another enemy bringing him down as well or out of the window for a one way trip to digital hell. You have a grappling hook at your disposal as well which will come in handy when trying to escape a particularly unfavorable situation. The tool is also necessary for traversing almost each level as you will use it to hurl yourself through windows, for example.
You can unlock abilities and gadgets by completing optional objectives in each mission which pretty much makes these objectives obligatory or else you’ll simply be at a disadvantage in the next level. These objectives are always the same – don’t trigger the alarm, don’t kill civilians and kill all enemies. The good thing is that completing these objectives doesn’t feel like a chore at all, doing a perfect run is extremely satisfying. The unlockable abilities and gadgets facilitate more diverse gameplay and range from being able to leave a decoy which will distract enemies for a couple of turns to teleporting near an enemy and stunning him.
Your next move will also depend on your enemies and your surroundings. Different enemies will follow different patterns. Ordinary enemies will aim and then shoot until they empty their gun clip at which point they will have to reload leaving you with a welcomed window of opportunity. Enemies equipped with assault rifles will shoot at the same location for two turns whereas samurais will charge straight at you even across great distances. As far as the surroundings are concerned, sometimes you’ll be able to strike unseen from the shadows whereas other times your progress will be hampered by mines and laser beams. Naturally, you can use these obstacles in your favor by jump-kicking enemies into them. While Ronin is a relatively straightforward game, all of these elements contribute to some engaging emergent gameplay as you try out different tactics each time. And even though the level design isn’t really open-ended, it is extremely important to survey the entire level first as that will provide some insight regarding the most optimal course of action.
Ronin is also a very stylish game. The visual style is relatively simple yet pleasing and clear. It actually reminded me of old Cartoon Network shows such as Samurai Jack. Certain characters reminded me of Professor Utonium from the Powerpuff Girls with their rectangular heads. Animations are also very stylish and smooth, although it would be nice if our heroine had some more execution animations. Overall, it’s a great art style. I also need to mention the superb soundtrack that sets the mood perfectly. Even though the track list is relatively sparse, it still greatly contributes to the overall badassery of the game. The main complaint I have with the game are the controls which simply do not offer the kind of pinpoint precision you require from a game like this. Make no mistake, they’re far from bad, but they could’ve still used some fine-tuning as it’s not really uncommon to fumble up a move as the jump arc is a bit fiddly to maneuver. Also, there is one extremely hard and annoying level which absolutely requires you to go about it in a very specific way. It simply hurts the emergent gameplay and even when you figure it out, it’s still really hard to complete. It just sticks out from the rest of the game.
Even though it can be frustrating at times due to its not-quite-perfect controls a bit of trial-and-error, Ronin is still a thoroughly great game thanks to its stylish presentation, innovative mechanics, emergent gameplay and well-designed levels.

Let me get the elephant out of the room first, this game is what I would consider a "REBOOT." When a franchise is stale, it tries to relive the successes of yester-year  (EX. Most Wanted (2005)) and sometimes it works, unfortunately for Undercover, the sales at launch say it was too late. Carbon had at least a 7 million unit sales DECREASE! Then ProStreet lost another 4 million unit sales at launch! Before you click away, this is NOT the same as bad, just for Undercover, it was a day late and a dollar short.
Gameplay:
The game tries to mesh ProStreet's engine, with Most Wanted's narrative format. This was an... INTERESTING result. We got control that was MILES better than ProStreet's, but still wasn't as great as Most Wanted (2005)'s.  There are new modes such as highway battles and outruns. These do add some variety, but don't really feel, (to me), warranted. The car selection is the best of the series. We got your typical street cars like your RX-8's and Camaro's, but then you got LFA's and Pagani's, holy ****,. that is awesome!
Graphics:
This is to me, the game's key strength. The shaders look real, and the textures look superb. The car modeling and damage are so fun to see your hood fly right off your car and fly away to no man's land.
Music:
Eww, I know most people bash on this, but to me this seems like a sign of how the times can change over the course of 4-8 years. Where'd did the good jams go?
Verdict:
Yes, this game has some issues, plenty. But most are not game breaking and this game gets too much hate despite no one knowing how tight this game's development was. EA Black Box/EA Canada was split in 2007. one team made ProStreet, the other made Undercover. Knowing what they accomplsihed with only half the team makes me want to give this game 4.5 stars, but I can't. It tries to be Most Wanted 2.0, but fails in terms of gameplay design and music choices. I can only give this a 5/10, which is not a bad score, in fact, five is a middle ground. It's the most subjective score I can give it.

This game was like playing a visual novel disguised as an RPG, which wasn't a bad thing at all. A couple parts feel a little farm-y, like the
minigames towards the end, but overall was very enjoyable on my first playthrough.
By the time you finish the game, at least the first time, odds are you've been able to guess the ending, but that doesn't make the choices feel any less impactful. In fact, for me, it directly influenced my endgame choices.
I definitely enjoyed playing it through, and even though I know how it goes, I'll be going for another few playthroughs just to see how my decisions change the gameplay and ending.
Overall, this game is probably good for at most 4 or 5 playthroughs if you're just looking to see the endings, but there are so many little subtle things that you can experience that don't directly impact gameplay... they're more of little side-events that you get to see, so there's definitely still room to enjoy the game beyond "I've seen all the endings" and I'll probably play a few more times through, just to explore... then I'll put the game away for a while until it feels fresh again, which I think it will. That's part of the beauty I see in this game: almost anyone will be able to relate at least somehow to the events that play out.
It's a shining testament to what people can create with the RPG Maker tool with a bit of creativity and a unique approach to game design.
