I gave Lawbreakers time to grab me, time to click, and it didn't, and here's why:
First of all, the game feels very unpolished. From the animations, to certain mechanics, it just doesn't seem to work very well. Let me ellaborate a little.
The animations. They're terrible. Every skill animation, every run animation, and any animation that is put right in front of the player (like those that the MVP's character does post-match) just look wonky. They're not in the least beat fluid and do nothing to characterize the player's Law/Breaker. They're functional, but they don't look good.
Also, now that I've said it, Charactization. I honestly can't, for the life of me, see why they decided to make this game a hero based shooter. Larger, more intricately designed, maps with weapon spawns and some level of character customization (Wherein every "character" is purely cosmetic) would have worked much better. I tried most of not all of the classes, and even found one that I felt suited to (Vanguard) but none of them were fun to use. Sure, they had abilities, but those abilities didn't really add anything to overall feel of the game. They were just functions of your hero and that's it. It's like that sat in a boardroom and said, "What if we had a class that did X, Y, and Z" then passed that idea off to programmers who did the bare minimum amount of work to make those ability function. There's just no thought given to how to make those abilities fun instead of just functional.
Also, the payment model. I have no problem with cosmetic lootboxes, but this game offers hero skins, weapons skins, stickers, and "kick imprints?" Oh and the character skins are not universal for both characters in a class. (As every class has two character, a "Law" and a "Breaker.") Also there are what six, or seven different levels of loot? It just feels like they took the model and pushed as close to the scummy-business-model border as they could without going over.
In the launch state of Lawbreakers, the game just doesn't feel fun. It's not smooth, it doesn't flow like an FPS, particularly an FPS boasting high speed combat, should. If you're looking for a fast-paced FPS go check out Titanfall 2. It's faster, it flows better, and none of the problems I've listed here infest that game.
All in all Lawbreakers is a functional beta of a game. It just doesn't have the level of polish needed to sustain a playerbase, and just like every other arena shooter that's come out in the past few years it will be forgotten and hold only a very small, niche audience. It's functional, but it isn't fun. Move on.

Name: Mark of The Ninja
Developer: Klei Entertainment
Genre: Stealth, Lite-Puzzle
Personal Thoughts: Not a bad game, the story is a bit rough but when it all comes down together well enough in the finale.
Mark of the Ninja is a stealth ninja action game from the developers Klei Entertainment which are famed for their work on games such as Shank, Shank 2, the survival game Don't Starve and lastly the incredibly fun new game Stealth Inc. Like many other of Klei's game the gameplay mechanic is incredible and true to life ninja story in which you are not a badass in a fight but instead requiring stealth to actually take them head on and has elements of puzzle in it although it is a bit light on that front.
Beautiful stuff, although unlike shank it's not handrawn due to the limitation of budget and time. The game sprite for guards, Ninja and background is beautiful to look at especially the background I suppose since the game primarily plays in black and white you won't notice all other sprites a lot.
The game has a dynamic tempo system where the action on-screen dictates what sort of music and sound you get. For most part the ambient music blends in well that you can hardly hear it most of the time. But when the action gets tough upbeat tempo accompanies you.
The Ninja, a tool of assassination. An agent of Destruction. A shadow that briefly appears before dissapearing, leaving death and chaos in its wake.
As a master of sneaking the ninja makes no sound as they move quietly through the level, hunting down their prey but even a master is not capable of hiding their sound completely which is clearly indicate by a circle. Hell everything that make sound in this game has a circle to let you know their radius.
Game has you traversing multiple level each with their own objective and while you can easily dispatch everyone to make the game easier and get more point that way it is far more challenging to just sneak past the guards and avoid them. IF you do want to kill them there are a lot of skills that you can purchase using points earned from completing levels and objectives that will make the job of killing guard even easier. Of course stealth people are not left out either, they have lots of tools at their disposal.
Everything in this game depends on line of sight and sound, guards can't see you in the shadow but can spot you a mile away in the lights and everything produce sound as I said earlier which is indicated by a circle. So far the whole system works very well, most of the time I got caught because I was too busy trying to quickly run through the level. Essentially nothing in this game is truly unfair or hard. There are also enviromental objects that you can use to hide behind, get shot and detected with and to destroy like in most typical stealth game.
That is until you play the New Game + Mode which severely handicaps you to the level of a normal human being and the game now being several times as hard. It's a 1 hko in that mode.
Like most of Klei's game MotN plays very well with little bugs and glitches and has an incredibly strong gameplay elements to back it up. Sure the story drags on a bit and the levels are easy if you take the path of killing everyone but that is an option I usually prefer. Overall great game, no bugs and glitches so far and great gameplay elements makes this a plus.
The special edition adds a whole new side story mission, new items, 2 new achievement and for the best part: developer commentary. These appear as balloons throughout the game that shows insight to the developers though on the game.
Scoring Methology [Courtesy of Meat King]:
-	S-Rank: excellent
-	A-Rank: very good
-	B-Rank: solid
-	C-Rank: satisfactory
-	D-Rank: inferior
Verdict: A+ Rank

Ok i really dont know where to begin with this game but I should say yes i would say try this game out $30 dollars is rather cheap and it is a really solid game overall. There are going to be the kind of people that are saying this game is a rip off of overwatch dont even give this game the light of day but really thats not even 1/2 the case of lawbreakers compared to overwatch.I am not saying all their ideas of this having some features that are somewhat similar but there is also so much that makes this game stand out from overwatch but there is also so much holding this game back like the comunity of overwatch players somewhat trash talking the game for being in the same genre and the fact that the marketing for this game was very limited to me i saw a ad for this once or twice but i needed to go and seek it out if i really even wanted to know anything about this game.
Lets start with some things this game does really well in:
1. The variety of roles with all thier own weapons and abilitys that make them feel unique to others
2.The focus on skill with everything you do there is little to none aimed or locked on abilitys its all focused and balanced around aiming and using your abilitys at the right time or else you will just die for nothing. With a side note where since it is focused on skill there is no hard cc the hardest cc is a short silence or a pretty heavy slow but there is no stuns or knock downs that inturupt the flow of combat making you need to stop fighting just to get out of the stun or hard cc.
3.The unique change from indoor gravity areas to outside areas where there is little to no gravity holding you back which is a vey big difference compared to overwatch since it would be like allowing mcree and rienheart fly like a pharah it just does not happen overwatch is ground focused while lawbreakers is ground and air focused
4.Special mobility options All roles have a mobility ability that allows them to move around which can range from sliding on the ground just charging in head first or even some more unique ways to move like using a lazer grappling hook to swing around or flying through the sky on rocket propelled boots
5.The way your key or ult ability works which is another key difference from overwatch you dont need to charge up your ult in this you can always have your ult ready if you just wait long enough most ults have around a 50 - 70 second cooldown so it is not just go in ult and then rinse and repeat because if you try the same thing over and over again someone will pick up on it and punish you hard.

Just as a not these cons are just my opinion and should not be taken as facts maybe you think one of these is a pro who knows

If you notice a decent amount of my cons are because of the lack of a player base then you should help support this game by getting it and even if you dont like it you can always return it but it is worth the time and money to at least try it since we would not want a great base for a game to fall by the side because of not enough players like battleborn

Story wise it's weaker than it's predecessors, no doubt...
The stories in DeusEx can basically be devided into three categories: main story, side stories, and "sub stories". Let's just quickly run over them so we are on the same page:
- Main story is what the game shoves in your face.
- Side stories is basically what you get optional quest objectives for.
- "Sub stories" are the best ones tho! These are the stories you have to pussle together yourself from various notes, snippets of dialog, or other observations - the game won't provide you with "map markers", "objectives", "progress indicators" or other abstract hand-holding of any kind for these.
Arguably the best "sub story" in HR is about who, or rather "what", Adam Jensen is... (because he might not strictly speaking be entirely human, and I'm not talking about augmentations here. There are some obvious clues, like Adam never taking augmentation drugs, as well as deeper ones like info on Adam's... um... "surrogate mother" lets say... but I don't want to spoil too much - go back and dig for it if you haven't found it! ;).
Aside from side stories which weren't shining gems earlier either, all of these are weaker in MD, and so is the atmosphere as a whole as a result.
However MD still has really nice semi-stealth fps style combat mechanics (and nice graphics), that is up a notch from HR, and it's some pretty good stuff! Which is kind of what this review boils down to:
Just pretend you can't see the Storage tab (a small tab in your inventory that opens the one-time-use compartment).
It will taunt you for an hour or two, but after a while you just kind of forget that it exist. Storywise it's a step down, but on a sale it's worth it just for the combat / sneak mechanics alone if you enjoy semi-stealth fps gameplay.
I stayed away for a long time just beacuse of all the bad rep, and at $50+... yeah I can kind of understand why people was seeing red. But now that the mob has calmed down, the dust has settled, and the pitchforks have been stoed away back in the barns... it's actually a pretty good game, and I actually regret not picking it up a little sooner.

Ok i really dont know where to begin with this game but I should say yes i would say try this game out $30 dollars is rather cheap and it is a really solid game overall. I would completly say play this if you are tired of playing other hero shooters like overwatch or you just feel that some things in overwatch dont sit right with you when you go to try to play it. There are going to be the kind of people that are saying this game is a rip off of overwatch dont even give this game the light of day but really thats not even 1/2 the case of lawbreakers compared to overwatch.I am not saying all their ideas of this having some features that are somewhat similar but there is also so much that makes this game stand out from overwatch but there is also so much holding this game back like the comunity of overwatch players somewhat trash talking the game for being in the same genre and the fact that the marketing for this game was very limited to me i saw a ad for this once or twice but i needed to go and seek it out if i really even wanted to know anything about this game.
Lets start with some things this game does really well in:
1. The variety of roles with all thier own weapons and abilitys that make them feel unique to others
2.The focus on skill with everything you do there is little to none aimed or locked on abilitys its all focused and balanced around aiming and using your abilitys at the right time or else you will just die for nothing. With a side note where since it is focused on skill there is no hard cc the hardest cc is a short silence or a pretty heavy slow but there is no stuns or knock downs that inturupt the flow of combat making you need to stop fighting just to get out of the stun or hard cc.
3.The unique change from indoor gravity areas to outside areas where there is little to no gravity holding you back which is a vey big difference compared to overwatch since it would be like allowing mcree and rienheart fly like a pharah it just does not happen overwatch is ground focused while lawbreakers is ground and air focused
4.Special mobility options All roles have a mobility ability that allows them to move around which can range from sliding on the ground just charging in head first or even some more unique ways to move like using a lazer grappling hook to swing around or flying through the sky on rocket propelled boots
5.The way your key or ult ability works which is another key difference from overwatch you dont need to charge up your ult in this you can always have your ult ready if you just wait long enough most ults have around a 50 - 70 second cooldown so it is not just go in ult and then rinse and repeat because if you try the same thing over and over again someone will pick up on it and punish you hard.
Cons:
Just as a not these cons are just my opinion and should not be taken as facts maybe you think one of these is a pro who knows
1.Rather small player base which can easly be fixed if more people are willing to try this game out its sitting around 2,000 players in the last 24 hours at the time of writing this
2.Some roles feel rather strong but it could end up being since most people are still new to the game and as a result i would not want the same thing to happen in this as overwatch where they nerfed bastion and torb rather hard to the point where they were getting slight buffs but i feel like i would need more testing to say for sure on this specificly talking about the two ninja melee style classes assasin and wraith where it just does not feel that great when they run up on you and just press and hold left click for a second or two and your already dead at that point
3.not the best match making but it most likely is because this game is new and it will sort out on its own a bit but its normally either you get stomped or you stomp although i have had some games where it has gone down to the last second where a team wins by 1 point
4.Lastly some times when i was in a party of 3 I would have a few matchs in a row where the game would not give us a 5th player so it was stuck with 4 v 5 which makes it be a rather unfair feeling when you just feel useless since you cant do much without the same amount of players
If you notice a decent amount of my cons are because of the lack of a player base then you should help support this game by getting it and even if you dont like it you can always return it but it is worth the time and money to at least try it since we would not want a great base for a game to fall by the side because of not enough players like battleborn

For any lover of stealth games, this is a must-have.
PROS:
-An awesome repertoire of ninja skills to either get by undetected, eliminate your foes with traps and ambush, or instill fear and cause panic. Different suits selected at the start of level gives you these varied styles.
-Smart AI that responds realistically to your actions
-Huge sprawling levels to explore, that are also decently varied, from asian to modern to desert, for example.
-Engaging story with many a punch, especially with the ending
-Stylish comic book art style.
CONS:
-Generic bad guys. Its hard to really understand why everything is happening, other than "they are villains that want to kill you and also like to make weapons to kill ninjas".
-Can be ridiculously difficult to get by undetected, esp. considering the limitation to 2 dimensions. May require great patience, precision and timing. Of course, you can always go berserk and get by the violent way.
-Lacks any kind of multiplayer or co-op
-Low probability of a sequel, given the ending. I hope there will be one though.
-Forced alarm sections was notably frustrating, given the focus and fun of stealth and "ghosting". Once an enemy is alert, esp. when accompanied by guard dogs, its stupid hard to get by undetected.
Negative point are mainly nitpicks, as otherwise the game is nearly perfect.
I highly recommend this one!

I got this game when it first came out and all there was to do was play in the living room, the bathroom and the kitchen. It worked well and although winning as a baby was easier for newer players, having a good knowledge of the house made victory very possible for the dad.
With the recent updates however, the house is so big that the dad cannot possibly anticipate the baby's moves, which is kinda the point of the game. I could baby proof the downstairs rooms while the baby teleports outside and drowns in the pool, or I could baby sit the pool and let the baby die in the kitchen. What the games now come down to is now the daddy's are forced to stand over the baby at all times, and if the baby manages to poison themselves you are forced to leave them behind while you find the medicine. During this time the baby can then instantly die or hide with very little chance of recovery for the dad. The solution to this was that the daddy could pick up the baby, but this kills the fun of the game. The daddy can pick up the baby, take him out front, and just wait out the clock and he'll win every time. Overall the game is somehow OP for both the daddy and the baby and just isn't fun to play anymore. If I made this game I'd make the newer rooms entirely separate maps. With the way it is right now though, I just can't recommend the game.

Neutralizing your opponents can be done in lot's of ways, also effecting the still breathing ones, when they detect the body (if you're too lazy to actually hide it). New gadgets are unlocked along the line to help you to accomplish your goals, but you can only use some at the same time, so you may try out several combinations or stick to your personal preference. At the least, this adds to the replayability of the game. If you think the game is too easy, you may choose to go for the 100% stealthy approach, without killing anyone except for the mandatory story related guards. So I played Lawbreakers during the Closed and Open Beta's and I learnt two really important lessons from those.
1) The Devs actually pay attension to the feedback they get and respond to it
2) This game is fun as hell.
This game plays like Unreal & Tribes had a baby. Between the fast and buttery smooth movement and the tight map design it really is a winner.
It is hard to describe just how good the movement in this game feels, hookshoting around the map as the Assassin or Flying around like a fighter jet as the Vanguard feels great. Even the classes that are less mobile on the surface still feel great and can come alive in Zero-G.
If you have even a small amount of skill you can get from one side of the map to the other without touching the ground with ease.
The funny thing is, despite how much has been made of the speed of this game I actually think it is slower than some of the other games out right now.
Every class has a decent Health Pool and no-one has a insta-kill attack or Ult. This means that usually the TTK is actually pretty high. It can seem fast since some classes have combos that do insane damage (The Juggarnaut has a Shot, Stab, Kick combo for example.) Which can one shot the weaker classes. However those are not fire and forget combos. There is no High Noon here. However if you are smart and don't let yourself get swamped then you can actually survive for a long time.
Another nice thing is the Matchmaking, aside from a few hiccups over the past few days I have not had to wait more than 30 seconds for a game yet. Even when playing at times with a low pop for my time zone (So say 4am) Add to that the fact that I have only run into one or two lag spikes and you have a a pretty stable game, although obviously if you have a bad internet connection you might not enjoy the same.
My only real problem with the game are the Loot Boxes that seem to have infected every game going. Whilst there are some really nice skins in the game I just am not a fan of the buisness model.
Aside from that the problem I have is that the game is too damn intense. I rarely play two games in a row as I feel like I need to catch my breath inbetween. You need to be paying attension all the time, not just to the visuals but also audio cues. There are barks to tell you if someone is above, below, beside or behind you and in zero-G you need that.
TL:DR
A fun, instense areana shooter with fast matchmaking and sweet movement and combat.

I'm so intrigued by these incredibly unique cult-classic 90's games. Whether it be Postal, Harvester, Dark Seed 1 and 2, Sanitarium, IHNMAIMS and so on. From the get-go, literally the first conversation you get engaged in, just immediately shoves some not-so-subtle social commentary right in your face and forces you to choke it down. You converse with your supposed "family", complaining of amnesia, but Steve being the kidder he is, is ignored and pointed in the direction of the lodge. On your way, you meet a quirky and demented cast of characters that (barely) help you along the way. Excuse me for my lack of information, but it's one of those game that you absolutely have to experience for yourself. Reading a synopsis or watching a walkthrough doesn't serve it justice in the slightest. It's a psychotic, disturbing and hilarious mess that everyone must experience.

I love puzzle games and there are a lot of puzzle games available on steam, from big to small, from serious to casual and many of them are really great and really fun. Unfortunately, Ichi isn't one of them. There are three fundamental traits that make a puzzle game great. One of them is that if you can think it, you should be able to do it. That is, once you figure out the solution, the implementation shouldn't be too hard. There lies the main flaw of this game.
The puzzles are pretty straight forward to figure out. In fact they are way too easy. But the problem is implementing the solution. It requires perfect timing and at this point Ichi ceases to be a puzzle game and starts to be a reaction / timing game. That is, you have to rotate an object at the exact right time in order to solve the "puzzle". It's not a bad thing per se but I was promised a puzzle game and  I bought this game in hope of solving puzzles. Puzzles are supposed to make you think. And in this regard, Ichi doesn't scratch my itch. Puzzles are too easy to be called puzzles.
To sum up, if you like playing reaction/timing games where you have to do things such as press a button at the correct time in order to advance, then you will like this game. But if you actually want to solve puzzles, you have to look elsewhere.

Unlike its predecessor, Cory in the House doesn't exactly come screaming off the starting line. Compared to That's So Raven, where you're immediately plunged headlong into a sexy story of intrigue and betrayal, this main quest can seem mundane, even perfunctory at times. But each time I stepped off the well-beaten path to blaze my own trail, it turned into a wild, open, exhilarating fantasy roleplaying experience, rife with opportunities to make use of its excellent combat. Even after over 100 hours with Cory in the House, it still tempts me to press on – there’s so much more I want to learn, and hunt.
Cory in the House is as dense and deep as the other Disney games in terms of RPG mechanics, and the overwhelmingly massive open-world environment has at once made that depth more intimidating, and in the long run, more rewarding. It’s difficult to express just how huge and open this world is: verdant, rolling fields liberally dotted with swaying foliage of every shape and size fill the space between loosely connected, ramshackle townships where people struggle to scrape by. A full day/night cycle and dynamic weather pull it all together, cementing Cory in the House's landscape as one of the most authentic-feeling open worlds I’ve ever seen. A handy minimap points you where you want to go, which might seem like a crutch, but honestly, without it, I’d have been hopelessly lost. That a world this size still feels so purposeful, and full of things to do is quite an achievement.
The one caveat on all that though, is the technical performance on both the Xbox One and PS4 versions. 30 frames per second was sometimes too much to ask, transitions between Cory in the House's two main maps are just a bit too long, and minor glitches do pop up from time to time. None of it ever impacted gameplay in any meaningful way, though it did compromise the beauty of the experience ever so slightly. Thankfully, PC players can expect a lot more. On a GTX 980, Cory in the House ran at 60 frames per second at all times on ultra settings.
This new open-world map obviously has ramifications for the structure of the story, and though there are flashes of greatness, the main story is ultimately the least fulfilling part of Cory in the House. You might call it another case of The Elder Scrolls Syndrome. Our tale begins as a multi-continent search for Cory's long-lost lover Maiara, and Sophie, his surrogate daughter. My single biggest issue though, is that it never becomes much more: the overly long main story is essentially just Cory running errands for people in exchange for information on Sophie's whereabouts. It effectively maintains focus and momentum, but it feels more like a wild goose chase than an intriguing mystery to unravel, like the one we got in The Suite Life of Zack and Cody.
Thanks to lots of excellent dialogue and voice acting there is some emotional payoff along the way, but it’s mixed in with too much padding in the form of meaningless fetch quests and collectathons. Every time I felt like I was on the verge of an interesting revelation, I’d have to suddenly stop to escort a goat, or search for a lost, narcoleptic dwarf. Heck, even Cory can barely hide his frustration with the constant parade of menial tasks at times.
It’s also worth noting that though you will get along fine without playing the first two games in the series, without the context provided by the Disney show, Sophie is more or less a complete stranger until the last quarter of the journey, which made it difficult to care about finding her as much as Cory in the House expected me to – especially given the slew of intriguing characters who are relegated to supportive background roles.
Thankfully, they all get chances to shine once you venture off the beaten path, and that’s where Cory in the House gets nearly everything incredibly right. Depending on your decisions in That's So Raven (which can be handily recreated via some dialogue early in the game), you’ll see lots of familiar faces returning to play a role in Cory's search, and once they have, they offer you a secondary line of quests that typically provide far more interesting scenarios to dabble in. Underground turf wars, assassination plots, love triangles, and unexpected alliances are all part of these optional romps. They’re all so meaty and full of rich story content that they feel like they should have been part of the main story.
The same can be said for a lot of the side quests you pick up in the field as well. Aside from the bevy of standard side-quests, monster lairs, and bandit camps generously littered about Cory in the House’s gargantuan land mass, you also get a bunch of monster-hunting Newt contracts to persue. Cory's quarry ranges from ethereal wraiths that need to be made tangible before you can harm them, to Foglets who conceal themselves in thick smog, waiting for a chance to strike. The payoff here is twofold: in keeping with the lore, these represent your most reliable stream of income, which is refreshingly significant due to an appropriately stingy in-game economy.
The other upside is that, more often than not, these hunts and other side activities provide interesting insights into a land being destroyed by war, and the many forces that play a role in shaping it. Best of all, you’re one of those forces. It may not shift the main story’s conclusion in monumental ways, but I often returned to places I’d visited earlier to find that a seemingly small decision played out in a very big way. There is no morality meter, no paragon or renegade rating. In the grayscale world of Cory in the House, there is only cause and effect; the decisions you make, both big and small, can legitimately change the world around you – far more so than most games that make similar claims.
Character progression and equipment choices are equally impactful. Relative to That's So Raven, I found that Cory in the House's RPG systems have been streamlined in some ways, and made more complex in others. In both cases though, the result is the same: a better experience. Simplifications to how you restock and use potions and oils makes them feel more practical and immediately useful, as you no longer need to meditate to do any of it. Sure, the old way was more in keeping with Cory lore, but in a wide open world, it makes less sense to expect players to predict and prepare for everything they might come across in advance. On the flip side, there’s a wider variety of powerful, interesting potions than ever, including those that greatly enhance mounted combat, and others that restore health as you cast spells (or Signs as Cory calls them).
Speaking of Signs, they’ve been improved across the board with alternate casting modes, and a wider variety of upgrades, making them impactful in every fight. It’s actually entirely viable to build a sign-focused Cory. I played him a lot like a Jedi actually, able to influence people’s minds in conversation, a powerful long range “force” push, and the ability to reflect crossbow bolts back to the sender (a returning ability that’s been made far more usable). The new skill system provides a good deal of flexibility while still rewarding players who want min/max for the best builds, and weapon and armor crafting is as deep and nuanced as ever, if not more so.
The Verdict: Though the straightforward and fetch-quest-heavy main story overstays its welcome, the option of joyfully adventuring through a rich, expansive open world was always there for me when I’d start to burn out. Even if the plot isn’t terribly interesting, the many characters who play a part in it are, and along with the excellent combat and RPG gameplay, they elevate Cory in the House to a plane few other RPGs inhabit.

Batman: Arkham Asylum is a pioneer which changed the landscape of superhero genre in the gaming industry.

It has everything you would like from an immersive world, great storyline, sleath, detective work and old fashioned brawling. What else do you want? ♦ Game: LawBreakers
♦ Release-date: August 8th 2017
♦ Developer: Boss Key Productions
♦ Publisher: Nexon America
♦ Platform: PC, PS4
♦ Homepage:
About the game
- 5 v 5 competitive arena/hero FPS set in a dystopian future
- Humanity blew up the moon and partially destroyed gravity on planet earth
- Play one of 9 different character classes with different styled of movement, weaponry and abilities
- Play one of 5 well known game modes with a special twist:
- Maps feature a Low Gravity Area that allows for verticality and mobility (shoot your weapon backwards to accelerate)
- All game modes are 5 vs 5 (Law vs Breakers) with symmetrical maps
- Core mechanics revolve around movement, aiming and timing abilities
Negatives
- Lack of proper tutorials to introduce new players into the zero gravity mechanic (mainly tutorial videos and a short sandbox)
- Player Base is smaller than most might like, but matchmaking works pretty well at time of publishing this article
- Some players will have issues finding games depending on location (Europe and US East are fine)
- Very steep learning curve for FPS beginners
- Characters are not as distinct and unique as they could be
Positives
- Every character has a extreme amount of depth in gameplay and allows players to improve their playstyle
- Movement, gunplay and the overall feeling are top tier
- Rewards players that really want to master their character and playstyle
- Extremely fair and fast netcode (Battle(non)sense Netcode Analysis)
- Clean and simple art style that intuitively guides the player
- Having symmetrical maps allows for balanced fights
- Well known game modes with a special twist by BossKey
- All future content like characters and maps will be free including balancing changes and bug fixes including Character 10
- Additional Skirmishes that add experiences like Team Deathmatch
Conclusion
- LawBreakers is hard to get into, but it rewards players for learning every single character to excel at combat
- The game respects your time and skill and wants you to take the challenge
- Every player coming from an Unreal Tournament or Quake background will find familiar mechanics
- LawBreakers offers a grittier, darker and more mature take on an hero-arena shooter
- It all depends on your preferences:
- Dark, Mature vs. Cartoonish, Exaggerated
- Movement, Aiming vs. Abilities, Team Composition
- Arena Shooter vs. Hero Shooter
- LawBreakers is a game that you can sink your teeth into, to set yourself up to a challenge and become a total badass in the long run

Unlike its predecessor, Cory in the House doesn't exactly come screaming off the starting line. Compared to That's So Raven, where you're immediately plunged headlong into a sexy story of intrigue and betrayal, this main quest can seem mundane, even perfunctory at times. But each time I stepped off the well-beaten path to blaze my own trail, it turned into a wild, open, exhilarating fantasy roleplaying experience, rife with opportunities to make use of its excellent combat. Even after over 100 hours with Cory in the House, it still tempts me to press on – there’s so much more I want to learn, and hunt.
Cory in the House is as dense and deep as the other Disney games in terms of RPG mechanics, and the overwhelmingly massive open-world environment has at once made that depth more intimidating, and in the long run, more rewarding. It’s difficult to express just how huge and open this world is: verdant, rolling fields liberally dotted with swaying foliage of every shape and size fill the space between loosely connected, ramshackle townships where people struggle to scrape by. A full day/night cycle and dynamic weather pull it all together, cementing Cory in the House's landscape as one of the most authentic-feeling open worlds I’ve ever seen. A handy minimap points you where you want to go, which might seem like a crutch, but honestly, without it, I’d have been hopelessly lost. That a world this size still feels so purposeful, and full of things to do is quite an achievement.
The one caveat on all that though, is the technical performance on both the Xbox One and PS4 versions. 30 frames per second was sometimes too much to ask, transitions between Cory in the House's two main maps are just a bit too long, and minor glitches do pop up from time to time. None of it ever impacted gameplay in any meaningful way, though it did compromise the beauty of the experience ever so slightly. Thankfully, PC players can expect a lot more. On a GTX 980, Cory in the House ran at 60 frames per second at all times on ultra settings.
This new open-world map obviously has ramifications for the structure of the story, and though there are flashes of greatness, the main story is ultimately the least fulfilling part of Cory in the House. You might call it another case of The Elder Scrolls Syndrome. Our tale begins as a multi-continent search for Cory's long-lost lover Maiara, and Sophie, his surrogate daughter. My single biggest issue though, is that it never becomes much more: the overly long main story is essentially just Cory running errands for people in exchange for information on Sophie's whereabouts. It effectively maintains focus and momentum, but it feels more like a wild goose chase than an intriguing mystery to unravel, like the one we got in The Suite Life of Zack and Cody.
Thanks to lots of excellent dialogue and voice acting there is some emotional payoff along the way, but it’s mixed in with too much padding in the form of meaningless fetch quests and collectathons. Every time I felt like I was on the verge of an interesting revelation, I’d have to suddenly stop to escort a goat, or search for a lost, narcoleptic dwarf. Heck, even Cory can barely hide his frustration with the constant parade of menial tasks at times.
It’s also worth noting that though you will get along fine without playing the first two games in the series, without the context provided by the Disney show, Sophie is more or less a complete stranger until the last quarter of the journey, which made it difficult to care about finding her as much as Cory in the House expected me to – especially given the slew of intriguing characters who are relegated to supportive background roles.
Thankfully, they all get chances to shine once you venture off the beaten path, and that’s where Cory in the House gets nearly everything incredibly right. Depending on your decisions in That's So Raven (which can be handily recreated via some dialogue early in the game), you’ll see lots of familiar faces returning to play a role in Cory's search, and once they have, they offer you a secondary line of quests that typically provide far more interesting scenarios to dabble in. Underground turf wars, assassination plots, love triangles, and unexpected alliances are all part of these optional romps. They’re all so meaty and full of rich story content that they feel like they should have been part of the main story.
The same can be said for a lot of the side quests you pick up in the field as well. Aside from the bevy of standard side-quests, monster lairs, and bandit camps generously littered about Cory in the House’s gargantuan land mass, you also get a bunch of monster-hunting Newt contracts to persue. Cory's quarry ranges from ethereal wraiths that need to be made tangible before you can harm them, to Foglets who conceal themselves in thick smog, waiting for a chance to strike. The payoff here is twofold: in keeping with the lore, these represent your most reliable stream of income, which is refreshingly significant due to an appropriately stingy in-game economy.
The other upside is that, more often than not, these hunts and other side activities provide interesting insights into a land being destroyed by war, and the many forces that play a role in shaping it. Best of all, you’re one of those forces. It may not shift the main story’s conclusion in monumental ways, but I often returned to places I’d visited earlier to find that a seemingly small decision played out in a very big way. There is no morality meter, no paragon or renegade rating. In the grayscale world of Cory in the House, there is only cause and effect; the decisions you make, both big and small, can legitimately change the world around you – far more so than most games that make similar claims.
Character progression and equipment choices are equally impactful. Relative to That's So Raven, I found that Cory in the House's RPG systems have been streamlined in some ways, and made more complex in others. In both cases though, the result is the same: a better experience. Simplifications to how you restock and use potions and oils makes them feel more practical and immediately useful, as you no longer need to meditate to do any of it. Sure, the old way was more in keeping with Cory lore, but in a wide open world, it makes less sense to expect players to predict and prepare for everything they might come across in advance. On the flip side, there’s a wider variety of powerful, interesting potions than ever, including those that greatly enhance mounted combat, and others that restore health as you cast spells (or Signs as Cory calls them).
Speaking of Signs, they’ve been improved across the board with alternate casting modes, and a wider variety of upgrades, making them impactful in every fight. It’s actually entirely viable to build a sign-focused Cory. I played him a lot like a Jedi actually, able to influence people’s minds in conversation, a powerful long range “force” push, and the ability to reflect crossbow bolts back to the sender (a returning ability that’s been made far more usable). The new skill system provides a good deal of flexibility while still rewarding players who want min/max for the best builds, and weapon and armor crafting is as deep and nuanced as ever, if not more so.
The Verdict: Though the straightforward and fetch-quest-heavy main story overstays its welcome, the option of joyfully adventuring through a rich, expansive open world was always there for me when I’d start to burn out. Even if the plot isn’t terribly interesting, the many characters who play a part in it are, and along with the excellent combat and RPG gameplay, they elevate Cory in the House to a plane few other RPGs inhabit.

Ronin is a sidescroller that resembles Gunpoint to a certain degree. It has a similar jumping and platforming mechanic, but is a lot more combat focused. In fact, the great combat is the game's main selling point. Combat, unlike regular gameplay, is turn based, with enemy attacks being telegraphed via tracer lines. If you, during your turn, move out of the tracer trajectories, you dodge the attacks.
Pros:
+Combat is fun
+Atmospheric soundtrack
+Game is challenging
Cons:
-Locked to30FPS.
-The Skill system. In order to get skill points, you need to complete all three optional objectives of a map, making the "optional" objectives not so optional at all.
-Paper thin story. There is almost no story at all.
-Controls could use some polish. The jump trajectory is unreliable.
-Linear level design. If you are used to Mark of the Ninja or Gunpoint, you will likely be disappointed
-Final level has no checkpoints. Unlike regular levels, you do not die instantly, but get a 9 round countdown that refreshes each time you kill an enemy. If you kill the final boss while the countdown is active, you get the Bad End, but if you manage to kill him and escape without getting hit, you get the Good End. Combine that with the great difficulty of the final map, and it is a recipe for frustration.
I really want to like this game, and if the aforementioned issues get fixed then I will adjust my review accordingly.

Outside of the length, the main problems reside in debatable design choices, like for example having your skill progression tied to repetitive and occasionally trollish secondary objectives. Level design is also unequally good and IMO lacks additional mechanics ; it is essentially hampered by the simplicity of the core gameplay. The transition into combat from stealth is also occasionally jarring with K&M.
But as I said, none of it is a dealbreaker and the concept is new and well executed enough to warrant a look.

The game plays like a cross between Gunpoint and Super-Hot, both games I love, and the fusion works. The influence of Gunpoint is obvious, the general aesthetic, the side-view planned jumping, the occasional stealth elements...all are clearly inspired by that game, and all are implemented quite well here. Super-Hot comes in to the combat, which is turn-based. Unlike what "turn-based" usually brings to mind, though, you don't go to a seperate screen where people stand around and hit each other in order. Instead, when combat starts you move a set distance (or perform an action) and then enemies get their turn to do the same. This repeats until either they or you are dead. It's *incredibly* addicting, and results in you carefully planning out complex series of moves to kill an entire room of gun-wielding thugs while only wielding a sword.
It's not a perfect game, but it's an incredibly fun one, that manages to tell a story in only 20 lines of text and one picture. Its developer deserves praise, and I eagerly look forwards to anything else they might do.

Intelligent, streamlined platform design. Very stylistic art choice really helps create atmosphere, I love the change in appearance when you jump out of the shadows into the light and back again. The indicators this game gives you are great, elements of interest are subtly pointed out to you without being obtrusive, everything melds so well together. There's a nice range of gameplay playstyles available within any given situation, which really stands in this games favour. Do you want to try and run decoys to distract them while hiding? Do you want to set up traps to incapacitate them? Do you want to creep up close and elminate them one by one? Or do you want to go full Rambo, run and gunning your way through the level? Choice is yours, and all of them can work based on the 'Way' that you choose to take, which give you different benefits (heavier armour, can use more items, have a teleport ability, silent running etc).
Plot is nothing fantastic, but it has some interesting elements to develop as it proceeds, with a nice twist at the end, that had me doing some serious thinking, and I still regretted my choice. That's the mark of a hard decision.

From the beginning of the game with the hitman and the casino owner/gangster wannabe to the politican election in Beaton to somehow inheriting Mark's car trouble in more then one way and lastly the threating to kill or killing of Sam for a debt she made less than 24 hours ago... all of these issues raise nothing but questions about the story or is just straight up illogical.
Why are the hitman and casino wannabe important to the story... why is the opening scene important at all? Whether or not I can truly reccomend this game is a tough call to make. While I have a lot of fun with this game, partly due to playing with a friend and making fun of it, and also because the game itself is fun enough on its own as well as the choices you make gives an experience different enough to add some replayability.
In short: the game has many interesting concepts (such as having a pessimistic view of the world, interesting choices that branch off into fairly surprising events) and carries a lot of potential, it does not live up to all it promises to be, sporting a predictable story (with some redeeming factors), sub-par writing and boring mini-games.
Of course this game has quite a lot of problems. First off I should mention that the mini-games or side activities, whether they be arcade mini-games or jobs your character does, are incredibly boring. I understand jobs being boring is related to how part-time jobs in real life are boring, but in a game that level of tedium should not extend for too long, which this game does. Also mini-games should be better designed.
Another issue this game suffers from is, with most games that follow the concept of having a diverse storyline that changes depending on your choices, is the illusion of choice. You have all these choices with all these different outcomes introducing you to all these different characters. But the characters are boring, stale and two-dimensional, and in the grand scheme of things it does not matter as the events are overall the same with minor alterations, and though the changes are significant enough to add some replayability, when I replay I find myself skipping most of the dialogue due how little is changed, despite choosing a different main character and love interest.
This game is not all bad though, the game itself is not boring as I can play it for hours without falling asleep, and some of its concepts are fairly interesting. One thing that should be noted about this game is that almost everyone in this world are not pleasant people, and you as the protagonist will have to choose things that bring your morality into question and being on the side of angels does not guarantee the best ending, something I can respect as that was always an issue with most choice-based games.
However the story itself is fairly bland and its themes are very not subtly thrown at your face. Often the script presents itself as some philosophical, thought-provoking or "deep", but instead it sounds more like it is just running around in circles spewing out words that feel as shallow as the characters saying them. It tries to be clever, but all it does is repeat messages found in a B-rated hollywood film. While these messages are not inherently bad, some are true enough in our modern society that it should be addressed, the delivery could be better.

Lawbreakers is a fast-paced high-mobility low-time-to-kill team-based shooter that focuses heavily on positional tactics and old-school FPS mechanics. With ultimate abilities that charge over time, classes that are treated like characters, and a focus on class interaction it’s hard not to compare the game to Overwatch. This game requires better dexterity with a mouse and keyboard than Overwatch to find success, while having less variety in class selection and utility. Most gamers will like this game less than Overwatch for those reasons, but this game is not targeting the same broad audience that Overwatch did. This is a game for hardcore shooter players, with a much higher skill floor overall than Overwatch.
The “low gravity” areas function more like water, allowing for movement in any direction, but also for extremely high-speed gun battles that carry over into areas of regular gravity, since characters conserve a lot of their momentum upon exiting these weirdo-spaces. The weapons feel powerful and manage to have a real sense of lethality despite the sci-fi implausi-future setting. The personalities of the characters are very hard to like, with some really unfortunate dialogue being spouted, but their skills and ultimate abilities are a real treat to put to use. Whether it’s firing lasers from their boots to fly, creating pockets of temporary low gravity, or impaling foes with explosive knives - they are mechanically memorable bundles of destruction and chaos.
This game is an anachronism in today’s market, but playing it feels like a shot of adrenaline straight from the 90’s that a lot of older PC gaming fans will appreciate (assuming they’ve kept their aim sharp enough to track humanoid targets moving as fast as jet planes).

This is one awesome simulator.

The game works, it's relatively pretty, there's still plenty of modding support, it's extremely boring with periods of stellar excitement, and you get to be a sub commander. It's great.
Now, really, if you play career... you are going to spend 90% of your time waiting to encounter some enemy ships. Not actually encountering them. But I don't even care. Because there's always something to do. You have to rearrange your crew every now and then to ensure they all stay healthy, and this is a simulation, what do you expect.
I'm impressed by the way the interface works. Lots of clicking on various GUI objects and things. I really like it. I wouldn't say everything is intuitive, but after a bit of fiddling around you can pretty much start to get a sort of workflow going.
Also, it's one of the few simulation type games I've played which doesn't look absolutely horrible while simultaneously running poorly.
But if you're honestly considering this game, ask yourself. Would you play ARMA without mods? If the answer is yes, perhaps you can stand being bored for long enough to enjoy Silent Hunter 3.

You know, as much fun as it is to run around guns blazing, mowing down wave after wave of infantry and making the world around you crumble and explode in a manner that would make Mr. Bay shed a tear... Sometimes it is nice to take a break from the braindead FPS games that flood the market to play a more mentally stimulating, slow paced stealth game. And this game certainly does it well.
It amazes me that for so long I never bothered with this title, but after it came on sale, I decided to give it a try, and I admit it was worth every penny. Gameplay is challenging, there is replay value in the game due to all the gear you are given to experiment with, such as insanity darts, spike mines, choking gas and more. The story is simple at first, but starts getting more complicated as you move along, sooner or later causing you to question your actions over time. And it is it done all with beautiful 2D artwork.
Sure, it can be a little frustrating at times, and sometimes it can feel cheap.. But if you work hard enough at it, it is all worth it in the end, and I like that feeling of when I manage to pull something off as I plan it.. or sometimes have something unexpected happen that makes things even better, such as driving people insane and causing them to kill each other in a panic.. Good times...
Sale or not, the game certainly will keep you busy for awhile, coming not only with the normal base game but a Gameplus, which ups the challenge even further while allowing you to use all the items you unlocked along the way. Speaking of, how often do you see Gamepluses anymore?

Ninjas do leave a mark it seems. Well, at least the ones we've seen in Klei Entertainment's side-scrolling stealth flavored platformer, Mark of the Ninja, in which players assume the role of a silent Ninja assassin, ya know, not the evil kind, but the kind that's on a meaningful crusade. Anyway, the game was initially released through Xbox Live Arcade back in September 2012, with a PC version following about a month later.
Don’t expect Mark of the Ninja to allow you to defend yourself if you fail at sneaking past soldiers, as this game has a solid focus on stealth. It does give you the option to fight back against your enemies if you are caught, however nine times out of ten you will most likely come out the loser. I did find it rather odd however that your character, the ninja, would use his sword to kill his enemies when undetected but would start using his arms and legs when faced with up to three gun wielding baddies at a time. It’s obviously a game design choice to cut down on action and punish you for failing, but I still found it distracting.
The premise is actually quite riveting story and it keeps you going. Sure it's a classic ninja tale, but who would say 'no' to a cool ninja tale? The storytelling is done by offering well-animated 2D cut-scenes between levels. The artists and animators who brought these cinematics (and the 2D character models) to life did an excellent job. The in-game dialogue is brief and to the point. Your clan has been crippled and your Master was captured, so you have to head out and rescue him. That's about it. Of course, things get a bit more exciting later on, but suffice it to say, Mark of the Ninja has a surprisingly satisfying plot structure for a platform game.
Moving around the game's environments is great fun. While a 2D side scroller at its core, Mark of the Ninja allows backtracking and climbing of the environments’ walls which gives a lot of freedom in deciding how you could make your way past enemies. It was extremely satisfying when I eventually pulled off the perfect getaway, and the frequent checkpoints that occurred prevented me from being frustrated.  The gameplay flows really well and can leave you feeling rather accomplished. Killing a room full of guards and hiding their bodies in the sewers in which you attacked them from, and then seeing their buddies walk in and look confused was a highlight for me.
The game awards points to the player depending on how well each level is played. Extra points are awarded if you locate certain artifacts that are scattered throughout each area. The points you receive can be utilized for upgrading the ninja's skills. Upgrades include unlocking various additional abilities such as new execution moves or other moves such as stronger punches, kicks etc.
The ninja you play as doesn’t speak, but the rest of the characters do. The dialogue is your typical ninja affair, with the words “power” and “consequences” being used like they’re going out of style, but it’s solid and when combined with the art design you really start to care about the other characters in the game. The ambient noises that you hear throughout the game are really well thought out as well. The further you are away from an enemy the more muffled their voice is, and the change in your footsteps depending on what location you’re in has a great emphasis on it, which keeps you guessing if you’re taking the best stealth approach or if there’s a quieter way around.
Overall, you might say this is one of the most enjoyable platformers I've played in recent times. Mark of the Ninja is a really nice surprise and definitely one of the best indie games I've ever played. There's not much I can criticize about it, other than the fact that it leaves no options for those who wish to resort to pure action during challenges. But if you're a ninja, what would you do? Jump into the fray, guns blazing? No that's not the ninja way.

I'm not usually a fan of more western style action games, but this game was a pleasant surprise. I know I have friends who have been raving about this series for years, but only recently got the chance to try it out. I was blown away. Since playing this, I've had the opportunity to try a couple similar style games, such as Shadow of Mordor, and I'd definitely say I prefer the Batman games, for a couple reasons. First of all, it's Batman, so there's not a lot of explicit violence and killing. I mean yes, you're punching and beating up the thugs, but there's little in the way of blood, and it's usually pretty clear they're just knocked out and not dead. I appreciate that, personally. Second of all, it's more structured than a lot of open world games. I struggle in games that just drop you into a huge open world and say "go". Luckily, Batman doles out the Asylum in pieces. Usually, you gain access to a new area after every story segment. So by the end, you're running around the island like you own the place, but you never feel overwhelmed getting there. I also enjoyed just exploring  the island looking for Riddler pieces.
In short, after playing this game I quickly picked up Arkham City and Origins the next time they went on sale. I'm highly looking forward to my return to this rendition of the Batman world.

This game does not cater to the lowest common denominator. It's a no-brainer that because of the skill floor this game will never have the player numbers compared to Overwatch. This is an arena shooter that does not hold your hand with tool tip popups or a "girlfriend" class (some character easy enough to understand that allows for immediate general ability.) The general time-to-kill is faster than Overwatch and Quake, but slower than Dirty Bomb. There is only a few insta-gib combo's in this game. That doesn't mean that every character is not lethal.
The shining star for this game is the movement system along with the zero gravity mechanic. It feels like a natural evolution from old Quake/UT games and I really can not play Overwatch or Dirty Bomb any more because they feel SO SLOW. While the new Quake Champions game has an equally speedy gameplay, their engine does not handle as well as Lawbreaker's, nor does QC have zero-g.
+Developers are super communicative.
+Very well optimized game. Runs like a dream for me.
+Movement system is the best I've felt in years.
+The balance between roles is very good. There do need to be some tweaks to some characters, however, nothing is gamebreakingly bad right now (if you know how to counter team composition and have willing / competent teammates.) (Yes, I'm talking about Gunslinger. No, Assassin is not OP.)
+The M rating. Not that I don't enjoy Teen rated shooters (gameplay above all else) but I've always prefered a grittier atmosphere in my games.
+No heal noodles or character abilities that negate that sick play you just made. All the characters are KILLERS.
+This engine can definitely keep up with the games speed. Servers have been very stable as well.
-This player count drama. Please make it free to play with a champion pack like Quack and Smite have done. It's a better business model. I have no problems finding games at 500 players quickly, so this complaint is not about lack of games. This game deserves to take off and have a scene but everybody has cold feet because of the oversaturation of arena shooters.
-CliffyB (the CEO? lead dev?) seems to have a huge ego. He helped make a great game though.. respect.
-Really not a fan of the Discord integration. I play with friends and we use Discord for personal comms and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥tting. Sucks we have to choose between team comms or using a different VOIP/not having personal comms while playing.

After playing this on console quite a lot, and being a big Batman and DC fan, I decided to buy this for PC.
It captures Batman as for what he really is; a badass hardened by traumatic experiences and many close death encounters.
The story is executed to a very good standard, encorporating a lot of the classic Batman villians such as the Joker (of course), Harley Quinn, Killer Croc, Scarecrow etc. It is also a rather simple story to understand as it features a standard plot to take over Gotham brought up the Joker, but in a way that truly shows off his evil genius.
The combat is rather fluid, if not unimpressive but it works. You have the basic combo chaining attacks with an element of counters.
The lack of some iconic characters such as Two-Face, Mr. Freeze and The Penguin allows the game to immersify the player into the other characters a lot more; making it feel not so crowded.
Graphics are superb, with near to no lag found within my first few hours of playing, even when loading into the main island.
There is an element of search and explore aspect, as you look to find certain Riddler Trophies as part of a sidequest to accompany the main story. There's also a stealth aspect as you look to avoid armed minions who can deal fatal damage, thus you have to intelligently pick your moment to take them out from above.
The voice acting and audio in general is rather brilliant, with many voice actors reprising their roles from some of the older cartoons.
The tone of the story is rather adult, as it should be for a Batman game. Featuring traumatic situations and murder.
All in all, this is a good game I'd seriously recommend whether you're a Batman fan or not.

I didn't realize I had written a review for this game. I was going to wait until I finished the game to give an overall review, but I want to rewrite the nondescriptive review I wrote apparently back when I only had an hour clocked in on the game.
So here is my experience: I like the game a lot. As of the writing of this review I have 12.3 hours played. The storyline is really cool and feels like one that you'd read in the comics, and Joker's antics are darkly humorous. Harley Quinn is a babe. I mean, she's a total psychopath... The game looks really nice, and even though it's about 5 years old, the graphics are still pretty neat. Unforunately, I don't know if it's the graphics or just its general optimization, but this game seems to take a fair amount to run. This computer can run Killing Floor 2 on almost all max settings and run well over 30 fps, but this game seems to vary between 20 to 30 fps. And I feel Killing Floor 2 always has so much more going on at one time (plus much higher graphics). The game loves its slow motion effects and while a lot of times its satisfying, like when you land the knockout blow on an opponent, sometimes it's a little overdone IMO. (Like the Bane fight and every time he charges past you there's slow motion and all I want to do is hurry up with the evasive maneuver). Nothing that distracts too much from the game though. Combat feels good and makes you feel like the Batman himself, and the gadgets are handy. Finding the Riddler's hidden items and stuff is fun too. Overall it's a pretty immersive game with beat 'em up and exploration elements. You also get to upgrade weapons, armor, gadgets, etc.
Now let me talk about some of my lesser experiences with the game. There are levels where you're up on ledges high up above bad guys with guns and you need to take them out without getting detected or else they'll drain your life with few bullets and perfect aim that can follow you as you move because you know, asylum inmates get sniper training apperently. But if you just grappel to a ledge like one foot away from you they lose sight of you (gotta love how enemies can go from stupid AI to perfect intelligent AI and regress back again). The first couple times this mechanic is done it's cool. It's definitely a Batman sort of thing. But then every few levels there's another room where you do the same ledge stealth thing. Then a few more levels there's another one. Then after you beat it this last time you go to the next room, do a thing or two that leads you to the next mission, backtrack to the same room you just had a ledge stealth level and yes you guessed it, suddenly there's more bad guys with guns in the same room so it's right back to the ledges with you. These levels aren't hard. It's just all about patience and if you don't blatantly screw up. But it's annoying that these levels keep getting copied and pasted every few levels. It would be one thing if it felt like the natural progression of the game and couldn't be avoided, but when you back track to the same place you were just at two seconds ago and suddenly there's more guys and you have to do it all over again, then to me it feels like they were a bit lazy and wanted to keep reusing that mechanic to try to make filler in between the other parts of the game, make it feel like there's more to the game than what there is. It's just so much waiting. And I admit, I'm kind of an impatient guy, but I didn't mind these parts the first couple times I was introduced. It just feels like "I've already done this let me continue the *story*." I feel like games follow a simple formula: Each level presents a challenge, and if you beat the level you've proved you can overcome that challenge, so the challenge doesn't repeat later because it doesn't have to and there would be no point. Imagine if in COD 4: Modern Warfare, after you beat the ghille suit level, snuck past the entire enemy army and everything, and two levels later, you had to backtrack through the same way. Then two levels later you had to sneak past another army that had a similar environment, so forth and so forth. Nobody would like the ghillie suit levels anymore because we already showed our stealth skills, overcame the challenge, and the mechanic was appealing because it differed from the norm of the game and stuck out as a stand alone level. That's what I kind of feel about these ledge stealth levels. They could have easily switched it up by having you sneak in different environment styles at least. So if you don't mind slightly repetitive gameplay and are a patient person, then this probably won't bother you too much in the game.
Another thing that was annoying is that this game can be inconsistent at times. Aside from the dumb AI switching to super intelligent AI in a split second sort of deal, there are times the game will tell you everything to do in a step by step kind of way and you're just like "yes, that's obvious I'm not dumb." But then they'll introduce some foreign mechanic or strategy or something and not tell you a thing, leaving you to run around blindly before finding this hidden thing or figuring out that you're supposed to use this control to do this. Similarly, sometimes it'll tell you where your destination is on the map clearly and other times, you can only see your destination on the whole island map rather than on your specific region too even when it's close by. It's those little things that can nag at you and make you wonder why it's not staying consistent. There have also been plenty of times where the game tells me to do this strategy and I'll follow it, the AI does the pattern they're meant to for the said strategy, then I'll screw up like a moron and when I retry, I do the same strategy as the game is reminding me, and suddenly the AI is acting in a totally different, disorganized manner (example, once when on a ledge stealth level I was supposed to throw batarangs until the bad guys claimed they would guard the door and then while they were in front of the door close together I could wipe them out quickly. But I messed up the first time around and the second time around, two the the bad guys went to the door when they said they were going to, but one of them stayed far away and I spent a half an hour trying to get him to do the pattern that he was claiming he was going to do but he wouldn't do it.)
It's a great game, though, and I do recommend it, just have some patience with it on some of the levels. It's one of those games where the good parts are amazing and you can't get enough of but the lesser parts are soooooooo frustrating and make you want to shut off the game for a while.

It could probably use some volume sliders...and some of the music loops began to get on my nerves, but snakebird is filled with some amazingly well designed puzzles presented in a pretty relaxed non-punishing way. You can freely undo any number of moves or quick restart, and you will almost certainly need to. Nothing timed or skill intensive. Features and concepts are introduced gradually, and even though it curves the difficulty pretty well I found the majority of the levels difficult enough to be interesting, and I never really felt like I was just going through the motions on some reused idea.
I chipped away at it a puzzle or two in a day and had a very satisfying experience overall. Highly recommended for anyone not immediately recoiling in horror at the idea of a puzzle game.

So Snakebird starts out decently enough but quickly devolves down into an obnoxious brute force "puzzle" game.
Here's the game in a nutshell. Levels are laid out as a square grid. You'll control 1-3 snakes which will each be a certain number of squares long. On levels with multiple snakes, pressing tab will select a different one. Some levels will have fruit. If it has fruit, you must eat the fruit with a snake which will make the snake 1 square bigger. Once all fruit is eaten, the exit to the level opens. If there's no fruit, then the exit begins open and you must navigate your snake(s) to the exit. The trick to the game is that the snakes will fall based on their current shape if they're no longer touching the ground. So you often need to shape your snake a particular way so falling causes it to land on a platform rather than a spike trap or off the bottom of the level. Snakes can also push each other if you ram another one, you'll often need to do this to get another snake to certain spots. At any time, you can reset a level or press backspace to undo moves as far as you want. If you die, the game automatically undoes your last move.
The music and graphics are fine. The game controls decently well. It starts out fine enough but quickly shows its ugly head.
Minor Quibble: If you're moving your snake around to solve the 'puzzles' and die on a level (and you will die many times) the game backs up 1 turn. If you have multiple snakes, the game selects the snake that died rather than the snake that moved. So once the game undoes your move, you'll go to move the snake you were using only to discover that the game has selected the other snake as the active snake instead. So you've driven that snake somewhere you didn't want it to go and have to undo moves and then select the other snake. This is a minor issue, but it will happen very frequently and is annoying. Why not just leave the active snake as the active snake when the death gets undone? I can't imagine what sort of idiotic reasoning the game designers had for making it this way.
So the biggest problem this game has is that each level isn't so much a puzzle as it is a brute force method of elimination. Most levels require that your snake(s) be moved in a specific manner. If you do not move in the exact manner the level designer wants you to, you will fail.  Quick example:  You need to move somewhere 4 spaces away, so you could choose to move (up, up, right, right) or (right, right, up up) or (up, right, up, right) or (right, up, right, up).  All viable right?  Well not in Snakebird.  In Snakebird, only one of those choices might allow you to succeed.  Now imagine your Snake is bigger and/or you have multiple snakes, all of which must move in specific manners.  This is what you do every single level.  All you're really doing is making a best guess as to whether a path you're taking is the right one until you either succeed or eliminate every possibility it contains and then do the same for some other path until you finally pick the right pathway. There's never really any moments where you get excited or feel good for figuring something out, you just go “Well, I guessed the correct path that 23rd time”. It feels as though the level designers made the levels starting at the end rather then the beginning, traced a specific path that each snake must make from the end back to a certain point, then set that as the start point, and then designed the levels around the pre-made paths. Levels are designed in a way that you could divide them up into several parts. You might clear 1 or 2 parts only to discover at part 3 that you didn't clear part 1 or 2 in the specific manner you were supposed to.  Have fun going back to part 2 or maybe all the way back to part 1.
After brute forcing my way through several levels, I'd had enough. I never felt like I was doing something thoughtful but instead was just punishing myself looking for that 1 and only 1 specific path. It feels like a mindless grind rather than something thought provoking that lead to a solution.
Edit: To further clarify since I've had some comments. I never claimed there's anything wrong with one pathway puzzle games, I enjoy plenty of them. The problem is that this one is a lemon. It offers nothing thoughtful.  Snakebird is a maze variant.  The best strategy for beating a maze?  Start at the end and work backwards, it's the same here in Snakebird.  This is a strategy I figured out for mazes by the age of 5-6.  If you consider tracing paths backwards to be thought provoking and a real brain burner, boy are you in for a treat. Consider this: All you do in the game is move up, left, right, & down and on some levels switch your snakes. Sounds incredibly simple right? We should all be able to beat a game this simple in a few hours right? So, how do you extend the playtime of something this simple? Easy, make it unfair.
People seem confused about the brute forcing parts, so I'm going to ELI 8 this for people. Let's look at how you play a maze, there are 2 methods.  1. Draw as you go:  You use a pencil, start at the start point and draw a path until you reach an area where you can go in multiple directions (a decision point).  You then glance at the maze and make a best guess which way to go.  If it leads to another decision point, do the same thing.  If it leads to a dead end, you erase your path back to the decision point, glance at the maze, and make a new best guess.  Repeat until you get to the exit.  2. Trace and then draw:  This works the same exact way as number 1, except you wait to draw your path until you've traced your way to the exit.  It's important to note that it doesn't matter whether you actually drew a path into a dead end or traced your finger into a dead end, you ran into the dead end.  They are the same exact things.  Mazes don't require intelligence to solve.  The best you can do at any given point is make a best guess where you should go and do that over and over and over until it succeeds.  This is brute forcing.  Now let's look at Snakebird.  How can you play Snakebird?  Well, there are 2 ways.  Let's assume we're on a level with 3 fruits.  1. Move as you play:  In this method, you move your Snakebird until you hit a decision point.  You glance at all the fruit and make a best guess as to which one you can get.  You then move your Snakebird to it and attempt to get it.  If you get it, you glance at the remaining fruit and make a new best guess as to which one you can get.  If you fail to get the fruit (either because you're too short, you block yourself out, you fall into the abyss, or fall into a spike), then you undo your moves until you're back at the decision point, glance at the remaining fruit, and make a new best guess.  Repeat until you get all fruit and into the exit.  2: Trace and then move:  This works the same exact way as number 1, except you wait to move your Snakebird until you've successfully traced a working path to a piece of fruit or to all fruits and into the exit.  Again, it's important to note that it doesn't matter whether you moved your Snakebird and fell off a ledge/onto a spike or traced a path where you realized your Snakebird would fall off a ledge/onto a spike, you still died.  They are the exact same things.  The problems with Snakebird are the exact same problems a maze has.  You're simply brute forcing best guesses until they work.  Again, it doesn't matter whether you're actually moving your Snakebird around or just tracing paths in your head, you're doing the exact same things.

Click on the comments, find the profile of “Edderiofer” (who does not agree with the way I reviewed this game) and click on his profile.  Then take 2-5 minutes to watch a video of him playing this game to see solid evidence that what I've written is entirely accurate.
