Gotta say this before I continue: THIS IS NOT OVERWATCH. Please stop saying that, and play the game for yourself before you compare it simply based off of watching a stream or some gameplay.
Alright. Now that that's out of the way I can talk about how ♥♥♥♥ing awesome this game is. Did you like Quake? Did you enjoy Unreal Tournament? Did you never play either of those games? Doesn't matter. This game is incredibly fun regardless of what you can compare it to, and it is unique in it's own way. Fast paced, and I mean FAST paced gameplay makes for some of the most intense firefights I've ever been in (and I was a machine gunner in the Marines, trust me, it's intense). Couple that with the smooth as hell mobility, and how your specific characters abilities interact and influence it, and you have a game where there are endless ways in which you can fight and win. Personally I enjoy playing as Vanguard; she can literally zip around the map like a fighter jet with a minigun attached to her arm. Simply awesome. The game modes are another awesome part of the game with very different objectives for each one. My personal favorite is Blitzball, which can be a really quick game of domination over the other team, or, for example, like my first match after release, a long tug-of-war match where the offense was amazing, and the defense was better, leading to a 20 minute battle of attrition where the winner was determined by the time running out (neither team made it to the required 8 scores to win). It was a blast. Let's not forget that there's blood, cursing, and hilarious results from dying in zero gravity where your body just flings off into the air in weird♥♥♥♥♥positions. Also, the loot system is pretty satisfying. It's the good ol' stash drops, loot crate, whatever you wanna call it kind of system, but the contents of the stash drops is just so much more fulfilling than other games with similar rewards. Whether it's a new weapon skin, armor for your character, a new logo for when you kick someone to death (it's various footprint images), stickers for your guns, or just coins so you can purchase skins yourself, there are plenty of things to look forward to earning through your levels.
So pros and cons time:
Pros:
- Very fast paced, intense gameplay.
- Different classes that cater to a lot of game play styles.
- Zero gravity combat is fun as hell, especially how it interacts with character abilities (you can propel yourself forward with the Titan's rocket launcher, for example).
- Hit boxes are way better than in other similar styled games.
- Various game modes that all feel different and can provide a good 20 minutes of intense back and forth.
- Fun maps
- Perfect game for M/KB
- Aesthetics are on point, not cartoon-y at all.
- Blood, curse words, and glorious deaths.
- Blitzball is fun as all hell, and the announcer is voiced by the same guy who voices Morty.
- Fun loot, and some bad♥♥♥♥♥exotic armor for the characters.
- The music is ♥♥♥♥ing amazing.
- It's 30 bucks. This game is priced so appropriately. Yes, it was supposed to be F2P at first, but I'm happy they didn't do that because it usually invites P2W stuff. There's none of that here. Yes, you can buy stash drops, but the contents of those drops are aesthetic and in no way help or harm your skills.
There's a lot more I could put in pros, but for the sake of not being too long of a post I'll end it there.
Cons:
- The fast paced nature of the game can throw some people off. Takes getting used to, but is very satisfying once you figure it out.
- Bad publicity. This game needed to be marketed better, not only to distance itself from Overwatch, but also to show people that they're getting a lot for 30 bucks. Already seeing articles claiming it's DOA, which just isn't true.
- Definitely needs more maps.
- Not really a con, but I'm wondering what the roadmap looks like for this game. I hope there's more skins added, more maps, and even more characters eventually. It's fine for now, but the game will have to be added on to so that it can have longevity.
- The game will fail simply due to people not trying it before judging it. It's 30 bucks, pay for it, play for a couple hours and then refund it if you don't like it, but I bet you will enjoy it anyways.
Honestly cons are hard to think about. I haven't found much I dislike about the game. I could possibly say that stash drops should happen more often, but then again, getting them for every level up is probably fine.
Either way, I think you should try this game out. It's very fun, it's not an Overwatch rip off, it's fast paced and intense as all hell, and it's only 30 bucks. Give it a go, you won't regret it.

Arkham Asylum's story takes place on the infamous mental institution full of thugs and super villians alike. Combat in this game is the first iteration of Rocksteady's FreeFlow Combat System. It is very impactful and showy, if not downright brutal. Compared to the later installments such City and Knight, however, the combat system doesn't have as many variations of special combos or the integration of quick gadgets.
The voice work is top notch, enlisting the efforts of Kevin Conroy as Batman and Mark Hamill as the Joker. Other characters are voiced by well-known voice actors and even some from the 90s Batman: The Animated Series.
Overall, this game is well worth its asking price and weaves itself deeply into the narratives of its sequels.

Overall, Far Cry 3: Blood Dragon is an excellent, if short, game. You can expect plenty of explosions, good combat, and general badassery from the main character, a cyber-commando named Rex Colt. Like all other far cry games there are several enemy bases scattered around the fully open world for you to capture. Raiding these bases provides you with an additional fast travel location, a shop location, as well as a side mission. You can reset all of the bases, filling them with enemies again, if you want to get more side objectives. By the way, the side objectives give you weapon upgrades, so you will want to do them. Apart from that, there is the extremely well-done main quest line, which is arguably the best part of the game.
Pros:
- Excellent main story line with diverse locations
- Diverse gameplay - In most situations you can either kill the enemies stealthily, or you can go loud and both will work
- Excellent graphics - Since this game runs on far cry 3's engine, it should be no surprise that the graphics are very good. However, the overall style of the game has obviously been tweaked from far cry 3 to fit the game's theme
- Good animations - The animations for reloads and climbing around and doing just about everything are all well done making combat fluid
- Good open world game - You can run around in the game's open world and find plenty of enemies and collectibles to keep you busy outside of missions
- Well optimized - This game ran at a completely solid 60 fps on my 4790k/gtx 780 at high/ultra settings, which is good when you consider how good it looks
- I could go on but I'll leave it like this
Cons:
- I felt that the game was a bit too easy. Even after putting it on hard, you can kill lots of enemies pretty easily in anything other than early in the game simply because of how many perks and upgrades you end up getting. I really would have wanted to see an insanity difficulty
- The game was short - I've completed the main quest in just under 12 hours, even while doing most of the side objectives and getting ~60% or so of the collectibles combined with some time just playing around in the open world. You can probably expect about 18-21 hours if you wanted to do a completionist playthrough
- UPLAY - Honestly, this is the biggest con about the game. The first time I installed it on my D drive (since I only have windows and a few programs on my C drive since it's an SSD), and it just wouldn't work after trying just about everything. I was about to return it when I decided I would put it on my SSD and it decided to work (WTF!). Maybe that will help you if you decide to get this game (which you still should).
NOTE: It may be possible to fix some of these cons with mods since the game does have a mod nexus, but I haven't lookied into it, so I don't know how good they are or how well they work with uplay
Overall, great game 9.2/10

All I can say about this game is that it is fun, really. What I'll do is take a negative review containing common misconceptions about the game, and hopefully shed some light on them.
"Unbalanced crap. The same characters that were a problem in Alpha are STILL a problem at launch... it's beyond me. This is supposed to be a game that is about skill but every character is on a totally different playing field. Most if not all the characters are practically useless aside from Vanguard/Battle Medic/Wraith. These three characters alone have so much mobility and damage it's beyond me how they even launched with them this way."
1. Unbalanced crap: this game is balanced. The reason people say that it is unbalanced is because the game requires actual skill, unlike games like overwatch, where your only skill is to pick the correct hero that corresponds with the enemy team and your team. In Lawbreakers, *everything* requires precision. Just because someone has better aim than you doesn't make their character unbalanced
2. Characters that were a problem in Alpha are STILL a problem at launch... it's beyond me: A beta isn't all about your enjoyment, it's about finding and fixing bugs so that there's a steady launch. I haven't come accross any major, game-breaking bugs yet since release (frankly there weren't many in the betas), which proves that BKP is actually trying. Even at that, they did something that was way beyond the call of duty- they actually balanced heroes in between betas. That's not really something you should expect from an indie studio that's competing with other big names in gaming. There is no magic switch that will balance a game. Every game has balance issues.
3. This is supposed to be a game that is about skill but every character is on a totally different playing field: *claps* well done, you have figured out how roles work. There are different roles and each of them are stronger in different situations.... How is that bad? Would you just want everyone running around with the same weapon and abilities? That would just get boring
4. Most if not all the characters are practically useless aside from Vanguard/Battle Medic/Wraith: This isn't true... The vanguard is the first character on the roster and for good reason. She is super easy to pick up and master. There is a very low skill cap, and the character is pretty strong. That doesn't mean it's overpowered or a must-pick, it simply means that casuals will have a way to do well. I do agree that the battle medic is a must-pick, though. If your team has a med and the enemy doesn't, you're most likely gonna win, but that's because it's a healer. For example, in Overwatch, if you were to go into a match without a single healer, how do you think you would do? I'm unsure why you put the wraith on this list... I mean, he was kinda overpowered in the third beta, but other than that, he's just another skill-based hero...
5. These three characters alone have so much mobility and damage it's beyond me how they even launched with them this way: This review gives off a certain vibe. It just makes you feel like he wrote it after getting destroyed in a match, so of course he's gonna blame the low-budget indie game devs
I chose to cretique this review in particular because it has a lot of common misconceptions about the game that I want to put to rest.

In the distant future of 2007 the world needs a cyborg hero and that hero is YOU!!!  Blood Dragon is a standalone dlc for Far Cry 3 and gameplay wise they're pretty much identical.  This is a good thing, because Far Cry 3 is very good.  It's an open world FPS with stealth and RPG elements thrown in as well.  The biggest difference in the two is how much more badass Rex Power Colt is than Jason Brody.  Not just in personality but in acutal gameplay.  In Far Cry 3 you start out with two weapon slots and very few skills meaning you need to level up, choose your new skills, and craft new gear to become badass enough to beat the game.  It makes sense in a game that's thematically about a regular person adapting to an extreme situation.  In Blood Dragon however you start out as a badass cyber commando and become an even more badass cyber commando by the end.  You start with all four weapon slots unlocked as well as quite a few skills that you had to work hard to earn in Far Cry 3.  You also have no control over what you unlock upon leveling up this time around.  In Far Cry 3 I  felt like I had to do some of the side missions and outposts to get strong enough to win.  In Blood Dragon I felt like they were entirely optional.  The side missions and outposts are still fun, but if you want you can rush throught the game in 5-6 hours.  Story wise the game's got a great sense of humor and doesn't take itself even the slightest bit seriously.  It's also almost as American as Broforce.  Overall great game, if you already like Far Cry then getting this should be a no brainer.

I recommend this game because of how much fun the game is, it's a fun little time waster that will have you burning hours into it, even at the highest levels. I've been playing this game since it originally came out on kongregrate and have enjoyed watching it progress from where it was, to what it has become now. Unfortunately as i will mention below, the game has become stale and used up after completing every achievement, and completing quite a few events. On the idea of events, I believe this may be my last event for awhile. My completionist personality isn't enough for me to keep coming back daily after having spent nearly 90 hours playing this game already; it just doesn't have enough replay value for that. Especially considering that you have to log in twice daily because of the 8 hour time gap, i don't even do that for MMOs with good dailies.
In essence, rewards for dailies are overused and honestly, quite annoying. It's a mechanic that exists specifically to keep us replaying the same content over, and over again so we don't recognise that we're actually running out of content to play around with.
To those at SadPanda, you've done a great job on this game and i appreciate the effort you're making to ensure your players have more content to play around with. But doing it as part of a daily system is just going to irritate people. And not only the people who don't have the time to log in twice with an 8 hour time gap. You're also going to irritate the people who sleep at awkward hours like myself. Not to mention the blatant punishment of new players by putting dailies on hard to reach girls. Dailies as a whole are just never a good thing. Perhaps they seem like a good idea to begin with, but eventually dailies end up making a game feel more like a job than the fun escape from reality that they are meant to be.
If you got this far in the review, thanks for listening to my rant, i encourage you to try the game for yourselves and decide your own opinion of it. Thanks again SadPanda for all the hard work you've put in.

This is an interesting game. Basically you commandeer a WWII Nazi submarine and hunt down enemy merchant and warships. Here's the part that I struggled with in this game and led to my disliking it: playing the game in a way that is most satisfying requires doing incredibly difficult things, things that require (OH F***) math! Plotting intercept courses, manual torpedo solutions, etc. all require a knowledge of trigonometry and angles that the tutorial does not cover. This presents a problem to people like myself who graduated a while ago and can't remember a thing related to math, other than basic concepts.
The reason I say that doing the above things is the most satisfying way to play is because when I played on easy settings, where the AI does all the torpedo calculations and course calculations, I felt like I was a lazy, under-qualified ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ captain who did nothing by himself and who inherited the position of captain because all other candidates onboard the sub were killed by chestbursters and the Alien. I felt cheap, in other words, because then it just became to easy. You might say "Geez dumbass, why not look up how to do these things on the interwebs and the internets?" Well, peeps, I did do that. And you know what? It made me feel worse, cuz I still didn't ever successfully intercept a ship.
Now, if you are in high school and have a fresh knowledge of trig and math, then you may like this game, because other than the incredible difficulty, everything else is great. The graphics are good, the sub exterior and interiors look awesome. No complaints there.
In summary, only buy this if you have an understanding of trigonometry and angles and will put serious effort into this game. Otherwise, watch "Hunt for Red October"

Challenging but rewarding puzzle game with a polished art style with colourfully animated design. 53 levels of solid mechanical puzzling fun!

"Snakebird is an elegant puzzle game."
This game is great because it's clear that each level was designed with a specific goal in mind that in order to accomplish, you must realize a new facet of the deep mechanics that make up the game. The mechanics are actually simple, but together they create some very deep interactions that you will need to fully grasp in order to complete the more challenging later puzzles.
However, Snakebird does not start off overwhelming and the basic mechanics are introduced gradually in the first few levels with a nice difficulty curve. Paying close attention to the "how" and "why" of the solutions of these early puzzles will be invaluable for finding the solutions to future puzzles.
Levels are spaced across a world map with each biome having its own mechanical theme or new puzzle object to interact with in addition to the snakebirds. The world map is laid out in such a way that multiple levels can possibly unlock from completing the previous one. This is incredibly helpful in case you get stuck so that you can go try a different puzzle in the meantime and return to the first one later with a new perspective.
Each puzzle itself is elegant and you rarely, if ever, NOT use everything in a level. Everything involved in a puzzle can be seen on a single screen at all times and there is nothing included to obfuscate the solution like extra objects to interact with that you don't need. There is a clear starting point with only a few pieces to work with, but the process to the goal remains interesting. If you get stuck on a puzzle, there is usually enough space in the level to move the snakebirds around to help generate ideas to yourself about what to do next. Otherwise, undoing your moves or resetting the puzzle altogether is just a push of a button away. It helps to be able to play around with the "puzzle pieces" that you're given to reach an ah-ha moment that gives you a new strategy to follow. Some levels will restrict your movement options quite a bit from the start, so deduction will likely play a bigger role in these puzzles.
The aesthetic charm and polish of Snakebird shouldn't be overlooked either. The colorful environments, relaxing music, and expressive faces of the snakebirds all create a pleasant atmosphere to soothe any pent-up frustration that you may experience while being unable to eat that distant fruit without falling to your demise in the briny sea below! There are also plenty of environmental doodads to click and mouse over should your mind wander.

I've been playing this game for the total of 251 hours, and I've enjoyed most of my time in the game.

Players could play in FFA mode, where it is a casual match of 4 people defeating each other until there's the last one standing.
There's also an experimental mode that allows players to have 1v1 match just like in the ranked one, but it isn't ranked.
The ranked match system is great, both the 2v2 and 1v1. It has these diamond, platinum, gold, silver, and bronze class to differentiate the players based on their achievement in the ranked match system. The matching system is also fair; it rarely pairs a low tier player with a high tier and vice versa.

Overall, the game is great, and I recommend it to everyone.

I really enjoy this game. It's incredibly fast paced, and a HUGE breath of fresh air when coming from Overwatch.
What makes it such a breath of fresh air is the fact that you don't have to hug your tanks and healers to do well in this game. Instead it's a true skill-based shooter, where the only reason you die is because you were bested by your opponent.
This game has a very fluid movement system, and it is so fun to use in Zero-G! For characters who don't have a jetpack or grappling hook etc., you can "blindfire" your weapon behind you by holding CTRL to propel you forward! This works amazingly and feels awesome when you've just snagged the objective from the enemy base and now you need to fly through the middle zero-g area of the map as fast as possible. Just jump, hold CTRL, and watch as you gain a ton of speed.
Each character in this game has their own unique abilities and loadout. Some characters excel at certain objectives more than others, and there is certainly a playstile for everyone here. And you may think "oh this is just another hero team-based shooter like Overwatch" but if you do think that, you are wrong. Overwatch is slow, and requires your entire team to hold each others hands as you get pocketed by a healer or protected by a big shield man (because shooting shields is fun in a shooter right?). In LawBreakers, there is none of that. You have the damage output, abilities, and movement to best your opponents no matter who you're playing. Yes even the "support" classes in this game (there are 2 currently) are highly offensive and can score skills on their own. That's right, you won't get jumped on by a tank as a healer and get killed because you have no dps, in this game the healers ARE dps and with the lack of rock-paper-scissors gameplay, anyone can outplay their opponent if they are skilled enough.
I highly recommend this game if you need to fill that arena shooter itch (Unreal Tournament, Quake, etc.) and if you're tired of having to hug a team and complain about "team composition" like in some other games...
I love this game, there's so much more to say. Please keep reading more reviews and consider giving this game a shot.

This game was my childhood. I'm biased of course, but I think this is a really great game whether you have nostalgia for it or not. For me, now I'm able to relive those blessed afternoons playing this on the WII- "Let me be Darth Vader!" "Stop throwing bombs at me!" "GO FASTER SEBULBAS GETTING AWAY"
It's a lot easier than I remember it- when I played this as a kid I paid a friend to beat Mustafar for me (he couldnt but still took my money). Now each level is pretty much 20-30 minutes on story mode. The game isnt really a challenge (aside from the bonus levels that ravaged my village when i was a child). I mean, it's sometimes tricky to get the minikits but never infuriating. There are some parts that feel very dated (I'm looking at that cutscene of the Slave 1 "taking off" on Kamino), but in an odd way the small bad parts are endearing. Let's just say you can tell it's aged, but it aged with dignity.
Bugwise, it's pretty clean. Good port. The only issues I have are the dumbass controls for p2 (if you don't have a controller) and the friendly AI not dealing damage. That's something I don't remember from back in the day, I remember relying on them to pick off stragglers? Also droidekas are overpowered as hell and it's BS to die twice doing the only lightsaber move that kills them, and also BS because you're basically invincible when you play with them.
Word from the wise, on the Hoth Ice base level with Han and Leia there's a part with a bunch of fans and a little truck that's practically impossible without P2 controlling C3P0, which means you either need to get a friend or grow another arm. That's actually the only gameplay issue I've seen, and I remember it infuriating the hell out of young me.

A potentially very good game marred by the plague that infects gaming and games developers in this decade, namely microtransactions.
Deus Ex Human Revolution is one of my favourite games of all time, right up there with the original Deus Ex in my opinion, and have rarely looked forward to a game as much as I did with Mankind Divided. It starts off well, and the story and gameplay are excellent, but the end is shocking. Not shocking in terms of the story, but in terms of how it feels like someone at Eidos cut the game in half so that they could sell the other half as another game later down the road.
And ultimately it's that pratice that I cannot accept. I could have gotten over the game having microtransactions, as annoying as they are, but when a game developer seemingly cuts a game in half to make more money, I cannot trust anything they sell ever again.
The integrity has gone out of game development and companies are now treating us gamers as nothing more than cash cows. Well, hopefully we can hit back where it hurts.
To anyone viewing reviews and thinking of buying this game: don't. It's not even worth £9.99.

Shooting them down increases a bar that gives you two features: 1)Triggers a short bullet clearing wave when hit if you have enough bar 2) When full gives you access to some screen clearing/filling burst lazers (by pressing a button0 that turns enemies, and their bullets if they die, into medals. Based on how many of them you collect a secondary bar fills that activates at the end of the lazer clearing burst that allows you to get melee with opponents/stage structures for more medals and score for up to 4 seconds.
You also have a secondary weapon that gets replaced with completly different ones by pickups in stages (found 3 different ones).

Great game that deserves alot more exposure. Lots of care went into enemy placement and patterns instead of just flooding the screen with bullets. 12 stages in Arcade mode, which is 7 more than you will typically find in this genre. 4 ships to start with, I've unlocked 2 extra so far from playing through everyones Story mode. Feels like a fusion of new shmups and the old Caravan shooters from the PC Engine era like Star Soldier. Has a much faster feel than other games, more focused around avoiding bullet patterns entirely instead of dodging them which is really fun. There's a primary and secondary weapon system, your main gun always stays but you can change your secondary, which is usually good to use against larger enemies and bosses. There are initially 3 different secondary weapons and I've unlocked two extra, one of which, the TT Drill is AMAZING. I unlocked them by playing the Story mode with the 2 hidden characters.
This game is also a good start for beginners to this genre as once you kill enough enemies it charges up energy for a shield. The same energy for your shield is necessary for points though, so getting hit can seriously ruin your potential score. New players to this genre don't care about score, but expert shmup players do, so you have a really cool mechanic that is appealling to both beginners and pros.
The scoring system is based around letting off a bomb (Which you charge up by killing enemies) when there are tons of enemies and bullets on screen, which turns them into stars that you collect and then your ship becomes a mini-black hole and you smash into as many enemies as you can to do massive damage and get more valuable stars from those defeated enemies before a timer runs out. I think the amount of stars you picked up in the first phase dictates how long the second phase is. This is really enjoyable and kind of reminded me of Crimzon Clovers Break Mode a little bit, or even the bullet absorption mechanics of Mars Matrix and Giga Wing.
The Story mode was interesting but a little verbose, if you want just pure shooting action then play Arcade Mode. Every character has their own Story mode to play through and you get to see the events of the game through their perspective with completely new dialogue from all characters. They did a good job of making every character unique, I loved the banter between Miho and Tatiana the best, I found the insults they slung at each other hilarious. The two hidden characters had a nice dynamic in their Story, with one acting as the straight man and the other a goofball. They also managed to make Pushpa and Thoreau sympathetic characters without going too overboard. The Story is based around a joint mission between nations to Investigate the Varstray: A giant hurricane thing in the middle of space that could hold the key to defeating self replecating machine things. It managed to keep me entertained and made me want to find out more about the world, which is what Sci-Fi is supposed to do.
I highly recommend it from what I've played so far, it's really well done. This game was unfortunately not featured on the front page of Steam so alot of people don't even know it exists. It deserves your support and way more attention than it got.
Also the game now has online leaderboards, full screen option and V-Sync thanks to a recent update.

Mark of the Ninja, one of those ninja games that really emphasizes the idea of being stealthy. That being said, this game also allows you to go all out with your ninja skills and tools to dispose of your enemies violently, but there is a certain sense of pride and reward if you play this game stealthily and sparing your enemies; assassinating only those who need to be assassinated. Like a true ninja.
Having played this game around 24 hours now, completed the story mode more than twice because of the achievements, and still finding new ways to finish levels, is now a rarity in games; yes this game’s storyline is linear, but the levels and how you want to accomplish challenges within the level is all but linear.
This was well worth the money I spent on it.
Story:
You are this unnamed ninja who has been chosen to bear “The Mark” in order to slay (if you so choose) your enemies who has attacked your dojo… That’s all you need to know for now.
I must say, the story was a tad predictable halfway near the end, but that didn’t stop me from finishing the game.
Story, may not be the most epic of stories, but the gameplay and art design more than makes up for the lack of “bang” in the story in my opinion.
Graphics:
It’s a 2D platformer. As in, the whole game is in 2D; 2D sprites with 2D backgrounds, and animated cutscenes.
I have nothing against 2D and in fact, love the art design in this game.
I don’t need Skyrim level graphics to enjoy the game, but this is also not hideous to look at one bit.
Love the little details, such as heat waves blurring the background as it comes out of vents. And that’s the thing about the game… The little details. They got it right.
Gameplay:
Okay, now this is where the game truly shines.
The gameplay is crisp, never did I feel detached as a ninja in this game, and once you have the controls down, it will become second nature to you. And that really is the key word. CONTROL. You are truly one with the ninja here. You are one with the game.
You can use certain items to distract your enemies to move away while you either sneak pass them or kill them when their backs are turned. You can also use the environment to do similar things; break a lightbulb and have the breaking sound distract the guards; wait until lightning strikes and have the guards get distracted by your transient image; and the list goes on!
There are a number of ways to deal with your enemies; like I said, you can either sneak passed them or kill them; use their dead bodies to scare their living comrades; inject poison fungus in one of them and have their comrade inspect the body only to get infected with the same poison; use your enemy to kill another enemy. The choice is yours!
I can’t point to any flaw with the gameplay really. And if there are any flaws, they just minor flaws that is simply outweighed by the near perfect gameplay.
Sound:
Music are what you’d expect from a stealth-minded game. It can raise tension, and it can pump you up, but somehow, I cannot say that these songs would be one of the more memorable songs. Sometimes I don’t even notice the background music playing.
Sound effects are alright, and that is honestly more important that the song, as you try and listen to the guards’ footsteps or their conversations especially if they think they’ve spotted you.
Sound department is on par with every other game really.
Replayability:
VERY HIGH. I emphasized that because I think it only took me 4-5 hours to finish the game, but it’s the achievements, the level seals/scrolls that I need to accomplish, that kept me going. Gameplay is superb so it doesn’t feel to repetitive because you can go through the level in a number of different ways.
And the Steam Achievements are honestly more possible than other games’ achievements.
If you are a die hard completionist, then you’ll love this game.
And for those who aren’t, well you’ll love this just as much!
In summary:
This is the best ninja game I’ve played in a long time, let alone, ever.
The thrill of being all stealthy, that “WTF” moment when you get caught, the number of ways you can finish a level… this is the ninja game we ninja fans/wannabes deserve.
High replayability as well makes this a no brainer purchase.
-Chan

In the distant future of 2007 the world needs a cyborg hero and that hero is YOU!!!  Blood Dragon is a standalone dlc for Far Cry 3 and gameplay wise they're pretty much identical.  This is a good thing, because Far Cry 3 is very good.  It's an open world FPS with stealth and RPG elements thrown in as well.  The biggest difference in the two is how much more badass Rex Power Colt is than Jason Brody.  Not just in personality but in acutal gameplay.  In Far Cry 3 you start out with two weapon slots and very few skills meaning you need to level up, choose your new skills, and craft new gear to become badass enough to beat the game.  It makes sense in a game that's thematically about a regular person adapting to an extreme situation.  In Blood Dragon however you start out as a badass cyber commando and become an even more badass cyber commando by the end.  You start with all four weapon slots unlocked as well as quite a few skills that you had to work hard to earn in Far Cry 3.  You also have no control over what you unlock upon leveling up this time around.  In Far Cry 3 I  felt like I had to do some of the side missions and outposts to get strong enough to win. One of the best stealth games I have ever played (and I play a lot of them. It's my favourite genre).
It's one of those "Easy to learn, hard to master" games.
Nearly every single level and encounter offrers at least couple paths and solutions to a problem. Quietly pick off guards one by one? Sure. Distract with a firecracker and  hide while they run past? Done. Destroy the lights and sneak through? Covered. Perhaps try a ventilation shaft? There's one. Plant some traps? Bye bye, guard. Bugger the stealth and punch/kick/evicerate target to the chorus of alarms? Do if you must, but that's not how we trained you.
You can even hang bodies for lamps for other guards to find, causing them to freak out and start firing at every little sound in sheer terror. Often hitting their coworkers and drawing other guards to investigate and join the mayhem. There's a lot of fun in watching half the guards in a level wipe themselves out in blind panic, before pouncing on a last terified stragler while he twitchily tries to watch all directions at once.
Ninja arsenal is nearly as extensive, allowing to customise gear to fit your playstyle. Multiple unlockable costumes with special effects each, distraction items, killing tools and various special takedowns.
NPC AI is fairly good. Guards react to sounds and sight and investigate glimpses of you. They can check vents, flash light around when looking and share jobs - one goes t investigate, the other keeps guard. AI is even better on New Game Plus.
AI is the source of my ONE nitpick with the game - sometimes guards can wonder into enviromental traps themselves and die, taking away "No kill bonus" points and ruining a perfect pacifist-ghost run (self-imposed challenge).
If you like stealth, this game is a must. Very well realised mechanics and simple controls with quite some depth.
Very highly recomended

Ah, Harvester, it's a classic full motion video (FMV) point-and-click game that has been both praised and scorned over the years. When it originally came out in 1996, many critics said that the game felt dated due to its delayed release, but these days gamers can't seem to get enough of this gore-soaked B-Grade title; save for the prudes who don't enjoy cheesy horror like Evil Dead, Basket Case, or even Silent Night, Deadly Night.
During the game, you play as an 18 year old guy named Steve Mason; trust me, you were always such a kidder, Steve. It turns out that he has severe amnesia, to the point that he doesn't even remember that he's engaged and set to be wed to a woman named Stephanie in three weeks time. No one in the town of Harvest believes that he has amnesia, which frustrates him to no end. During the time that you will spend in the small town of Harvest, population 51, you will meed a variety of wildly eccentric and somewhat wacky characters, all who have their own personality quirks; a deputy who is obsessed with jerking off to nudie mags, Stephanie's father who is off his rocker about meat, a crazy school teacher who thinks that the best way to discipline her students is by beating them with a baseball bat, gay firemen... the list just goes on and on.
Well, it turns out that Stephanie has just as severe of a case of amnesia that Steve does. The goal of the game comes down to getting in to this mysterious, secret organization known as The Order of the Harvest Moon, whose headquarters are located at the Lodge. Steve needs to join them prior to the Harvest Annual Blood Drive Donation at the end of the week, which is mandatory... and perhaps deadly. The gameplay is separated in to days, and as such you will play through a total of six days (some with night events) and three levels of the Lodge. The entire game, if you're using a guide, will take around 7-8 hours to complete; if you're not using a guide, it could take you upwards to 20 hours to figure out the complex puzzles and how to initiate the game moving from one day to the next.
Harvest is a fairly large town for having such a small population, it has 18 locations to explore; although some of them you will only end up visiting once or twice. There are just as many characters to interact and converse with, as well as to potentially murder. That's right, Harvester also features a fighting mechanic; left clicking lets you examine, pick up, and use objects, while right clicking lets you attack. You will find a large amount of weapons to use during the course of your playthrough, all which can be individually equipped via the inventory screen. Not only are you able to kill people, but once you reach the later Lodge levels, there are monsters that you will have to take out as well.
Surprisingly, this title has aged incredibly well in both looks and functionality. The abundant FMVs are riddled with gore, cheesy dialogue, and bad acting; even though they're low quality and slightly pixelated, they're still incredibly enjoyable to watch time and time again. It's even worth it to go out of your way to explore all of the different ways that Steve can die, and to interact with all of the characters as many times as possible to view all of the cutscenes. Talking with people in the town of Harvest will show "key words" that you can select that act as topics for discussion, though some disappear after speaking about another subject you can type in any keywords that were available; this is one retro game where keeping a pen and paper handy is actually still useful.
I could go on singing praises about Harvester all day, but sadly the Steam version has a few kinks that will most likely never be worked out. For some people, the game crashes often; this did not happen to me. For a lot of people, the FMV cutscenes, which are arguably the best part of the game, will refuse to play; this actually did happen to me, and you do miss out not on just a lot of the fun stuff, but a lot of the story as well. There's only one known fix for the latter issue, and that's to lower the frame cycles in DOSBox to 8000. Doing so makes the gameplay infuriatingly choppy and sluggish, fortunately most of the FMVs are located on the sixth day, and only sporadically throughout the rest of the game.
Even with the problems that weigh this port down, Harvester is an amazingly fun, low-budget horror title that's seething with blood, gore, intestines, crude phallic jokes, bad acting, cheesy dialogue, and hilarious FMV cutscenes. Some of the more memorable moments for me were when the deputy was caught jerking off, and finding the children eating their mother; not to mention the countless sessions of dialogue that will stick with you, such as the meat obsessed father of the bride. If you're a fan of old B-Grade movies like the ones I listed in the introductory paragraph, or if you played and enjoyed games such as Sanitarium, Phantasmagoria, and I Have No Mouth and I Must Scream, then you will absolutely dig Harvester. However, for a dollar more you can purchase it on GOG and avoid any potential issues that the Steam version has.

The best Batman game ever made.  As the first in the Arkham series, all the conventions the game presented, including the third person camera view, takedown varieties, gliding/batline travel, the complex fighting system with tumbling/evading/blocking/counters and the universe's general aesthetic "DNA" were all new and fresh.  The story was simple fare: enter Arkham Asylum, and stop the Joker and his enlisted bosses, through technology/subterfuge/force, from holding the institution.  The ending was a bit of a cop-out.  The story wasn't anything amazing and didn't have any lasting implications in the Batman universe.
Despite it all, the game *feels* good. It moves/travels/fights as Batman should.  Possessed of some legitimately tense moments, the game also exhibits a Batman that we remember from the comics.  Unlike successors that have suffered from feature creep and a series of issues, Arkham Asylum is very linear, thankfully enough.  The game moves briskly and with purpose as you work your way towards the conclusion.
Definitely worth the time if you can get it on an 8 dollar Steam sale.

I have 300+ hours on Overwatch and no matter what the comparisons are,
LawBreakers is incredibly fast, responsive and reactive. It's unforgiving and incredibly satisfying when you play well but infuriating when you get demolished.
The game modes are actually good, and Blitzball is great fun.
Cosmetics come in forms of crates - like most games these days - and you can buy more crates - but you get one for levelling up and they dish out credits for duplicates and even watching the tutorial videos so you can buy more with them.
Even though the hero roster is pretty small right now, each one plays completely different and will take a long time to master.
The one thing I will say that can be a positive and a negative - the skill floor is very low, and the ceiling very high. Meaning if you're bad at this game you'll know it and it will remind you at every opportunity. It can get annoying.
If you're good at this game then you'll know that too, from the nVidia highlights features (which is awesome) to the end game rating and achievements.
The visuals are decent, and it performs pretty well at launch. Rarely dips below 60fps and I don't have the best of machines by todays standards, running at 1440p on a GTX970.
If we're going to compare to Overwatch (which everyone seems to be doing) then the difference is that LawBreakers is purely focused on the skill of the individual player and outplaying people, whereas in Overwatch you're only as good as your team and your team comp with counters. Lawbreakers doesn't have counters or isn't THAT focused on team comp, but a group of good players playing their desired class will definitely play better. Thing is, even if you're a top 500 Genji, you still rely on that Ana ult or Zarya ult. In Lawbreakers, you can just rely on your aim and mechanics with your class to win the game for you and your team.
The other comparison is that - unfortunatley, compared to Overwatch, the characters in Lawbreakers are pretty forgettable. They don't reallyt have much soul or personality - in fact that's non existent. All you'll be referring to when playing is the class - not the character. That's where Overwatch is in it's own class with Blizzards typical attention to detail and fleshing out the visuals and art style.
Generally, I would say that if you like the look of this game and you're looking to scratch an itch of a fast paced arena shooter, I would pick this game up. Whether you have Overwatch or not.

This is not a stealth game, This is not Gunpoint, You cannot turn off these hints.
This actually all very good advice, Ronin is not about making a plan of how to get to the top floor without being seen, it's not about discovering the truth of a mystery without making noise.  It's exactly what a tale of a Ronin should be, revenge, destruction, and badassery.
Your best bet is to go with the flow in this game, use your rope to smash through the window and cut the guard by the entrance in half. No one noticed you? Hang half of the others from the ceiling, but then you get spotted by the super speed samuri! Jump next to the window, then jump away and watch him hilariously throw himself out the building to fall to his death after hitting some electrified wires. Your turn stops with you hanging in midair, you throw your sword at the guy at the far end of the room and land infront of another. You summon your sword to you and it flies into his back!  Launch yourself to the wall to avoid the stream bullets from the guard with the submachine, wait a turn, then cackle evily as you now have two whole turns to finish hims off any way you want becuase now he has to reload and then reaquire you. Jump to him and use your grappling hook to close in... but another default guard sees you and your rope swing doesn't clear his aim. A single tiny bullet hits and you fall to the ground clutching your wound.
The guards will come better equipped with all sorts of gadgets weapons and abilities, but all it takes is a single bullet to kill you. The really good news is that you get a checkpoint every time you enter or exit a room. this means plenty of retries that don't force you to comeback across the map, because there is going to be that room that takes 20 tries. You may get respawned dead center of all the guards, but that's because it was the only entrance to the room.
Your biggest advantage is that Ronin is turn based, plan where your gonna go and who you slice next with all the time in the world. Your turn can even (and often) end with you in midair with a nice selection of methods to dispose of the baddies. The skills can only be activated by action points, and the action points can only be acquired from stunning and killing enemies. At five points you trigger limit break wich resets your points but gives you a whole extra turn, which could be a godsend as that was all you needed to tackle the annoying guard about to set the alarm. Or it could be really annoying as sword throwing would have been really more helpful at the moment.
Your skills are granted points for completing these optional objectives:
-Killing all enemies; not a stealth game, you can be stealthy, but loud is suprisingly more fun and rewarding
-No alarms; there isn't a guard standing next to the magic game over button, you have 8 turns to at the least get his attention
-Kill no civillians; this is where your stealth play is pretty much most used, simply avoid lights to dodge the chatting civvies in some sort of puzzle fashion
Spending your skill points will mold how you paly the game, deciding which you will get more use out of is frustrating, especially when there is so many cool choices.
As for downsides, (to this fantastic game!):
-The transition between combat turns and roaming can be disorienting. You can use the pause button at any time, but if you use it when you thought you entered a room unoticed and press it right as combat starts you may think you're still roaming and lose that valuable first turn since it's your skip turn button during combat. Or think it's still combat and not notice the guard calling the alarm isn't paused, the pause button and time pause for jumping can save you there sometimes.
-The objective for almost every mission leading to the bosses is go to the computers and press the button to auto hack. Some other challenges would have been nice. Since making your way through the building and guards is the main challenge and often very different and fun, that one should slide.
-The optional objectives are also all the same. They feel more like requirements since that's how your skill points are earned, and you NEED those skill points. Minibosses and optional fullfilment objectives could have spiced things up.
-As mentioned the limit break "extra turn" can be very unhelpful in certain situations. The mechanic will add a layer to tactics, but an accidental stun can lose that sword toss you really needed and that will cause you some gray hairs more than once
All in all, I loved this game. It's not to hard, not to easy. It's nice to see someone create an action game that doesn't sell off of hype or humor. Ronin tells you what it is, and does it very well. I'll even say it, I had more fun with this than gunpoint, and I loved gunpoint.
-9/10
-Minus one point because the "optional objectives" don't feel very "optional" or "objective", some more creative optional objectives would have been fun.

I'm reposting some of my old reviews because I adopted an easier to read format (and because for some reason I can't edit my old reviews)
Mark of the Ninja was released in mid 2012 originally for the Xbox Live Arcade and eventually released on Steam. It is a 2D side scrolling Stealth game which delivers gameplay which heavily emphasizes stealth combat (either Lethal or Non-Lethal). It has then received several critical acclaim from both players and critics alike.
The player takes on the role of "The Marked One", an unnamed Ninja from the Hisomu Clan during the modern (relatively futuristic) world. After a massive attack by a heavily armed and technologically superior mercenary group on your home Dojo, the Marked One awakens to find himself tagged by mysterious tattoos which grant him unrivaled skills and ability. Use this new found powers to drive away the invaders and uncover their plans.
+ Excellent art style with high resolution art works (essential for a 2D game)
+ Fluid and very responsive character animation
+ Excellent Stealth mechanic that places some Triple A titles to shame
+ Quality sound design (which is very important in a stealth game)
+ Good character progression that accomodate different playstyles
+ Fun (and fair) puzzle mechanics
+ Very responsive controls specially with controllers but...(See CON #1)
+ High replay value
+ Relatively large levels with hidden collectibles but most importantly...(see below)
+ Mission objectives can be approached and completed in multiple ways
- Keyboard controls are a bit complex and and may need getting used to
- Some puzzles are repetitive and frustrating
- Black and White ending (NO SPOILERS): - This game suffers from the Mass Effect 3 Syndrome where the player chooses between ending A or ending B regardless of how you played thus leading to...(See below)
- Not much incentive to go with the Non-Lethal path (which, to be honest, is a lot more challanging and fun)
- No non-lethal option for Bosses
GREAT GAME. Mark of the Ninja delivers one of the best Stealth experiences since Thief: The Dark Project. The fluid Animation, sound quality and excellent art work gives life to the world.
It's well worth its full price with its high re-playability and beautifully crafted level designs. It is HIGHLY RECOMMENDED for long time Stealth players and casual players alike.

LawBreakers is a modern take on the fast-paced arena shooter developed by the folks at BossKey Productions. The game cleverly uses areas of the map with low gravity zones mixed with a large variety of different roles to offer a breath of fresh air and something truly exciting to play in this era of remakes and reskins. I play games very competitively and when I saw the announcement trailer for LawBreakers I thought this was going to be the perfect game for me. A modern, fast, and fluid shooter where skill matters most. I put over 120 hours into LawBreakers through the Alpha and Beta tests before the game even launched and I planned on putting in many, many more. However, the playerbase of the game is currently little to none, so matchmaking and finding fair games are not an easy task for the game to handle. The folks at BossKey are some of the nicest and hardest working people I've ever had the pleasure of getting to know, and I'm hoping they find a way to revive the playerbase for this wonderful game, LawBreakers didn't deserve this.
Here's what I think BossKey should do.
I think they need to make LawBreakers free-to-play. This would most likely be a good way to rejuvenate the playerbase and get some people playing again. I am looking forward to seeing how BossKey handles the future of the game, and I'm hoping to play more of it in the future.

Best WW2 Submarine simulator game I ever saw.
There is a sequel, however it takes a look at the Pacific Ocean rather than the Atlantic, and the association created by making a game about German submarines in this area immediately sinks us into the movie "Das Boot".
For 2005, this game has the most depth out of all the other naval simulations that exist, and there aren't too many of them, which is quite a shame.
The game itself, is easy to learn but hard to master, especially when enabling the realism settings, such as dud torpedoes, no external camera view (meaning that you are limited to the periscope which, in terrible weather really gives you a feeling of what it's like to be in endless ocean) etc. etc.
It's a game better played with a cup of tea, prepared for hours of searching for enemy ships or convoys, planning an assault and getting away (or maybe returning). It's quite simple.
But the idea - of making ships go to the bottom (that's very well detailed as well) simply grabs my attention irreversibly.
If you're into ships, this game is one you should try.
Although it's nearly 10 years old, a marvelous mod called "The Grey Wolves" breathes some life into it, while a small but friendly community on
keeps this legendary game alive and sailing.
I'd say it's quite sad that we don't get these types of games more often.
Also, yes - this is probably better than Silent Hunter V at least without mods (not many of them (up to today - 23/07/2014)).

A decent buy for a buck, not much more.  Gnomoria has little promise and now that the dev has essentially shut down all accounts related, there is no promise for fixes.  It has a great base and some nice additions over other builder games, but that's where it ends.  The additions cause serious issues.  When you start the game, if you don't know any better, you'll crash repeatedly.  (That is, if you aren't a Mac user, who bought the game because it stated it was Mac compatible and found out it wasn't, at all, and never was.)  You will only find out - after a forum search on why it doesn't work for you - that you'll need to disable half the games mobs.  Once you can stomach that, you'll manage to get the game going.  But you'll learn to save often, especially before any market transaction as a combat engagement or a market trade crashes the game.  But if you can suffer endless annoyance through that (clearly, my hours in the game show I can), you'll finally reach 40 gnomes and start struggling with lag.  It took many "failed" empires and many lag crashes to teach me a lesson that I should have learned.  A game with bad mechanics can't be replayed a little differently here and a little differently there to hope to grow.
There is no fix for this.  So just as you start a rhythm, get the game going and feel confident mining, you'll get gobsmacked with massive lag that just cannot be fixed.  You'll go on searches for hours among the Steam and Reddit threads to see if any computer changes can help with lag, only to find out that the game itself was essentially coded to lag out and eventually crash at this point.
It gives you so much hope in the first few years and rips it away just as you have it going smooth and hope for an endgame empire.
No such luck.  So for a buck?  Maybe.  Otherwise, not so much when so many other games are similar and don't have constant crashing issues that we know will never be fixed.
(As a secondary note, I suggest checking the dates of reviews, especially those of curators which weighed the overall reviews heavily.  They were up to two years before the game was declared "released".  Many of those reviews are based on fixes that were promised but not implemented or features that were allegedly upcoming but never came.  Feel free to read these reviews to make these notes for yourself.)

This one's a tad difficult to review.
Gnomoria's a bit of a mixed bag. While it was released feature complete, it also has some leftover, possibly gamebreaking bugs. So no matter how stupid this whole !ABANDONED! !FINISHED! argument going on in the reviews might seem, both sides are right ... in a way. Lemme put it this way - the game's "done". But it's not technically dead, look up tacyn's mod in the workshop, it adds a crapton of stuff like new enemies, plants, trees, resources, craftable items and equipment, decorations and work stations. It's easy to install and also lets you pick from multiple options regarding all of the changes like trade overhaul, smelting and technological progress.
I'd probably be more annoyed by this whole situation if I didn't get it on a 3$ sale some years ago, while it was still in very early access. It looked promising and in the end - I don't feel cheated. Throughout the EA, Robo did iron out the bugs and solved the issues in a pretty swift manner, while also adding some features and options requested by the players. A lot of issues and negativity were created when he released a "roadmap", that wasn't really a roadmap. It was just a list of things that he would like to eventually add into the game, more like a memo or a wishlist of sorts rather than a set-in-stone development plan. It was pretty quickly removed and if I recall correctly, never properly explained, so in a convoluted way - misunderstandings are perfectly understandable. Also, Robo's departure from the project was handled very poorly, and while I can totally understand WHY he did it, he created a lot of hostility and if he ever comes back from the dead to make another game - it'll come back to bite him in the♥♥♥♥♥ big time.
But enough of that, let's talk about the game itself.
Gnomoria's a DF inspired sandbox strategy/city builder that has thrown away the epic size and depth in favor of accessibility and graphics (though to be fair, DF's not as deep as some people would claim). The scale's much smaller, the game's more focused and streamlined and the mouse controls are supported by the ability to use rebindable keyboard hotkeys, so it controls just fine.
Once you're thrown into the main menu, I recommend checking the audio settings first, where you get to choose between the 2 versions of the soundtrack - the oldschool 8-bit and a typical, "orchestral" version.
After that you should probably try and start a new game, where you'll get to create a game world first. You can choose the world seed, the general shape of the landscape, change the difficulty settings and select the mods you're going to use. You can also preview a small, central chunk of the area soon-to-be-generated. First of all - deselect the goblin tunnelers and the beetles, that single step solves 90% of the issues you'll have with the game. All the underground mobs have weird spawn rules, which wouldn't be a problem if not for the fact that beetles can multiply, so if you don't know how to handle them (and they're one of the stronger mobs) or are unaware of any nearby caverns, after a few in-game years you'll notice the fps drops and if you won't handle them there and then - eventually the game will feel more like a slideshow and eventually your save will become unplayable. Goblin tunnelers are less obvious, but equally unpleasant to deal with, since the tunnels they create can sometimes (not always) become corrupted and will lead to crashes or broken game tiles. So you deselect those suckers and *BAM!* your game experience is so much better now.
So now you've generated your map and finally you're there, on the first day of summer at 7:22 in the morning, looking at a small expedition waiting for your orders. You're given some basic tools and a few days worth of supplies, from here on you're on your own. Not much to say here, it's the meat of the game and it works perfectly fine ... well, almost. You might have some problems with the military gnomes, sometimes they act erratically, either ignoring the training sessions they're supposed to attend, getting stuck next to a wall and eventually dying of thirst or not equipping the gear assigned to them. What worked for me 100% of the time - select the training grounds, clear all the squads from the schedule, save the game, go back to the main menu and reload the save, assing the squads back and all will be fine. It's an annoying 1 minute of "work" every X-number of hours, but hey, at least it's fixable. Also, miners and woodcutters make poor soldiers, since they will attempt to use their tools as weapons roughly 50% of the time. This one's a bit harder to work around, but luckily, even when not as good as proper weapons, the tools still benefit from better metals used in crafting (only for combat, copper axe will cut trees at the same speed as the iron one would) and their damage types are good, so it's not as big of a problem as it could've been. People mention multiple different issues, but those already mentioned in the review are all I've ever encountered.
I didn't really talk a lot about the basic gameplay itself, but lemme put it this way - if you know DF, you already know what you're getting, and if you don't - think Minecraft with isometric view and lack of direct control, you give orders and stuff gets done.
You start small, with bare minimum of resources and couple of gnomes, already assigned to some basic professions. You gather resources from the map to create workshops. Workshops are your crafting centers, you'll need 'em to make tools and equipment, create more filling meals, access advanced resources etc., you can also easily automate the majority of the production as long as you can keep the unrefined resources flowing. The whole world is block based and other than the workshops - there are no prefabricates, you'll have to create stuff from the grounds up, one block at a time. You'll also have to dig down, to get to more valuable ores to forge better weapons and armors. In the meantime you'll be attacked by goblins and some other hostile creatures. Everything you craft and build will directly influence your Kingdom Worth, which will also impact the strength of enemy attacks and the amount of gnomads that'll join your kingdom each season. Speaking of which - there are 4, no tileset changes, but nothing grows during winter. Lack of tutorial doesn't help too much, but the game's quite straightforward anyway, just apply common sense and when in doubt - mouse over the "?" buttons present within every workshop and building menu.
Other than that, I've only crashed once, and that was back in the early access and was caused by a known and now fixed issue, so ... not bad, not bad at all.
Now if you excuse me, I've a kingdom to run. Toodle-oo!

Gnomoria is "inspired" (in quotes, because it's really a complete copy/clone) of Dwarf Fortress with graphics.  There's no notable features in Gnomoria that isn't present in Dwarf Fortress, so there's no new systems to see/explore.
However, Gnomoria is full of bugs/glitches.  Every 30 minutes or so, a gnome will glitch out, refuse to move or respond to commands, and die of starvation.  Every 1-2 hours, an area of the map will corrupt itself and have areas of black space (no tiles) appear in the middle on certain z-layers.  After 15 hours, my save game would no longer load and all my progress was lost.
In addition to these game-breaking bugs, lots of small bugs and incomplete/missing features.  The dev claims this the game is "finished" and moved on to other projects, but being "finished" was an early access being randomly pushed into release and then never updated -- even to fix game-breaking bugs.
Compared to other titles in the base building/sandbox space (Factorio, RimWorld), this game is not worth buying at any price.
What you see is what you get, the dev made the game playable, but only just. It's a descent Dwarf Fortress Clone but there are others  out there.
This had promise.  Abandoned by the devs.

I have nothing nice to say, but I have put near 8 hours into the game and spent money on it, so I am going to vent a little.
Always Sometimes Monsters isn't just a let down on my expectations, it's a let down of a game. It fails at the one thing a game should always prioritize on being: Fun. It fails as being fun. It fails at telling an immersive story. It fails at pacing. It fails from a control standpoint. However it doesn't fail on one aspect. It doesn't fail at being a chore. It's so anti-game that it hurts me. I hate being overy critical, but when I invest the time and the climax is a massive disappointment, I can't help but be this way.
Is it the fault of the developer? In my opinion, I don't always believe so. Sure, it's easy to blame them cause I mean they did create the game after all, but it was their vision at the end of the day, and they weren't wrong for producing it. However, it is their fault for having a premise, and making it a long grind of futility and boredom. It's so damn boring.
I can go into more details in a future edit if people REALLY want me to but every other review has done a good job of dealing with the details. I just wanted to vent over how disappointed I was.

Always Sometimes Monsters definitely the best Newgrounds-esque game I've played (insofar as it is RPG Maker, but with more effort than most games of that type).  And it's precisely the type of game that makes me wish there were more options than a thumbs up or thumbs down.
The game isn't bad.  Like I said, for the tech level the devs were working with, I'm actually very impressed.  But the dialogue and the writing is so damned pretentious and unrealistic that I found myself rolling my eyes at every second sentence.  It honestly felt like reading something a 16 year old would write after taking his first course in philosophy.  And for a game that puts so much on its story, that's bad.  It's really bad.
As for the game itself, why would I want to play a story where the character has a less interesting life than I do?  As soon as I found myself homeless and working odd jobs for money, I needed the story to keep me in the game.  And as I mentioned, the story is too full of itself to carry the experience for me.  I'm a fan of indie games, and I really wanted to like this one, but I couldn't bring myself to give it a really fair chance.
I can't recommend the game, but if it's the type of story you're into, and you can stomach the writing, there's something there.

Need For Speed Undercover. Intended to be a true successor to Most Wanted (The 2005 version...not Burnout Paradise 2), this game has received its fair share of hate and throughout all of these years, i never understood why to be perfectly honest. After the less then stellar Pro Street, i was extremely hyped for this game at the time and when i played it, initially i thought it was an absolute blast and lived up to Most Wanted in every way.
But again, that was in 2008. How does the game hold up to today's standards?
Well. Suprisingly well id say. Its not even close to how good i thought it was back in the day (Bare in mind, this was back when i loved racing games and i was a Total NFS fanboy) but its still a pretty exciting racer and the hate it received wasnt exactly what it deserved. It truly was the last TRUE Need For Speed, before the series would become Burnout (Hot Pursuit was basically Takedown, MW2012 is Paradise 2, as stated). That being said, lets get a few things out of the way. If your expecting a truly engaging story with memorable characters, unexpected plot twists and perfect pacing with pitch perfect acting...then just stop, like seriously. The story is completely disjointed and random. Stuff happens for no reason and characters come and go without any rhyme or reason. And the cutscenes...my god...the dialogue is without a doubt completely unbearable. Most Wanted and Carbon were cheesy, but in a way that gave it style. Here, it just feels forced...that or these people cant write or act at all. A particular character, Rose, is without a doubt the worst. Her dialogue is just the worst ive heard in awhile. Suffice to say, im sad that the story failed. The idea of being deep undercover of some kind of crime syndicate always intrigued me and EA couldve really did something here.
Anywho, enough of the story. The racing and cop chases are where this game strive off of and i feel that while its not at the heights of Most Wanted, its still good enough that you can see yourself having allot of fun with this game. The sense of speed is crazy, and the car handling is less torpedo like and allows you to casually cut corners like a pro, which goes really far into making you feel like a real bad♥♥♥♥♥ The courses are layered out with plenty of ways to overcome other racers and you always feel like you have a chance even if the race isnt going good. Then the police chases, which is one of my personal favorite mission types, are just pure intensity, particularly when your Wheelman level goes up and the odds against you get higher and higher. Also, i love the small touch of being able to press a single button to hop into another race on the spot. It allows you to simply hop into a match without surfing into map screens and i for one love the small touch. The game is extremely easy to run too. Throwing it on max settings shouldnt be too difficult and 60FPS isnt going to be far from reach either.
This might be a preference thing, but the keyboard controls are Meh at best. You can totally work with it, as i found it atleast playable...but if you have a 360 Remote laying about, or any other form of Gamepad, id highly reccomend using it. The game feels much more slick this way and it really pays off.
Now for the things i didnt like. The AI is inconsistent to say the least. In races, expect to always see the opponents lag MILES behind you. Even towards the end of the game, this happens pretty often. Im under the assumption that you could EASILY beat this game with the starter vehicle, which is kindda sad. Then theres the "Master Races" which is the perfect showcaser of why the series frequent use of Rubber Banding is a joke. You literally have to ensure you make NO mistakes...yet even when your doing perfect, someone will be glued to your♥♥♥♥♥like a Magnet and side swipe you when your close to victory. You can try to rear end them but they stay glued to the road as you plumet to the side of the road in shame. At these moments, i really wish we had the progression of Need For Speed Most Wanted, where the game got more and more difficult as you made your way down the blacklist. Hell, even Carbon with its Rubbery AI had a feeling of progession. As for the cop chases...they have issues too. Dont get me wrong, they are still fun, but the Police are just too forgiving. Cops often stand back, allowing you to easily out run them, and even in the higher intervals, they give you space to escape being boxed in. Also for whatever reason, they eventually call off all their units after awhile, abruptly ending a chase. The only thing that really gets you off guard is the Spike Strips, but thats only because you never even really see them.
In the end, the game is definetly flawed. But id say its worth it. Especially now that its cheap and easily attainable through Steam. The racing is fun, and the chases can be a blast. The awful story and Inconsistent difficulty drag it down but nowhere near to the levels of a bad game. Its a solid racer and if your looking for something to play, look no further. PERSONALLY though, if you still have a Playstation 2 or a Nintendo Wii (Or a Wii U even), id reccomend hunting down a copy of Need For Speed Undercover on one of those consoles. It may not be the prettiest versions, but the AI is much better and consistent, the cars feel and handle better, the cop chases are a challenge and it just overall just feels more like a Most Wanted sequel then this version does.

This game is an amusing romp through the world of DLC gone rogue, and it's quite enjoyable. It pokes fun at all the tropes you'd expect, and does it quite well. For a couple of quid, it's a decent game, and for that reason, I recommend it.
There is a but, though. It does its thing quite well,
, perhaps too well, as I'll explain in a second. The first campaign, plain old DLC Quest, is fine. You can finish it in 30-40 minutes without overly rushing, and it's enjoyable for that time. But let me tell you a tale of Live Freemium or Die. That turned into, for me, an hour long play session that remained funny, but stopped being fun. The primary issue is that the second campaign plays on the Fetch Quest trope a little too well, and starts to run the joke into the ground pretty quickly. It's making a point, and I get that, but I'm sure there must have been a way to make that point without making the game quite such a tedious pain in the backtracking butt.
The tl;dr of this review is that the game is generally fun and worth the entry price...
You should just know what you're in for on the second campaign.

2d stealth game with alot of freedom on how to play, go for nonlethal or kill enemies with any variety of tools, fun progression and hidden collectibles.
The game starts off a little confusing but the controls are very intuitive to pick up.  The game is broken down into sets of little puzzles, often involving you to kill/sneak by guards in order to open up access to the next area.  The environments are varied from a sewer level to a mansion, to a castle etc.
At the end of each level your total score is tallied and you get a certain amount of upgrade points which can be spent on perks, or new ways to solve puzzles.  The game has a huge amount of freedom on how any one play through can go and be solved.
The art style is unique and reminds me of samurai jack, while the animation is very fluid.  The environment is drawn in such a way that you can almost always tell what you can and what you can't interact with.
Overall the game is extremely enjoyable.  If more stealth games played like Mark of the Ninja I could call myself a fan of the genre.

The integrity has gone out of game development and companies are now treating us gamers as nothing more than cash cows. Well, hopefully we can hit back where it hurts.
To anyone viewing reviews and thinking of buying this game: don't. It's not even worth £9.99.

Not much to say except it's a lot like Overwatch but with different game modes and, obviously, low gravity, and it's amazing. Some of the characters are very similar, some mechanics are similar, weapons are similar, but because of the low gravity it changes EVERYTHING about how the game plays out. It changes how you get around the map, how you play the objective, how you fight others, how you play as a team, pretty much everything.
I've been in since the alpha and never once has this game failed to disappoint me in any patches or updates throughout the time spent working on it. None of the characters really are super overpowered nor is any weapon, like in other online games. In fact, every patch has just added good content to it, and I expect more good content to come in the future.
Every character is different. They all use a different main weapon, ranging from knives to a grenade launcher, to a minigun. I feel the "E/L-Shift/Q" abilities system was ripped straight from Overwatch, and often times you might forget about them, but they were still done well.
The graphics are nice, the gameplay is chaotic and interesting, the voice acting is surprisingly good, and no characters are especially overpowered (from my experience). I rate it a 9/10.
Plus it has Justin Roiland doing his Mr. Meeseeks-ish voice for the Blitzball so it automatically is a good game.
