The Good:
+The story is very engrossing.
+The fighting that batman does is awesome.  It is very simple in nature, but can be very fun as you pull off combination after combination.  I recommend a gamepad of some sort.  I used the XBOX ONE controller.
+The taunts the characters give when you die is hilarious. Seriously, this to me was the funniest part of the entire game.
+Excellent voice acting.  Mark Hamill's Joker is awesome.
+If you love Batman, you will love this game.
The Bad:
-Boss fights are unforgiving, even on normal difficulty.  I had to repeatedly retry a boss fight multiple times in order to beat it.  This was especially true for the end of the game.  However, it isn't a great game until it's at least a little difficult.
-Those riddler challenges are very annoying to track down, but are the only way to gain every tool Batman has.
-Detective mode makes things 1 shade of color.  If you play, don't sit in this mode all the time.  You will miss the beauty of those graphics.
-Zooming sucks with nvidia surround unless you fix the overall FOV to 150 and the zoomed in FOV to 45/60.  I found out the hard way when solving riddler puzzles that the detection zone was in the top right somewhere.  I had to apply the fix here:
for z key with an FOV of 45/60 depending on what I was trying to solve. 45 worked for zoom for most of the game, but I had to change it to 60 once to solve one puzzle.  I also had to constantly fix the overall FOV by binding it to spacebar (see link) constantly to avoid zoomed in faces in conversations with AI.
-The health bar for batman and boss enemies with nvidia surround appears on the left and right monitors respectively.  They should have been on the center monitor instead as it made it very difficult to gauge batman or an enemy's health.
Overall score: 9.0/10.0
Why aren't you playing this already?!

+ Voice-acting is spectacular; dialogue stays true to the lore, and lines are competently delivered (with the notable exception being Gordon's character)
+ Combat system is simple, fluid and enjoyable; attacks are well-rendered, feel as though they have weight to them, and offer the player an opportunity for great finesse
+ Detective mode is an excellent mechanic, and adds significantly to gameplay
+ Myriad unlockables and collectibles scattered throughout; character bios, therapy audio files, riddler trophies, etc. are all fun to collect and do well to showcase the lore of the franchise
+ Mechanics are refreshingly varied and intuitively introduced; the way that Batman's utilities work to influence the environment is applaudable in its implementation
+ Devs showed great care in the nuances of design; Batman's suit shows gradual accumulation of wear and damage, and his beard shows visible signs of growth as the story progresses
+ Platforming mechanics are near perfect, and the game does much to encourage their utilization; problems can often be tackled in many different ways depending on how the environment is utilized
+ Audio design is superb
+ Boss fights require a healthy balance of reflex and making on-the-spot decisions
+ Environmental detail is excellent; the devs clearly took great care in modelling the island, and the quality really comes through in the final product
+ Game's engine runs smoothly and efficiently
- Facial animations are atrocious
- Abysmal variation in enemy mob design; game relies heavily on a copy/paste approach
- Very poor variety in voiceovers for secondary characters and enemy mobs; it seems as though all support characters are voiced by 3 or 4 individuals
- Textures have not aged well, and contrast sharply with quality in lighting
- Standard enemy mobs have one, solitary KO animation; this animation is used uniformly throughout the entire game, and it is a decidedly ugly one at that

Are you a fan of games like call of duty and overwatch? Do you enjoy running around as an invisible dude with a sword that can 1 hit most people in the back? Do you like non regenerative health? Then this is the game for you! This game features 7 unique characters each with their own unlocks for playing and leveling them up. Some characters, such as the shadow (affectionately nicknamed "invisible sword ♥♥♥♥♥" get a cool sword that can 1 hit people from behind as well as your choice of guns from dual automatic pistols to SMG's! Also he's invisible while sprinting. Other characters, like the wraith can use snipers, that tend to 1-hit most characters on bodyshots. He's also invisible while standing still. I don't play the other characters much but they're alright I guess. The game has a pretty fast pace for most of the gamemodes (fast time to kill from what I've noticed) and the characters can move pretty fast at times.
The game features a crate system where after each game there's a chance for a crate to drop, but unlike most other games with a similar system the crates don't cost any money to open, which is a real nice change from other games (Looking at you, counterstrike). There are 10 maps and most of them are pretty small but there are a few decent sized maps. If you play a lot of first person shooters like call of duty, counterstrike, halo, you'll feel at home in this surprisingly good game. There is a bit of a skill gap where some of the older players can completely destroy some newer players but since I've played thousands of hours of first person shooter games it wasn't much of an issue.
PROS
-cheap (only 6 bucks)
-surprisingly good
-Reminds me a lot of call of duty: modern warfare 2
-Many unique playstyles generated from the characters
-perks system
CON
-No weapon costumization yet (not sure if it's being planned but it's not that big of an issue)
-Low player counts (You can still find a full server to join most of the time, but there's not really much of a choice if you don't like the people in the server you're playing or if you don't like the gamemode/map that's being played
-Some bugs (expected in an early access game), some maps have environmental sounds that are DEAFENINGLY LOUD AND NO SOUND OPTION WILL LOWER IT BESIDES GOING INTO WINDOWS SOUND MIXER.
-no offline/bot play (that I can find), which could be a problem if the game where to die sometime down the road.
I rate this game a solid 8/10 in its current state and would recommend you to buy it if you're a fan of multiplayer first person shooters

Game is obviously a work of love and passion. More than anything though, it is FUN. Finally, the arena shooter comes back in full strength and resides in its proper home, the PC. The "one more game" itch drives the game forward and makes each round interesting.
Three things initially drew me to this game:
1.) It was built and designed with keyboard and mouse first. I'll support any shooter that puts PC first. Why? Because they tend to be more accurate and have less hand holding. Shooters today always feel really dumbed down to include lots of people. I call it "console-itis". Much like movies dumb down obviously rated R movies so that they can get more kids to watch it, the same goes for PC developed shooters.
2.) I've been a big fan of Cliffy B's work since the first Jazz Jackrabbit and more specifically, Unreal. (That's right, he made amazing games on the PC before Xbox). I LOOOOOOVE Unreal and all its iterations. I grew up loving Unreal Tournament and I couldn't wait to get back in. Another game that I miss is the Tribes games. Fast, vertical combat with class based weapons.
3.) You can KICK. Nothing makes a game more fun than a kick function. Wish all games included one.
LawBreakers incorporates all of these things flawlessly. It's like a group of kids who grew up on 90's shooters got together and refreshed the genre.
Now People are going to inevitably make OW references due to Blizzard HEAVY marketing and saturation. The questions of "Which one is the Genji?" and all that BS will come up, but keep in mind this is a SKILL based shooter, not an ABILITY based one. The better shooter can over power the best of characters and players. If you lose, you only have yourself to blame, not the game. No ******* hand holding here.
There is plenty of teamwork involved, but you can definitely turn the tide with good skill. I'm excited to see where this game goes.

With the final chapter of Rocksteady's Batman: Arkham Trilogy out, Batman: Arkham Knight, I thought i should give my thoughts on the Arkham Games that I own on Steam. First Off, Batman: Arkham Asylum. Arkham Asylum is a very fun game with a very interesting story. This game follows Batman, who has just taken Joker to the infamous Arkham Asylum compound. The Joker takes control of the Asylum when he has killed the guards with him. Batman must face iconic Batman villains such as Harley Quinn, Bane, Scarecrow, Riddler, and more. The freeflow combat that everyone loves is in this game, but isnt as fleshed out as I wanted it to be. Many more things needed to be added to make the Arkham Experience the best it could be from the get-go. The predator rooms are very fun and challenging. And of course, The boss battles. Some of the boss battles are't that great like Joker and Bane, but some of them are some of the most creative boss battles out there like Killer Croc and Scarecrow. Overall, Batman: Arkham Asylum was a pleasant suprise in 2009 (a time when superhero games sucked). I very much recommend this game, Batman fan or not.

Great stealth game with an awesome art style. Challenging and clever game mechanics make this fun to play in lots of different ways, rewarding the player with different unlocks depending on their playstyle.

Imagine yourself hiding behind a potted plant or clinging to a ceiling grate, killing enemies with certain moves and making your decision to reveal the fate.
Many titles in popular culture have given ninja dazzling appearances. For its very characteristic, blending with stealth gameplay and a metroidvania style, Mark of the Ninja imprints the stock character quintessentially on the history of video games.
I was attracted by the game’s art style at first glance. Dignified atmosphere rendered with dark-toned colors. The brief brushwork of the protagonist’s design is just irresistible. When it comes to action, the depth of background is gorgeous thanks to the multi-layers well-crafted by the talented artists. Appropriate blur effect not only adds artistry but also improves tactics.
In the name of a dedicated assassin, the scoring system rewards player after successfully performed a silent kill, tossing bodies inside carts or even getting passed through by the guards undetected. Completing secondary objectives of each level matters equivalently. Resulting in getting “honor” to redeem new ninja tools and moves, which could significantly widen your options dealing with the puzzle.
Personally, I think the game set a benchmark of side-scrolling stealth game.
I played the game using keyboard+mouse, but the control sucks when sneaking around in a hidden-place, sometimes it just doesn't work. Since it’s a console ported game, a controller is highly recommended for the original experience of gameplay.

Like Puzzle Games? Like Puzzle Games That Actually Challenge You. THEN YOU NEED TO GET THIS GAME!
I'm an avid puzzle game player and stream puzzle games most days. I was recommended this game by one of my viewers and I'll be honest, looking at the images on the store page, the game didn't stand out to me because of the "2D Game Design", but I decided to go with my gut and give it a go. boy am I glad I did.
I've just finished streaming all the main game levels. the game mechanic seems very simplistic at first, but don't be fooled. I've played so many puzzle games which have a great concept, but it feels like developers have 'given up' mid way through and what you end up with is a game which is very broken, very easy, or ends up complete trial and error. Not the case with Recursed.
Each area introduces a new mechanic, and gives you a few simple (tutorial) levels before throwing you in at the deep end and combining with previous mechanics, which is where the real mental agility test comes in.  it has taken me 11 episodes, and 13 hours to complete the main game, and some episodes i only solved 2/3 in an hour sitting, so be prepared to not work things out straight away. just have a break, clear your mind, and come back to it.
All in all, i think recursed has been my game of the year, which last year went to The Witness. At time of writing, I'm having a small break, but still have the bonus content to play (which by the way is all included in the price, although i would happily pay a couple of quid for extra content) and I'm really hoping that Portponky has continued to bring new items and mechanics to the game.

Tl:dr – Ronin is a side-scrolling action-platformer, with turn based combat, that adds a fresh perspective to the stealth kill genre. Great atmosphere, music and combat system allow this game to shine where others have lacked. Currently in early beta access, it feels complete enough to warrant the purchase. With a skill tree allowing new abilities to be unlocked, retribution will be swift on the ones who have done you wrong. I definitely recommend giving this a shot if you are looking for a fresh challenge in this genre.
Full review below and link to article
IndieGamersUK -
Ronin a side-scrolling action-platformer developed by Tomasz Waclawek and published by Devolver Digital. I’ve played games published by Devolver before, all of which are extremely stylized and unique. Ronin does not disappoint, and I quickly fell into the world that this game was portraying.
The first few levels serve as a tutorial, getting you into the swing of the games play-style. You control your street ninja by jumping, wall climbing and slicing through levels. Complete the 3 optional objectives in each stage (avoid triggering the alarm, kill all enemies, spare civilians) and you’ll earn a skill point which you can then spend on various upgrades to how your character can attack. They call these Limit Breaks.
The most interesting aspect of Ronin is the combination of a turn based combat system with free-flowing movement. Each level consists of a combination of buildings with locked doors, windows and elevators. Each building has computer terminals to hack, and bad guys to kill; it’s your task to work your way through them. The moment you are spotted by the enemy the game switched to the turn-based system, allowing you to plan out your attack. Enemies’ bullets or movements will be reflected as a red line that shows the path they’re going to take to attack you. Once the turn has ended you make your next move by either jumping on them, for stunning purposes, or by cutting them down with your sword. Kill enough enemies and the skills you’re able to purchase come into play as your limit break goes up, allowing you to perform more elaborate sequences. Throw your sword, create a decoy, or even teleport to an enemy to gain the advantage. The odds are often against you, you but with careful planning, and the right combination of skills, every fight is winnable.
There is a story underpinning Ronin, although it’s a bit cryptic. You aren’t even sure what your name is, or the true meaning behind some of the bigger targets you will have to go up against.  It appears someone did you wrong and you’re on a crusade for retribution. The boss fights offer interesting scenarios, requiring even more careful planning to defeat them and their cronies. Enemies are fairly varied. There are agents with pistols, super agents with machine guns that fire for two rounds and a samurai who is just a PAIN in the♥♥♥♥♥to kill. There are also civilians that can be killed, but that should be avoided unless you plan on not earning your coveted skill point. If the civilians see or hear you, for example if you break a window near one, they’ll trigger the alarm. They’re almost as dangerous as the enemies shooting at you!
Each level felt familiar but there was enough variance to keep me interested for the 7 hours I played. There are only 2 music tracks, but both are great and really add to the atmosphere. I wasn’t able to finish it as the last mission is real crazy, but I was engaged throughout and really enjoyed my time. Once I finish the game I’ll update on the story more so be sure to check back for that.
Rating – 8/10

If you've got a fair bit of patience, and enjoy combat puzzles, there's a good chance you'll like this game. The turn-based combat works very well, and turns most fights into puzzles based on the positions of your enemies and yourself, and what jump arcs you choose to take. When you get it right, you'll feel like a badass. When you don't... hope you don't land in a position where every escape route is covered.
There is stealth, though there are many areas you'll have no choice but to fight through. Player reflexes are also a bit more important in some stealth situations, too, since you may need to very quickly try to get out of an enemy's field of view, or move around into position to take someone out before they call out an alarm. Some occasional annoyances there, but I'd recommend learning how to deal with suspicious enemies, because some fights are much easier if you can pick a few people off first, and the hanging assassination isn't always an option.
The difficulty on NG+ can be frustrating, but most levels have pretty good checkpointing. The occasional exception can cause some headaches, though.
All said, and even with the frustration I felt on a couple levels, I'd recommend this game. Also, there's a demo! It's good for giving you a basic feel for how the game plays, though the difficulty does ramp up well beyond what's available in the demo.

The game will constantly tell you that it is not a stealth game, however to complete New Game + and get all the skill points in the first playthrough, you WILL need stealth and a lot of it.
The tutorials are a little bare, I found out that you can extend and retract your grappling hook in the final mission, meaning it's obviously not needed but it was never explained.
Combat is very strategic and will often take a few goes to redo on the later stages, however that is a major draw of the game. If I were given one word to describe the combat, it would be satisfying.
As I have already mentioned, the stealth aspect is a very large part of the game, when getting an alert will remove the chance of you getting a skill point.
The graphics are ok, nothing amazing but they are very clear.
The only story is told in writing between boss kills. As such, I didn't really read the story.
Overall, I recommend this game if you played and liked Gunpoint. If you aren't sure, try the demo. I personally spend an hour and a half playing the demo, enjoying myself before I decided to take the plunge.

"Turn-based ninja" is a strange sort of description, but they managed to make it work.
It's a game about dodging between bullets, swinging from the ceiling, kicking goons in very nice suits out of tenth-story windows and dying because throwing your sword at a dude, while cool, isn't always the best choice.
There's the occasional bug, but save points are frequent and given how often you die- to surprises, miscalculations and simple stupidity -they're not much of an issue.
There's a fair few reviews mentioning things like stealth or things which weren't in the version I played; I'm inclined to think it's a misapprehension.
People hear "ninja" and think "stealthy murder" when it's really more like "Kill Bill". There IS stealthy murder, but it's an occasional thing, usually so that you'll be able to go loud later on without worrying about being machinegunned from four directions simultaneously.
It WAS hard, but I didn't especially notice it at the time; too busy having fun.

You like puzzles? Easy to mid-range difficulty? Some challenging puzzles?

Walk away. Come back. Still feel like you're looking at some Mandarin translated from Finnish using an abacus with missing beads? GOOD. You're doing it right!
Now lay down and zone out like the single-celled organism you actually are.

I'm not sure how I feel about this game.  Let me be clear: I wouldn't recommend this game to everyone.  I would recommend this game to people who are fans of Batman and comic book heroes and whatnot.  I'm not particularly one of those people, and to people like me, I don't know that I would recommend this game.
Bear with me, there's gonna be a lot of comparisons to Assassin's Creed.  Specifically, I've only played AC2 and AC4, so those are the ones I'm thinking of.
It's a weird combination of stealth and action.  It's more of a stealth game than Assassin's Creed (more solid mechanics for effective stealth), but it requires you to partake in it's action combat.  The action combat is more robust than what you find in Assassin's Creed, but much less robust than full-on action games like Devil May Cry/Bayonetta/Metal Gear Rising.  In a lot of ways, the combat feels overly simplistic--it feels like it plays itself as you press X at the right rhythm.  Batman literally just flies across rooms punching dudes several meters apart at the press of a button.  There's more to it than that, but that is the core of the combat, and I don't find it particularly fun or engaging.
So, that brings me back to the stealth.  Fairly early on in the game (about where the game reads 20% completed at the main menu, I would say) it introduces a mechanic where enemies that are knocked out automatically set off an alarm that lets every other enemy know they've been taken out.  I absolutely hate this.  Now, I've talked about this with someone who is a Batman fan and they liked that aspect of enemies knowing you're taking them out and putting fear in their hearts.  I am not a Batman fan and therefore do not give a single ♥♥♥♥ about this weird bat terror fantasy.  When I'm stealthing and I'm in scenarios where I need to take out all the enemies to proceed (as is often the case in this game), I want to be a ghost.  I want to take out everyone without anyone having any idea I'm coming for them, even as their friends all disappear.  I'm the type of person who played through Deus Ex: Human Revolution as a pacifist ghost (I might not have the achievements, at least not pacifist, because I accidentally killed someone by knocking down a wall and didn't realize it until 15-20 hours later).  So, to me, this type of stealth gameplay feels very one-dimensional and uninteresting--it lacks the options I would like to have in my approach when I'm playing a stealth game.
Aesthetically, this is the comic book Batman with a spandex looking outfit and a stupidly wide jaw.  He looks terrible.  Again, I'm not a Batman fan or a comic book hero fan.  Aesthetics, particularly those of the main character, are almost too important to me, as it makes the game a lot less likeable that the character I'm playing as looks like a moron.  If I'm going to play as Batman, at least give me some kind of option to be the much better looking armored Batman in the vein of the recent movies or SOMETHING.
Finally, this is a game where you're using Detective Vision a lot.  I hate that.  Detective Vision is so useful that it's hard to justify not using it.  Unfortunately, this means you're playing the whole game in very few colors, which is really irritating, because it looks a lot better when you're not being smothered by this seemingly necessary thing.
All that said, I think people who like Batman and the comics will probably like this game a lot more than I do, so I will recommend it.  If you don't care for Batman, you might like the game for its mechanics more than I do.  I just don't find it to have the depth that I would like to see from either of its core gameplay elements.
My personal rating: 3/5.  Not a bad game, but not a good enough game on its own to get past the need to be more interested in the subject matter to like it more.

: Rocksteady Studios
: Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment
==========
Batman. One of the world's most popular superheroes. The Dark Knight first made his appearance in 1939, in
. Since then he has appeared in countless other comics, several films, several animated series, and a nice handful of video games. Arkham Asylum is the first of the 4 currently available mainstream Batman video game titles. For a long time most gamers considered movie tie-in or superhero games to be....well, sub-par and not very impressive or satisfying. Just look at Superman 64. Wait....don't. Let's take a look at Batman and see how he fares.
==========
The Joker has hatched yet another plan; a plan to bring Batman to Arkham to have him face all the criminals he’s put away there. Yes, the inmates are running the asylum, and Batman aficionados are going to get a full dose of Jim Gordon, Oracle, The Riddler, Bane, Harley Quinn, Killer Croc, Scarecrow, Victor Zsasz, Poison Ivy, The Joker, and others. Themed similarly to the graphic novel of the same title, it is nonetheless a completely original adventure as Batman fights his way from one side of Arkham Island to the other rescuing Gordon and guards, doctors and nurses and others, while putting a stop to The Joker’s nefarious scheme.
Batman: Arkham Asylum does one thing extremely well: It puts you in the shoes of the Dark Knight. It makes you feel like you ARE Batman. You have all of the signature gadgets available to you (not all at the start, of course) and using them to solve puzzles and beat down baddies is a complete joy. The combat system that started in this game has since been emulated many times by other game franchises (Shadow of Mordor, as an example), but none of those are anywhere near as good as the Batman titles. I can only describe combat in this game with one single word: fluid. Batman’s motions are fluid, continuous, and definitely not a set of disconnected moves. He looks like a martial artist (as he should), not the sort of jerky puppet that so often happens in these games. The way Batman moves across the screen, punching and kicking foes in a storm of punishment is simply breathtaking. You have a lot of different combos and actions you can take, depending on your unlocked upgrades which are bought using EXP you earn for doing nearly everything. Enemies have a symbol that appears over their heads when they are abotu to attack, in reaction to this you can hit a button to instantly counter that attack and keep going. There are several types of enemies, each you have to approach and deal with using different tactics. Enemies carrying riot shield will shrug off your punches, while enemies with knives will slice you up if dealt with head-on.
As said before, Batman has all his gadgets available to him throughout the course of the game. His batclaw (grappling hook), Batarangs, smoke bombs/pellets, explosive gel, and even a decrypter. Most of these gadgets can interact with the environment, and you will be using them in this manner very frequently...which further adds to the feeling of you being in the Dark Knight's shoes. Most of the gadgets can also be used in combat to disorient or stun foes. My only complaint is that every encounter is a picnic. You can easily take down 10-12 foes in a small, confined space without any of them laying a finger on you.
==========
This game is simply stunning, graphics-wise. Even today it still stands up next to newer games being released. The amount of detail that went into just about everything you see on screen is amazingly sharp, very well-rendered, and crisp. Arkham isn’t just dreary, but classic gothic horror dreary. Batman glides with the ease of an athlete, with his the cape swaying with his paces. You can see characters breathing, which is always a nice touch in my opinion. As the game progresses, Batman's suit actually begins to look more and more beatup/tattered after so many battles. Every character, whether hero, villian, or supporting role, has a very defined look. The best one by far is the Joker, and why not? He is literally the star of this game.
==========
One of the best things about Arkham Asylum (and most of the subsequent titles) is that almost every character is voiced by their Batman: The Animated Series voice actors. This means that Mark Hamill (Luke Skywalker!) is reprising his role as the Joker, and my god does he nail it! I cannot picture anyone else ever voicing the part of the Joker as well as Mark Hamill does. Batman is voiced by Kevin Conroy, who has played this role/voice since 1993, in nearly every animated feature and video game with Batman in it thereafter. This includes the Justice League and Batman: The Animated Series. Their inclusion makes this game feel authentic, and lends to it a nice atmosphere.
The accompanying music to every scene in this game is very dark and fitting. You definitely feel like you are in Batman's world. It's the usual dramatic Batman fare, which sets the tone of each area and encounter.
==========
Initially, the game ran beautifully. Not a problem whatsoever. But the longer I played, the more I started noticing a short 0.5 - 1 second stutter that only occured every 20-30 minutes. It did not affect my enjoyment of the game, nor did it hinder me at any point, but it was noticeable. Aside from that small irk....there were no other issues with this game during my 31 logged hours. It ran at a near perfect 59-60 FPS at all times.
==========
Batman: Arkham Asylum is very nearly the perfect game. This game is as close to 100% as I’ve ever seen. It's damn close to a masterpiece. It's a game everyone should play at least once, especially if you are a fan of the Dark Knight. Your collection would just not be complete without it. Likely an entire generation will go by and never find a better gaming dollar spent.

The story surrounding Harvester and the concepts of Harvester are actually surprisingly interesting. It's a game that suffered a lot from being in a transitional period for computer hardware and software, and the manufactured controversy angle it went for completely fell flat on its face as Harvester missed its initial release date by two years.
Harvester does a lot of things other games get credit for but all the way back in 1996 (technically as early as '94 if you cut the developer some slack). While it's under developed puzzles and ludicrous content (the gay firehouse and ability to kill children strike me as two elements definitely unlikely to fly in modern times) make it hard to recommend for gameplay purposes, and the end 'boss rush'-sequence borders on unfair, this game does three things well: metafictional commentary, ludonarrative harmonium, and actually interesting content (the aforementioned boss rush has one fmv sequence that is genuinely disturbing and I really dug that).
This game taunts players and crafts a self aware and self reflexive narrative that is enjoyable for its timeliness. This preceeds many great games that experiment with the meta, such as Metal Gear Solid and Undertale for two easy examples. It's also a lovely time capsule in how to approach these elements and how public thinking on video games was truly absurd at one point.
It is also a game that possess very poor gameplay. It wasn't good when it came out and it isn't interesting in retrospect. That said, many of the gameplay choices are fascinating "in concept", but more importantly, and especially with the game's central twist in mind, many of the design choices make sense within the context of the game world. This doesn't make it fun to play as the combat is bad and the puzzles are lazy, but in more capable hands some of it's more noble failures could have been executed interestingly.
Lastly, this is a game that is full of schlock and absolute trashiness. My brother and I actually played through this whole ordeal together, and for large parts it fails to be horrifying and it fails to be shocking. Even at time of release, much of its most disturbing content was at best in poor taste and at worst completely uninteresting. That said, this gives is a b-movie kind of charm. Scratch that. It gives it a z-movie kind of charm. The terrible fmvs are enjoyable kitschy, but on the rare occasion this games content actually works in its intended fashion (off the top of my head, the peeping tom next door dad is a sequence that is gross but deservedly so, and the trials of the lodge have a few moments of actually dark content) by George it actually works. And you almost want to root for the game for that.
Basically, if you have a Sunday to kill, maybe a few beers, this is a game worth playing for that kind of "are you kidding me, this is so stupid" kind of entertainment. I'm solidly recommending it because let's plays exist and the game also goes on sale frequently. Plus, you can expedite many of its worst elements via cheat codes.

I'm a longtime fan of FMV point & click adventure games, so I'll always be very lenient when judging these games. But Harvester just doesn't cut it. To review an adventure game, we need to talk about the setting and the story a bit, so the following may contain small spoilers, but don't worry: real spoilers will be hidden like so
.
You play Steve, who wakes up in the town of Harvest with amnesia. He doesn't remember anything or anyone, but everyone seems to know him and everyone seems to know he has amnesia before he tells them ("they heard about it"). On top of that, everyone looks bizarre and everyone acts completely psycho. Everyone except Stephanie, who's supposed to be Steve's fiancee, but they both don't remember anything. You see, Stephanie has amnesia just like Steve. Steve will go explore the town to find out what's going on.
At first, it's fun to explore the town and talk to the people, who are all complete nutjobs. But soon, the behavior of the main characters becomes outright unbelievable and you won't care much what they have to say anymore, you will just keep playing because you're curious to know what is going on and what type of creatures these so-called townspeople are. To discover that, you need to gain access to 'the lodge'.
Gameplay is classic point and click. Find items, combine them in your inventory and use them on things or people. There are a few points in the game where I had to look up a walkthrough. When I read the solution I never had the feeling it was completely impossible to guess, but it would sometimes have taken me hours to come up with it myself.
Once you enter the lodge, the gameplay changes drastically. Fighting becomes a large part of the game. Now in my opinion, an adventure game shouldn't become a fighting game all of a sudden, especially when it has a combat system that's just awful. And the most infuriating part is
But you persist, because you're almost at the end of the game and you haven't even received the smallest bit of information about what the hell is going on. And then, the final cutscene explains the plot, and it's the biggest anticlimax in an adventure game ever.
Nah, I don't recommend Harvester. The first part is somewhat fun, but the second part isn't and the ending just makes you want to shout cursewords at your screen. If you're looking for a good FMV, I recommend Gabriel Knight 2. Phantasmagoria isn't bad either. I even enjoyed Phantasmagoria 2 more than I did Harvester, and people who played both these games will know that's a bold statement ;-)

One of the things I demand from any game is that is draws you in & immerses you in the experience it's trying to create.
Silent Hunter 3 does that massively.
The premiss is simple; take your U-Boat out, reach a pre-determined sector by what ever course you want, patrol it & try to sink any enemy ships you find. Simple, easy to remember.
That is, until you get dud torpedoes that cheat you out of that BIG score, a swarm of aircraft just won't leave you alone by swooping down time & again, your crew are all exhausted, an escorting destroyer is determined to depth-charge you back to the stone age, sweeping over you again & again while you desperately try to contain any damage & sneak away to safety...
The game allows you to fast-forward the cruising bit, you don't strictly have to return to base once you complete your objectives, you can program each torpedoe manually or let the game manage it, manage & train up your crew, upgrade you sub, go whatever route you want, sink what you want, Silent Hunter 3 really is what ever you want it to be.
If all you want is to drool over high resolution textures & realistic faces, go somewhere else, but if you want a fairly unique, utterly immersive & tense gameplay experience, Silent Hunter 3 really is a great game. Highly recommended.

Let me start off by saying, I really loved the game. I've been waiting for years for a game like this, as I grew up on Halo multiplayer, UT and Quake, and always wondered why there weren't more games like this - So to finally have this arena-shooter style of game with all the new bells and whistles of popular "modern" shooters was so refreshing. I find games like OverWatch boring and TOO team-dependant - I just like fragging, whereas OW insists heavy team work.
But now, I've realised why this type of game hasn't been done sooner.
Is it fun? Yes. Is it hard? Yes. Does it have longevity?.. I don't believe so.
This game requires no heavy team work. I pretty much jumped into a game, hit play on my Spotify playlist and went ham on the enemy team. Infact, I barely cared whether my team won or lossed, as long as I racked up some kills. The objective was inconsequential to me. There is no incentive to work together with your team, or win matches. There is no "strategy" element that requires heavy communication with your comrades. There is no competitive mode.
It's basically, "Oh my team lost. I got 25 kills though! Booyah!"
This game NEEDS a competitive mode, and soon. Or it will fizzle out. Maybe a competitve TDM mode where killing so many other players actually has an impact on the game, or is the difference between winning or losing. A competitive mode where your skill directly effects the outcome of the game. Because right now, it doesn't make a difference. It's too "casual".
I heard somewhere this game was aiming for eSports status - And it won't get there without a competitive mode, and will instead be dead in a month (Like Reflex, Toxxik, Quake Champions).
Can I recommend it? No. Not how it is now.

Deus Ex Mankind Devided is the most under appreciated game of the franchise for no good reason period.
Some people complain about micro transactions, while there is no real need to really spend money for them because you can easily collect all the stuff you can buy with microtransactions with a little afford if you're the explorer type who really likes to check into every corner of the game like I did.
Back to the game, yes, the backstory-conspiracy is kinda overused and at this point I really ignored it for the most because the flesh of this game is the world itself. The side-notes, quests and happenings within the world are interesting for most part and I really enjoy myselft moving through it. The world is so emersive that I easily can forget about the dated animation after just a while and just remember that for most of the time the Deus Ex franshise has never been a pinnacle in graphics. The first Deus Ex looked terrible even for the time it was released in but like its successors it managed to let the players dive into its world. I for myself can hereby confirm that if you are an older player of the franchise you will get into the game very fast because you'll see and feel alot of the charm that made the first game special. An improvement in almost every way over Human Revolution. The smaller scope means a much richer, more detailed story to be explored.
It doesn't feel as blockbuster as the previous game, it's much more... refined, both in story and experience. It didn't have to bear the burden of establishing the characters and world, as the first game, the novels and the comics which came before it served that purpose. So it had the freedom to explore its themes and the protagonist more deeply.
To some, this translates into "What the hell is going on I just want a start, middle, end and conclusion" which is fine, but not a formula this game seeks to answer to - it responds "none of that matters, and that's the point" which could be seen as pretentious but, given the body of work it's contributing to, fits perfectly - given that it's a game about questioning everything, it's apt that it prompts players to question the game itself as well. If Human Revolution was Blade Runner Theatrical, Mankind Divided is definitely Blade Runner Directors Cut.
Definitely worth playing at full price, and a must-have when it's on sale.

I'm not one for superhero games, in fact, I don't really care much for superheroes in general. I'm a hipster, I like Spawn! But that's beside the point. Batman Arkham Asylum is beat-em'-up kind of game that moreso tests your reaction timing and ability to adapt moreso than actually beating up the enemies compared to Bayonetta or Devil May Cry.
The music is a little on the bland side, its pretty generic.
PROS
- Arkham Asylum stands out as a game with a simple and easy combat system, terrific voice acting, a decent story, and level design (that more or less infuriates me in how confusing it is sometimes).
- Excellent character portrayal, Joker is meant to be crazy while Batman is a brooding intellectual type, and boy, did they nailed it. If you're a big fan of the Batman universe, then you're definitely in for a treat. I'm not, but I still enjoyed it.
- A small island with a giant♥♥♥♥♥and needlessly complicated facility  to explore, there's not much to explore, but its there. To, uh, you know, explore.
- The Arkham series is the best game to try and make you feel like the Batman, and it does a pretty good job at doing that.
CONS
- Puzzles! Puzzles! Depending if you love 'em or hate 'em, its pretty well done here. Except the Riddler, that's kind of more annoying and tedious than anything else. The Riddler's riddles are well done, but the trophy collecting...ugh, remove that and I'd slap this as a pro.
- Joker gets caught by Batman, Batman puts Joker in prison, Joker has a plan to break out, Batman screwed up, Joker is free,  Batman tries to stop Joker. This is your typical Batman vs Joker relationship that has been going for decades. Its nothing new, its just normal at this point and it'll never change. Mainly because Batman is against killing people.
- For the Batman, you aren't very equipped at the very start to tackle much of anything, its a little sad, considering Batman is supposed to always come prepared for any kind of situations. I'm aware its more for not overwhelming the player all at once, but when its necessary to have those gadget upgrades to go back and hunt Riddler trophies, backtracking becomes a chore to scavenger hunt for those.
A very good game that withstood the test of time, most games created during the seventrh generation looks very bad when you go back to it, but not this one! No sir, this game is definitely a good pickup, even if you're not a Batman fan like me.

Mark of the Ninja is a 2D, side-scrolling stealth platformer set on a beautiful comic book-esque backdrop with a stunning atmosphere and superb mechanics. It's is also one of the highest rated games on Steam with a 98% user recommendation rating. I picked this up in the sale but even at full price; it's worth every penny.
You play the part of a nameless ninja in an intriguing story of present day conflict between ancient ninja tradition and the prospect of modern day technology impacting and infiltrating the dojo. It's a simple, yet surprisingly engrossing story which is told through animated and cartoon rendered cutscenes. The presentation is absolutely slick throughout.
The game mechanics are well-implemented and easy to use although a controller is somewhat of a necessity as some manoeuvres are tricky to master along with the wealth of movement available. You can attack, hide, hang, scale walls, use lethal and non lethal weapons, an array of equipment and use the environments to your advantage. For a basic 2D game; the amount of ways to approach situations and complete tasks is quite incredible.
The main story of the game can be completed in about 10 hours but the replay value here is significant. On completion; you open up a harder version of the game which is extemely tempting. The game is also score-based and ranked online so you'll be eager to improve your overall points tally for each mission as well as unlocking everything the game has to offer including achievements. It truly is a sublime package.
Overall; Mark of the Ninja is one of the most successful games ever to hit Steam. It's a 2D platformer that simply delivers in all aspects. From the beautiful backdrop to the fantastic movement mechanics; it really does tick all the boxes that puts many major titles including many stealth ones to shame. A tremendous accomplishment.

There isn't a more 1980s first person shooter, I don't think. It's a nice throwback to the future (??) that is, the 1980s vision of the future. Take the dark future from Terminator, make it a little more generic and a lot more neon and add some zany stuff for flavor and you've got Blood Dragon, a TC for Farcry 3. Michael Biehn even voices the protagonist.
It's a short game but I thought it was better and more interesting than vanilla FC3. Funny how that works.

If you are old enough to remember the 80s, or at least have seen afew 80s era action/sci-fi movies, this game is a great tribute to and parady of that era.  As a game, it's a condensed version of FAR CRY 3 (smaller map, fewer collectables/objectives, linear skill progression, etc) with a 80s era futuristic coat of paint (think night-time with lots of neon).  Same shooter with stealth elements as FAR CRY 3 but with the added benefit of no fall damage and a super fast run/swim speed.  Also, lots of good humor in the story and comments made by the player-character throughout the game.
Some have complained that the game is too short and doesn't have much replay value.  In my view, this is actually a good thing.  I completed the game in 11.5 hours and enjoyed it the entire time.  Unlike the original FAR CRY 3, I never got sick of invading yet another enemy camp, hunting yet another animal, or scouring the map for collectables. I was ready for FAR CRY 3 to be over well before the actual end while Blood Dragon never overstayed it's welcome.  I got this on sale a long time ago for about $5-$8 if memory serves so I can't complain about 11.5 hours considering I spend more than that when I go to a 1.5 to 2 hour movie.
If you are looking for a good stealth/shooter with RPG elements set in an 80s version of 2007, you can't do any better than FAR CRY 3: Blood Dragon.
PS.  This game does require you to creat an account for and install Ubisoft's UPLAY in order to play.  UPLAY is stupid and annoying but other than initial game setup, didn't cause me too many issues

I’ve always been a sucker for ninjas. When I was a kid I was obsessed with the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: the cartoon, comics, and action figures. Soon that obsession expanded to all things ninja and samurai. So when I first heard about Klei Entertainment’s stealth platformer Mark of the Ninja, I knew I’d love it. I picked it up last year in a Humble Bundle, played it for one session and then moved on to something else. I enjoyed the game but for whatever reason I wasn’t ready to play it then.
Cut to 18 months later and I was finally prepared for my journey of the ninja. I’m only about 3 hours into the game, so this video is mainly a first impression. I’ll get this out of the way immediately: Mark of the Ninja is a beautiful game. The high contrast art style is striking, with amazing fluid animation throughout. The cut scenes are memorable and reminded me of classic Japanese-influenced animation like Samurai Jack.
Along with the superb visuals, Mark of the Ninja delivers generally tight gameplay. Occasionally the controls got away from me, but I think that’s more down to my impatience rather than anything else (more about that later). So far I’ve unlocked a few new ninja abilities (ninjabilities?) and you’ve got the freedom to approach the gameplay from a number of different angles.
The stealth mechanics in Mark of the Ninja are really well done. You get a visual representation of how much noise you’re making as well as how visible you are to the enemy. This works both ways as well, as you can see an enemy’s footsteps when you’re hiding out of sight. Some enemies can find you even if you’re hidden and as you get further in the game you’ll have to adapt to new environmental hazards.
After playing for a few hours, I’ve discovered I need to be in a certain frame of mind to play Mark of the Ninja. If I’m not relaxed enough I’ll soon grow impatient with the environmental puzzles and blow a stealth takedown or fall into a laser. I can only play for short periods, when I’m in the right state (with a balance of relaxation and alertness). Normally I like to dive right into a game and play for hours but I like that I need to experience Mark of the Ninja in small doses. Means I’ll be able to take my time and enjoy exploring the game.
I’m glad I’ve finally taken the opportunity to properly play Mark of the Ninja, a great example of focused gameplay and development. This is one oversight I’m happy to correct.

I’ve always been a sucker for ninjas. When I was a kid I was obsessed with the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles: the cartoon, comics, and action figures. Soon that obsession expanded to all things ninja and samurai. So when I first heard about Klei Entertainment’s stealth platformer Mark of the Ninja, I knew I’d love it. I picked it up last year in a Humble Bundle, played it for one session and then moved on to something else. I enjoyed the game but for whatever reason I wasn’t ready to play it then.
Cut to 18 months later and I was finally prepared for my journey of the ninja. I’m only about 3 hours into the game, so this video is mainly a first impression. I’ll get this out of the way immediately: Mark of the Ninja is a beautiful game. The high contrast art style is striking, with amazing fluid animation throughout. The cut scenes are memorable and reminded me of classic Japanese-influenced animation like Samurai Jack.
Along with the superb visuals, Mark of the Ninja delivers generally tight gameplay. Occasionally the controls got away from me, but I think that’s more down to my impatience rather than anything else (more about that later). So far I’ve unlocked a few new ninja abilities (ninjabilities?) and you’ve got the freedom to approach the gameplay from a number of different angles.
The stealth mechanics in Mark of the Ninja are really well done. You get a visual representation of how much noise you’re making as well as how visible you are to the enemy. This works both ways as well, as you can see an enemy’s footsteps when you’re hiding out of sight. Some enemies can find you even if you’re hidden and as you get further in the game you’ll have to adapt to new environmental hazards.
After playing for a few hours, I’ve discovered I need to be in a certain frame of mind to play Mark of the Ninja. If I’m not relaxed enough I’ll soon grow impatient with the environmental puzzles and blow a stealth takedown or fall into a laser. I can only play for short periods, when I’m in the right state (with a balance of relaxation and alertness). Normally I like to dive right into a game and play for hours but I like that I need to experience Mark of the Ninja in small doses. Means I’ll be able to take my time and enjoy exploring the game.
I’m glad I’ve finally taken the opportunity to properly play Mark of the Ninja, a great example of focused gameplay and development. This is one oversight I’m happy to correct.

On the negative side, I don't think there's much to say. Everything I'd nitpick about is concerned with minor interface/control issues, Given the speed with which some of those have been resolved already,  I'm sure that there won't be much to complain about in a few weeks.

Less of a stealth game, more of a flashy, bouncy massacre. And it's actually a plus for me.
Turn based combat is great, allowing the player to plan their jumps and other actions. Grab walls, use the grapling hook to swing, collide with enemies making them fall or just cut them right away. While simple in the beginning it offers quite a few strategies later on. The character can teleport, throw her sword, use decoys, throw shurikens to stun enemies etc. You decide what suits you the most by upgrading the skill tree.
I find the gameplay to be a decent mix of skill and luck, so if you lack one, you can compensate with the other. It's worth mentioning that the game is hard in a good way, not the frustrating way. Finishing a tough part can be really satisfying.
On the minus side, the story is pretty simple, but I didn't find it to be a huge disadvantage, bacause I like the gameplay anyway. As the game is in early access few things need some upgrading. For example there are some empty places in the skill tree, that are only used to unlock more advanced skills later. I think those empty spots should be filled with actual skills or different kinds of bonuses. I also experienced few crashes, but none of them were gamebraking and they usually happened after I died anyway.
Action oriented (for me)
Satisfying, turn based fights
Different skills, resulting in various fighting strategies
Challenging gameplay
The gameplay is a good mix of skill and luck
Simple story
Some non-gamebraking crashes
Skill tree requires some additional skills or bonuses
7.5/10 (recommended)

I'm not one for superhero games, in fact, I don't really care much for superheroes in general. I'm a hipster, I like Spawn! But that's beside the point. Batman Arkham Asylum is beat-em'-up kind of game that moreso tests your reaction timing and ability to adapt moreso than actually beating up the enemies compared to Bayonetta or Devil May Cry.
The music is a little on the bland side, its pretty generic.
PROS
- Arkham Asylum stands out as a game with a simple and easy combat system, terrific voice acting, a decent story, and level design (that more or less infuriates me in how confusing it is sometimes).
- Excellent character portrayal, Joker is meant to be crazy while Batman is a brooding intellectual type, and boy, did they nailed it. If you're a big fan of the Batman universe, then you're definitely in for a treat. I'm not, but I still enjoyed it.
- A small island with a giant♥♥♥♥♥and needlessly complicated facility  to explore, there's not much to explore, but its there. To, uh, you know, explore.
- The Arkham series is the best game to try and make you feel like the Batman, and it does a pretty good job at doing that.
CONS
- Puzzles! Puzzles! Depending if you love 'em or hate 'em, its pretty well done here. Except the Riddler, that's kind of more annoying and tedious than anything else. The Riddler's riddles are well done, but the trophy collecting...ugh, remove that and I'd slap this as a pro.
- Joker gets caught by Batman, Batman puts Joker in prison, Joker has a plan to break out, Batman screwed up, Joker is free,  Batman tries to stop Joker. This is your typical Batman vs Joker relationship that has been going for decades. Its nothing new, its just normal at this point and it'll never change. Mainly because Batman is against killing people.
- For the Batman, you aren't very equipped at the very start to tackle much of anything, its a little sad, considering Batman is supposed to always come prepared for any kind of situations. I'm aware its more for not overwhelming the player all at once, but when its necessary to have those gadget upgrades to go back and hunt Riddler trophies, backtracking becomes a chore to scavenger hunt for those.
A very good game that withstood the test of time, most games created during the seventrh generation looks very bad when you go back to it, but not this one! No sir, this game is definitely a good pickup, even if you're not a Batman fan like me.

A 2D stealth game with a good assortment of level design and lots of earnable goodies based on performance. Things like costumes completely influence how you would tackle a mission. One costume removes your items that harm people, and even takes away your weapon, but makes running completely silent (sprinting is usually fairly noisy), and you get extra items to draw guards' attentions elsewhere. There is a favorite costume for most any playstyle.
Another enjoyable thing is that the levels, while they don't get impossibly hard, they do get hard enough, and give you enough freedom, that you are able to make use of your entire arsenal in creative ways. An issue I had with Gunpoint was that I never had any moments where I established a situation where I had an awesome domino effect of events that was flashy and effective. Mark of the Ninja has you think on your feet in many situations, without the ability to sit and make a plan. However, you can take some damage, so not all is lost if you're spotted.
My favorite moment was using a costume that incites terror in enemies upon seeing a dead body. (As opposed to hunting down the player and becoming more alert. Terrified enemies will fire wildly and more importantly, not call in alarms) I killed a guard, then threw his body into a room of 3 other guards. Upon seeing the body, all three guards opened fire at it, the forward 2 guards being killed in the process. The lone guard, reacting to a new dead body, stumbled backwards, and off of a ledge, falling to his death.
These kinds of defining moments are what make the game reward tactical thinking, and exploiting every advantage of your costume to give you that sense of fulfillment. Feeling like you've used your character's abilities to their extent in certain situations, while it leaves you wanting more, doesn't give that icky feeling of "I never reached my potential."

I started playing the game without watching any walkthroughs, or anything.  I was never able to even get to the lodge.  How could this be?  I was stuck.  I had to go look for a walkthrough.  I realized the first problem.  I didn't pick up the pen and quarter from the drawer.  Of course, I should have been looking around my room, and opened the drawer.  Well, I did.  I clicked on the bookshelf, and I only got a description and I clicked on the closet next to my bed, and I only got a description.  I assumed that everything that can be examined would only be examined.  To prove my (incorrect) point even more, I tried to open the oven and cabinet in the kitchen.  None were able to be opened.
So, how could I differentiate between stuff that can be opened, and stuff that can't?  Well, there isn't any way.  I can’t even have my mouse over the drawer to know weather it can be opened.  I always get the “examine” cursor, so I would have to click on everything that has the examine cursor.
The same thing goes for items, but there aren’t that many items that are able to be picked up, so it’s not that bad.
It's not that the game is too hard, but if I have to click on every possible thing that can be opened (or look at a walkthrough), it just becomes tedious.
There could be a way to make it possible to know weather something can be opened after being examined, or if it would just be able to be examined.  A glow could be possible.
It does take a little bit of realism out if there is a way to know weather something opened or not.  It is needed to examine everything to know weather there is something important in it.  Then everything that can (in real life) be opened should show the contents, but since that would take too much time to program, and it would have nothing to do with the game itself, it would be good to only let things that are needed for the game to be able to open.  Since it takes a little bit of realism out, it would be a good idea to go a little bit further and have a way to know weather something can be opened or not just by looking.

I picked up this game in the hopes of playing a stimulating and accurate submarine hunter game.
When I first loaded this game up, to my dismay, it runs is a lower resolution, not at my 1080p resolution of my monitor.
The lower resolution of the game made me almost want to put it down, but I persisted, albeit with the somewhat weak visuals.
Within a few minutes I realized this game has a very steep learning curve, but one that I have found reasonable as time goes on.
This game is complex and appears to be realistic( I have never been in a submarine). Lots of control panels indicated your depth, c02 levels, pressure, different kinds of deck gun shells, torpedoes, etc.
The complexity of this title is appealing, as it leads to more in depth gameplay and I like that. It took me about 3 hours to figure out how to maneuver my uboat somewhat decently, fire off the deck guns, and launch torpedoes terribly off the mark.
Just the training has left me feeling a little eager to try myself in real(albeit simulated) combat.
I continue the training and work on my torpedoes. They bounce off, they miss, they are in limited supply. Its moderately frustrating.
The visuals continue to be unappealing, and I decide to drop the game. My opinion is that a game of this type requires better visuals, and therefore I dropped it. I am not sure if I will try again, but I doubt it.
For this reason, I do not recommend the game, even though I have, on many occasions, been able to look past visual elements without an issue.

Looks so adorable and polished that you'd think it'd be another Angry Birds type puzzle game that you can just turn off your brain and enjoy.
But in reality, it's a brain-punchingly hard puzzle game. Each puzzle introduces some new element, or new arrangement of elements, and you have to figure out the perfect technique to interact with it. You can easily spend half an hour just fiddling the birds around until you have a breakthrough and realize that you have to set one bird up
, so that it can catch a falling block without the bird becoming trapped or unsaveable. Luckily, after the first few levels you can start skipping over levels, so if you don't reach a breakthrough you can just come back to it later. And when you finally complete a particularly tricky one, it really feels like you've accomplished something!
Also, the snakebirds make very silly noises that literally had me giggling aloud while playing.

Snakebird is, despite its colourful appearance and charm, one of the hardest puzzle games on Steam, if not one of the hardest games.
I'm going to start this review by telling you to watch the first trailer provided for this game, as it explains the basic mechanics better than any text can do, and also highlights how incredibly complex such a simple game mechanic can be.
In terms of production quality, Snakebird is absolutely fantastic. The art is done
and perfectly reflects the outward simplicity but underlying complexity of the puzzles themselves. Every object in the environment is meticulously designed and work together perfectly to create a cohesive minimalist design.
The music is done by Carl Karjalainen, and isn't too eye-catching (ear-catching?) - but this is probably a good thing, as if you're planning on completing Snakebird you're going to hear all of the tracks a
of times.
But these are mostly besides the point - I don't know many people who buy a puzzle game for its soundtrack, so you're probably reading the reviews to find out what the puzzles are like. To be extremely blunt: if you don't enjoy feeling stupid, don't buy this game. It is INCREDIBLY difficult, to the point where even 10 levels in (out of slightly more than 50) it's already harder than the final levels of most other popular puzzle games. By the mid-game each step requires 50 steps of planning ahead to make sure you're not going to move yourself into a corner, and there's virtually no room for error with nearly every puzzle requiring nearly exact moves to complete it correctly.
It should be noted that this difficulty is
arbitrary or forced. The developers aren't making deliberately obtuse or tedious puzzles just to drag out the runtime, and every single puzzle makes complete sense once you work it out, using the relatively limited set of features in extremely clever ways.
Personally, I think that this game is fantastic, both in its production quality and in its fiendish difficulty, but it's definitely not for everybody. You have to absolutely love difficult puzzles to enjoy this game, and you'll get frustrated extremely quickly if you aren't used to that kind of challenge. If you are, though, there's basically no better option for training mental acuity.

7.5/10 Beautiful gaming experience dragged down by it's clunky UI, stopped short story-line, and poor optimization.
Story 7/10
The story for this game was a little lacking, as the ending (no spoilers) was very sudden, but wasn't even a cliff hanger just a flop over the finish line so to speak. Other than that though this game has great characters and tense scenes of persuation and uneasiness. There is a scene (again no spoilers) in which you are unsure if a certain character is really who they say they are and it is apparent in the dialouge. Very solid story with a great feel, a concrete world and lore to back it up, if not for a lack luster ending would have really stood out for me.
Atmosphere/Immersion 10/10
Wow, is this game immersive! The "open world" this game provides is very small, but EXREMELY DENSE. Every corner of this game has secrets and new characters to uncover, you truly feel like you are in a military controlled neighborhood. Don't go into this game expecting wide open spaces like other Open-world games, rather think of it as an Open-town game. This game gets the perfect score for atmosphere, because unlike many games today, it truly transports you to the world of Deus Ex.
Mechanics 8/10
This game has very similar mechanics to DE:HR but very much improved upon. This game adds a lot of new gadgets to have fun with and tons more combinations to use. The way this game approaches levels however is where it truly shines, you can truly go anywhere, if you think of a solution to your problem you CAN do it! The open ended nature of the way to approach any situation differently is a nice reminder of games like the original Deus Ex, System Shock, and the newer Dishonered. I must also add the new UI for this installment is very clunky and hard to grasp, but I didn't particularly mind too much.
Performance 5/10
Here is where the game gets bad... The optimization is very poor with this one. I played the game with a 960 which at the time of playing this game was a high-mid-range card and I often got 30-40 FPS on medium settings, very disappointing for a game that looks as great as this. Many settings in the game critically impacted your FPS way more than it should, I got a definate Arkham Knight PC vibe, but of course, not nearly as severe. I experienced 5 crashes throughout my playthrough of the game, all towards the end, which seemed to be cause by playing with Direct X12 enabled. Long story short, only buy this game if you have a mid-high range GPU, low-range GPUs I'm afraid will give you a very poor result.
Overall I feel this game is amazing and goes back to the franchises roots as an experience, rather than simply a game. However the performance really drags it down for me.

Recursed is a game about what Recursed is a game about.
Ahem, sorry, I'm thinking of INF (Ludum Dare 37 entry). Lemme try again.
Recursed is a puzzle-platformer. The goal of the game is to get to the goal (a giant floating purple crystal) by solving puzzles. As in a standard platformer, you can move around and jump (three blocks high, in fact). But if you're holding an item, you can only jump two blocks high (you can however throw items horizontally). Already this is a pretty novel mechanic I've not seen in any other game; there *might* be a game I've played where you merely can't jump when you're holding an item, but that's just not the same. Point is, Recursed does some neat stuff with this mechanic, as it's the focus of a fair few puzzles in the game.
But of course, that's not actually what Recursed is about. No, Recursed is a game about what Recursed is a game about.
Ahem, sorry, I'm thinking of INF (Ludum Dare 37 entry). Lemme try again.
There are three types of item you can pick up: keys, which open doors; blocks, which you can stand on; and chests, which are rooms which you can bring items into and pick them out of. The first two are standard puzzle fare, but it is the third that's where the game is.
"But," I hear you cry, "Isn't that just the same as rooms being linked to one another? I can't
see how that would give deep gameplay!"
And here lie two subtleties. The first one is that since chests are items, you can also pick up chests and bring them into other chests. This changes which rooms are connected.
But that still doesn't get at what Recursed is about. No, Recursed is a game about what Recursed is a game about.
Ahem, sorry, I'm thinking of INF (Ludum Dare 37 entry). Lemme try again.
The second subtlety is this: Entering a chest does not actually move you to another room; it instead creates an *instance* of a room, which is destroyed when you leave the room. So what's the difference? When you re-enter the room, it re-creates the *original* instance of the room. So, for example, you can take an item out of the room, then enter it again and find that the item's respawned. And it is *this* subtlety that creates the puzzles in the game.
Using this, you can, for instance, pull chest A out of chest B, then put chest B in chest A. Then pull another copy of chest A out of chest B, and put it back into chest B, into a third copy of chest A. Be careful, of course, because if you leave the first copy of chest A now, chest B will vanish into the aether, and cannot be gotten back (which probably means you've borked the puzzle).
This unique sort of action in a game could only ever be dreamt up by a madman. Truly, Recursed is a game about what Recursed is a game about. And yes, this time I
thinking of Recursed, not INF (Ludum Dare 37 entry).
Unfortunately, at some points, you have to think like a madman to solve the puzzles. That's not to say the puzzles are *unfair*; rather that they require such a weird modus of thinking that I've yet to wrap my head around the game. Contrast this with Stephen's Sausage Roll, the Best Puzzle Game Ever™, where the levels themselves usually tend to guide you towards what to do; the levels here are either doing so in a really arcane manner, or not at all. That's not always a bad thing, though, but it does mean that you'll have to experiment a lot more than most (and often don't really get as much feedback when you've done something right or wrong).
Complementing the game quite nicely is a rather catchy soundtrack (unfortunately not a fractal one, but either way it's been stuck in my head the past few days), and some nice humour ("This green stuff smells terrible! I hope it's not poisonous. *deep sniff*").
Despite its lack of level signposting, Recursed is a game about what Recursed is a game about. It is unique in terms of mechanics and brings a lot to the table in terms of that.
(SEE EDIT), I still recommend it highly, with the caveat that you'll need some patience to get through it.
Also, screw Rolling Shapes and Soko Match (formerly known as Flow Match). Those two games can chuck themselves into a chest which I'll happily remove from existence for them, because they're that bad and I've mentioned in my previous reviews that I would slag them off from time to time.
EDIT 17/09/2017: Having finished the game now, I can definitively say that it's somehow
than Stephen's Sausage Roll! If you are a fan of puzzle games, you DEFINITELY do not want to miss this. The main mechanic is just so rich and the secondary introduced mechanics complement it so damn nicely. And unlike SSR, chances are that this game is of complexity class Undecideable, not just in PSPACE!
Also it has a level editor, so there's that too. And the free in-game expansion is pretty sweet too. I hope another one's on the way for the game's anniversary.

I sunk at least 40 hours into the PS3 version back when it first came out, and re purchasing it on steam was interesting, the first time I played it I simply thought "well, this is s**t" and quit after 20 mins. However, having gone back to it in a more tolerant mood, I'm now in love with it all over again. The 2 most off putting aspects of the game are the car handling (only to begin with) and the graphics. But once you get used to both of these, its an enjoyable open world racer with a decent sized map, good car choice, better customization than most modern racing games, and really damn fun police chases.
When you first play it you may be very put off by the bizarre and immensely unrealistic handling of the 200sx that you start with, it basically feels like its got the worlds tightest suspension set up, and the worlds most grippy tyres. Therefore the car will understeer heavily round all corners before suddenly lurching violently out of control if pushed too hard. But a few tuning adjustments and suspension upgrades later this is greatly reduced, and once you get onto driving the skylines, evo's etc the handling model suddenly stops feeling ridiculous and starts feeling like a good old arcade racer.
The main downsides are....
-Short and poorly told story (But I like the premise none the less)
-Empty and fairly lifeless city
-Dated graphics
-Car handling takes a lot of getting used to
-Difficulty fluctuates (Starts way too easy, then gets pretty hard)
The good parts are.....
-Fairly large and well laid out free roam world
-Decent car selection
-Good customization
-Police chases are a blast
-Variety in race/activity types
-Cars sound nice and soundtrack is good
-AI actually make realistic mistakes which allow for varied and unpredictable races
So if you want a good old open world need for speed game for the purposes of picking out a nice tuner, pouring large amounts of time and money into making it a badass street racing machine, and then smoking some other racers or playing with the cops, then Undercover is perfect for you.
If you want modern graphics, realistic driving, atmospheric worlds and memorable plot/characters then this isnt the game for you.

First in the Batman Arkham series, this game amazed me. I was immediately hooked for these games. Why? Well, it's succedes on so many levels.
Firstly - the story (no spoilers). Story is one of the strongest components of Arkham Aslyum, it's well written and voice-acting is great (original Batman and Joker voiceactors - Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamill - actually voice the characters in the game) and the villains are very well characterised, with many iconic and somewhat less iconic from the comics appearing in the game. It is full of comic book and its own game lore.
Gameplay - Rocksteady developed a revolutionary, new type of combat for these games. It's very fluid and varied and is exactly the opposite of button mashing fiasco. It actually teaches you that you shouldn't button mash everything. 1v1 boss fights can't be more epic than they are already and all are actually challenging even on normal difficulty. Of course, you can change difficulty level if you're either a casual or hardcore gamer.
Graphics and performance - the game is developed on Unreal 3 engine and they really look good even now in 2015 (looking back, game was released in 2009!) when you compare it. It has additional options for PC that make your game look better than the consoles and also, ultra textures. Performance plays quite well, I myself had no performance problems whatsoever.
In conclusion, if you're a Batman fan, buy it. If you aren't, you will be.

This game makes me regret not getting into PC gaming until I was already in my 20s and Quake/UT were relatively dead. It's fun as heck. Yes, there's a little similarity to Overwatch, but think of it this way. Where Overwatch has its roots in TF2 and MOBA games, Lawbreakers has its roots in Quake/UT. It helps that it doesn't have Blizzard's design philosophies behind it, either. There aren't any hard counters (Titans blow up Assassins, but Assassins can still get in and wreck you, or just run away), ultimates are powerful but not automatic game-swingers, and it never feels like you're smashing your face against a wall at the end of the match. Winning isn't just a combination of well-timed button presses, but requires you to actually be good at shooting.
Also, the lobbies don't kick you out at the end of the match; you can stick around and continue playing with people, which leads to more fun times. I have been complemented on my play more times than I ever was in Overwatch. One time someone cried that "everyone is already playing OP heroes, can't wait for ranked", and everyone else laughed him out of the match. The community is great, and the number of new people who I see saying "wow this game is great" is awesome.
Speaking of ranked, currently the game feels like Halo 3's unranked mode, which was really fun but a bit disorganized and casual. There's no ranked mode, only one big quick match pot. I'd like to have some control over the gametypes I play, and it would be nice to join a bunch of other guaranteed tryhards. It's not stopping me from having fun, though.

Lego Star Wars: The Complete Saga is the six star wars movies told in lego form. Each episode is split into six chapters, so there are 36 levels of lego silliness to enjoy. Each level has different objectives like collecting enough money in each level to get "true jedi," collecting ten minikits to make a vehicle to use in other levels, and the red brick that gives you abilities to purchase (with ingame money, as it should be). On top of this there is free play, that lets you have fun in each level instead of playing the story, and even other levels outside of the original saga like challenge modes. There's a "super story" that tests how fast you can complete the six chapters in an episode in succession. So in terms of gameplay there is a lot to do.
Lego Star Wars is definitley a completionists game, with things to collect wverywhere you go. There's minikits, red bricks, characters, true jedi, and lots of money. Your progress is tracked with a hologram by the shop in the hub world of Mos Eisley cantina. Even this cantina has loads of things to do like make custom characters, view ones you've unlocked, go outside the cantina and look at vehicles, and a two player challenge mode (everything in the game can be done with a local co-op partner).
Given that this game was released in 2009 the graphics are dated compared to the Lego Star Wars: The Force Awakens game and others. There is also a lack of co-op over the internet.
I would definitley recommend this game to people of all ages, people who like star wars, and completionists of all levels.
