Arkham Asylum is a good, perhaps great, beat’em up game with a fairly engaging story full of Batman’s most iconic characters, the most memorable of which is your encounters with Scarecrow. It’s not a perfect game as I have a number of issues with the game design but many of those are nitpicky issues and don’t detract from something that is incredibly well made with astonishing production values.
I have to admit something secret. I never really completely loved the Batman Arkham games. At the time of this review I’ve only played Asylum and City. With the new Batman Release I decided to go back and replay Asylum (and will get to city too) if it was just as okay as I remembered it or if I’m just some kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ who can’t see the 10/10 masterpiece everyone else sees. And upon revisiting, it was better than I remembered it but also I still could see things that I found unsavory to my personal tastes.
I can’t lie, there are some things I think this game does extremely well. I can’t fault it for being one of the slickest and highly-polished games of its time. The game still looks and plays so well even today. One thing that really stood out is the texture work. It is better than some modern games. They also made good use of the unreal engine, loading times are short, almost unnoticeable sometimes, and UE’s infamous texture pop-in is nearly nonexistent. Some of the lighting effects make some areas just absolutely gorgeous, even though there were a couple of areas that looked kind of washed out. Overall, even though this game came out in 2010 it is still stunning in 2015.
A lot of the level design is also really good. The game has a habit of trapping you in a room with a bunch of dudes so it is linear but in this case I would say it leverages its linearity to its benefit. The map is modular, meaning that it is a bunch of battle arenas strewn together but each area acts out as its own small scale sandbox where you can use Batman’s various gadgets in different ways to take out the room’s patrolling foes. It almost plays like Deus Ex or even a Metal Gear game in some ways, but where those focus more on stealth Arkham Asylum takes a more character action game route with some light stealth.
And, that combat is the big draw here, well for most people. I have to make a confession. I’ve never really, well, been in love with the combat of these games. I think I finally figured out exactly what bothers me and that it is too arcadey. Don’t get me wrong, I think it is well made it’s just not the kind of fighting game I typically like. Games like Assassin’s Creed suffer from this too, though AC gets the added benefit of having really enjoyable freedom of movement mechanics. Early concepts of this game was that it was going to be a rhythm based game, not unlike DDR, which is strange to think about with the tone of the final product, but with how the combat plays it is incredibly obvious. You basically hammer the attack button until you get the visual cue to hit the counter button and when there are knife dudes you have to use the stun button before you can continue hammering the attack button. There is even an upgrade that allows you to get higher combo scores for timing your attacks better, like a rhythm game would. The combat, especially in the early game, doesn’t really require you to use your movement stick much at all during a combat sequence because the way Batman will auto target the nearest convenient enemy. It wasn’t uncommon for Batman to be hitting one guy to then do a flying side-kick all the way across the room even though that enemy wasn’t actually viewable on the screen at the time. I don’t know. I have to admit the combat looks really slick and cool. I mean the animations are astounding, but I can’t help feel a little detached from the situations. It’s a bit too, video gamey.
Speaking of video gamey, another stupid dumb gripe I have with this game is its character upgrade system. I don’t mind character upgrades but in certain games it just does not work and I would say this is a good example of how one just doesn’t work. First of all it does not really make sense in the canon of the game. Like on one hand, how does having beaten up a bunch of dudes translate into spending that experience on my suit gaining more armor somehow, but it also does not make sense with Batman’s character. Like, wouldn’t you think he would have brought at least some more of his gadgets with him? I guess the purpose of the game locking off certain gadgets is to give it an almost metroidvania appeal. But where those games withhold gadgets and weapons to allow clever backtracking to new areas that were previously inaccessible for tangible rewards like health powerups and hidden levels or even actual game progress, Arkham Asylum just does it to hide Riddler trophies for the most part, which is a bit underwhelming. I’d rather have had all those gadgets at the beginning because then the whole game would have been as fun as some of the later game fights were.
If I had one last thing to complain about I guess it would be the characters. Aside from the Scarecrow encounters and the Joker’s voice acting nothing really grabbed me. The characters are all pretty one dimensional and yeah I get it is based on the comics portrayal and it isn’t like those are considered Faust or something but I wish they could have had at least some stronger characterization and made Batman more than just a power fantasy rich guy getting a kick out of hurtin’ crims, but then I guess that’s just who Batman is really.
I have a few other minor complains, like how annoying it was to watch a little cutscene every time Batman took off a vent cover, but I think that’s enough negativity. I think the game is good, maybe even great. It’s got a lot of fun moments and while I thought the characters were kind of bog standard I thought the story was fun to watch. It’s a well-polished, cinematic weekend romp that is sure to entertain.

This game is pretty much a dream come true for me- I was a fan of other class shooters like Overwatch but it was too "rock-paper-scissors"-y for me, but this game is balanced in such a way that allows every class to go toe to toe with each other- which is Heaven for a healer main like me.  With that said I will focus on the negatives of this game- since you can find the many positives from other reviews.
I have four main criticisms...
1.  The Ranking/MMR System- This is actually really good overall, but there is one major flaw.  The way it works is that you are given a grade based on your personal performance at the end of the match (D-S+), which is good, but.....  Leavers are already a big problem in this game and you can be thrown into a match in progress if someone leaves.  So I was put into a game that was 0-2, there was only four people (including me) on my team, and the enemy team had the uplink and was at 95%.  I only had time to load in, pick Battle Medic and heal a couple people, and then the match was over.  The game then evaluated my performance as if I had been there the whole time, and was given a rank of D, which tanked my grading, putting my into B tier when I was A tier.
2.  Some of the ultimates are really underwhelming compared to others.  The Vanguard's Starfall and the Battle Medic's Defense Grid pale in comparison to ults like the Gunslinger's Equalizer or the Harrier's Convergence, and speaking of ultimates....
3.  Character stacking is way too strong.  3 or more Wraiths/Gunslingers/Assassins etc. can absolutely dominate a match.  One Gunslinger using Equalizer is scary enough, two or more using it is a guaranteed team wipe.  Multiple Wraiths can just instagib you with their knives like a horde of (pardon the pun) wasps, and so on and so forth.  There really needs to be a character limit, so you can have at max two of the same class.
4.  The Wraith is still a bit too strong in my opinion.  He is not OP, but in a game so focused on mobility, especially vertical, a guy with a slide, a melee that causes him to lunge forward, and a triple jump that resets instantly upon contact with the ground allows him to move like a rabbit on cocaine, allowing him to utterly dominate.  The characters best suited to deal with him (Titan/Juggernaut) are all very close range based, and the Wraith is effective at close to medium range, with his SMG being fairly accurate and his explosive knife doing lots of damage, so a good Wraith can just keep their distance and still do fine.  My problems with him are summed up by something someone else said, "The Wraith feels more like an Assassin than the Assassin".  Whether or not the devs decide to tone him down or not is in their hands, until then here are some tips to deal with a pesky Wraith...
If you are playing as Titan- Crisper is love, Crisper is life
Gunslinger- Warp backwards and use the Warp Combo (Warp and right click)
Assassin- Your melee is faster than his, so close that gap and use it, just dont miss
And finally- The kick is your best friend
Obviously all of this is subject to change, but as of August 8th, 2017, this game is an 8/10 for me.

So I do recommend this game, but I caution you all before you commit to $13-20 AUD price tag. As of 06/01/2015, the game is labelled as Early Access, but it is in fact complete. The devs want to bug test and get feedback before the June release (unless it's pushed back again).
It is a simple little game presented in a simple art style with a minimalistic approach to character progression. The soundtrack is wonderful if a bit understated. Completing missions is a combination of stealth, turn-based combat, and puzzle solving. There is a sense of being a powerful ninja that can dodge bullets and clean out an entire room of hostiles with a careful tactical approach.
However, the game mechanics are seriously flawed. Completing missions is more about memorizing certain patterns, and repetitively jumping around to avoid being shot or cut down by samurai. There is also an attrition factor in that the longer the fights going, the more likely you are to get killed. You might say that tactics comes into play here, but they don't. The player has little in the way of tactical capability; special abilities require a power gauge type device to fill before he/she can use an ability - it is filled by stunning and/or killing enemies - and if you find yourself in the endless jumping phase to avoid getting killed you will most likely never fill the bar. Additionally, you can't use the abilities unless you are in mid-air which presents additional problems because if you spend a turn to jump into the air, you run the risk of depleting the gauge rending the special ability useless.
The platforming aspect of the game is also perplexing. The jump indicator (represented as an arc) often indicates that you will land in a certain area, but then drops you onto a platform that is in the way, often times leaving you in the path of a stray bullet (one shot one kill in this game).
The level design is interesting to begin with, but overall boarders on the too easy or the absurdly difficult.
The game itself is not so much challenging as it is extremely frustrating, relying on handicapping the player to make it difficult, more than sophisticated game design that tests the players ability to think laterally.
The story is so-so. A simple revenge story with two endings depending on how the final mission goes for you.
So if it's so bad why do I recommend it? Because the game has a lot of potential to be a fantastic little distraction, but falls way short of the mark because of flawed game mechanics. The ideas might work on paper, but in practice they not so much.
If you want to kill 5-8 hours get it, but I'd say wait for a steam sale.

I'm going to start this by saying that I got the Humble Bundle as an early Christmas present and while trying to decide which one of its awesome games to play first, I set my hands on Always Sometimes Monsters just because it was an RPGMaker-made game (and I have a huge soft spot for their minimalistic supremacy). Also, this review is going to be an unusually long one for me because I haven't spazzed over a game of this category in so long, even if it looks pointless.
A crudely beautiful game, Always Sometimes Monsters is what they call "a life simulator", setting you up in one of the worst life scenarios possible: broke, jobless, homeless, loveless. Trying to fight back all the obstacles and win back the love of your life, you decide on your own destiny with every single option you make, which is the essential point of this game. All the elements of storyline, pixel graphics, and soundtrack construct step by step an immersive feeling into the plot, which is unfolded, again, with every step you take and every option you make.
The story starts off with an interesting allusion, which then brings you into the game experience itself. It's hard, it's stomach-churning, even far-fetched sometimes when striving over the edge to be real, but it never fails to serve its primary goal: life isn't meant to be easy. Gamers up for a good story will know this one isn't disappointing... until you reach the end of the game. With so many choices in-game it's nearly impossible to know you're doing what's right according to the game without a walkthrough (I am guilty of that, but solely because I wanted my love back), though this was an element that really hurt my feelings as I was suffering along with nearly everyone in the story, and even after replaying the game with different characters, I was still left quite confused and unsatisfied with the elements of the "eternal ending". The fact that the interpretations are left open for the player to make is a nice thought, but I still am not sure I enjoy this in games. Moreover, the small easter egg popular arcades are a nice touch, although most likely not replayable and serving their purpose for the image and only. (Swedish Pac-Man with meatballs anyone? Damn yes!)
Nevertheless, all the choices possible raise up this game's replayability for me, so I will definitely spend more time into it. I also have to congratulate the developers on their initiative to create a "character selection" box regardless of gender, race or sexual orientation, as well as on the implementation of the selection as a node into the allusion that starts it all. I also enjoy the fact that they actually put themselves in the game, since, in my opinion, their dialogues construct extra food for thought concerning the game. I know I'd love to do that if I was a game developer.
The average decent RPGMaker pixelly graphics are able to set up a real-like atmosphere in the city, combined with the morose darkness of the backstreets, but there's nothing else to say about them. As for the dialogues, they're captivating yet full of orthograph mistakes (and I really am someone who doesn't like being a grammar nazi) which should be fixed.
The soundtrack... What could I possibly say about the soundtrack?! Fresh, stylish, retro feeling while still modern enough, rinvigorating and immersive! Laser Destroyer Team outworked themselves on it and it's undoubtedly a fine piece of work. Every little piece or loop helps set the mood and captivate the player, it's really catchy. It's a nice thing the LP is available through Steam as a preview of their work, although it's really worth it to support them on their Bandcamp and get the EP and XP too (in all honesty, I'll always wish for a physical copy... Christmas wish found!). It's a complete and on the spot soundtrack.
Long story short, this game had a huge impact on me as I'm quite sure it has on many others. Intriguing storyline and graphics, smooth gameplay, disappointing ending, stunning soundtrack.
This game has made me question the severity a lot of things in life. There was one day I was at the supermarket and I saw a vagabond roaming around the aisles, so I stopped and thought just for a moment, what if that was me? It was actually another confidence boost to show myself that there is tougher stuff out there that can be overcome, and for that I couldn't be happier. I'll definitely replay this game more than once, because I really want to find all the secrets, and totally suggesting it to anyone who likes themselves a good story, so long as they can forgive the mistakes in its existence. This game has changed me and I'm grateful for that, and I'm really interested in clearing out anything hidden in the game. And who knows, "maybe I could translate the game for free"! Haha. Or probably make a comic about it. With a personally envisioned happy ending to satisfy those who didn't like the one in the game, haha.

Mark of the Ninja is foremost a stealth game. It's definitely got some platforming/action elements, and those are fun too, but its heart longs for the cover of darkness. The designers clearly understood what made people love stealth games like Thief, and they focused in on all the fun parts. If you're a fan of stealth games, you will very much enjoy this one because they did it right.
Those of you that haven't played stealth games (or at least, good ones) will probably enjoy this one nonetheless, if you liked Dishonored or Hotline Miami. I realize those are sort of disparate examples, but what they have in common, HLM in particular, is that while they look like action games at first glance, they're all really traversal puzzle games. It's about figuring out how to beat a room, which route to take around the guards, which strategy to employ in a particular place and time. That's the secret heart of stealth games - puzzles, but with tricky execution - and Mark of the Ninja captures that to a T. Every level has multiple routes and options, and between the progression and customization options and the achievements, there's a lot of replayability as well.
For such a cheap title, it's got stylish visuals and really responsive controls (a must for this sort of thing). Definitely one of my favorites in this genre.

Rather unsatisfying, simplistic little puzzler.
About 2 hours in and having completed (with an "A" grade) almost all of the 60 official levels in the game, I've yet to find a single one of them even remotely challenging (and therefore rewarding) to figure out. And yet, I still feel like those levels have taken far longer than they should have to complete, for two reasons;
First, because the pace of gameplay is so gratingly slow. The level starts, and within a few seconds it's pretty clear how to solve it - and you are left for several minutes just watching the ball crawl its way back and forth across the level before you can move on. Worse, maybe you overlooked something, and need to make a minor change to the sequence in which you collect the circles - so you must start again, and crawl your way along the same path again... This sense of boredom is only made worse by the extreme simplicity of the graphics, with the result that every level looks so similar as to barely be distinguishable.
The second, and probably more significant problem, is the control system. Having been designed entirely around touchscreen support, they are an overly simplistic "left-click-anywhere-does-everything" affair, with no alternate or rebinding options. It wouldn't seem like a big deal, as the game mechanics are so limited - and, as far as rotating and activating or deactivating bumpers, if you've got a smoothly functioning mouse there's no real problem. The second control mechanic of drawing lines, however, becomes unnecessarily clumsy with these controls. If, for example, you need to turn a bumper then immediately draw a line, or vice-versa, this imprecision can easily trip you up and force you to restart the level - taking us back to problem #1.
Overall - as a lover of puzzle games, I became so bored as to find playing the game a chore after less than 2 hours of gameplay - which in any case, was enough to grind through almost all of the levels. Unless it's 95% off, I'd recommend avoiding this one.

I know I'm very late posting this review, but I'm going to do it anyway.
TL;DR:
Pros:
- Smooth combat system (choice of beat-em-up or stealth)
- Be the Batman. Use his gadgets.
- Learn more Batman lore than you knew existed
- Engaging and new plot
- Dynamic Dialogue
- Appealing art style and graphics
Cons:
- Controls on Mac were a little hard to get used to, but you can change your keyboard bindings, and I believe you also have the option of playing with a gamepad.
Breezy's full review:
Batman: Arkham Asylum is hands down the best video game based on a comic that I've ever played and one of the best games overall in my collection. I remember playing the demo at my local GameStop and being sort of skeptical as it just seemed like another beat-em-up. Flash forward to about 5 years later and I'm so glad that I was wrong.
The story is refreshing and encapsulating. The dialogue is great (a lot of times humorous, a lot of times epic, only sometimes corny). Like everyone else says, the combat system is the most fluid I've seen in a video game, though I much prefer the "Predator" style of combat (taking out enemies stealthily) in the game. Being the Batman and getting to use all his gadgets (Batclaw, Detective Mode, explosive gel, batarang (in the form of the normal, multiple, explosive, and remote controlled)), and appearances by both the Batmobile and the Batwing were definitely a treat.
I honestly have to say that the Riddler trophies were my favorite part of the game. When the trophies were first introduced in the game I really had no intention of collecting all 240 of them. But the developers did something very clever and linked character backgrounds to most of the trophies. Some of the trophies take the form of interview tapes with Arkham inmates, Chronicles of Arkham (cryptic messages left by Amadeus Arkham to be found and deciphered), or simply scanning the environment as a visual answer to one of the Riddler's riddles. Of course, there are actual trophies you can find, but I much prefered the ones that would provide some background on the characters. Before this game, I had minimal knowledge of the Batman universe. When I discovered that the trophies could actually unlock character bios (and some nice viewable character trophies), I became obsessed with finding them. Through the character bios and other various forms of the trophies, I became educated on more of the Batman universe than I thought I would want to know. But don't get me wrong, every detail about a character or asset in the Batman world interested more than the last.
Actual gameplay wise, I probably beat it in about 12-13 hours. However, as you can see from my hours played, I spent a lot more time in the game than that. What was I doing? Collecting trophies, of course. Also, I spent several hours in the challenge maps where you rack up points by seeing how long of a combo you can get on enemies or you complete predator challenges, where you must knock out enemies in a specific way (i.e. break through a glass ceiling to take out an enemy). The GOTY Edition DLC  offers you the choice of playing as the Joker in these challenge maps, and it's pretty awesome and a nice change of pace from playing as Batman.
End note:
My only real prior knowledge of Batman came after Christopher Nolan's Dark Knight Trilogy and that was about the extent of it (besides watching a few episodes of the animated series growing up). The movies were great, expecially the Dark Knight, but they didn't really expand on the Batman universe, but instead focused on dark realism. This game, however, seemed to capture the wonder and atmosphere of the Batman comics and various animated series. I guess you could say that Batman has gained a Batfan. Thanks for reading.

Mark of the Ninja is probably the most fun I've ever had with stealth-based gameplay.
There are countless good things I could say about this game, but it's all been said before, so I'll focus on the thing I personally found most important: Player Choice.
Every situation has countless different equally viable ways of playing it and yet the game maintains a feeling of challenge.
Pass through the entire game killing no more than three people? Sure.
Be a deadly shadow that leaves an endless trail of corpses in it's wake, with noone ever seeing more of you than the horrifying fruits of your labour? Go ahead!
Go toe to toe with your enemy, perform impossible acrobatics, dodge bullets, and beat the enmy into submission through superior force? Why not?
There is a very small number of unfortunate choices on the part of the developer, which can easily be forgiven but on a canvas as pristine as this one, they are rather glaring.
- You have to do a silly, easy but obnoxious quicktime event every time you perform a stealth-kill, otherwise the kill will be loud and messy. This can be circumvented by wearing the Hunter's garb later in the game but it's just unnecessary and adds nothing to the gameplay.
- Later in the game the levels will be filled with enemies you cannot stealth-kill without some setup (usually using items, which are very limited when using the aforementioned Hunter's garb). Using items to kill them is simple enough and they are easily avoided so they do not really increase the challenge, rather they just seem to arbitrarily limit the effectiveness of one particular, otherwise extremely fun and fast-paced way of playing the game.
- There seems to be no mod support. That's the big one. This game is absolutely made to have a map editor. The amount of amazing gameplay you could squeeze out of this game through player-created maps is practically endless, so it's hard understand why this was ommitted.
Tl;dr
Amazing game with a few unfortunate downsides.

Are you wondering whether to buy this over Silent Hunter 4 or 5?
Although SH5 has had some substantial attention from the modding community, it still has a way to go, so I would hold off on that one.
SH4 features US Navy submarine warfare in the Pacific theatre. If that tickles your fancy it is equally as good as SH3.
SH3 features German U-boats in the Atlantic theatre in WWII. It has adjustable settings for difficulty, which the game deems "realism". These features include whether the game will just automatically lock on to a target and automatically set your torpedoes upon them, or whether you would like to do the calculations yourself. Let me tell you there is a significantly rewarding feeling when doing the calculations yourself, waiting for what seems like an eternity for the impact, not knowing whether the torpedo will hit... then you see it happen. You almost can't believe it. Such a great feeling.
This game isn't about instant gratification. There is a lot of planning involved and you will have to figure out how to best intersect with your targets' headings. It is really rewarding though, and I can't say that about a lot of games.

Let me just start by saying there's currently only 3 hours of game time on my account for this game, but I played it for about 10 hours in the open beta before it was on Steam. A lot has changed since beta, but the concept and execution are the same, and the game has vastly improved as well. The absurdity of this game is what makes it amazing.
My favorite things about this game:
- Finding new and creative ways to kill myself as baby. I never have to rely on the same way to die each match.
- Using Dad strategies to overcome whatever kind of baby I get put up against. All babies play differently.
- Countless hours of fun with friends. The only reason I don't have many hours on this game is because my friends have been too busy to play lately, but once their lives have settled down a bit, we'll be back at it again.
Now, here are some of the negatives:
- Baby favoritism in random matches. This is the big one, but it cannot be held against the developer. I strongly advise anyone NOT to buy this game unless you have friends you can play it with. Random online matches are only fun for a little while. You might get lucky and find someone who won't leave when it's their turn to be Dad, but most players will leave once their turn as baby ends and they have to be Dad during the next match. I've had it happen dozens of times, no matter what time of day, or what day I play. Most people just want to be the baby, which is why having friends who play is so much better. You can alternate characters and not have to worry about your partner leaving the game.
- Glitches. Every game has 'em, but this game has quite a few. Some baby deaths don't properly end the match, so you have to leave the game session and start a new one. Anyway, this is an extremely strange retro horror/adventure game with a KILLER( ba dum tsss) sense of humour. You walk around different areas looking like a character from Mortal Kombat and you can access the map at any time to travel to different parts of a small, weird town.
This is one of those old games where figuring out what you are supposed to do is next to impossible and a walkthrough(at least, for me anyway) is almost mandatory to beat the game.
You play as a young man of nonspecific age who wakes up not knowing what the hell is going on. All around town the people are really creepy and weird. There's a military guy who has no legs or groin who guards a nuclear missle base sitting in town, there's a house with some old wasp lady(who doesn't factor into the game's story at all. you don't even have to go to her house to complete the game), there's a butcher shop with blood everywhere and dead cats all over the place and there's a giant druid-looking building called "The Lodge".
You find out that you're supposed to try and become a member of The Lodge by the end of the week and to do so you have to complete tasks for the really cool guy who runs it. A guy, who talks with his mind in an awesome voice.
I don't think I would have been able to figure out what to do honestly but basically in completing the tasks you will talk to all kinds of people and the story is littered with creativity and incredibly dark campy humor. In this story you will see many cutscenes with the bad actors being hilarious in front of crappily animated early-3D backgrounds and it's a wonderful sight to behold. It seems as if the developers thought of everything as there are so many secrets to be found through dialogues and doing things in certain orders that triggers funny responses and, in some cases, exclusive death cutscenes. Any time you die it will trigger a cutscene of the main hero being brutally murdered in whatever manner you managed to die in the game.
I think that if you like the early Peter Jackson films like Bad Taste or Dead Alive(known as Brain Dead in some countries) then you should really consider giving Harvester a play and maybe even look at walkthrough to see what this game has to offer. Once you complete all of the tasks and get into the lodge finally you have to complete the "trials" of becoming a lodgemember and it's really cool to see what lies inside. It's a huge building with so much personality and creativity around every corner and once you get through it you have access to an awesome twist that explains what is going on and a choice between two solid endings.

It's a FPS where you get to hear the voice of Cpl. Hicks making fun of the entire genre, there are TRON-colored dinosaurs that shoot lasers... and everything's beyond Meta, in a delightfully self-referential kind of way.
It's basically what I wish FPS games would do more of- good, clean Fun, rather than "shoot hundreds of people in the midst of some Tom Clancy novel".
The mechanics are nicely thought-out, with a clear sense of progression and good solid shooter mechanics, including a lot of mobility options; the weapons are pretty well-designed and the gameplay is challenging in places, with a genuine sense of exploration and different options, including stealth runs.
That this game was basically just new content slapped onto Far Cry 3's engine belies what it delivered, which was genuinely entertaining through most of the plot and it had, if anything, a better sense for completion.  And it runs very nicely on modern rigs.
It's not perfect:  some of the gun balance is a bit off and some weapons don't progress well into later gameplay, there is very little real variety in enemy types, and once you're past the midgame, you've pretty much seen it, other than the crazy level designs.  There's a lot of exploration that took you to new places, but not new situations; arrive, kill everything that moves, get the upgrade, move on.  But, given how this game came about, it's largely forgivable; these are minor blemishes on an otherwise-enjoyable title.

After finally finishing the story mode and most of the DLCs (above all, Scarecrow Nightmare), I have enough experience and knowledge of the game to make a bold review.
The game, from start to end, tells you it's going to be about mysteries that need to be solved, places that need to be scouted, and enemies that need to be put down. And of course, there isn't only the Joker, you will have to battle a handful of other much more powerful (but not as intelligent) villains.
At first I read the description; "explore every inch of Arkham Island", and I thought to myself "I am limited only to Arkham? Well that can't be big enough, this game is going to be short!”, On the contrary, the island is extraordinarily well designed, and quite extensive. A speedrunner can finish the game within 2 hours, but anybody that has ever played an Elder Scrolls game will squeeze the gameplay hours off this game. With most of the DLCs and all the story, I invested over 10 hours in this game.
The combat system is simple, yet it never gets boring. The AI is beautiful, enemies actually feel smart, and combat can be tricky. But the best part is the Assassin’s Creed-like stealth part of the game; if you want to, you can take out enemies without even engage them in combat, one by one. The remaining enemies will react accordingly; they will get nervous, scared, terrified, and more aware of your current situation.
I can go on for pages explaining how well designed, well written and beautifully set this game is. But that experience can only be truly known by playing the game. It’s a no-brainer; you get it whenever it’s on sale. Don’t be fooled by the old styled menus and by how obviously this game has aged, it is still one of the best third-person, action/thriller games. And of course, as serious and concrete I want this review to be, we can’t oversee the obvious appeal this game has; it’s Batman.

This is a 10/10 puzzle game. Here's why:
- Simple, clever and fun mechanisms, introduced gradually
- You can tell a lot of thought and effort went into the design of each level
- Levels never feel too big or overwhelming, while being very challenging at times
- Levels never feel repetitive
- The game mechanisms are fully exploited, making you really learn its world and rules
- It has secrets
- Nice, challenging ending
- Nice, relaxing music
- Adequate graphics (2D with a mixture of 3D in some places, and some cute animations), though graphics are not the main goal of the game
- Comes with an extra set of levels that introduce a new concept
- You can create (and find) custom levels, which means that if you really liked it you can continue playing it even after you finish the main story
I had so much fun playing this game! I consider it at the level of other puzzle games like Braid, Snakebird, Portal, Antichamber, The Talos Principle and The Witness. I know these other games might have better graphics, but in this kind of games what I look for is a well thought, fun and challenging puzzle game (though I can tell graphics and music in Recursed have soul and love put in them). So if you liked any or all of the above games then this game might be for you.
The fact that there are no negative reviews of this game up to this point is also a very good sign.
Oh, and if you like recursion, you'll like it even more.

For some puzzle games, when you get stuck at a certain point, the strategy becomes "try everything with everything, and maybe something will work."
Recursed is NOT one of those puzzle games.
If you get stuck in this game, the strategy becomes "get yourself some pen and paper and use your brain." Sometimes the strategy becomes "play another level and come back to this little demon later." At least once so far for me the strategy has been literally "sleep on it."
Puzzle games that manage to avoid giving the player the option to brute force their way through difficult parts are few and far between, so when a rarity like Recursed comes along that simply doesn't allow you to turn your brain off when you're playing it, you've gotta treasure it.
You've also gotta hate it for giving you a massive headache but that's beside the point.
Well worth the price of admission.

A mind-boggling brain workout.  From the trailer I thought it would be simply messing with the chest rooms like a straightforward puzzle game, but the mechanics are far more complex.
The chest rooms are all temporary.  You can take items out and then when you go back in the state of the room will reset.  When you're going into a chest that's in another chest (layering instances) the rooms previous to the one you're in will keep their items.  You can move chests around, take them out of the rooms they're in, put them into new rooms to create different paths through the room layouts... duplicate chests... put chests inside of the rooms they lead to...  The game quickly makes it clear that the chest-room structure does not work at all in any real world sense.  The chests are not like doors.  The rooms are not quite "rooms" either.
Otherwise it follows the standard theme of puzzle games where additional mechanics are introduced gradually so you learn at a steady pace.  Eventually you'll have to learn to cause paradoxes!
A really fun puzzle game that hurts your brain a lot. Definitely worth it even at its current price.

Mark of the Ninja is a 2d stealth game by Klei, the same guys who made Shank and Shank 2. The same buttery fluid animations and art direction are present in Mark of the Ninja. Quite frankly, the game looks amazing in motion. Once you get the hang of the controls and the environments, you put whatever the current-gen protagonists of Assassin's Creed are called to shame. That's inadequate, you make the free-running elements in AC look like a geriatric with a crutches by comparison.
The story, so far (I've yet to beat it), is rather straight-forward stuff. You've gotten inked by your clan's tattooist Dosan, with ink which heightens your senses and gives you a convenient array of abilities that are mainstays in video games. But the downside is that the ink burns you out, and will ultimately drive you mad. So you've taken this Mark, in order to undertake a mission to safeguard your clan's existence.
And once you've completed your task, you're going to kill yourself.
Before that though, truckloads upon truckloads of henchmen are going to get theirs.
Alternatively, they will not even know you were there.
Klei made the Shank games. Shank games are 80-ish action homages as sidescrolling beat-em-up. MotN is the AC/Batman/Splinter Cell/Tenchu/Sneak-em-up treatment of a sidescroller. You have essentially complete freedom in how you choose to undertake your missions. And by how, I mean the level of lethality and bloodshed that will befall those who made the poor career choices that culminated in ending up on the wrong side of your blade. Or those ninja traps you will unlock or buy eventually. Or, you will just quietly slip by them. Hiding in doorways, behind potted plants, crawling past them on the ceiling, grappling from lamp-post to lamp-post above their heads, sneaking in the vents below or above them. The sneaking is really good. Like REALLY good, REALLY good.
Your equipment at first consists of firecrackers for distraction, a sword for stealth killing (kills are executed like a QTE, but not nearly as annoying. You press a direction and X to cut someone up), and that's all you got at first.
Later on you get a grappling hook, spike traps which work like land mines, smoke bombs and more fun stuff to play around with.
There are challenge rooms you might encounter (they look like gongs), which mix up the regular levels by being more of platforming challenges/puzzles. They use the normal game elements to complete, which manages to both freshen up how you think about the environments and traps/hazards in the game, as well as giving you a fresh lease on how to approach situations in subsequent levels.
I know a lot of game reviews fall prey to the pitfalls of hyperbole and similes, and I've already planted my foot firmly in that territory. And I kinda detest that. But honestly, it's impossible to do it when talking about MotN.
The stealth&stalk bits are great. The array of gadgets are groovy, as is the techniques you unlock with honor points as you complete levels. Some of them are different types of stealth kills, while another lessen the sound you make while sprinting, or allow you to string up dead guard from lamp posts in order to frighten other guards senseless. You can actually terrify guards to the point of them losing it completely, where they just start shooting wildly at everything they see or imagine they see. The only downside so far, is that sometimes it's a bit wonky whether you get the bonus for hiding bodies or not, and you might have to drop them a couple of times before it registers. Or possibly that's just left in there as a reference to Metal Gear Solid games. I'm not putting it past these devs, this is obviously a labour of love.
This is definitely a high-score type of operation, and I'm gonna come back to these levels.
You're scored on stealth kills.
You're scored on sneaking past guards closely while remaining undetected, and on distracting them.
You're scored on equipment kills, on terrifying guards (and the possible resulting friendly fire), and hiding bodies.
In each level, you can find 3 scrolls which tell the story of your clan and how it came to be, and what led up to you taking on the Mark in the first place. These also give you a point of honor each, which is used to purchase upgrades inbetween missions or at banner stops within levels.
There are also 3 seals per level. Seals are the same thing as optional objectives or challenges.
These seals fall into Path of Hunter, Combat, Nightmares or Shadow.
(Names subject to making-up by me, just now, seeing as it's late and I can't be arsed to start the game to be correct.)
Completing enough of these nets you new outfits with special pros and cons. For instance, the sneaky suit silences the sound of running feet, and allows you to carry 2 distraction items in your loadout. But the tradeoff is your sword.

In the following wake of Batman: Arkham Knight being pulled from Steam due to complications and statistics of poor performance and graphical fidelity, not to mention the ton of negative reviews pointing its fingers at a triple-A release, I decided to go back to the first game that started it all, and what an excellent adventure that this game was.
Let's go down the list:

Ichi is a "one-button" puzzle game in which the goal is to safely direct an automatically moving line to collect golden rings. By clicking the mouse, you can make red triangles rotate and blue triangles appear / disappear; by holding down the mouse, you can draw a grey line where the moving line is. The moving line can bounce off of these, which is necessary in order to change its direction of movement. There are also other obstacles like breakable blocks, warps, switches, and death spikes.
The base levels are a bit on the easy side, but I still enjoyed solving them. I particularly liked figuring out the correct places to draw grey lines — there's some light reflex challenge involved in drawing the lines while trying to ensure the triangles aren't pointing toward spikes at the same time. Additionally, a level editor and currently over 50,000 user-created levels are accessible through the game's main menu. A simple, chalky aesthetic and some nice tunes make this a relaxing puzzler to play overall.

I got stuck. I almost made a refund because of the incorrect claims in the negative reviews. Then I started quickly solving the puzzles that seemed "impossible"... and it turned out they are very easy once you understand what you're actually doing.
So I decided to help anyone who's on the fence and has read the negative reviews.
- It's not true that the game doesn't slowly introduce you to the basics
- It's not true that the game doesn't have different locations with different gameplay themes
- IT IS true, that the game gets difficult very, very quick
- IT IS true, that if you believe that you are smart, and in reality you're not, the game will crush you without mercy
- It is not true that the puzzles are complex, but random. No, they are very meaningful, but if you're not smart enough, you won't be able to understand the meaningful pattern behind the solution, even if someone shows it to you. Just like any other difficult logic game, you have to visualize what you want, your final goal, and what prevents you from getting there, but here you also have to rely on your spacial reasoning and that's differently developed in different people.
There's a risk that the game may not be for you. Have you finished "English Country Tune" or "Stephen's Sausage Roll"? What about the hardest secret levels in "Sokobond"? Was the last level of "Open Doors 2" relatively easy for you? What about any Alan Hazelden game, like "Boxes love boxing gloves"? You didn't need a walkthrough to get through "The Witness", did you? If the answer to any of these questions is "Yes", than go ahead. If not, try the demo. (There is a demo, even if it's not on Steam). And don't give up immediately. Give it time. Good luck.

Alright, so I won't harm this game by giving it a negative review, because did not deserve that. That being said, it's far away from being perfect, but here is a my little backstory:
So I got this game from my friend, played two games and decided to write a negative review and don't play it at all. After about a month a developer of the game actually added me to friends and asked me kindly what I didn't like about the game and if I could give the game the second chance, cause he felt it was a little bit rushed experience for me. Well, he was definitely right, so I decided to play this game once more. And hell yeah I had some fun - it felt a bit something like a CoD Class based game. It has nothing to do with the Overwatch though - classes change your HP and the loadout you can use. Also you can use two out of couple passives, that gives you more damage while you're being attacked or more HP overall. No skills, just that. It's much less dynamic, but it doesn't mean it's a bad thing. It's worth adressing, cause I heard that a lot that this game is Overwatch-like. Teamwork does not exist at all, that's why it reminds me more of a CoD. Yeah, most of the game modes you play with a team, but you don't need to cooperate at all to win and that's how it looks actually - I didn't care about my teammates at all, it was just me. Developers' studio is not big, so the game is not either. It got some fun game mods, really great maps and many weapons, but after you play a couple of matches it feels like it has nothing else to offer. Don't get me wrong, the game is really fun and it's in its early stage so they're definetely gonna add some great content, but that feeling got really strong for me. Also, there are some balance issues - mainly weapons. Some of the reviews mention the revolver, that takes a long time to get and deals so massive amount of damage that it's stupid to use other weapons. Overall, the game feels like it should be free to play (that's actually what I thought it would be) - the animations, graphics and not so much gameplay content. But 7 dolars/euros is not that big deal either and I think this game is worth it - it has great potential and devs are listening to community, they're definetely worth supporting. I know that the game is gonna get more expensive a bit, but they're planning to do discounts on it, so if you catch one - at least try the game, maybe it's gonna be your jam, because it's a good game - it's rather is it good for you or not.

When I first heard "Stealth game with turn-based combat", I was very skeptical about how that would work. But RONIN executes this idea very well. It's not turn-based in the sense that every character in the battle gets their own turn, but rather all actions play out in segments that are about a second long. Time stops in between these segments and you see red lazer sight-ish lines that show where all enemy shots/attacks will travel, and you aim your jumps to try and avoid them, while attempting to put yourself into positions that allow you to attack your enemies. It's a very interesting design idea that turns combat into a perilous touch-and-go puzzle that rewards you for planning ahead and baiting your enemies into leaving openings for you to exploit.
However, this system can be both engaging and infuriating at the same time. It requires an incredible amount strategy and precision EVERY turn, and punishes you for even the slightest mistake. Fortunately, check points are frequent and I never found myself getting frustrated at how much progress I had lost, just in the sheer amount of variables you have to constantly keep track of in order to keep the battle playing out in your favor. It definitely takes some getting used to.
One thing I've personally enjoyed is the amount of actual combat the game asks you to participate in, and how forgiving it is when you're spotted by an enemy. Most of the stealth games I've played have a system in place that disincentivizes engaging in hand-to-hand combat with enemies, which is fine. They are, by their nature, supposed to primarily be about stealth. But this often leaves me feeling like a coward who runs from a fair fight so he can try to ambush his opponents while their defenses are down, instead of the badass ninja you're supposed to be. But RONIN actively promotes hand-to-hand combat, and rewards you for killing all of the enemies in a level. This is obviously a personal opinion, but it is a different approach to creating challenge in a stealth game than what I've traditionally seen.
If you'd like to try a brutally difficult game that has a very unique take on the stealth genre, you can't go wrong with RONIN.

RONIN had the chance to be a good game, but it's so damn hard it's near impossible to enjoy. I might even go so far as to use the term 'broken'. There's lots of level texture variation but very little variation in gameplay - and it becomes a tedious slog to get through a single level. Let me go through a few bits and pieces in depth.
Stealth is
missing. You can either get through a room without being seen or you can't, and most of the time it's the latter, which is upsetting. You'll hope to see multiple entry points to a room like in Gunpoint, but as the 'hints' that appear ON EVERY TURN will tell you 50% of the time, "This isn't Gunpoint." There is usually only one way into a room, which requires you to run right into full view of all the enemies and limits your stealth to linear hallways.
A novel way of playing, with the turn-based platforming combat.
, if you could move outside of jumping during the combat. You can't. You are restricted to jumping, no movement or crouching or anything like that. You also crouch after certain jumps seemingly at random, so you'll never know if the jump you're making will take you under the line of fire or not. I would (un)happily agree with other reviewers that the second boss is simply learning the directions to jump in for half an hour or more of tedious trial and error. This does not make a fun game.
Sadly, it also suffers from clunkiness. Climbing is particularly bad. It tries to copy Mark of the Ninja and falls flat on its face.
Your combat is basically jumping at people and then severing their arteries with a large sword. However, everyone but you has ranged weapons, and it becomes a refreshing form of combat in a way. However, jump-kicking people also affects your jump arc, which means you will almost certainly die because you accidentally kicked someone and passed directly into the line of fire. Another unfunny hint screen: "The jump arc is a lie."

Probably one of the best games I've ever played. I enjoyed every bit of the game, truly, but here are the key parts.
The first thing that I instantly noticed was how well the introduction was created. The first scene was a little bit bewildering and confusing since I had no idea what was happening. The first scene took only like three minutes, and that's when the magic began. The way the character and the lover were chosen and introduced was clever. Whereas most games have the character creation not really tied to the story or it's just there at the beginning related to nothing *looks at the Elder Scrolls IV* the character creation really made you feel like a part of the story right off the bat. One of my favourite bits was that you can choose anyone to be your character and you can choose anyone to be the significant others, and whom you choose doesn't have a whole bunch of effects. Sure, there might be a few gay innuendos from the friendly neighbour or some racist butt faces being racist against you and your *black friend (his boss)*, but there isn't anyone saying it's wrong.
Because that's not what this game is about.
As the developers have stated, the game doesn't care. It doesn't care if you decide to sell the dog to be a police dog, a fight pit dog, or return it back to the owner. The charm about this game is that it's not up to the game to make you content with what you do. There isn't anybody patting you on the back for doing the right thing (something that doesn't exist in this game, as you'll see) or someone telling you that you're a screw up if you do the evil thing (also doesn't really exist), it's practically only you who will be the judge of you. If you feel like you did the wrong thing, then you did the wrong thing. The game doesn't care, and it most likely won't impact you. If you feel like you did the right thing, then you did the right thing. Again, the game doesn't care.
What really makes this game great is what I said before: it's special to you because you make it special. It's just you doing the things in the game, with very little forced upon you. You can take that screwdriver and pawn it off simply because you're short on cash. Whoever owned the screwdriver might be mad, but you don't see it, it doesn't effect you negatively. You benefit, he loses. Or you might decide to not accept the bribe. You lose some, others gain some. It's take or pull, but it's what you make of it. Have fun.

It wasn't a game where you can just get the best ending by just rushing to the end and picking the right dialog, it was focused on choices and life decisions that can cause your own story to end suddenly by taking the wrong turn in life.
There are some flaws that I felt made the game feel annoying at some points like the boxing minigame or earning enough income in a short time open up another dialog option later in the story but without knowing all this beforehand you'll be left with just one thing, your own personal choice. Anyway, this is an extremely strange retro horror/adventure game with a KILLER( ba dum tsss) sense of humour. You walk around different areas looking like a character from Mortal Kombat and you can access the map at any time to travel to different parts of a small, weird town.
This is one of those old games where figuring out what you are supposed to do is next to impossible and a walkthrough(at least, for me anyway) is almost mandatory to beat the game.
You play as a young man of nonspecific age who wakes up not knowing what the hell is going on. All around town the people are really creepy and weird. There's a military guy who has no legs or groin who guards a nuclear missle base sitting in town, there's a house with some old wasp lady(who doesn't factor into the game's story at all. you don't even have to go to her house to complete the game), there's a butcher shop with blood everywhere and dead cats all over the place and there's a giant druid-looking building called "The Lodge".
You find out that you're supposed to try and become a member of The Lodge by the end of the week and to do so you have to complete tasks for the really cool guy who runs it. A guy, who talks with his mind in an awesome voice.
I don't think I would have been able to figure out what to do honestly but basically in completing the tasks you will talk to all kinds of people and the story is littered with creativity and incredibly dark campy humor. In this story you will see many cutscenes with the bad actors being hilarious in front of crappily animated early-3D backgrounds and it's a wonderful sight to behold. It seems as if the developers thought of everything as there are so many secrets to be found through dialogues and doing things in certain orders that triggers funny responses and, in some cases, exclusive death cutscenes. Any time you die it will trigger a cutscene of the main hero being brutally murdered in whatever manner you managed to die in the game.
I think that if you like the early Peter Jackson films like Bad Taste or Dead Alive(known as Brain Dead in some countries) then you should really consider giving Harvester a play and maybe even look at walkthrough to see what this game has to offer. Once you complete all of the tasks and get into the lodge finally you have to complete the "trials" of becoming a lodgemember and it's really cool to see what lies inside. It's a huge building with so much personality and creativity around every corner and once you get through it you have access to an awesome twist that explains what is going on and a choice between two solid endings.
-------------------------------------------------

From the darkest heart of 1990's gaming comes one of the most unabashedly ♥♥♥♥-ed up games FMV technology could create.  The characters and situations are so terminally freaking weird that I honestly felt like I was high for the first hour of the story.  As the game continues it progresses from merely strange through to disturbing and finally ending on outright horror.  By the end, blood and gore are omnipresent, and it all becomes so over the top it's laughable while still being gross.
Unfortunately that wonderfully odd ambiance is broken due to two flaws in the game.  Some of the puzzles tend to be on the more obscure side, as in nearly impossible to figure out unless you have a walk-through guide.  Fortunately, steam provides one.  Also, you'll want to create numerous separate save files at various points throughout the game, since you *can* get locked into situations were you may have neglected to pick up an item which was critical to completing the game, but it's impossible to backtrack to retrieve it.  However, I only found this to happen in one area late in the game.
Final verdict:  if you can work around the technical flaws and enjoy weird atmosphere and offensive humor with campy acting, give this a try.

There are also little bits of polish such as your player character getting dizzy if you mash left and right.
However, one major gripe I have is that filling rooms with water is a major mechanic yet the water level is not indicated in any obvious way. You must simply figure it out by trial and error. Because the number of rooms in each puzzle is typically small (1 - 5 rooms) I never had issues remembering what the fill lines were once I started experimenting. But the design is otherwise very crisp, so this one oversight stands out a bit.
Gripes about the water aside, the mechanics are very unusual. I would give more details but the trailer already does a good job describing the general idea and I felt the specifics were more fun to figure out on my own.

(I have many hours played offline)
Turn 1
I have just taken control of France. Half of what is rightfully mine is held by the English. I begin preparing at once.
Turn 25
I probably overprepared, but I have many huge armies ready to attack the English.
Turn 30
It was a lightning operation. England lost its territory in France in a few turns, but now I had to choose: Make peace, or finish them. I choose the latter.
Turn 45
England had alot better castles and armies than I thought, but I outnumbered them 5-1. In the end, I won, taking control of the Southern British Isles.
Turn 85
I spent the following 40 turns buidling up my cities and castles, bringing the whole of the British Isles under my control, and waging a few succesion wars against Spain, who I finally took control of after a few dozen turns of war. Aragon fell under the control of Spain beforehand, so I basically owned northern Iberia. France seemed to be a dominant nation in Europe. I planned to have a unified empire stretching from Ireland to Vienna, Lisbon to Prussia. There was only one, very, very LARGE problem-The Holy Roman Empire.
Turn 125
Hoo boy, this war went crazily. I first invaded every province I could. I took the 2 layers of HRE provinces quickly, but then the HRE counterattacked in their Italian Provinces. They played a dangerous game, choosing to try to take Paris ASAP and cripple my economy (City where I recruited most of my units). If they failed, I destroyed their main offensive army and get a load of new provinces in Italy. If they won, I most likely would lose all of my territory quickly, as I didn't have a good enough economy to produce huge armies in every area, and I would probably lose the game. I was making an army in Spain, when the Moors attacked and forced me to fight on 3 fronts (Iberia, France, and Germany).
Turn 126
The time has come, the seige of Paris is over, the Battle for Paris is on. They have thousands of somewhat inexperienced foot soldiers, mostly spearmen, around a thousand archers, and a few catapults. I have Hundreds of Archers and Crossbowmen, with about 500 mounted knights, All veterans of wars of expansion. I have 4 Dukes in this group. I also have only about 5 units of Spearmen. The battle was tough.
I split off 100 knights and a Duke to take out their catapults. It works, but the troops are cut off. They tried to make it back, but we were encircled. I sent out all but my worst knights and my King. I surrounded my King's troops with a square made up of the spearmen, and hope the knights win. My Knights did great, tearing through the enemy's cavalry, suffering few losses by enemy spears, but heavy losses from their volleys of arrows. At last, the enemy killed my knights. However, they suffered extreme losses by the arrows that have been pelting them the whole battle. They still fought on, breaking down a wall, and charging in with everything they had left. Their final general led the charge, and was killed instantly from the spearmen defending. With that death, they retreated. They retreated all the way back to Vienna, with my armies close behind.
Turn 147
The battle of Vienna.
If you've read this far, you're probably invested in this game, so sorry to dissapoint with this part.
I had so many troops, that when my first assault failed, and my second, and my third, that they hadn't gotten the chance to retrain their troops. They finally lost enough men to be taken down. The final charge, led by my King, a veteran from the battle of Rome (Oh yeah, that was a thing, wasn't actually interesting, just a simple, take down the walls and charge in seige) was glorious. He charged with 500 extrememly veteran Knights. That was the end. The enemy's forces instantly broke, and were all captured. And that was the end to my glorious campaign. I could've kept playing, but no major empire had risen to challenge me. They all kept fighting each other. I probably would've put the Byzantines under my protection and conquered all around me, and I started too, but it felt like a chore, winning battle after battle just to fufill the need for an end to my quest. The gameplay mechanics are pretty fun and it's replayable by virtue of the different play styles on offer but, based on what I consider a Deus Ex game to be, it fails to meet its potential due to a severe lack of locations, a lack of diversity in objectives/pacing and also an underwhelming story.
My playtime was 39 hours but over 33 of these were in one place; Prague.  Then there's 2 hours or so in Golem city, which admittedly is beautifully designed with a huge attention to detail.  However, the rest of those 4 hours are made up of a miniscule 3 main missions outside of Prague and Golem City.  In fact, one of them is the tutorial level.
If you take a list of the main missions and places to see in the original DX and compare them to Mankind Divided, it's absolutely laughable.  There's very little sense of adventure or variety here.
The game designates missions by M for main and S for side.  M17 is the last main mission but don't let the number 17 fool you, MANY of those so-called main missions are simply things like, 'Go back to HQ and see Jim', or 'Go back to your apartment and speak to Alex'.
There are a lot of side missions, and they're good as side missions go, but they're a poor substitute and in the end you'll spend 30+ hours in Prague, dealing with petty criminals and a variety of odd balls and people down on their luck or you'll be acting like some kind of cat burglar while you collect items and XP.  Great if it were in ADDITION to a large variety of main missions but as the core meat of the game I was very disappointed.
Buy this game for the fun of the 'play it your way' gameplay but don't expect anything like the original version in terms of an epic story, variety of locations/objectives and the questline.  In the words of the great JC himself, 'What a shame'.

This has been (since beta) and will be my review for this game. This is my personal opinion on the different aspects of the game.
**Playerbase**
* The playerbase is something everyone is worried about. I personally don't think it's too low to get enjoyment out of this game. I've never had issues finding matches and for the most part the matches are as fair as can be. I've never felt like I was stomping or being stomped (although sometimes forget to play the objective, and even though the people you're playing with are mechanically good at the game, you still stomp or get stomped based on objective play.. I think that will change the longer the game is out.) So all in all, id say if it looks fun to you, and you are able to responsibly drop 30 bucks, don't let the player base hysteria scare you.
**Skins (Player and weapon)**
* Some of the player skins at the blue level are just as sick as the ones at the boss level. A lot of hours went into making them look this good.
* There are A LOT of skins. Being that they have to make a LAW and a BREAKER skin, that takes a lot of time. They all also look very nice.
* When you jump from one rarity to the next, it is never a boring recolor.
* The colors are iridescent (exotic+), try inspecting a weapon and moving it around, take notice of the colors as the light hits them from different angles.
**Maps**
* The maps are generally, well thought out and work well with most modes.
* Polish, these maps look very polished, there is a ton of detail both big and small.
* They *feel* good, when I finally got used to the maps, they all felt really well, they flowed nicely for the type of fast paced combat we have.
* Zero-G works really well with the map designs, it takes some slight getting used to, but it just feels right.
**Animations**
* Nothing looks really funky as far as movement goes, I haven't really encountered broken animations for anything, they all seem fluid and just work.
* Reload animations, can we talk about some of the cool reload animations? Enforcer? Gunslinger? They're all awesome.
**Sound Effects**
* Call outs, if you listen sometimes you can hear "Above you!" or "Below you!" type call outs and even though by the time you hear it and process it they can be a mile away, it is still a very nice touch.
* Banter, the characters will sometimes spout off banter after killing an enemy, generally this is linked to lore and is a pretty neat addition.
* For fun, titan rocket jumping has the best sound effects... "EUUAAHG, EUAAHG, EUUAHG"
**Account portraits**
* These are just awesome, especially the advanced(green) ones because they're animated.
**Dev Presence**
* Devs have been very active on a lot of platforms including but not limited to their official forums, the LawBreakers discord, this sub, and twitter.
* They tend to listen to the community and make changes in a way that takes the problem at hand and fixes it, but in a way that doesn't nerf the offender into oblivion.
* They're all super good people, hop in the discord and if one of them are on they'll sit and chat with you about whatever.
**Price point**
* At its core, it is 30 dollars. Not sure what the translates to in other regions, but that seems pretty cheap considering the caliber of game you're getting. If you pick this game up and spend only 30 hours in total on it, you've paid 1 dollar per hour of entertainment and I don't see that as being a bad investment. Plus for like 10 bucks more you can get some awesome skins, what's not to love?
**Misc**
* If your game crashes and you're in a group you can relaunch the game and you will still be in the group.
* You can allow anyone in your party to invite people to the group.
* Sandbox mode, great for people who want to try out new classes/maps.
* The combat feels very fluid, the netcode is very good in this game, it has been proven to be similar to that of current AAA titles. (YouTube "Battle(non)sense Lawbreakers" and watch the videos.)
* Ults are a great utility, but they game is not based around them like some other AAA titles. The game favors skill over ults/abilities.
* The twitch integration is a pretty cool feature, although I do not stream I can see it being pretty useful for those who want to, or do.
* Custom games, some games don't ship with it at all, others take time to implement it in such a way that it is already implemented in the BETA version of this game. A bunch of different nobs to turn and tweak, if you and some friends want to screw around it can be a nice change of pace to disable every class but titan and have air wars, or see which wraith is superior, etc... Plus spots for spectators if you wanted to organize some sort of tournament, or something of that sort.
* I am sure there are tons of things I have missed, but overall my personal opinion of the game is that it is a very well put together game that is fun, fast paced, and for me worth the money. I desperately wanted to love Legacy of Kain Defiance. But I played this game far too late.
Amy Henning's phenomenal writing bleeds through. The fantastic voice acting from luminaries like Michael Bell and the late Tony Jay are a delight. But the game's repetition, repeated levels, backtracking, and shallow combat just wear away at you.
In 2004, this game would have been a delight--and it most likely was. But age hasn't been kind to it. Its levels feel too simple. Enemies feel too cheap and numerous. Objectives can be unclear.
The story is still worth it, even if it ends on that damnable cliffhanger. Legacy of Kain: Defiance is a hard game to love, but  the meat is very much worth the time. You may want to wait until it's on sale, though. Those statue enemies are just way too numerous for how unfun they are to fight.

Watch the cinematics on youtube and give this one a pass.

One of, if not
 best stealth game in recent history. It provides all the information required without becoming blatant or easy, and removes the tedium of having to watch long pathing sequences or re-doing long sections due to silly mistakes. At the same time, it offers a myriad of different solutions to any given problem and never uses unfair design to create fake difficulty.
Similarly, its upgrade and customisation system, while not particularly deep, offers further variety and options to be explored and exploited. Add in NG+ and the extra options provided by the Special Editions and the replayability is surprisingly large.
The visuals are clear and simple without becoming simplistic or (overly) cartoony, with proper feedback and warnings on all actions and hazards. The audio similarly provides accurate and crucial feedback on what's going on outside your field of view (especially in NG+ where that field is restricted). At no point will the deaths feel cheap or the errors seem like anything other than your own fault for not doing the (in hindsight) really obviously right thing.

Legacy of Kain:Defiance continues the story of  crunchy Vampire Man and Captain No-Jaw.
Taking place right after Soul Reaver 2, in the distant future of 2003. Kain infiltrates the Serefan fortress, and by infiltrates I mean he kills everyone, in search for Moebius, the world's worst liar.
Meanwhile, Raziel is kept prisoner by that♥♥♥♥♥♥Elder God, who refuses to allow Raziel to enter the material realm unless he swears complete allegiance.
Raziel, who is the world's best liar, convinces the Elder God for a moment that he does submit and then escapes while also kind of looking like Spider-Man.
So starts the journey anew as Kain and Raziel go on separate paths through time to find Moebius and punch him in the nuts.
Defiance is the first time in the series that you can play as both Crunchy Man and No-Jaw. I guess they figured since Raziel got two games, and Kain got two games, now they have to share one like poor children on Christmas.
Both characters play the same, save for a few combos. The big difference being that Kain gives your neck a little nibble, while Raziel just flat out tears your soul from your body.
Hardcore.
Legacy of Bane: Airplane separates itself from the other games in the series quite a bit. While The others were more like adventure games with combat here and there, Defiance is more around the line of Devil May Cry. There is a bigger emphasis on combat, which isn't as bad as it was in Soul Reaver 2 because of the new combat system that's actually built around fighting more than one shmuck at a time.
Humans make up the majority of your enemies, much like both Blood Omen 2 and Soul Reaver 2, although other critters make their presence known throughout the game. It is kind of disappointing because
it samey to just fight and kill all the enemies.
Luckily, Kain and Raziel have enough moves to keep it entertaining. Not only do they have different combos outside of “hit hit hit give em the♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ but you can also pull off air combos, combo extenders, and dodges that are more than just jumping backwards once.
Even with all these changes, Defiance still has a big emphasis on story. Because of the time traveling nature of the game, you spend a lot of time revisiting areas you've seen from previous game. It does a lot to cement Nosgoth as a world that actually exists and where people actually life instead of just a big series of levels that just so happen to be in a place called “Nosgoth.”
The voice acting also, once again, takes it home. Michael Bell and Simon Templemann practically made the characters their own, giving the characters quips and mannerisms that wouldn't sound right coming from any other voice. Luckily, the game is split in half between Kain and Raziel so you get a good earful of both of them.
So whats wrong with it? There was stuff wrong with the other games, right?
Well yeah.
Still didn't get the controls right, although now it recognizes your controller as an actual controller, so you got that going for you. Also you should probably turn Vsync on if you don't want the game exploding on you.
There are also reoccurring puzzles that drag on way too long, but other than that, the game is pretty good.
I managed to get through the entire game no problem this time without having to change to a different port.
But if you're so inclined, Legacy of Kain: Defiance is also available on the Xbox and Playstation 2. No Gamecube version though, throwing you off after enticing you with Blood Omen 2 the year prior.
The Legacy of Kain series was a blast to play through after all these years, though they did kind of wear on me after about two weeks of going through each game. It was nice to travel through Nosgoth and revisit a story I basically forgotten over all these years.
It doesn't really matter what platform you play any of these games on, but it's probably easier if you play them through a console, for at least some of the games.

Loving the game so far but it definitely has its flaws at the moment. These flaws mostly lie in the grade/rank system and I hope will be sorted in the near future.
The gameplay is a blast with each class feeling unique,smooth and relatively balanced and all the game modes are fun to play when your team play the objectives.
The grade system in my opinion is pretty terrible, basically the more points you get the higher the grade you get. This is where the problem lies as short games in which you dominate will still yield little points. This gives you a bad grade despite doing well. Further more if you join an ongoing game late you can end up with the worst grade possble as you will earn little to no points at all. All in all skill does matter, however having a long drawn out evenish game where you do well is when you will get the best grades possible.
Leavers are also a problem at the moment and the grade system doesnt help this either. There is no punishment for leavers so you can freely leave if you know your grade is going to be low and cheat the grade system all together. This leads to losing teams quite often losing members for the rest of the game. This results in the leavers not getting graded and the losing team getting graded poorly.
Pros: Good smooth gameplay thats well balanced, pretty skillbased and also really really fun.
Cons: Bad grade/ranlk system that can be abused which can encourage leavers. The game also has no penalty for leaving games early.
Thats my two cents. Done this on my mobile so hopefully not too painful to read. Cheers.
