Ichi is a fun little puzzler that shines all in the right ways. No doubt, a pencil like written board and little touches of pencil eraser make you feel like you are playing on the notebook at break time between classes back in the school years. It is a game meant for all those players who loves a chill out at evening with a puzzle game. The game keeps you addicted and the feel of paper background makes the game just the best. It is a one button to click kind of game that requires quick finger and a good reaction. I find it to be an incredibly charming game with well designed puzzles. It is a simple enough at first, but gets more challenging as it progresses. The first few levels are simple and easy, but as you progresses the levels become tough and difficult. You control a ball that travels round the screen and it must bounce off against the walls and triangle objects that are placed all around the board. The triangles can be interacted easily with the tap of a screen. The ultimate goal is to collect all circular objects with the less taps as possible. To finish a level you need to manipulate objects on the board through tapping, like rotating triangles, toggling buttons, drawing temporarily walls and so on. How well you finished a level determined by a grading scale where A is obviously the best completion grade, like in school. If you don't like the inbuilt levels of the game or you have an idea for genius level, you can create and share the custom level. It is easy and simple to use the editor. Custom levels created in number of thousands make the game endlessly playable. I would recommend getting this game. It is great and deserves a chance for everyone.

And that's where I start! In a rundown, bum-filled city with a day to procure $500 to pay rent because apparently I'm that irresponsible and that's only the first 10 minutes of the game! Freaking Adventure Quest up in this ♥♥♥♥♥!
The little observations my character makes are a mixture of deadpan snark and actual emotion. When you pick a choice between being a complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ or actual decent human being or at times neutral, the dialogue corresponds with it. I find that in some RPGs your character is secretly aligned with a temperament already and if your choices go against that temperament that you have built up or is already in place, your choice is played out halfheartedly, which is lame. So what if I want to change my character's outlook half way through?! The puppy needs a home! I don't care if I robbed that game's safe of their start-up money two minutes prior, I'm a changed man/lady/sprite-thing!
This game is a slice of life, find-your-own-way, make-ends-meet, there-are-quite-a-few-ways-you-can-go-about-this, but-don't-♥♥♥♥-it-up-too-hard-ya? RPG that I settled into almost immediately. The problem with ME, not the game, is that I'm so indecisive. I'm that person who has at least three fingers on different pages when reading Choose Your Own Adventure books (one joke from Family Guy comes to mind "AAah! a dragon! Lois my finger was on the page! Do you see it Lois?! Do you see!") so making big 'this or that' decisions in this game was nail-biting and I glanced at one of Steam's "Perfect Ending" guides just to see if I was heading in a relatively good direction on my own (I was, hurray for me!).

SH3 is one of those games that you need to invest time in. It is a perfect example of a "Dad game," as Yahtzee Crowshaw once put it. It's meticulously detailed, and you must learn all of the different eccentricities of the sub to be a great captain.
It uses the real-life technological limitations from WWII to define the gameplay. Want to fire off a torpedo? A standard gas-powered torpedo leaves a trail of bubbles in the water, which ships can detect in advance and will swerve to avoid your torpedo. You can fire an electric torpedo, but you'll need to be close, or else the battery in the torpedo will die and it won't reach your target. SH3 is filled with these sorts of tactical nuances that really make it satisfying to play.
Difficulty is customizable. It can be as simple as "point the periscope at a target and shoot," to manually identifying and anaylizing your target's position relative to your own. Difficulty is increased by making the game more akin to real life (limited air, limited fuel, no periscope stablilization, etc.) This helps tremendously, since beginners can relax the difficulty while they familiarize themselves with the ships' systems.
The player is awarded more renown following a mission with high difficulty, compared to a mission with a lower difficulty setting. Renown is SH3's version of experience points. It allows you to 'purchase' upgrades for your sub like improved batteries, hydrophones, conning towers, or even a completely different sub altogether. Medals are awarded after each mission, which you can assign to your crew. This is probably the single most satisfying part of the game; the medals allow your crew to function more efficiently, thus improving things like torpedo reload times.
There's a lot to cover here, so let me just wrap this this up by saying that this is probably the best simulation game I've ever played. I find myself coming back to it every couple of weeks. It's aged quite horribly, but I don't care, since the gameplay is just too good. Forget the sequels in this series, SH3 is the best.

I must say, many people complain about it not being finished and all, but really, it is. Game is more than playable. It is true that the developer, after releasing the game in its final form, completelly disapeared from the forums and left his main website unsuported (also the game wiki, which was great but now is in shambles). This left everybody who was following the development of the game (such as myself) with a "i want more!" feeling, since it appeared that he was going to do more for the game.  That was indeed halved, and many promissing  future features never did take off. But it is not fair to say it is not a finished game. Not only it is, it is also pretty bug-free, and its funcionalities work just fine.
Also, it must be stated that with only a few mods (available via steam workshop) the game gets even better. I specially like the ones by "Tacyn", which expand the game's enjoyability manyfold. So saying it is dead is just plain wrong.
That being said, this game does cater for a specific kind of player. It's a very open build and survive game, with blocks and resources,  recipies and craftables etc. So if your aim is to have a storyline, an "end game" crisis, characters, etc., this is not for you. If your architect itch is ... well, itching, than this is for you, as you can build pretty much anything you can imagine. A 10 stories castle with wind-powered steel doors and moats? Do it. Have your gnomes upgrade from eating raw ingredients, to having variead meals? Done. With some mods you can even raise spiders and harvest their silk, and tailor hats with it! Wanna build a 'hall of heroes' with gold-statues, to raise your town worth and attract merchants that offer more specialized goods? You got it.
Done it all and got tired? Delete the game then. In a month or two, reinstall it and play it all over again. In that sense the game's replayability is huge.
I admit, it is hard. In several maps I can't get those gnomes to survive enogh time to get a basic industry going. Or before I had time to build the simplest of defenses, a goblin attack wiped everybody out. In that sense the game can be indeed arid. Like "banished", with worse graphics but ten-fold the possibilities. But that is not the same as saying, as many people did, that the game presents you with nothing to do, or that it is boring. That is simply untrue.

Once upon a time, there was a game called Dwarf Fortress. It was a magical game that spawned infinite stories for those willing to read its tea leaves of finely-detailed content, from the most epic slaughter by rampaging elephants down to the tiniest thoughts and details of its dwarven citizenry.
And the masses looked upon Dwarf Fortress and said, wow, these stories are fantastic but are you really going to make me learn hotkey controls to use this mess of a UI? And you can't see a hill except as a series of layers of dirt?
And so many, emboldened by the newly-released Steam Greenlight and Steam Early Access, took it upon themselves to remake Dwarf Fortress in their image. Some of these early attempts died on the vine, like Towns and Spacebase DF-9. Gnomoria is the most long-lived of these early re-imaginings, releasing to 1.0 status after three years of early access. Instead of dwarves, it's gnomes, and instead of ASCII and tiles, it's 3D isometric graphics, and instead of a hotkey-driven UI, it's a graphical mouse-driven UI.
And Gnomoria, in many ways, delivered on its promise of being "Dwarf Fortress, but properly 3D." Players create a colony, dig underground (but not too deep or too greedily), create an economy piece-by-piece, and defend themselves from unruly neighbors.
However, time has moved on, but Gnomoria hasn't. Gnomoria's feature list at its 1.0 release in 2016 is still nearly identical to Dwarf Fortress circa 2013, without nearly so much of the flavor that attracts so many to Dwarf Fortress. And more games have come along that evoke the magic of Dwarf Fortress without resorting to mimicry - Rimworld for small-colony storytelling, Factorio for intense production optimization. And even Dwarf Fortress itself continues to evolve and outpace Gnomoria, not only through the development of its core gameplay, but also the development of mods like Stonesense (isometric 3D, like Gnomoria) and Armok Vision (fully 3D visualization).
As a game releasing to early access in 2013, Gnomoria made sense. As a game up for purchase in 2017, Gnomoria no longer makes sense except for those interested in the history and design of Dwarf Fortress and the games surrounding it.

Arkham Asylum is a great game that really brings Batman into the videogame world and does it exceptionally well.  The game can be effectively separated into three parts: stealth, comabt, and exploration.  All aspects are done well and serve none feel tedious or boring throughout the game.

Batman can't take too much damage from gunfire so the key is to remain hidden the whole time.  There are many ways to defeat guards, from just seeking up behind them to grabbing them from hidden vents in the ground.
-Combat flows well and combos feel satisfying.  Heavy blows make you feel powerful, just like Batman himself.
-Exploration could also just be called running around, but finding hidden trophies, interrogation tapes and other things if fun and gives entertaining insight into the games villians.  It's not necessary but it is fun.
The game is great, even if it over shadowed a but by Arkham City.  A great and worthwhile purchase.

This is one of the best puzzle games I've ever played. It takes a very clever and deceptively simple mechanic and allows you to layer it with insane complexity.
As good as it is, it hasn’t exploded in popularity. I haven’t seen it on any game of the year lists (my own included; I hadn’t heard of it till after Christmas, but in retrospect it would have been near the top). I think this comes down to a few things: 1) It’s very difficult to solve, 2) It’s very difficult to describe, 3) It’s a very pure puzzle game without much fluff.
Some more complaints: The sound track only has a couple tracks and they’re like bland Christmas tunes. The VO is very quiet and I always have to turn up the volume, stop moving, and strain to listen.
Most everything else is great! The visual style is interesting. It looks like a pixel art indie game, but when you pay attention most objects are rendered in 3D. The puzzles are excellent. Everything feels impossible until you’ve figured out a genius new way to combine the game objects. I can feel it changing my brain. I also feel like I need to lie down after a few levels and unravel my thoughts inside thoughts inside thoughts. This is one of those games where getting stuck means you should take a break and come back later.
The hidden stuff and extra mechanics added in an update are also an interesting tangent. I can’t bring myself to find all the secrets, but it’s probably several more hours a mental gymnastics if you need more.
So, if you like difficult puzzle games (Lolo, Braid, Ico, Snapshot, Talos Principle) give this a try.

A nice example of how not to make puzzle-combat.
After first few starting levels(approximately 5-10 minutes) overall fun and engaging game process turns into repetitive one-way to solve puzzles, in which you have to play a "guess what's on my mind" game with designers of levels.
Stealth is non-existent - literally every other room is only accessible through one entrance, every other - through two (way to learn from Mark of The ninja).
Most rooms are boringly easy. Others are painfully hard - they require perfect execution and a lot of luck.
For example, main difficulty of second boss consists in a sheer amount of enemies in the boss room. I discovered only one single way to clear that room - a very specific way, which I had to add 40 minutes of repetition and memorization and random guessing. When I actually did it, there was no sense of accomplishment - only reason i accomplished it this time and didn't on other tries was luck. On this moment you might ask - what is luck in a game with no random numbers? Well, the problem is that lifeblood of this game is tiny, almost uncontrollable twitches of mouse that completely change course of almost every action. Taking the same action with just a bit of mouse twitch could turn it from best course of action to a total disaster.Due to this, I can't even imagine playing this game with controller.
Amount of meaningful decisions you can actually make is really minor - action points for unknown reasons deteriorate every turn, and on most turns only thing you can actually do is run(jump) for your life. Overall, it just turns every fight that is not to easy to engage you into a long streak of endless jumps, during which you simply hope for a lucky moment when nobody will actually shoot at you.
Soundtrack is great. Nothing else I can say about it.
Art style is decent, although completely copied from mark of the ninja, with a little nice twist of taking-itself--less-serious.
Overall, this game could(and, probably, still can) have a huge potential, but a set of mechanics and  level design promote only extreme caution and endless repetition, not creativity and proper choice-making. Unless something really serious is done to both those aspect of game I doubt it can be really enjoyable.

I remember playing this when it was a 3 level demo on itch io maybe a year ago. I liked it then and I liked it now. The game manages to remain frantic while essentially being turn-based. It's neatly tactical and the pace is basically defined by the player. The environments may seem a little stale currently but it's basically to be expected given the content matter of the game.
Our protagonist's jump arc is finicky to work with and for some reason he can't do an arc that is short horizontally but tall vertically. He's kind of an all or nothing about his jumps. Furthermore there are strange inconsistencies in how the protagonist will choose to kill a person, I'm sure they're all based on distance from and position of target, but I've loaded a checkpoint and moved down some stairs and immediately had a samurai get ready to strike me while I chose to kill a regular guard, sometimes leading to me striking the guard and moving just out of range of the samurai and sometimes leading to me striking the guard and being slaughtered by the samurai. In both instances I start this from the position of the stairs and choose the exact same path and it seems in both cases the samurai is about the same distance away.
This wouldn't be an issue if you could choose the length of your strike the rest of the time, but instead it's entirely based on positioning, which is something of an arbitrary gameplay restriction.
Another such arbitrary restriction is that although you can use the scaffolding parts as floors that you  can travel through from below, you cannot use them as ceilings that you travel through from above, meaning that you cannot hang bodies from them. You get used to it quickly, it just seems like a bizarre restriction on the gameplay and you wouldn't expect these restrictions to be in place.
This sounds like I'm panning the game but these are just minor issues, it's an engaging game

Don't let the charming graphics and the simple one-button gameplay fool you, because this puzzle game - which is about navigating a ball through a level by changing the objects in it to collect all of the golden rings - offers a lot of interesting mechanics that are often combined in such way that you'll scratch your head a couple of times before that glorious 'Aha!' solution comes to mind, reminding you of how clever some of the levels are. The levels are well-designed in such way that they introduce the mechanics very nicely and will teach the player to actually think ahead about how to get to all of the rings.
While the well-made level editor provides a way for the community to make their own levels and share it with others, most of the levels are overly-simple - sometimes even completely empty - and add only white noise to the content of the community. Most likely this is due to the achievement you get for 'Uploading your own level', which is obviously redundant, considering the community content 'fallout' it has created.
In conclusion, I really enjoy playing Ichi for its charms and interesting use of mechanics. The level-editor adds a lot of creative freedom and replayability to the game, but the developer really has to think of a way to make sure that players cannot just upload an empty level for the purpose of getting an achievement. Other than that, I think that Ichi is definitely worth it's price.

WRONG MOVE, BUDDY, NOW YOU HAVE TO LISTEN TO ME RANT ABOUT HOW GOOD EVERYTHING ABOUT THIS GAME IS!
The combat is God of War pre-GoW.
The story is superbly told. It's rich in philosophic themes and makes you think. The vocabulary is also rich.
Free Will vs Fate is a major theme through the series, but especially this game. I can't think of many other games that tackle this subject material, and this one does it so supremely well.
It uses time-travel, addresses the paradoxes it creates and FIXES THEM?! That's some Dragon-break-level writing. Clever as hell.
The voice acting is second to none. I cannot think of a game with better voice acting. Kain's voice actor nails every single line, Raziel's isn't bad either, and The Elder God's (RIP) is so perfectly fitting, I cannot imagine it being another voice in any way.
For its time, it was graphically impressive, the world of Nosgoth is still very rich in detail. Just pixelated detail (oxymoron?). The environments are truly fitting to the material, and the spirit world creeped me out when I was younger. ("...someone... help?")
If I had to find a negative about the game... it would be that it didn't get it's deserved sequel to actually tie everything together, but even in that this game still manages to give you a satisfying ending. It's just that friggin' good.

If you have played the Soul Reaver games, you will probably be absolutely horrified by the camera controls (or lack therof) in this game, at least I was. I went as far as trying to install a 3rd party application to make the camera more akin to the earlier games. When that didn't work out, I begrudgingly decided to give it a go anyway. Don't despair! It IS possible to get used to, and in the process you get a kind of increased cinematic feeling, which is very suitable for the epic scale of the story at this point.
Throughout the game you will encounter both boss fights and puzzles, but honestly nothing as inventive as Soul Reaver 1 and 2 respectively. Be that as it may, the enjoyable combat system and ever-present epicness of the story, is quite enough to make me give this game a resounding thumbs up.

I was excited to play this game when I first saw it appear on the Steam store.  It looked like it was going to be a thought-provoking, deep experience where people would be able to compare the different choices that they had made and the outcomes that resulted from them.  I was wrong.
Though on a first playthrough it is easy to believe that the choices that you are making change the story, a second playthrough (or even a bit of research) quickly prove otherwise.  At best your choices make a minor difference that lasts about as long as the next scene.  At worst, there is literally no difference at all.  Once you discover that the choices in the game don't matter all that much, your second realization is that the story is rather bland as well.  I'll avoid discussing the ending for the sake of those who are reading this review but still wish to give the game a chance but I definitely suggest not getting your hopes up.
As far as the story goes, there were several parts that entertained me and (while still having the belief that choices affected the narrative in a major way) seemed promising.  On the opposite side of that, there was plenty in the game that drained the fun out of it.  The vast majority of the jobs in the game were an absolutely terrible grind.  This makes it so that earning money is less of side quest and more of 'you know, I think I'm going to skip eating today' moment.  Call that realism if you'd like, though I prefer to enjoy myself the entire time that I'm playing a game.
Overall, the game was okay up until the discovery of an extremely linear storyline and downright bad after it.  It had potential to be a great game if the developers had put a little more heart into it.

A classic case of an initial concept losing its way.
Play the first few hours, read reviews or previews, and you'll see an emotionally-driven story about choice and fate, where you're penniless and broken and have to go on a difficult journey to getting your life and partner back.
However, all these concepts get abandoned and by the end you're left unfulfilled, with cop-outs and odd character behaviour along the way, until the game is telling you you're a broke bum who desperately wants your ex back, when in fact you the player are ACTUALLY full of money and don't give a crap about the ex because s/he's a jerk.
You might go through hell and do drugs if it meant getting the love of your life back, but would you do it just to go to someone's wedding? No, but the game apparently thinks people do that.
As a cop-out, you even get to make some choices about the actual plot. As in you decide who dumped who, and why. But this one 'choice' hidden away in a conversation, a couple of hours before the end, is what impacts the ending most of all, without even alluding to it. Madness.
In one person's story, you dumped a girl because you wanted to bang some more chicks, then changed your mind and crashed the wedding and she came crawling back. In another player's story, you got dumped and now you're acting like a crazed stalker to see her again and ruin everything. In another, you may not give a crap about her. The game, however, is adamant that in each scenario you're going to the wedding to crash it or be a wuss and do the whole "I just want her to be happy but I still love her" shtick, and likely end up depressed anyway. Because the plot isn't as flexible with choice as it wants to say it is.
Other little things about the game can make it frustrating. Press space to speed up the text, and you might end up accidentally making a choice that pops up without the usual pause, and you'll have to reload your most recent save. Play Blackjack and if you and the dealer have the same hand (a 'push'), you still LOSE.
In hindsight, my hours would've been better spent playing something else.
That's what I call a very good game.

It is safe to say that war provides the most popular structure within games, so when faced with the prospect of taking up 'yet another war game', people can be forgiven for choosing to spend their time elsewhere.
Let me contest that idea in relation to Silent Hunter III, or SHIII (coincidentally a sound you might make a lot whilst playing the game). The war is definitely going on out there, but you're merely a boat in the ocean and your focus is your orders, your crew and the deep waters immediately out around you. In historical writings this ocean arena is referred to with reverance for both sides playing a high stakes chess game in an isolated battlefield with little of the political discolourings of the mainland.
One of those games to draw you in and hold your attention across many hundreds of hours.

Mark of the Ninja is a great example of how much more important gameplay is than graphical fidelity. This is a familiar sentiment, but Mark of the Ninja embodies it. The control scheme with a 360-controller is excellent, and the game gently ramps up the difficulty as you gain proficiency with the controls.
The length is perfect; the game never feels repetitious. A single playthough should take you 8-10 hours, and it's rewarding the entire way. There's decent replay value, as the game will give you higher scores, more tools and techniques, and Steam Achievements for more careful playstyles. I especially appreciate the leaderboard, where you can compare your performance to that of your Steam friends.
There's another notable feature that's built into the gameplay that may go unnoticed, because it's an absence, not a feature: there is no difficulty slider. Mark of the Ninja offers exactly as much challenge as you want to take on. If you want a casual experience, the game is challenging but only rarely frustrating. If you want an expert-level challenge, there are challenges built into each level that you can attempt or ignore. For example, no kills, no detection, incapacitating certain soldiers, putting out every light, putting out no lights. There's no difficulty slider that puts in more or fewer enemeies,  or makes them more or less alert. It's a brilliant design. And - it does this on the fly. Some of these challenge goals appear mid-level. Two players can play the same level and have an entirely different experience. The game gives you just as much challenge as you would like to take on.
Mark of the Ninja is a superbly designed game. Give it a go.

Understand, first and foremost, Gnomoria is something unheard of to the crowd that likes these kinds of games; Fully released. As of this writing the version on Steam is the released product and the game is not abandoned as some have claimed. Many of the negative reviews currently on Steam have nothing to do with the game itself and are about the developer stating he has finished development and this has led some people to decry the game as an unfinished product. This is not the case, and many of them do not state or list relevant detractions from the game aside from their feeling it is unfinished. The developer did not finish all the features he intended to, but he left the game in a well-beyond playable state that is beyond a fair few other Greenlight games that never make it out of alpha or beta states.
I first heard of Gnomoria a few years back and at the time it had a small bit of hype for it's aspirations to be an in-depth but still penetrable city and resource management game. The premise is simple enough; You start as a group of gnomes, you have a small amount of starting resources and your goal is to build and maintain a prosperous settlement. To do this you need to mine for ores, clear forests, farm food and materials such as cotton, build structures and outfit your people. You manage what each individual Gnome can do via a Profession system that ties certain tasks to each profession (A miner mines, a woodcutter cuts wood, and a rancher fruitlessly tries to corral your animals) and understanding it, as well as the game itself, will be your key to victory.
Let me state, I love this game. It's one of my favorite games to just turn on and let run when I need to kill time and it's perfectly easy to pick up and put down, yet like most city and civ management titles it's hard to actually stop playing. I spend a lot of time doing projects to reach some goal and find myself needing to do other projects to shore that up and it turns into this interconnected maze of projects that each feel fulfilling when you complete them.
Each Gnome has it's own skills and each profession uses certain skills which makes managing your gnomes a key and fun part of the experience. The game has wild animals and monster invasions which provide most of the incentive to militarize your settlement and add an extra ticking clock to the survival of your settlement.
It is not an easy game to dive into. Your first few settlements, without the benefit of Steam guides or other resources, will crash and burn. You have to keep food stocks up, drink stocks up and your kingdom has a Value which is the combined total of all the resources and structures on the map. This value attracts more Gnomes to your settlement, but also factors into the strength and rate of enemy attacks which means you have to be able to adapt your defenses as your population and value increase. This makes each settlement lost a learning experience and very rarely will you not take something away from the experience.
It is not perfect by any means. Despite it's light feeling, the calculations and processing required can make bigger maps or older computers chug a little and sometimes the AI feels a little clunky in how it determines pathing, often leaving gnomes taking the longer routes or unsafe one when shorter/safer ones are available, but this rarely impacts the experience for me.
There is a lack of variety in some things such as metals and farm-able resources but what is there is easy enough to understand and the combinations/products you can produce can easily be enough to overwhelm yourself with. There are some small complaints like the music being a bit chippy and the sprite work being basic, but they both work fine and they do not detract from the experience.
Overall, I highly recommend this game and urge you to give it a chance in spite of the negative reviews currently in place. I do not deny the game has problems, but the game is absoltuely playable and a good, easy to slide into game for this genre. In terms of cost versus enjoyment, it is well worth the money and you could easily have less fun and less time spent in much more expensive games. You can benefit highly from the guides and resources in place and mods will add some depth for those seeking a deeper, more varied experience, but this does not take away from a great game.

So I bought this game recently cause it was on sale, and also because I watched a playthrough of it a long time ago. It tells the intriguing story of a young man named Steve, who finds himself in the mysterious town "Harvest" after waking up with amnesia. The town is populated with a couple dozen people, most vastly differing from one another, producing a nice cast of memorable and unique characters. Steve, the main character, is personally my favourite. I love his dialogue and I found myself connecting to him and his situation -- something that doesn't usually happen for me.
Throughout the game you will uncover the secrets of Harvest, most opening up more questions than answers. This adds to the mystery of the town, producing a nice spooky vibe which fits it's horror genre. While playing I found myself simultaneously laughing, crying, and cringing; it's the perfect combination of humour and disgust. You can't help but feel pity for Steve, who like you has no idea what's going on or why he's there.
A warning to anyone squeamish: This game is not for the lighthearted. Though the graphics may be older, some of the cutscenes are surprisingly brutal, and without going into too much detail, very gory. There's no real jumpscares though, which is nice. Just be wary that at any second a cutscene could come out of nowhere. There's child/baby death in this game too, which may (understandly) bother some people. In general, the farther you progress the more gory it gets. So if you are faint of heart, I advise you not to play this game.
PROS:
-Great story with somewhat satisfying conclusions
-Amazing characters
-Not afraid of it's audience
-Decent voice acting
-Great cutscenes
-Graphics aren't bad for an older game
-Steve
CONS:
-Fighting is lackluster
-Some may find endings unsatisfactory
-Gets pretty weird (it's for you to decide if this is a good or a bad thing)
-Dead babies, mutilated children, wounded cats, blah blah blah
-Too many wasps
-Steve is a kidder
All in all, I highly recommend this game to people who enjoy classic horrors with unique charm and a weird, crazy plot. If you're looking for a game that'll make you question what the f**k is going on, then this game is for you. If older graphics really bother you then they may be a problem, but personally they were good enough to make me genuinely scared at some points (which is good enough for me). Basically, just buy this game. I promise you you won't find another one like it.

At some point in the past I binge played Dwarf Fortress, enjoying the experience as far as the interface and graphics would allow. Seeing Gnomoria I had high hopes that this would be more or less the same game but with a more tolerable interface and graphics.
Starting out, the game seemed solid. The interface is better, if still far from perfect, the graphics are tolerable and everything seemed fine at first.
Similar to Dwarf Fortress you will fail a couple of times before you get the balance and learn what to build in which order. Pretty soon you realize that the game is a lot shallower than Dwarf Fortress however (for better and worse). Less to build, less to manage, less “to do”.
This would be an okay game with a potential for many hours’ enjoyment, if it was not for the HORRIBLE PERFORMANCE BUGS. The developers have failed at the implementation of the AI/pathfinding to the point where a game with as few as 20 dwarfs/gnomes can become unplayable even on high end hardware.
Prepare to lose your colony to the “performance death” (e.g. if you happen to block the path of attackers or your dwarfs) long before you reach the “end game”. The UI becomes less responsive and over a few minutes the game slows to a freeze. No error message or crash, just a freeze that cannot be avoided or recovered.  Do not get me wrong, there are plenty of crashes too, but those are recoverable. But once your colony has started to freeze, you can only start over. Until it happens again.
Do not waste your time on this game. It will only bring you frustration and disappointment. What a shame.

Gnomoria is a complex kingdom management game in the same vein as Dwarf Fortress.
The starting point sound simple enough: You've got a handful of gnomes, a few livestock, and enough food and water for a few days. You must direct your gnomes to build a kingdom in which they will live. Simple, right? Wrong. It turns out that building a kingdom from scratch is no simple feat. You only have a limited amount of time before hordes of monsters will show up and attempt to slaughter your settlers. You'll need a sword (or many, many swords). But to make a sword, you need bronze bars to make it. Bronze bars must be made of tin and copper. Tin and copper need to be mined. Mining is dangerous and may force your gnomes to come face to face with monsters deep within the earth. All of this just for a sword, which is most definitely not the most complex thing you can make.
As you progress, you'll need to get a feel for the supply chain required to make things. You choose which gnomes do which jobs, you choose the priority of their tasks, and you hope that you don't make a mistake somewhere because production will halt if you do, and there's nobody to hold your hand and tell you that you forgot to assign a gnome to burn wood into charcoal for your torches, and that's why none are being made. You'll make mistakes. You'll lose dwarves. You'll see your kingdoms be completely obliterated from one small band of goblins or a rogue golem or a horde of subterranean insects. It's all part of the game.
But that's the fun of it. It's not an easy game (though not as tough as Dwarf Fortress), but it's quite rewarding to see your kingdom grow and take on new challenges. It's great to build a giant, walled marble city with trained archers wielding steel crossbows at every entrance. It's satisfying to build systems of gearboxes and axles which power mechanisms which keep enemies out or deploy traps against invading giants.
Overall, Gnomoria is a really great game for those interested in the kingdom management genre, but be aware that it's not a game that's simple to pick up. You'll fail a lot. It's part of the game.

*WARNING* This review is highly biased towards the Super Smash Bros. games*
As someone who has played the Super Smash Bros. series extensively, I looked into this game hoping it would be an interesting spin on the platform fighter genre. However, upon entering the game, I was pretty disappointed.
Overall, compared to Smash, the controls felt extremely clunky, and pretty unresposive at times. The overall feel of the game seems very cheap, hoping to reap off of the nostalgia people may feel from the Smash series.
There is also quite a large lack of balance in the game, especially with this new update, making air fighting being the only viable option. Smash managed to give each character movesets that could work with either a ground or air playstyle, while also giving a bit of preference to each character.
The fact that this is a free to play game also works against it, making it, from what I've seen, a bit of a pay to win game, due to how underpowered the starting characters feel. Sure, Smash added some unbalanced DLC characters, but only with the latest release, and since then they have made attempts to balance them extensively.
Overall, Brawlhalla feels like an unbalanced, lackluster spin on the formula Smash has established and mastered, and feels like a cheap money trap  to make the game more enjoyable, or requiring a hefty amount of playtime.

After all these years I finally took the time to play Batman: Arkham Asylum and damn it was good fun!
From the progression of the storyline to the iconic fighting system which has been copied some times already, this game is worth your bucks.
With a small but fairly open world we progress our way with batclaws, explosive gel and our cool detective mode. This detective mode lets you scan the area and see enemies behind walls and also detects if they have guns on them. Jokes on you, you're Batman and of course limited to your fighting skills and tech toys to stop the thugs from the prison, NO GUNS! But with that in mind the great fighting system that let's you take it out on big groups of small and big thugs with easy counter attacks, jumps over the heads of the enemies and more moves like instant takedown or throwing guys around.
The graphics are a little older and the cutscenes look horrible with a very low bitrate for today's 2015 standards, but it's all acceptable and still looking really nice overall. The sound is a bit unrealistic the way it is reflected, but it's delivering the atmosphere more scary tones. In fact, Arkham Asylum is a really scary game and the special parts against Scarecrow really do their part.
The bossfights deliver some challenge though they are not changing over the course. Except for the 2nd biggest fight with Poison Ivy, the bossfights are mostly the same way like you encountered Bane the first time. Dodging, punching, retrieving. But nonetheless, it's still good fun! The final fight against our main antagonist The Joker could have been a bit more spectacular, but I'm hoping on future titles to bring me more fireworks.
TL;DR
A fine game for people who need a witty challenge and like a thrilling atmosphere! The Batman universe is well presented and gives us even more background story when you're willing to search the collectables.

Wild Animal Racing is the first game of the Wild Animal Series, A series well known for its challenging gameplay and excellent world design. The first thing you see when you launch the game is  a splash screen of the games title with the main character (The Giraffe) in his signature red car. you also see "made by Paul Bird" underneath the title, a subtle hint to the secret bird boss later in the game.
You can play single player with the expertly programmed AI or if that isnt a challenge enough you can take your chances and face off against some of the worlds best Wild Animal Racing fans (You might even be able to race me #1) Or if you are feeling a bit more intimate you can invite a hot date over for some split screen couch co-op action, Something that will ensure your date goes home thoroughly pleased.
There are 6 characters to choose from all representing the animal kingdom (sorry humans this isnt a game for your kind) each of them has thier own unique racing style and gameplay abilities, the shining examples being the lions ability to blend in with the sand on the desert levels to give him that extra edge or the rhinoceros' secret ability to ram other racers with his horn to knock them wildly of course.
The soundtrack is amazing and has become an instant classic in my home, I have already made the beautifuly orchestrated underwater theme my ringtone. The wonderfly orchestrated soundtrack compliments the gameplay in ways ive never seen before, It slowly builds up for the first few laps then breaks into an almighty crescendo upon the final stretch filling the player with a sense of awe and wonder at the fsat paced action.
Overall this game is a master piece of game design and is not for the faint of heart, if you love high octane blood fueled animal racing action then this game is a must buy for your christmas list.

Recursed is a puzzle platformer with the platforming being pretty basic and the puzzle design something very unique.
There is no story in this game,it is basically out and out puzzles with the level selection screen giving you an idea of the game and it is wonderfully done. There is a short tutorial which you can read before you start the game.
The gameplay basically is that you solve puzzles using chests which have the properties that once you get inside them they spawn a different room. Now the puzzles come for example with you basically starting in a room with a locked door and the chest having the key. You go into a chest which spawns a new room get the key and return back to the prior room to unlock the door. This is the basic puzzle mechanic and there are some very interesting puzzles designed around them. there are puzzles where if you submerge the chest in water the room gets flooded. The first 4 levels of the game are a bit repetitive but not that difficult and easy to breeze through. Then comes the last 3 level sets which introduces some new objects and those are pretty complex and difficult but gives you immense satisfaction on solving them. You basically unlock the next set of levels by collecting gems which are one each in the prior levels. There are also hidden gems which you can find out which are very cleverly placed and require some critical thinking to get to that part. The level design is stellar in this game especially the last 20 levels which if you are a hardcore puzzle gamer would give you immense pleasure to solve. i solved about 15 of them and the rest were too difficult for me. This would appeal to gamers who like logical puzzles. The failure states in the later levels are so abundant and one of the failure states leads you to a completely different puzzle which is excellent puzzle design.
The graphics are very simple and include a 2d character that you control. There are hints provided by a talking ring which you encounter in all the levels. The hints are very vague and basically explain the new mechanics which keep the game fresh and take it to absolutely epic difficulty levels.
Highly recommended if you like logical puzzles. The game's name basically is taken from recursion in programming languages and boy the puzzles use that mechanic in some very intelligent ways. If you feel bored after the first 4 sets of level do continue ahead as before I mentioned the last 3 sets of levels are devilishly difficult and require all your puzzle solving abilities to be used. there are certain mechanics when you are experimenting with a level and it strikes what has to be done is so rewarding.
The only critism are the controls which are a little finicky with respect to throwing objects and stacking things which you would need to do a bit. but that is only a minor gripe. A must buy for fans of puzzles platformers who like extremely difficult logical puzzles.

NFS Undercover is maybe the most casual, plain and simple game of all serial. To call it arcade... well, I remember arcades of 80's, so it is definitely not an arcade! It is very sub-arcade, in the terms of controls and the whole gameplay.
Yet I'm not so determined to absolutely NOT recommending that game. You see, that depends from where you are looking at the whole NFS bunch of games. If you are one with NFS Underground, you maybe found Undercover less colourful, but acceptable. Same goes with the fans preferring NFS Underground 2 the most. Now, the biggest group of fans, I know, love the Most Wanted. For them, Undercover will be quite bleak in terms of contest. The police there dumb and slooow, the contenders, for the most time, also not showing you any challenge.
Undercover has its own nice features, sure.
First, the soundtrack. It's the best from the whole serial, I still have more than dozen tracks from there in my playlist.
Second, the cars. There are quite a bunch of roaring road monsters for every taste, with the only downside that you should invest some time in the game to get to the sweetest ones.
Third, Maggie Q. I'm not a fan of her, yet she certainly make the atmosphere a little less boring.
Still, it is not enough for me. You see, my favourite NFS is Porshe Unleashed, so I can certainly tell you from my biased point of view, that all driving in the Undercover is boring as Mr.Obama speeches. The physics of driving is under every level of comparison. Maybe it is similar to the driving in the Watch Dogs, but hardly better. I've played Undercover on the PSP platform, but even there I was not really engaged in the races. They were not attractive even on that tiny piece of hardware, and PSP is not rich with the racing games at all!
So, the only good thing I believe you can get from buying Undercover now is the little fraction of the same drive that gathered NFS so many fans with Underground and Most Wanted titles. So far you can't buy any of those great games on Steam, maybe you'll get desperate enough and go with the Undercover.
My mark is 5.8/10. If you try to look a little harder, you'll find so many better racing games on Steam, than that. Yeah, they won't be calling Need For Speed, so what?

I miss this series' storyline. Defiance has the best combat gameplay in my opinion, in terms of just 'how good it feels to swing a sword." It also mixes things up by having you alternate in each level from playing as Kain to playing as Raziel, and so on and so forth, with each on his own journey in Nosgoth, taking care of business.
"Forging the Soul Reaver" is a bit overused, though. You'll repeatedly imbue your sword with a different element to get through a different lock. I think this is a bit lazy on the part of the developer, and would have preferred something less repetitive. That said, switching characters helps to get rid of that, along with a nice amount of cutscenes throughout the game (about 1 hour and 50 minutes, which you can actually watch on YouTube if you only care about storylines. The series has a good plot and if that's your plan, Google to figure out the order of the games and watch their cutscenes in the appropriate order.
This is a pretty good PC port, featuring mouse and keyboard controls with button mapping that works (couldn't use a mouse in SR1, and button mapping wasn't working properly for me in SR2). Striking an enemy with Kain's sword sounds like striking a person with a blunt object, which is a little silly, but it's still pretty satisfying for a game that's approaching 15 years old now.
I do recommend the game because the gameplay is pretty decent and the cutscenes/story are rather entertaining with exquisite voice acting.

As someone who loved Human Revolution, I was extremely happy with how Mankind Divided turned out.
, I do recommend you adjust your expectations when getting into this game:
1. This game is about Adam Jensen's work at Interpol and the fallout of Human Revolution's ending. This game does not focus as much on the conspiracy plot as you might expect if you played Human Revolution. That doesn't mean it's given very little attention though.
2. The game does not put too much emphasis on the side characters from Human Revolution, except for a couple side quests.
Once your expectations have changed a bit, I think the game becomes far more enjoyable.
+ The gameplay is incredibly good and pretty much a straight upgrade from Human Revolution. While the stealth approach is pretty similar to HR in how you do it, the levels themselves are pretty well-made and in most missions you have more than enough options to approach any given situation without being seen (there are a couple of outliers though, where there seem to be only 2 ways to go). The guns blazing approach is
and much more fun than I thought. The guns feel and sound great and are extremely satisfying to use. Weapon customization also makes the loud approach much more viable, because of armor piercing rounds and EMP rounds.
+ New augmentations have been added and they are a good addition. In early game you're limited in how many experimental augs you can use at once (for balancing purposes), but you're promised a solution to this problem early on in the game. The augmentations themselves are integrated well into the game, highlights being Remote Hacking which is a must-have, and the Icarus Dash which is very good in the late game for quickly moving from cover to cover. Two more examples are the Nanoblade, which can do amazing area-of-effect damage and is really fun to use, and the TITAN aug, looks absolutely incredible and makes you shrug off bullets for a massive badass factor.
+ The level design is top-notch and most levels are on par with some of Human Revolution's best levels (if you haven't played HR just know that it's as good as you want it to be) with a couple outliers as I mentioned before. Highlights are the Palisade Bank and the final mission, the latter being one of the best level designs I've seen period.
+ Side quests are pretty much all great and there are 12 in total. The game doesn't make them overly difficult to find so you don't have to run around Prague wondering whether you missed a ton of side quests. On my first playthrough I only missed one of them (hint: check the sewers).
+ Voice acting is universally good, although the accents from Czech citizens takes some getting used to. Adam Jensen's voice actor has greatly improved from the previous game and is the highlight of the voice acting in my opinion. He has more emotion in his voice and doesn't overplay the smoker-voice, which I felt he could do in Human Revolution.
++The great voice acting also makes the couple of dialogue boss battles that the game has much more believable and interesting. All of them have a certain tension to them and the dialogue is written to cover multiple approaches to a conversation (such as dodging the question / being up-front / talking cautiously).
+ Prague is a great hub and has plenty to explore, from apartements to store basements to general buildings. I feel like the aftermath of Human Revolution was presented well here, although there were times where it can feel very on-the-nose.
+ The game has 3 acts, the third of which is so good I don't even know what to say. I'll spare you the details for the sake of spoilers, but it feels very tense and uses Prague's hub world in a creative way.
+ Music is just...I'm running out of words that mean the same as 'great', but the soundtrack really is fantastic. It also makes the guns blazing approach more satisfying because of how good the combat music has become.
+ Visually the game is very beautiful, but do know that the game no longer takes place in a Cyber Renaissance like Human Revolution did. The black/gold aesthetic is used more sparingly, and while you won't see it very much in Prague because of how the city now shuns all things Cyber Renaissance, other locations like Golem City do make plenty of use of it. Also fun fact, both Adam and a certain NPC still have the black/gold aesthetic, which fits considering what they've been through in Human Revolution.
++If you have a high-end PC, the game will probably look phenomenal if the promotional pictures are anything to go by. I played the game on fairly low settings and I can totally see the promotional pics being in-game footage with graphics options turned up.
- The main plot is decent and above average when compared to most RPGs, but it doesn't reach the heights that many were hoping for, mostly because of what players such as myself expected after the previous game. Adam's work at Interpol and the series-arching conspiracy plot are played as two separate stories that end up intertwining. Unfortunately, neither have the necessary tension or personal stakes to make it as grand as the game wants it to be, excluding the final mission. The Versalife Vault mission is an exception though.
- While most of the new augmentations work well, some of them don't feel very useful. Tesla is meant for hitting multiple targets non-lethally, but with how non-lethal fits much more with a stealth approach, it's weird that Tesla will randomly cause enemies to turn hostile (red) rather than just orange. While I can't fully confirm it, this could mess with some achievements (like completing the game without ever being seen, i.e. not turning on any alarms). Besides Tesla, I haven't found much reason to use the PEPS augment and the bullet-time augment just takes up way too much energy.
- Although I can't tell you how the game runs on a high-end PC, on my fairly decent PC I couldn't crank up the video options as much as I wanted (my 2 gigs of VRAM could be to blame though). Check out PC gaming websites for more in-depth information on how the PC port is.
~The Assault and Tactical packs are not worth it.
~The in-game microtransactions are single-use (!) and feel forced on by the publisher. Do not spend any money on these under any situation.
~System Rift is okay, get it if you like the main game as much as I do but you're not missing very much.
~A Criminal Past is a must-buy if you like Mankind Divided and in my opinion it's the best mission in the entirety of Human Revolution and Mankind Divided combined.
It's worth the €50,- price tag, but if you find that a bit too steep then you'll still get plenty of bang for your buck if you buy the game at €30,- or less. The main story is fine, but not as good as expected after Human Revolution. The side quests MORE than make up for this however. The gameplay is incredible and gameplay-wise it's one of the best action RPGs I've ever played. For me, the game was worth every cent.

Don't let their cuteness fool you, Snakebird(s) is a deceptively challenging puzzle game that will have players twisting their minds as they twist and wiggle the charming titular characters around it's many levels.
Sharing classic video game rules for snake behavior, eating fruit extends the snake one segment changing the areas that can be accessed.  It'll take a steady hand and a well planned diet to reach the goal!

It's an unexpected candidate, but in my opinion right up there with
and
. That being said, refer to the Downsides and Caveats below for some things to keep in mind in deciding if you specifically will like it.
The mechanics are very simple and (with one or two exceptions) almost completely self-explanatory. There are only a finite number of possible moves at any given position. Yet, from level two or three, you will likely get pretty stuck. Moreover, you will be absolutely baffled at how you got stuck on such a clearly simple level: you know an easy solution must exist, and it's going to be completely obvious in hindsight. (If you don't believe me on this, just watch TotalBiscuit struggle with it on Youtube. He spends 7.5 very painful minutes on level 2. He then spends 6.5 additional painful minutes on level 3 before giving up.)
So begins a series of excellent, completely solvable, but extremely difficult puzzles. You are lucky if you don't get stuck on almost all of them. They aren't tedious or just a matter of brute force. Rather, as with all of the best puzzle games, you must piece together techniques and strategies you have learned in previous levels to get you through more difficult ones. Each level involves careful planning: working backwards, figuring out what sequences of subgoals might get you to the end, and using process of elimination to rule out impossible sequences until you find one that works. Many levels
impossible and (another aspect of all great puzzle games) you will feel like a genius when you solve them.
There are over 50 puzzles (I won't say exactly how many to avoid a minor spoiler); I got about 16 hours of playtime although of course it will be more or less depending on how quickly you solve them. That's a little under 20 minutes a puzzle, on average, but the hardest ones must have taken me close to an hour each.
Definitely worth it for $7 in my opinion, although I got the game for much less in a humble bundle. Note, however, that you can get full game as a mobile app for $4.71 (on Android; probably similar on iphone) if you want to save money that way, and don't mind playing it on a phone.
It's probably the cutest thing ever to present such a huge challenge. I was expected this to be a cute little puzzle game I'd blow through then forget, but I can't beat level 3.

Lead your Snakebirds to a portal eating fruit in the meantime. Sounds simply? ...Not really.
The vast majority of puzzle games are way too easy for me. Snakebird was a total astonishment. There are a bit over 50 levels, but it took me long hours to complete them all. Don't be deceived by a sweet graphic design, this game is hella difficult.
The great advantage is that a player isn't forced to complete levels in order. Solving one level reveals few more so when the player is getting tired with inability to solve the damned level he is able to try and fail in few more.
Strongly recommend to everyone who likes challenging puzzle games. The rest... oh well, I recommend it to you too, but don't be surprised if you will fail on level 3 ;)

TLDR; It's a good game. Buy it, play it, love it.
Alright, It's that time again. A new Batman game is upon us, and it's time for us dedicated Batman fans to play through all previous Batman entries in anticipation and to remind ourselves why we love these games in the first place. That being said, the Arkham entries are fantastic, this one in particular is no exception.
The game can essentially be broken down into 3 segments (2 primary segments and 1 minor. Combat, Stealth and the occasional detective investigation. Each mode has it's way of growing on you and making you feel connected to the Dark Knight himself. The combat, in my opinion, is the meat and potatoes of the game. In this entry, it's very well executed, but with a lesser degree compared to the other games. This should be obvious, being the first entry in the series. If you've never played any other Arkham games, you certainly won't notice. If you have though, it feels a bit less refined, polished and with the obvious lack of gadgets and little nuances. Fantastic nonetheless and there's nothing more satisfying than zipping around a room at the (relative?) speed of a bat and smashing a nameless henchmans face off the wall.
The stealth really comes to life in these games. In these predator segments, you mostly rely on gargoyles to zip to and from, mostly undetected. Of course, no predator mission would feel complete without your trusty detective vision to help you analyze the situation, down to very personal details such as the henchmans heart rate and mental state. These segments can be fun and I enjoy getting to sneak up on an unsuspecting thug and introduce him to the wrong end of batmans hands.
The detective segments are rather few and far in between, however, still an interesting mechanic that let's you get a sense of Batman's detective abilities/ overpowered Batman computer and visor. The game mostly walk you right through these scenarios, so there isn''t much effort involved.
To sum up the experience, It's Batman. If you haven't played any other Arkham games, I'd say this is the best place to start, as you truly do notice the difference as each release comes out. Even though Batman: Arkham Origins is technically a prequel, there are far more mechanics and features in the game in comparisson to Arkham Asylum, making this the logical Starting point, in my opinion. Also the game does not allow you to free roam an entire city, of course, so you would not feel as though you've downgraded your roming space if you start with this game.
It's a great game overall, definitely does a good job of drawing you into the atmosphere and makes you feel as though you are stepping into the shoes of the Bman himself.

Usually I find it difficult to recommend any game that tries to be "retro" - but usually this is because indy developers use retro as an excuse for low effort, low quality shovelware.
Far Cry 3 - Blood Dragon is an exception.  It has a charming retro veneer, satirising the 1980's perfectly, while underneath is the full Far Cry 3 engine.    Gameplay is identical to Far Cry 3, although the excessive modification to the source game covers that up extremely well.   You could approach this game without having played Far Cry 3 and you would never know the heritage.
Technical implementation - Based on best of breed Far Cry 3's Crytek engine, top tier with all the expected PC graphics settings, incredibly smooth gameplay. It's highly polished - no glitches or issues.  You can jump straight in and go.
Gameplay - Based on Far Cry 3 but with some cool additions like radioactive dragons and things.  Short but very enjoyable storyline.
Art - The retro "cyborg" view is annoying at times but that's part of the theme.  The cutscenes and great voice acting from Terminator/Aliens' Michael Biehn as well as the over the top humour complement the flawless technical implementation perfectly.
This isn't a low budget DLC for Far Cry 3, it's a complete and polished game that stands well on its own merits and should be enjoyed by FPS gamers, 1980's fans, and gamers who enjoy a quality product.

An 80's throwback and obvious passion project, Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon is a solid, open world-ish, mini-dose of Far Cry 3 doused in neon lights and electro synth beats.  This stand alone expansion is short (10 hours for my play through), but densely packed.  The gameplay consists of capturing enemy installations on an island map, completing side missions to upgrade your weapons, and ripping out the mecha hearts of your cyborg enemies for experience and cash.  Abilities are unlocked by just leveling instead of the more complex Far Cry skill tree system, but it feels more like a streamlining instead of an afterthought, allowing you to focus on the gameplay.  Guns blazing, satisfying stealth, or throwing aforementioned mecha hearts into an enemy complex to attract the nearly invincible, eye lazering blood dragons, you get to decide how to approach each situation.  Finally, the ultra-campy humor, retro NES-style cinema scenes, and Terminator inspired sound track round out this time capsule of a gem, topping it off with Michael Biehn (aka Cpl. Dwayne Hicks, aka the original Kyle Reese) grumbling out the best action star since golden age of Arnie, Stallone, and Van Damme.
Buy if you love everything 80's, definite buy on sale to enjoy playing a game the developer had just as much fun making.

A very clever space-manipulation puzzle game. Everything in Recursed (graphics, story, music) exists to serve the puzzles, so if you don't enjoy puzzles, there's nothing for you here. If you do enjoy puzzles - particularly puzzles with keys, locks, platforming, and green-tinted objects that are unaffected by your space powers - then you're in for a real treat.
The core mechanic is this: when you leave a room, its contents revert to their original state. This may remind you of old games like Megaman, where the hardware didn't have enough memory to remember the entire level at once. An enemy that followed you out of a room and then back into it might be duplicated, while an enemy that wandered off-screen would be erased. If you've ever thought that would make a good mechanic for a puzzle game: you're absolutely right. Recursed is that game.
The puzzles are masterfully designed. Many of them hinge on a single insight, and solving them will make you feel like a genius. There's lots of room for experimentation, and lots of opportunities to see how the puzzle elements interact that really makes you feel like you're learning the rules of this world. Even if what you've learned doesn't help you with this puzzle, it will almost certainly come back in a later one.
Recursed encourages these moments of discovery. Sets them up, even. At least once in the game, you'll have a question about a particular mechanic, and you'll set up an experiment to find out the answer... and the game will reward your curiosity. "Well done", it seems to say. "You spotted a cool thing, and I didn't even have to point you towards it." (And then you get a diamond.)
The game introduces its concepts very gradually, letting you experiment and master each one before throwing a new object at you. The first world doesn't even use the core mechanic, it just lets players familiarise themselves with the platforming and lock-and-key mechanics. Which is appreciated, because there are a couple of subtleties (the ability to throw objects, in particular) that veteran gamers may not expect, so they'll appreciate the slow start.
The green objects in the fourth world are something of a turning point. By then, you ought to understand the basic mechanics of Recursed well enough, and you'll have discovered that some things are impossible within the game's rules. Green breaks those rules, turning the discoveries you've made so far on their head, making some things possible that were impossible, and opening up new areas to explore. But unlike the start of the game where you had no idea what to expect, this time you'll have a framework to fit these new ideas into, and you may even think of a use for green objects before you see the puzzle that demonstrates it. It's from this point on that Recursed's puzzle design really shines.
With that high point in mind, I'm a little let down by the later areas. The new mechanics introduced are less obvious than the ones before - acid brings little novelty over water, and fissure jars are strangely complicated compared to the rest of the game's elements. But the new expansion The Oobleck Conundrum remedies this very well, as oobleck has a very simple behaviour from which complex and interesting puzzles flow.
The final level is one for the books, as well. Everything you've seen throughout the game comes back for one last hurrah, a final boss of a puzzle that uses all the most advanced tricks you've learned. Yet it's ultimately simple enough that you can beat it in three minutes, when you understand the solution. Worth playing through to the end.
The game took me about twelve hours to beat all-in-all, including the expansion. There's not much reason to play it again once you've gotten 100%.
Also, after I did beat it, I caught myself checking what I was holding before leaving my bedroom. 10/10, would attempt to use game mechanics in real life again.

Awesome game for programmers that teaches functional programming:

- Leaving room = returning from function
- Moving objects between rooms = passing parameters for function (there are objects with copy semantics and move semantics)
- Many more...
Controls are fine, music is well suited for long hours playing. Great game.

Granted, the graphics are a bit of a throw back to the 90s and the game does not quite have the sense of humor of a game like Portals, but the underlying idea using recursion is one of the most original I have seen in a while.
The game starts of fairly simple, but difficulty ramps up quite quickly once you are past the first 20 levels. The title of each level sets the theme and often hints at the eventual solution. There are lots of clever puzzles in this game and I particularly liked that the solutions are often quite different and there is little tedious repetition. Controls work well enough for me using keyboard, although a controler might work even better. The hard part is always the puzzle aspect.
I really liked the game and if you like puzzle games this one will likely keep you entertained for many hours as well.

Unfortunately, out of all the Two Tribes games available on Steam, this is the only one I cannot recommend not because the core gameplay isn’t well-designed or it isn’t a unique take on an obstacle course puzzle platformer that focuses on momentum. The biggest problem with EDGE is the most damnable for a game; the controls were not properly designed to be played on computers whether you use the keyboard or a controller with analog or D-Pad method.

Had I not played RUSH and Toki Tori beforehand and known EDGE came out afterwards, I would have assumed that EDGE was the first PC port done by Two Tribes. Knowing this isn’t the case, however, the issues associated with its control-schemes as well as its steps back from the quality of a port that RUSH was makes EDGE feels behind the times rather than cutting edge.
In order to illustrate the many issues associated with its controls, it’s important to understand what the game requires you to do and how the input method is incapable, with the options available, to work with these demands. EDGE uses an isometric grid-movement system where you control the direction of a cube in one of four directions that can be toggled to set the up-button in the North-East or North-West direction. When you press a key/D-Pad/analog stick, the cube leans towards that direction depending on how long you hold the button/stick as well as how much inertia you have. Timing any change in direction with relation to its speed is important for the platforming challenges as well as speedrunning these courses. In order to use both the wall-edge mechanic for traversing obstacles with wall-grinding as well as the usage to gain more time, the controls cannot make every press of the button translate into a shift in direction. The result is a puzzle game that relies on reflex challenges with a heavy emphasis on precision without the ability to have constant textile feedback to make precise movements.
To explain these issues in a less technical manner, imagine playing Super Meat Boy where his arms and legs were cut off and he is forced to roll around levels from a diagonal view with the same control inputs and use his momentum to propel him. On top of this challenge, imagine the Tony Hawk Pro Skater games’ grinding system where you balance the direction of your skater with relation to the balancing bar now without a visual aid to communicate your level of balance.  As a result of all these changes—the camera, the control-method, the usage of speed, and the visual feedback—there is far too much information blinded from you that adds unnecessary difficulty to an otherwise fair challenge because all the necessary information should be given to you.
The bloody, meaty skater cherry on top of all these issues is that there is a simple control method that would mimic the touch-screen feedback and responsiveness at everyone’s computer, the mouse. Had the game used a cursor and a mouse-button to determine the direction as well as the momentum of the cube, EDGE wouldn’t be nearly as unresponsive to the point where it feels unplayable in sections where the fraction of a second of a direction change could spell death in overshooting or undershooting the obstacle.
Unfortunately, without being able to deal with the frustrating control methods, there is no way to assess the rest of the game or to discuss the variety of challenges EDGE offers with its minimalistic style. The only positive things I can say are the additions from the Extended version do not feel like gimmicks as the edge-tilting mechanic is properly used for obstacles that could not be completed any other way; the small tutorial marks on new mechanics are simple enough to show you how to perform a new challenge while being optional hints; and the soundtrack is a consolation prize that I wish I could buy to get something out of the game on Steam.
If nothing else has made up your mind whether to get this game or not, I would suggest you either play the demo on the PC, which thankfully Two Tribes’ games all have demos, bless their hearts. You can then purchase the Two Tribes bundle if you want to attempt to play the PC version—there is no level editor and the only thing you would probably miss out on are the Steam Group community levels—or you simply purchase Edge Extended on iOS or android after trying out the demo available on Steam.

A word to fellow female players: if Bearverly didn't sell you on the game, then hopefully this will.
I first discovered discovered Crush Crush through an update on Yandere Sim and was slightly interested since I enjoy casual and otome games, but I was highly skeptical because dating games with an all-female cast tend to be very...
, I guess, for lack of a better term.  With the huge boobs and the cliche writing and the blatant blatant pandering to horny boys with disposable income.  I looked at the screenshots and read the dialogue and decided that since it didn't look to be an all-out ♥♥♥♥♥ fest and it was free, I might as well give it a shot.
You can tell by the number of hours I have clocked into this game how well that turned out.
The characters are engaging and full of personality.  They're funny, they're angry, and they clearly have lives outside of the protagonist.  Since they all more or less start out disliking you at the beginning of their routes, you have to actually get to know and befriend them to advance.  Let me repeat this: if you're not even friends with a girl first, they don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about you romantically.  That is a huge breath of fresh air compared to most of the romantic content I've ingested before.
Like Hunny Pop, the game takes a harem approach to courting the girls.  Unlike Hunny Pop however, the girls are all aware of eachother and the fact that you're dating all of them at once, so if you have any reservations about lying and cheating to a girl you've romanced, no worries: they genuinely do not care.  (Well, with the exception of Yandere-Chan, for obvious reasons, but despite her hilariously inept attempts to murder the other girls in order to be your one and only, she still seems to get along with them fairly well.)
As for the gameplay itself, I'm going to be blunt.  This is not a game that you play for hours on end.  This is a game that you boot up every so often, play for a few minutes to an hour or two, and put away again.  It's a clicker, but everything you need to advance through the routes takes time, so you're going to have to do a lot of waiting.  After having the game installed for a year, I largely play once a day for half an hour or so, depending on how far I am into the routes and whether or not I should prestige again.  (Speaking of prestiging, I know the game is free and all but listen: do yourself a favor and buy some diamonds to add extra prestige to your hobby timers.  It makes a world of difference and you will find yourself wondering why you didn't do it sooner.)
(I also highly suggest you get an autoclicker to deal with late-game girls like Rei who require tons and tons of clicks to advance.  Your fingers will thank you for it.)
The game's timers and progress bars keep running even when you have the game closed, and will continue to do so for a week, so no worries if you forget about it for a few days.  You can play as male or female and switch between the two at any point as much as you like, so bonus I guess if you're gender fluid.  The game has like four or five events per years, so something to break up the monotony, but be warned that you can't really expect to complete the events unless you've unlocked at least a few late game girls.
All in all, very pleased with this game and cannot wait for the hinted all-male sequel.

This is the second game produced in the Total War series. You can see its age in some ways. Perhaps most importantly, this is the game just before the break-out hit of Rome: Total War. The mechanics that Total War games are famous for... had not yet been fully created and implimented. In this game, moving into a province will automatically incite a battle at the end of the turn, so there is not slow movement of multiple armies to bury a foe under... or to be buried under.
That said, you can see some of the mechanics beginning to take shape. And it still had good play. Just don't expect it to be "modern". And maybe get it when it is on sale.

For curiosity's sake, Medieval 1 is fun to play, but unless you're super nostaligic for this game you'll probably wish you were playing one of the later entries.
