As an old hacknslash fan I expected to like Torchlight 2. Running around killing stuff, collecting items and gaining exp is right up my alley. Plus it has a lot of positive reviews. Turns out it is not for me.
The minimap is almost useless, no matter if it is sitting in its default spot in the upper right corner or if I move it in the middle of the screen with the hotkey M. This isn't a problem in every area but some of them are huge and then this shortcoming becomes apparent.
Related to this, there is so much backtracking involved... I don't know why they did this. But the quests keep sending me through territory I already cleared. Why? To not fight/loot/gain levels for a while? I really don't get this.
The waypoint system is also extremely crappy. A given area from one act can only be selected if you're in that act. If you are in act 2 and want to travel to some act 3 location you first have to venture into the act 3 town. Only then will the waypoint interface let you select the area you were aiming for from the beginning. Diablo 2 did this better more than a decade earlier.
It feels like every second enemy has some sort of leap back/run away/fly up in the air and be out of reach for a while mechanic. (The last one I'm not sure how it is for ranged characters. I only played a Berserker.) Those type of stupid enemies are in every game of this genre. I know that and I grudgingly accept it. But in TL2 it is so freaking often, it really breaks up the flow of the combat. Chasing those annoying little ranged enemies reminds me of the succubi of Diablo 1 and certainly not in a good way.
The rest of the fights are mostly okay. Nothing more though. Diablo 3s combat is so much better, it is ridiculous.

This game has promise.  Gun play, always a concern for FPS, feels really good -- similar to how
Dirty Bomb played at release before they messed up the gun play months after. Dirty Bomb might have switched it back, but I quit the game, as did many, after they made that change.
Here is what I initially said about Dirty Bomb, and I think it applies to Ballistic Overkill: Think Counter-Strike (gun play) meets Team Fortress 2 (objectives) meets Call of Duty (fast pace)... on steroids. A variety of weapons, great gun play mechanics and smooth movement meets team objectives/goals.
It's an alpha, so there are some minor bugs here and there, and perhaps some slight balancing needed (definitely not as much as others would like to whine about, but then again, I have played *a lot* of FPS games). These are amplified because of the fast pace and quick TTK.
If I'm not mistaken, this runs on the Unity Engine, which is what Rust is also based on.  Read the issues that Rust has had on latency and hacking issues during it's development.

I love old games like this one. At the time the different genres of gaming weren't so clear-cut as they are today. Not having the imperative to be separated in perfect little boxes in order to identify a game as "adventure", "action" etc, resulted in games like Harvester. A game with heavy adventure elements, timed events, combats, different weapons you can actually aim and use, ammo to manage and of course, many deaths.
There is a weird exhilarating sense of freedom in that lack of genre labeling in gameplay. You can't follow the patterns modern adventure games use, so even simple things may have an unexpected aspect to them. This kind of freedom in a game's design makes it more interesting -and of course, at times, harder to beat.*
Unfortunately Harvester also carries with it the sexist tropes of the era, so if you can't stomach good old sexism, a touch of homophobia, gratuitous sex scenes, ladies in lingerie and violence against women then you should probably choose another game. I was able to enjoy it despite of this, but I can't say that this will be the case for everyone.
*But, thankfully,  in case you get stuck, it has one of the most beloved "features" of old games: cheat codes. N00b players everywhere, REJOICE!

Ichi is a little "pong" puzzle sandbox game developed by a small Dutch indie studio.
The look and feel of this game is quite good. There are 2-3 endless music loops, with trumpet, flute, strings, piano and guitar
During gameplay you have rotateable or switchable triangle bumpers to change the direction of the quick moving "pong" ball. On walls the ball is reflected except if they have spikes - then you die. Another interesting elements are a divider, switches or swirl portals. A special ability is to draw a grey reflect line per left mouse hold which is useable once. The main purpose of the game is to collect all yellow coins in a level without dying. That's all. In the standard levels you have also a bonus  for minimum use of actions.
But then you'll find the level creator and begin to generate your own puzzles. After you published them, they can be played by other players, rated, tagged and you earn each time a gamepoint your level is played. So try to make popular puzzles. Unfortunately the game points are highly neccessary to reach at least the 1000 points achievement. It's a real grinder.
You must play or generate tons of rubbish empty levels to get this last achievement. The base game should you take 5 hours of playing but the further point collection bind you even longer. I needed over 30 hours.
One small tip: You can change your game resolution if you press ALT+Shift on startup.

I really enjoy puzzle games that you can play for a set period of time and go back to later, like Kami and Toki Tori 2+. Ichi easily falls into the fun, but challenging puzzler category.
If you like "simple" puzzle mechanics (move the ball to pass through all points) that progressively get harder, then you should really enjoy this game.
The aesthetics are nice and simple and make me think of Ballpoint Universe because the background looks like blueprints drawn on grid paper. The music is nice and cheerful, however, I listen to my own music while I play.
The controls are very simple (mouse only) and instructions are given whenever a new mechanic is introduced. The learning curve is minimal, however, the levels get very challenging, and obtaining an "A" grade for each level can be extremely difficult when you reach the later levels.
In Ichi, your goal is to get a ball to pass through a number of points, in as few moves as possible. Initially, all you have to do is manipulate triangles by click the mouse, causing them to rotate - and change the trajectory of the ball when it comes in contact. Spike hazards on the walls are introduced, and you will see new mechanics like the ability to toggle solid triangles with a mouse click, or even drawing lines on the board to change where the ball will go.
You can also create your own levels and play others', greatly adding to the playability.
The game is a great time puzzler and I've added it to my time fillers between games (or just when I want some down time), alongside KAMI.
Very good, challenging puzzle game, grab it if you are interested.

Brawlhalla is a competent, albeit simplistic platform fighter.
At its core, Brawlhalla is a game about distance: choosing a character with reach to hit without getting hit, about dodging backwards or forwards to avoid getting hit, about camping the sides while the other opponents rack up damage on each other, about hurling bombs from a safe distance for easy kills.
The meta revolves around guns, sycthes, and lances. Guns are short range but devestating, sycthes are quick and have moderate range, and lances can be used to skitter around the arena like a cocaine-addled toddler. Characters have three sets of attacks: unarmed, main, and sub... each with differing movement speeds and moves.
Fights begin in the Unarmed phase, where all attacks have the force of an enraged gnat. This lasts until item drops begin, roughly around the ten second mark. For the first thirty seconds after, attacks will be made, but no player will have reached killable potential yet. This marks the beginning of the fun phase. For the next three minutes, players will trade blows and points in a frantic-ish race to beat down the others.
Each week, a different rotation of temporary characters is available for use. By spending coins (earned in-game), you can permanently unlock characters. It takes roughly six hours of free for all madness to earn enough dosh for the newest character, around three for the oldest. Despite the timewall, I don't feel cheated: most of my time has been spent levelling up my favorite, Lord Drax, for new character customizations.
The individual character level meter adds a sense of progression to the game. By levelling up your character you can unlock new character colors and stat-modifiers. Yet another level meter - the player meter - measures your overall progress. I'm currently level 21, with two characters permanently unlocked.
This game is defined by what it doesn't do, by as much as what it does: counters are omitted, no rage/comeback mechanic exists, and there is no dedicated grab button.
Overall, Brawlhalla is a passable brawler. But it sits in an uncomfortable gulf between casual and technical, one that hurts the competitive aspect and the party aspect alike.
And I can't help but play it.

I played this until I noticed it's a puzzle game that deliberately hides portions of the puzzle. I consider that a fatal flaw, like crossword puzzles that lean on knowledge of movie stars, writers, and made-up abbreviations. I'm ok with puzzles that seem not to lay out all the information, but this is a game about moving a cube around where very early on, objectives are completely hidden from view and require multiple "leaps of faith" that are more "leaps of guess" since you're more likely than not to just go tumbling off the level and back to square one.
It's one thing to hide things in an action platformer, but in puzzle games, I expect every thing I might be assessed on to be either visible or inferrable from the information at hand. I don't count the expectation that somewhere, hidden behind the visible level, there's a platform and a hidden tunnel or two as "inferrable information". What I mean by inferrable information is thinks you can deduce from either explicit information, or from combining previous inferences. I don't get a thrill from blindly solving mazes.
I have no idea how important such trashy design becomes later in the game, but it was present very very quickly and thus dashed my interest very very quickly.

I do not recommend this game. It was part of a Humble Bundle I bought, but it wasn't worth the time. It's pretty short at around 8 hours, but I was never really engaged by it. Always Sometimes Monsters is a solid effort by a small studio, but it's not worth your time. In the first 90 seconds of the game, you're given the option to shoot a person who approaches you. Unless you're a big fan of boring exposition and tedious gameplay, I recommend using your weapon.

Starting with the positive: this game clearly succeeds in its objective. It offers the player several moral choices which influence the story. It gives the player a few opportunities to reflect on these choices or discuss them with characters in the game, and it avoids labelling any particular choice as the "right" or "good" one.
There are a few things, however, which make this game difficult to recommend:
* Most situations are extremely contrived, being even further removed from real-life decisions than most soap operas. Do I let my friend die or commit a major criminal offence to save his life? Do I confront a murderer or run away and never tell anyone?
* The mini-games are terrible. They're more difficult and less fun to play than the 30-year-old games they imitate
* The characters are a bit one-dimensional, including (frustratingly) the player character, whose emotional baggage pretty much dictates the plot of the game

Well, see what comes out of fervently wishing for something. I've loved the indie puzzle revolution of recent years, I only wished for more difficult, more challenging puzzles, because it was really celebration time if a game produced at least a few levels that made your neurons sweat a little. And now enter Snakebird, a cute, nice-looking little game, which is really a ruthless killer of a puzzle game in candy-flavoured disguise.
Snakebird wants you to collect all the fruits on a level and proceding to the exit with every one of your characters. Eating a fruit grows your snakebird with one unit, gravity works in the game, some levels provide you with simple items to help your progress, while the environment sometimes wants to kill you. There. That's it, really - and a collection of really, really tough levels, which manage to be hard without being unfair.
Snakebird is easily the best (non-construction) puzzle game I've played in a long while - I bow before the greatness of the people who designed its levels. For those who are looking for a serious brainy challenge - highly recommended.
The difficulty curve is not balanced at all, you go from easy as a pie to this is hell in 2 just 2 levels.

My problem with this game lies in the extreme narrowness of its solutions, despite the apparent breadth of ways to approach each puzzle. What I mean by this is that it's not enough to solve a part of a puzzle, you have to solve it by making the exact moves the developers envisioned, otherwise the next part of the puzzle will likely be unsolveable, however as you have no way of knowing this, hours of frustration await.
I consider myself a puzzle game enthusiast (I'm particularly fond of the masterful works put out by Zachtronics) and the difficulty in Snakebird is beyond anything I could have imagined. I note that most of the positive reviews here have less than 2 hours of play time and if I'd done a write up after the first dozen puzzles this review would likely be amongst them, however I don't review games unless I've finished them or have lost interest. Sadly, Snakebird falls into the latter category.
It's not a bad game, but when I'm railroaded into solving a puzzle from one particular angle, despite the illusion of a plurality of angles being available, I feel that the game is not being fair.

I have a lot of fond memories towards the first Medieval title which ended up with me replaying it once more with close to all factions. It definitely doesn't deserve all the mixed reviews based on compatibility issues with Win10. I'm using Win10 myself and I might have had the occasional crash but it was nowhere as drastic as reviews here might suggest. Apart from the technical side, Medieval is one of the, if not actually the most beloved game of the entire Total War series to many.
By today's standards I'm personally missing things like army stances, agent actions, general abilities and traits, unit abilities and more formation options, but in its core, Medieval was brilliantly balanced without all these newer generation options and it still plays flawlessly fluent today regarding its timeless mechanics.
On the graphical side it hasn't aged too well, but even with newer titles in the series coming close to eye candy, Total War was never about visual appeal in the first place, but about tactical acuity and planning long military campaigns dozens of turns into the future. It looks abysmal in the first 30 minutes of playing, but it is able to engulf a players consciousness just the way it did 15 years ago.
I personally can and will recommend any Total War title, as I have played and loved all of them, but Medieval will always have a special place in my heart as it was the first Total War I played.

This game is soooo deep.

Recursed is a game of nested structures, patterns, loops, paradoxes, and of course recursion.
Imagine a set of Matryoshka dolls where somewhere down the chain, one of the embedded dolls contains the first outermost doll itself again, with all its contents repeating, which means that deeper down it will again contain itself, and so on. Or imagine two different sets of Matryoshka dolls, the first one containing the second one, and the second one containing the first one, both sets interlacing each other forever. These are the kind of structures that Recursed requires you to construct in order to solve platforming puzzles.
Rooms are chests that you can pick up, carry around, and enter in. By nesting them in other chests, you can shape the world by creating intricate entangled configurations that allow you to reach places otherwise unattainable.
The fun aspect of the game is to make mental maps of such knotted networks of chests, and to keep track of the relationships between rooms as you change them. It is an abstract mental maze of endless loops and infinite regressions. And when you get lost in that maze, it feels like rather than being lost in the game, you are instead lost in you own mind, since you are the one making the layout of that maze as you go along.
There is more than chests to the game, new gameplay elements are introduced throughout. For each new chapter, it starts straightforwardly but ultimately the concepts are pushed to the very limits of their imaginable uses. The puzzles are quite inventive and the difficulty can reach very high levels that will push you into extreme mental contortions.
I absolutely recommend this game to anyone who enjoys puzzles relying on logic and mathematical ideas.

A word to fellow female players: if Bearverly didn't sell you on the game, then hopefully this will.
I first discovered discovered Crush Crush through an update on Yandere Sim and was slightly interested since I enjoy casual and otome games, but I was highly skeptical because dating games with an all-female cast tend to be very...
, I guess, for lack of a better term.  With the huge boobs and the cliche writing and the blatant blatant pandering to horny boys with disposable income.  I looked at the screenshots and read the dialogue and decided that since it didn't look to be an all-out ♥♥♥♥♥ fest and it was free, I might as well give it a shot.
You can tell by the number of hours I have clocked into this game how well that turned out.
The characters are engaging and full of personality.  They're funny, they're angry, and they clearly have lives outside of the protagonist.  Since they all more or less start out disliking you at the beginning of their routes, you have to actually get to know and befriend them to advance.  Let me repeat this: if you're not even friends with a girl first, they don't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about you romantically.  That is a huge breath of fresh air compared to most of the romantic content I've ingested before.
Like Hunny Pop, the game takes a harem approach to courting the girls.  Unlike Hunny Pop however, the girls are all aware of eachother and the fact that you're dating all of them at once, so if you have any reservations about lying and cheating to a girl you've romanced, no worries: they genuinely do not care.  (Well, with the exception of Yandere-Chan, for obvious reasons, but despite her hilariously inept attempts to murder the other girls in order to be your one and only, she still seems to get along with them fairly well.)
As for the gameplay itself, I'm going to be blunt.  This is not a game that you play for hours on end.  This is a game that you boot up every so often, play for a few minutes to an hour or two, and put away again.  It's a clicker, but everything you need to advance through the routes takes time, so you're going to have to do a lot of waiting.  After having the game installed for a year, I largely play once a day for half an hour or so, depending on how far I am into the routes and whether or not I should prestige again.  (Speaking of prestiging, I know the game is free and all but listen: do yourself a favor and buy some diamonds to add extra prestige to your hobby timers.  It makes a world of difference and you will find yourself wondering why you didn't do it sooner.)
(I also highly suggest you get an autoclicker to deal with late-game girls like Rei who require tons and tons of clicks to advance.  Your fingers will thank you for it.)
The game's timers and progress bars keep running even when you have the game closed, and will continue to do so for a week, so no worries if you forget about it for a few days.  You can play as male or female and switch between the two at any point as much as you like, so bonus I guess if you're gender fluid.  The game has like four or five events per years, so something to break up the monotony, but be warned that you can't really expect to complete the events unless you've unlocked at least a few late game girls.
All in all, very pleased with this game and cannot wait for the hinted all-male sequel.

You click/wait until it gets slow, then you reset and progress faster each time.
You don't want to take time?  Spend money, buy gems.
Or you can earn gems in-game through achievements and use those to upgrade like spending money.
You want to *support the devs because you like the game?*  Spend money.
I don't understand people that call the game a scam or say the devs are using cash-grab tactics.  The game is FREE and at no point is the primary game limited by a pay-wall.  Outfits and such do cost money.  Guess what?  Someone had to develop that stuff.  They spent their time and talents to make it for you and they're asking something in return since the game does not contain ads or any other way to make money off people playing.
If you have a job, would you do that job without being paid?
Of course not.  If you're going to flip burgers and smell like grease at the end of the day or have to wash concrete out of places you'd rather not mention, you'd expect to be paid for these things.
Anyone who feels entitled to everything for free really needs to develop something worthwhile themselves and give it away for free, just to get some perspective on seeing your time and efforts float off with no recompense.  Yes, I know, many artists do this, but now give up your day job (assuming you have one), give away your work for free, and place hope that someone will pay you for the efforts you've given away.

I love this game... I really do, but I know it has issues.  Before getting into the issues, i would like to tell you to at least give the game a chance.  It's free, you won't lose anything.
The grind in this game is the worst i have ever had the displeasure of seeing.  If you want to try using an LMG, you have to either pay around $50, or grind for anywhere from 30-100 hours depending on how skilled and lucky you are.  This is only slightly more than the other weapons, like a bolt-action rifle or a decent smg.  And that's just to unlock the damn thing.  To actually buy it will take another 5-40 hours depending on which class you play.  The grind just keeps getting worse too.  Recently the only real way to make cash (piloting) was nerfed again, instead of doing the smart thing and raising other classes credit rates.  There are also some guns that cost more than tanks, planes, and cars, which makes sense I guess, but isn't very realistic.
A lot of gameplay problems are caused by non-gameplay issues.  For example the matchmaker will pit players who have just started playing and still have starting gear with 1000+ hour veterans who will tear them to shreds, leading to a dull one-sided game.  This also tends to make the other problems come to the forefront.
The tanking in this game makes no sense to me, and mostly relies on how far into the grind you are.  If you have the top tier tank for that weight class, congrats!  You will now destroy all your enemies with ease.  If you don't, get ready to be repeatedly destroyed before you can get any damage off.  This problem only gets worse in war, were your ♥♥♥♥♥♥ light tank can and will fight heavy tanks.  An old issue for tanks aswell is the anti-tank weapons.  It takes one infantry on a bike to easily destroy any tank in the game.  And you'd think it would be harder to take out heavy tanks, but it is infact easier as they are too slow to run away.  The only advantage they have is it takes one more AT shot to kill them, which rarely helps.
Infantry also will struggle against tanks if no one on your team brought AT weaponry, as the free panzerfausts provided on each map are sparse, weak, placed in easily camped spots, and hard to use.  Infantry vs infantry combat comes down to who has the better modded gun and better badges most of the time.  There are also snipers everywhere in the maps as  the dense forests provide excelent cover.  It doesn't help that snipers can 1 shot you if you aren't wearing heavy set gold.  The repair costs for weapons you mod are unbelievable, and any form of explosive, including those so important AT weapons, are so expensive you might as well not even have them because you can't use them.  Recon suffer from having nothing to set them apart from an infantry sniper except for the camoflouge badge and there armored cars.  The camoflouge badge makes it so the game doesn't show the kill cam on you, so you can basically never be detected if you hide far away.  The armored cars are also super OP, they're escentially light tanks, but faster.
Planes are the worst balanced part of the game.  The starting recon planes are useless and can be shot down by literally anything, even normal rifles.  The medium planes are dominated by the yak if Germany doesn't have two infantrymen go pilot to bring their total to 6.  America really got the shaft on medium planes, no one flies them, they're hard to aim due to the lack of gun convergance, and have bombs too small and hard to aim to do anything.  Then 3 new medium fighters got added and only one of them was remotely useful.  The american and russian ones are utter garbage, and the german one is just a slower yak.  Then the heavy fighters are dominated by the p-38 lightning who go uncontested and are just flying tanks.  Fog maps are a death sentance, but i'm not sure if they even show up anymore because reto is so bad at communicating to the playerbase.
The game itself runs very poorly as Reto decided it was a great idea to try and build there own engine with their limited resources.  If you don't have a stacked PC you'll have to turn the down all the graphics settings and possibly the resolution making it impossible to see anything more than 100 meters away.  Then there's the time Reto broke their own sound system.  They tried making walls affect the way things sounded, but ended up completely screwing up the way that things like distance and direction came through.  Someone shooting right next to you could sound like it was from a mile in the other direction.  Though this only affected part of the community, and I believe they fixed it, this just goes to show the incompetance of Reto.  And when people did find a way to fix this by removing the feature with a custom patch, Reto removed this solution.
I'm willing to give Reto a little lee-way because they're such a small company, but that isn't an excuse for how bad they are at their jobs.  I honestly believe they have tasked marketing, customer service, PR, and all of the interactions with the community down to 1 person who just masquerades as a couple different people because we get actual news from them so rarely.  When we do get news though, it's usually pretty small.  Reto also seems to be incredibly bad at keeping promises.  I remember they said 3 new maps would be out by the end of the year (A couple months at the time).  That was almost a year ago, and they have released nothing that I know of about these maps.  Instead they put a new map on the prototype server which I am sure will also go nowhere.  Those maps where desperately needed too, there are only 10 maps in total.  Granted they are big, and they each have 4 lines, you'll have gotten bored of them fairly soon.  Retos updates are usually small too.  It's rare an update is more than a few minor graphics changes or balance changes.  Reto doesn't even tell you all the times when these happen.  They once made it so shooting the para-planes didn't give you experience or money.  And they didn't tell anyone!  They just did it and hoped no one noticed.  They thought none of us would notice.  That just shows how little they actually respect and care for their players.  When people make criticisms, often times their posts will be deleted or closed with out Reto even taking any of them into account.  There well known player by the name of TheFlyingCow has talked to them, met them in person, and even guest starred on dev streams.  He made a forum post compiling the most common legitimate complaints and suggestions from the community.  So far only a few of them have been taken to heart, and they seemed to be already in the works.  The updates that actually do change the game seem to be taking the game in a downward spiral.  Bad weapon changes, updates screw up peoples performance, introducing new bugs that don't fix old ones.  The double shot glitch has been around for years and has still not been fixed.  Reto can't even get balance changes right.  They either nerf something into the ground, or buff it to god tier before nerfing it.  Reto doesn't even give buffs.  They just keep making weapons nearly unuseable.
This game still has so much potential, but until Reto steps up their game it won't reach it.  The only reason this game is still alive is because it's the only one that fills its niche.  Once something steps up to it, it'll be like the death of tf2 all over again.  Who knows maybe it'll make Reto finally start to change, and make the game better.

text: Still fine but less greater than Deus Ex 3

Adam Jensen: "Where I come from cops are supposed to be the good guys."
Aid worker in the Utulek complex: "On what planet is that?"
Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is the second installment in the beloved franchise's Adam Jensen storyline. Jensen, now a double agent working for the Juggernaut collective led by Janus and Interpol, is assigned to find the culprit(s) behind a train station bombing in Prague. The story exarcebates itself into a consipiracy of global ramifications once more, in time. The story is still a step down from Human Revolution, but I consider this not a flaw by itself. The story is a more down-to-earth type of scenario after the events of Human Revolution. The Adam Jensen series of Deus Ex was intended to be a trilogy of games and it shows. I won't spoil the plot, but there are many story threads that are left loose after the ending credits. The story here is still good, though. And definately one which I enjoyed a lot.
The story in Mankind Divided involves a lot of topics that are now prevalent in the real world, namely racism, bigotry, and predjudice. This political theme with terrorism and law-making may or may not be your cup of tea, but I personally enjoyed it. The game does not spoonfeed you any political message, however.
The gameplay is very similar to Human Revolution. Adam can roam the streets of Prague and hack or break his way into pretty much every household or storage. Once again, you can utilize a stealthy or non-stealthy, lethal or non-lethal approach however you see fit. There is also a special achievement for never setting off any alarms or killing people, including bosses. Some augmentations available are new, but there certain oldies make a return as well, such as the Icarus landing system, Typhoon, and Strong arms. Some of the augments are throwaways, however, and rather useless.
Technically speaking the new graphics engine is pretty GPU-intesive and can crunch your graphics card's prowess really easilly. The variety of settings is commendable, giving ample opportunity for everyone to tweak the game to your liking. The game is not badly optimized, just very heavy. I encountered some bugs and glitches, mainly audiobugs and some floating textures. Occasionally, the game also crashed to desktop. The animations are still terrible, however. The movement of the character models resembles that of animatronic pirates in Disney World.
A tempest in a teapot emerged when it was revealed that the game featured microtransactions. You can play the game from start to finish without ever seeing them in-game, and you can max out your own Jensen with all the bells and whistles without resorting to any pay-to-win scenarios. It was confirmed that Eidos Montreal was forced to include the microtransactions in the game pretty late into the development cycle. Who forced them? You guessed it, the publisher, Square Enix. Shame on them.
There is a breach mode available, but this is nothing but a waste of time. A NG+ is also available once you finish the game, letting you get back into action with all previously acquired praxis kits and augmentations.
The game took me a whopping 31 hours to finish, so it was definately not short. However, if you pay less attention to the world and its inhabitants, you can inadvertently skip much of the content, like side-quests and mini-missions. I recommend everyone to take their time with the game and savor it.
Pros:
+ A play-it-like-you-want experience which supports multiple playthroughs and styles
+ A game world filled with stuff to do and find, more so than meets the eye
+ Proper amount of gameplay (anywhere from 15 to 30 hours)
Cons:
- Immersion is hindered by jagged character animations
- Bugs and glitches
- GPU-intensive, eventhough the game doesn't look particularly demanding or beautiful
Adam Jensen's newest outing is a good one, despite certain flaws. While there may not be a new Deus Ex game for a while, Mankind Divided proves that the market for enthralling singleplayer games is far from dead. The Adam Jensen story line is left unfinished in Mankind Divided so now we can only wait for a sequel.

Independently of its sequels this is one of the best games of 2016. Solid shooting mechanics coupled with an extensive set of possible aug-configurations make the game rewarding and fun.
The story is well developed and ambitious, but suffers from being a slightly predictable variation over the theme of the last three main installments in the franchise, which makes it difficult to woo the player.
The game does depend on you as a player to "supply" part of the role playing. For example the experience is more intense and rewarding if you stick to your invented moral compass and not just roll with what seems most convenient in every situation.
Bottom line is that there are few games like this, and although you could always argue it could be better it is still one of the best as long as we do not compare to what basically amounts to childhood memories of DX1.

I have to be honest, this one was a let down.  If you don't want to read the rest of the review: Go buy Prey instead.  It's a fantastic game in the same vein as Deus Ex, and it manages to do just about everything this game does, but with more polish and better mechanics.
Mankind Divided is functional but I encountered several bugs on the first play through, many of which required complete re-loads to an old save.
The inventory system is absolutely godawful.  Many times it glitches, requires repeat clicks, is slow and just generally clunky.  Which is a pain because you have to use it a lot to balance the small space you have.  Don't even get me started on the forced and completely repeated conversations you have to have every time you talk to a vendor, only to sell your items using a computer anyways.
The default hotkeys for abilities are the F keys on PC which is a terrible decision.  You can and should remap them, because it's about as clunky as it can be to place them there, and it clearly lays them out as though they were on a D-Pad for a controller.  It feels like a pretty terrible port from console.
Many abilities feel underwhelming, and some just downright useless.  Add in that they're hard to activate, and many times it's faster to just skip them entirely.  Especially if you haven't remapped them off the F keys.
Which brings me around to... My Biggest complaint: About halfway through the game I realized it's just not that much fun.
- Enemies are predictable and easy to deal with on every difficulty.
- Mechanics for hacking are essentially just a random roll of the die, with your odds altered by abilities. (The exception is remote hacking, which I actually enjoyed).
- Vents are obvious and everywhere, and they all look identical. Too hard to spot the giant vents? Use vision and they literally make them glow. (They'll also let you make lootable items glow, for the ultimate in lazy).
- Most conversations don't have any variance at all, and the few that do are easy to guess (or if that's too hard, they give you an aug that tells you the "right" options).
- Side quests are WAY out to the side, most without any real tie-in to the main story line, and several that just kind of leave things hanging.
- There's no real feeling of consequence to your actions, good or bad.
- The AI is... bad, police/nuetrals will shoot you on the spot for hacking if they see you, but you can happily walk in and pick up everyone's credit chips without getting even a second glance.  Literally in front of them. Oh, and using a multitool to hack for you is apparently not going to get a second glance.
- The combat AI is just as bad.  Enemies drawn by noise can be taken down in literally the same spot until the room is empty. Make some noise, wait, press Q, repeat. "Gee golly, better go investigate the noise. who cares if all my buddies are missing, and that suspicious pile of bodies near the noise is absolutely not a problem!"
- And to add insult to injury, they want you to use a phone app to scan items you can pickup in game. Or earn extra items by buying their phone game.  Which they hint at continuously.
So eventually I just wanted the game to end.  Which it did, in a fairly lackluster finale. Which is honestly too bad, because the setting itself is actually pretty damn fantastic.
The setting is hands down the only redeeming factor in the game.  It's well thought out and immersive. It's too bad the rest of the game really isn't that great.

Phew.  What to say about Deus Ex: Mankind Divided.  I am giving this a tentative thumbs up, but if I had a choice it would land somewhere square in the middle.
Story Wise - Human Revolution is much more engaging & interesting.  However, if you are a story-oriented player, it's always interesting to see where Adam ends up after Panchea.
Gameplay wise - We see some additional augmented abilities, which can add a dash more fun to it.  Otherwise, it's an old hand after playing Human Revolution.  Everything is as expected here.  I actually had about 7 praxis points I never spent in this game.  I was reserving them in case I needed to pick up a useful augment during the boss fight, but that turned out to be a bust.  Supplies are extremely plentiful, even on Give me Deus Ex difficulty.
Boss? What Boss?
Big problem for me, although I thought the boss fights in Human Revolution were weak, the boss fight here is practically non-existant.  Although, technically there IS a boss to fight, he'll die if you just give him a cross-eyed look. (and this was on the hardest first play thru difficulty to boot).  You think I am being hyperbolic, trust me, I'm not.
I've not yet ran through on I Never Asked For This (NewGame+) thus this critque is applicable to first playthrough highest difficulty.
Summation:  If you're looking for something to really challenge you tactically in game play, this isn't for you.  If you enjoy story-centric games and are a fan of Deus Ex, might as well grab this on sale.  I really enjoy playing Adam, and seeing where his story goes, I just wish, the game tested his badassery a hell of a lot more.  It's a soft recommend.  Very soft.

This is a 2D side-scrolling stealth game where you play as an unnamed ninja protagonist who gains mystic powers from the tattoos (the titular "mark") that are granted during the plot.  Your clan is under attack from mercenary forces and you are to protect your home and defend your clan's honor.
Upon beating the game, you unlock a new game plus (NG+) option that gives additional replayablity.  To summarize, the story is awesome, the gameplay is original, and you should definitely play this.

The Plot - For me it's OK. It looks a little foreseeable at begining, but it acquires some philosophical aspects, such as the ninja code of honor, the most positive quality in my opinion, what creates a reflexive and excellent end.
The Gameplay - The best feature in this game, Beacause there is a total freedom in the behavior of the player in the game. You can be a stealth player, not more natural, it's a ninja game, but nothing willl stop you if you kill a guard, but remember that you will reach more points if you don't kill anyone or don't activat the alarm. However, the symbols of the game are the puzzles. There are many of them, of variables difficulties, in objective or secret forms, what makes the duration of the gameplay get more extended (between 15h~20h depending the style you choose) but not monotonous, and without them the game would be very easy.
The Graphics - For me it's OK. The 2D scenarios give the game an old school appearance, but the movimentation are very fluid and the well animated cutscenes give a modern view of the situation. Wth the 2D, there isn't many details in the ambients, but, in the gameplay, it haven't made any difference anyway.
The Soundtrack - Excellent, especially in the end. The instrumental musics mix with different situations and ambients in a perfect way.
Result; I think the game is one of the best in Steam, it isn't expensive, at least in my country. This one worth be played.

A thoroughly enjoyable 2D stealth platformer. Tight and responsive controls, nice art style, decent game length, and spot-on sound effects and musical score are all tied together with a good story to make this a very enjoyable game. Levels are open enough that you typically have a few choices on how best to attack (or avoid) obstacles. As you progress you will unlock various tools of the trade, allowing you to better hone your play style. The game handles equally well with keyboard & mouse and with a controller.
My only issue is that Mark of the Ninja is not overly challenging until late into the game. A fairly minor issue, as half the fun is playing with the AI.
I'm hopeful there will be a sequel, or even another game from Klei Entertainment in a similar vein as Mark of the Ninja. Though even if this stays as a standalone experience, I'll still enjoy returning time and time again.
I would gladly pay the full asking price of $15 for this game, though it regularly goes on sale. Highly recommended to pick up whenever on sale.

A throwback to the 80s where cyborgs, aliens, lasers and mutated beings were the norm…or at least we thought there were…You are a Cyber Commando and your mission is: To Save the World. An over-the-top FPS shooter with great soundtracks and a cyberpunk setting. Quite the reminisce if you ask me.
Straight out from what the future would’ve looked like if you were imagining it from the 1980s. Neon lights, multicolour lasers and robotic arms are seen throughout the entire game. Some might even say they are too bright.
It’s a very simple – “get the girl and save the world because you’re the only one who can do it!”. I guess it’s the 1980s and this would be the norm, but it just seemed a bit too generic for me really; they should’ve tried something more unique as with sticking with the original theme. Nonetheless, the game will feed you a ton of 80s references and over the top comedy that will keep you entertained for the rest of the game.
Do I even need to say anything here?? I mean it’s just pure awesomeness with everything about the soundtracks. Especially the voice acting and the minigun sound…they are so satisfying to hear.
You either go in quiet and unnoticed or just go in full metal mode and barge in the room with your shotgun, it’s up to you. You’ll have fun either way. The weaponry, the enemies and the vehicles are well refined to have an enjoyable gameplay. The only downsides are the random frame drops when the game AutoSaves and it requires Uplay for you to be able to play.
Asking for £11.99 is a bit too much for the amount of time you can complete this game (around 6-8 hours), it’s not worth the ‘pound per hour’ if you’re wondering that. But it is certainly worth getting when it goes on a sale. Then I’d totally recommend it.

You may find yourself pushing forward just because you want to discover all the unreal wonders of Harvest.
Unfortunately the game is not remastered or anything, it's emulated through DOSbox with most of the inconveniences of the initial release, very low resolution, cutscenes problems, infamous twitchy and not-fun-at-all combat.
Another huge problem would be second part of the game, it revolves around combat and is more linear, like most of the other point'n'clicks.
What's more about that part is mandatory item hunting, as the game does not allow the slightest backtracking then, which means that if you haven't picked up a crucial puzzle piece and saved on only one slot.....well, have fun starting from monday.
I picked it up knowing what it is, and for those who don't, but are curious- some guides/walkthroughs and multiple saves may make the game playable instead of tedious.
I like some of the more original and funny games like this one, but then again- I always was a kidder.

It's a shame, because this game was delayed two years for the programming alone, which seems to have done more harm to the project than good.

$5 might seem a bit steep given the simplicity, and I'm not sure of the point of it coming in a two-pack at all, but it is actually a solidly-made game and easily worth the cost. Plus, if you end up really loving it, you're not going to run out of things to do in it - there's over 21,000 user-made levels even after you beat the 60 that ship with the game.
(Note: I beat all but one of the premade levels back before this game was on Steam and haven't really been interested in playing it again, hence my relative lack of achievements/playtime here. I still recommend it, though.)

Awesome little puzzle game. Like advertised: easy to play, but damn it can get twist your brain in a knot. The goal is to collect all yellow rings in the level with an orb that bounces around automatically.

Ichi is a simple looking puzzle game where you guide a yellow ball through a maze with the goal to pass through all the gates before you die.  The simple conceit is that you control the maze with only a left-click of the mouse.
There are various elements in the maze, blue triangles that reflect the ball 90° red triangles that also reflect the ball 90° but also rotate 90° with each mouse click, another sort of triangle that can be turned invisible at a click allowing the ball to pass through, objects that are destroyed after a single hit, teleporters, switches and splitters that spit out 2 balls for twice the fun!  Every click will change the state of the maze, you can't set and forget, you have to constantly adjust and watch the ball like a hawk.
Though the most important tool is if you click and hold the mouse, you can draw a single use short grey wall where the ball is currently traveling.  As you get to the higher level puzzles you will have to reflect the ball multiple times a level to succeed.  Whether it's a bug or intended, there is a small but noticeable delay from when you click and hold and where the wall starts and this will have to be taken into account.
The graphics are quite good, the game is presented as though drawn in pen on graph paper though the mobile origins are obvious, giant buttons!  Levels range from simplistic to quite challenging and you receive a grade from A to C based on the number of moves, clicks, you make.  There is also an easy to use editor and an inbuilt publish and rate system with more that 20000 levels available online!
While there are only 60 official levels, there probably should have been more, in the release and you'll probably be done with those in 2-3 hours, this is a fantastic little puzzler presented with style that's very worthy your time.

Ichi's blueprint philosophy extends into the design beyond the colorful and inviting crayon aesthetic. While it comes packed with 60 premade levels for you to complete, these are merely a teaser for the main course that is making and playing user created levels. It's a one touch game with more depth than it gives itself credit for, but is simple enough to be instantly understandable to anyone that gives it a go.
As I said, Ichi is a puzzle game that relies on a single touch to interact with the various mechanics within levels, with the goal being to bounce your ball around the screen collecting all the dots without running into spikes or getting overzealous with your taps (which will earn you a lower grade). The items you control start off simply, with triangles that rotate or disappear with a touch, but then evolve into more complex tools from switches to portals and various others which add upon each other to make puzzles more complex and engaging. Despite this, my biggest issue with Ichi is that all the developer made levels are surprisingly easy, to where I rarely felt any challenge from them up to the very end. Ultimately they act more like a tutorial to the user generated levels than something to fill a game with in their own right.
Thankfully, with already 20,000+ created and more popping up every day, there are tons and tons of absolutely brilliant user created puzzles that will give you a far greater challenge if you want it. A handy tagging and rating system makes sorting through them easier than you'd expect, and a simple (if slightly over restrictive) editor allows you to forge your own puzzles should you feel no one has made one that's just quite right for you yet. It took a long time to get here, but in the end Ichi is just as much fun as it was when I first played it ages ago long before it managed to get on Steam, and can recommend it without reservation to anyone interested in an immensely easy to put up and hard to put down puzzler.

One of the best stealth games, hell, one of the best video games period.
This game just gets everything right in the gameplay department.  Nothing feels cheap, and there was never a time where I dies due to cheap controls, and there was not one game mechanic that I thought didn't work.
One of my favorite things in this game, is you basically choose your own difficulty with your play style.
Want to do a no-kill/no alarm playthrough, where you only kill the 2 enemys required to progress?  That's your hard mode.
Want to stealth kill everyone, and make sure nobody's left alive to see you?  That's your easy mode.
If you do a no-kill/no alarm playthrough, you will feel so accomplished once you win.  You were sneaky to get past the 100s of enemys without being seen, by planning out your movements and paths, and that's a fantastic feeling.  This game is also very forgiving, no matter how you play.  There are no lives, so that means if you mess up on an optional objective, just die, or restart from last checkpoint, and you can have another go.  This also goes for when you are trying to not raise alarms, so if you get seen, just let them kill you, and it won't register that mistake at the end of the level.  And from what I've seen, there are no punishments for dying, so you can retry as many times as you need to.
The idea of being able to see how loud your actions (or anyone else's actions, for that matter) are, by seeing a circle around said action as fantastic game design.  You can even see your enemy's line of sight, so you can effectively plan around everything.
Literally the only thing I can think of that might be annoying with this game is the voice acting is a bit lacking, especially in-game.  But even with the "meh" voice acting, they still managed to make the story and gameplay engaging!
Also, I'm not spoiling anything, but damn, this game has one of the most powerful endings I have ever seen.
Klei did a fantastic job with this game, and I hope for more DLC, or maybe a sequel(or prequel) at some point!

Mark of the Ninja reeled me in with its smooth gameplay and interesting stealth mechanics, but after spending time with it, the game seems to have some serious flaws, especially when trying to stay non-lethal. I will cautiously recommend this game due to some design decisions and bugs that impeded my experience. I'll go over some of my major issues with the game while also heavily recommending that people play through this 2D game as stealth-action first before doing attempting a non-lethal playthrough, at least until you have more unlocks. You can easily revisit chapters for replay or go straight into New Game +.
I'll start off with the line-of-sight or fog-of-war system. I don't enjoy blurring in my games for the most part. I tend to turn off depth of field, motion blur, and other things of the sort. Mark of the Ninja has some kind of fog-of-war system where sections of the level will become blurred if your character can't see it. This can become detrimental when it comes to spotting climbable surfaces (especially ceilings) resulting in confusion where there shouldn't be any. This is due to fog-of-war blurring out the surface,
. I tend to figure it out after x number of deaths/restarts. It's a very annoying game mechanic to deal with when just trying to navigate through a level. I suppose there's Far Sight, but sometimes the foreground interferes since everything the environment becomes mostly teal. I've only used that skill for navigating through trap rooms or when I need to find out what switches affect since it requires you to be stationary. Far Sight:
The checkpoint system is downright annoying. Adding a quicksave/load would've alleviated a lot of frustration. It's not fun to repeatedly kill the same four enemies or navigating through the same section just to reach the part that troubled me. I had multiple instances where guards didn't behave the same way despite doing the same things and they'd change the direction they're looking at resulting in a raised alarm and manually restarting to the previous checkpoint to repeat the process. Twice, in two different levels, I triggered a checkpoint right before an alert went off and died soon after. Both times the game respawned me, but counted those as detections which I found out at the results screen. Another section had me platforming through a couple screens before I could finally try my hand again at attaining a scroll undetected. These checkpoints turn a fun game into a tedious and boring experience. I could've saved so much time if I could load the game right at the part where I'm having trouble instead of constantly heading back to a checkpoint. Occassionally, the checkpoints will put you in a different spot than usual too. I don't know why.
I've ran into maybe only a handful of bugs, but in the level "Above A Bottomless Chasm" I forced myself through its incredibly frustrating and buggy last part. Your character is trapped in a room for a set amount of time and you must survive until the door opens so you can escape. Over half an hour, the game gave me two checkpoints at the halfway mark, one that inside of a hiding spot directly in front of a dog (they can sniff you out and alert nearby guards) while the other placed me in the darkness by some door. The first one especially was incredibly infuriating since there was no way to disable the hound. I spent dozens of deaths trying to figure out how to escape the dog in a way where it wouldn't bark and alert all the guards. After many attempts, I finally succeeded by throwing multiple darts at it repeatedly to break its AI so I could make my escape. I ended up dying and restarting in that other checkpoint in the darkness. It could've improved my situation were it not for the second problem.
The second problem with Above A Bottomless Chasm besides its bugged checkpoints in the last room is its bugged detection of dead dog(s) that I didn't kill which results in an alert. Yes, that's right, the enemy releases poison which kills their own dogs, but the enemy soldiers will "discover" the dead dogs and raise the alarm. This bug results in all that work staying in stealth being thrown out the window. That's a big slap in the face when you spend a lot of time in a level only to be robbed of your accomplishment by an unavoidable bug. I say unavoidable because I restarted many, many times to try and save the stealth rating only to consistently see an alert that I didn't cause pop up. Here's my solution for those that reach this part, immediately kill as many soldiers as you can hide before the poison starts popping up everywhere.
Stealth kills have an unnecessary quick-time prompt (direction + x) that isn't consistent with enemies depending on your approach. I dislike them and they occasionally force me to restart when I mess one up. Just try and take it slow; make sure you're reading the direction correctly.
Other than those aforementioned issues, I do really enjoy the game and there are very fun ways to dispatch enemies in the game. There are so many ways to kill enemies that stealth-action is really the way to go the first time around to maximize your enjoyment. I really like the spike mines, killing opponents from hiding spots, causing chandeliers to crush soldiers, and using smoke bombs that have been upgraded to choke enemies caught in it which make them vulnerable to executions. The variety is quite nice, especially when you make use of the environment, your distraction items, and lethal items.
The stealth involves not just the use of items and killing techniques, but taking advantage of the darkness, creating openings by destroying lights, and avoiding the line-of-sight of enemies. So what can a person expect? You can use hiding spots, move between hiding spots if they're close enough, throw darts at destructible lights, turn off lights by destroying fuse boxes, and moving between lightning strikes or risk being exposed. The darkness is important for you since most enemies can only see directly in front of themselves unless they have goggles, a flashlight, or are dogs. Dogs have a sniff radius; give them a wide berth. You can also hear enemy footsteps when they're not in view and use that to sneak around or ambush them. This game does a pretty good job at making you feel like a ninja. Oh, and don't forget to hide the bodies to earn extra points and not raise any alarms.
Finally, you can expect some platforming, usually in the form of avoiding lasers, scaling walls, and grappling places. The game also features challenge rooms hidden within levels which emphasizes the puzzle/platformer aspect of this game since they're abstract.
Alright, go and have fun. Don't start off as non-lethal since the game isn't balanced in its favor until you know the levels; the enemies in the levels; what loadout to bring, certain enemies require different tactics; and have most of the unlocks, many of which aid stealthy or non-lethal approaches. It's been more than 15 years since the dawn of the Wild Animal Racing franchise on PC and the series is still going strong. Indeed, since its inception Wild has become a household name, seeing six iterations, over 10,000 tracks, and spawning millions upon millions of players worldwide. Every version brings something subtly different to the table, and everyone seems to have a favorite amidst a franchise that never quite changes, but never really stays the same from game to game. Ask players which characters they prefer, what levels top the list, and which items need to stay or go, and you'll get as many diverse responses are there are gamer types. And yet, most PC fans will agree that the Wild Animal Racing games are enjoyable single-player experiences and addictive multiplayer ones.
Supposing you're new to the phenomenon -- hey, this is Steam after all; you might come from that coveted "blue ocean" corner -- Wild Animal Racing, like its predecessors, is a pick-up-and-play racer drenched in zoo themed characters and overrun with outlandish track designs. You can race against foes or engage them in vehicular battle -- not with guns, mind you, but spiked wheels and missles. This is a Steam game, remember. The concept may seem downright childish as you read about it, but the end experience is both charming and fun.
Wild Animal Racing has never really been full-blown "hardcore," and neither has it been wholly "casual," a truth that Paul Bird has fully embraced this time around. Wild Animal Racing comes complete with three Grand Prix speed classes – 50cc, 100cc, and 150cc – with the expected unlockables after that. Each character fits distinctly in a race class, has specific light, medium, or heavy cars to choose from based on that class, and there's of course a healthy dose of local multiplayer via classic versus ad battle modes. If you grew up with Wild Animal Racing, you will not find the Steam iteration full of pioneering new play modes, which might prove disappointing for some. At the same time, though, Paul Birds's series was founded on a winning formula and we can therefore sympathize with any reluctance to break from it.
Still, there are some welcomed additions. Not only does Wild Animal Racing for Steam ship with a Noose -- a shell that encapsulates the neck and makes the process of dying more believable -- but now there are bikes, Animal support both on and off the tracks, 32 total stages (half new, half classic), as well as a few new items thrown into the mix. It all feels and looks like Wild Animal Racing, mind you, but the extra bells and whistles are definitely recognizable But you knew that. The real question here is how exactly the game plays, what works and what doesn't, and whether or not you need to start sending hate mail to Paul Bird for screwing up your now-teenage baby.
Overall, Wild Animal Racing is extremely rewarding and we take into account the Noose (yes, we just complimented a suicide tactic…), the inclusion of IR and non-IR supported menus, the seamless integration of console Animals, and never-ending laundry list of SteamConnect24 and Steam Wi-Fi Connection features, the continued support of traditional control schemes, the retro levels, and much more. For the thick-minded, Wild Animal Racing offers a seemingly never-ending amount of content. Some of it you'll love and some you won't want to play through a second time.
For the first time ever on a Steam console, the online portion trumps the single-player offering, and we'll explain why. Both 50cc and 100cc races are fine in Grand Prix, though the exclusion of the Wild Animal Racing-like cooperative two player GP is a serious misstep in our opinion -- you can certainly go in and create your own GP competitions, but they work separately from the normal GP cup progression. Road Cup is a bit boring, World Toar starts to mix things up with some decent track design, Rally Cup really starts to take off with some superb levels and true innovation, and a Magical Cup that rounds things off with one of, if not the, best LSD trips  in franchise history.
Overall, I give this game a 10/10

Snakebird is one of those rare games that feels absolutely solid.  Presentation is great.  Controls are great.  Difficulty is superbly devious.
It seems simple:  Navigate all the snakebirds on the screen, to the rainbow portal, eating all fruit on the level in the process.   But you will learn to hate gravity.
The graphics and solid controls takes one back to Super Nintendo days and are a joy to look at.
But the heart of this game is the superb puzzles.  53 levels to complete in total.  Millions of hair strands to remove from your head in the process.
No two levels are the same and yet, sometimes you solve a puzzle purely on luck.  Try to do the same level a second time and you have no clue how you completed it the first time...
Even though most of the puzzles are super hard, stick with it.  Figuring out a level feels extremely satisfying and most of the time you learn something that will help in the coming levels.
Greatly recommended for anybody up for a serious challenge.

The purest, most effective stealth experience available, in a novel 2D environment. This game perfectly pitches character progression and challenge, marrying atmosphere and threat with power-fantasy.
It's in actuality a puzzle game; if you are detected and discovered, the punishment is rarely less than swift death and a fast reload. Perhaps punishment is the wrong word, as the game never penalises you for failing to outwit one of it's systems, but challenges you to do so with all the timing, strategy and grace of a true ninja. This approach to stealth is something many other titles avoid, especially AAA games with long loading times, which give players to option of fighting their way out of their mistakes. While this may avoid frustrating players with constant failure, 'Mark of the Ninja' proves that less is more when it comes to the mastery of stealth.

Where do I start with this...
Need for Speed Undercover has been bashed, beaten & overall just despised by the entire Need for Speed community, often described as "one of the absolute worst Need for Speed games ever made". But, judging you see that giant blue thumbs up, you obviously can tell that I don't think that way.
Now, those of you who really hate long reviews (because there's gonna be quite a lengthy one ahead), here's a short pros-n'-cons review to not waste your time:
+Can run on a toaster
+Great soundtrack
+Huge car selection
+Easy-to-follow story
+Simple controls that are even very playable on a keyboard
+Visuals are passable
+Gameplay is rather fun
-Story is inconsistent and highly forgettable
-Visual glitches regarding the sky & the sun (sun flies from one part of the screen to the other while the sky spins in a nauseating fashion)
-Horrible racer & cop AI
-No "Perfect Start" (a prominent feature in Most Wanted, Carbon & World)
-Steam Overlay (unfortunately) does not work with Undercover, due to EA not patching out the old, outdated Steam Overlay DLLs in the game's files
If you just want a racing game where you could really care less for story & want one that can run on your toaster computer, then yes, NFS Undercover should fill that niche for you quite nicely & I recommend the game for the price it's asking.
Now then, short review done. Let's get on with the long review!
I'm not gonna bother with a brief synopsis of the story, since that's what the store page basically tells you. But what I will give will be my thoughts on the story. So. I think the story in Undercover is garbage. It's very sloppily put together. Some characters come & go without a proper explanation, some characters are given NO INTRODUCTION and just sort of...appear, other characters for some reason or another just swap roles mid-story, eh, you get the point. I get that it's to be expected that a racing game will have a terrible story, but back when this game was announced & being promoted like the next best thing, it tried to take itself seriously, with all the trailers & promotional videos. So, yes, the story is trash, introduces characters & gets rid of characters periodically & tries to take itself way too seriously, which is why I don't like it & find it very forgettable. It shouldn't take you more than 10 hours to beat the entire story, I, for one, beat the single player campaign in around 8 hours & now am doing my second runthrough on the Steam version of this game, just for the sake of adding in more gameplay hours.
Before I move on to the meat of the review, being the gameplay, I wanna briefly go over the game's visuals. They look...passable. Now, I've had the pleasure of experiencing this game both in 1080p Ultra Settings & 360p Very Low Settings, and generally - I am impressed with the framerate. The game (for the most part) is very consistent with the framerate on newer hardware & back when my good PC was still alive & played this game for the 8 hours it took to complete the single player campaign, the framerate was crazy-stable at 60 FPS, with sometimes dropping below when there were too many cops at once, which is understandable. As for the visuals themselves, everything in the game world, including the road you drive on & the water beyond the shores looks "alright" at best. Yes, Black Box has done MUCH better in terms of visuals in Carbon & even Most Wanted, but I don't think the game looks ugly by any means, but certainly doesn't live up to the 2008 year it came out on. And the audio? The car sounds are remarkably pleasant to listen to, giving off the feeling that the car you drive FEELS like an actual car and not a freaking go-kart. The soundtrack is picked rather well & there are a handful of songs I don't like, sure, I like most of the soundtrack.
And now, we move on to the meat of the review - the gameplay. Need for Speed Undercover's gameplay tries to emulate the critically-acclaimed gameplay of Most Wanted & Carbon while trying to introduce enough new things to stand on its own. First of all - the controls are great. Every car feels very responsive & turning even with the slowest of muscle cars while using a keyboard, not a controller or wheel, felt super reliable & the car showed no signs of delayed turns or any kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t some racing games usually have, which is great, as great control is what makes the game great. There are, however, a few things I really don't like about the gameplay. Gone from Most Wanted & Carbon are perfect starts, which require to get your speedometer stick on a certain part of the actual speedometer when it changes color to give your car a bit of a necessary boost when you start, unless you want to drag on for about 30 seconds, trying to catch up to your opponents. Thankfully though, Undercover's AI is built around the lack of perfect start, so it's not like they'll speed up instantly, no, they'll generally start out at pretty much the same pace as you do. NFS Undercover has a multitude of game modes, with a few brand new game modes, never-before-seen in any previous Need for Speed game, or even any sub-sequent games - Jobs & Highway Battles. Briefly about the other game modes - they're standard fare what you'd find in other Need for Speed games - you got Circuit, Sprint, Checkpoint, Outrun (making a return from Underground 2) & Police Events. About those "exclusive" game modes, as it were. First - Jobs. Jobs are essentially your character stealing a car & then driving said car to a drop-off point, meanwhile cops are after your♥♥♥♥♥and your goal is to escape the cops & get to the drop off point. This game mode doesn't have a time limit of any sorts, so you can breathe in relief, however - some jobs do have damage meters, which are rather easy to deplete. Highway Battles are sort of glorified high-speed canyon events from Need for Speed Carbon, just with♥♥♥♥♥♥tons of traffic & only 1 stage. The goal in Highway Battle is to get ahead of your opponent & lead by 300 m (or 1000 ft if you're using the Imperial system) whilist trying to not wreck your car with the insane amounts of traffic around you. These 2 exclusive game modes are generally executed very well, with the opponent AI sometimes being crafty enough to try and block your path by purposefully pushing traffic cars into you & they take advantage of every opportunity to overtake you and make your day horrible, should you ♥♥♥♥ up midway in the race. Making a return from Need for Speed ProStreet is domination, but this time - instead of completing an entire area to "dominate", dominations are handed out if you can manage to beat the developer time for each race in the game, not counting Jobs. Early game, beating the developer "domination" time is quite easy, but later down the road - it gets more & more difficult. For Customization - if you've played ProStreet & seen that game's insanely expansive customization system, then Undercover will bring nothing new and you can jump straight in. But for the new guys? I'll throw it out there right now - customizing your car (other than its performance) does nothing and won't give you any benefits like in ProStreet. They're just there if you want your car to look nicer, but be warned - if you will ever decide to play online (which will happen only if you have someone who plays this game after 7 years), your vinyls that you apply to your car will not be shown. Why? Who the hell knows, but they disabled it. I haven't spent much time in the customization menu myself, so I really can't comment on anything here.

For such an old game (the second in the Total War series), Medieval Total War still has its attractiveness.
The point of this game is similar to most other Total War games: take everything over and expand your empire (or at least that's the way I play my Total War games). The graphics for Medieval are old and outdated (as expected of a game this old), and they actually resemble Shogun 1 a bit. The gameplay is very similar to Shogun 1 as well, but it takes place in Medieval Europe. You can build buildings and units in each place, with certain buildings granting extra money, perks, or unit building capabilities. Once you gather an army, you can engage in an RTS battle or just choose to autoresolve the battle (I autoresolved most of the time cuz I'm lazy). There are four scenarios I could play: Vikings, Early Stage Europe, Mid Stage Europe, and Late Stage Europe. I chose Early Stage Europe and the Danes (since they started off as just one little fort). I continued to conquer half of Europe and expanded my small Danish Empire to be larger than all the rest of the countries combined. However, the game started to get glitch later on and it kept crashing every time I wanted to end turn.
Overall, Medieval 1 is better than Shogun 1, though very similar, but can be rather entertaining to play as a whole.

The single-player game is fairly good for a GTA game. Worth $30-40 and your time, I'd say. The world itself is fun to explore, and the typical GTA shenanigans are, as ever, a staple to laugh yourself silly with. The driving, fighting, and gunning are all satisfying.
The single-player falls flat when it comes to the characters. They are all hateful spiteful human garbage. That wouldn't be so bad, but this game feels too over the top in terms of the humour. There are no sympathetic characters, there are no grounded interactions, and the entirety of the world itself is one giant sardonic orifice raining down diatribes of hate and sarcastic drivel on your head.
In past games we've had anchors (straight-men) to help us realise the audacity of our characters, as well as the lunacy of some of our friends. But this game is missing any sense of the mundane in favour of the constantly ridiculous. This feels more like a Saints Row game than a GTA game.
I still mostly enjoyed the single-player experience even if the game was trying to constantly cut me with it's supposedly sharp socioeconomic and political mini-rants. I got tired of the writing and the characters, but I was still (mostly) interested to see their stories pan out. That's the single-player.
The online, or GTA Online, is a mess. The loads are ludicrous, even on a fast connection and the game installed on an SSD, and are a near constant issue with jobs/missions often requiring a load. If you're not waiting for your own game to load, then you're likely waiting for someone else to load into the mission. It feels like you spend more time waiting for things to happen, than you do making things happen. The online economy is a heavy grind. It would be considered a heavy grind in a free to play game. But it's not a free to play game, it is a full price game that demands that you either play dozens of hours to achieve the tiniest of gains, or to pay real money for shark cards. Poorly named. They ought to be named whale cards.
The game demands an extreme amount of grinding to achieve much of anything. Dozens of hours are a drop in the bucket for this grind. The game does not respect your time and is balanced around you buying in-game cash with real money.
Surely for all that grind you have some assurances of a stable, cheat free, product? Nope. The game is riddled with hackers who will kill everyone in a match with the stroke of a button, or they'll lock your character so you cannot move, they'll empty your inventory of all of your hard earned weapons and such, they'll crash the server, or they'll crash your game, or they'll shower your character with items or money in such a way that they'll get you banned for a few days or weeks. That's right, the greedy publisher and devs of this game have offloaded most of the stress of the multiplayer onto their customers, without sufficient checks to keep the integrity of the game itself secure, and so have rendered the experience moot. When hackers can permanently ruin a character you've made, leaving you with no recourse, what are you supposed to do? The PR and marketing for this game avoids the tough questions while shoving more micro-transactions down your throat.
GTA Online is a disgrace. I reinstalled for the first time since release, and played some hours to see what was new. I had missed most of the new content, 'till now, and was curious to see if the game had finally reached a worthwhile state. As you can tell from my above comments, I am not pleased. Things are worse. The lobbies always have a few cheaters in them, about half of the remaining players will hunt you without reason, and the remainder will keep to themselves. Rarely you'll meet some nice seeming folks, but any crew will quickly fall apart as the missions require a high degree of coordination. Unless you have friends to play with, don't waste your time.
The online is a mish mash of ideas, but none are very well implemented.
GTA Online is the fixture of GTA V. There are no expansions or DLC coming for the single player game. If you can find the game for cheap, buy it and play the campaign.Ignore the online component, it exists to part you from your cash.
All of the added content in GTA Online is grind heavy, expensive, and ultimately not worthy of your time. Play a game that respects your time, and isn't just trying to get into your wallet.

Mark of the Ninja is a side-scrolling 2D action game that can be played to varying degrees of stealth. As an xbox port, the game plays best with a controller, (it ought to be a requirement) so bear that in mind if you plan on purchasing it. That said, the game is completely worth the money as I can think of no other action game that does stealth so well.
The game itself is not so difficult; it can be completed rather quickly if one wishes. The real gem in this game lies in the replayability; challenges and achievements that are fun and set to just the right level of difficulty. Multiple "costumes" (altered game mechanics) and a wide variety of skills/tools allow for a range of playstyles.
Mechanics-wise, the Mark of the Ninja leaves nothing up to chance or question. Success is based on skill and everything about the environment is communicated to the player with visual cues. If the player character dies it is always the player's fault. No "bad rolls" or "cheese" here.
While not a story driven game, the story in Mark of the Ninja does have merit for reasons I cannot explain without spoiling it. Just suffice to say that the player will do well to pay attention to the graphics.
In short, I wholeheartedly recommend this game.
