You might think that this game is like every other Lego game out there. And to be honest, you would be pretty much right. But. Because there is a but (there always is). It was the first of this kind of lego game. Or, more precisely, it is the combination of the first two, the Lego Star Wars games (duh).
To those who played them separatly before, I say this : they took the first game, and got rid of what was infuriating to make it more diverse, like the second one is. And then they added the two games together, which means that you do not need to have a saved game of Lego Star Wars I to fight the Emperor with Jar-Jar and a young Boba Fett (I don't recommand trying that, btw).
To those who have played other Lego games, I say this : it is no open world. It is quite linear at first. And there is nothing original here : you play through the movies. But it is funny, it is easy to beat (you get through the missions in under 3 hours), and you will go through it many times if, like me, you are a completionist.
To those who have never played a Lego game, I warn you : if you happen to like this game, you might lose yourself in the Lego franchise. As I mentionned, it is quite easy to beat it "normally", that is to say finish the story mode. But that is when the real fun starts. You have much to unlock, discover, search... You can go back to any level to play it with unlocked characters, to look for secrets and secondary objectives. And that is without the bonus levels. Also : you see Vader show Luke a picture of him and Leia together to prove that they are related. Just saying.
In short, it is well worth the price. If you happen to have an Xbox controler, that is. It is dreadfull to play with a keyboard (no mouse allowed). You have been warned.

Harvester is a classic point and click adventure game originally released in the mid 90s. upon purchase on steam, It comes with a journal article basically stating stuff about violence in video games. So you can expect an epicly gorey and surreal adventure. You'll want to try and explore every area of the game and you'll be surprised or shocked by some of the stuff you'll see.
If you remember the classic point and click adventure games, then you'd already know the fundamentals of playing this game. Click on things, Pick up items, Heavy dialog from various NPCs, Work out cryptic puzzles, Think about using an FAQ. All those natrual moments of point and click adventures will come to you. So if that thrills you, This is a title to pick up. If you need an extra push on the decision... here's the story.
The beauty of this game is basically waking up not knowing a single thing. You dont know where you are, who you are, or what you are meant to do. and after briefly talking to various people in the town, You find out you have amnesia. As you discover parts about yourself, you also learn the town you are in is not exactly like other towns. You have your average buildings like Schools, Police station, General store but the largest building in the centre of the town is The Lodge. No one in town knows whats inside but you'll need to gain access to it. If you manage to succeed, You might be lucky to actually understand what the whole story of this game is.
As for the violence and gore? Well there's definately a lot of that. There was several settings and scenarios that may upset some people and if I could admit, there was one particular scene I came across which even I was shocked by. The FMV movies have some porno-intro style acting but it gives the game a unique touch.
It might feel dated now, but the story and the enviroment you are traveling through. It feels like a surreal bad dream and for some reason, when things are so creepy or unusual we cant help but be curious to get more. So I'd say if you can get this game, Grab it.

Harvester is a point and click horror/adventure game from the 90s.  What sets it apart from other games in its genre is how insane it is.  This game has things in it that would not stand a chance at making it into releases today.  Sure, blood and gore are pretty common today, but when it involves children, it's just completely taboo now.  Not surprisingly, Harvester has a pretty decent sized cult following.  It was hit hard when it was released by negative criticism for its gameplay but mostly for its content.  It definitely broke no ground with its gameplay and its content is pretty shocking.  I found the tone of the game to be just perfect.  It is just creepy beyond reason.  Kind of like a cheesy horror flick or something.  The characters are so over the top with their insanity it almost makes you feel uncomfortable.  The game has humor, but the humor is also...insane.  I really love it.  Check it out.  It's cheap and worth the ride.

"You always were a kidder Steve...."
A cult classic point and click adventure game from 1996 that managed to spark quite a bit of controversy at the time of its release due to its graphical violence and generally messed up and twisted themes . You play as a character called Steve who wakes up in town called Harvest somewhere in the 50's. He doesn't remember why or how he got there, and he can't recognize his not-so-idyllic family. Pretty soon he starts to realize that things are very, very wrong in this small town. And the only one besides Steve who realizes this, is his soon-to-be fiance who lives next door. The true nature Harvest will unveil as you progress through the game.
Gameplay is exactly like you would expect from any point and click adventure game from the 90's. You walk through different parts of the town gathering stuff and trying to figure out whats going on while talking to all the peculiar characters in the town. The game has its share of some flawed and obscure puzzles. The game also has some extremely clunky combat elements, but you won't be needing combat till much later in the game, so it doesn't really matter.
You can also kill every character in this game if you want to, but you'll be sent to the electric chair if theres any witnesses around.
Graphics are pretty abysmal by todays standards, but I think it just brings more charm into this game. Not to mention all the greenscreen cutscenes which were so hilariously bad that they were funny as hell.
Overall, this game is a rare gem and should be played by anyone who enjoys old-school adventure games and/or downright ♥♥♥♥ed up games.

Heyo folks, End World Gaming here to share an excerpt from my review for The Novelist by Orthogonal Games.
The Novelist is a first person adventure game with some stealth elements. The game puts you in the role of an unknown creature/ghost that, more or less, spies on the inhabitants of the house. The creature can impact the inhabitant’s life choices but it’s neither benevolent or evil, but based on your choices, it can impact their lives in good or bad ways.
The current inhabitants of the house are the Kaplan family which consists of 3 people. Dan is the father, who is a novelist who’s hit a roadblock on his current book. Linda (Dan’s Wife) who is seeking to bring her family closer together. Finally, their son Tommy, who is a young boy who is having trouble in school.
The game revolves around a central question “Can You Achieve Your Dreams Without Pushing Away Your Loved Ones.” It uses this as the basis for the gameplay.
In each chapter your objective is to learn their current wants. To do this you must read notes, letters, diaries and look at pictures to discern what they want. Once you’ve found all the clues, you’ll need to step into their memories to find further clues. Once every clue has been found simply read their mind and the final clue will be revealed. If you’re playing on stealth mode, you’ll have to do this without being seen. In story mode you’re free to walk around freely.
Once you’ve found the final clue for each character you’ll be able to choose a single character’s want to finish off the chapter. Be careful with your choice because choosing one will make the other 2 characters disappointed and will cause them to have a negative outcome. If you manage to stay hidden and uncover the final clue for all characters, you’ll be able to choose a compromise which will force a neutral outcome but still make the character somewhat happy. This will leave only one character with a completely negative outcome.
Your choices impact the ending to the game and because there’s multiple choices to make with multiple outcomes, the game has a lot of different endings as well.
Overall, The Novelist is an adventure game with a powerful message. It’s also a deeply personal game as well and you really get to know the Kaplan family and their daily struggles. It’s also sad to see the negative outcomes that each character is faced with as well. In the end I had Dan abandon his book because to me, his family was more important than wasting away while writing a book. It’s a touching game all around and it does a really good job of putting what’s most important into perspective. Very well put together game.

An affecting little story. The main game elements are as strong only as the players connection to the characters; thats a pro and a con depending on how strong a player feels about the situations therein. I loved this little game with its touching and bittersweet tone. It produced a couple of agonizing moments as family situations sortof become cost benefit analyses for the player but the choices felt real and their consequences did too and thats hard to acheive.
Perhaps a breath too long -as the seams of the mechanics become all too clear towards the end- but regardless it is a lovely little work that shows games can be just as morally and narratively powerful as other mediums whist giving autonomy to the player. A beautiful look at family life and the pulls of dreams, work, and responsibilities.
The Novelist allows players to reap the rewards of their choices and also have to live with choices that may impact negatively; its sortof like juggling guilt, and its fantastic.

I really enjoyed this game. While slow moving, the characters have depth and the story arc is enough to keep engaged those players who are interested in deeper, meaningful examinations of human interactions.
It would have been helpful if the tutorial had explained how to choose a compromise, though. I tried several things but never found it. I learned that the compromises are chosen in the B&W scenes between chapters, not in the next chapter as it says in the game. Also, I have no idea why there is a history of the house. Is that setting up a sequal or did the dev start a story arc and just forgot to finish it? We may never know. I did enjoy that the choices I made had consequences, not just in game play, but in how the characters finished their slide down the mortal coil.
All in all, I spent a lovely evening playing this game with an emotionally gratifying story. If you want a quiet, slow, relaxing game that lets the player experiment with life choices, all set to a beautiful soundtrack, this is the game for you.

This game is quite on the depressing side but I guess that is the point of it.
You play as a 'ghost' who is trying to figure out what everybody's motives are and then choosing what decisions the family should make. The sad part is that your decisions are always going to hurt at least one of them and it is always going to end up being hard on all of them because of that. The reality is that the game follows a troubled family to begin with so there is only so much you can do to better their situation. The game really made me think what kind of creatures we as humans are and how deeply our decisions reflect our psyche.
Overall I see what the game was trying to portray and I really like how all of these decisions you make result in different endings. The game has quite a replayability value for that alone but only if you can bear the pressure of a depressed family with two very distant parents and a love-seeking child.
Other than that I had some framerate issues which caused me getting nauseated and I had to lower the resolution of the game noticeably in order to run it properly which was not expected from such a game at all.
At the end I really don't know if I would recommend this game. Not to everybody for sure. It's not fun nor is it very philosophical. It's just very heavy with raising psychological self-reflecting questions. What would you have done? What is the right thing to do? Who has the right to be helped and from what action can as many people as possible benefit or at least people as possible get hurt?
If you play games for fun or if you want to cheer up, then no, don't buy this game. Don't even think about it. On the other hand, if you feel like helping others and self-reflecting then this is the game for you.
For me personally, this was too heavy of a load but that's what the game was trying to empathize, so I'll give it a recommend.

This is a very simple but punishingly difficult puzzle game. It starts off fairly straightforward, but progresses rapidly to seemingly impossible situations. I am sure there are subtleties to the movement that I have not yet learned, but as it stands, I've actually reached a wall where I can't solve any of the available puzzles. Still, the game is extremely well crafted. The graphics are colorful and crisp, the audio is unobtrusive, and the controls are as simple as it gets. All you have to do is have your little snakebirds eat all the fruit and make it safely to the rainbow portal. But good GOD it's hard. Luckily, it's the kind of hard that, when you figure it out, it's immensely satisfying. So, if you're in the mood for an extreme puzzle challenge (honestly, this is probably the hardest puzzle game I've played on Steam), this is your game.
Excellent puzzle game. I love the sound effects and the birds. Blue Bird is my favorite.

Game of the year for 2015 (for me, anyways).
Ranks up there with English Country Tune.  Many puzzles simply look impossible upon initial assessment.  The mechanics of the game may initially feel counterintuitive
, but are consistent and fair.  You start to develop the snakebird wiggling skills and techniques that give you an extra block or two you need, learn the proper positioning of snakebirds, and formulate the conditions required to achieve your goal.  The puzzles are elegant, tight, and reduced to the essence of the concept they intend to teach you.  Hypothesizing, testing, discovering, removing a patch of your own hair, and finally solving impossible-looking problems is so gratifying.  As with the best puzzles you sometimes feel like you have discovered a loophole in the fabric of existence.
Graphical style and music also very appealing.  A very polished work of genius.

If you're a puzzle game enthusiast looking for a new and unique challenge, this game will make you very happy.
It is:
SMART: The levels are designed to make you discover the intricacies of the game's mechanics. As the trailer suggests, the levels are often set up to suggest an initial strategy that ends up not working, giving way to a seemingly insurmountable barrier, and the fun lies in finding the trick that gets you past it.
SUCCINCT: In some 50 levels a number of mechanics are introduced (multiple snakebirds, pushable blocks, warps) that keep things fun and new. None of the levels seem redundant- I really found myself learning something new in each level.
DAMN CUTE: And the cuteness correlates a bit with the game's functionality. When a snakebird's head is moved next to a spike, it gets nervous. Next to a fruit, it looks happy and excited. The pastel-children's-book visual style, along with fun synth music and sound effects, work very well. Bravo.
Comparison: This has a similar genius to Stephen Lavelle's commercial games (English Country Tune, Stephen's Sausage Roll). If you're a fan of those, you'll love this (and vice versa).
PWYW for this as part of the current Humble Indie Bundle (until Tuesday 6/21 midday), but honestly this gem is a steal at full price.

Pretty fun game, as a person that really enjoyed the game Ballance, which is amongst the first in this 'genre', this game seems very much like a modern carbon copy, but I can't say it's a bad thing, since the game does improve in a lot of aspects. Visually and not to mention feature-wise, as there's more types of blocks in the game, however it seems to have stuck to the standard three-ball system.
The biggest deal is the level editor & user levels. There are a lot of user levels made that are of pretty great quality, and overall the editor is quite intuitive. Unfortunately the base game doesn't actually feature many "vanilla" levels, and some of them are of really poor quality, but it's counterbalanced by all the user levels. Considering the game doesn't have nor need a story, it can only benefit from that.
I can recommend the game, although there are also some otherwise minor issues:
Achievements will only be received after exiting the game - they don't seem to work during the game.
The tutorial is pretty much pointless - and in my experience it didn't even work properly.
Random language errors across some menus, such as finishing a single-player mission.
During a multi-monitor setup the game launched on the leftmost monitor as opposed to the primary, and it was a bit of a hassle fixing the resolution, but it worked out eventually.
As for some suggestions:
Allow us to use mouse camera as well, or at least adjust the tilt of the camera.
Expanded zoom option/button so that we can see more of what is around us, without needing to go down a path off-screen we just find out it's locked.
Multi-heighted parts in the level editor should show multiple levels while tab is pressed. (Such as ramps should specify the height change)
Extra score nuggets (or whatever they are actually supposed to be called) and 'keys' should attach better to the player. I find myself rolling away from the score points until they accumulate and eventually reach me just from me standing still. This is not an issue as the points are received instantly anyway but overall it's kind of weird.
Half of the text in the game isn't even english!

Not as complete as Ballance, Lacks the great levels that made Ballance so good.
The level editor is unfinished and difficult to use.
Overall: Get Ballance It's a better game. This is alright, If its free or ever completed (fixed).

Have you ever wondered what the gaming world would look like, if you had to pay DLC for even the silliest things?  DLC Quest answers this question, in a humorous adventure to save not only the Princess, but also the world.
DLC Quest's gameplay plays like most side-scrolling titles.  You can do the typicall running and jumping, as well as attacking.  The catch, however, is that you have to "buy" these features as DLC.  To do this, you have to find coins that are hidden around the map, and buy them in the shop.  It's a very interesting way of changing up how the game works, and is also an analogy of what could happen if DLC is used in a bad way.
Graphically, DLC Quest looks pretty solid.  It looks like a nice upgrade from the typical 8-Bit NES offerings, and work very well.  The soundtrack and sound effects work too, and sound very nice.  The soundtrack may be a bit repetitive overtime, which may annoy some, but it's still pretty solid.
As far as playtime is concerned, the game can be finished anywhere between 1-2 hours.  Possibly less.  As the game costs around $3, this is pretty much up to you if you think it's worth your time.  I think it's definitely worth going into, though if one is sceptical, I recommend waiting until it's on sale, as it goes on discount quite a bit.
Overall, DLC Quest is a fun, interesting look at how DLC can ruin the gaming world, and one that one shouldn't miss.  I highly recommend it.

Note: Might come back to this and add a handle to the cup; I'm still soaking in the game in its entirety.  It's amazing how much can happen in a couple weeks, no? I commend those with the coffee stained brain able to soak in so much and still have the energy to give birth to an array of content regularly without as much as a pee break.  Augmented bladder?  Yes, please.  I hope you enjoy this little review/character study and the Deus Ex series, including this offering:  Deus Ex: Mankind Divided.
Overview/Adam Jensen
The theme of betrayal, multilayered conspiracy, and mankind turning against each other is relevant. We're continually fighting injustice, ignorance, and greed in the real world.  Often times the fight is simply navigating the highway of information presented. It’s hard to accept the individuals or vested entities capable of manufacturing senseless violence and fear, but we have no choice but to respond.  It has happened and it will happen again if nothing is done.  And like Jensen, we must try and find the wisdom to be able to confront and defeat the enemy without becoming it – or worse.
Agent Adam Jensen and his underground counter-terrorism unit are tasked with uncovering the reason, stopping, and preventing certain entities from carrying out their disruptive, violent schemes.  Jensen is very much an outsider within his own task force as opposed to the toast of town he was at Sarif Industries, his former employer.  He’s very much the same Jensen we remembered from the previous game; a smooth operator, with a knack for penetrating enemy lines, and asking the hard-hitting questions.  Given the option, Jensen delivers diplomatic alternatives to his signature knock-out punches, but often he is left no choice but to incapacitate those immune to reason. Jensen can be cruel and calculating by his own admission and subversive “hack-tics.”  If you haven't read your e-mail yet, he probably has.  And the pistol in your locker?  Jensen may have borrowed it and left a note.  He has no qualms about defending those he loves by any means necessary.  When Adam seldom retracts his precision augmented eye-gear, I see a compassionate human being beneath the machined lenses...
May no amount of metal or bionics define or deprive a man of his soul; his ability to love and create; his will to take up and lay down his life.
"Sometimes to love someone, you got to be a stranger."  -Rick Deckard (Blade Runner 2049)
Graphics and Sound
AAA when it’s all working.  Sometimes the lighting, while brilliant, can be distracting.  Animations tend to paint a stiff upper lip instead of a fluid conversation.  Again, when it’s working as intended, everything is crisp and extraordinarily detailed.   Voice acting, sound effects, and music are well-done.
Gameplay
Mankind Divided is very much down to business, and the feel of the combat, stealth, and weapons feels better than ever.  Even the stun gun lost its happy-go-lucky, white-out roller design.   There are many ways to fry an egg, but some paths are exponentially more satisfying IMO.  (Please, take my word for it, hacking robots is deliciously satisfying.)  The game rewards you for a playing the missions covertly, but I do not believe Jensen has anything but dry ice in his cybernetic veins when the time calls for him to act.  You’ll find out which augmentations – experimental or not – you prefer.  I highly recommend TESLA’s experimental work.
EDIT - OK, I finished it.  I slaved away for the Pacifist Achievement. The only killers in my playthrough were hacked robots turning on their masters and puddles of electricity.  As long as you don't directly murder someone with your own hands the achievement is secure. >.> This is good because a particuluar mission required the sometimes cruel, sometimes kind mistress known as Death.  So it goes.
CRITICISM:   Well, I looked at the other reviews, and I saw where a lot of people were coming from in their criticism.  (Their reviews have bullet points, for goodness sakes!  Wizardry!)  I was a big fan of the previous installment in Human Revolution, so I looked past some of the glaring oddities glittered throughout.  Yes:  * bugs, weird voice overs, animations, etc, etc, etc.
I personally couldn't ignore the main story and antagonist in this game wasn't satisfying or even really all that interesting or believable.   There was a feeling of,  "To be continued . . .  "  I hope they do, even if it takes awhile!  I want to know these chracters and how the story may or may not flesh out.
Complimentary Digression:  I couldn't help but think of Deus Ex when I watched Blade Runner.  There's sort of a connection there, but I won't spoil it beyond saying Jensen isn't the only one who knows his way through a wall!   Blade Runner with this game's mechanics would be pretty cool, right?  Or maybe elements from Blade Runner incorporated into Jensen's universe?

The game took me 18 hours to complete, but that is because while playing I went back in saves to explored every possible outcome of each situation and to hear all the dialogue possible in each conversation depending on the questions I asked or answers I gave. If you rush through the game you can probably beat it in half that time.
A few technical tips if you do pick up this game.
Save often, especially later in the game. The game allows you to save 25 times before having to overwrite old saves. This is for 2 reasons. One, there are a lot of situations where there are different outcomes depending on what you say or do and you may want a recent save point to try out all the options without having to go back to an old save and repeat a bunch of stuff. Two, this game is run through DosBox and it has problems with skipping some of the cutscenes.
In the DosBox settings (steamapps\common\Harvester\dosbox_windows\dosbox_harvester.conf) you will want to set a certain cycle number to play at and then use the cycle down and up shortcuts (ctrl F11 & F12) while in game when you get to a cutscene that was skipped. I used these settings, but you may need to adjust them a little for your computer: cycles=28000, cycleup=20000, cycledown=20000, aspect=true. When a cutscene is skipped, load the previous save (beginning of that conversation if you are saving a lot), press F11 to drop the cycles down to allow the cutscene to play and then press F12 to bring them back up so the game plays faster and smooth again. I had to do this on probably about 20% of the cutscenes, the others played fine. You can also adjust your mouse sensitivity in the DosBox settings. You may notice that your mouse cursor moves horizontal faster than vertical, I could not fix this.
You may want to get a pen and paper while playing. When you talk to people in the game, new subjects will appear that you can talk about just like in most point and click games, but in Harvester you cannot click through every subject because sometimes when you pick one subject the others will not be there after. There is a box that says "other" and you can type in subjects to talk about, but you have to remember the exact title of the subject. I chose to write down the subjects each time I talked to someone and then crossed them off after I did each one. That way I can type in the others that disappeared and get to hear all the great dialogue. Try swearing at your mother, lol.

This is a fun game but somewhat antiquated feeling if you've played the newer Lego games and then go back and play this. For those who may not know, this is a combination of 2 original titles - Lego Star Wars and Lego Star Wars II: The Original Trilogy. I have played neither of those but from my understanding, their recreation in this "Complete Saga" is pretty faithful to the original games with some minor changes here and there. One of the nice bonus features is that they let you play the original version of 2 stages from the first game and you can tell that they definitely made some improvements in terms of the maneuvering and physics on those stages. However on one of the stages they also made it a lot easier by essentially removing certain goals that have to be met throughout the stage to continue.
On the whole thoguh, if you've played most any Lego game before, then you know what to expect. If not, then expect to smash a lot of stuff, play as a lot of different characters from the Star Wars series and use those characters' various abilities to progress through stages and find the insane amount of collectibles, if you so choose. As with most Lego games, this game goes almost overboard on the sheer amount content and collectibles that you have to play and find to achieve 100% if you're a completionist like me. This one really almost wore me down and I feel that they maybe put a bit TOO much, but you certainly get your money's worth.
All in all, if you're a Lego game fan and/or a Star Wars fan, I would recommend this game. It does a very good job of staying mostly faithful to the Star Wars movies, while taking some creative liberties in order to keep gameplay consistent. It also has the light-hearted humor throughout that the Lego games are known for and I think that Star Wars fans will appreciate most of it. Again though, be prepared for a slight feeling of antiquated controls and mechanics if you've played newer Lego games, sepcifically Lego Star Wars III: The Clone Wars because they have definitely continously made gameplay improvements over the years.
Looking forward to LEGO TFA's!

I found this game touching and creative.
For those who want to experience how a decision can affect others, this game is for you. If you do not enjoy experiencing a story without a "true" ending, this game is not for you.
-Pretty suprised with the mixed reviews, I found this game meaningful.
-Do you pursue a career or leave behind your loved ones?
- What can you do when a compromise between decisions need to be made?
- How can you find a solution where everyone can be happy or satisfied?
Simply, you play as a "ghost" who helps a Novelist with his choices. Make a name in the literature world whilst balancing out family commitments or just pick one?
- Simple click and point , discovery game.
-A lot of thinking involved. Makes you rethink about your actions and how they currently affect others too.
- You can play as a "ghost" or "stealth mode" (either you sneak around or become invisible)
- If you play on the stealth mode- you have to hide in light sources (lightss, lamps) so you dont' "spook" the Kaplans.
- Like a novel, you discover the story within chapters. These chapters are loopable so depending on your action, the chapter order changes slightly.
- You discover the memories and thoughts of the characters- the novelist, his wife and his son.
- Ghost whisperer: After discovering a bunch of clues and reaching a decision, you " whisper" the decision to be made and the result and consequences unveil.
-Minimalistic Art- Not much to be said about it, I feel like the plot and gameplay is much more important.
-Loopable ambient soundtrack- It's pretty peaceful , slow drones of melodic piano. Changes sometimes.
- Typerwriter- I actually love the typewriter sound.  It just makes the game feel peaceful.
This is an extra section because I felt like it was interesting.
- Subtle subliminal changes can be witnessed due to the choices you made. Especially with Linda (the Wife) and the more noticeable ones (the kid and the novelist) .
- Loved the use of extended metaphors :)
I love playing this game at night. It's just that peaceful. Overall, it's a simple , minimalistic but meaningful game about decisions and how they affect ones relationships, and the balance between work and family. :)

This game has the most touching and relatable story I've experienced in any game. It is about ordinary humans, with ordinary family problems. The premise is simple: A father who
to finish writing his book despite his writer's block, because if he doesn't the family will be bankrupt. Meanwhile the wife feels neglected, and their disabled child needs the father's care and attention to get a fulfilling life.
This is where you as a player comes in, in the shape of a ghost who can affect the surroundings in the house to steer the family members in the way you deem best for the family to not fall apart, juggling with compromises as any family has to do.
That is really what the game is about: Compromises. No one single family member can get all that they want or need, because that would be to forsake the others, and this is exactly what makes the game relatable.
No other game has actually made me feel bad about what I do to the extent that The Novelist does, and that's exactly why I think everyone should play this game. It can actually make you reflect on your own life.

Winter Sports Trilogy is (I think) an Olympic game. Though not all winter sports all available to play (such as Hockey), the game will provide some replay-ability and fun. I'll start with my absolute favorite sport in the game : curling. Much like bocce is on grass, curling is about the same on ice. Most controls throughout the game are quite basic and most time is spent either setting up or executing quick button presses. In curling, you (as the thrower) throw the rock down the ice and inform your teammates when to sweep. There are two skiing events : downhill and jump. The downhill is relatively fun and they've added a few more buttons to make it immersive (carving and crouching).
The jump is quite basic where you need to keep your balance as you're going down the ramp and in the air. Landing is also another skill required to successfully complete the event. Biathlon is a neat event as well where you have to keep your heart rate below a certain amount or else the player begins to fatigue. Going up and down hills your HR (heart rate) will change and the frequency in which you press the buttons will need to adapt as well. Shooting is quite simplistic and the ability to hold your breath also exists (as most sniping games). Crouching is also available in the event and is extremely useful when going downhill to rest your character. Speed skating is an okay event where you essentially have to press two buttons synchronized with the skaters legs. Snowboarding is another okay event. They literally took the fun out of it as there is no real freedom. You can move around on your own will and jump when you need to jump. When it comes to a skill or a trick, they give you one and you must obey their QTE (quick time events). This totally took the fun out of the event as you leave real time a few times during the event. Luge is pretty basic and specific in where your launch matters and where your steering is really difficult to control (especially with a keyboard).
Upon starting, you have to keep in between two orange lines that are marked on the ice. If you start getting too close to one side, the side of the screen will slightly blur to indicate you are too close to the walls. Even though this event is a bit dull, it does gives the player a bit of insight into the sport. Skeleton is essentially the same thing. Figure skating has the camera following the performer and while they are doing their tricks, the user must complete QTE's which comes from the left and right side. Lastly there is bobsled which closely resembles luge.
The visuals are okay and not completely out of date. Although a bit boxy at times, a lot of the animations (such as the dancing mascot) is appreciated. There is an atmosphere thankfully. The sounds are okay and are suitable for what they are supposed to signify. The announcer are completely another thing. There is an English guy then an American sounding ex-athlete who consistently banter about random topics. The English dude will talk about the sport and commentate (at times). To fill the void, the English guy will start bringing up controversial topics about the ex-athlete how he got called a "bendeho" by an Argentinean diplomat while he was performing. Some of the conversation topics will have you scratching your head wondering how did this sneak into the game. The menu is pretty easy to navigate and provides most of the options you need for adjusting options. I have to admit, they did a pretty damn good job here. Only complaint is the same song they use over and over.
Overall, not a bad game. I would (HIGHLY) recommend purchasing on sale as I got this game, Axis football and a few other games for under $3. It is not the greatest sport game in the world, but may be the only thing for sport enthusiasts on steam.

The other two games, biathlon and downhill skiing, are included in Winter Sports as well, but the mechanics are not as detailed as they are in the solo versions.

This is what would become if Call of Duty and Overwatch had a baby (perhaps with some Counter Strike genes thrown in there too). Ballistic Overkill is an enjoyable FPS that doesn't take itself too seriously (hence the price tag), but definitely has potential to be a contender for Counter Strike, Overwatch, Call of Duty, etc, upon full release.
Pros:
- The FPS-RPG element creates a development and growth aspect ashamedly missed by Valve with Team Fortress 2 (which is similar in ways to B.O.)
- The variety of classes enables constant experimentation, mixing and matching character perks with unlocked weapons.
- The UI/menu is lovely. They've really put effort into the little things like screen transitions and navigating between characters.
- The aiming mechanics are impressive, particularly when sniping.
Cons, hopefully to be cleared up in full-release:
- You can't update a character's loadout entirely while connected to a server during the intermission - you must leave the session and return to the menu. That's a little frustrating, particularly when you unlock a new weapon.
- The movement mechanics are a little clunky and wooden, not on-par with the pure and fluid movement found in Call of Duty. But then - that's Call of Duty, which costs 10x the price of this game...
- Lack of maps and thus repetition, hopefully plenty more to come in full release though.
Can't wait for full release. Keep it up!

This game feels different enough from other FPS games that you should give it a shot and see how you like it. Every class in the game has their own unique feel. The movement is especially what makes each class unique, and I don't mean different walkspeeds. Assassin can grapple through the arena, Vanguard is a literal jet airplane, and the Titans can rocket jump to their hearts content. Add in low grav, and there's another layer added to the movement of the game. You don't want to be a sitting duck in low grav with a gunslinger charging his shots towards you.
The game modes are what you'd expect from an FPS. They're simple enough and the UI tells the player exactly what's going on at each point in the games. Teamwork is encouraged and with how simple it is to understand each of the game modes, it's as if everyone is always on the same page. I recommend playing it if you want something faster than what's on the market currently. Cruising through zero g alone is worth the price of admission.

"The best stealth game ever made?"
Not sure about that. I would still give this title to Thief 2. That said, Klei seems to have a talent of creating brilliant games no matter what genre they reach for and MoN is no different.
Great artstyle mixing western-style animation and Japanese themes. This 2d stealth game allowing for variety of approaches. You want to sneak? You can. You want to murder everyone in the room? You can. You want to murder one guard and hung him high to terrify other guards, who the fall to their deaths, or shoot other guards. You can.
While levels aren't complex as in earlier mentioned original Thief games or Hitman: Blood Money, they are designed well enough to allow for different paths and encourage exploration. Add to that really solid game mechanics which allow you to make your own path if you feel like it, by distracting enemies or taking out guards in ways not specifficaly designed by creators.
The UI makes sure that whatever you do you know hom much noise you make and who and how can hear you.  Thanks to this you always know how much noise you make and can plan your moves accordingly.
Anything bad? The writing could be better. While the story is pretty solid and the little "Haiku scrolls" you find in every level are brilliant, I am not a big fan of the dialogue in the game. It is just too dry and character-less.
Still, a must buy for anyone even remotely interested in stealth games.

This review should enlighten all who are still unsure whether or not to purchase this game.
There are far too few acceptional ninja games out there today, many of which lack the certain emotion and feeling of what it is like to be a true master of the shadows. Mark of the ninja gives you that experience.
The key element which makes mark of the ninja stand out more than any other stealth assasin based game which I have personally played, is atmosphere. every touch of detail, lighting, art style, and animation is perfect. The shift in music brings a certain balance between silent and deadly, to intense and heavy combat. With cerain levels having various weather effects it makes the player feel even more on edge and truely puts you on the edge of your seat, whilst at other times being the calm before the storm as you slowly pick off your enemies one by one.
Of course this is all based on how your play style adapts the world around you. Whether you wish to bypass all enemies and go for the "ghost" style gameplay. Or if you preffer using an asrenal of deadly traps and fear tactics, it's all here in one package.
The key to being a good ninja is movement, from scailing tall buildings, crawling through vents, or leaping from wall to wall, the way you use the enviroment to move is essential. Hiding in the shadows and above enemies goes as far as your creativity.
You start the game with nothing but the shadows and a blade, as you advance further through the story you begin to unlock seals which help you learn new techniques, and unlock more of your precious tools to assist you in meeting your objective however way you choose to play each mission.
Whether you wish to be invisible or a monstrosity that brings a new level of terror to your enemies, you will find the right skill or equipment to accomidate your needs.
Worried about not getting the hours out of this purchase? Well to be honest I keep coming back to it, with multiple paths and suits to keep each playthrough unique and enjoyable.
The only thing I could point out not necissarily to be a negative, but certainly something the developers should take into account is a level editor. It would make this the perfect ninja game (in my opinion) to create some kind of level design which could be shared over the workshop, so you can challenge your friends to see who is the better warrior.
That being said there is an extra dlc for Dosan's tale which is worth the purchase. Various side challengs which help you unlock more seals, and a new game plus once you beat the game for a bit of extra challenge and further replay value.
With a fantastically writen story which hooks you in right off the bat, and each level offering that little bit more to keep you going without feeling bored. This is the best ninja game I have ever played, and to me that's a huge deal since I am a big ninja gaiden fan.
£10.99 on steam currently and worth every penny, personally I would of been happy paying £20 for this experience.
So for my final verdict i shall rate this product as 9.8 out of 10
the only .2 missing would be the level editor and some more dlc to keep this title going strong for future years.

NOTE: IF YOU HAVE NOT PLAYED DWARF FORTRESS, THIS REVIEW WILL BE MOSTLY MEANINGLESS.
Most of the reviews do not understand this game at all.
This game is an almost exact copy of Dwarf Fortress, except with many of the extremely horrible aspects of the UI improved. Any negative review written by someone who doesn't mention Dwarf Fortress in any way should... well, not exactly be ignored, because they really do have a point. It is insanely difficult and frustrating to get into this game. But just know, there is a game called Dwarf Fortress, which has all of Gnomoria's downsides to a much greater extent, and yet is generally agreed to be one of the deepest and most satisfying games ever released for the PC by a surprisingly large dedicated playerbase. If Dwarf Fortress is a good game, then Gnomoria certainly must also be a good game.
But if you're a fan of Dwarf Fortress, then you already know what all of the bad reviews are saying. You can bet that if DF got put on steam, it would garner exactly the same hugely negative criticism: impossibly buggy, horrible UI, horrible graphics, brings your computer to its knees in the late-game, etc. Make no mistake: Dwarf Fortress's UI is atrocious. And yet, the game has such incredible depth that it is beloved anyway. Once you become competent at it, though, once you actually understand what you're doing and develop the muscle memory required to drive the UI, the game is magnificent.
Well, Gnomoria is essentially the same exact thing, except the learning curve is about half as steep, and the end-game is about half as deep. No pun intended.
I started out as a Dwarf Fortress purist, just played Gnomoria a little because it was in the same genre and it seemed decent enough to give a shot. Nowadays, when I go back to Dwarf Fortress, I am *amazed* that I ever thought such a truly awful interface was playable. All of the super aggravating aspects of DF are just gone in Gnomoria. Many of the things in DF you would need external tools for (Dwarf Psychiatrist, autotask, many of the dfterm functions) are included in-game natively. They're far better integrated.
Also, much of the unnecessary crap around the edges has been eliminated. Why on earth do you need to generate a whole 1024x1024 world when your fortress, and the absolute boundary of your gameplay experience, will be contained in a single 3x3 square of it? The idea of of generating a huge pool of starting locations is that (after waiting forever for your CPU to do the horribly intense calculations involved) you can select the very best starting zone on the whole map, and so get a skill-based advantage. But this is just another stupid barrier to entry; should new players be penalized for not knowing that the 'aquifer' tag on a particular tile means that any mines they dig will fill up with water? When barely less than 1% of the map is even inhabitable, why even bother? Gnomoria just generates a 3x3 tile guaranteed to have access to all resources and with low variance when it comes to bad luck like large surface lakes or elevation changes.
I dunno, there's lots of stuff like that, little ways the game has been improved by cutting out some in-retrospect-unnecessary element. The reason the "game was abandoned" and "development stopped" was because they had finally brought the content up to where DF is.
Now, when I feel a hankering to play DF, the program I actually open is Gnomoria. I think you'll come to the same conclusion, if you try it out.
If you're familiar with Dota, then you might remember a game called Heroes of Newerth. People were sick of having to use Warcraft 3's interface and scripting engine for Dota, and it was obvious that some change needed to be made, so some rich fan developed a whole external engine, and built dota as its own game, and it was therefore much easier to do things that are hard to do in the warcraft 3 map editor. He changed the names of all of the heroes, but, for the most part, their abilities and gameplay stayed the same (although, as a fan, he had a couple ideas for new heroes that he soon implemented). And it was a thousand times better than playing Dota 1 on Warcraft 3.
And it had its own problems, of course, but they were nothing like the problems of a decade-old
game. So all the dota players flocked to it.
(Later, of course, Valve published Dota 2 and then HoN kind of died or something? I don't know what happened to it, everyone I know switched over.)
Anyway, I see Gnomoria as being the HoN to Dwarf Fortress's Dota 1. It changed all the names of everything, even renamed the dwarves to gnomes, but the actual gameplay is exactly the same. Except all the problems with using an ncurses-style command line interface for a GUI are fixed, much like HoN fixed the fact that players couldn't reconnect to the game in Dota 1. I think it's a good analogy.
So I think this game is worth getting, if you're a DF fan looking for perhaps an even better DF experience.
...if you *haven't* played Dwarf Fortress, on the other hand, well. This game might be *easier to learn* than DF, but it is still a very far cry from easy. You will probably have a ton of trouble understanding how to do things like build workshops or plant crops. The UI will fight you. Your basic understandings from other games will be actively hurting you. Your gnomes will die repeatedly while you are alt-tabbed out looking at the Gnomoria Wiki's "Getting Started" page. It will take you a long time before you understand what you're doing. You probably won't enjoy it. And so I don't recommend this game to you.
But that doesn't mean this game shouldn't exist. DF has an enormous following, and (let's be honest) there really *ought* to be a version of it that doesn't have such a truly unbelievably bad interface.

Don't compare this to Overwatch, even if it also has heroes.
This isn't about how you use your character. It's how you shoot. Gunplay is the most important factor in LawBreakers.
Granted, the composition of your team can be a major factor, you don't always need a support character.
Anyone can be killed by anyone. In Overwatch, you can't always expect to run in as Reaper and take down a Roadhog. DPS, Tanks, Healers are more important in OW than they are in LawBreakers.
I was able to take down Titans and Juggernauts as Assassins and Wraiths just because I had better aim then them.
This makes it a way more leveled playing field. The characters don't matter as much. They're just there to help you decide which weapon/kit works best for your gun preference.
And there's also the fact this game is honest about what it is.
As Cliff said, it's like Coke versus Pepsi. Some prefer one over the other. I like both Coke and Pepsi, they both taste great and I have an equal chance of getting diabetes with both.
With Overwatch and LawBreakers, I like them both, and I have an equal chance of getting tilted with both.
There's also the fact that it's THIRTY DOLLARS. Cliff doesn't ask for much. Just players. Try it out! You'll get more than enough of an experience in two hours. Then you can decide if it's something you want to stick with.
I refuse to let this game go down like Battleborn. We've had more than enough time to get a refresher on the hero shooter genre. And this game does just that.
If I'm getting too frustrated with OW, I'll play a couple rounds of Lawbreakers instead. And vice versa. Both are fantastic games.
Seriously, try it out.

Typically, I'll forget how heartwrenching the remaining bugs are and give it a go... get 20-30 hours into a new world and things just start devolving to buggy madness.  :(
-Gameplay-
I call it macromanagement, as you can't give any direct orders to the gnomes.  Instead, you configure the gnomes to do certain tasks, then make sure the necessary workshops and resources are also configured.
-Bugs-
"Retreat to equip uniform" is THE most frustrating of incomplete features.  Always happens... a key gnome rushes into battle with a wheelbarrow instead of retreating to grab a crossbow and gets murderized by an ogre.  This isn't a "quirky bug", it's sheer frustration.  Absolutely nothing you can do about it.  That gnome that spent 10 years perfecting his crossbow skill and is a wicked shot?   He's going to kamikaze against a two-headed ogre weilding a pine bucket full of hooch cuz... reasons.
Cascading stockpiles... doesn't really work, sadly.
Beetles.  Maybe not buggy, but definitely bad mechanics.
Mant SFX will get stuck on a certain location, and continue to chitter away, years after you slew it.  One of several reasons I mostly play without sound.
Floating helmets?  I dunno why.  They dance merrily about my kingdom.
Performance... Not great.  Single-threaded and will crush any PC once there are too many objects.  The better the PC, the more it can handle, but I've seen redditors set up big battles when they know they can let Gnomoria run 3-4 hours uninterrupted.
-Overall-
I LOVE THIS GAME.  I wish some of those bugs got fixed.  :(

The Legacy of Kain series in one of the best and most detailed and intriguing series you could ever play in your life.
It has a great gameplay and the music is iconic. The story is so intricate it will take you at least 2-3 playthroughs and being very attentive to dialogues and of course having played the 3 previous games Blood Omen, LOK: Soul Reaver, BO2 (not so relevant, worth playing tho), LOK: SR2. After that you can understand the story and what's going on. This way you will have a better understanding of what the characters are talking about the entire time.
At first I played the games as a kid. Defiance was played in 2004 by me, shortly after it came out. As a teenager I found vampires very cool and everything, but honestly I could not get half of what they were saying, although I had played SR and SR2 previously. I replayed the game at 28 and I must say, I really enjoy this even after 12 years. The graphics have aged a bit, but they will never make the game,
If anyone's reading my review I give you two alternatives:
- Don't play the game. Save yourselves the trouble of getting all the stuff done. If you play the entire series, without including the Blood Omens, it will take you at minimum a good 50-60 hours at first. They are long and the first two SR dialogues are unskippable. You will live your life without having played one of the gems in gaming but you will be calm and carefree.
- Play the game and you will enjoy one of the best written and performed games in the history of gaming. With one of the richest stories ever told. My personal favorite OST in gaming, Fully detailed environments and characters and what not. But the game ends... At a critical point. They have stopped all further developing of the series with like 10 cancelled games. You will not be calm. You will want to see the ending to the story, but there is no ending... THERE IS NO ENDING!
Choose carefully!
I chose to play the series and I am still tormented. I have replayed every game in the series a lot of times but unfortunately the answer lie not in the past anymore. I have to move on, but I can't. This review is baing written in 2016 after having successfully completed the series one more time. And the ending is as hurtful as always. A black hole, that sucks inside all the rest of the series.

CONs:

Always Sometimes Monsters is an RPG developed by Vagabond Dog to simulate survival in modern society whilst driving forward a constant storyline revolving around your chosen character and partner that you choose at the beginning of the game. The responsibility of choosing your own way in life and making important decisions really grabbed my attention when playing through this. It is not your average RPG in which you play a linear story making choices that don't necessarily affect the state of the world and the relationships you have with the people in it, Infact, the choices you make will definately affect the world around you and the way that you are treated by other characters definately towards the end of the game.
The visuals are pretty standard for an RPG of this type, but the attention to detail is definately worth a mention, If you want an interesting visual experience and a great story, this game can definately provide you with both. There are a few graphical problems, particularly with the Hospital Lobby area, the food plates seem to be hovering in mid air and are being eaten by people standing at the ends of the table instead of being sat at it, I don't know if this is a known problem, or if vagabond intend to deal with it, but it isn't an experience ruiner for sure, so don't let it affect your opinion too badly.
The music in this game is incredibly atmospheric, and provides a lot of mood setting for the particular towns and areas. The Laser Destroyer Team did a great job on it and they should be proud of the masterpieces that they produced. One of my favourite tracks is 'Hit the Town', and I suggest you give those a listen if you're into 8-bit themes.

If you're a casual puzzle solver and not tempted by achievements, you're in for a light treat. Solving the levels can be tricky, but checkpoinits and infinite retries make it inevitable if that's all you need. Get the game on deep sale because it won't take you very long.
Difficulty and gameplay time ramp up fast if you want a decent score like "B" or "A" on every level. You'll need some patience to redo levels over and over until you get them right. Any sale price is worth it.
And if you want all the achievements, be prepared to retry levels dozens of times as you shave a few seconds off them here and there. Cheating's not really an option... you need dexterity and skills to achieve the best times. The game is worth the full price if this is your idea of fun.
I'm in the last group. Dying over and over is frustrating, but getting that "S+" is hugely rewarding. Clawing my way up the global leaderboards, a fraction of a second at a time, is even more satisfying. That's why I'm S+ on 34 levels so far, and why I've enjoyed most of the 57.5 hours it took getting there.
Update: I'm sorry to say, I hit a wall on the achievements and gave up. I may find a walk-through for the level I'm stuck on, but right now I'm not that tempted.

Very short, very well-made, and very sweet stylized game you have to play. Like any other game of this genre, it is a sort of exploration, so you should not expect that much of a gameplay, and certainly not try it if you hate indie games. However, for those involved with a story, who like the plot over mechanics of slashing enemies and solving puzzles, this is a perfect game.
In this short story-rich adventure, you have to juggle a person's life, setting his priorities, and see the results envelop him, and unwrap in front of you. You'll have to whether balance job, fun, and family, or choose one, or forget about one in favour of two. There aren't any "good" or "bad" choices or endings, you just have a life in your hands, and it up to you where to direct it.
The game requires a lot of patience, as, as much as any indie adventure, it revolves around careful reading and listening, which isn't a task everyone is up to. But I got
by it, spending four hours straight on it, from the very beginning to the very end, and couldn't let go. Small pieces of lore here and there were priceless, enjoyable almost more than the story of the main character itself.
Among the minuses, uncustomizable and a little confusing key bindings, and the language used. It took a while to understand what the creator meant via his tips, and the basic mechanics and "compromises" could be explained much better, else you can be completely oblivious to what this means, unless you search through discussions to understand it.
I'd also love for tehre to be a "replay chapter" option, at least after the endgame, as I am very curious about some choice might've been made, because, hey, the game is just good enough to leave you struggling with some of them!

This is one of the games that keeps me coming back to play it over the years. Released on Steam long after Medieval II, this game has better medieval immersion than its sequel. This is because of small things like unique historical provincial title (Count of Anjou, Prince of Antioch, etc), Roman numerals after reigning monarch's name (Pope Urban II, King Henry V), the granting offices of Marshal, Constable, etc to the monarch's vassals. They disappear in Medieval II.
You'll rarely find yourself have nobody to grant the governorship of a province of yours to. You can appoint any unit commander to become one. In Medieval II, only generals and adult male royal family members who can and they're often numbered less than the province you own. There are random appearance of general available for adoption to your family if you have more provinces than your generals. This is by chance and you can't have a governor for every province you own anytime you want.
This game is also more challenging than M2TW. One of the reasons is the unit control in battle. Controlling is better in M2TW. If you manually control a missile unit engaging enemy unit in skirmish, constantly double clicking to run away when enemy getting closes, your unit would eventually rout and won't be recoverable. The game consider that unit commander is a coward. You can't rely on the game's skirmish mode at certain situations. This is true for both MTW and M2TW.

This was one of those games I wouldn't normally be interested in picking up if it wasn't for Steam sales. So i grabed this quite some time ago on sale and only just got around to finishing it with 12 hours of play time so it's an average length story .
As far as the story goes, I played the game in bits all spread out over a year so I can't fully remember the whole plot but for a cheap 2d side scroller game I'd say the story is better than some AAA games out there today.
The game controls are ok for keyboard and mouse but I had a controller plugged in and it was showing the 360 button maps on the screen so I decided just to use the pad which probably felt more fitting for the gameplay.
The combat in the game is very basic and can get quite repetitive, but jumping up from an air vent, stabbing someone in the back and dragging them back down the vent with you never gets old.
I did like the stealth mechanics in the game and the enemies/puzzles get more tricky and harder as you progress. The ninja's near the end can be very annoying to sneak past. The side puzzle rooms were also fun and although most of them were fairly easy to figure out they did change up the gameplay for a bit.
All in all, Mark of The Ninja is a decent game and worth picking up for a cheap price but I did find myself near the end just playing waiting for the game to end because it was getting repetitive quick.

This game is really fun! Reminds me of the old-school arena shooters of yore but with some character classes and fast-paced game modes thrown in. The low-grav twist makes learning this game interesting and excelling at it extremely exciting.
* High production values, from the in-game tutorial videos to the eclectic soundtrack.
* Classes are unique and fun, each one feels like a completely different way to approach combat and objectives.
* Objective-based gameplay! The game modes are exciting and reward focus, they all have opportunities for some big plays.
* Navigating in low gravity is extremely fun once you wrap your head around it.
* Ayy dem graphics is gud~
* Cosmetic loot. Some neat stuff to earn, particularly the bootprints that display when you kick a player to death.
* Character design. Characters have a mix of realistic faces and random sci-fi outfits that aren't very distinct. Luckily the UI allows you to easily distinguish who is who in a match.
:
* While the maps are very pretty and some of them are visually distinct, they can feel kind of samey and ultimately most of them are the same general layout. More variety playing with sizes or sightlines would have been appreciated.
* Just don't expect anything you shouldn't (singleplayer content, etc.) and you'll be fine.
Should you buy this game? If you wanna go fast and fly high and master a high skill ceiling with some interesting classes, yeah! If you want something chill or lore-heavy where the time-to-kill is over five seconds, nah. Stop comparing it to other stuff and just have fun.

This game is a masterpiece; I don't understand all the hate. It could be because I played it months after release, with the bugs mostly patched out and the optimization fixed (played it on High with the framerate never dipping under 60 with a rig that's slightly below the recommended specs).
The writing is wonderful, the graphics are wonderful, the soundtrack is subdued but does the job, the gameplay is excellent. The attention to detail had me floored. As you explore the world, you're constantly stumbling upon funny or moving stories of the local people, well done ads, secret passages etc...
The ending is not as grandiose as DX:HR's but it does wrap up this game's storyline well while leaving room for sequels.
My only reproach is that the beginning is incredibly slow. There's a short first act in Dubai which is great, but once arriving in Prague the game slows down to a crawl, though perseverence is greatly rewarded a few hours later.
I would heartily recommend this game to absolutely anyone with even a remote interest in video games.

I've given this some long and hard thought. I'll start with the good things.
It's beautiful, large chunks of it have wonderful attention to detail. The enormous open world that can sometime look photorealistic in the right light and distance is great. The ability to run a wanton criminal empire is great, the driving is alot of fun and loving detail has gone into the sheer number of different cars, bikes, planes and boats available. There is an in game purchase system, that isn't lootbox based. A bunch of the missions and races and whatnot are good fun in coop and there's lots to do. I'm hooked, and may be coming back to it a long time, if the annoyances below don't kill it for me eventually.
Unfortunately, there's so much wrong with it that I can't possibly give it a positive review.
1. Ridiculously expensive.
The in game purchase system is preposterously expensive, and dramatically unbalanced. Eight million in-game dollars buys you very little indeed, and rockstar has the gall to charge you 75,- euro's for that. It's ridiculous. I've found myself paying it though, but it gives one a feeling of disgust and dirtiness. Rockstar does not get my sympathy and I will think three times before ever buying another of its games.
2. New players.
If you haven't spent say ~200 euro's on in game dollars, you're ♥♥♥♥ed. There is nothing to help new players into the online version of the game and the complete lack of any sort of balancing means that you will be constantly slaughtered in ambushes or one sided exchanges in freemode untill you reach end game levels of cash which you need to bring something like 500 euro's to do or thousands of hours of gameplay and even then you will still be subject to the general freemode balance problems.
3. Balance.
Heavy military hardware is far to cheap, relatively. Freemode is dominated by ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s flying gunships hiding and griefing anyone who is trying to make some in game money which they don't really need anymore since they've already got all the cool gizmo's. Freemode pvp gameplay is a sequence of one-sided exchanges and ambushes and respawning is so close together that after the first death it's just a matter who spots who with a sniper rifle first. It's inane. Rockstar needs to look at open world pvp games and learn from them. APB has a system which is far from ideal, but dramatically better than what's going in in GTA online freemode.
4. Hackers.
They're incessant and constant. Rockstar doesn't seem to want to do anything about it. You can't tell me that it's impossible to put a sanity check on the means by which someone was killed or what happened in the minute or so before someone switched sessions. Or they should talk to the OpenIV developer and include anti-cheat code in that software. if you can't detect tanks being dropped on a helicopter in mid air, you're incompetent, rockstar.
5. Story mode.
No female character? Seriously you can't write a story which has three switchable characters ffs and you can't make one of them a woman? You have got to be kidding. Of all its numerous shortcomings, this is almost the most glaring. The previous four can be attributed to rockstar's inexperience with online pvp environments, but not including a female character in the main storyline requires actual long term ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ vision. If story mode had a decent female character, I probably wouldn't visit online at all, its so full of jerks and hackers.
Not catering to female gamers in the main story line and the intolerably bad protection of new players is really bad business by rockstar and I'd be having a serious words with them if I was one of their financers.
The sad thing is, most of this is all that hard to fix which would make it magnificent. As it stands, it's just barely tolerable and since I've run out of other games that are holding my attention, I'll stick with it untill something better comes along.

This game is freaking awesome. I don't generally like stealth games, but I had watched an extra credits video that mentioned the game and thought "Huh, this could be fun" And it is. For the sale price it is unquestionably worth the price of admission. For normal price, knowing what I know now, I'd still buy it.
And it does stealth really well, everything is streamlined and easy to understand with little time sitting still. The guard AI is simple and easy to understand, and othing terribly shocking comes from nowhere to murder you unfairly, making the times you do fail (And you will, so many times) that much more infuriating.
And there's the NG+, which I'm convinced was designed specifically to infuriate players, as it takes all the awesome things the game does for you and takes them away and it just reinforces how well it's designed.
It's also the best use of music I've seen in a video game, changing as the situation requires while keeping background elements constant to not feel jarring.
Just get this game. It's awesome.

This game is pretty bad, but for $2 it's hard to argue with. I don't know how many people these days have played or even heard of Ballance, and I have no idea how many other games are similar to Ballance or what Ballance got its ideas from, but Puzzle Ball feels like a worse made version of some of those other marble puzzle games.
Either way Ballance is rather old, and doesn't have a level editor. The puzzles in Puzzle Ball are pretty fun though extremely easy, but with the level editor the possibilities are endless but since I'm not a creative type I doubt I'll see much use out of it.
What makes the game bad? The music is terrible, a mouse cursor always flashes in the middle of the screen, the menus overlap, there's no 'next level' option when you beat a level, you can't actually close menus in 2-player mode without exiting the stage or restarting the level, deaths are rather meaningless since there's no lives or penalty that I can see, and only about half of the vital text is in English, the other half in Dutch or something. This made the tutorial totally useless, but the idea is pretty easy: use WASD or the arrow keys to guide your ball to the end using two other ball types (a stone and a paper mache ball) to solve the various puzzles. Each ball is better at different things, like paper being able to go over water (but wood can't float enough apparently) and stone being able to do some heavy hitting and fall through glass.
Other irks are the vertical split screen, horizontal would do better on some monitors and having the wider angle is easier to see anyway. It takes too long to load a level, I don't know why it has to do each individual block over the course of 10 seconds (and this on a not-weak-by-any-definition computer). The level editor has a block limit (come on we're on the PC here) and I wish a few of the graphics blended in a tad better. There aren't nearly enough actual levels (or scenarios) which I'm guessing is the purpose of the user-made levels, which, as you expect, range from absolutely terrible to waste of time impossibly hard. I also seemed to unlock achievements while idling on the home screen, and I'd get the same achievement 13 times after that. Weird.
What's good about it? The controls are good, the graphics are good, the puzzles are good, and this game is cheap as Puzzle Balls. Value wise this is a great buy, but game wise it still needs work and feels unfinished, or at least "we worked hard on this game, it's close enough, let's release it without smoothing out the rest" finished. So far best Steam Wallet buy but least favorite marble puzzle game buy.

This game is what a game needs to be, fun above all else, say what you will about Ubisoft and I will agree, but this time they did quite well at remaking the 80-90s visuals.  While the ride is short, around 6 hours if you clear most of the outposts and side missions to level your character up, since it is a Farcry 3 game it’s very open and has a level of replayability.  The story is good enough with the cutscense using old school 16 bit still images which again add to the old school feeling of the game.  However what it doesn’t do is take itself serious, this is a comedy game make no mistakes and the comedy that is there is fairly solid though younger players who did not live though the 80s and 90s might not get many of the references or be able to fully appreciate what the game is showing you.
The game’s style is great though the scan lines might give people the wrong impression about the visuals of the game though they do seem to muddy up the image a bit.  However with everything being neon in tone it’s not hard to find objects, enemies and animals within the game.  Blood dragons are by far one of the coolest natural animals that you will see in many games and they fit very well within the universe, they are also a force to be reckoned with, before you gain the highest level that is.
The one major advantage of this game is that once you to get to the highest level and max out most/all of the sub missions you will feel like a bad♥♥♥♥♥ unlike in Farcry 3 which was at times rather bland once you gained your full powers.  The arsenals are awesome though some are more useful then others, some are more customizable then FC3 while others are less so however the important ones you do have the ability to make almost every weapon 10 times better.
If any of this sounds good to you then by all means buy it and enjoy, whether it be for the humor or the fun gameplay you will enjoy your time spent playing FC3: Blood Dragon.

However, it has just the right amount of customization, the cars are very fun to drive no matter if it's a tier 1 or tier 4 car. The game world is diverse for driving, though again, not in apperance. There's winding country roads, city areas, and long highways where you can take your car all the way to the top of its abilities. 252mph seems to be the speed limit in this game, with a fully upgraded Bugatti Veyron. The police system is just a tad too unforgiving, but it's relatively simple and it is a very, very easy game to learn and quite difficult to master. The game is oftentimes too simple in the beginning no matter what car you choose, but if you choose the wrong car later in the game, you'll have a hard time beating the game. Highly recommended considering its base price on Steam is $10. One playthrough will last almost 20 hours.

Always Sometimes Monsters is a heavily narrative focused adventure game that visually appears much like a classic Final Fantasy title but plays more like a point and click adventure. You take the role of an aspiring writer whose career and relationship collapse and you travel across the country to win him/her back.
During your journey you will constantly be making extremely difficult decisions in very grey areas. The entire experience of shaping this character's journey is unbelievable and unlike most “chose the red option for bad and blue option for good” narratives, Always Sometimes Monsters makes you dig into your own conscious, having to make tough calls when facing a challenging (but not outrageous) time constraint.
All the way through the adventure, you must balance moral choices, making enough money to get by, patching together your last hope of a writing contract, and making sure you don’t starve in the streets. The developers should be incredibly proud of the story they've crafted through Always Sometimes Monsters.

Always Sometimes Monsters deeply connects to the realism of life. It connects to love, work, money, friends and ultimately the path to finding true happiness.
Without spoiling too much about the story, you start out with your character, a writer. Your manuscript is not getting published; your behind on your rent and your partner has left you. Without a cent in your pocket and no home to go to you decide to travel across the county to win back your ex that’s getting married in a month. Through the story you go through a few cities trying to make enough money and interacting with the people and world around you. This game will really question your moral code and really ask you the question of how far are you willing to go to do something.
The gameplay is heavily based on the choices you make and the consequences of that. Some of the jobs you do in the game could be a little bit tedious but it is to simulate the tedious work you would do in real life. ASM has many points in the game where you could do some extremely shady things and it will really question your humanity. However you choose to play the game will change you path and the consequences will determine your ending. As the days progress and you have less time to get to the wedding you realize things will not get any easier.

I think Vagabond Dogs took the right step in making it on RPG Maker. The soundtrack is also pretty good. The music is pretty good to listen to and it doesn’t get annoying.
In all even though ASM doesn’t look like a lot on the outside the game is truly a worth it game. The character selection is unique and the replay ability factor to this game is amazing. I recommend buying it. This unique little gem will stick to you for a really long time.
