'Tis a simple game, but a rewarding one. You are an entity that resides in a summer home. The Kaplan family has decided to rent the place to get away from it all and to help make a fresh start. Dan Kaplan is an author struggling to finish his latest novel, Linda Kaplan is a painter trying to reach out to her husband, and Tommy is a little boy struggling to read that wants to spend more time with his Dad. Your task is to discover what is on their minds each day and determine what decision should be made, which will make one family member happy and disappoint the others, though you can meet one other person halfway and compromise. The trick is to make sure everyone feel satisfied. It's up to you if you want to have one character completely have their way, focus on two, or try to balance all three. Your actions have consequences and change the relationship dynamic among the three. It's a game that encourages multiple playthroughs, which I've yet to do.

(small spoiler) The game often seems very ambiguous about the choices the user is forced to make. For example when Dan wanted to go fishing, his son wanted a sofa fort and his wife wanted to wash the ugly sweater. ALL those things could've been done and for some reason the choices were extremely important without any hint.

Unfortunately, I don't recommend this game. Though the basic idea is charming, it is so redundant. I was expecting something compelling, a psychological thriller in which you have to draw conclusions from details and behaviours. But no, the characters barely interact with each other, you just wander in the house, finding letters, journals and notes in order to find out what are their struggles, you read their memories to discover what they are longing for, and then you propose a solution. Either way, someone is unhappy. My story didn’t end so well, in fact. Even if I did try to help them!

The Novelist is a simplistic, narrative driven game, but with a really thoughtful story. The choices and compromises that you have to come to are interesting, and create a story you become involved with. It's a fairly slow moving plot, the perfect thing to sit down and play for a relaxing afternoon. I will say that replayability is limited, despite the narrative choices, and I found it difficult to complete again due to the slower pace, but as a whole I throughly enjoyed my time with this game, and the ideas and concepts that created it. Would recommend to anybody who likes narrative driven games that make the audience think and be drawn into the story.

I got this game on sale and while I enjoyed it, it is definitely not worth buying for the full $15. I think I paid $5 or under while it was on sale, and I feel that that's a fair price. The game, while it has replay value to reach different story outcomes, only lasts about 1.5-2 hours on the story mode playthrough. You could probably squeeze 5-10 hours out of it (with the replays), depending on how much you enjoy the game and your play style.
The choices you have to make affect the way the story flows, but it's basically like an interactive visual novel. I was satisfied with my first playthrough and ending and will probably replay another story mode to screw everything up, and then play once more through the stealth mode just to experience it.
I didn't notice any bugs and the navigation is simple (mostly due to how small the setting is - you are confined to a single two-story house). I was pleased with the art style and found the setting to be quite nice, although I do wish the ocean was textured better (while it blends with the art style, it does look a bit stagnant). Some tree movements (blowing in the wind, or pine needles falling) and ocean water movement would have been a welcome addition. The house also felt a bit empty for its size, but it didn't take away from the gameplay at all.
Overall, it's a nice story and experience on a sale price, but I wouldn't recommend getting it for full price.

If I were stranded on a desert island, but inexplicably provided with a gaming PC and allowed only a single game, this would certainly be it. A lot of titles have come and gone over my life, but there is something magical about this game that maintains a hold over me, even now.
Fans familiar with the franchise will recognise the game's format. At its heart, it's a turn based strategy game, composed of two arenas.
In the first, you pore over the campaign map to manage your provinces, generals and armies on the macroscopic level. You control your economy by tweaking taxes, maintaining a trade network and constructing improvements to your provinces. You recruit troops and agents to fight for supremacy through martial power or subterfuge. You plot, scheme and strategise to guide your faction to victory.
In the second, where your armies meet those of your enemies, you fight on the battle map. Here, you enjoy microscopic control of your units, making careful use of a variety of troop types to defeat enemy armies.
The gameplay is deep, thoughtful, enjoyable and memorable. Indeed, whilst newer TW games look shinier, their gameplay does not reach the same depths. The sheer scope of ways to play is unmatched. Moreover, the simpler campaign map is much easier for the AI to handle, resulting in genuinely rewarding and complex campaigns.
The game also triumphs in its smaller touches like the texture of notification parchments, the gentle soundtrack, the emerging personalities of generals, the wealth of historical information.
But my favourite feature, the one that dwarfs all others, is the replayability. Every campaign is different. Sometimes you'll see the AI perform spectacularly with one faction, only to see it destroyed swiftly in the next campaign that you play. Plus, there are multiple periods in which to play, and so many strategies.
For the belligerent, one can focus on martial power and grind enemies into the dust. For the shrewd, one can exercise soft power by hoarding riches, then bribing enemies and relying on mercenaries. For the underhanded, one can employ a variety of agents, be they assassins, spies or diplomats. Or you can mix all three!
Furthermore, every campaign is itself a wonderful journey. Every nuance contributes to the immersion. A faction rejects my alliance? I'll remember that when they leave their rich provinces poorly defended. Former master general becomes a violent drunkard with waning loyalty? I can assassinate him, frame him for treason, put him on trial for heresy or cart him off to govern a province far away. King is weak and ineffectual, rapidly losing influence over his generals? Let's do everything to stir up disloyalty and simply support the rebellion in the ensuing civil war, quietly removing a useless leader and a minority of misguided loyalists.
In this way, each campaign tells a story, much like the history of any nation. Winning a campaign is not just about the victory itself, but about telling a story fecund with the brutality, avarice and intrigue of the Medieval world.
So, whenever I jump into a new campaign, I am reminded of these previous games; every faction is held accountable, in my own mind, for its betrayals and underhanded moves in previous campaigns; every province has a memory that makes me smile.
And every campaign is a new challenge, a new story.
Sure, the game has its flaws. The battle map looks horribly dated and the later games improved heavily upon this, particularly with the siege features. But the game holds up beautifully well across the board and contains far more depth on the macroscopic level than supposed sequels.
Why is it doing badly on Steam? Well, lots of people are having crashes. There are fixes out there, but maybe it's not working for everyone. It's a shame really, but I wrote this review to tell people that the game is enchanting and that they should not be perturbed by reports of a few crashes. Patches have come; fixes are known. Indeed, I love this game so much, I wrote an extensive crash fixing guide for the community.
To sum up, fans of the franchise who came late, or strategy veterans looking for a new challenge, I implore you to try this game! It is a wonderful experience and a triumph of video gaming.

LUMBERMANCER is an action adventure game from Roger von Biersborn. Before we go any further, I just want to say that I backed this game on Kickstarter and I’m proud of it. Let’s get rocking.
The Good
Let’s take a moment to address both the title of the game and the profession of the character that you play as in the game: Lumbermancer. As a bearded male who has a proclivity for dressing in flannel, the term Lumbermancer thrills me at a spiritual level.
The art is wonderful. There isn’t a single thing in this game that isn’t entertaining to look at. Just wait until you have your own little log men slicing through ghosts like sausage. It’s seriously delightful.
The story of the game is one that I feel we can all identify with in some way: it’s one man’s quest to get himself  a sandwich. While the quest shown in the game is easily far more epic than going to your local sub shop, it is, nonetheless, relatable.
The Bad
Absolutely nothing.
The Meh
Due to a physical limitation, I play nearly all games with a controller rather than a keyboard and mouse. I feel like this was an important disclaimer to put before my next comment which is more of a personal nitpick than an actual complaint. Sometimes, it becomes tedious to control both the Lumbermancer and his logs at the same time using the joysticks. However, I can see how using a keyboard to do this would be vastly easier.
Verdict: Yea
If you weren’t a Kickstarter backer, this game is only $3.99 on the Steam Store. I can’t think of any actual reason to not get this game, play it, and enjoy your time spent doing so.

An diamond in the rough, Aeternum is a western made shmup that could not borrow more from Touhou in style or design. You play a demon girl (And later a couple of other characters) flying through a school, blasting trash enemies, dodging huge piles of bullets with a tiny hitbox, and meeting a quirky anime girl, with whom communications immediately break down a fight starts. The bosses have timed and scored patterns with bonuses for clearing them successfully without getting hit, as well as time out options to support the game's pacifist mode, but the trippy visuals when they engage them is pure Touhou. Enemies drop power items that boost your power, which also doubles as your bombs, and of course there's a Touhou style autocollect line if you can advance far enough on the screen. Dangerous but rewarding.
This game doesn't really WANT to murder you though; bosses drop a full bomb's worth of power each pattern you clear. And if that's not enough, on Story mode you get nearly infinite retries so long as each death  just throws you back in with much less power and you can keep coming back as long as your power doesn't hit zero; a boss would have to utterly destroy you for that to happen. Not to say it can't and won't, but the game makes the bosses work for it, yet it feels like the gamer dignity wounding charity it is. The story is charming enough and worth the trip.
For the veterans, an arcade mode drops the story chatter and the infinite respawn gimmick, as well as four difficulties to meet you wherever you like on skill level from a walk in the park to a walk through Detroit with the wrong gang colors while Pyramid Head, Nemesis, and the T-1000 are after you for your past, present, and future. Bullet patterns are elaborate, colorful, and spammy in a Touhou-esque manner. An extra boss, again Touhou-esque, concludes the story in a clever manner that leaves it satisfying and also whets my appetite for other games in this goofy universe.
There's a lot of competition in the indie shmup market these days, but Aeternum is worth your time if you have any love for a Touhou style bullet hell.

A side scrolling shoot em up that reminds us of Choujikuu Yousai Macross (Famicom 1985) and the gradius/parodius series (many platforms).
It has a story and chibi Anime and fantasy theme in it too.
Why? Because they wanted to.
It’s being a long time since we played a title of this genre and it’s a nice reminder of what has changed since the Nintendo Family computer.
We really didn’t like the mix of a fantasy, magic school genre with a side scrolling shooter. Yes we are aware Twinbee and Parodius did similar back in their time.
Regarding game mechanics we quite like the include the focus and graze system. This reminds us a lot of Choujikuu Yousai Macross which also allowed you to change the size of your hit box. The shields aren’t a bad idea either. It’s not immediately obvious that the 2 characters you can play as have different shields and different power ups.
Speaking of powerups we would of preferred a system like Raiden with 2 or 3 colours and missiles OR Gradius which had a bar at the bottom allowing you to select which power up.
One thing to note it is critical you play this with a modern controller e.g. an xbox controller. A DPAD of the Famicom/NES or SNES days or keyboard keys would not give you a good experience.
It's also interesting to note that autofire is the norm these days. I wonder how this would play without auto fire.
The pacifism run and arrange mode were good ideas but we played arcade mode the most.
Local multiplayer!
This type of game lends itself to it. One more person to dodge those bullets with you and help you shield would have played well.
On this note perhaps even online multiplayer.
We were also didn't like using X as the default to shoot and were glad to to remap it to A.
Do you like learning patterns and weaving through a screen full of obstacles? In other words do you like honing quick responses?
Do you like chibi anime art?
Is happy and chirpy chiptune/pop music your thing?
On the other hand you can think...
Are you a gamer who doesn’t have the patience to practice their reaction time?
Do you really not like anything cute?

--OVERVIEW--
I just got this game on release day, and I must, say, it's surprising! Puzzle Ball is, in essence, a spiritual successor to marble-based games like Marble Blast Gold, Ballance and Marble Madness. Being a lover of Marble Blast Gold, I thought that this couldn't hurt and gave it a try. After playing with a few of the scenario levels and checking out the level editor, I must say that this game is amazingly fun for 3 dollars. This game is not as much of a skill platformer as others in its genre, but is more of a puzzle, like the name implies. Figuring out the order in which to accomplish challenges for a high score is important, as some points can be permanently missed if you don't do them at the right times. However, there is never so much chalenge that you will get angry at the game, as the game does live up to its "casual" tag This, the beautiful graphics, and the relaxing music combine to create a surprisingly fun experience, as watching each levels' mechanisms come to life is fascinating, and there is some satisfaction in completing each level.
--THE EDITOR--
In addition, the level editor is quite easy to use, as the description states. It is a simple "pick block and place" style editor. However, the camera and controls of the editor are a bit weird, so there is definitely room for improvement there. Other than that, there isn't too much for me to say about the level editor, as I'm not into taht sort of thing.
>NOTE: There is a "level budget," so you cannot make infinitely big levels! :(
--MENUS--
This is where my criticisms start. After launching the game, you will be treated to a small graphic informing you of the controls. There seems to be no way to bring this up again besides restarting the game. After dealing with the graphic, you will be treated to a menu with no logo and four buttons: "Levels," "Editor," "Options" and "Quit." Clicking "Levels" takes you to a bland screen with the 11 scenario leves shown, with the options to look at user levels. Clicking "Editor" throws you straight into the editor with no options or preparation screen. Selecting "Options" brings you to an options screen where you can edit your screen resolution, quality (idk what this exactly means), your languages (choices of English, Russian, and Dutch), something called "Image Resolution" (I really have no idea what this does), your sound/music volumes, whether to be fullscreen/windowed, bloom, and SSAO. There is no way to rebind key controls, although they are standard (WASD) and you shouldn't have trouble with them. While the menus certainly are functional, they are bland and lack depth; but as this is a 3 dollar game, it is acceptable.
--PROS--
>Interesting gameplay
>Very nice graphics
>Relaxing music
>Infinite replayability with the level editor
>Good learning curve
--CONS--
>Only 11 built-in levels
>Lame menus
>Some typical functionality missing (rebinding controls, advanced graphics, etc.)
>Small music selection
--VERDICT--
>9/10<

This game along with it's entire collection have been a cherished treasure of mine. Too bad itll be one short since Legacy of Kain: Blood Omen can't make it a complete set.
Main Plotpoint(s): After the events of Soul Reaver 2, the player with be running through consistently switching playthroughs between both Kain and Raziel, 500 years between each other after the paradoxical instance in the Sarafan Stronghold. Raziel came close to being absorbed by the Soul Reaver until Kain freed him and prevented another predestined course of events. Now both Vampires are on their entwined journeys to discover more of the truth behind their destinies and to hope that there is still a chance to defy Fate.
-A wonderful story, exposition, and ending that makes you feel like you're reading a fantasy novel. The characters are well thought out as well as most of the environments. I really want to take a field trip in the Sarafan Stronghold, The Pillars, and the Vampire Citadel. It feels like spots to just take a break with a book and some tea.
- Playing as both Kain and Raziel were truly an experience as each character's story always seem to intertwine as you journey in the same spots that are spaced out between 500 years.
-The combat mechanics are a little more dynamic than in the previous games, but still pretty meh as there weren't many moves to work with. You can gain EXP to gain a total of 5 combos. So yeah. Dodging a messload of enemies at once becomes a fight for life! You can't go in a beat em up like God of War, they'll ignore that♥♥♥♥♥♥and give you a hard time.
-The puzzles this time around are a bit more watered down than Soul Reaver 1 and 2, but the game makes it up by using different elemental reavers to solve them. It was fun.
- The Camera. OH MY GOD THE CAMERA. Back during the old days of fixed camera positions in games, this hurt me the most. Every room has it's own fixed point of view and you can only pan the camera's view away. When this happens, I spend 5- 10 seconds trying to find where the hell I am. It's even a pain because it makes the platforming a total illusion. You can't tell how far you are from gliding to another platform until you fall off and start over.  This goes especially wrong with Raziel as with his movement. When you stop, he kind of has some ice physics going on for a brief second.
- Overall: Pretty damn good game. But it's terrible to play with a keyboard and mouse. Get a compatible gamepad.

Great game. Played it on hard and it took me roughly 25 hours to beat it. Once you're done with the story, you still have a bunch of special challenges to beat (both combat and stealth related) and it doesn't even end there. Then, if you can, you still have a ton of hidden riddles around the asylum that are a lot of fun to find.
As I could not beat the challenges (I warn you, they ARE hard)I uninstalled the game after beating it to the end for the first time, and just a few days ago I decided to install it again (for which I blame Marvel’s Daredevil TV series, which made me want to punch thugs and feel like a superhero once again) and well, I 100%’ed the game this time and can only recommend playing it.  I easily just put another 25 hours in the game, and had a lot of fun along the way. This game *gets it*. You really feel like Batman, the combat flows, the animations are well done, there are no loading screens to speak of, the game looks beautiful and the story and the appearances of the enemies are kind of justified. And, if you want to want to learn more about the characters, you have a bunch of entries about most of them. The gadgets are fun to play with, but I admit that it’s kind of annoying how convenient everything is for Batman. “Oh, I’m stuck in this island… never mind, I have several batcaves in every corner of Gotham, mwahaha!” The game is perfectly adapted to the PC, almost no FPS drops, and if you are Spanish or if you are learning Spanish, I recommend playing it in that language, as the quality of the dubbing and of the translation is extremely well done. I think this is one of the very, very rare occasions in which I prefer a dubbed product rather than the original. But yeah, that’s just my opinion. Anyway, congrats to everyone who participated in the Spanish localization of the game.
And among the best moments of the game, I loved the parts with Scarecrow in them. Extremely interesting and engaging, and trying not to spoil too much, there’s this particular part that resembles the now classic  fight against Psycho Mantis in MGS1. That was genius and I loved it. We need more mind-blowing, scary stuff like that in video games.

If you enjoyed the movies/series/comics, you'll definitely like this game.
So yeah, if you still haven't played any arkham games, you should definitely give this one a go. It's your chance to be Batman, should I really say anything else? *vanishes*

I've just finished it, and I kinda don't know what to say.
It was funny and rather engrossing. In the middle, I thought the game was going to take a downturn, but it didn't. It totally held my interest the whole way through. They do a good job of both doing a (sort of) life sim and telling their story (trying to get a few cities away, with no money, to go to your ex's wedding).
Huge plus points for the fact that you get to pick both your gender AND your partner's gender. It really is a massive perk to me to be able to play gay in a game (and, probably had a bit to do with my level of engrossed as well).
I really have nothing bad to say about this game. Well written, funny, sweet, tender, it packs a lot into its environments and populates them with interesting characters, some of who's stories I never got to the end of (FK, for example, I wonder what happened there). Much like life. And the way they tie in the end with the beginning (which I had forgotten all about) is great.
A huge factor to note is the moral dilemma's that the game throws up. One minor example, for example, some girl asks you to buy her drugs. You can take her money and buy her the real stuff, or spend part of her money, give her fakes and keep the change, which was what I did. But the next time I saw her, she was woozy and sick and I felt really guilty (and also lost an avenue to the game, which I didn't realise until checking later!). So yeah, some choices have big affect, some don't, and like life, you never know which is which.
Tldr; Just buy the thing and enjoy being a struggling writer who lost the love of his life and is doing everything he can to get back to him. Quirky, well-drawn (in both senses of the word), well-written, varied story-driven game. I'm already eagerly awaiting their next game!

This is a very difficult game to assess. It's well worth playing, but isn't without its frustrating aspects.
It has some great writing - interesting characters, hilarious moments, and others which are quite touching and thought-provoking. However, the tone is quite odd. It jumps from dark and meaningful to silly and self-indulgent so frequently that it can be quite jarring.
Despite the adult themes, it's hard to ever take it too seriously. Homelessness and poverty are worthy topics to address, but it's undermined when fishing in the local pond and sleeping on a mattress in the street are actually better options than buying food or paying rent. Still, perhaps that's a decent way to handle it; it would be an ordeal to play the game if it was too dark.
The steps required to get a decent ending are quite unintuitive. My lazy female author avatar not only can but pretty much needs to be a champion boxer (and/or save-scumming gambler) to end up well! Other options for gathering the required money would have helped.
It's also a little odd that my host and potential mother-in-law isn't bothered that I nearly killed a toddler and then ransacked his backpack for toys as long as I admit that it was wrong!
Still, there's something compelling about it. There's some aspects of a really good story there, and though it tails off a bit towards the end, there's enough good elements to keep playing through to the end. The devs deserve particular credit for giving you a range of character options, and adapting a fair amount of dialogue to reflect that.
It's a very solid effort. Hopefully the devs will learn from it and come back with an even better second game.

Too plodding and slow paced to be the kind of reaction based platformer it wants to be. Edge also relies on deaths you couldn't possibly know are coming the first time through, which is just cheap. It's a shame, because in many ways the levels are very well crafted, for the most part-there's clearly a lot of thought that goes into certain aspects of the design, but the execution is sorely lacking.

There's a particular style of game that seems to rub everyone the right way, and I'm not sure if it has a name or not. It's that ultra-minimalist look found in REZ, Lumines, and Chime, lots of right angles and primary colors, attended by a light-electronica soundtrack and synthesized voice. Everyone loves it for some reason, maybe because it feels like a friendly sort of futuristic. EDGE is another puzzle entry in this unnamed genre, but it does a lot more than just ape a popular aesthetic.
EDGE is so named because you control a perfect cube, pulsating with color, that rolls around on its edges. This isn't the imprecise flailing of Gravilon or square golf balls in Golf With Your Friends, this is precision movement across a grid of blocks suspended in some vast void. Holding the arrow key in a direction makes the cube tilt that way, and holding it long enough will make it tip into the next grid space. Your cube can tilt up elevations equal to its height this way as well, allowing you to scale stairs. Feathering the button lets you balance on your edge and rack up Edge Time, a bonus scoring mechanic that can also save you if a platform drops out from under you.
This tight control scheme is the cornerstone of EDGE, because the sprawling levels will assemble all manner of paths, tunnels, platforms, and obstacles to navigate. Some might have you following a one-block-wide path, some might have you flipping to and from speeding platforms, some might have you tumbling across falling blocks, and so on. There are even some complex scripted level features like robots and trains formed out of the moving landscape. Each level has a theme to match, and it is always presented in some recognizable way using the basic two-tone blocks that comprise everything.
You'll come across a number of colorful prisms in each level as well, which factor heavily into your scoring. Time is another factor, as is how many deaths you racked up. You can die, in a sense, by plunging off the side of a level. Sometimes this will be because of a flip in the wrong direction, other times it will be because an obstacle shoved you into the void. Regardless of what gets you it will happen often, but you lose very little thanks to the copious checkpointing in each level.
It's a simple premise, but the execution elevates it to something special. EDGE is polished to a mirror shine, with sharp graphics, a pumping soundtrack, and lovingly-crafted levels. There's around a hundred of those levels to get through, and the challenge is steep enough that it'll take you quite a few hours even without locating all the prisms. And mastering the movement of your cube is extremely gratifying when you finally start pulling off complex flips across harrowing hazards. After just a few levels you'll see why EDGE deserves to be counted among those classic games I mentioned above, and its look and feel are the least of many reasons.

This game is pure perfection.
The first of the Arkham series you dive into Arkham Asylum in the hopes of stopping the Clown Prince of Crime in his evil doings. Playing as the brooding Dark Knight you have an array of items at hand to help you defeat the goons and mutated enemies of Arkham Asylum.
I played this game so much on the xbox my disc broke!! I enjoyed the story mode, it was exactly how a Batman/Joker story should be featured. Harley Quinn was also a intergrated part of the game, showing the twisted and abusive relationship between the Joker and Harley.
Graphics reflected the game, dark and brooding. Although good they could have done with a little more attention. I enjoyed the look though as it gave the game its atmosphere. The characters exuded personality, the Joker (voiced by Mark Hamill) was his usual, crazy self with his laugh down to perfection. You could tell the voice actors went all in because of how their voices gave their pixel counterparts a life of their own.
The controls of the game were easy to master and moving Batman was easy. The controls flow especially through fight scenes moving from enemy to enemy easily and gracefully. You level up with XP to gain better and stronger equipment and better finishes to easily take down those annoying goons that roam the grounds. You have detective vision which means you can follow trails, scan evidence and see enemies. You have the usual gadgets such as the Batarang and the Bat Grapple to more unusual gadgets such as Explosive Gel which is useful for breaking walls, floors and blowing up enemies to the Cryptographic Sequencer which hacks into panels, overloading them in order for you to get inside otherwise inaccessable areas!
The one thing I enjoy about this game is the Riddler Trophies. This was fun for me to go around and try and find. His riddles were the trickiest, trying to find out exactly what his riddle meant and where you were meant to find the area to scan. So much fun and you don't feel like you are grinding for the trophy/achievement. Also you have a certain amount of Joker Teeth chattering about in different parts of the Asylum which count towards the Riddler.
Recordings are also dotted about on the patients of Arkham. From Harley to The Riddler you can hear what they said in their interviews with the doctors of Arkham Asylum.
I also loved the Nightmare parts, going after The Scarecrow you end up in the deepest recesses of Batman's nightmares. That was fun to play through except seeing Scarecrow about ten feet tall!! In these parts you have to take your time and make sure you don't get caught by his gaze!!
You can also play arenas where you take on waves of enemies. This was fun for when I just wanted to sit and kick the goons asses. I don't really have much to say on that part except it was awesome!!
All the usual Gotham characters make an appearance, Joker, Harley, Scarecrow, Killer Croc and Poison Ivy. You have Barbara Gordon (Batgirl) on the line helping you through your quests. Jim Gordon appears in the first cut scene and the last.
In my opinion this game is 9.5/10. Good graphics, good controls and a beautifully indepth story. Well worth a play!!

1: Redefines what a superhero game should be; upgrading equipment really impacts how situations are approached, making each encounter unique.
2: Riddler Trophies are addicting to collect, solve, and uncover; best of all collecting them awards XP which can be used to quickly unlock upgrades for Armor, Gadgets, or Takedowns.
3: Level design is genius and aesthetically pleasing; as the story unfolds the island continuously changes to reflect the plot.
1: Startup Issues are not uncommon and can be a headache to solve without prior knowledge; saves can become corrupted and inaccessible.
2: CTD’s and FPS Issues can sometimes occur in certain locations; these issues can be fixed with some editing of the game files.
3: Steam queries and prioritizes Cloud synchronized files regardless of Steam settings; which can result in “General Protection Faults”.
My Thoughts on Batman: Arkham Asylum,
I was skeptical that any superhero game could ever be “good”, especially after the horrific Superman Returns game, but Batman: Arkham Asylum wasn’t just good it was Rocksteady’s magnum opus. The storyline is fabulously written and expertly performed by Batman: The Animated Series veterans Kevin Conroy, Mark Hamill, & Arleen Sorkin. Gameplay mechanics are flawless and so fine-tuned that even years after its release they remain unrivaled by anything but others in the series.
I’m not going to sugar coat it; this game can become a real pain to get up and running if your experiencing startup errors like the dreaded “General Protection Fault”. FPS issues are not too much of a concern but I tend to get a slight slowdown in the bell tower but nothing so extreme it hinders my enjoyment.
Overall if you’re not a fan of Batman or superhero games in general this gem will certainly help you see the light but before you run off and buy it I suggest you cool it for a moment and pick it up on sale for $5.00 bucks instead of the listed $19.99… and while you’re at it grab the sequel Batman: Arkham City for $5.00 too because I guarantee you’re going to want more Batman after the conclusion and sure you can do some fun challenge maps but that’s only going to increase your appetite for more Arkham.

Wow. I've never played a game quite like this one. I mean sure the themes are pretty run of the mill life simulated problems but the way you play through them was unique and fun.
You're a ghost of some sort who spies on a family as they take a whole summer vacation away from home. You focus your attention on Dan primarily and how he should balance his carreer and his relationship with his wife and son. You have the ability to see their thoughts and travel into their memories to learn more about the situations that beg for resolutions as well as things laying around the house like journals or letters. If you uncover all the clues you are granted the ability to choose one perfect outcome and one outcome that got compromised. You can't make everyone happy so someone is always gonna be disappionted. The trick is a balancing act in and of itself and almost ballbusting to figure out how to get a happy ending.
Something I didn't like was that everything revolved around Dan. No one seemed to be able to make their own happiness which frustrated me. I would've liked to see some of the disappointing outcomes to end with their own improvements. For instance, Tommy (the son) wanted to have his friend sleep over one weekend but I chose not to honour that one. One of the clues suggested that his friend's parents were open to housing Tommy for a weekend so instead of that route getting an absolute disappointment, it would've been cool to see Tommy just asking his friend if he could stay over there independent of what Dan decided. Linda (the wife) had one such out come I guess but it still woudla been nice to see them thinking for themselves a bit so their happiness didn't ride of Dan all the time.
Other than that, the story telling aspects are great. The music is atmospheric and tone appropriate. It is a pretty ok I'd say. Thumbs up!

DLC Quest is an indie game that serves as a playable mockery of how extreme some developers are about selling you DLC. It's a funny joke...For a few minutes. The game only has 1 joke: "Haha, isn't it crazy how bad DLC can get?" and it's true, DLC can be crazy. Developers like Paradox are especially guilty of this, as they cut out entire mechanics that are practically CRUCIAL to their games so they can eek out some extra pennies.
But the game's main problem is that it simply has nothing unique up its sleeve. It just wants to serve as a "Take that!" to DLC-whoring developers. Making a game was not high up on the list.
I couldn't finish it as I just got so sick of the joke being repeated ad nauseum and teethless gameplay. Hell, I don't even think I got halfway before I slammed my head down and yelled aloud "I GET IT, DLC SUCKS, TELL A DIFFERENT JOKE OR GET OFF MY HARD DRIVE." Naturally, it just replied "Isn't DLC just the worst? Wanna buy your horse armor DLC? :D" and I closed the game, bored to tears.
Even at $3, I'd argue it fails to live up to what it charges. (My rule of thumb is usually $1 = 30 mins - 1 hour for fulfilled value, with some exceptions.) If you don't mind buying a game that has no game and only 1 joke to tell, then you'll probably get some entertainment out of DLC Quest. However, I'll point people to better games like FTL, Binding of Isaac, and even *shudder* Undertale instead of DLC Quest if they want a good indie game.

Played through nonlethal. Spent countless hours exploring, reading people's emails, and shamelessly save scrubbing. I then went back and played through HR again to finally do The Missing Link and it made me appreciate this new engine MD is running on.
I'm working on a second playthrough now to try the new DLCs. Just like any immersive sim, if you do nothing but the main story, it will be short and underwhelming.
In comparison to Human Revolution, the controls (using a controller) are fluid, inventory managment is also far more forgivable, addition of armor piercing and emp bullets for most guns, smart vision looks and works better, the new battery meter has longevity, and you can now use optical camouflage to hack unnoticed indefinitely.
I could see myself putting another hundred hours into the game.

Final thoughts:
Environmental Detail - The game is absolutely packed with detail, so much that even my 1080GTX can't hold a perfect 60FPS. Character models look great, but the animations leave much to be desired, especially the stilted dialogue animations. Also, you will see the same male/female models copy and pasted not just for the pedestrian NPCs, but for the side-quest givers as well.
Loot: Resources are so prevalent in the environment that they make merchants redundant.
Exploration - It's fun but much of it is vapid and ultimately unrewarding: seldom does breaking into apartments or store basements lead to side-quests or unique loot. However, I do appreciate that the game respects your curiosity and exploratory inclinations. Anecfore: There's an area (theater) in the game that I decided to explore as part of a different mission, and I was surprised how large and complex it was. I uncovered the vents, I punched through the weak walls, and didn't find much. However, an hour or two later I was sent to that same location as part of a mission, and sure the guards were restocked, but the environment was as I had left it. That was pretty neat-o.
Level Design - My greatest disappoint with Mankind Divided is how tenuous the skill progression is. No matter how you play, you will become a jack of all trades. It's a great shame too, because the game does an admirable job of providing you various ways of navigating its environments. The only time you really have to commit to a particular style of play is only truly relevant during the opening hours. It's apalling that all of the skills cost the same across the board and it really doesn't take long before you have all of the skills that you want.
Summation: skill progression is far too lenient to enforce a particular style of play, and it's a shame since the title has the level design to support it. the hub based setting is a bold move that I would like to see carried into the future with more thought put into fleshing out the more pedestrian areas (apartments, stores).
Things I would like to see as a player/fan of classic/new Deus Ex:
-enemies impervious to stun (must be stealthed around or killed)
-obstacles that cost more than ONE (yes, "1") multitool to overcome
-a much, much, much smaller STARTING inventory
-much higher priced skill costs
-I would like there to be two forms of stealth takedowns: a longer, but quieter, choke AND a faster, but much louder, takedown that can alert guards
-(this will never happen, but I think it would remedy my gripe against Mankind Divided's progression) I want to see the "overclocking" feature overhauled. I would like for there to be a system in place whereby you can only have a certain number/combination of agumentations enabled at any given time. this could be tied to the difficulty you're playing in. think of them as loadouts, you spend your skill points to unlock Augs and need to equip them strategically. Assuming the next title will be hub-based, it would give players a great reason to return to the Doc. when out on missions, the player could choose to deactivate an aug to enable a new one (that he's saved skill points for) and not be able to re-configure without returning "home" to the doc. Of course this won't happen, since the game actually has a quest where the overclocking restriction is COMPLETELY lifted. what a shame.

Human Revolution was my first entry in Dues Ex. Quite enjoyed that game. Interesting characters, locales, missions and so on and so forth. This, on the other hand, felt like a letdown in comparison. Sure, my favorite part of the game, the hacking is still in the game and is as good as I remember, everything else just felt... boring. Most of the time I felt like I was doing chores. Doesn't help that you're in a single city split into two, completely uneven parts and you have to travel back and forth all the time for missions, be it main objectives or side objectives. And a lot of the city was just empty space. Looking back at it, the bank was the most fun part if you had the right augments and could find your way around it. Otherwise every store was the same, every building was more or less the same.
Gameplay itself was fine as far as I'm concerned. Since I played non-lethal, I felt no major difference to Human Revolution. Except that maybe sneaking around was easier as less obstacles were put in your way or you had more than enough tools to get around them. Oh, and the ledge grabbing was a bit wonky at times.
Story felt short and totally incomplete. Either they cut parts for DLC (which I'm not gonna touch even though I have them, just not interested) or they were trying to set up for a sequel(-s). But at least the side missions were somewhat interesting.
As for characters it felt like they were there only as set pieces. Nothing more. Frankly, you could've replaced the with cardboard cutouts and you would've achieved the same effect. They were just bland and uninteresting. And for some reason they were more or less the same. All disgruntled and against you. And the villains are not much better to be fair. The 'true' villains, if you will, are at least somewhat interesting, but there's too little interaction between you and them to actually matter. And the "surprise" during credits frankly is not even that. Won't spoil it, but it was fairly predictable already halfway through the game.
All in all I felt disappointed. While I kept remembering the flashy China or dark and broody Detroit from Human Revolution. Not to mention Panchea which was a great ending zone. I think all I'll remember from this is the metro and constant ID checks.
tl;dr
Get it if it's on a sale and you want some more augmented fun, otherwise I'd suggest to steer clear from this one. At least at full price.

Alright, fam, so first of all. I have soooo many more hours clocked into this game than Steam is showing. I am mostly playing in offline mode and I also played a lot of it before it even hit Steam.
This game is a masterpiece. Simply put.
It was my first Total War game. It made it one of ,if not my favourite gaming franchise.
Being released in 2002 it holds up really damn well to today's standards.
The premise is simple. Total War. Military and diplomatic simulator. But its mostly war. Be ready to destroy every other faction on the map to please your inner warlord.
The game is picked up pretty easily. The mechanics are nothing to be scared off. Nothing on a Paradox Interactive level of complexity. However, it is quite the challenge to master it and beating a campaign on Expert requires some solid learning and skill. The gameplay is rewarding. In terms of AI and difficulty I dare say it surpasses most of its successors. And it's not just the more organized region system to be thanked for this. The Battle AI handles itself and the Campaign AI knows when to attack or when to abandon a province.
Factions play differently from eachother, factors like starting position, religion and culture mean a lot. There are 3 starting dates you can choose from which change the gameplay significantly and the Viking Invasion expansion is also an entire monster on its own. You can fish for mods on the internet and trust me, they are worth it.
The diplomacy system has less features than any of the newer TW games. You are basically restricted to bribing, allying and organizing royal marriages. Not having diplomats and princesses actually affects your gameplay. Now, despite the fewer options diplomacy is more reliable, allies are not complete backstabbing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, alliances are tied really quickly, AI factions usually make the right decision in choosing between two allies and not a single game will be the same. Individual nits are assigned their own named leaders which are given their own stats like loyalty, piety and others. Micromanagement and immersion are perfectly implemented. The construction system encourages variation in city building and region management. (Features that have been completely bareboned in the newest installments)
The army system is in my opinion one of the best TW has ever offered. I am especially impressed by the mercenary system, units which you can only recruit by building an Inn. And it's exciting getting travelling vikings or Italian Militia fighting for you, Spain, in Northern Africa. The autoresolve system for battles works perfectly. You have to take in account not just numbers but bonuses, counters and especially the rank of your general. And you will need the autoresolve system because here is my first con.
Battles are outdated. You can fight them, you can win them, you can enjoy them. But coming from newer games the interface is clunky, you can only zoom in so far and the graphics are barely pleasant.
Back to graphics, the campaign user interface, the menu, the portraits and the overall artistic style of the game is timeless. There's something enthralling about it and it really captures the medieval atmosphere, especially combined with the glorious soundtrack. Yes, the soundtrack is divine, immersing, flawlessly medieval.
Overall, the gameplay is top notch and you will find yourself pressing for the next turn more than you'd like to. If you can enjoy the sprite battles even better. Medieval 1 is a perfect example of a game that can resist time by simply having solid features.
9/10, the price is totally worth it.

Go home now". Come-ON!
- And the last point is a bad bug (even if I'm pretty sure it's just matter of negligence). You play on this pixelart maps. They do have, obviously, borders. There are natural, randomized obstacles like trees and bushes, and also dangerous ones like lava pools. It often happens that one of this obstacles is near the top/bottom border of the map, and they are always at the same distance from it, that is the exact distance to let a player pass between the border and the obstacle. Now this game really takes me back to my younger years. 2D side scrolling games are what I was raised on so needless to say I was immediately interested upon seeing this. Add to that a modern edge and a stealth system that works better than some AAA titles and you have a recipe for a fantastic gaming experience.
You start off with fairly limited powers but accumulate more as you progress through the story and more combat and stealth approaches become available. What I particularly love about the game is how powerful you feel. It's been said that in this game you are not the 'hunted' but the 'hunter' and while in some stealth games you can feel somewhat overwhlemed, that never happens here.
The story is fairly generic if I'm brutally honest but it works, and it's not the story that keeps dragging you back in, it's the solid gameplay, excellent mechanics, fluid controls and wonderful presentation which will leave you wanting more. Not only that, but this is a game you'll want to play again as there are simply so many ways to tackle each level. Using a combination of the tools you have and your own intelligence you can turn even the most seemingly difficult situation to your advantage.
Put simply, Mark Of The Ninja is a truly excellent platformer which outshines many of the big names in stealth as far as I am concerned. I  would highly recommend this even at full price. It's a beautifully crafted, expertly designed and truly addictive solo experience. Exactly the kind of game I like.

I went into this game unsure of what to expect.  I've always loved Klei's art style, and while I utterly suck at Shank, I found its gameplay to be very tight and enjoyable.  However, I've had very little exeperience with stealth games and the hype for this was through the roof, which is usually setup for disappointment.
I came out of my inital twenty hours with a new additoon to my favorite video games of all time.
Let me be the first to admit, this games narrative is probably its weakest aspect.  It attempts to emulate the kitschy ninja and martial arts movies of old, and while that's something I should love, I found the excectuion to be lacking.  A lot of the voice acting is pretty flat and there's a glaring thematic inconsisentcy to the gameplay's focus on true ninja techniques and the narrative's emphasis on the western misconception of "honor" among ninja.  However, that's easily overlooked thanks not only to the incredible job done with all other aesthetic qualities, but also the gameplay itself.
This game is so ludicrously elegant.  So beautifully designed, fluid and engaging, that I almsot can't believe actual humans made it.  Humanity implies fallibility, and the core mechanics of this game have none that I can think of.  Every limitation is deliberate, every ability satisfying, every animation goregoud and fluid.  It all comes together to deliver on the game's central conciet: making you feel like a ninja.  Not an unstoppable badass with a hood and katana.  Not a one-man army that happens to dress like a feudal Japanese spy.  Not a barely-clothed cheesecake factory with a sharp fan who giggles and calls herself "kunoichi" while all the straight male gamers bend over backwards to call her a strong female character.  A NINJA.  An honest-to-god shadow warrior who strikes hard and vanishes into the night.  The core mechanics of this game and the vast majority of the way those mechanics are implemented are SUBLIME.
Unfortunately, there are some areas that are pretty "bleh."  In particular, the laser puzzles are fine when first introduced, but quickly become so tedious that I find myself ready to rip out all my hair at the roots and mash on the keyboard with my bloody disembodied scalp.  And there are some items that I pretty much never used due to how difficult it was to make proper use of them in the vast majority of situations.
But in the grand scheme of things, these are truly minor things, and all in all, this game is absolutely incredible.  I'd dare say it's a masterpiece.  One of ther finest blends of all the elements that make a game engaging and peerless in the way it presents a pop culture touchstone so often reduced to a generic mook, a skin for a typical Mary Sue protagonist, or a Big Bang Theory-level "nerd humor" punchline.  Play this goddam game before I sneak into your house and throw dusk moths on you while you sleep.

I picked up Always Sometimes Monsters (ASM) through the recent Humble Bundle for $1 (Had three free copies of Insurgency, so why not?). I went into the game expecting very little from it and to uninstall it after 30 minutes, but I couldn't stay away from it.
I can see why, from the screenshots and all, a typical gamer wouldn't play this game :
-Pixel graphics (hit-and-miss)
-Really slow paced and to be honest, unecessarily draggy kind of gameplay
-Somewhat boring introduction to the narrative. (One wouldn't stay very long for this game, I would imagine)
I wasn't blown away by the game in the first hour of playing it, but it kept me playing. And why? I simply just wanted to find out where this journey would lead me, and not so much whether or not I would be able to achieve my goal.
The goal of the protagonist is essentially, getting the love of his life back. who was about to get married. Knowing that this goal was unreachable, I still just wanted to know how the story unfolds. Why? Because the protagonist was in a pretty ♥♥♥♥♥♥ situation and I wanted to see if it gets any better.
Apparently not. Everything just turns to♥♥♥♥♥♥
I was extremely disappointed at the story, and at myself. To be honest, due to its draggy gameplay, I took most of the 'shortcuts' (do one thing that I knew had a bad outcome as compared to doing three things which took more time but was more morally sound) but still stuck pretty true to what I'd do, and did some others that were morally sound to balance things out. It's interesting how these things strike back at you towards the ending and make you feel that your miserable and ♥♥♥♥♥♥ end is somewhat justifiable, and that's what's so f**ked up about it.
It is such a sad game. Don't expect fun, don't expect happiness, expect a hell of a guilt trip. It's more than a sad ending, it's a miserable one, which isn't very common in games nowadays, and is a good change of pace, but this might be way too much for one to handle. The plot twists (somewhat?) are EXTREME but yet predictable, as they're quite hard to believe.
I will not play this game again, but I will suggest this game to people.

So, I was really excited for this game. I saw the initial trailer and thought that it looked great. I kept an eye on it when it was released, but it was a little bit more than I like to pay for games. When I saw that it was included in a Humble Bundle, I jumped at the chance to get it.
If you can stand the thought of an RPG without combat of any sort, and you like to read a LOT, I recommend this game. I wouldn't exactly call it an RPG, though. It's more like a Choose-Your-Own-Adventure book. You move through the story, making moral decisions and seeing the results.
The gameplay and writing starts out very strong. The story quickly hooks you in, and there's a lot to see and do in Dogstown, the first area. However, each area after that has a little less detail and fewer interesting things to do. It seems like the writers started out strong and then ran out of steam.
The game is actually pretty short. I finished it in just under 9 hours. There is some replay value in it (making different choices to get different endings), but not really a ton.
I'd give it a 7 out of 10 rating. I like the philosophical area that the game designers were trying to explore, but they have this weird love/hate relationship with the story tropes they use. They present some pretty cliche tropes, but then they don't reward your for following through it them.
Random thoughts:
-For the love of GOD, can there be more than a single microwave in the damn game?!?! I finished the game with the same three HotPockets that I started with, because the only microwave is in your starting apartment. There are NO microwaves in any of the convenience stores, none in the apartment you stay in, none in the trailer and none in the house!
-From the inital previews, they made it sound like you could choose any race/gender/orientation to play. You can, but the initial character selection process is VERY unclear. They needed to add more information about what you're choosing when you 'toast' people in the first scene.
-One thing that really bothered me was your 'best friend'. Throughout the game, you are told this character is your best friend and there's nothing you wouldn't do for each other. However, you are never given any reason why this is, and you don't get to see much of the relationship that made them friends. Building a rapport with this characters is pretty crucial to the later parts of the story, so the writers needed to "Show, Not Tell" in this case, and they missed out on doing that.

Nice concept, many flaws.
CONS:
- No graphic settings available, you can't set the screen resolution or play it fullscreen. You can maximize the window, but it'll keep the Windows menu bar in the bottom and the game's own window bar at the top.
- It's buggy. The main character will freeze randomly or when it's killed. If it freezes randomly, it
come back to life if it takes damage from an enemy. If you were killed, you can't do anything else besides exiting the game (there's no way to go back to the main menu)
- Now that we're talking about the main menu, I'm not sure if it qualifies to be a "menu". A proper, more clear menu with options, play, load, etc. would definitely be better
- No co-op mode. At least having a local co-op mode would greatly improve the gameplay. It's funny (but difficult) to control both characters at the same time, and I guess that's part of the game concept. But having the two game modes (solo and co-op -option to play with someone else, each player controlling one of the characters) could be very funny.
- No achievements, no trading cards. This game is begging for achievements, and with the cute artwork it would be very easy to create th trading cards and the required backgrounds/emoticons/badges.
- Did I say ir's difficult?
PROS:
- Cute graphics, nice story and game concept
- Simple enough to play from the beginning but also has quite a few things to improve the gameplay (upgrades)
- It's difficult, but because it is challenging, it achieves its goal to keep you playing
Conclusion:
Nice, casual game with a great potential, but still has a lot of room for improvement. It's worth the price when on sale ($0.99-$1.49) but at a $4 retail price I would expect it to be less buggy and that the developer will continue to add features to the game (proper settings, a real menu, local co-op mode, achievements, cards, etc.).

Mark of the Ninja is a 2d stealth game based around, well, ninjas. The core gameplay is based around hugging shadows, dodging around enemies, and then stabbing them in the back. It is well implemented, and the display is usually very clear about what is visible and what isn't, including your sprite, which turns black if in shadows (similar to Sam Fisher's Christmas lights). You also sometimes have the option to sneak past guards and leave them undisturbed, kill them from the shadows, or kick down the front door and try a fair fight (much like the Ghost/Panther/Assault options in SC: Blacklist). This can add some variation if you get a little bored of just crawling through vents.
The story is good, and although quite simple, it did keep me guessing right until the end about the mental state of my character. The extra depth added to the Dosan character in the Special Edition DLC is also excellent, as are the new items provided.
PROS
- Beautiful art style
- Good core gameplay
- DLC is good value
- Reasonable depth and replayability (New Game+)
CONS
- Simplistic plot
- Sometimes gets a little "samey"
That said, those cons are relatively minor issues and are more subjective than objective comments on the game. I probably only found some levels samey as I played through the whole thing in a few consecutive nights...
Bottom line: If you don't like stealth games, avoid MotN. If you like stealth games, then this will probably be one of the best purchases you can make on Steam. For me, as 2D XBLA/PSN/Steam releases go, this is the best game I've bought, and I'm sure I will beat New Game+ a few more times too.

As a team based arena shooter Lawbreakers benefits the opportunity to combine the charms of either, but falls flat trying. The presentation is definitely double A, everything feels very polished ranging from sounds to animations. Sadly the intrinsic mechanics face naive fundamental issues.
Considering the team/classes based aspect it clashes with it's inherent nature of allowing the good to run rampant. A team composition really isn't a necessity and is more or less just there for variety. Problem is some weapons and abilities shine in but specific scenarios, whereas others fail to find any impact. In original arena shooters this problem was tackled by allowing everyone to carry any weapon and giving everyone the same movement capabilities. Lawbreakers does not hestitate to put classes in the game that are worthless in anti gravity, and on the opposite end of the spectrum classes that obliterate everyone in the right hands.
Then the arena shooter aspect is too, poorly executed. The game allows unrestricted movement to an extent of pure frustration. Quake and UT fans will very quickly recognize this too. The movement in Lawbreakers is absurdly spastic and knows little patterns. It also adds a new vertical dimension making thinks even more hopeless for those trying to track their targets in close quarter. In long range zero gravity favors the hitscan classes as it's slow and clumsy. Instead of strafe jumping and wall jumping / sliding Lawbreakers allows movement that changes your direction at the click of a button in max speed. Resulting in a chaotic unoverseeable mess.
Lawbreaks is alot of fun for a few hours. It looks good, feels fresh but ultimately fails to innovate by breaking the premises of it's aspects.

I've enjoyed the Deus Ex games through the years. Few other games offer the creative use of space that this series does or the rewards for exploration. This was a great game and flowed well, with options within options of ways to complete your tasks. If you just rush the main story you'll miss half of the game.  There is the main story of bad guy attacks you, you hunt down bad guy, figure out who he is and stop him. But there are lots of smaller side stories about the events and lives of those living through this time. Having to deal with the results of what happened from the last game.  The majority of the game is spent in one city, Prague. Normal games you would run through the city to start a mission, and you can do that here also. But this game the city itself can be missions, and there is almost as much to explore that is not the main story line. There are almost as many side missions as main, help solve a murder, help figure out what happened to a guy in the sewers who's lost his mind, disrupt drug trade, work for or against organized crime, human trafficking, runaway groom, illegal check points, the list goes on. It's not main story arc related stuff always, but they are interesting explorations into the world left from the last game. Being a Deus Ex game there is stuff to learn every where, on computers, books, personal notes, or the old fashioned way people talking. Also the number of options to complete everything made me feel like I was choosing how the game would flow instead of following a one-way path. Even the final boss, I could discover his kill switch, I could disable him and knock him out keeping him alive, or I could fight him to the death. Is a door blocking your way? Hack the keypad... too hard? Maybe that guard, note, computer in the office has the code to unlock it. Can't find that code? You could move that fridge and use the vent behind it to go around. Can't find a vent? Maybe climb to the second floor and open the window and come down the stairs. Can't climb to the second floor? Maybe you can punch through the wall of the adjacent building and make your own way in.
It's this freedom that makes this game so enjoyable. Do I kill everyone I meet? Maybe I knock out everyone I see and hide the bodies so I don't raise an alarm. Or maybe I just slip by completely undetected and leave everyone to their own lives.
Few games reward you for playing how you want to play, or even allow you the option to choose how you will play. If you explore more than just the main story line you'll be rewarded.

I recommend this game with a heavy heart if and only if you can get it on sale. Do not spend more then $30 for this game. I had fun playing this game don't get me wrong there but it had so many flaws that prevented me from liking this game especially how it ended, more on that later.
Pros: It had great gameplay that was fun and non-repetitive. In some situations there was more then one way to take on a situation. The voice acting was done well and believable. The story was compelling and drew me in. There was a variety of weapons and being able to mod and upgrade them was a nice touch. I like the rpg element of earning talent points to unlock abilities.
Cons: You earn Praxis kits (talent points) to unlock new augements (talents) or upgrade ones you currently have, how ever when it comes to combat ones they few entirely useless or unnecessary. For example you can unlock the Typhoon ability which is not only the strongest offensive ability you can get it is also an AOE ability. I never once used it in this game because i never felt the need to. In the first game i remember using it multiple times to defeat bosses. Use the cloaking ability to get out of a sticky situation, run up to the boss and spam Typhoon a few times to take out a chunk of the bosses health or finish them off.  In this game no such situation.  Which brings me to my next problem, bosses are practically non existent and the ones that can be remotely considered boss can be killed with a few well placed head shots so they die in like 30 seconds maybe less.
As with combat augments the weapon upgrades and mods are useless, well mods less so. You can spend crafting parts to upgrade your weapon stats. I maxed out all the stats on my pistol and comabat rifle and they felt no stronger or more accurate then it did at base stats. The silencer and scope mods are completely useless. The enemies are alerted to your presence and know exactly where you are after the first shot, so no point in sniping and no point in reducing the damage of your gun by equiping a silencer. Laser sight and combat sights mods are the only usefull mods for they actually help with aiming.
The game punishes you for doing a lethal play through by giving you less xp so there for you earn less praxis kits, so if you want to unlock as many augments as possible you have to do a stealth play through. Also doing a full lethal run and gun play through is impossible seeing as the last level is a stealth mission where you fail if the enemy is alerted to your presence. About half through the game it start leaning heavily on stealth or you will quickly get over whelmed and killed on certain missions. I do not like stealth games, I don't mind a little bit of stealth here and there but I don't like being forced into it for a large chunk of the game.
Now for my biggest complaint and BE WARNED THIS COULD BE CONSIDERED A SPOILER. The game ends so abruptly, how was I supposed to know that a guy you see twice through out the game that you know is a lackey to the big bad would be the final boss to the game. A boss fight that was SO ANTI CLIMATIC. The boss fight if done the way they want it done doesn't even take place at all. For you see to get the TRUE ENDING you have to save your boss, a senator and a group of hostages while defeating the "final boss" in a certain amount of time and the only way you can do that is to use the remote that you were supposed to find if you did a good amount of snooping and exploring. A remote that activates a kill switch that the big bad implanted into the final boss incase he ever turned on them. What makes it better is that there were no clues, warnings or any leading/segway that lets you know that this mission you are going on is the last one in the game. Its sneak around, rescue these people, kill a flunky and.....cutscene then credits. CONGRATULATIONS YOU BEAT THE GAME. WTF....its over? Thats it? How.....unsatisfying. Do you want to know the ending cutscenes are? A reporter giving you a news report and Jensen telling you that he is planning on going after the big bad. So a lame reporter wrapping up the side stories in the game for you and a unsatisfying cliff hanger telling you they plan on making a 3rd game that we might not ever see is what we get for a reward for playing their game and getting sucked into their story.
The game felt very incomplete, I feel like I bought a game that was only 2/3 done.

SUMMARY: It's a decent value buy at the $15 mark, DLC / Season Pass best avoided. Game's fun, story's meh. Runs about 20/25 hours for a regular-speed playthrough.
===========
:: Technical
Deux Ex: Mankind Divided (hereafter DE:MD) is pretty and plays well. I encountered 1 crash bug in a full playthrough (while triggering weapon customization at the tail end of an autosave - couldn't reproduce), but I ran into zero game-breaking or progress-halting issues.
There were some minor sound balance issues in some areas where environmental sounds or music made it difficult to hear NPC conversation, but nothing that made me put the game down or even tweak my settings.
I did have to crank down anti-aliasing despite having a hexacore I7 chip backed by an nVidia 1070 GPU. Something about their implementation of MSAA feels off; I couldn't hold good performance while it was turned up.
:: Story
DE:MD picks up after the story of Deus Ex: Human Revolution, plus a couple of years wherein extra story elements were crammed. The game ramps up fairly quickly though the initial trips through Prague seem like they're dragging - then you realize Prague /is/ the main game setting, as it's where all the side missions happen, and they take up the bulk of your time. This is more of a hub-game, not a destination-game.
Unfortunately this is where my big criticism is; DE:MD's story comes off as half-baked. By the midpoint of the game they've ramped up the scope of possible conspiracies to involve Everything and Everyone, then by the time the game finishes you realize it still involves Everything and Everyone That's Still Alive. None of the main plot points are resolved by the game's completion and there's a completely naked telegraph for a future sequel (which, due to poor sales, is unlikely to happen any time soon).
The "Story DLCs" that were released include one prequel mission and one "this also happened" mission without wrapping up any of the loose threads. The game won't bring you closure.
:: Verdict
DE:MD was worth playing if you enjoy stealth/action types of games. I wouldn't pay anything near full price; wait for sales or historic lows.

I honestly do not know why this game continues to be criticized by reviewers on Steam. This is my second favorite Deus Ex game behind the original. I liked it quite a bit more than Human Revolution. The single hub was very well fleshed out and was fun to explore. I am pretty sure I will find plenty of new areas to check out in my next playthrough. I played the director's cut of Human Revolution right before my playthrough of this game and there weren't any new surprises after my 3rd playthrough of that game. I felt that game, which is much more highly regarded, has not aged well and I blew through it in about 20 hours. This game was criticized for it's length and I felt it wrapped up nicely in a reasonable amount of time (well of 20 hours for me).
The consumable DLC, some of which comes with the deluxe edition, really does not seem to add much to the game. Paying real money for praxis kits or new weapon skins does not show up in the game. It is done through external DLC. There are so many praxis kits in the game I was running out of things to upgrade. The deluxe edition comes with 5 extra praxis, not 50. The weapons are not better than the weapons you find off of enemies. So really, what is the big deal? So many games have these loot crates and yet gamers eat those up. I hate them in online games. They ruin the balance. At least in a single player game, it is between me and the game if I choose to buy my upgrades beyond what can be done typically through the story. Online I am getting owned by someone with better weapons and they also level up faster. Pay to cheat is more like it. So we are ok with it in games like the Battlefield series, but not here. Sure. Ok. Seems fair.
Beneath the consumable DLC is a great Deus Ex game. My only problems with the game had to do with how it brought my PC to it's knees (low settings and long load times) and unskippable credits. That was it. I loved it otherwise. It was fun to upgrade weapons. The side missions were fun. The main plot and setting was cool. The graphics, if you have a rig that can handle it, are top notch. The ending was way better than Revolution. If you are a fan of the other Deus Ex games, you really should pick this up. I grabbed it for $25 on sale and it was well worth it. I plan to play it again to try different choices.

Medieval and Shogun are great examples of art from adversity. Wonderful atmosphere and immersion thanks to memorable music, crunchy sound design, beautiful campaign maps, and a plethora of creative design decisions. These games still have the most generous and interesting historical battles in the entire series, as well as the most competent AI, both on the campaign map and in battles. Even though the battle maps and pixelated units are a far cry from where the series is today, the excellence in design of the first two TW games still shines through and makes them worth playing today.
The cons: Medieval has a disappointingly passive campaign AI. It loves to make alliances and rarely declares war. Also, while the building system offers much more flexibility than recent games in the series, becomes seriously tedious to manage once you have a large empire.
Recommended for fans of the series who want to explore its early heritage, and for those (like me) who loved this game back in the day and want to relive those memories.
