In a treacherous game of greed and escapades a princess gets kidnapped under the watchful eye of her lover. Now, in a fatal game of cat and mouse, facing almost insurmountable odds, he must overcome his limitations and embark on a journey to … buy more stuff, because he can’t even jump over obstacles let alone walk left and the shopkeep is the only one selling these abilities to him. DLC Quest (2013) contains two adorkable little satires by Going Loud Studios in which players go through the motions of everything that’s wrong and right about video games of the early 2010s.
Included in this bundle are the original DLC Quest from 2011 and its sequel Live Freemium or Die from two years later, 2013. Although the first game is loads of fun, the second is falling in the same trap as too many sequels before it. In order to understand what is wrong with the second game, it might make sense to have a brief look at the first one. Shall we?
DLC Quest starts in such an “unfinished” state that the player character is just a still image. Part of his task to save the day is to buy enough additional content (gear and mechanics) to beat the bad guy. To do so, “Player”, as he is called, has to talk to the townspeople, listen to their funny antics, and collect enough coins in a game that takes around 30 minutes to beat the first time around. DLC Quest’s humor is easily understood by anyone, even by those who are unfamiliar with video game tropes and who have no idea what DLC (downloadable content) are, which is key to good comedy: Reference jokes should still be funny even when the source material is unknown to the recipient. Luckily, the mechanics match the humor in both playstyle and simplicity.
The controls themselves are as easy as in the first Super Mario Bros. (1985) on the Family Computer with “Player” attacking with one button and jumping with another. The entire adventure can even be experienced with either a gamepad or keyboard. Despite that, one tiny problem is that the controls are a bit slippery so that the valiant hero might slip off of a ledge or two while attempting to jump on to a platform. Luckily, he can’t die and there’s little punishment for not making a jump. This also means that the game relies mostly on its humor over challenge. With all that said, what’s the deal with the second part?
Live Freemium or Die picks up right where DLC Quest left off. This time around, the world is somewhat bigger and more mazelike with checkpoints, deadly spikes, and different townspeople. Glossing over these additions, the two major problems of this title quickly become apparent: It is still lovable and quirky, but, the creators failed to see what made the first one work.
The game’s core problem is in its design, which can be seen in three aspects, the game’s mechanics, its humor, and its length. The protagonist can now wall jump and there are death states that will teleport “Player” back to the last checkpoint he touched. The controls are still as slippery as in the first entry, but there is a stronger emphasis on platforming with some coins only being reachable after successfully wall jumping across gaps. Depending on whether or not “Player” missed or skipped a checkpoint, dying might teleport him back quite a bit. Though not too difficult for semi-casual players, the more elaborate platforming gets slightly annoying, as it substitutes quality content with busywork and a pay-off that is just some in-game currency. And just like the mechanics, the humor as well could have used some revision.
Just like its predecessor, this title too heavily relies on comical dialog, yet multiple (not all) jokes are referential and can only be understood by those familiar with core gaming trivia from the mid-1980s to 2012. One character in a cave, for example, is a direct reference to Markus “Notch” Persson and tells “Player” that he used to love mines but was now into space. Persson, the creator of Minecraft (2011), was developing a space game titled 0x10c at the time Live Freemium or Die came out, but had indefinitely halted the project in 2013. Sadly, unless players know about this or other things that were popular in gaming at the time, they won’t understand several of the game’s antics, while others familiar with the subject matter will simply say “Oh, yeah, that was a thing back then” instead of finding them funny. Despite a couple of jokes still putting a smile on one’s face, they are overall not as good as in DLC Quest and, due to the level design, are too few and far apart from one another.
While the platforming and jokes are minor bumps, the biggest complaint I have is that Live Freemium or Die is too long. The game should have ended at the latest, right after retrieving the “Box of Various Supplies” in an area called “Allan Please Add Zone Name” with an entire Cave Zone cut out as well. The way it is now, its world is too large and mazelike for what little there is to discover. It may only take an hour to play through the entire game, but, thanks to the level design, feels much longer and drags on. With these issues, Live Freemium or Die suffers under the same predicament as many sequels before it: It tries to focus on and dig itself into a couple of aspects the developers liked about the first game instead of taking a step back and to try and see if the product as a whole is still fun to experience. While the title still has its moments and the ending is hilarious, it does not reach the same level as its predecessor.
Does this double pack come recommended? DLC Quest would definitely be worth getting over the weekend, if there were such a thing as video game rentals. There isn’t really any replay value to both games and, with a combined playtime of one and a half to two hours, players will have seen everything there is to see through the course of one afternoon. I really like the art direction in both games and the music is awesome. I loved the humor in the first title and would love for my readers to play it as well, but I’m not that big a fan of its sequel and think that people wouldn’t miss out on much if they didn’t play that one.

A great stealth game with a decent amount of diversity, not thrown in all at once. Easy to learn, hard to master. Good replayability: has nice achievements, challenges for each level ("seals") and exploration for hidden stuff. If you're good at it, you'll be able to get upgrades faster. Upgrades are not like "in your way", but they are still very useful: new ways to kill, to move, to trick people.
Classic stelath with light exposure and sound as your main foes. A great number of ways to handle just about anything with either lethal takedowns (in many ways!), clever distraction (like scaring the s**t out of people), or just avoidance ("don't mind me, just passin' through"). All spiced up with cartooney yet serious art style (Klei is good at it!) and good audio (music and SFX).
Challenging if you want it to be: in New Game+ (unlocked after normal playthrough) things are pushed a bit towards realism: you can't see behind yourself, you can't visibly determine sound's detection range. Nothing forces you to try it though, there's not much to miss without it.
Not without its drawbacks: since it's stealth, it's often dark in there. And some really crucial elements are sometimes difficult to detect. And controls are clunky when it comes to precision moves (even "focus" doesn't help much with that). When it doesn't though, they are great: responsive and mostly express your intentions fast.

The things that hold this game back are: the slightly old sound design, the awful camera (infact platforming is the most dangerous part of the game as is it's hard to tell where you'll land), and obviously this game never got a sequel and never really ended. The camera is especially unfortunate since there are a couple of good environment puzzles.
If you can deal with the bad you'll find this time-traveling hack & slash adventure a worthy sequel to Soul Reaver 2.

If you have two monitors use only one (windows icon + P shortcut = computer only) to avoid problems with launching, and don't bother with the trainer that gives you the SR2 camera, it's not much better and sometimes creates bugs.

I loved Quake and Unreal far back in the days of old arena style FPS.The only game that held my attention aftyer those days were Halo. From 2001 all the way into the end of Halo Reach, until the dreadful Halo 4 was released, FPS games were all I played, they were in my blood. Since 2012 my love for the genre completely died, Halo was all I had and nothing matched that magic since then. I tried getting back into Quake and Unreal shortly after hoping to reignite that love to no avail.
Then comes Lawbreakers. I've had my eye on the game for awhile, participating in the past 3 betas, it was until the last beta I realized, "this is it." This is the game that gave me my love of competitive FPS games back since 2012, Five years later, I am falling in love witrh the FPS genre all over agin thanks to this game.
I played Overwatch for awhile only to be tired of it and have it grown stale on me. The causal, cartoonish approach that made the game so popular to everyone, detered me from the game in the end. This game has been compared to Overwatch since its announcement as an "Overwatch Clone" just as Overwatch was labaled a "Team Fortress Clone." This game is a hero based shooter from Bosskey, headed by Cliff Bleszinski the legendary developer behind Unreal Tournament and Gears of War. But after we clear the fact this is a hero based shooter, Every similarity with Overwatch ends there, the two games are nothing alike.
This is very much a movement based game where holding still or not knowing how to take full advantage of the movement system will 100% be your downfall. Because the game is movement skill based, you have to have your aim on point at all times. Much like the old FPS games like Quake, Unreal, Tribes you have to move as fast as you can while being able to track your enemies at the same time. The game is very much a skill based game. Unlike Overwatch where every hero has very clear advantages and disadvantages, some heroes will do well against others, and everyone has a counter, that does not exist in this game. Every single pick can hold their own against any other class in this game, it might have more trouble than others, but there is no hard counters in this game. The only hindrance is your own skill in this game, there are no free insta-kill supers in this game. Every super you have to aim and work for your kills. Not even the Enforcer's Bloodhound Rockets are guaranteed, if you can master the omvement you can evade them (However it's not easy to do if you aren't expecting them.)
Everyone should at least give this game a go, it will not be everyone as it is a skill based shooter in which you have to work for every kill in order to get it. But once you get the hang of it this game is a complete blast and 100% worth the $30 price tag. It fills that old competitive arena FPS I have been itching for since 2012. While not completely classified as an arena FPS, it takes all the elements and mixes them up nicely with the new takes that seem to be in every FPS nowadays, to make a fun, fast, hectic shooter that I have needed in my life. Thank you Lawbreakers <3

Kevin James stars as Paul Blart, a Segway-mounted security guard at New Jersey's West Orange Pavilion Mall. Having repeatedly dropped out of the New Jersey State Troopers' academy test (low blood sugar makes him pass out without any notice), lonely single dad Paul takes his job too seriously and lives with his mom and daughter -- and he hasn't had a date in so long that they set up an online profile for him. After meeting lovely new kiosk owner Amy (Jayma Mays), Paul thinks she could be the one to look past his schlubby exterior to the sweet, courageous man inside. To prove himself to her, he stays in the mall to try and save her and a group of other hostages captured by a group of young criminals on the hunt for a huge identity-theft score.
IS IT ANY GOOD?
At first PAUL BLART: MALL COP just seems like another broad, brainless Adam Sandler-produced comedy aimed at teen and tween boys. But as the plot thickens, James' teddy-bear of a protagonist actually begins to grow on the audience. Despite the many fat jokes (which are thankfully not aimed at Raini Rodriguez, the cute, chubby actress who plays Blart's daughter Maya), there's none of the raunch that's defined Sandler's signature brand of humor. Blart doesn't make apologies for who he is -- a food-loving, mustachioed, unfashionable man who loves his job and his mother and daughter and would risk his life to save any innocent mall shopper.
The physical comedy is surprisingly well executed, with James pratfalling with the ease and grace of Chevy Chase or Buster Keaton. Mays is like the second coming of Anna Faris, and the acrobatic, skateboarding crew of criminals put on an entertaining cat-and-mouse chase around the mall. The mall, it should be noted, deserves its own credit, since the movie prominently plugs many a store -- particularly an extended scene in Victoria's Secret. So, yes, this is a broad, silly comedy filled with consumer brands -- but it also has, embodied in its brave buffoon of Paul Blart, heart.

The Novelist is a pretty interesting take on narration in games. In control of a ghostly presence you have to wander around a house, trying to understand the personal issues of its inhabitants by listening to their conversations and exploring their memories. The game is basically made of two main elements : stealth and story decisions.
In order not to get spotted by the family you will have to hop between lamps, which act as hiding spots. In each chapter your main goal will be to figure out a path through the house that will allow you to follow the characters as they move around. It can get pretty tense, especially when they decide to turn off lamps at certain points.
After you have gathered enough information about the situation at hand - each chapter being centered around a particular event that the family has to deal with - you will have the option to choose between multiple outcomes. Without revealing anything, I can tell you that the later decisions are very tough to make.
Overall, and though the game has a very limited scope, I found The Novelist to be an intriguing attempt at narration which managed to hit home for me on several occasions. Being interested in novels and writing certainly helps since it allows you to relate more easily with the main character, and understand the struggle he's going through. I would be interested in seeing a bigger and more complex game with the same ideas but I would definitely recommend The Novelist to those of you who are interested in narrative experiences.

I've never written a review of a game before, but Snakebird is so criminally underappreciated I have to make an exception.
The mechanics of Snakebird are very simple. There isn't a great way to explain them with words, but if you watch the video, you'll see the core idea very quickly - it's like the old-school game Snake, except our dear snakebirds are subject to gravity. There are a couple twists on this formula, but they are also very intuitive. The focus is not on throwing mechanics at you, but on puzzles that force you to push those mechanics to their limits.
This is the hardest puzzle game I've ever played. Not because it's full of cheap tricks, or because of randomness (a la Candy Crush), or because it's complicated - the puzzles are (mostly) fair, they're just brutally hard. It's the Dark Souls of puzzle games. If that sounds good to you, this game is for you!
Also, although the game is difficult, it never gets too frustrating, because once you solve the first few puzzles, you'll have a bunch of puzzles unlocked at any given time. Which means you can always bang your head against another wall. Plus, the art is delightful! My favorite part is the expressions of the snakebirds. When you leave them hanging next to spikes, their eyes are terrified and imploring; when you leave them next to fruit, they gaze at it desirously; and the rest of the time, they look at you like they're too cool to be in this puzzle. It's more endearing than it sounds.
I hope the creators of this game come out with many more like it!

Já tinha ouvido falar muito bem da Série Arkham, mas nunca havia dado uma chance. Então, com o lançamento próximo de Batman Arkham Knight, decidi jogar todos os Arkham, em ordem de lançamento. Batman Arkahm Asylum te coloca na pele do herói mais sombria da DC Comics, o nosso querido Cavaleiro das Trevas, The Batman. Você entra no jogo em meio a uma rebelião que ocorreu no Asilo Arkham, lugar onde os criminosos mais perigosos de Gotham são mantidos e estudados.  E quem começou essa rebelião foi aquele louco sádico do Coringa. Conforme você entra no Asilo, percebe que tem algo errado além da rebelião, e depois de algum tempo, você percebe que Joker foi quem tramou todo o teatrinho, inclusive a captura dele próprio. Conforme a história avança, você percebe que tudo já estava tramado há muito tempo, e no meio de suas insanidades, Joker te coloca contra alguns dos piores vilões do universo do Cavaleiro das Trevas, como Bane, Poison Ivy, Scarecrow e Killer Croc. No início do jogo, a história não é muito imersiva, e você acaba ficando meio alheio ao jogo. Mas após um tempo de gameplay, as coisas começam a esquentar e você fica mais imerso na ambientação que o jogo proporciona. Ambientação essa que é simplismente fantástica, pois você passa pelos mais variados ambientes, como o exterior do Asilo Arkham, uma Batcaverna no subsolo do próprio Asilo, Jardins Botânicos, celas dos internados em Arkham, e por aí vai. E todos esses ambientes extremamente bem detalhados e cheios de pontos secretos para proporcionar ao jogador momentos em stealth, que é bem valorizado no jogo, pois Batman é um herói que luta com as próprias mãos, então enfrentar um cara armado correndo pra cima dele não é uma ideia muito inteligente. E o combate de Arkham Asylum é um dos principais pontos fortes do jogo, pois é extremamente fluído e satisfatório. Os combos encaixados te dão uma sensação extremamente prazerosa, e a fluidez dos movimentos dos Bats enqaunto bate é realmente impressionante. Ah, mas não adianta só apertar o botão de bater que você ganha de tudo e todos, pois haverão momentos em que até mais de 20 inimigos lotam a sua tela para te matar. E pra isso, existem os counter-attacks e as esquivas, que funcionam do jeitinho que devem. Só o counter que as vezes deixa a desejar, e te faz tomar muita ♥♥♥♥♥da pelas costas. Todo o esquema de leveling é bem útil, te possibiltando adqurir novos combos, novas skills, ter mais HP, ter mais proficiência com seus artefatos. Ah, e eu não poderia deixar de falar dos artefatos, pois eles são os personagens principais do jogo, juntamente ao Batman. Com eles você faz de tudo, desde dar stun em inimigos com a Batarang, até mesmo excalar paredes com a Batclaw, sem contar os outros artefatos que são extremamente úteis para a jogatina. Os gráficos do jogo são muito bons e bem detalhados, com um estilo único, misturando os traços realísticos com os cartunizados. A dublagem e a sincronia labial dos personagens não é muito bem detalhada, principalmente a do Batman, que às vezes só balança a mandíbula pra falar, sem expressão facial nenhuma, e com uma voz que não combina com o personagem do jogo, justamente pelo fato da voz transmitir uma certa emoção e o personagem não. A trilha sonora é boa, mas em certos pontos é bem repetitiva. De modo geral, Arkham Asylum é um jogo explêndido, que só não alcançou o seu potencial máximo pelos entraves da época em que o jogo foi feito. 8,5/10

Harvester is a great game, but it's not for everybody.
It claims to be the "most violent adventure game of all time," but "most disturbing" or "most offensive" might be more appropriate.  As well as exceedingly violent, the game is also homophobic, misogynistic, and generally rife with unpleasantries; be aware that the game is designed as satirical self-parody, intended for consenting adults only.
Concerning gameplay: what begins as an interactive B-movie eventually evolves into something quite different, along the way featuring plenty of tongue-in-cheek commentary on violence and death (within the video game medium and without).  Mature adults will laugh at the game's goofiness and gore, but will also understand the point being made using all the blood and insanity.
Save often, use multiple save files, and expect lots of reloading.
It's rubbish, but fascinating rubbish, like a terrible movie.  Totally recommended for people who like trashy horror movies; avoid if you won't "get it".

1996 DOS point and click adventure, Satire/ Horror/ Fantasy/ Sci-Fi.
By todays standards highly flawed and highly recommended.
Cons :
- B grade poor quality FMV.
- Politically incorrect and potentially offensive.
- Occasional illogical puzzle/ item use/ combo common for the genre and time.
- Horrendously janky combat mechanics, primarily confined to the games third and final act.
Pros :
- B grade poor quality FMV.
- Politically incorrect and potentially offensive.
- Especially dark, twisted, amusing and interesting cast of characters.
- A rare ancient gem, the subject matter and themes aren't things you will find explored in contemporary games too often if at all. A relic from a bygone era deserving of its' cult status
The games worst aspect is its combat, no question. The first 2 acts are traditional point and click style with the 3rd heavily incorporating combat additionally. Whilst you CAN kill people in the first 2 acts there aren't many reasons to do so and there are consequences, many of them fail states. So when it came time to unleash I found it a welcome change of pace which added a nice, albeit frustrating at times, survival horror element towards the end. I managed to quite enjoy it despite its shortcomings but I understand why that isn't a popular sentiment. The timing of attacks is mostly luck but choosing the right weapon can make things a lot easier. Also there are opportunities to talk your way around some confrontations.
If you are a horror fan (particularly if you have an eye for satire/ social commentary) and are craving an interesting story (even if, like myself, you aren't overly fond of the point and click genre) you owe it to yourself to pick this up at some point and persevere 'til the bitter end/s.
If you're the type to take the Metacritic score into account I advise you to take note of the disparity between the critical and user reviews.
There's also a GOG version if you'd prefer.

If you like The Behemoth's games, you'll like this. The art style and humour definitely take cues from those guys and I'd say it's a resounding success on that front. The lumbermancer, the enemies (and the way they die), the lumber being manced, everything just oozes personality. In a good way, not the way things normally ooze, which is pretty gross.
There's not much else to say that won't be repeating the "About This Game" section in a significantly less witty fashion, but I'm gonna say it anyway so that you're hopefully double-sure of what you're getting into. This is a small game. It's got four areas, each with different enemy types and a unique boss at the end, a shop where you can upgrade your lumbermancer, an endless level that (surprise) goes on forever, and allegedly a secret boss that I haven't found because it's a secret. That's really about it. You could see everything the game has to offer in maybe ~4 hours. Now, it'd be an enjoyable ~4 hours and only set you back $5, but this is a Sunday morning, play-while-you-drink-your-coffee game. You won't be playing this months from now. You'll probably finish it in the same day you buy it. That's something you should be fully aware of going in.
All in all, I'd recommend it pretty highly. It's a great way to kill some time and the price is right for what you get. The game's got tonnes of charm and you can tell it was a labour of love. Plus, your money goes towards raising Roger's cholesterol when he inevitably uses it to buy pizza instead of paying his bills, so that's nice.
Hope you enjoyed that pizza Roger.

I honestly would not recommend this game. Also note that I was actually excited for this game before it was released. I'm going to do my best to avoid all spoilers.
I love indie games, I'm a fan of retro graphics. I'm a huge fan of storytelling type games even if it has minimal gameplay.
But this game has a very weak narrative that just doesn't make sense if you try to analyze any of it past the base level. All the 'twists' don't make sense. It feels forced and contrived at points.
Also the moral choices feel about as subtle as a bat to the face over and over again. Most of the choices were extremely obvious, back away from this situation or somebody dies.  But the 'moral choice' was always much longer in terms of gameplay time which meant more boring 'minigames' and by the time I was halfway through I just wanted the game to end to see how the story finished.
Also quite a few of the moral choices weren't obvious in terms of the game forcing you into the situation first and then asking you to reconsider. I'm already there man, and there was no dialogue to just say no from the start so might as well see how this plays out.
I got pretty tired of half the music looping after about 15-30 seconds.
It felt like any message they were trying to deliver was basically drowned out by all the archetypical stereotypical characters they presented in the game. Yes, they weren't trying to say 'all drugs are bad mmkay' but it felt that way. Yes, they weren't trying to say 'religion will set you free!' but it felt that way. The writing didn't express the author's intent as much as it did the characters moral values which were always extremely black and white. The authors definitely wanted a grey moral area but I felt it lacked the execution to do so.
Ah well, I feel like the dev could make a promising sequel/game from what they've learned after making this game.

I honestly do not know why this game continues to be criticized by reviewers on Steam. This is my second favorite Deus Ex game behind the original. I liked it quite a bit more than Human Revolution. The single hub was very well fleshed out and was fun to explore. I am pretty sure I will find plenty of new areas to check out in my next playthrough. I played the director's cut of Human Revolution right before my playthrough of this game and there weren't any new surprises after my 3rd playthrough of that game. I felt that game, which is much more highly regarded, has not aged well and I blew through it in about 20 hours. This game was criticized for it's length and I felt it wrapped up nicely in a reasonable amount of time (well of 20 hours for me).
The consumable DLC, some of which comes with the deluxe edition, really does not seem to add much to the game. Paying real money for praxis kits or new weapon skins does not show up in the game. It is done through external DLC. There are so many praxis kits in the game I was running out of things to upgrade. The deluxe edition comes with 5 extra praxis, not 50. The weapons are not better than the weapons you find off of enemies. So really, what is the big deal? So many games have these loot crates and yet gamers eat those up. I hate them in online games. They ruin the balance. At least in a single player game, it is between me and the game if I choose to buy my upgrades beyond what can be done typically through the story. Online I am getting owned by someone with better weapons and they also level up faster. Pay to cheat is more like it. So we are ok with it in games like the Battlefield series, but not here. Sure. Ok. Seems fair.
Beneath the consumable DLC is a great Deus Ex game. My only problems with the game had to do with how it brought my PC to it's knees (low settings and long load times) and unskippable credits. That was it. I loved it otherwise. It was fun to upgrade weapons. The side missions were fun. The main plot and setting was cool. The graphics, if you have a rig that can handle it, are top notch. The ending was way better than Revolution. If you are a fan of the other Deus Ex games, you really should pick this up. I grabbed it for $25 on sale and it was well worth it. I plan to play it again to try different choices.

I honestly have to say this is one of the best licensed games out there. Scratch that, one of the best action adventure games out there.
The reason why this game is so great is that it has strong gameplay, great visuals and an awesome soundtrack and it doesn't rely on being a Batman game to fool people into buying it. Don't get me wrong though, this is a Batman game, from beginning to end. Rocksteady have crafted one of the most unique and well designed gameplay experiences of the action adventure genre that suits the Dark Knight perfectly. This is particularly impressive considering most licensed games do it the other way around: trying to fit the characters into an already existing gameplay style. This game does exactly the opposite and that's what makes it so incredible.
Speaking of the gamplay style, it is a healthy mix of action combat bits, stealth sections, environmental exploration and even some minimal platforming and detective bits. All of these feel distinctly Batman-y in every way though so don't be fooled into thinking this is just another generic action adventure title.
The combat sections in Arkham Asylum do a great job of making you feel like the Dark Knight. They are very unique as they focus on timing your strikes and flowing smoothly into each next move without ever braking your combo rather than the standard button mashing and long button sequence memorization in most games. In fact the actual button sequences you need to remember are very minimal. Most of the game you will spend only using two buttons really: attacking and countering. The attack button does what you can imagine but the counter is a bit more interesting. It allows you to automatically counter incoming attacks indicated by the little Spiderman-esque lightning bolts that appear on top of enemies' heads when they are about to attack. This may seem like a very simple system, and for the most part it is, but even though the system is easy to get into, it is hard to master as it requires a lot of timing to execute properly. It is truly brilliant and it's no wonder it's becoming the system most game devs have started using. It just makes you feel like a badass.
The stealth is equally as interesting and fun although it is more standard stuff. The focus here is using your environment to your advantage to take out threats without being seen. To do this you get a wide variety of options for silent take downs each as satisfying as the next. The only thing I need to say here is that these sections don't feel slapped on like they do in most other action games. They really fit and are great fun.
The environmental exploration is in the form of Riddler trophies and riddles. Dotted around the island there are many question mark trophies placed by the Riddler. Sometimes to get them you just need to find them but sometimes they require a certain gadget or upgrade to be obtained. The riddles themselves are about scanning a certain landmark or object that answers the riddle for the said area. Don't worry though, it's never anything too obscure like in the old point and click days. No leaves in the corner of the Arkham mansion need to be scanned. These trophies are very rewarding to collect both in a literal sense and a personal accomplishment sense.
The story and visuals are great and fit into the Batman mythos amazingly. I won't spoil much but it's great fun for fans of the Dark Knight and even those who don't care about Batman might enjoy it. It's very well written and voice acted.
The only con I see is that the game is sometimes easy to get lost in due to the dark bleak environments. You do have a map though for that but it is still a minor annoyance. The bosses are also pretty weak as you only get one type of them for most of the game. I feel like they could of been so much more.
That said, the cons are very small and this game is an absolute diamond for any Batman fans and fans of good games in general. Highly recommended to everyone. 9/10.
Still the best Batman experience available without investing in a cape and rubber suit.

One of the better Steam ports of the Legacy of Kain games. This and Blood Omen 2 were the only games compatible with a xbox controller. The steam verison of Soul Reaver 1 was unplayable and not optimized at all for modern hardware. Soul Reaver 2 worked great, but was not compatible with my xbox controller. Regardless, I enjoyed this series and can see why it's labeled as one of the greatest gaming series. Players really need to play Blood Omen 1, Soul Reaver 1 , and Soul Reaver 2 before diving into Defiance, which concludes the series. Blood Omen 2 is really more of an afterthought and side story that doesn't really effect the overall series. LOK: Defiance feels more balanced compared to the previous entries with the best of Kain and Razial merged together in one. Once again, the presentation is really well done here. The combat system is a bit more developed than the Soul Reaver series, but still feels a little unpolished. The only complaint I had with this game is that the camera angles are truely terrible, which will cause frustration and headaches due to dizziness! They should have used the camera system from the Soul Reaver games. Anyway the puzzles and abilities are more than less pretty good. As linear as this game is compared to previous entries in the series I still managed to get stumped on puzzles. I got lost in the game mainly due to the annoying camera angles. Other than that the game serves as a good conclusion to a epic series.
PROS:
+ Superb presentation. Concludes the epic LOK storyline with amazing voice acting and music.
+ Visuals still hold up well
+ Boss Fights!
+ Play as both Kain & Razial! Each with their own unique abilities
+ Combat is deeper and more complex than Soul Reaver games/ Blood Omen games.
CONS:
- Terrible fixed camera angles will effect the experience, but will not hamper it overall.
- Combat is not as polished as it should be and can get a little repetitive

P.S: For those who are having issues/crashes, here's a fix:
1)Run the game.
2)Open Task Manager.
For Windows 7 or older:
3)Go to the Processes tab. (Second tab from left to right)
4)Find and right click the defiance.exe process.
For Windows 8/10:
3)Go to the Details tab. (Second tab from right to left)
4)Find and right click the defiance.exe process.
5)From the menu, click Set Affinity.
6)A window will pop up, showing a list. In the list you'll have the following: <All Processors>, CPU 0, CPU 1, CPU 2, etc. (depending on the amount of cores your CPU has, you'll see that many in the list. Note that the first core is counted as CPU 0, so if you see, for example, from CPU 0 to CPU 7, those are your 8 cores.)
7)From this list, uncheck everything but CPU 0. This will set the process to use only 1 core from your CPU.
8)Now you can tab back into the game and play. Enjoy!
NOTE: You will have to repeat this every time you relaunch the game, as it's not a permanent change. This should however fix crashes/graphical issues/cutscene stuttering. I did notice a micro-stutter after the intro going into the first cinematic, but aside from that every other cinematic will run fine.
Another fix you can apply to the game (fixes some graphical issues for Windows 10):
1)Go to the game's installation folder. (Should be in your Steam\steamapps\common\legacy_kain_defiance, or in whichever folder you installed the game in)
2)Right click the defiance.exe.
3)Go to Properties, then to the Compatibility tab.
4)Check the "Run this program in compatibility mode for:" box, and then select Windows XP Service Pack 2.
NOTE: This is a permanent change, as in no need to redo it, unlike the previous fix.

Though Lawbreakers seems on the surface like an Overwatch clone with some low-grav gimmicks, it's really got more in common with classic twitch arena shooters like Quake and Unreal Tournament. Even the new Quake Champions seems slow by comparison. If you like your skill ceilings high, your action fast, and your characters varied, this game is fantastic. Your first couple matches might be rough, there's a fair amount to learn, but there's a decent interactive tutorial that teaches you most of the advanced movement, and if you want to learn even more there are videos for each class in the client that tell you multiple little tricks and tips. There's still room for polish, the HUD could be clearer etc., but if you like fast-paced shooters you will *not* be disappointed by Lawbreakers.
Highly recommended for fans of UT, Quake, and arcade dogfighting games (if you don't believe me play Vanguard).

From the creators of the acclaimed beat-em-up Shank, comes a stealth game that blindsided gamers: Mark of the Ninja (MotN). Why were we blind sided? We had no clue it was going to be THIS good!
MotN is obviously a stealth game where you play a nameless ninja in search of vengence for the man who destroyed his hometown. As you can probably guess from the generic cliche of a plot, the story is nothing to write home about. At all. You've got your excuse to slaughter everything in your path so what are you waiting for?!
Our protagonist is specially chosen to bear tatoo "marks". It essentially acts as phencyclidine (PCP); heightening his senses, reflexes, and strength, but all at the cost of his diminishing sanity. The plot only continues to disappoint with its choppy story telling, brief and hyper fast cutscenes, and the confusing, rushed dialogue/writing. The plot was definately the after thought. The 2 endings that last about 4 seconds each do nothing to ease the failure.
Thankfully, that's about where the cons end. The only other drawback is the music, which mostly consists of lame percussion segments.
Now on to the numerous pros! The voice acting is fantastic. Especially your guide, Ora. Her voice perfectly fits a ninja, and she performed well as a narrator. All the guards have many, many recorded lines, so they have many variations to "the light broke!" preventing their voices from becoming too stale. The jumps have a nice "whoosh!", throwing kunai have a satisfying "shing!" as they cut through the air, gun fire, alarms, gongs, katanas piercing flesh, or the haunting sound of crows' "caw", the sound delivers in every detail, save for music.
The graphics have a slick, water-paint art style that fits the mood very well. Each mission has well thought-out light/dark segments and are never cluttered. The player can easily see the layout and it all has a very "vidoe game-y" feel to it. Character sprites and enviornments also are well detailed.
The gameplay is where MotN won all the hype. By pressing move keys, you are automatically "sneaking" which can be turned to sprint by holding the shift key. You can jump, climb almost any wall, use a grappling hook to hook onto street lights above, throw kunai to knock out lights or draw guards, and many others. "Intuitive" is the word that comes to mind. It all flows so smoothly.
When you sneak up to a guard to kill him, you left click which zooms the camera into you and your victim. A prompt will appear telling you to hold left click again, then swipe left or right, giving each kill a little interactivity. Succeed, and it's a silent kill. Fail, and you might as well set off an ambulance.
Of course, what is a ninja without his cool gadgets? You have many at your disposal that you unlock as the game goes on. If you perform well, you are even awarded points to unlock more gadgets, more special attacks, or gadget upgrades (such as remote detonation of distractions). Just don't upgrade the smokebomb. Trust me.
The U.I. is what makes the game run so well. By watching circles emit from things, you can see how far the sound is traveling, and use this to distract guards, or go undetected entirely. They also detect guards not in your line of sight by emitting from their footsteps. It's a terrific, visual metaphor. The U.I. also shows you were you can use your hook to scale buildings or escape danger.
The game additionally boasts so many options for each situation, and rewards you for all of them. Do you want to kill everything with your sword? How about with a gadget instead? Knock down the chandilier to wipe them out all at once? Or my route: distract them and slip away, leaving them untouched?
Aside from all the bloodshed, MotN also brings great platforming segments such as using switches to open/shut doors to avoid the infamous RED LAZERS OF INSTANT DEATH, or climbing around a moving platform to avoid MOAR LAZERS OF INSTANT DETH!1!!11. They really do get quite creative, and are very challenging, but rewarding when you end up on the other side unscratched.
My favorite new idea they bring to the table is the ability to "terrorize" guards with other dead bodies. Terrorized guards move more predictably, and don't search thoroughly...but for whatever reason, suddenly their bullets arch around objects to hit you.
With terrorize, you can lure guards into shooting each other in panic, scare them off of a rooftop to fall to their doom, or walk right up to them and cut them down. It's a brilliant mechanic and I hope it and more like it catch on in the stealth genre!
Final Verdict: MotN is a very well polished stealth game that delivers in almost every category. The plot leaves much to be desired, and the music could be much better, but that's not enough to stop Mark of the Ninja from earning a 10/10. Nice work, team.

This is not Naruto-style ninja with earth-shattering ninja-magic and standing in the open and talking for all to know your identity.  Rather, this is a very fun 2D side-scrolling stealth platformer.  You get rewarded for not being detected, and severely punished for being detected, both by the immediate score penalty and by nearby guards suddenly turning on long-range flashlights and searching everywhere.  The check-point system is generous though, which makes experimenting and rewinding failures not too punishing.
I personally enjoyed the story (no spoilers!), and I felt that the scripting, voice acting, and music were excellent for this particular take on ninja.  I recommend good sound and playing this in the dark!  This is not a psychological thriller, but it does have it's share of sudden surprises if you are not careful and alert a gurd or trip a sensor laser or you get too close to a dog.
This is single-player campaign only.  The campaign took me about 6 hours to beat on my first playthrough, including a generous number of checkpoint rewinds because I was generally bad at being a ninja.  Fortunately, this game is meant to be replayed, offering a New Game Plus mode that ups the difficulty a bit and lets you keep all your achievements and unlockables from the previous playthrough.  I am currently on New Game Plus mode and trying to go full stealth, and it is fun!
Definitely worth the money.  This is a great game for playing an hour in the evening after work, or for unwinding for a few hours on the weekend.
Extra Credits was spot on with this game.  It has easily earned a place in my top favorite games of all time.  Very well designed.

This game is insane. Very fluid, fast, and skill based. Don't listen to idiots that compare this game with overwatch, it has a lot more in common with quake and unreal tournament.
Overwatch has slow rock paper scissor style gameplay where characters are more or less locked into a certain role and playstyle.  Lawkbreakers is the opposite of that. Team comp doesn't matter much at all and medics can top frag and do insane DPS.
The selling point of the game is definitely the unique movement and momentum system. You can build momentum in low grav through movement abilities, shooting behind you, and you can preserve it outside of low grav through bhopping. Characters like the assassin can attack from virtually any angle, and most characters can go from one side of the level to the other in seconds. The verticality in this game is unmatched and I cannot recommend this game enough to shooter fans.

Plays like a free-to-play Nexon shooter. Guess what? It was published by Nexon.
The moment you log in, it already asks you for your money to purchase micro-transactions. Skins this, avatars that. Why not give me a bunch of stuff I can pick and choose from the get-go?
From the clustered, dated looking menu from 2007 to the weird music in the background, the game doesn't feel like it justifies a hefty $40 CAD price tag. At best, I'd pay $10.00 for the experience. The game modes available are limited; there is no single player campaign or any PvE for that matter. You're only given 2 options when clicking play, 'Quick Play' or 'Custom Game'. That's it.
I'm not sure why this game is getting raving reviews on Steam but I feel like they're being trolls. Either that or they're being paid to give stellar reviews.
As a shooter, what it tries to do is to be unique in terms of verticality. It does this well. Other than that, it isn't unique.
I give this a mediocre review; a 5/10. Feel free to disagree. I didn't write this review in spite, but I wrote it in disappointment. I wish it were better.

Gnomoria plays like a simplified, isometric version of Dwarf Fortress, but with much the same degree of freedom for the development of your little kingdom. You start with a small group of gnomes, seeds, bandages, yaks and a few other tools to get yourself going and must quickly, but not stressfully, resolve a number of problems: building shelter and beds, setting up workshops, getting your seeds planted, pasturing your livestock, initiating diplomacy and trade, obtaining materials for basic weapons and armour, and perhaps most importantly, figuring out how you will keep intruders out before too many seasons pass.
As the game progresses you grow your kingdom to take in greater numbers of gnomes, improve your productivity, skill up your gnomes and try to balance the wealth of your kingdom and food reserves against having sufficient defences to hold off those who might covet them. You can build basically whatever type of structure you desire with the completely rebuildable environment, and a basic selection of mechanisms allows you to build many interesting Gnomish contraptions to make life more easy for your gnomes, or more difficult for your enemies.
It's definitely not a perfect game, but conceptually it has been well designed and what has been put in is well executed. There are often many complaints of bugs, but I personally do not seem to come across any of them (other than the easily resolved wheelbarrow/bucket/sack hauling bug).
While there is plenty of content in there, is best picked up on sale as it's extremely unlikely to ever end up being complete, as development has finished at 1.0 and the extent of modding support, as well as the size of the modding community, is unlikely to be able to fill the remaining gaps in the game. That said the game is extremely playable (and replayable if you like these types of builders), and offers plenty of variety.

LawBreakers scratches an itch for a fast paced FPS that I haven't had since the golden days of Tribes: Ascend.
Overall, I recommend this game to anyone with a similar yearning for a competitive FPS that isn't so bound on ults like Overwatch. In short, OW has more focus on team play, while this has more focus on frags and personal FPS ability.
Aim is key in LawBreakers, as most of the engagements come down to whoever best uses their character. During the development cycle, Cliff Blizenski has claimed to have put a lot of attention to detail in terms of balance and core gameplay experience, and I feel it reall shows.
I haven't played enough yet to discover all balance issues, but apart from some hiccups in Blitzball I believe that the game will follow a slow growth trend, or at least maintain a dedicated playerbase, which is one of the biggest fears I have come across regarding this game.
To sum up my my feelings about this game, I'll give a pros and cons list for brevity:
PROS
>Fast paced FPS Action
>Emphasis placed on FPS ability rather than meta strategy
>Generally, everything is fairly balanced at launch, thank the betas
>Devs seem dedicated, game is backed by Cliffy B
CONS
>The characters aren't very well done, they all look samey and uninteresting. They match the colour scheme of the game, but a lot is left to be desired in this department. There's two characters for each class (one for each side) but good luck getting me to remember any of the characters names
>This game shares a lot of similarities with OW, to the point that it feels slightly like a clone. However, I feel like this is more fun, so despite that I prefer this game.
>A lacklustre marketing campaign has left concerns on the table as to whether the playerbase will be sustainable in the long run. I personally believe it will; but I may be wrong. Therefore, I expect a small, dedicated playerbase (that I will be a part of) that will grow slowly over time.
SUMMARY: This game isn't for everyone, but if you're like me and you want a different competitive arena shooter, then you will enjoy this.

This is one of the best stealth games that I've played. This is what you would get if you combined Gunpoint with Assassins’ Creed, if you were to take only the best elements from each. Everything in the game feels fluid, tactile and responsive. More than that, it is a game that encourages you to experiment with different play styles. I’ve played through the entire game, including the DLC, and I’m still having fun playing through again to experiment and take different approaches to levels. The art style is fantastic, and the story is sufficient to provide a nice framework for the game.
There is a lot that this game gets right, but one thing that sets this game apart from many other stealth games is the pacing. You never spend too much time standing around waiting for a guard to walk to a certain position. Irrespective of whether you want to kill everything in your path or try to slip by everyone undetected, it is possible to progress quite quickly, especially once you start getting the hang of the game. Also, if you get spotted you can still fight back, and if you get killed you never lose too much progress. 2D platform games don’t get much better than this, and if you are a fan of stealth games you absolutely have to have this.

I greatly enjoyed The Novelist as a nuanced choose-your-path story with lightweight stealth gameplay elements.
As a parent and someone for whom artistic/creative work/life balance issues are a big part of life, the choices and story resonated with me more than any game in recent memory. Even though it hit home for me in a way that it might not for most, the empathetic writing should allow anyone (parent/creative or not) to identify with the characters and become invested in figuring out which choices will lead to their desired outcome.
I liked that there was no obvious "right" answer in many cases, as "right" shifted around depending on each character's needs and perspective. Despite having to make some tough choices, the gentle music, sound effects, and general pacing of the game helped make the whole thing a relaxing experience, leading to introspective contemplation rather than stressful regrets when a tough choice was presented.
As for the idea that you're a ghost who possesses light fixtures in order to move around unseen and influence the life of a family, though a bit of a non-sequitur if you think about it too much, I enjoyed it and found the tone of it somehow complemented the mood and subject matter of the rest of the story. I wouldn't be surprised if opinions varied here though.

To some degree I did feel the game got a little repetitive when you have to start hunting for the new clues to move the game along each time but the story was good enough that I got immersed in it. I originally wanted to hate the characters but in the end I felt the writing was good enough to help me establish a connection with them and forgive them for their foibles, making them feel a little more realistic and somewhat loveable.
If you enjoy story-based games such as Dear Esther and Gone Home, you'll enjoy this too.

The Novelist takes an interesting and novel enough approach to a choice-based game. I liked the basic gameplay of choosing between the three characters' wishes and exploring their home/memories, although it made every level feel largely the same. I also enjoyed the general atmosphere of the game and thought it was executed very well. I do wish that the choices affected the game a bit more than they did - as it is, a chapter's choices change the ending to their chapter, the placement of some objects around the house, some thoughts the characters have, and the endings seem more quantitative than qualitative (choose everyone's choice enough times and everyone lives happily enough, don't and some people are happy while some suffer).
But overall, while the story's nothings exciting, it's very easy to relate to and empathise with, and the execution makes it an enjoyable experience as well as a well thought-out work of art.
I'd recommend buying this game, but given the short play-through time and existing but limited replay value, I'd only recommend getting it on sale.

Out of all the games I played in 2015 starring elongated narcoleptic birds, Snakebird is my favorite.
The premise is pretty straightforward: Steer your snakebird toward the exit.
Like in the classic Snake game, your snakebird's head will move in the direction you choose, its tail following behind. If your snakebird eats a piece of fruit, its tail will grow one segment longer.
Unlike classic Snake, your snakebirds are not self-driving, they are affected by gravity, and there are sometimes several to control within a single level.
If there is fruit in a level, you must collect it all to unlock the exit. In addition, you must guide ALL of a level's snakebirds to the exit, not just one. This might not sound like that big of an obstacle until you realize that some levels require your snakebirds to climb on each other to advance.
These are not easy puzzles. There are a few basic stages to ease you into the rules, but then you're thrown right into the heavy stuff. Thankfully, the game is not purely linear. When you solve one level, the levels adjecent on the world map will be unlocked, regardless of how they are numbered. This is a feature that I worry will be overlooked by a lot of people, and more puzzle games would do well to incorporate it. I couldn't tell you how many times I got frustrated on a puzzle, then left to play a different puzzle, and returned later with success.
Another great feature: the game remembers every move you make on a given attempt, so instead of having to restart a stage every time you fall offscreen or land on spikes or get yourself trapped, you can hit Undo as many times as you like.
There are multiple methods of controlling your snakebirds, but my personal recommendation is the skip the mouse during puzzles and use arrow keys to move, Tab to switch between snakebirds, and Backspace to undo.
If you're looking for a timewaster, you might not have a very good time with this one. If you're looking for actually difficult actual puzzles that require thought and planning, you should strongly consider Snakebird.

Always Sometimes Monsters is a RPGmaker "life sim" where you play one character whose objective is to attend his/her ex-bf/gf wedding in a distant city.
So as you may think, this game first lets you pick from a small range of characters (because they couldn't make hundreds of sprites) to get the protagonist and then you choose who will be your partner (and later, your ex). Both can be guys, girls or an heterosexual couple, the game let's you decide how you'll get more involved with the story there. For example my first gameplay I chose a lesbian couple.
So the game centers around making you think about what path is best to accomplish your goal, and then make you reflect on your decisions. You need money in order to get to San Verdano (the city hosting the wedding), so you'll have to work, steal, lie... or not. The game leaves all that up to you. You can get the money by legal means, or walk over people to get what you want. You also need to eat and sleep, so you'll need money for that as well.
The game involves drugs, sex, killing people, stealing and a bunch of references and jokes. So if you enjoy this kind of things you may like the game.
But so far I've described to you the overall feel of the game. now I'm gonna get a little bit harsh on it, so I warn you:
FROM HERE THE REVIEW HAS "SPOILERISH" OPINIONS, IF YOU PREFER TO GET INTO THE UNKNOWN, DONT READ THIS.
Ok so the game has mainly three wrong things.
- The first one is the poor writing of the story. At first the plot is real good until you get to a point where you ask "why?". And this repeats from then on. Poor character development if you ask me, and this will make you mad if you can't stand weak plots. Also, you "decide" why your character wants to go to the wedding, so you expect it not to be a "romantic rescue" if you don't want it that way. You just wait.
- There is "almost" no consequences from acting douchy or well apart from the rewards. I've done a lot of♥♥♥♥♥♥ Help people who needed it, sell drugs, try to do an honest job... . And the only bad things that will happen to you if you go commiting crimes or just walking over people is... the moral remorse? Which may not matter to you at all because well, it's a ♥♥♥♥ing game.
- At the end of the game you'll get a fusion of the last two points. The only way you'll face your "mistakes" is by talking with some character, and well, that's it. You'll have to defend yourself from accussations of doing bad things, if you did any. But you'll have an excuse for all of them so it doesn't matter at all. But the worst part is that, not only it actually turns out that you are ON A ROMANTIC RESCUE, but you figure it out too late. In a game where you can act maturely, you are expected to fight for your exs love (even if you chose your character to decide to forget her), other way you'll find yourself in one of, what I guess, many ♥♥♥♥♥♥ endings. Again, thanks for the poor writing.
END OF "SPOILERS" HERE
So this is a game that makes you decide in every minute, with poor writing but a fun story and minigames. Only one of the many endings this game has is "good", and if you play the same way I did, you'll find yourself in any of the bad ones.
Also it fails to deliver the message in the game's title, as you build your character from zero and make all the decisions for him/her, so you won't feel bad about doing bad things if you just wanted to play that way.
Anyway, buy it if it's cheap, but don't expect a great game. It's still fun and a nice experience, but I warn you, if you try to behave maturely and nice, you'll get butthurt as hell. 6/10 too much meh.

Always Sometimes Monsters isn't like whatever you're thinking it is. The game opens on a scene where you meet someone in a dark alley as you're attempting to quit your job as a contract killer. I see what people are getting at in downvoting this game. The story can be overly dramatic at times, it is limited by its RPGMaker engine, and you don't ever have quite as much freedom as you'd live. It is a diamond in the rough. I think it is an ambitios attempt at a kind of RPG we haven't seen often before but is becoming more common in that it attempts to explore a modern day, realistic fiction setting.
I believe Always Sometimes Monsters succeeds in its goal of causing the player to face themselves and the actions they're willing to take to win the game. There are no monsters to be slain, no magical items to retrieve, no experience to farm, only seemingly mundane choices that seem arbitrary at first, but can later (and often) have a profound effect on your world. Maybe not THE WORLD itself, but your world. You're not out to save the land from evil, you're on a journey of self-discovery. I found myself intrigued with the decisions I found myself facing, and at the end I was so disgusted with the ending I recieved, I loadrd a previous save to change my character's fate. I believe that reaction crosses Sometimes Always Monsters over from being merely a game to serve as a distraction and moves it towards an artistic piece worthy of discussion. Like a painting, you may love it or you may hate it, but the fact that it made you think and feel anything is an indication that the piece succeded in its goal.
If you can get it for $10 or less or as part of a Humble Bundle, I highy suggest giving it a whirl. It does have a little replayability, as the selection of your character's race, gender, and sexual orientation do impact the game world and there are multiple branches you can take to complete the story. The endings can be lumped into 5 or 6 different branches, but Always Sometimes Monsters, like life, is about the journey and not the destination.

I played this game initially before Med2, a game which I was terribly addicted to. With the death of my desktop, I installed this beauty for a measly $2.50 (thanks, Steam!). To say the least, it has surpassed it's value ten fold. "Is it really as good as a $25 game?", you ask. The answer to that question varies from  "THOSE PIGS BROKE OUR ALLIANCE!" to "Watch them flee. I love watching the enemies flee." and even "I... I lost!?". Losing never felt so good. It leaves you changing your view from "How could my idiots let me down?" to "How could I let down my brave soldiers?".. that's a lesson you can carry to victory in ANY game.
-
The gameplay. If you don't know this game, let's just say the obvious: It's responsible for funding a team who would create the most celebrated and brutal historical war simulation games, ever. Yes there are a few NOT made by the Total War team that are amazing, this is true. However, would those games have been as good if the Total War franchise didn't exist? I think not. The Corvette didn't become the 650 horsepower sternum-crushing monster it is becase there are no other cars in the world to compete with, right?
Play as several factions, each one like a historical counterpart. The Total War team skirts historical inaccuracies by saying "Before countries, there were only kingdoms", or something to the tune of that. It doesn't matter that it's not 100% historically delicious, this is a strategy game first, history channel lesson second.
Raise armies, make alliances, fight pitched battles. Switch between campaign map mode, which resembles what a grisly old emperor might look over to play war games with his neighbors; and battle mode. Battle mode is where the soldiers you chose to fight get to live up to their duties. This is where the middle ages greatest leaders made their names. Where they won their spurs. Thousands of soldiers fighting to the death, following your careful command. Battles lines are formed, archers are readied, cavalary are signalled and the fates of a kingdom, of and empire are decided!

-
One of the biggest problems with retro gaming is compatibility and dealing with the graphics. This game hurdles those problems (for me).
I have a laptop with no-name hardware, backed by some watered down Radeon card from years past. Retro PC gaming isn't as simple as consoles, however my hardware didn't hesitate to show it understood how to process MTW1, although I may have installed a wrapper. (If you don't know what a wrapper is, look it up. Glide wrapper, D3d, Direct Draw for example, make your graphics card able to read the outdated or defunct engines of years past. I installed one for D2 which may have made a difference)
The graphics are spot on, the menus crisp and animation as claymation as the day it came out. That sounds like a bad thing to some, but remember that the early 2000's is a hard pill to swallow when you're dealing with small scale 3D modelling. It's far better with the enhanced 2D style, especially for gamers who remember just how awesome MYTH 1 and 2 were, compared to 3. Imagine Diablo 2 with horrible nearly PS1 era 3D models. Wicked bad. The resolutions, I suspect, were updated. Running this game on higher resolution on a bigger monitor only makes this game better. All of the usual resolutions are available, max at 1920x1080

NOT SOME OVERWATCH CLONE -
LawBreaks is awesome it is the cure for having played to much Overwatch. Despite what you may have heard this game is no overwatch or team fortress 2 clone. If you had to classify it I would say it is a mash up of old school quake and team fortress combined with the gun play of newer modern warfare type games. The game consists of 5 player teams across a bunch of different maps. The game types are a couple variations of capture the flag, king of the hill and capture the point. Unlike a game like overwatch that is very dependent on a quality team make up in Lawbreakers you have still win with two players that don't know what to do and our playing the wrong character for the map. This is refreshing because you still have a chance to win even if you are down with half the objectives already claimed. Game typically last for about 10 minutes but on occasion against equally matched teams they can go for the entire 20 minutes. The gun play is very tight and the weapons feel weighty. As far as I can tell the netcode is running really well and the hit boxes are accurate to the character models. Right now I believe Wraith is a little OP given the range of his weapon and his speed but all characters are viable.
Pros:
- Great gun play
- Good net code
- Quickly match into games
- All heroes viable across different game types
- Quality graphics
- Unique IP from small studio that plays like a AAA title
- Great game for teamwork
- Multiple routes to victory not a rock paper shotgun type of game
- Not pay to win
- Highly addicting gameplay.
Cons:
- No aim toggle (player like destiny, Rainbow six siege, COD, Battlefield, etc. *Sad*)
- Blitz ball team can be carried by one player that knows the map and is playing a quick character
- Some heroes are less viable at higher levels of play
Questions:

Suffice to say, I don't think I've ever laughed, clapped, and cried at any resolution in a game before in one single sitting.
Defiance is the exception.
Return to Nosgoth as the legendary vampire Kain and the fallen wraith Raziel as they struggle to defy the machinations of fate itself.
Pros:
-Resolution to one of the most shakespearean tales told in gaming.
-Alternate between Kain and Raziel throughout missions, each armed with different tools to progress in one area where another may not.
-Combat provides engaging mechanics to keep one interested
-Puzzles, albeit somewhat less intensive than that of the Soul Reaver series.
-Good gamepad adaptation compared to previous installments.
-Vae Victis!
Cons:
-Camera angle is more remniscent of Devil May Cry games and not that of the previous installments, leading to some frustration especially if one is using a keyboard.
-Combat encounters can be rather repetitive at times, despite the intriguing mechanics provided.
-Graphical glitches can be somewhat apparent on more recent Nvidia cards, such as Raziel's wing membranes and Kain's cape physics breaking at certain points in the game.
-If running multiple cores, one may need to manually lower the priority to 1, as some cutscenes have the capacity to freeze and have the script misfire to play them.
Do I recommend this? Hell. Yes. I recommend the entire series if you haven't played it yet.

Good game. Still stands tall, and even though its studio is no more, the creators had enough foresight to enable quite extensive modding in Torchlight II. This alone extends the possible content expotentially - with merely 3 mods installed, my game got upgraded with around 20+ classes (compared to original 4) and the level cap, along with loot tables and enemies got extended up to 999th level (cap is somewhere at 100th lvl in the core game, iirc).
Gameplay-wise it's what you'd expect - a hack'n'slash dungeon-crawler with hordes upon hordes of enemies to destroy, and class-specific abilities to use. Additionally, you'll find "spells" - spells are independent of class and anyone can use them by looting them randomly and placing in one of your four spell slots (the spells can be exchanged to different ones, obviously).
There's also your pet, which has a mechanic that goes well with the gameplay - even if you're in the deepest of the dungeons, you can pack your pet with loot and send it back to the nearest town to sell it for you. It's good when you're having too much fun and don't want to break your momentum with a town visit, but your inventory is full. Or if you're out of potions/scrolls, because you can order your pet to buy them for you.
Sub-mechanic for your pet is fishing. Sounds silly, but helps. You can find fishing spots and either complete a minigame to find some random loot and fish, or use a dynamite to clear the pond without the minigame, but with less total loot. Every fish has its own type and when you feed a certain type to your pet, it transforms into a more powerful creature for a while, to help supplement your own skillset.
And most importantly - you can play co-op with your friends.

I see what people are getting at in downvoting this game. The story can be overly dramatic at times, it is limited by its RPGMaker engine, and you don't ever have quite as much freedom as you'd live. It is a diamond in the rough. I think it is an ambitios attempt at a kind of RPG we haven't seen often before but is becoming more common in that it attempts to explore a modern day, realistic fiction setting.
I believe Always Sometimes Monsters succeeds in its goal of causing the player to face themselves and the actions they're willing to take to win the game. There are no monsters to be slain, no magical items to retrieve, no experience to farm, only seemingly mundane choices that seem arbitrary at first, but can later (and often) have a profound effect on your world. Maybe not THE WORLD itself, but your world. You're not out to save the land from evil, you're on a journey of self-discovery. I found myself intrigued with the decisions I found myself facing, and at the end I was so disgusted with the ending I recieved, I loadrd a previous save to change my character's fate. I believe that reaction crosses Sometimes Always Monsters over from being merely a game to serve as a distraction and moves it towards an artistic piece worthy of discussion. Like a painting, you may love it or you may hate it, but the fact that it made you think and feel anything is an indication that the piece succeded in its goal.
If you can get it for $10 or less or as part of a Humble Bundle, I highy suggest giving it a whirl. It does have a little replayability, as the selection of your character's race, gender, and sexual orientation do impact the game world and there are multiple branches you can take to complete the story. The endings can be lumped into 5 or 6 different branches, but Always Sometimes Monsters, like life, is about the journey and not the destination.

7/10: As a struggling writer who receives an invitation to the imminent marriage of your ex, your only hope for a career hinges on handing in the journal you are writing as you struggle to get across the country in time for it. Things get "problematic" as they are wont to do for protagonists.
The game begins with what I did not realize was a character selection process. In choosing who to take a drink from and who they talk to outside, you are in fact setting up not only yourself but your significant other as well! After that initial party where you get signed though, you soon find out things have not been going so smoothly for you. As a player, you get to step in just as you're getting evicted and utterly broke.
At its core, this is a narrative game that tasks the player with accumulating enough money via interactions to proceed to the next scene. Still, only a fraction of events that deal with story and character development really earn you the money you need, so a good portion of the games "challenge" feels like grinding as you put in double shifts at the factory. Still, I didn't really feel challenged by the tasks so much as obligated to deal with them for the sake of the story.
That being said, the story is interesting. The story may shift dark or light depending on how you choose to approach the issue of dealing with people and situations along the way to the wedding, but the central theme of love and loss stays the same regardless. Any more than that would be spoiling it though.
As far as advice, I suggest buying a fishing rod as soon as possible in Dubstown. It's about $100, but fishing lets you avoid wasting money on food, which helped speed things up a bit for me. Also, once you finish whatever stories you have in an area, just work morning and afternoon shifts at local temp agencies. The Tofu Factory in Dubstown and the Grow Op in Beaton seem to be the most profitable, but you can try investing in the Sandwich Stock Market on the side or gambling to get some money too. Also, collecting all the Indie Heroz figurines gets you nothing!
Overall, it's a good story of love and what one may do for it. Maybe you think that love is all you need to justify becoming a fiend. So how many of your morals would you compromise to see them again?

Most of the reviews here explain the good about this game so I'm just going to skip that part. I do recommend this game. It is a unique arena shooter and it does a lot of things right. But there are some flaws that I am concerned about due to the nature of the game itself, so they may not be easily fixed. Of course, it's only a few hours after launch as I write this review, so I'm giving a lot of slack to the developers.
My main concern is with certain heroes who are unbalanced (of course), and most of this is due to the structure of the maps and, to be straight to the point, how small the characters are. Now this might sound stupid, but hear me out. In comparison to the maps, each character is VERY small for an arena shooter. Even the tank(ier) heroes. I have no problems with this, as it increases the skill ceiling, requiring more aim and precision. However, I do have a problem with how fast/small characters constantly dominate the map. And they dominate
. They cannot be punished easily because they are so fast and so small and deal massive amounts of damage in such a short amount of time. Tankier heroes don't do enough damage to be able to kill these massive DPS characters, who are not
squishy enough. I am specifically talking about Assassin and Wraith. Meanwhile, characters with similar HP who are much slower like Gunslinger are defenseless against these fast characters because they have no easy way of escaping.
You're probably thinking that this is an easy fix, but it actually is not. Due to the nature of the game, LawBreakers is based GREATLY upon vertical movement. Wraith, for example, can triple jump, and the cooldown resets the instant he hits the ground. Not to mention the anti-gravity which sends every character flying. This (again) becomes a problem for precision-based characters like Harrier and Gunslinger (Harrier not as much, but due to his weapon type I feel I should include him).
Due to the fast and vertical movement and many objects to easily maneuver around, characters like Gunslinger who are meant to annihilate players from great distances are useless. Also, the headshot hitbox is a joke.
Oh, and Nexon chose to allow character stacking, so if 3/5 are Assassins, it becomes a clusterf**k of Tarzans swinging around on grappling hooks.
Just an opinion.

For a game that's mostly remembered for its infamy as "the goriest game of all time" a title it could possibly still hold due to the fortunate lack of baby blinding in more contemporary videogames, Harvester does have a surprising amount of merit despite that.
The dialogue is funny and engaging, and the puzzles - while not particularly mind-blowing - aren't awful and obtuse, and the combat mechanics weren't aggravating to any extent. I almost had fun accidentally punching children in the face when I meant to talk to them. The relatively small overworld map was enjoyable to watch change throughout the game's timeline, and a massive amount of the game is optional - from hidden weapons and rooms to entire areas of the overworld map having absolutely no effect on the plot (The Wasp Woman and Military Base in particular).
What Harvester tries to be is a dark comedy with a few sobering morals. Age has changed what it is though, from an era where FMVs and basic 3d modelling were standard to one where their very existence is hilariously archaic.
The game hasn't just become camp, it's become on of the most stupidly camp games you could - and should - ever play. The absurdly gory deaths are no longer shocking moments, they're punchlines - watching the digitized actors dramatically spread eagle on 3d rendered backdrops that could pass for a high school student's school project results is so bad that it's brilliant.
I'd recommend Harvester to anyone who's in for a camp adventure in the vein of watching 13 year olds from yesteryear try to be dark and cool, and doesn't mind always being a kidder, Steve.
Be warned, however, that this isn't a true port - it's DOSBOX. Expect some graphical glitches, minor mechanical fiddly bits, rare but annoying crashes and I did on occasion have a few FMVs refuse to play. Just something to keep in mind.

The game's overall premise, "violent media (television shows, video games, etc.) are causing children to become more violent" might have been true in 1996. Actually the trend of juvenile violence relating to video games has experienced a downward trend since the formation of the ESRB in 1994, so the premise is no longer true (and here in 2014 we can laugh about it). But the overall message is obscured by the game. Its only concern is to get you to play "minor pranks" that will ultimately turn Steve into a serial killer. As the game goes on, it gets more and more ridiculous. The newspaper boy has a pistol that he'll shoot you with if you don't put the newspaper outside (the game even acknowledges the ridiculousness of that), Loomis the sheriff's deputy is beaten with a newspaper like a dog by the sherriff if he catches him beating his meat in a jail cell, a teacher actually beats a child's head in with a baseball bat for asking a question during a nuclear bomb drill, the firefighters are all gay and drive a pink fire truck. The list goes on and on. It was rather nostalgic to play an old point and click style adventure game, but there are far better ones. That's not to say this one is easy, the graphics are so pixellated sometimes it's hard to tell what's what. A grey rectangle in the distance is a drawer that you need to open to get a screwdriver out of. I'd recommend playing this only to see the sheer ridiculousness of the game.
