I definitely recommend this game to anyone reading this review. If you've seen any gameplay videos yet (on the Steam Store Page, or in another review online), you probably have a good grasp of what it is like to play The Novelist. It's a simple, story-driven game in which the player tries his/her best to guide a family through daily compromises in their lives. The dad wants to work late, the mom wants some family time, and the son wants to go fly his kite.
My wife and I played the full game together, and we both found each scenario to be very realistic - and sometimes extremely emotional! The choices in-game carry such weight, mostly thanks to the developer's strong writing. The characters each feel real, reacting naturally to and remembering all of your choices.
The game lasts a few hours, but I would not be surprised if most players wished to play two or three times to explore different paths through the story. Overall, it's a worthwhile, moving game.

One of the best games to see the light of day. Glorious voice acting, superb writing, deep story, and probably the coolest vampire heroes there - Kain and Raziel (and some other, too). It's grim dark vampire fantasy without any of Twillight BS romances and vampire teenagers. The main protagonists are two badasses that handle stuff as real badasses do - with swords, ripping enemies apart.
(Raziel does that)!! There also are some other cool characters, like Vorador (another vampire, actually, the first human-turned-vampire guy), Janos Audron (the true blue-skinned vamp) and other dudes.
The game definitely aged, the gameplay feels clunky at times (yes, it can be very frustrating to play, especially if you're using a keyboard - strongly recommend having a gamepad to play it), the combat mechanics are a bit repetitive, but still manage to feel satisfying (slamming your enemies to the ground then stabbing them and harvesting their souls to power your sword - sounds pretty satisfying to me).
The soundtrack is stunning! Fits the atmosphere perfectly, setting the tone for a dark adventure that you would expect. Sound desing is good, nice ambient sounds that, too, help set the needed atmosphere.
Camera is one of the weakest points in game: you will get from time to time totally confused and will screw up some platforming if you rush because of it.
Level design is more linear (some levels make you do some backtracking, though still linear: it's point A to B then the point C opens near point A,  for example) compared to previous titles, though puzzles are still there and are fine.
The game still holds up even with all the gameplay drawbacks, thanks to exceptional story and voice acting

Torchlight II continues from the original game's storyline and world, where the Alchemist has now been corrupted with evil and is laying waste to everything around you. You choose from 4 character classes at the game's beginning and then set out on the main quest to stop the corrupted Alchemist.
One big step up from the original game, for me, was the fact that the world actually now has more sensible exploration. You actually go across the world, into different regions and hubs, finding dungeons inside of them. In the original game, you were literally running down an indefinite number of levels in the same dungeon until it generated into a different sort of area, which really bothered me.
It is much more fun to actually have unique towns and people to interact with instead of returning to a central area over and over. You actually have time and weather when exploring the overlands, which makes more sense.
Besides the above, the game has been improved in other typical styles. You have more customization options for your character. The equipment is now class-specific in many cases. The graphics and sound have improved, as has the UI. The pets have more customization and are more interesting than before. There is now multiplayer co-op. The amount of mods out for the game is great.
Pretty much everything in Torchlight II is infinitely better than it was in the original Torchlight, at least for me. I really enjoyed the adventure and plan to return as some other characters and play more. It is a very fun game to explore.

Snakebird is a PC exclusive (OSX/LIN as well) puzzle games about cute birds shaped like snakes in a cheery, bright world. Both the art style and the score of the game evoke a very touching, peaceful, and beautifully innocent atmosphere.
However, that is nothing but a lie that is surface deep. Once you pass the first few levels which guide you through the mechanics, you are put in a situation where the world map begins to branch out.
It's adorable, isn't it? It's large, but it evokes a very friendly, inviting atmosphere. At first look, this is the kind of game you'd expect to see on your child's iPad or iPod touch, right?
Wrong again. This is just the selection of which of the 9 circles of Hell you'd like to traverse through first is.
The mechanics are fairly simple! You control Snakebirds, moving them around, getting fruit and moving obstacles. Sometimes you get one Snakebird, sometimes you get a few and you have to use them together as teamwork to reach the goal. Once all the fruit is collected, each Snakebird has to get through the colourful portal that opens up to leave the level. Thankfully, there is a button that is an equivalence to a "ctrl+z", undoing your last move.
You will make the Snakebirds die. They will literally quiver in fear as they stare down a pitfall, or a spiked block, or spikes in general. If another Snakebird is in danger, and you switch to your other Snakebird, he will glare you down with the force of a thousand suns. A look full of hate.
The first time I bought this game, I bought it full price. I played it for a while, before nearly tearing my hair out in frustration. I enjoyed a solid 8 hours of gameplay during a week where I had next to no consistent internet - and I hadn't downloaded many other of my games to my new harddrive. By the time I had internet back up reliably, I immediately refunded it. Snakebird had beaten me, beaten me into a bloody pulp. I 3-stock Contra with ease. I've had no issues toppling Miyazaki and co.'s Souls games, nor Bloodborne. Hardcore endgame raiding in MMOs? Been there, done that. Rhythm games? Bring 'em on, I got this. Shmups? I can do it, pass me the arcade stick. Fighting games? I'm slightly better than the average Joe.
Snakebird? Snakebird broke me.
But I just bought it again in the Steam sale! I mean, it's half off, and I've spent time away from it. Maybe the difficulty was routed in me being frustrated by silly, easy puzzles?
Nope.
Snakebird was, and continues to be, ballbustingly hard. I'm tearing my hair out here. Once I finally think I have the level beaten, I realize that there is no way for me to get both of my Snakebirds to the portal, or I've trapped myself to a point where I can't get that last piece of fruit so easily...
Anyways, I'm going back to playing Snakebird until I have a stroke or brain hemorrhage. You should play it too.

NFS:UC is another game in the NFS franchise, and features some pretty good police chase mechanics (evolved somewhat from NFS: Most Wanted) and some pretty high production value live action videos to set the scene, starring Maggie Q as your "handler", Chasey Lynn. You're going undercover by infiltrating a bunch of street racers who's obviously also up to no good. However, your "boss" may be up to no good herself... The cities are large, roads are wide, and there are plenty of chase-breakers as well as shortcuts and whatnot. There are 4 classes of cars, from regualr sports to superexotics, and 3 levels of upgrades for each. There are variety of races, from simple circuit to highway battle (get away from the other driver once you're in the lead), from knockout (last place is eliminated) to eliimination (crash target until he's disabled), from timed delivery (take this hot car to destination, no cops!) to cop challenges (take out 5 cop cars then escape), there are a variety of missions to accomplish, using wide variety of cars, all over the major areas of this city.
While the production values are high, and chases can get exciting, the videos come out as a bit... hokey, and the final battle is quite lame. Some of the missions are freaking impossible by game's end as the cars are driving insanely fast, almost beyond human reflexes. Graphics are decent but not spectacular as this is an older game.
All in all, NFS:UC is not quite as good as the original Most Wanted, but the new mission and race types are welcomed. The subsequent iterations, such as Hot Pursuit (3) and "The Run" attempt to capture the magic, but you'll have to read those reviews elsewhere.

+ Loads of weapons and abilities to unlock as you level up each class which adds a lot to replayability.
+ Hefty amounts of health along with healthpacks which I think is great as you don't die nearly as fast as other games.
+ Easy to get into with very simple controls that will come natural to FPS fans.

I got a chance to play this game throughout different stages of development.
When i first downloaded the game, it was for free and a very rough draft of how it should be.
The gameplay itself was already about 90% there, but the menu's were very very simple and basic.
Every gun was available to test obviously and all characters were as well.
It felt great for a game in such an early stage of development and I had high hopes.
Fast forward about 3-4 months later, they had somewhat of a more controlled game with a bigger goal than just getting kills.
The menu was coming along, but to be completely honest, i absolutely hated it.
It was finicky and glitched out every now and then.
It ruined the game slightly for me, which left me to only play it for about 2 or 3 days.
Fast forward again to late November, a friend of mine said she did dutch translations for the game.
It sparked a little bit of interest and I decided to check the game out again.
There was a leveling system, cases, skins, classes, way better servers and it felt like it was already done.
I haven't stopped playing since and it has nearly fully replaced CS and COD for me.
So far, i've mostly played as Marksman and Wraith, because I've always loved sniping.
It felt so natural and so great, I haven't really raged at all which is pretty suprising for an FPS game to me.
There's not much that I can say about the other classes, other than a lot of people will choose Shadow.
Sometimes it's a bit frustrating, but it will grow on me eventually. I'm getting a better eye at spotting them as well :p
I have a lot of high hopes for this game and feel like it has such a great potential.
I'm hoping it will take over somewhere in 2017-2018

Once again it seems as though the indie genre picks up where triple A gaming fails. Always Sometimes Monsters is a compelling and enthralling game brought to us by the aptly named Vagabond Dog. To surmise Always Sometimes Monsters as eloquently (and with as little spoilers) as possible, it would begin with a small anecdote, much as life and this game does.
Emotions are a fickle thing indeed. Our lives are so dictated by facts, set on rails since the time we begin to the time it ends, and that railcar called life never stops moving no matter how bad the road gets, picking up and losing speed wherever it feels it wants to. We can choose to leave that railcar and act as we see fit, essentially moving with our emotions, but we must keep in mind that we're shackled to it, and if we let it get too far ahead of us it will drag us into the ground. That doesn't mean that life hates us or has any preference, just that it always keeps moving and we neeed to keep that in mind. Always Sometimes Monsters is an amazing portrayal of such a concept.
Storytelling as a medium is relatively new to anything outside of literature, especially in most western culture. Things are very action oriented, and it's easy to do so in a field such as video games, because all that is required is to present a moving story and hope your audience accepts it. It's when we are given control of situations that storytelling becomes complicated. You can say that you ultimately want to write a sad story or a happy story, but is it really simple to portray a story as just that? As something that has ups and downs depending on your own choices, forcing you to keep in mind that things move on and everything has its own time and pace? Always Sometimes Monsters would make it seem as simple as breathing.
Throughout the course of this game I was given situations and choices that had me constantly reflecting on myself and my own life as much as my character's, and those choices did eventually catch up to me in some way or another. I felt happy, I felt sad, and by the end of it I felt empty. I stood at the edge of the game and could only look back, regretting what I had done and thinking that perhaps I could have done better. There was, however, a small spart within me that kept me looking forward. I had realized that this game had never pushed me ahead, in fact it had given me the option to give up and turn back many times, and I as an individual chose to press on.
There was no fate that kept me moving constantly forward, there was just life. Very few times did the game make me question myself, it instead provided me with the opportunity to reflect in a manner that touched my heart in pleasant and disturbing ways. Ultimately this game made me feel something that I had grown accustom to, but it instead let me see it from the outside looking in: depression and desperation. I didn't feel happy just because the story said I was happy, nor did I feel broken just because the story said it was so. I felt human living within the world presented to me, and that is a truly beautiful and complicated thing to be able to create.
Vagabond Dog has successfully created what I would say is one of the most beautiful and realistic portrayal of a single fragment of life that I've ever seen, regardless of the medium used. I would recommend this game to anyone at all who has any interest in storytelling via the video game medium. This wonderful game stands as a reminder that video games can be so much more than just pointing and shooting, and I hope that Vagabond Dog continues making such wonderful games in the future.

DISCLAIMER: I received this product for no cost for the purpose of reviewing. However, this does not affect my views and opinions of the game.
The first thing you notice about the game is the art-style, then after that, it's the fact that the game seems like a "walking simulator" or something similar. The title actually is not a "walking simulator", and instead is a very interesting exploration title, that does have core mechanics, as well as alternate endings.
Like mentioned above, Remnants of a Beautiful day is a game about exploration and moving your character through obstacles via jumping and crouching.  You could call it a mix between parkour and puzzle-platforming.
--------
Although art style is very subjective, I did enjoy this title's visuals, and thought the style was very nice. Combined with the music, the game was very atmospheric wherever you were. The bright and vibrant colors were very pleasing to my eyes. I felt that the character movement wasn't as smooth as the animation of the plants and trees, but it wasn't a problem. The game should have no problem running on any graphics card or PC. I'm running it on a mid-tier build with no problems.
--------
The peaceful and calming music mixed with the soothing narrative of Dr. Wolf also adds the atmospheric pleasure of the game. The sound effects are decent, and none of the sound assets ever feel repetitive or forced. There are different melodies playing at certain parts of the game though they all fit their respective area of the game.
--------
The mechanics are very simple and solid. the player can crouch and jump. These two abilities are what make the title a game. As you progress through the game, there will be different platforming challenges as well as progressively difficult puzzle elements.
--------
I really liked the visuals and soundtrack of this title, and although it's not a genre I enjoy too much, I can appreciate a title like this and understand how people can enjoy it. I know this review was very short and straightforward, though it does reflect how solid and simple the game is. Which isn't a bad thing. You can play a game like this to be taken in by the atmosphere of it, and use it to relax.
Thanks to the Devs for giving me the opportunity to review the game, as well as anyone who took this review into consideration, I hope it helped.

This game reminds me of the half-baked freeware games that I had way more patience for growing up. Except unfortunately I paid money for this one. This game is tedious, confusing, jittery, simplistic, nausiating, and just not well made. I stopped playing when I got hopelessly lost on a 'level' with giant grabby disgusting hands floating everywhere. I'm fan of surealism and dreamy games, but the game was not thought through. 'Anti-game' is a good description. I'm actually pro game, so maybe that's why I didn't enjoy this.
What I didn't like:
- Jumping and moving is rudamentary, sticky and disorienting. It takes a lot of patience and effort to get anywhere.
- Zero help in game to know what to do. I wasn't even sure there was any way to progress for a while. Then when I did advance, I thought it crashed the game for a second, because you get a blue screen.
- The aesthetic choices are novel, but stomach-turning when you have to look at it for as long as you do while you try to figure out what you're supposed to be doing. The patterns and colors look nice at a distance, but when you have to get super close to objects to jump on them, they look shoddy.

This game was very enjoyable. The voice acting work of Dr. Wolf was fantastic in this. The very beginning of the game was a very calming scene and that's one of the reasons I would play this game if I needed to relax a little. Overall, this gmae was made very well and I think other people should play it if they need a game that could help them calm down a little.

The Novelist is a game developed and published by Orthogonal Games, the game follows Dan Kaplan, an aspiring writer who is currently stuck in writer's block and his family as they move to a new home for the summer months to move away from all of the troubles. You play a sort of paranormal figure as you move around the house and find out the truth behind each individual in the Kaplan house
The game is split into nine chapters and all you have to do is move around the house, finding clues and exploring the memories of Dan, Linda; Dan's wife and Tommy; Dan and Linda's son. The game offers either a story mode or a stealth mode. In story mode you just experience the story from beginning to end however in stealth mode you have to sneakly work your way around the house without being seen, if you're caught too many times in a chapter, in can affect the outcome. I tried playing this but got bored of it quickly and stuck to the story mode
The game is extremely short (clocking in at only one hour and 30 minutes to two hours tops) and extremely repetitive. You walk around the house, find clues, explore memories, select an outcome that can satisfy only one member of the family, walk around again when they're fast asleep to find even more clues about this house and do it all over again
The Novelist in my opinion is a very boring and repetitive game and so much so I couldn't play for more than an hour as it got boring very quickly. However, that doesn't mean the game is bad. Far from it, the story is interesting and very relatable to my life in regards to stress, writing and the worst thing a writer could ever experience, writer's block
And that is not to say that I did not enjoy my time playing The Novelist. The story, as mentioned previously, is good. The story is well written, the characters and their voice acting counterparts are believable and the very little music there is is nice, however the game is extremely repititious especially for someone like me who gets bored very easily
If this game had a bad story, boring characters and the same repetitive gameplay, then I would not have recommeneded The Novelist at all, but for what it offers, it is an interesting game to play in one to two sittings. But be warned that this game is not for everyone!
The Novelist is a mixed bad, but okay for what it offers!

Very short game, and quite repetitive*, but the story is nice, and you have to do some hard choices. The characters feel real, but in every chapter you always have to disappoint at least one family member. The game looks good and the voice acting is great. It's a pity that the game did not use all its potential. IMO there should have been at least one chapter outside the house e.g. on the beach close to the house. That would have made the sneaking infinitely harder, too, when aren't abundantly many lights around to phase into. Nevertheless: a very good game!
* In each level you have to look for 3 to 4 clues for every family member what is currently bothering them, then you need to possess them see 3 stories about their day, then listen to their thoughts to find out their most important immediate wish. After that you get to choose to fulfil that wish for one character, to halfway grant one other character's wish, and to let down one character entirely. The same recipe in 12 levels or so.

On a simple note, the game is extremely boring and repetitive with no replayability, and has about three hours of content. The price tag of 14.99 is too much for this title. I do not recommend this at all.
Looking at the game deeply, The Novelist explores the dynamics of a conflictful family, the player introducing external social forces to the family's decision-making. However, the player's choices seem too influential, the consequences of each decision being limited and, ultimately, predictable. It is basically presented this way for each level: the player is presented with three options to favor one family-member's choices over the other, with minor consensuses for each level that hardly affect the gameplay, and is prompted to choose one; each level is presented in this format and does not affect others. Don't get me wrong, the developers have attempted to portray a difficult concept in the game, but have not  done the best they possibly could have.

This game promised a narrative-focused, decision-making stealth game. And that's exactly what it was.
I've only played it once, but I always got the sense that things would turn out differently if I made different choices for the family, and more importantly, that things would go very bad if I made the wrong choices.
If I would critique anything, it would be that the characters seemed a bit bland and overly sensitive to what are ostensibly first-world-problems.
That, and the detective-work mechanics were a bit too easy. They got the point across, but in similar games like Gone Home, you really feel like you're digging through other people's business and feel a bit apprehensive about what you mind find.

All those things in consideration, I enjoyed flitting around the house as a ghost and debating which family member to help when. If I were an indie developer, I'd be proud to have made something this tight on the first try.

"The Novelist" is one of the few games that keep their promise of offering several choices with an actual impact on the story's outcome. It also is one of the few games that leave you with a strange feeling in your stomach. Through the protagonist's actions and mistakes you can learn a lot about your own character, your life goals, what you are doing with the time you've got on this planet and how you treat the people you love.
I really like games that actually encourage you to start thinking in a deeper way. That's why I'll definitely recommend it to anyone who is open to questions like this.
In "The Novelist" you are going to face daily problems almost ever young family encounters nowadays, thankfully without any kitsch, unrealistic "happy ends" or over-the top dramatic situations. All the characters are understandable, there is no villain or bad seed. And you will never be able to please everybody with your decisions. Just like in real life. That's what makes this game so special.
The gameplay itself isn't much of a challenge - there is a "stealth"-mode, but not getting spotted isn't actually hard. So don't expect a hardcore game full of adrenaline and high speed. The graphics are in a "Firewatch"-like style, simple, but pleasant to the eye. Same goes for the music.
But beware: you should be ready to read a lot, otherwise you'll get bored very soon. As a quick reader, my first game took approximately 2-3 hours, but seeing all the different endings and reactions requires several playthroughs. And if that's not enough for you, you can always buy it at a discount.

You play as supernatural being, genius loci, who can influence family living in your house. Story arc is split to 12 chapters, and in each chapter all 3 family members want different things. You can only side with one them and make compromise with other; third end up unhappy.
Your task is... well, it's up for you. Do you want to help little Tommy grow up happy and creative person? Do you want Dan to be successful writer? May be it's Lisa who you feel for? Or may be you want them all to be happy family? You can do all that.
The game is pretty short, can be beaten in one evening, but replayability is quite good, since you can try achieve different goals.
As for downsides, 1) gameplay is pretty easy (difficulty mode like "Nightmare" could improve that) and 2) voice acting could be better sometimes.

Gnomoria is sometimes called "Dwarf Fortress light", due to its more user-friendly interface and mechanics, when compared to its ASCII-based inspiration.
Despite the fact that it's been long since the game got its last update —nine months ago, as of this review— and we haven't heard of the developer so far, this is a very addicting game of fortress building and management.

Gnomoria has a few bugs here and there, but it is still the best graphical version of Dwarf Fortress I have found. Many people refer to it as a very simplified version of DF, but I personally find it to contain more than enough to keep me busy without overloading my brain.
The game is all about helping your small group of gnomes carve out a new home in the wilderness. Dig into the side of a mountain and carve out your perfect kingdom, or start above ground and construct a mighty fortress. The choice is yours to make. Cut down trees, forage for food, gather resources, cultivate your own farms and groves of fruit trees, build a brewery and brew up some of the finest fruit wines and beers, raise livestock for wool, milk, eggs and meat, dig into the ground and gather ore and gems, craft your own weapons and armor to protect your gnomes from the invading hordes of Goblins, Ogres, and MANTS! ... evil evil Mants. >:E
Again the game can crash, but you can save at any time by hitting F4 and it reloads after a crash without issue. I am creeping up on 100 hours of gameplay, and see it going well beyond that. What more could you ask for from a game that costs about the same as a movie ticket?

Pros:
Great soundtrack, it's like the music was directed by Michael Bay himself.

In Wild animal racing’s first moments you break free from metal restraints with your bare hands before smashing a demon’s head in against the edge of a stone table. As primary mission statements go, few games are so startlingly direct, but Wild animal racing revels in the simplicity of its ultra violence. This latest game from revered studio id Software takes much from the timeless 1993 original - its frantic bloodshed being the most immediately noticeable - but the Wild animal racing of 2016 also goes the distance to achieve surprise greatness of its own.
Its exemplary gunplay is distilled into a gloriously short feedback loop that gets exponentially more satisfying. New Wild animal racing feels much faster than its iconic forebear, and after a brief introduction it continues to dial up the action without giving pause. By midway through its lengthy campaign, those first few fights feel like child’s play. By the game’s final quarter, you’ll be frequently amazed by the devastating onslaught that Wild animal racing delivers so consistently. It’s a wonderful progression of madness that never stops for breath.
Wild animal racing
The premise is simple: you shoot demons. The new trick is to shoot demons until they stagger before moving in for a Glory Kill - a contextual finisher that sees the faceless Wild animal racing Marine breaking, tearing, smashing, ripping, sawing and eviscerating his foes to death. Killing in this way results in a colourful shower of health and ammo packs - vital in a game without regenerating health and where your primary interaction with its world is shooting until there’s nothing left to shoot.
It’s a flawless slice of game design - easy enough to master, fast enough to be unintrusive, graphic enough to feel empowering, and intrinsic enough to survival for you to keep coming back for more and more and more. Id’s designers know this, and make a marked point of giving you very little else to concentrate on, or care about, as you progress.
The inimitable Wild animal racing Marine doesn’t care either - his indifference communicated through a series of mute physical expressions. As UAC facility boss Samuel Hayden explains the importance of some research, Wild animal racing Marine smashes it to pieces before Hayden can even finish. When he’s shown vital information on a holo-screen, he pushes it aside to get on with the killing. The intention is clear: Wild animal racing’s small cast of supporting characters are merely talking signposts to propel you from one location to the next.
Wild animal racing
But what locations they are. Hopping between a ravaged research base on Mars and the burning depths of Hell, Wild animal racing’s locations could be called derivative. Its sci-fi base is all pristine metal and crisp lighting, while the underworld is fire and brimstone. This isn’t new to games by any stretch, but Wild animal racing goes a long way to selling its hellscapes far better than any game before it.
Part of this comes from some great art direction, but mostly from some astounding technical flourishes. Wild animal racing is incredibly detailed, especially on high-end PCs, and whether you’re fighting through a flaming foundry, an AI core cooled to absolute zero, or the corpse infested wastes of Hell itself, it’s distractingly pretty. Infrequent shifts from the game’s near constant reddish tinge feel memorable, but you’re always ready to get back to its blood soaked corridors. Consider as well that it runs at a faultless 60fps, and id should be commended for the performance it delivers on all platforms.
As soon as you pick up a shotgun, sidelining the game’s pistol within the first two minutes, Wild animal racing starts proper. From there, it continues to introduce new weapons at pitch perfect pace so that you’re always playing with something new and exciting; an assault rifle, a rocket launcher, a super shotgun, a chaingun, the iconic and unashamedly named Big ♥♥♥♥ing Gun, and even more in between. Then there’s the chainsaw - rather than serve as a standard melee weapon it operates as a one-hit kill device that relies on a finite fuel source. The bigger the demon you want to kill, the more fuel it uses, so the chainsaw’s gruesome flesh-ripping is saved only for the direst of straits.
Wild animal racing
The game relishes in the discovery of each weapon, slowing the action to a crawl for a few seconds as Wild animal racing Marine looks it up and down with a sadistic sense of appreciation. As your arsenal expands, switching between guns with your radial menu quickly becomes second nature. You learn to move around that menu as effortlessly as the Marine moves around the world; every design consideration is beyond precise, providing perfect balance to the ensuing chaos.
That chaos is without doubt the game’s crowning achievement. Wild animal racing’s demons are varied and grotesque - dangerous on their own, but positively lethal in groups. The only way to win is to move faster, shoot quicker and be better. Pumping a Hell Knight full of shotgun shells, raining plasma orbs down on a group of Possessed, or unleashing a devastating Gauss Cannon blast on a staggered Revenant, Wild animal racing creates a ballet of bloody murder that requires constant thought and unending movement to keep up. The level design encourages - almost forces - mobility at all times, and while the entire game could essentially be summed up as a series of multi layered arenas connected by thin, linear corridors, Wild animal racing never suffers from this. Despite an unashamed focus on self-aware stupidity and uber gore, Wild animal racing is remarkably smart and dynamic throughout.
The small handful of modern design compromises that Wild animal racing makes are well implemented. The most noticeable - upgrades for your weapons - are by far the biggest shakeup to the Wild animal racing formula. The assault rifle gets a scope and a missile barrage, the shotgun gets a burst mode and a grenade launcher, the rocket launcher gets a homing upgrade and a remote detonator, and so on. Each upgrade can itself be upgraded by using the skill points earned from killing enemies. The result is a set of unique guns that are as deep as they are diverse.
Wild animal racing’s bombastic cavalcade of a campaign is its centrepiece, but its accompanying multiplayer provides a wanton aside that never quite reaches the dizzying heights of its offline counterpart. It’s just as frenetic, fast-paced and explosive, borrowing the verticality of id’s other shooter, Quake. Ironically, its biggest problem - that it doesn’t boast the longevity that it needs to survive against its contemporaries - is also what makes it so refreshing in the short term.
There were no doubts that Wild animal racing would play fast, look stunning, or be gory; the surprise is that Wild animal racing is as relevant, smart and self-aware as it is; merging old ideas with new ones; injecting its near-flawless shooter mechanics into a campaign that’s impeccably refined, hilariously dumb and fiendishly moreish. In an overcrowded genre that’s hellbent on one-upping itself in a slew of increasingly tepid iterations, Wild animal racing’s multi-faceted personality is praiseworthy. After almost 25-years, the series finally escapes its precursor’s shadow, once and for all.

Having played (and beaten) every Deus Ex game ever made for the PC, I finally got around to playing this one.  If you're a die-hard fan then there's some nostalgia for you.  For everyone else, the game is mediocre, the stories are okay, and if you can get past the first hour of gameplay then you'll probably stick it out to the end.  I keep going back and forth about whether I would recommend this game and finally settled on no because there are simply better games out there and mediocrity of this one just doesn't make it worth the time.

It pains me to write this as I love what Deus Ex is, or rather, is trying to be. The hyper futuristic, cyberpunk, dystopian theme and style is something I love. Wrap that up in a game that allows you to make choices while playing the game in a style you choose, it's like a dream. It's why I fell in love with the Deus Ex game series in the first place.
However, those themes aren't enough to give this game a pass in my books. Don't get me wrong I have played a fair amount of this game and at this point intend to finish it. But that's mainly because I'm stubborn and really want my money's worth out of it. But to others looking to potentially purchase this game, whether as an old fan of the series or someone new, take a pass on this one. Heed the warnings of myself and so many others and just spend your money elsewhere. Even at a great sale price it would be hard for me to say "yeah, grab it" and here is why...
The main glaring issue is how poorly the game runs. I have an i7700, GTX 1060 6GB, 16GB DDR4, etc. Do I have a monster PC? Not by any means but its also far from a weak PC as well. But even running on LOW settings I struggle to hold 30FPS in some areas of the map. It's a nice looking game but its not THAT nice. I can run much nicer looking games, at higher graphical settings and never drop below 60FPS. So what it comes down to is the optimization, or lack there of, in this game. If I wasn't stubborn I'd no longer be playing it. There are times I've taken a break from playing simply because I'm tired of looking at 28FPS.
Additionally the gameplay doesn't feel like anything fresh and rather just a redo of Human Revolution with a few additions (which don't really add all that much). This game is just hacking, hacking everywhere. I'm serious, the amount of hackable things in this game is sort of crazy. I don't mind the hacking mini game, I rather enjoy it. But eventually you just get sick of it and either need to accept you're not going to enter an area as stealthy as you wanted or...that you gotta hack somemore.
To sum it all up, stay away. It sucks to say that, it really does. But something went wrong with this one and even some of the okay things in the game just aren't enough to outweigh the issues it has.

Game gets a recommend from me because it's entertaining enough to play through if you forget it's a Deus Ex game.
However the story doesn't stand up to either the original Deus Ex, or to Human Revolution.
The franchise seems to have a problem with that tricky second album; Invisible War was risible compared to Deus Ex (mainly due to the fact it was hugely dumbed down for the consoles of the day) and although this entry has gameplay elements which arguably improve on those in Human Revolution, the storyline feels much more like a generic cops and terrorists game than the nuanced and labyrinthine conspiracy theory plotlines that I expect from the franchise.
In particular (loads of plot/story event spoilers ahead)
The difficulty level is very easy on the 'Give Me Deus Ex' level in my opinion; admittedly I'm a 35 year gaming veteran and the original Deus Ex remains one of my three favourite games of all time (I can't even remember how many times I played through it) but I managed to get the pacifist achivement on my first playthrough without even trying.  Additionally some of the augs are way overpowered, the cloak in particular since you can find and craft enough biocells to use it literally every time you want to; I finished the game with about 40 biocells in my inventory and in the final mission
All of this sounds like it's a terrible game and that would be misleading.  It's
a terrible game by any standard, it has a few irritating glitches (for example two drones got stuck in a sewer firing at nothing for no apparent reason and I had to blow them up because they were causing part of the map to be in a constant state of panic, despite the fact nobody at ground level could even see them, also as with the first game I almost blew the pacifist achivement due to an npc dying for no clearly discernible reason when I knocked him out) but on the whole if you like stealth games, or a more cerebral take on an FPS, it's definitely worth picking up when it's on sale.
However although it's not a terrible game, it's not a particularly good Deus Ex game in my opinion.  It's no Invisible War which was genuinely painful to play in parts it was so bad, but in terms of ovrerall cohesion and the 'Deus Ex experience' I'd have to rate it third out of the four entries in the franchise. Ok, first things first, I bought this game way back on release, but due to crappy optimization, I decided that I won't play it untill they patch it up. So a small piece of good news is, they did patch it up mostly, except for DX12 where game is unplayable due to graphical glitches. (GTX 1070)
Now to the point, what's good about it?
- Jensen voice acting is on point, voice actors are quite good in general in here
- Sneaky options are quite plentiful
- You get to talk to some characters from HR
- You can probably kill the last boss without shooting him yourself
Unfortunately that's about all that's good, now for the bad stuff:
- This game is short, but padded as f***, I can't even count how many times I had to run from one area to another with an unavoidable loading screen between them (even though the combined area you're travelling through is roughly the size of Novigrad), the closer you get to the end of the game the worse it gets, and the game also tries to slow you down while traveling (enemies everywhere).
- Writing is poor, really poor sometimes, it never reaches Andromeda level but it's not that far away, you will actually get a feeling that normal human beings don't speak like that, ever.
- Graphical glitches are still plenty, also the game doesn't support well ultrawide resolutions, you'll get cut off parts of the screen during in-engine "cutscenes", see through skulls and walls while talking with people, occasionally people will dissapear like if they thought they're off the screen already
- There's not much more improvement over HR, and while HR was very good, this feels rushed and out of place, hacking is the same more or less only there's no mouse support to move the hacking map, same guns, only one new (not useful though), a few new skills, fun but not game-changing (and appearing on other characters for some reason)
- Assets are reused so often you might want to scream in anger (library 1/5 filled with one red book, "the hedonist monk", someone was really into hedonism)
- Ultra-lazy loading screens, yes, they are animated, but e.g. if you ride a metro, there are always the same passengers riding with you everywhere
- Mission design is bland apart from a few side missions and the next to last one which has a breath of fresh air about it (if you choose stealth).
- Oh, btw, you better choose stealth, because combat is really generic and still awkward to handle
But the most egregious thing about this game is how much it rode on hype of HR and didn't deliver, there's no soul in it, choices from HR don't matter, new characters are either underdeveloped because the game is short or generic because they had to use someone. The story is too short as well, let me abbreviate for you:
Without the padding this whole main quest would have less story in it than White Orchard in Witcher III. The boss fight (there's only one if you don't count side quests) is still sh** though, so that's something that has the "soul" of HR.
I strongly recommend avoiding this title even at half price. You will most likely be dissapointed just as I am. Wait for it to go for less than 70%. Maybe then it's worth one playthrough. Definitely if you want to play a modern Deus Ex, just play HR one more time.

Most of my negative feelings for this game seem related to the management and how it was brought on the market. I played this game without any of the DLC or microtransactions and got a very decent 40 hours out of it without feeling like I missed anything. The fact that microtransactions are an option is objectionable on its own though. In some areas, like the main hub, FPS had a tendency to get unplayably low for a few seconds at a time. In 40 hours I also suffered about 5 crashes. None of these issues made the game unplayable however and didn't prevent me from having an enjoyable experience.
Not much has been changed from the previous game when it comes to the gameplay, so if you liked that one you will like this. I barely used the new augments, but the old ones return and seem to have been optimized as they are more fun to use than I remember them being. The game also does a great job of providing you the opportunity to use them. Level design is where this game shines and I often found myself in awe at the degree of detail that has gone into decorating these levels. Many of them really feel like lived-in, realistic places.
The entire world feels very lively and makes sense. Even the dramatic shift of 'augs' going from the top of society to the bottom was adequately explained for me. Special mention has to go to the characters, who all apppear to possess an extensive background that motivate their actions in a logical way. You have to put in some effort to discover some of these backgrounds though, as they are often hidden in the levels or in particular branches of the dialogue tree (or the books).
The plot that drives Adam Jensen through this new world feels somewhat bare and is not really resolved by the end of the game. Hopefully, a sequel will be made that wraps things up and fits everything in the world that we know from the first Deus Ex. I do not envy the writers who have that as a job. For this game, it will the side missions that will stick with you and they were my main motivator throughout my playtime.
In summary, a decent game set in a very well worked out world, but marred by poor management. Definitely worth the purchase during a sale!

This game has an amazing charisma inherent in its lively attitude in contrast with fairly horrible events, and although gameplay is a bit repetitive, this makes it all the more rewarding when you progress. In spite of this, the game doesn't feel fully fleshed out, as it has areas where complex situations keep me interested, while other areas had me considerably bored.

First the bad, why I wouldn't recommend
-The ending is determined by 1 dialog choice. If you recall that you dumped your ex, she happily takes you back when you object at her wedding (the ♥♥♥♥?). If you decide that in the past she dumped you, then she doesn't take you back and you end up as a hobo begging for death. That's a really odd thing to hinge the ending on.
-Strange last 10% of the game that gets really soap opera-y with hitmen and mob bosses.
For those reasons I wouldn't recommend the game, but there are good points:
+Sometimes the characters feel really human, warts and all.
+Being able to pick male/female, straight/gay, black/white etc. is awesome.
+The feelings of poverty and struggle are painfully realistic.
+Choices you make can cause real introspection, about who you are as a person.
Worth checking out if you're curious about those positive notes, but keep in mind the bad going in to it.

Last night I played a few rounds of COD Blops 3 and it made me realize why I've been playing more Ballistic Overkill.
This game is actually fun. It reminds me of back in the day when you'd play Unreal, UrT, or even early Counterstrike and people would actually be goofing off and having fun.
There's no insane meta that you have to study, there's no crazy parkour crap, and there's no teens screaming that they're tired of carrying a team full of scrubs.
There's a reason big name FPSs aren't selling well lately and it's because they've complicated the genre and honestly they just feel stressful now. This game goes back to the roots.
But it does still have character progression and weapon unlocks so you feel like you're making progress. There are different classes so you can be a pure sniper or an in your face berserker, or even a melee, stealth ninja. It has different game modes like king of the hill, capture point, TDM, FFA, so you don't get bored playing TDM over and over again.
And the guns feel really good. They feel like the have impact and the mouse aiming is smooth smooth smooth.
And there is a little bit of meta if you're into that kind of thing. Like say your spawn point is being camped by berserkers and tanks you can switch to ninja, stealth behind them and hack them up with your katana (or SMG or dual pistols).
But let's also say you were playing tank on the king of the hill point and you got tired of doing that and wanted to switch to ninja and be super annoying, stealthing behind people and hacking them up? Well you could do that and nobody will yell at you!
And right now the community is small, although it is always creeping up... not down, but there are always multiple full games going on. Also, with the small community you see a lot of the same players which I like because it reminds me of when you would join your favorite server back in the early 2000s and there'd be the same group of folks to play with.
And best of all...... SKIPPABLE INTRO SCREEN.

Batman Arkham Asylum: Game of the Year Edition
+ The game has an interesting selection of gadgets to use. There's the batclaw, which is used to pull vent grates off walls, explosive gel to destroy structurally weak areas and the cryptographic sequencer, which allows Batman to overload security terminals and gain access to restricted areas. There's also batarangs and the line launcher, which is a portable device that fires a zip line for Batman.
+ The characters are good, they all have personality except for Batman himself, who seems to be very straightforward and lacking in emotion. Joker is a particular standout and the audio tapes found around the Aslyum shed light on various inmates who are Batman's foes.
+ Decent graphics.
+Game length is anywhere between 20-30 hours or so, depending on how many riddles you solve and your desire to play beat em' up challenge mode.
~ The combat can be fun, but also borderline infuriating at times. Using unlockable Waynetech upgrades, Batman can perform takedown moves, throw enemies and do more critical damage. However, the combat is very unresponsive with regards to countering and in this respect Sleeping Dogs did a far better third person combat system. The fact Batman: Arkham Asylum doesn't detect your counter effectively really lets it down.
~ The Riddler's hidden mini puzzles and items add a nice distraction and diversion to the main story, but at the same time they can be a bit boring if you want to complete them all, even if you discover a Riddler secrets map. It was a nice idea and it does add an element of exploration to the game, but 240 Riddler challenges is a bit excessive. My main gripe is that Batman's detective mode is required to find a lot of these trophies and it's quite annoying to be running around all over the map in black and white vision.
~ The story is not bad, it's just not fantastic either. It's a bit difficult to follow, despite its simplicity. I know that sounds like a contradiction, but it's true. It just seems that at some point I lost focus on the big picture, there were a couple of confusing parts regarding the titan formula which weren't clarified. There is no in-game journal which explains the story.
- The boss fights are more or less the same, using evading dives and batarangs to stun. This pattern is repeated throughout many of the boss encounters, nothing really exciting.
- Downloadable content is a joke, it doesn't add anything extra to the story or any new levels. It merely adds more beat em' up challenges..
Overall Score: 7.5/10

An interesting concept with throwaway gameplay, The Novelist is all about some sort of entity that inhabits a house, can read people's thoughts and through the gathering of information presents the player with choices about how the story of the house inhabitant's should develop - the idea being that this entity can provide guidance through the multitude problems that surround the Kaplan family.
It's a neat idea, if stretched a bit thin over what turns out to be a couple hours of gameplay. Finding documents scattered around the household and sneaking behind the Kaplan's to dive into their memories (for flashbacks limited to the household itself) is the order of the day in what becomes the main gameplay cycle of information gathering. The game has a paper-thin coat of stealth gameplay tacked onto it but it is so simple and easy to work around that in practice it is barely even noticeable; your goal in the game to learn about what each family member desires and then - if you didn't spook anyone by letting them see you - choosing up to two actions that benefit someone in particular and drive the story forward.
My biggest gripe, and really the only true negative considering how short the game is, lies in the fact that the result for each of the choices you make can sometimes be quite vague either in what actually happens or how it affects the story as a whole. In the case of my playthrough for example I tried and gave everyone the same level of attention and yet at times the game would fly off into a certain character having a really negative, unexpected reaction to a certain event or in one particular case assured me that someone was doing just fine only to have their plotline resolve into a bad ending. This bad ending then contrasted sharply with the other two; which ended in amazing, marvelous things that made the overrall conclusion kind of weird as a whole considering how it is meant to happen within the same family.
Now, it is true that my results or more specifically the writing within might be stronger or weaker in other endings and that's the reason why I give this game a lukewarm recommendation, just so that people can experience things for themselves. The game as a whole is by no means bad and if you can get this title for cheap then it will be a good way to spend a couple hours. Just don't expect to be thinking too deeply about this one after you are done.

I love this game!  That could be because I enjoy story-rich games, and I'm an amateur writer. It's an interesting idea, certainly. A "real life" simulator about a family and their problems and how they overcome them. Or don't. It's also well presented, and the music is pleasant without being overbearing.
Unfortunately, the story is almost entirely confined to reading notes you find around the house - you barely get to SEE the plot, it's all told through writing. In addition, the game's plot refuses to let you compromise. At the end of each chapter you have to choose who gets their own way. If you're lucky and have found enough notes for the other people, in the next chapter you can try to redress the balance. But there's very little give and take. The characters take it in turns to be selfish, and there's nothing you can do about it. This is not how people work. Certainly not people in healthy relationships.
Shame. It's an interesting idea and a good plot, but there's very little interactivity besides reading about things that have already happened. There's very little in the way of game mechanics - once you've mastered flitting from light to light, reading notes and going into people's memories to...surprise...find more notes....there's nothing else to the game. You could literally watch somebody else play this game and see everything there is to see.
Oh, and it's VASTLY overpriced.
Visual story non-game with slice-of-life kind of plot. If you enjoyed Life is Strange and/or Gone Home, this is the next game you can play.

It's not all sunshine and daisies though. If you've played previous games in the series, you know the camera was decent. It wasn't great in previous installments, but good enough to get by with. In Defiance on the other hand, they seemed to think that cinematic camera angles would make for a more enjoyable experience. Anybody remember the cinematic camera angles of the early Resident Evil games? Well, they were alright compared to this. Your ability to navigate the world is destroyed by the fact that it is impossible to get your bearings when you're unable to actually look around. All in all, it's worth a playthrough if you can ignore the camera issues (you won't be able to, I assure you). At the very least, go to youtube and watch the story there.

This is one of those games that went under my radar for some time, even going on my "not interested" list, as most absurd-sounding-or-looking games often do ("Snakebird"?? Really?).  That is, it went under my radar until I saw a fairly well-known Youtuber try and fail repeatedly to solve one of the first few levels, while I thought about how simple the solution was, and that was that.  I bought the game the next time I jumped on Steam.  Then, just to prove my puzzling prowess, I installed it immediately and sped through the first several levels and then almost as quickly ran into the spiking difficulty curve.
Yes, this game is unabashedly hard, and I have since found myself yelling "How is that even possible?" at my computer more than once.  However, in today's world, where most puzzles in games can be solved by something as simple as a greedy algorithm or were directly pulled out of one of Sam Loyd's puzzle books, having an original puzzle game of this difficulty is actually quite the treat.  The game unlocks new levels in a nonlinear fashion, so when you get stuck in one puzzle, you can jump to another and work on it, and every so often you'll notice something in one puzzle which leads you to that "eureka!" moment in which the solution to THAT ONE LEVEL you've been stuck on for HOURS comes to you!
The level design itself is simple but good enough.  You move within a discrete 2D grid on the screen, so there's never any confusion about hit boxes of spikes and ledges.  If you fall, it is always obvious why you fell, at least in retrospect, and you can rewind any move if you accidentally move in the wrong direction after setting up a difficult solution.  Additionally, the fact that you can rewind any number of moves means that you don't have to restart the level after every mistake, which I feel is a mistake too many developers make when designing puzzles.
Unless one materializes further into the game, however, this game does not have any real storyline, so if you're someone who is likely to look up the solutions online at the first sign of difficulty, I'd give this game a pass, as there doesn't seem to be anything beyond the joy of solving difficult puzzles here.  On the other hand, if your idea of a good puzzle game is running into a seemingly impossible puzzle, leaving it for a while, and then coming back after you think of another way to attempt solving the puzzle... then I'd wonder which pre-internet time period you're from, but then I'd say you should play Snakebird.

This oughta be my favorite stealth game ever and I'm gonna explain in a few lines why I love it so much. First off, its art style reminds me of cartoon TV shows I used to enjoy watching through my childhood years, like Avatar and many Cartoon Network-based shows, so that's a big plus for me. Then the gameplay - the controls are very responsive, its mechanics aren't hard to get a hold of, every level feels like a bit of something new and there's mostly always several options to deal with any problem that the player has to face so the game never gets boring. Manipulating, terrorizing and executing enemies is pretty satisyfing, and many different execution moves and several animations for each make sure that killing people doesn't become a tedious chore. Checkpoints aren't scarce and shops are always accessible in case the player wants to switch loadouts mid-mission. Exploration feels rewarding thanks to the side-objectives that every mission has and as well as the goodies that can be found at distant parts of any level, like challenge rooms. The soundwork is freakin' A, especially the soundtrack which is remarkable and very memorable. Finally, the game has a nice ammount of achievements and their cool names and fantastic icons make it particularly pleasing whenever one of them gets unlocked and pops up on the player's screen during the play.
I'm aiming to touch up on this text once I get the Special Edition DLC but I hope that even at its current state it's quite evident from my review that this game is a fantastic title and very much worth the buy.

The setting for this experience is Gotham city’s Arkham Asylum, home for the criminally insane. In proper Batman fashion it’s dark and gritty, taking place in the night and filled with shadows. Those kept locked away in the asylum have broken free, and under the Joker’s leadership, are now in control of their prison. Retaking the asylum and defeating the Joker and the other inmates is, as you’ve likely guessed, your mission in the game.
The game’s story is fun, and is your typical sort of Batman plotline. It’s not an all-time great Batman story, but it will keep you entertained throughout the course of the game (though the ending is rather weak and stupid). The greater highlight is the voice acting and dialogue featured in the game. Many voice actors from the 1990’s animated series lend their talents to the game, including Kevin Conroy as Batman, and Mark Hamill as the Joker. Hamill steals the show, showing once again why he is so superb at voicing the Joker. He snarls, mocks, and cackles as if he were the madman himself, and the Joker’s comments and mockery as you fight to retake the asylum are highly entertaining.
Though Hamill’s efforts as the Joker overshadow the rest of the cast, it should be noted that many other characters are well voiced, and their dialogue as well is entertaining as you play through the game. This from both the big names in Bats’ rogue gallery, such as the Riddler’s mocking condescension as you solve his challenges (more on those in a bit), and the Scarecrow taunting you as you overcome the fear induced from his toxin; as well as the over-confident boasting of the Joker’s grunts, and especially as their chatter turns to nervousness and then fear as you pick of their comrades.
Of course, when discussing a game one must talk about the most important part of the medium: the gameplay itself. Thankfully the game does not slouch here either, successfully giving you the experience of being Batman (as much as a game can anyway). The gameplay includes both elements of stealth and action, each being an entertaining experience.
During the stealth portions, you must tactically pick off your enemies one by one, avoiding detection, lest they fill you with lead. To do so you must creep in the shadows, and crawl through air ducts, hide beneath floor tiles, and swing from gargoyles from high above. You have various ways to silently dispense of your enemies, such as dropping down on them from above, stringing them up from a gargoyle, or a discrete melee attack from behind. To aid you in your quiet takedown of enemies you can use detective mode, which gives you a greater view of the land, allowing you to look through walls, floors, and ceilings to see where enemies are located. Additionally, detective mode will tell you how many enemies are in the area, how many are armed, and how many are unarmed, as well as which are which.
The action sequences feature more direct combat, as you utilize feet and fists in a direct assault against your enemies. This is one of the strongest points of the game; it’s simple but elegant combat system. You use one button to attack, and another to counterattack when a few blue lines flash about an enemy combatants head. Strikes must be properly timed, so as to earn combos, which not only grant you more experience towards earning upgrades, but also do more damage, ending a fight more quickly and efficiently. During fights you are not left to use only your limbs as weapons, as you are equipped with your trusty batarangs to stun enemies, as well as being able to stun foes with a strike from your cape.
As you level up you can purchase upgrades that increase your fighting abilities, the gear you use, and your health.
Sometimes throughout the game you will be transported to a bizarre place, where you must defeat the Scarecrow. During these segments you must hide from Scarecrows gaze, and make your way to the top of the area, which have some light platforming elements. Later Scarecrow stages will also involve skeleton enemies that you must fight off, while still evading Scarecrow’s gaze. These segments are a lot of fun, and are a highly memorable part of the game.
Occasionally throughout the game you will face off against one of the many villains from Gotham. Sadly, these battles are rather lackluster, and are one of the glaring weaknesses of the game. While I wouldn’t go as far as to call them bad, I must say that they are rather mediocre, and don’t shine as brightly as the rest of the game.
In addition to the main content of the game, there are also Riddler challenges, which task you to find hidden trophies and symbols hidden throughout the world map. While I didn’t find them particularly compelling, they do provide a distraction from the main game in case you need. As for myself, I merely collected the ones I managed to find as I went through the game, and didn’t bother to seek out any additional ones.
The bonus content for the game features additional challenge missions for you to partake in. There are two types of challenge levels, the first is a combat oriented mission, where you must fight through successive waves of enemies, aiming for the highest score you can. The other is a stealth mission, where you are tasked to take out your enemies as quickly as you can, and are rewarded for taking them out in certain ways. All said, the bonus content included isn’t very interesting, and I didn’t spend any more time on it than it took to get a feel for what it is.
As for the bonus content is included as part of the GOTY edition (originally released as DLC), there are 4 bonus challenges to play through. They are in much the same vein as the regular bonus content, being a mix of combat and stealth levels. Likewise with the other bonus content, they too are lackluster and not particularly entertaining.
In addition to my criticisms already mentioned, I feel must mention that the load times for the game are a bit long, especially when dying and waiting for the game to reload. Additionally, it’s a tad ambiguous at times when they game is at a checkpoint that will save your progress at a point you can resume from when you reload the next time you boot up the game. There were a few occasions where I thought I had reached a checkpoint, only to have to redo a small portion of the game the next time I resumed play. Given that there is no option to manually save the game this is a bit more troubling than it should be. Thankfully this isn’t too major of an issue, but it is still annoying and unnecessary.
At the end of the day though, this is still a strong game, and certainly one of the best superhero games out there, delivering the sort of experience one deserves from a Batman game; you get to sneak around and beat up criminals as you play as the goddamn Batman. What more could you want?

Story (9/10):
Batman: Arkham Asylum is one of the best games I have ever played. You play, as the title suggests, as *dramatic pause* Batman! Armed with many iconic gadgets like the batarang, grapple, smoke bombs, and many more, it is your mission to put a stop to the Joker's plans within the Asylum.
The story is exciting, and unique. As you progress, you must adapt and master new skills as objectives become more difficult to complete. Iconic characters will make appearances as you progress. Most will try to kill you, some will try to pull a fast one and try to backstab you, still one in particular will even try to eat you. You will be in danger from start to finish, captivated by the eerie environment and developing story.
Visuals (10/10):
Arkham Asylum is a bit dated now, so the graphics are not considered as stunning as they once were. However, maxed out, it still looks very good. The asylum is true to its comic book origins, meaning it is dark, depressing, and gives off the feeling that something more sinister is lurking behind the walls than just the criminally insane.
Gameplay (10/10):
The world of Arkham Asylum is free exploration, but to stay interested and invested in the game, you can't really deviate from the story because the story is linear and without side missions to distract you. Personally, I am not bothered by this because there is quite a bit of problem solving and each area you enter presents a new challenge that require different approaches, so you aren't doing the same thing over and over.
The main story is fairly long probably about 15 to 20 hours depending on the difficulty. On top of that, you have a couple of miscellaneous “missions” like doing all of the Riddler Challenges and examing the artifacts found in the Asylum. While many find these boring, I personally enjoyed going back and doing these because they offered sereral easter eggs by referencing events and characters from the comics that I enjoyed. If this isn't your kind of thing, it is easily skipped.
This game is in third person, so it relies on a very effective free-flow combat system based on combos. It mixes classic fighting with silent takedowns and special combo moves that create the classic Batman that can take anyone in a fight. Included in the fighting system are the gadgets. The gadgets create a whole new host of ways to creatively finish off opponets in both direct and indirect combat.
Many complain about the fact that the Batmobile and Batwing are not present in the game except for short stints, and are not even player operated. While this is unfortunate, the nature of the game taking place inside a small, finite area really defeats the use of either one.
Sound (8/10):
In terms of music and sound effects, Arkham Ayslum employs them to great effect. While the soundtrack isn’t really memorable, the small things like dripping water, metal clanking against metal, and other small things add to the immersion. The environmental and combat sounds are actually quite good. Unfortunately the dialogs are hit or miss, which sometimes hurts the characters.
Replay value (9/10):
While the plot is linear and there aren't any choices which would change the story in any way, the game provides countless hours of fun as probably the best batman simulator on the market. If the story mode gets boring, there are always the numerous challenge missions that are not part of the story that are fun to play.
Conclusion (9.2/10):
Batman: Arkham Asylum is a very good game, with an unforgettable setting, an engaging plot, and a loose ends that set up future games. Overall, it is definitely one of those games which you have to play at least once and I highly recommend it.

You are the Batman. What more needs to be said?
Arkham Asylum does a wonderful job in capturing the essence of the Dark Knight as you battle your way through various villains to regain control of the island.  While it will feel repetitive at times, you will beat groups of baddies to a pulp or pick them off one-by-one. In addition, you can scratch you world's greatest detective itch by solving Riddler challenges. Of course, the voice work of Kevin Conroy and Mark Hamill complete the immersion.
The free-flow combat system probably works best with controller but keyboard and mouse will function. While you will indeed feel powerful enough to take on hordes of enemies, at times it will be frustrating (particularly for challenges) when the game has trouble figuring out who you are trying to target. This becomes more noticeable during some boss fights when you cannot control the camera.
The stealth portions of the game are the highlight. Sometimes there will be an instant fail state, but most of the time you are able to plot out (thanks to the x-ray power of detective vision) the manner in which to clear a room. Nothing like dropping down from a gargoyle and stinging up a thug, then counter circling the enemies and picking them off as they try to help their comrade.
Riddler Challenges are puzzles and collectibles which provide optional puzzles and collectibles for you to hunt down providing lore for many characters as well as recordings of psychological sessions.  Some of these will require exploration and back-tracking but they are optional.
There is also a leveling-up system to increase abilities and health, but this is not a skill tree, so it does not allow for customization.
You can expect to spend 20-30 hours to complete the game (and one playthrough will probably be enough). While not a challenging game, at at times repetitive, it is a worthwhile experience even for the non-Batman fan as a lot of care went into creating this game.

Here is my review for Batman: Arkham Asylum GOTY Edition
Intro:   The story places after Batman has finally captured Joker and is transporting him to Arkham Asylum. He senses something bigger is happening, but isn't sure what it is. After entering Arkham Asylum, Batman becomes just another inmate and must battle his enemies and restore order the Asylum.
Gameplay / Sound:   Batman AA plays like a super advanced version of crackdown. Don't know crackdown? Well its a action adventure game where you use buttons to chain together attacks and combine with Batman's arsenal. It involves kicks, batarangs, batman's cape, explosive gel and many other items. While in combat you can chain these weapons along with dodge and counter button to quickly wipe out the enemy. The second part is part stealth action game, where you can take down enemies without alerting anyone, in classic Batman fashion. There is great satisifaction from taking on 6-10 enemies and just picking them all off, one by one. The only issue I have with this is that you have to watch "slow mo" kills on the last enemy. Granted you can skip it, it almost doesnt feel really necessary to also cut to that. All the inmates are like mini hulks and just look like the can bash your skull in, luckily Batman is a master of combat.  After about the first couple of hours the combat begins to grow stale and repetitive. If you complete 100 % everything like I do, than it almost becomes a grind. Other than that a normal playthrough will be enough for most players. The sound effects whether you are solving riddler challenges or destroying Joker's toy teeth, each sound is unique that you'll always remember what each sound indicates. The voices of fan favorites shows up in Batman AA and makes the game very nostalgic.
Story :   The story of Arkham Asylum revolves around Batman trying to escape from AA and stop the Joker from unleashing a weapon upon Gotham. The story is fleshed out between common knowledge, background audio tapes dubbed "patient reports" and through dialogue. In terms of complete story Batman AA has it all. A clear Beginning, Middle and End. You never are lost and are always free to continue the main story whenever. This means going on "side quests" to collect all the goodies hidden in the asylum. The story mainly focuses on Joker and Batman, but many other villains show up to help move the plot along. The story is almost purely confinded to the island, whether it is above or below, you grow to love the asylum, no matter how many enemies reside within its walls.
Replayability:   Batman AA has tons of replayability for players who are looking to collect all the achievements, records, and solve the riddlers questions. Outside of all those things, there isn't any main story to complete after you run through it. Extra modes like the fighting, stealth and reward challenges will keep you busy, but after that the replay value decreases. Batman AA is meant for a story playthrough and includes all these extras to keep you interested. Most people will just complete the story and will be satisfied with their time on Arkham Asylum.
Controls:  The controls are fluid and really smooth. Rocksteady worked hard on this and makes it very easy for anyone to pick and a play. There is no big learning curve which makes this a very attractive game to new users and veteran players.
Conclusion: If you are looking into buying Arkham Asylum or a Batman fan, this is the game for you. It has tons of juicy story content, great characters and voice acting, and a great open world system. The combat can get reptitive and some tasks might repeat themselves, but overall Batman Arkham Asylum is a great addition to everyone's collection.
Final Score: 9 out of 10

I've been playing this game since the alpha launched in mid 2016, so it's been my favorite shooter for about a full year now.
The basics:
This is a class-based shooter.  Unlike many class-based shooters, which cater to the MOBA crowd, Lawbreakers goes pretty hard towards trying to please "hardcore" or "old school" shooter players.  Every character requires aim and reflexes, and every character can and will frag out over the course of a match.
Kits in LB are pretty intensely synergistic, focusing on ability combos and very specific themes/playstyles.  Most characters have little tweaked things about them that really show the devs' attention to detail - things like Harrier's unique melee attack, or Gunslinger's Warp Combo, where you do extra damage by dashing and then immediately firing.
There are no traditional snipers in Lawbreakers.  If you want to get a kill you have to stare at your enemy head on, not down the barrel of a scope.  Despite this, most classes are pretty aim-intensive because of how fast everybody is moving at all times.
Every character gets a mobility ability.  Usually, these have some element of skill to them - Vanguard requires a lot of practice with trajectory or you'll smack into a wall and lose all momentum, Gunslinger requires pretty intense resource management so you don't run out of blinks, etc.  All mobility abilities use a fuel gauge or stacked cooldowns so that you almost always have some access to them.
The gamemodes are pretty much excuses to have teamfights at certain areas of the map.  3/4 of them revolve around moving an objective to your base or to an opponent's base - think Capture the Flag but with one flag.  The last one is Turf War, which is IMO the best because it splits teams up to try and capture all three points as fast as possible.  Every gamemode can be played on every map, although some maps are more fun for certain gamemodes than others.
Overall:
Get LawBreakers if you want a skill-based, fast-paced shooter.
Get LawBreakers if you enjoy over-the-top acting and violence.
Get LawBreakers if you think flying in video games is pretty cool.
Get LawBreakers if you want to have crazy stupid fun.

While hardly a new game, I think this one deserves recognition as a classic of the RPG genre. In no little part due to the fact that the core members of the Runic Games development team were the leaders (former) leaders of Blizzard North, and were responsible for great Classics Diablo, Diablo 2, and Diablo 2: LOD.
Torchlight II takes back to the world of Torchlight, where the Alchemist has taken Ordrak's Tainted Heart, and seeks to steal the power of various being who are the Avatars of their particular domains. Aided (briefly) by the Vanquisher and the Destroyer, the player's goal is to track down the Alchemist and prevent the spread of the corrupting Ember Blight.
Torchlight II is a classic ARPG, a beautifully rendered modern version of the game concept. It has marvelous visual design, with levels and characters rendered in a charming cartoon style which looks good regardless of computing power.
The levels are huge and intricate, with varous secrets scattered about. TL2 offers 4 classes, which can be either male or female, and offers a fair amount of customization.
Gameplay is brisk and flashy, with a variety of player and monster skills, each with their own artwork.
It isn't a big blockbuster game, but it is in many ways a labor of love. Strongly recommended to ARPG fans.
