Great to see this game released on Steam! I first saw it on Facebook a while back and was captured by the iconic Crysis-like map design. When I launched the Steam version I was impressed by the animation and UI quality. The gamefeel is really snappy and rewarding, with better optimization than many f2p games I've played. Unlocking new weapons has both visual variety as well competitive synergy, where few secondaries feel underwhelming. Big props for the akimbo gangsta aim down sight animation too! The impressive variety of classes feels decently differentiated but not all of them have interesting active abilities. The most notable ones were shadow sprint, sniper cloak and explosive resistance. When compared to a game like Dirty Bomb or Ghost in the Shell (Stand Alone Complex - First Assault Online) their characters have more team impact and things to do when enemies are respawning. Being able to do some more tricks could really spice up this game, such as a class with quick jetpack jump, a spotting sentry or decoy grenades. Melee weapons are cool in this game as well, maybe bounching throwing weapons or left hand shields could spice up the static cover design.
TLDR; I really see myself playing this game as my go-to fps quick fix when I want to warm up and don't want to die and wait in BF/OW/CS matches that affect my stats. This has excellent aim practice feel and I hope the new maps have more of the lush crysis-feel that first drew me in. I also hope there will be more dynamic game modes like COD Headquarters.
Tip to the devs: I think you can use free weekends as good way of drawing in new players, where paying customers get earlier access to your new maps, classes and guns. That is a good way of balancing them and charging those who play the most with a one-time fee once they already like the game. I rate the game 9/10 for the price and EA-stage it is in :)

It seems like many games nowadays are doing this style of slick clean UI with simple boxes and colors, and I think it usually looks tacky and stylistically clashes with most games, but in this game I feel it perfectly matches the slick style of all the characters and weapons, and works great. Another thing that should be mentioned is gameplay and performance. Just to get it out of the way, this game performs excellently. Even on my crappy prebuilt school computer with an AMD APU, I get 40-60 frames at a bit under my monitor's resolution. I must say, however, the servers are absolutely ATROCIOUS. I'll go into a quick match, and despite having decent internet, I'll have 500 ping and not land half of my shots! I'm not sure what is to blame for this. Regardless, in general the online play is bad for one reason, this being that there is not enough people playing this game. In quick play, the ideal to just jump in and have a few matches, takes about 30 seconds to find a game, and it's usually only a lobby with about 6 people, who you've already likely played with in previous matches. Now quickly onto gameplay, there isn't really much to say about this except that it's excellent, really! It's perfect fun, tight fps gameplay that mashes together all the perfect features of the best in the genre. So TL;DR, great game, main gripes being not enough players, bad server lag, and underwhelming visual upgrade. I'd really reccomend it, especially for it's current price of $6.99!

QUICK NOTE ON PERFORMANCE: I have Windows 7, intel CPU and an AMD graphics card, which seems to be the best PC spec for the game. I haven't experienced a single bug or crash with this setup.
Medieval 1 is, for me, the best of the Total War series. The risk-style campaign map offers the best strategising compared to the 3D campaign maps in the follow up games, which the AI never managed to properly make use of.
Here, it is a cutthroat, tense battle of wills at each end of game turn as you wait to see if a faction sends their giant army stacks into your territories. Many tough decisions have to be made when it comes to balancing your forces. It's perfectly streamlined and never gets bogged down.
The battles, too, are superior to the follow up games. Units take their time climbing hills, slowly whittling eachother down in combat, allowing proper tactical changes during battles. You truly feel like a general directing a battle, unlike the 5 minute mass brawls of Rome/Med2 which ended up resembling some Benny Hill inspired, fast forwarded mess.
The game engenders that feeling of intrigue and epic storytelling more than any other TW.
So, if you feel your PC setup can get it running properly, I heartily recommend picking this up. It's arguably one of the very best PC games of all time and still holds up remarkably well.

The Kaplan family has temporarily moved to new house, led there by the husband and author, Dan Kaplan, who is suffering from writer's block. But it just so happens that the house is haunted by a spirit. But not the "built on an indian burial ground" kind of spirit. This is not a Stephen King video game (a.k.a. Alan Wake). Instead, it's more the "greek muse" kind of spirit. Which is a nice change actually.
In The Novelist, you play this spirit, flitting from light bulb to light bulb, reading minds and searching memories to discover everyone's desires influence the decisions of Dan towards the best possible outcome. This game is about balance. Balancing Dan's writing career with the individual needs of his family while still maintaining strong family bonds. While I only played it through once, I got the strong feeling that there's definitely better choices and compromises to make. You can form a limited idea of what the outcome from Dan's actions will be and how you influence Dan probably depends on what you prioritise. Do you prioritise Dan's book being a best-seller? Or prioritise Dan's wife breaking to the local art scene? Or do you help the son make friends at school?
The Novelist is simple, in looks and execution. There are only three characters and you never see yourself (or even if you have a material form). I did feel that there could have been a bit more effort put towards the character models, especially the faces, in order to feel a bit more empathy towards them. But, thanks to some decent voice acting and good writing, I don't feel that the characters are as robotic as they look. It's a simple, short play through, with limited, yet solid re-playability. I'm not sure if it's worth $15 US, but definitely worth a play.

A moral choice management sim presented unnecessarily as a first person perspective game.
The moral choice is stretched over several days and ultimately takes the form of helping one of three people. Irritatingly (and unrealistically) the choice is zero-sum, meaning that whenever you choose to benefit one of the three you simultaneously harm the other two. Because of its zero-sum nature, you cannot 'win' this game - there is no way to play it so as to achieve a 'better than expected' result - you can only choose how you want to distribute the benefit/harm.
The choice takes the graded form of 'Help this person the most' (+1) vs. 'Help them a little' (+0) vs. 'Harm them' (-1), meaning that in a sense it is possible to reduce an entire playthrough to an (implied) balance sheet. You get a bit sick of navigating the environment and interacting with everything only to find that there is no strategy to the game and you're just as well picking a random character when deciding who to benefit/harm.
Dont waste the time or money on this, trust me when I say its a painful playthrough.

This has to be by far one of my favorite games. It is the only stealth game that will seriously make you consider your choices when you approach a situation, yet it does not overwhelm the player at the start of the game. There is no tutorial, but rather the game itself plays out like one, allowing you to learn new tactics and new ways of approaching difficult situations in your own way at your own pace.
It is unparalleled in it's ability to immerse you in the role of a ninja. You don't even get to know the protagonist's name just because that's how ninja's are - ones who embrace nothingness. You can kill everyone, kill noone, or anything in between. The simple fact that this game can be completed without killing a single enemy when enemies can completely overwhelm you, kill you very quickly (guns hurt, who would have thought) is absolutely stunning and shows just how much thought was put into each and every situation. I highly suggest playing through on either extreme end of these choices (no kil or kill), but you don't have to stick to them entirely.
That of course doesn't even mention the fact that you can use very fast reflexes and the games tight controls to execute strategies that allow you to change the way an encounter works entirely, taking enemies off guard entirely, putting them into states of panic, destroying lights to distract them and allow you to slip through the shadows, throwing nonlethal darts to make them run towards you so you can make a quick escape with that diversion... the list goes on and on. Every decision you make is entirely unique to you and how you decided to move forward through the game.
From start to finish, this game has a good story. Make sure to watch the launch trailer for some extra backstory and the E3 trailer to hear the full song and see the very basics of how the game plays.
When you listen to the song in the E3 trailer, remember it. You will hear it again in game and it will suddenly make sense. If you can't understand the lyrics:
" The more of you
The less of me in space
Sound travels fast
With mark
And blade"
Overall this game is a bit of a sleeper hit and if you enjoy stealth-based games or the ninja theme, I strongly recommend you buy this game.

This has to be by far one of my favorite games. It is the only stealth game that will seriously make you consider your choices when you approach a situation, yet it does not overwhelm the player at the start of the game. There is no tutorial, but rather the game itself plays out like one, allowing you to learn new tactics and new ways of approaching difficult situations in your own way at your own pace.
It is unparalleled in it's ability to immerse you in the role of a ninja. You don't even get to know the protagonist's name just because that's how ninja's are - ones who embrace nothingness. You can kill everyone, kill noone, or anything in between. The simple fact that this game can be completed without killing a single enemy when enemies can completely overwhelm you, kill you very quickly (guns hurt, who would have thought) is absolutely stunning and shows just how much thought was put into each and every situation. I highly suggest playing through on either extreme end of these choices (no kil or kill), but you don't have to stick to them entirely.
That of course doesn't even mention the fact that you can use very fast reflexes and the games tight controls to execute strategies that allow you to change the way an encounter works entirely, taking enemies off guard entirely, putting them into states of panic, destroying lights to distract them and allow you to slip through the shadows, throwing nonlethal darts to make them run towards you so you can make a quick escape with that diversion... the list goes on and on. Every decision you make is entirely unique to you and how you decided to move forward through the game.
From start to finish, this game has a good story. Make sure to watch the launch trailer for some extra backstory and the E3 trailer to hear the full song and see the very basics of how the game plays.
When you listen to the song in the E3 trailer, remember it. You will hear it again in game and it will suddenly make sense. If you can't understand the lyrics:
" The more of you
The less of me in space
Sound travels fast
With mark
And blade"
Overall this game is a bit of a sleeper hit and if you enjoy stealth-based games or the ninja theme, I strongly recommend you buy this game.

Brilliant game, but not for the faint hearted.  Unless you have experience of other skill based shooters (Quake/UT etc), you will need to spend some time learning the movement mechanics and learning to aim accurately against fast moving targets.
If you are the type who quits at the first hurdle, this game probably wont be for you, but if you are willing to put the time and effort in to 'git gud' and learn to play, you will find this a very rewarding game.
The combat is fast and intense, and the adrenaline rush you feel when you pull off a clutch save in a Blitzball match is worth every death.
At this price, I thoroughly recommend it.  The game is polished to a high standard, it runs well (I get 100+ FPS with a GTX 680), the netcode is up there with the best of them, and the soundtrack really gets you revved up for each match.  For a team of 65 people, they have made a very impressive and fun game.

Arkham Asylum is, in a word, awesome.
Still, it's not a
game:
, which is a damn shame (and they fixed this flaw in Arkham City).  Even though you experience a diverse range of villains and locations around Arkham Island, your exploration is still mostly limited to hallways, air ducts, and swinging between rafters/gargoyles.
, especially without the ability to set waypoints on your map.  It's easy to get turned around on the island, and re-checking the map over and over is more work than following a "Go this way" arrow.
Sure, you've finally won and Joker is back where he belongs, but you'll find yourself saying "Wait, it's over already?".  Arkham Asylum gives a solid 20 hours of gameplay, even without finding 100% of the Riddler side-quest items or the challenge maps.  But when the credits rolled, I didn't want it to end. Well, I guess that's what Arkham City is for.  I recommend buying both games together, just to be safe.

Mark Of The Ninja, Where do i even start. This game, is BY FAR, THE MOST *gets shot* ......... *mumbles while dying* ...most amazing stealth game ive played.......

Mark of the Ninja is an expertly crafted 2 dimensional stealth game made by Klei Entertainment
Plot: The game follows the main character, The Ninja I will call him as his name is never said outright, through his trials as the marked champion of the Hisomu Clan. The leader of the Clan, Master Azai, decides that The Ninja must be given The Mark, a series of tatoos that will grant him great power, however The Mark also causes the bearer to go mad and before that he must commit suicide. The games plot then follows The NInja trying to find and kill the man who attacked his clan, Karajan, discovering betrayals from his friends, and eventually deciding his own fate.
Graphics: The game looks amazing it has very detailed artistic, almost comic book like visuals, which complement the gameplay well with very dark areas and bright contrasts. The NInja himself is, throughout most of the game, just a black silhouette with red accents from his tatoos/masks. This works very well as it is easy to see him onscreen regardless of how dark it is and he and his companion are the only characters with so much bright red on them.
Gameplay: The game plays very well on P.C. and aside from a few framerate issues, mainly in the bonus challenges, the game is smooth as butter. The controls are simple and easy to get used to and the mechanics work very well. The main focus of this game is stealth, it follows traditional ninjas very well in this aspect as if you are spotted, you lose points and are most likely going to die. Also the game discourages killing enemys by giving you an enormous bonus if you finish the level without killing anyone. In the game you are able to hide in many places, distract guards using sounds, and creep around areas using vents and grapple points. The controls are smooth and have no delay. Altogether the gameplay is excellent.
Everything Else: I thoroughly enjoyed this game, but it does have a few flaws, the biggest one being that it is very short. There are only around 10 missions and the game can be finished in a matter of hours. There is a DLC but I have not played it or researched it so I don't know how much it adds. There are quite a few hidden bonuses and in game challenges to complete though, adding a good amount of time to the game. In the game there are also alternate suits for the ninja which add different abilities. Most of these are quite interesting, such as the Path of The Mark and the Path of Silence but  a few such as the Path of The Hunter are somewhat useless.
Conclusion: This is a great game, the main game is somewhat short, but there are bonuses to keep you coming back. The gameplay is excellent, the graphics are beautiful, and the plot is extremely good, as you would expect from the group that made Don't Starve, with it's mysterious and enticing backstory. I recommend this game to anyone who enjoys stealth games.

2-D platformers should not require you to move around with the analog stick! I mean, that's just obvious, isn't it? But in Mark of the Ninja (and come to think of it, Shank 2), you're encouraged to move around with the analog stick because that's also the aiming mechanism and you literally cannot hit targets using only the directional pad! So you're left with two solutions: either cumbersomely switch from analog to directional as necessary, or have your character twitch around looking up or down when all you want is to go forwards.
If this ends up being a design gimmick from Klei entertainment, then the only thing I can recommend is that they go back to game design school because moving around the stages is a chore on analog. NO, KEYBOARD CONTROL FOR 2-D PLATFORMERS IS AN EVEN WORSE IDEA.

Snakebird is a difficult puzzle game with simple mechanics. What makes the game so challenging is how well thought out all of the puzzles are. This game is not for everyone, but anyone who wants a challenging puzzle game will surely be pleased with Snakebird.

Each area in Snakebird introduces new mechanics that serve well for making a variety of different puzzles. Every puzzle feels very unique and the gameplay always feels fresh. If you are stuck on a level, go on to a different one and come back to it. Snakebird will not only test your puzzle skills but also your persistance. People who are very impatient will struggle to finish this game.
Forget about the fancy graphics and mindless entertainment that a lot of next-gen games are giving nowadays. Snakebird forces whoever plays it to think and provides a good challenge for those who enjoy puzzles. The creators of Snakebird are ingenius and deserve more attention than they have been given.

a name every criminal fears. A part of the "Holy DC Trinity", the Dark Knight is a character everyone knows and admires. One of the best comic book characters ever created, he has a personality unlike any other. Every piece of work published on him, every movie made on him, was either brilliant, or a failure. When someone decides to work on such an iconic character, the expectations from its followers are so high, that they are often never met. That was why when Rocksteady Studios, the London-based British video game developer, were to make a videogame on Batman, knew that it would either have to be a breakthrough, or a disappointment. Rocksteady chose to give it their best shot, and came up with a masterpiece the world had seldom seen before:
Called the "best comic book videogame of all time", Arkham Asylum is a class apart. Based on the relationship between Batman and his arch-nemesis Joker, the game is full of plot twists and turns. It lets you be the Caped Crusader, and experience what it is like to be him.
The game has it all. Fighting criminals as the best martial-artist in the world? Check. Solving crime scenes with intricate gadgetry? Check. Spreading fear among goons and henchmen? Check. The game is an all-in-one experience.
You explore the sprawling Arkham Asylum as you find secrets and slowly uncover the sinister plan behind the Joker's doings. On the journey, you come across your worst enemies, and fight them to move on. No boss fight is the same, and no part of the game feels stale. As you progress, you unlock the Bat's tools, and use them in interesting ways to take down thugs and unlock new areas.
One of the best things about the gameplay is the combat system aptly named the FreeFlow Combat System, where you string chains of punches, kicks, and takedowns to mobilise huge groups of hostiles. Taking down armed thugs is even more interesting, as you think of ways to get past them without attacking them head-on. The fact that Batman is human makes the game even more challenging, as there are no special abilities or attacks akin to other comic-book games. It's up to the player to use the gadgetry and combat mechanics in creative ways.
The soundtrack and graphics are simply amazing. The music creates enough tension to keep you focused on the game, while the graphics and visual effects immerse you into the gameplay. Overall, the videogame is a wonderful example of game developers doing things right.

Mark of the Ninja is a 2D side-scrolling stealth game from Canadian developer Klei, makers of Eets, Shank and Don’t Starve. To put it simply, Mark of the Ninja is a 2D mash-up of Batman: Arkham Asylum and Ninja Gaiden. However, unlike those two, it is a stealth game through and through. It is a true ninja game. Ninjas weren’t open field warriors, they prowled in the shadows only striking on completely unaware enemies in total silence. And this game will make you feel like a true ninja.
This is achieved through great level design and fluid mechanics which facilitate experimentation and don’t penalize you for slight mistakes. Instead, the game grants you the tools and abilities to recover and vanish from sight once again to try a different approach. This design philosophy is crucial as it so effectively bypasses the trial-and-error tedium that plagues stealth game so often. There are almost always multiple ways to tackle each situation. You can try to distract the guards with your assortment of gear, you can take out the lights, or you can simply try an alternate route through the level. Every level can be completed without killing anyone or even without being seen at all. On the flip side, you can choose to slaughter absolutely everyone. This freedom of choice and emphasis on player experimentation makes Mark of the Ninja truly engaging and rewarding. However, there aren’t any notable setpieces or particular design variety, even the range of enemy types is slim.
The controls are absolutely superb. All the moves and assassinations flow wonderfully and are achieved effortlessly without having to battle your control input of choice be it a controller or mouse/keyboard combo. The graceful ballet of stealth and death is heightened even further by the fast and fluid animations, although more assassination animations would have gone a long way to make it even better. Each level also has a hidden gateway which will transport you into a challenge room. This is mostly designed as an environmental puzzle requiring you to bypass certain obstacles such as lasers in order to get to a reward item. These challenge rooms are well designed and offer a nice change of pace.
Mark of the Ninja will take you on a trip through Asian landscapes including urban and rural areas as well as a Eastern European fortress and a brief Middle East stint. The visual style is definitely nice enough, but it rarely impresses and it feels kind of similar throughout. The same can be said of the soundtrack, it fits well with the theme of the game, but it doesn’t stand out in any way. The truly disappointing part is the storytelling. It is an absolutely awful mish-mash of predictable cliches, lazy writing and poor voice acting. It’s incredibly boring and uninteresting. This is such a shame because a compelling narrative could have elevated the gameplay and the design into new heights by providing much needed context. As it is, it’s just sort of there for the hell of it. But at least the storytelling isn’t intrusive and doesn’t take away from the gameplay in any way.
Mark of the Ninja is a very enjoyable game with engaging gameplay and emergent level design that is an easy recommendation to any stealth fan or any video game fan, for that matter. However, I can’t escape the feeling that it simply lacks some sort of an unidentifiable element that would elevate it into the territory of a true modern classic.

Mark of the Ninja is a 2D side-scrolling stealth game from Canadian developer Klei, makers of Eets, Shank and Don’t Starve. To put it simply, Mark of the Ninja is a 2D mash-up of Batman: Arkham Asylum and Ninja Gaiden. However, unlike those two, it is a stealth game through and through. It is a true ninja game. Ninjas weren’t open field warriors, they prowled in the shadows only striking on completely unaware enemies in total silence. And this game will make you feel like a true ninja.
This is achieved through great level design and fluid mechanics which facilitate experimentation and don’t penalize you for slight mistakes. Instead, the game grants you the tools and abilities to recover and vanish from sight once again to try a different approach. This design philosophy is crucial as it so effectively bypasses the trial-and-error tedium that plagues stealth game so often. There are almost always multiple ways to tackle each situation. You can try to distract the guards with your assortment of gear, you can take out the lights, or you can simply try an alternate route through the level. Every level can be completed without killing anyone or even without being seen at all. On the flip side, you can choose to slaughter absolutely everyone. This freedom of choice and emphasis on player experimentation makes Mark of the Ninja truly engaging and rewarding. However, there aren’t any notable setpieces or particular design variety, even the range of enemy types is slim.
The controls are absolutely superb. All the moves and assassinations flow wonderfully and are achieved effortlessly without having to battle your control input of choice be it a controller or mouse/keyboard combo. The graceful ballet of stealth and death is heightened even further by the fast and fluid animations, although more assassination animations would have gone a long way to make it even better. Each level also has a hidden gateway which will transport you into a challenge room. This is mostly designed as an environmental puzzle requiring you to bypass certain obstacles such as lasers in order to get to a reward item. These challenge rooms are well designed and offer a nice change of pace.
Mark of the Ninja will take you on a trip through Asian landscapes including urban and rural areas as well as a Eastern European fortress and a brief Middle East stint. The visual style is definitely nice enough, but it rarely impresses and it feels kind of similar throughout. The same can be said of the soundtrack, it fits well with the theme of the game, but it doesn’t stand out in any way. The truly disappointing part is the storytelling. It is an absolutely awful mish-mash of predictable cliches, lazy writing and poor voice acting. It’s incredibly boring and uninteresting. This is such a shame because a compelling narrative could have elevated the gameplay and the design into new heights by providing much needed context. As it is, it’s just sort of there for the hell of it. But at least the storytelling isn’t intrusive and doesn’t take away from the gameplay in any way.
Mark of the Ninja is a very enjoyable game with engaging gameplay and emergent level design that is an easy recommendation to any stealth fan or any video game fan, for that matter. However, I can’t escape the feeling that it simply lacks some sort of an unidentifiable element that would elevate it into the territory of a true modern classic.
7 OUT OF 10 (GOOD)

Finally, a ninja game that acurately portrays the ninja! This game is a masterpiece in terms of character accuracy and gameplay. Prepare yourself for an epic adventure that places you in the shoes of an unknown man who happens to be the champion of  an ancient clan of ninja assassins who were attacked by a group of dangerous mercinaries. Perhaps the best aspect of this game is the sense of looming danger in every stage. This game is out to get you; everything is far more powerful than you are and if they find you, they will kill you; And if the enemies don't get you, the traps will. You have to cautiously and careful plan out every action you'll take when approaching danger. Don't think that you can just kill everyone and be done with it; enemies are often in pairs or near traps so killing them is not an optimal solution. Think of this game as a metaphore for real danger (you don't just go rushing in, throwing your life away - Arin Hansen's quote from sequalitis). Should you decide to kill, you will be blessed with some of the most thought out and crafty killing methods in video games. In addition the few characters in this game are some of the most memorable and loveable ones you'll ever experienced (I even loved the main villains). Simply put, this game is well crafted and is a great buy for anyone's library...

* * * * - Lawbreakers Closed Beta/Open Beta Review - * * * *
This game is pretty damn great, it certainly gives me the break from Overwatch that I so desperately needed.
The gun play with this is quite unique, fast paced, zero-gravity combat and comes with a skill ceiling that is actually quite high, so for someone who really enjoys their first person arena shooters, this is a game for you.
The game has mostly capture and defend game modes, such as 'Overcharge' and 'Uplink', both game modes are very similar only that the Battery can be charged by either team and both teams have to capture it to win. Uplink on the other hand, both teams must charge it in their base to raise their score to 100% in order to win a point for their team.
'Blitzball' is a game mode that sort of reminded me of the game mode 'Grav-ball' from Halo, all be it without the Hammers. In this game mode (Sort of a bit like Gravball) the ball spawns central and both teams must take control of the ball and dunk it in the enemy teams base to score a point, this is best of 8 I believe. (Also the ball sounds a bit like Morty and it talks a load of balls to the player holding it.)
The characters in the game are really fun to play and as someone who plays Overwatch quite regularly, a few of them feel similar to a few of the hero's from there for example: Vanguard = Pharah, Enforcer = Soldier 76, Battle Medic = Mercy etc.
There are I would say a little bit of balance issues with certain classes that could be improved upon but let's be honest, every game like this that has some sort of class system and operators or hero's, will always have one thing stronger than the other.
The low gravity combat makes it really fun to play and I actually only picked up on this in the last beta, that you could shoot behind you with your weapon using ALT and propel yourself forward in the zero-G zones if you are feeling a little weighted down. (And also gat one or two people in the process if you are lucky.)
All in all I am looking forward to this games release, and I hope that it takes off nicely. A really good change of pace.
(NOTE: This was a review on the Beta testing of the game, NOT the official release, this is to help people form an opinion on what I have experienced from testing the game and give them my thoughts.)

Arkham Asylum is an incredible Batman experience as it succeeds it what a Batman game should be like: allow you to be Batman. Its gameplay, story and design all make you feel like the Caped Crusader and is one of, if not the best licensed title we've ever gotten.
Arkham Asylum's story pits the Dark Knight against a plethora of classic villains from the Batman's rogues gallery who are all pawns in the Joker's master plan. Honestly, the story on its own and Rocksteady's take on the Batman mythos are worth so much just on its own. The way they cleverly write the whole rogues gallery essentially into this game, either through story or easter eggs, is genious at least. It also happens to be one of the best Joker stories in recent memory.
Just story alone really makes this game, but the fact is that the gameplay is also insanely good. And I'm not just saying that because Batman, but because all the game mechanics and level design are excellent in their own right! The combat system this game crafted has been copied by so many games already. The simple freeflow combat mechanic where you can counter enemies' attacks and keep your chain going is just simplicity at its best. The stealth portions of the game are also very good with level design giving a hand in those sections.
All the gadgets available to Batman are useful and do very different things, not only in combat and stealth, but also in puzzle-solving, collectible hunting and platforming. The Metroidvania style of gameplay and Bioshock type ambience also really make the game's atmosphere really shine and make for a dark and gritty Batman story. They also explore and enliven the Asylum which is usually not shown too much. The whole concept of spending the entire game on the Asylum with all your superpowered nemeses, during one night is genious and they have managed to pull it off perfectly.
Even if you're not a Batman fan, you'll become one after playing this game. Gameplay and story are all excellently crafted and add to this essential Batman experience. This game is most definitely worth your time.
A must-buy!

Short version: a great game any sci-fi/rpg/stealth lovers should play.
Cons:
- loooaaaddddiiiinnnnggggggg time (shut your av down to save a few minutes)
- sequel that will never happen, letting most mysteries unresolved
- main quest not as world-wide as the previous one
- soundtrack less enjoyable than HR's (the ending theme is good tho)
Pros:
- great environnemental narration
- side-quests really interesting
- visuals really good
- nice gameplay (it's a lot easier not to kill someone by mistake, remote piracy aug is a must)
- more a cop story (save the neighbor) than a spy story (save the world)
Long version:
I don't understand people saying this game is a failure compared to Human Revolution.
Sure, the scope is less.
You're mainly in one city, and only get out of it for "dungeon" levels.
Yet, the player witnesses by himself the slow fall of Prague from democracy to apartheid, with all the phases in-between. It begins with checkpoints, some restrictives laws, then more controls, curfews, more laws, forced deportation.
Where HR was more philosophic, asking the player to make a choice not for the game's future, but for our own world, MD is more a warning about things to come if we let fears and prejudices dictate our societies.
Yes, the main quest isn't that interesting.
There's a lot less to dig in, when you compare with the first released trailer. Where is the boy we should have helped from the cops and then decides to join the terrorists ranks?
I met the main antagonist after 40 hours of gameplay. And his motivations are... unclear to say the least. At one point, I though he was triple agent, helping me indirectly for another hidden agenda. But, no.
He's just a soldier waging his own war to the world. All the steps between are standard blockbuster scenario.
But that's not the main point of MD.
MD's main focus is the city itself, how it evolves, its inhabitants and how they cope with the events.
In that regard, MD is a success, boasting one of (if not the best) environnemental storytelling in videogame history.
Unlike classic RPG, quests aren't given to you.
You have to look for them. Around a street corner, inside an apartment, behind a garbage bin.
Sure, there is an info dealer who can direct you to points of interest. Yes, some side-quests show themselves to you. Yet, most of them appear naturally, while exploring, or just passing by.
The glitch and the copycat are the two side-quests which represents how questing should be handled from now on: surprise, mystery, danger, trap, emotional stake.
Unlike RPG, lore isn't force-feeded to you.
You have to look around, read mails in an ordinary computer, move through tossed beers, broken utilities, burned painting or manicles on the walls (cf look closely in the Dvalis Theater), to understand the inhabitants' personnal stories.
Nothing complies you to do so. But it's still here, waiting.
The story of the mom who died in the rumbles of the station, the hope of young artists trying to get out, the despair of a father who has lost his daughter to Dvalis lies.
Some complains about the game are the characters. Too one-sided, quite boring, nothing enthralling.
Indeed, some of them are.
The "rival" is so-so. The big bad is "monolithic". The love interest is inexistant. Alex is more a plot device than anything else. The crazy aug specialist has potential, but is only used at two points in the game.
I barely met (stun-guned is more precise) the Dvali boss, despite hearing about him all the game long.
But others shine.
Adam's boss, who must both deal with global terrorist attacks, illuminati manipulations, a gay divorce and a daughter tortured to death by TWM to force him into augmenting her (and probably blackmailing him later with a killswitch).
The Rabiah's recrutor, whose sincerity and pragmatism are harshly treated by the police forces.
Samizdat team. Of course.
Hobos and homelesses, pouring out some nice philosophies or social critiques if you take the time to listen to them.
Smiley and Chang are funny to speak to. Chikane and weapon sellers ( "Tars is the man!" "F***g Clanks!!" ) too.
The female cop trying to do her job despite the general anti-aug policy. The shrink (aka Madam Photograph? ) and her shady behavior. Helle and the professionnal killer.
So, yeah, the writing isn't poor, it's different. The player has to play for it, to dig, to deduce, to speak to, to listen to, to look at every doors, windows, posters and props.
It's "show, don't tell" made into a videogame. The story is right here, it's up to you to unravel it.
I admit, MD is less a surprise than HR.
There isn't much novelty. The game stats speak for themselves: barely half the players have used any of the new augments.
The breach mode, I did not play. I'm here for Deus Ex. And Deus Ex is solo.
There're strange choices in the first hours of the game.
Why the station bombing isn't playable? It should have been a great scene, forcing the player to explore and act in a crisis (save Alex or save random people? ).

Sometimes superficially compared to Risk because of its use of "Regions" and armies that occupy them in the strategic aspect of the game; Medieval: Total War is, like Shogun: Total War before it, a very unique sort of game. You play as a sort of "animating spirit" of a nation and guide it on to glory, honor, and conquest across Europe, North Africa, and the Middle East. Gameplay involves two main aspects: the Campaign Map and the Battles that are fought to resolve military actions on campaign.
In the Campaign Map you have armies, agents, regions, and the castles in regions.
You make economic choices such as the risk management of the unrest that higher taxation causes, which buildings are most beneficial to a region's income and whether or not you can protect the investment in that region, and whether you want to leave your titles of land to the men who are most loyal, leave them to the men who can manage the agriculture the best, or wait for the uncommon man who fits both criteria and will be a true asset to your rich interior regions.
But along with economy and land come those who covet it, and war that claims lives and land is part of the game. Your military infrastructure permits your recruitment of navies and armies, and your military strategy regarding the movement of those armies is just as important as if not more so than your military tactics regarding battles. To defeat an army of your strength in a clean victory that pushes him back to another region is one thing. To completely outmaneuver him, annihilate the majority of his forces in detail, and leave his pathetic remnants holed up in their keeps in lands they no longer control is another, and the difference is when and where you fight your battles.
In the real time battles things are much more straightforward: you have your men, they have theirs, and not everyone who enters the battlefield is leaving it.
Analyze your troop composition, analyze their composition, analyze the terrain near yourself, analyze the terrain near them. Do you wait for them to make the first move, and act upon what they are committing to? Do you take the initiative yourself, hoping for (or in the best case, assured of) getting an advantage that will take you a step closer to victory?
Your units have their own varied personalities. Sometimes they fight you. The impetuous feudal knights who charge home into the enemy may plainly refuse to disengage on your order or, in the worst case, attempt to and fail as they are cut down because only a portion of them followed the order. Highlanders ready and willing to slaughter are themselves not so stiff of character and from just a volley or two or archer fire may break and flee as their pathetic discipline proves to be their downfall. After you lose this battle, those very same highlanders may prove themselves to be your greatest asset as the enemy pursues you and your men charge downhill out of the woods, slaughtering and turning the enemy mass in the face of such raw force.
To conclude, Medieval: Total War is certainly a unique game and a satisfying one if you appreciate a test of both your strategic and tactical skills. I recommend if you play this game to avoid savescumming every turn to outmaneuver enemy armies. It takes a lot of the challenge out of the strategy when you know exactly what your opponent is going to do next when he cannot do the same with you.

Find out what screen resolution your computer is set at.

Arkham Asylum is an incredible Batman experience as it succeeds it what a Batman game should be like: allow you to be Batman. Its gameplay, story and design all make you feel like the Caped Crusader and is one of, if not the best licensed title we've ever gotten.
Arkham Asylum's story pits the Dark Knight against a plethora of classic villains from the Batman's rogues gallery who are all pawns in the Joker's master plan. Honestly, the story on its own and Rocksteady's take on the Batman mythos are worth so much just on its own. The way they cleverly write the whole rogues gallery essentially into this game, either through story or easter eggs, is genious at least. It also happens to be one of the best Joker stories in recent memory.
Just story alone really makes this game, but the fact is that the gameplay is also insanely good. And I'm not just saying that because Batman, but because all the game mechanics and level design are excellent in their own right! The combat system this game crafted has been copied by so many games already. The simple freeflow combat mechanic where you can counter enemies' attacks and keep your chain going is just simplicity at its best. The stealth portions of the game are also very good with level design giving a hand in those sections.
All the gadgets available to Batman are useful and do very different things, not only in combat and stealth, but also in puzzle-solving, collectible hunting and platforming. The Metroidvania style of gameplay and Bioshock type ambience also really make the game's atmosphere really shine and make for a dark and gritty Batman story. They also explore and enliven the Asylum which is usually not shown too much. The whole concept of spending the entire game on the Asylum with all your superpowered nemeses, during one night is genious and they have managed to pull it off perfectly.
Even if you're not a Batman fan, you'll become one after playing this game. Gameplay and story are all excellently crafted and add to this essential Batman experience. This game is most definitely worth your time.
A must-buy!

As much as I love this game, I have to say that it's not for everyone. First of all, you should understand that this is the last part of Legacy of Kain pentalogy. Yes, pentalogy. Unfortunately, the very first part, Blood Omen, is not sold by Steam. Shame, because it's one of the best classical RPGs. But back to Defiance.
Gameplay-wise, this game isn't really special. It's a specific hack-and-slash game with several action adventure elements. There are some very frustrating moments with cameras and it's best played on gamepad (though I had some problems with remapping the buttons). If you are a keyboard player, then no problem, but you'll need to change the controls to your liking. You can't really change the graphics and even though the characters or environment don't look very bad, it's evident that the game was released in 2003. And, since this is the pentalogy's conclusion, if you don't know the story, you'll miss the best part of this game.
Now for the good parts. First of all, for the first time in the series, the game is not only about Kain (Blood Omen) or Raziel (Soul Reaver), but about both. In odd levels you play as Kain, in the even ones as Raziel. Though both are similar in their range of movements and controls, there are some significant differences (Reavers, realm-shifting). This changing of characters allows the game to run two separate, yet connected story lines. To continue, Legacy of Kain series have always been known for atmospherical, original music (by Kurt Harland). The soudtrack is flawless. The characters are memorable, they've come a long journey and I can honestly say that Legacy of Kain has the most developed and believable characters I've seen in the gaming world. The voice acters did an amazing job - my personal favorite is Michael Bell as Raziel, but there isn't a single poorly dubbed character. And the story. If you like complicated, dramatic and epic stories, Legacy of Kain is the best you can get. The story combines both personal tragedies and events that affect the whole world of Nosgoth. It's very strong, some scenes will just leave you breathless.
To conclude - even though it's somewhat linear and the gameplay shifted from action adventure to more hack-and-slash type, the game is fun and I recommend it. I'd say that even a person who never played a Legacy of Kain game before can play it and enjoy it, but if you want a truly memorable experience, play the previous games and save this for the last. It's a great finale of an escalating story that no fan of epic stories should miss.

Not one of the strongest entries in the LoK franchise, although not the worst either. It's a fairly good game. The story is brilliant, as always, as is the voice acting. The gameplay is a bit of a mixed bag.
To start with: the camera. The camera is no longer a chase-cam, like the last 3 games. Instead, it's a kind of Devil May Cry camera that shifts, rotates and generally gets on your nerves. It frequently changes when you are in the middle of performing a precise action, like jumping - which screws up what you were doing.
Secondly: too much repetitive combat. Okay, to be fair, the other games have also suffered from this, but LoK seems to simply have more of it. It gets tiresome and I found myself avoiding combat wherever possible. Certain levels have you running backwards and forth with wave after wave of enemy re-spawning after every battle. It gets annoying very quickly.
Those things aside, the rest of the game is pretty solid. It looks lovely, sounds great and the puzzles are a little more diverse than titles such as BO2. Story is great and it is good fun to be able to play both Kain and Raziel (although bar some animation differences, they play very similar to each other). The main difference between the two is that Raziel is blessed with more engrossing puzzles, while Kain is simply given more enemies to mash. Raziel also has the spectral realm to play around in, which of course, Kain does not have.
LoK fans will like it (as I have), but it leaves you wondering just what they could have accomplished with the format - and such a shame that certain elements were not improved upon.

Compared with Batman: Arkham City, this game may feel more packed, but it provides a great storyline, if not better than Arkham City's. The atmosphere is executed perfectly, especially with certain scary parts of the game (not only Scarecrow's parts). All the characters are great and have a real reason for being in the game. Collecting Riddler's content is a huge part of the game, unlocking everything else as well such as a ton of backstories and character bios which are very interesting. I actually began playing this a while back, but I stopped because my computer couldn't handle it (it's not a gaming computer), so I instead played Arkham City, which ran more smoothly. However, after a while, Arkham Asylum ran just about as smoothly so I played it again. I was playing Normal difficulty up until playing about 12 hours, 3/4 of the way through the story. I then made a new file and put it to Hard difficulty to stack all the achievements, and the game only took me about 6 hours (I completed it that day). Not only that, but I also was able to finish all the other content, meaning challenges and Riddler trophies/riddles/extras. I already have every achievement, and they are fairly easy to get. Be warned that Hard mode was a little more difficult than I thought, even though I was decent at combat and such. Another thing to be wary of is that the keyboard and mouse make it hard to control gliding, so I eventually changed to a controller, so keep that in mind. All in all, a great game especially for the price, and it is great to have a part of the amazing Rocksteady Batman trilogy.

This game has slow gameplay, but is still satisfying to play. I know not everyone will be into it, but keep reading if the following interests you, and you should know, this game faces realistic problems, and the game's adjectives present a very depressive situtation. You play as a spirit that lives in a house, where a family of three decide to spend their summer. These family members contrast in what they want, and how their summer should be spent. The father Dan wants to finally finish his second novel. The Mother Linda wants her husband to spend more time with her, have a closer family, and to pursue a possible future as an artist, while the son Tommy just wants to enjoy the summer, and isn't fully aware of the family's problems.
As the spirit, you have the ability to observe these characters, read their memories/thoughts, find clues about what they want around the house. Once you discover what they want, you decide at the end of each chapter, who shall get what they want, and then you can follow up by giving a compensation to a second member (Not as good, but better than a depressing event for that character), while the third will get a depressing event. As the spirit, you can whisper to Dan at night, and pass what you decide on to his own thoughts.
There are 12 chapters in the game, followed by an ending decided by the relationships that you've created between the characters, and your final choice. The game becomes more interesting as you feel for the tragedy that each character is going through because of your decisions, and even more so, if you are trying to keep everyone happy, similar to how I did. The problems that the family faced hit pretty close to home, which makes it even more tragic as they repitively face problems, and often feel empty, and disconnected.
Like I said, there isn't a huge amount to gameplay, but if you're interested, I'd recommend trying it. It took me about 3 hours to complete it once, and I don't plan to play again, but there are other changes that can be made to the story. However, I do not feel that is enough personally to create replayability. Price is a bit high, I'd recommend trying this game if you see it to have a decent sale.
Do you wish for the son to have a happy childhood more than Dan's acomplishment in completing a quality novel?
Do you focus on your son's education struggles, or your own problems?
Do you target Dan's drinking problem to help Linda?
Do you wish for Linda to have a real chance at becoming an artist over Dan's career?
Do you wish to destroy the family's already faulty relationship for their careers?
And BTW, I ended up with two of the three characters happy after such a depressing game, so I'm pretty sure that's good.

People are comparing this game to Overwatch and expect it to be what Overwatch is.
Spoilers. It's not.
This game is nothing like Overwatch. Sure, it is classified as an "Arena Shooter" but that is pretty much ANY similarity it shares with OW. The game plays nothing like the former. It's fast paced, hectic with a HIGH skill cap. That doesn't sound like Blizzard's baby at all. The classes all feel unique in their own way and the implemented gravity system makes things just awesome.
I have only put 7 hours into the game so I can't be thorough with my review but it is pretty incredible. I think it delivers a  great experience, a different experience. For $30, you really cannot go wrong here. The developers  know how to make games and I have full faith that they will do what it takes to allow this game to succeed. The number of players playing at the launch may be a bit alarming, but like their other games, they will ease players in with long-term updates and generally great communication and patches to make the game better and better. It really is unlike any other game I have played, and coming from someone who has not really played anything but SMITE, no game has really interested me like this in a long while.
The mechanics are fluid, easy to learn but hard to master. The games are team-based but individual skill can pretty much single-handedly pull your team to the top if you play well enough. My only issue right now is that some guns don't really feel "heavy" but with feedback I'm sure some will be adjusted. The graphics and the maps are very nice to look at and play around with. I would recommend anyone to give this a try. It's a breath of fresh air and hopefully many more people will be able to see that as I have been able to.

Casually, Brawlhalla is a great game to have fun with if you have friends. Easy to learn quickly. Just download it and start beating up your friends in this simple 2D platform fighter. Tons of game modes and flexibility means you can play with any number of people online and offline in many different ways. And it's free.
Unfortunately you only get six playable characters (out of 34 at this point) if you don't buy the All Legends Pack or SLOWLY earn in-game gold to buy them.
However, if you want to play competitively I advise caution. The game is still in Early Access and constantly changing (for better or for worse). Blue Mammoth Games seem to be trying to figure out how to balance a game without the usual components of a fighting game (blocking, grabbing, proper ranged attacks) for competitive play.
Outside of having to buy the characters, there is no pay to win anywhere in sight. Microtransactions are cosmetic only.
Expect plenty of toxicity and salt in ranked modes.
If you're fine with all of that, great. You might enjoy ranked modes or organized tournaments. Brawlhalla's active community and large playerbase ensure you can easily find human players to compete against and help you get better.
Try it for free and maybe you'll stick with it.

This game is amazing.  I usually don't beat singleplayer games, or take a long time to do so, but Mark of the Ninja was different.  I was HOOKED.  I couldn't stop playing it.  The different suits, changing you play style, the different distraction and attack items, allowing you to sneak by or take out guards in new ways, the upgrades, letting you try out new kills and abilities (parachute cloth), everything about this game is just great. ====EDIT====
If you get this game, I would personally recommend getting the DLC.  The DLC comes with a new level that is challenging and interesting, Developer commentary (presented in a very cool way), a new costume/path, which takes away your special abilities and makes the game feel much more realistic, and two new items, which are very helpful and can get you through tough situations.  As of now, you only get one level with the DLC, but personally I am hoping they will add more, as well as more costumes/paths.  It would really get people (like me) who have beaten the game (a few times) and unlocked all the stuffs back into it, trying out new things they add.  I also would absolutely love it if they found a way to introduce a multiplayer co-op aspect into this game, because it would make this (already very good) game hundreds of times better.

The difficulty ramps up quickly, so expect to take breaks when you get frustrated. Edit: it looks like some players have concluded that the puzzles in ths game can't be solved except with brute force. I would strongly recommend not using brute force in this game. Yes, it is a simple grid based puzzle and so backtracking algorithms will eventually yeld solutions, but at the cost of enjoyng the game or learning from it. If you get so frustrated that you want to just brute force a level, take a break and let the puzzle percolate in your subconcious for a bit. I promise you that brute force is not a major part of solving the puzzles.
Finally, an exercise: prove that solvability of a Snakebird level is NP-hard (no portals!).

I have played this game for 701 hours and 2 years now. I've tried this game competitively, I have reached the highest ranks (as far as my region goes). I've spent close to  $50 dollars on this game. Here is what I think of this game.
Brawlhalla is one of those games that you will tremendously enjoy. It's got several different game modes, competitive, casual and private options for multiplayer. It's got a training room which has expansive options for learning how to play the game. This game has one of the best developers working behind it. They even have their own esports department, and tournaments are featured on the main menu frequently. Loads of options that you can have when playing this game free to play. You will have fun playing this game: if you're looking to play casually. Spend maybe 60 great, intense hours with your friends! Download this game if this applies to you. However to the 40% of the population who wants to try this game to reach the top, read on.
Playing ranked is whole different game. Although it has a great esports scene, this game is severely broken and terrible at the high levels. The main problem is this: there is no punishment for running away. What makes a fighting game a fighting game is that two opponents are essentially forced to battle out in an arena, with intense action and adreneline everywhere. However, in Brawlhalla at the highest ranks, you're essentially trying to bait each other out and parry. Defensive play is the only option if you want to win the game. Let me put it this way: a good story has a beginning, conflict, rising action, climax and a resolution. In Brawlhalla, although there is conflict, it's often either you chasing someone, you losing to someone who waits for you to attack first, or you doing the above. There is no rising action. So when a match finally ends, is more like a flop. This game will feel terrible and there's nothing you can do about it. Some weapons are incredibly overpowered as well. The developers do not make a good attempt at trying to make all styles of plays and weapons viable. Like the disaster game which is League of Legends, there's always a pool of weapons and legends that are considered top tier, before they are pulled off. Where as some weapons make reading very hard (10+ different options to escape and punish back), some weapons feel like 50-50 or you lose the entire game.
In essence, Brawlhalla is a fun an excellent game that should be played with many of your friends. It's almost guaranteed you will have a great time. However, this game lacks extremely at the higher level. Just look at a clip from a tournament that happened yesterday: a PRO PLAYER (has earned money from this game), actually TWEETED MIDGAME, because his opponent resolved to a style where he was just waiting for punishes.
. Trust me, this is how 60% of all matches turn out.
TL;DR: It's an excellent game for playing casually. Don't invest time into it if you're going to play ranked.

After playing Deus Ex Human Revolution (Predecessor of Mankind Divided) multiple times, being one of my favorite games, I looked forward to Mankind Divided. In short, Human Revolution a game with multiple paths and options, with a great storyline of conspiracy which you have to discover and uncover yourself. You can really invest yourself into the story.
The start of the game was, in my opinion, one of the weak parts: you're dropped right into contact with multiple characters and situations of whom you've never heard of before (except in the trailers), but whom are apparently well known to the main protagonist. While these connections were introduced rather sloppy, you do get to know them about two hours in.
The storyline overall is very good. The feeling of being kept in the dark was fun, as it led to many surprises to which you can react. The main story changed the rest of the universe as well, which makes you feel like you are really making an impact on it. The story connected to the previous games as well (With Human Revolution being the past and the original Deus Ex as the future) in a way that made sense. Multiple sidequests with connection to Adam Jensen, being old aquaintances or connected to the atmosphere and his opinion about them. Some sidequests are randomly found, which made solving those mysteries much more enjoyable.
The atmosphere of the game is great, you see the division of "Naturals" and "Augs" and the results because of it everywhere around you. The main protagonist can also strike up multiple conversations on the workfloor with colleagues, which made them feel like more than just random NPC's by having discussions or building up friendship even if it doesn't alter the storyline at all.
The combat has been vastly improved; in Human Revolution the normal pistol was an unchallenged king out of the other weapons, but in Mankind Divided each weapon has their own merit (Some large open fields for the sniper rifle, different types of special ammunition, effective range and piercing, etc). Gunfights have more glasscannon than bullet sponge enemies, which is something I enjoy as well. Adam's health felt quite low, but I haven't tried out the Titan shields yet, which should give Adam Jensen a much higher survivability. Some situations felt poorly planned, some ambushed start you in a 3v1 situation without cover, making it hard to find cover or take them out fast enough on the highest difficulties.
The stealth system was improved as well with multiple phases like panic, hostile and searching. Although this was already present in the predecessor, it's more fleshed out in Mankind Divided by making the stages of NPC's known from the start. The ability to pull enemies with you behind cover in hand to hand combat also was a quality of life improvement, making the game react more to your intentions (Because you almost always want to hide bodies).
The amount of possible paths to locations was even bigger than in Human Revolution, making every playstyle viable instead of a choice between vents and following the main path; almost every floor was a new maze of possibilities.
The cityhub felt a little less diverse than Human Revolution which had a wider variety of scenery with Hengsha and Detroit, as Mankind Divided only has Prague and a small moment in Golem City. It was, however, much more impressive than it's predecessor as the area's changed much more because of new events. Shops are all over the city, which made selling items and buying new ones quite easy. Shop interaction was kind of flawed; you have to sit through 4 one-liners of the NPC which narrow down to "I sell items. Please buy items?" before you get access to their computer (which contains their wares), and exiting wants you to confirm your exiting multiple times.
There is only one bossfight in Mankind Divided compared to Human Revolution's multiple, but it doesn't feel like this game is lacking them.
TL;DR:
It's a great game, a worthy successor of the earlier Deus Ex franchise.

This standalone expansion to Far Cry 3 takes place on a neon-hazed island where you, a cyber-soldier, must take down a former comrade and save the world. Filled to the brim with 80's references and one-liners, this shooter is basically a love letter to all those movies we binge watched on VHS.
+The story is told through old DOS style cutscenes. Choppy (yet endearing) animations and corny dialogue keep you entertained throughout. There are various visual and verbal references to 80's pop culture, so the story will definitely be appreciated by buffs of that time period.
+Fantastic visuals. Very pretty game to look at, even if the neon can sometimes get almost a little too intense. The main character has a variety of animations that are well-designed and fun to watch.
+Voice acting in the game is thoroughly enjoyable. Michael Biehn (Terminator, Aliens) voices the main character and is the main attraction of the game. Every line is ridiculous, and his gritty delivery makes it all the better.
+Music in this game is great. Might be one of my favorite soundtracks of all time. It's very inspired by movies like the Terminator and the Thing, so there's a lot to enjoy here. It helps set the tone for the game and really makes the lackluster fights more fun to get into.
~Gunplay isn't as good as it should be. Like Far Cry 3, a lot of the guns feel very underpowered and just don't have enough pop. There are some weapons that avert this (like the shotgun), but otherwise it feels like you're shooting a BB gun. Running around and just stabbing people can be fun, however, even if it doesn't take much skill. Whenever you're injured in combat, you have to heal yourself--this means going through a healing animation over and over again. At first they are fun to watch, but after a while they get tedius. You'll find yourself just wanting to jump back into the action.
-Lots of filler missions. The main story isn't that long, but there are plenty of collectibles and outposts to capture. These activities aren't really that fun to complete. They let you unlock more weapon attachments and level up your skills, but the game isn't hard enough to warrant chasing these objectives down. Like many Ubisoft games, the side quests don't actually add anything to the game, only serving as minor distractions or achievements for completionists. Some people may like this, but I don't.
VERDICT
It's a short game, but you have to keep in mind this was only released as DLC. For a standalone expansion, this is excellent. It delivers a fun story, has memorable acting and one-liners, and is a lot of fun to play through. The side quests and collectibles detract from its light speed pace, but they are entirely optional. Blazing through the story in one go is the best way to experience the game. If you're a fan of the 80's, look no further. This game is for you.

I was seriously gonna recommend this game... but I didn't.
You start in your bedroom, waking up from a tormented night. Clicking on stuff gives most of the time funny descriptions.
Like "this plastic plant has been recently watered", "this plastic plant is dying" and many other very funny variations. This plastic plant joke will become a true inside joke throughout the game. Then you get to the living room and find a kiddo watching black and white TV. The first dialog happens when you will ask him one of the following questions:
- Who are you?
- Who am I?
- Where am I?
That made me seriously LMFAO.
Well, you got the picture. All the game is like this, with absolutely crazy people, funny dialogs, and incredible stupidity. The acting is bad -- on purpose. However the voices are good.
This game is a point and click adventure parody. But it's not just that. The main story will keep you playing. How comes you know about color TV when those rednecks have no idea it exists? Why don't you remember anything? Why are they... so strange?
You will encounter lots of people in this small town, from a waistless vet protecting a nuclear site, to "feminine" firemen and a teacher that loves to have a ... "goodtime" with little children... This town is completely crazy and you will definitely want to know why and how you did get dragged into this crappy situation.
I had lots of fun the first day in the game. Talking to everyone, blackmailling people and stuff. However, you will get stuck pretty quick, having no idea what you should be doing. Items’ purposes are hard to figure out. I was so stuck that I had to check the walkthrough -- just to know where I was supposed to go. “Damn, yeah, I missed this tiny white pixel which was a light switch”... and so on. Very frustrating.
What really turned me down was the end of the game, which is super lame. All was going fine, with your everyday weird routine, like giving the newspaper in the morning instead of being it given to you, chitchatting with people about commies and gay firemen, peepholing on your GF and watching her undress (eheh). Until you reach... a certain point where the story goes litteraly FUBAR. No more plot, no story, no details anymore. You will just whack you way till the end of the game... and learn the truth. Everything will be explained don't worry. But... that will be super lame.
Overall this game is good for a solid 3/4 of the story. But the plot dissapoints. The story feels so unfinished, what a letdown. There are bugs too, so save often on different slots. The combat system is super  s h i t  but that's meant to be. Some FMV scenes are a bit disturbing which were the cause of the game ban in various countries. But, even though there is an excess of blood and violence, all of that is not serious. We are in a parody all right.
Unfortunately, this was not enough -- for me -- to recommend this game.

This is the epitome of what a good, horror point and click game should be.
The puzzles in this game while difficult, are fairly creative and enjoyable. Some of the tools you need are hard to find, and it can get a bit frustrating at times; However, the game does have tips, and once you figure out the solution it really feels like you've accomplished something. The gameplay is standard for the point and click genre, but there is some combat thrown in. HERE'S where the game gets a little nasty.
The combat is terrible. It feels clunky, unresponsive and boring. This would be forgivable if it were sparse, but during the last third of the game it's almost the only thing you do. In fact, the entire last third of the game is probably the weakest part, simply because of all the combat and that the area you have to trudge through is feels very disjointed.
The atmosphere is fantastic. I really felt alone while I explored the town, and the fact that there is no clear goal from the start made me feel all the more involved. I was really interested by the town of Harvest, and I really wanted to learn more. In fact, the story is a big part of why I kept playing. Along with the fun puzzles and creepy environments, the story really pulled me in. I was interested in the world of Harvest, and I wanted to see the mystery unfold.
Character interaction makes up most of the first third of the game, and its done very well. All of the characters are unique and memorable in some way, from the meat obsessed father of your bride-to-be, to the school teacher who punishes disobedient children with a baseball bat. Some characters will die, some characters will evolve into something much more sinister.
Though the graphics are dated, the world feels like a lot of detail was put into it, and I couldn't help but feel creeped out every time I stepped into the mortuary. The soundtrack contributes to this feeling, with tracks ranging from a relaxed radio tune to a tense nighttime heist.
Throughout the story, you are forced into more and more uncomfortable situations; Maybe you start by scratching a car, but soon enough you'll be burning down a diner. After every task you complete, you are able to talk to the townsfolk and witness their reactions to what's happening around them. I felt immersed in the world and interested in what everybody had to say.
The cheesiness does show through sometimes, though; when it did, I couldn't help but laugh. This game mixes humor and horror perfectly, allowing for some scenarios that other games don't.
For instance: There is an armed gaurd (who happens to be missing both of his legs) you talk to at  a few points during the game, and you soon find out that he controls a group of nuclear missiles that could cause a holocaust. If you continue to talk to him, he will accuse you of being a communist. If you do not persuade him that you are not, in fact, a "pink-blooded commie", then he will shoot you in the forehead and then accidentally set off all of the missiles (with gore out the wazoo, of course).
Its scenes like these that help to keep the atmosphere campy and fun despite the serious undertone of the game, and I feel that it makes it one of the most memorable point and click games that I have ever played.
Average game time will differ depending on the person. Some people will skip most of the dialogue and rush through the game, while others (such as myself) prefer to "smell the roses", so to speak. I personally recommend playing it at a moderate pace, because if you go through it too fast you might miss some of the great scenes and fantastic writing. It took me about nine hours to play through the game at a fairly slow pace, talking to all the characters and examinating all of the objects. It is possible to beat this game in around five hours, but that's if you're really rushing.
All in all, this is one of my favorite point and click games of all time, despite the lazily implemented combat and bugs. So if you can stomach the gore and enjoy some campy horror every once in a while, than I would highly recommend this game. I can guaruntee that if you enter with the right expectations and an open mind, you won't be disappointed.

"There are many facets of cheating in online games which make the creation of a system to stop cheating very difficult; however, game developers and third party software developers have created or are developing[10][11] technologies that attempt to prevent cheating. Such countermeasures are commonly used in video games, with notable anti-cheat software being GameGuard, PunkBuster, Valve Anti-Cheat (specifically used on games on the Steam platform), and EasyAntiCheat.[12]
Exploits of bugs are usually resolved/removed via a patch to the game; however, not all companies force the patches/updates on users, leaving the actual resolution to individual users."
They seem to take the "leaving the actual resolution to individual users." part way too literally.
The only unbearable problem with the game is modders/glitchers in my opinion, but nothing really gets done about it.
Most games will do a small patch every few days when they've found an exploit that can be abused in order to prevent cheating, but with TakeTwo/Rockstar you can expect a patch every... 4-6 months. After the patch there's usually a ban wave, which will give you a splendid week of modder free playing time. The other 16-23 weeks though? lol, good luck.
To give an example of how bad the modding is; I have played in approximately 30 sessions over the last 4 days. I left ~5 of those sessions because I was content and felt it was a reasonable time to get off the game. The other 25? Well, either server crash from modder trying to spawn too much money at once, or the entire lobby was just blowing up repeatedly and getting teleported around and having their weapons taken away. Oh, and vehicles don't save you - they'll just force eject you from them. You can also be frozen so you can't move your character, or modders can spawn 1000+ planes on you at once, crashing your game. Switching lobbies doesn't save you, because there's another malicious modder in the one you're loading into already.
To reiterate, it's a really fun game. One of the best I've played, actually. But unless you're going to play invite only sessions or instanced missions, it's not currently worth the frustration.

The Novelist is a game that falls into that bucket of games that aren't exactly interactive experiences like Dear Esther, but still not nearly as involved gameplay wise as the majority of mainstream FPS games.  The title sees you patrolling the Summer home of a frustrated author and his single unit family as some sort of "presence" or "ghost".  There are two distinct game "difficulties", in the first you can patrol the house on foot (I assume its on foot, the player's avatar is still a bit of a mystery reserved for hints found in the notes scattered through the levels) without the NPC's noticing you.  The second takes on a more stealth-based approach, requiring you to hide from the family as you peruse through their thoughts and belongings.
Basic gameplay involves you searching through the house and possessing the thoughts of the family to determine what the hopes, needs and feelings are of each family member.  You can navigate through traditional walking or via possession of light fixtures.  After you discover enough information to continue, you can either stick around to get the rest of the missing information, or make a decision on how to influence the father's thoughts.  After a you commit to your choices, the house switches to night, where you can discover notes relating the experiences of past denizens of the house and finally pass your decisions on to the father.
The story threads hinge very much on which characters you choose to make happy at the end of each day, and the choices directly effect the NPC's moods and relationships with each other as the Summer progresses.  You can go the route of making everyone as happy as possible, or focus only on the needs of a single family member depending on your decisions.  The house looks pretty and has just enough detail in it for you to have to search for clues during the day without getting lost in the clutter.  For a game that depends a lot on moods, the characters have somewhat blank painted-like faces, a smart decision on their part as now the characters con convey their mood via body language instead of heavily involved face posing.
As someone entering the working world trying to balance time between family, career, and hobbies, the game really clicked with me conceptually, and though its very subtle in its pace and approach to gameplay, I still found myself enjoying it for the duration of a Saturday afternoon.  Length (~3 hours) may be a consideration for some, so waiting for a discount might make it more of a bang for your buck.
