The games starts with you witnessing three family members, Dan (husband/father), Linda (wife/mother), and Tommy (son), going on holiday for the summer so Dan can concentrate on writing his next book without all of the distractions that being at home brings. Needless to say that even going away from home with family members will still bring it's own distractions as the family members each have specific things that they want to do whilst they are away, which don't generally include just letting Dan get on with his book.
There are two ways to play this game - story mode, or stealth mode. I chose to play the game in story mode as I just find stealth generally too frustrating, and I believe that from what I got out of the game's story-telling, I definitely made the right choice personally to remove the stealth element.
Your role within the game is to observe the three family members. From your observations you will find out what they each want from a particular moment in time, and from there you can choose your preferred outcome for only one character, and if you have the time and inclination to do more investigation around the house for each remaining family member, you can potentially choose a compromise for another character who didn't get their first preference. Your decisions will have an effect on what happens in the future so choose wisely, and obviously someone will always end up being disappointed.
You play as a ghostly presence within the house - one that can either walk around the house in plain sight (being careful not to get spotted, if playing in stealth mode), or one that can possess the lights/lamps within the house to travel without being seen. You can only be spotted by the family a small number of times in stealth mode per chapter, and after that you lose your ability to influence the choices the family make; however in story mode you can walk around at will which I found to be a much more enjoyable choice for how I wanted to play the game.
In order to find the outcomes for the family members each day, you do this by reading notes/books/pictures that are strewn around the house, and by reading the memories of each family member and walking around the house playing as each character in turn finding clues as to what they would like to achieve.
I found this game to be incredibly atmospheric. From the music to the cell-shaded visuals, it gives a sense of isolation in the big house on the cliff. Seeing how this (almost) visual novel plays out from your own choices I found to be a very personal and emotionally engaging process. I would also praise the voice acting as it really adds to the personality of the characters and the ongoing story.
It is a little frustrating at times having to walk around the whole house at least 6 times if you want to find all of the outcomes/compromises for the characters, particularly when the family are all walking around doing their own thing, but in general that still didn't spoil the atmosphere for me. There were a couple of moments where the outcomes and compromises that I had to pick seemed a little bit unrealistic in terms of how quickly the family could seemingly start to fall apart, but I managed to pull it together enough for each character to get a mostly positive ending for all family members.
This certainly isn't a game for people who want something action-packed, but if you want to be engaged with somewhat challenging decisions, character relationships and atmosphere, this would be a game I'd recommend trying, though I'd maybe wait for a sale to pick this up, as this is a short 2(ish) hour play-through for a £10.99 price-tag.

Free to Play.  Great World War 2 action in multi-player FPS mode and an RTS side to it to boot!  It's in constant development and always improving.  You start as a soldier fighting in FPS mode on reasonably large capture point maps (20vs20), working your way up the ranks and acquiring equipment by spending game credits you earn while playing.  You can bypass the grind by spending real money (purchasing gold) but true experience is only earned by putting in the playing time.  Once you are high enough level, you can acquire troop assault teams (AT's) that can be deployed on the war map.  Choose your faction everytime a new war starts - USA, Germany, Russia.  You can have multiple soldiers of all tyoes (Infantry, Recon, Tank driver, Pilot, Paratrooper) and in all three factions if you want but in war mode you can be only one faction for the current war.   After moving your AT's on the war map to attack or defend a city, you can then join the battle in FPS mode... using your (or anyones) AT's as the supply for your battle!
New players are not typically thrown into battles with experienced players but until you earn enough experience to be put in harder matches, the wait times to be matched with similarly novice players is a bit longer then usual.  Be patient, it's worth it.

Being a compilation of the first two LEGO Star Wars games developed by Traveller's Tales, The Complete Saga stands resolutely as a lot of bang for your buck. Particularly if you're a completionist because finishing the game as-is will probably leave you at about 50% completion rate with plenty more to find in form of unlockable characters, gameplay gimmicks and additional levels.
As a game it's your action adventure fare with platforming as you go through the entire movie hexalogy. I have to point out the game does suffer from having vehicle levels with extremely loose controls that simply end up getting in the way of things, though. The Complete Saga even retroactively adds some vehicle sections to prequel episodes to keep the entire experience consistent. It does benefits from eschewing voice acting in favor of simple gesticulation which leads to a lot of funny scenes as characters try to convey some plot points. Speaking of characters they operate based on different types ranging from Jedi and Sith aka Force users to droids and bounty hunters, each with their own specific utility which you will need to use in order to complete each level to its fullest. In practice this means you'll be going back to already finished levels in order to complete them as you unlock more characters. You'll also be spending omnipresent studs you gather throughout the game as currency to unlock things.
This write-up may seem to be a bit all over place, but that's because I find myself fighting for words. It's a really great game and should not be dismissed as a cash-in game, not even close. Just beware – completionist mentality is recommended.

LEGO Star Wars: The Complete Saga was one of the first video games in the LEGO franchise I played and which made me come back and play more LEGO games and now this title again. That being said, I find 60% of the time I spent on the 2007 title I was hard-pressed not to put the game for good. Controls and scripting have improved so much with later games that it is just a hassle to deal with their state in this game. Plus, I don't understand how over a decade after games came to PCs there are still unskippable cutscene.
Recommendation: I started to play this game because it's a LEGO game and kept at it because I like to 100% a game. If you think, that description fits you as well and you are prepared for some discouraging game design, I'd say, go get the game. Same if you think you're satisfied with only going through the story missions once - this was quite fun. Otherwise you may just want to get a newer LEGO game. They are objectively better.
+ LEGO game
+ The Star Wars saga retold
+ Loads of characters from the Star Wars universe (+1 extra)
+ Lots of levels
- Outdated controls
- Immaturely scripted "player 2"
- Immature camera / point of view
- Flying missions include long and unnerving sounds
- Unskippable cutscenes
- I repeat, unskippable cutscenes
- Reward collection policies
Brace yourself. What follows is as much a review as a rant, read as psycho hygiene, and thus may transport negative feelings.
Why "60% of the time"? Well, it took me about 40% to get through the story mode, the rest of the time was spent bringing the savegame to 100%.
The game has an in-built requirement for replaying levels if you want to get to 100%. AFAIR each story level, and there are many, requires the completionist to play it at least four times. There are quite a few levels outside the story, a welcome diversion. Replaying levels, of course, also restarts the connected cutscenes. Of those you can skip the very first story cutscene, which is directly followed by another cutscene you cannot skip. Throughout each level you'll encounter more transitional cutscenes - none of which are skippable. I actually want to follow the story of a game so I'm cool with games requiring you to stick through cutscenes. Still I would strongly advocate to make every piece of a game that takes up time but doesn't provide game play to be skippable at the player's discretion. The game already got the player's money and shouldn't unnecessarily commandeer the player's time. I had times when the game actually felt like a boring chore.
The controls are somewhat outdated. When running into a "steep" inclination you usually cannot jump. This is right away irritating because it takes away the functionality of one of the main buttons without apparent explanation. I guess, it's because you're supposed to slide on steep inclinations - a nicer device to limit levels than invisible walls (which are also in the game) - and at the bottom you're sort of halfway on the inclination. There are some places where you can slide into stuff in a way that makes it very hard to slide around them which is nevertheless the only option - except for quitting - since you cannot jump at the time.
Stairs are usually a device to ease ascent, in this game they often fail to do so. You're often better off just jumping up stairs. In case they are winding you'll notice that the game is a bit lacking in providing a sense of depth. Although the camera is not too close to the ground most of the time, the camera often jumps between certain pretty fix position, then swivels. This in combination with upwards movement can lead to unfortunate angles.
When playing in "free play" you can effectively choose two characters that enter a level and the game will provide a number of further characters in a way that all skills necessary to complete a level's secondary goals are available. You can then switch between those characters. I couldn't figure out how the game sorts the extras and so had to learn them for each level.
You're always running around with at least two characters. That way you can play as one or two players. The extra character(s) can be quite a hassle. If there are fewer players than characters you can tag and change the currently played character. When you're running with more characters it can be hard to change to the wanted character. When attacking something extra characters are often in the way as the auto-aiming rather hits an extra than anything else. Sometimes extras are blocking you sometimes they keep their distance when you want to tag them. NPC cooperation, e.g. when having to pull two levers at roughly the same time, is still a bit lacking in this game.
The problem with camera angles is even more problematic with ingame rewards, mainly LEGO studs that act as currency in the game and are also part of secondary level goals. Reward collection policy in LEGO games has always been an issue with me, right from the first time a stud vanished into an abyss. So what about the camera? The studs in this game do not have a shadow so their movement in 3D space is somewhat hard to follow. Sometimes you can translate from the movement of another stud moving on the screen plane, i.e. at a right angle to the player's line of sight. Why do you need to follow movement anyway? Most ingame rewards vanish after about 4 seconds which is relatively short. Most ingame rewards are not collectible right away, i.e. studs usually have approximately a second after they appear in which they are protected from collection. Some rewards drop down an abyss or jump behind a wall right away. If there wasn't the argument that there are basically always more studs to collect I'd find that unbearable - so I'm only somewhat upset. Also, game designers were aware of that as is evidenced by the fact that certain levels change policy so that every stud is automatically collected.
My policy would have all studs collectible right away, no time-related vanishing, no jumping through walls and always dropping a shadow.
The game has a few dead-ends, i.e. places you can get to but cannot get away from without quitting a level. There is also a bit of unnecessary tunneling. Example 1: In free play despite having a character that can theoretically make it across wide abysses the game still drops you into the abyss because it just wants you to take the scenic route. Example 2: Some silver object cannot be bombed unless some other object has been built despite the object to-be-build and the silver object never interacting.
There are a few flying missions. Whenever you happen to collect a power-up - which due to bad visibility cannot always be avoided - the game starts to make an unnerving sound for the duration of the power-up. Later in my game I simply turned off sounds altogether.
Again, I recommend LEGO Star Wars: The Complete Saga to those that don't mind playing only the main part of the game or have a high tolerance against boredom when 100%-ing.

This game is... more enjoyable than NFS:MW 2012, which I spent like $60 when it came out because of the MW name, and I hate it so much.
Undercover is a game that gives you a feeling that they rushed too hard during development, so it lacks testing, refinement, and thoughts. It carries quite a few promises, but is very disappointing.
Pros:
1. Fast-paced action easily makes one EXCITED!
2. A good collection of cars.
3. A nice world to roam about.
4. Cut-scenes are quite well made.
5. Chances are that you buy this game when it's on sale, very cheap.
Cons:
1. Physics is ridiculous, when crash happens, all cars seem to have infinite mass. Mario Kart has better physics and makes more sense. NFS is not famous for physics accuracy, but this game is way too off-scale.
2. If you drive manual, you will easily feel that the cars' torque-rev relationship is pretty ridiculous.
3. Brake is so ridiculously powerful, and the car has ridiculous amount of grip.
4. They hired Maggie Q and others to make nice movies, so it seems that they focused on SP. However AI is ridiculous. Anything controlled by AI just makes no sense.
5. AI racers seem to be "given" speed and accleration. Sometimes I can have 200 feet in the lead and I am faster round the last corner, but the second car just acclerates ridiculously and robs my first place. It feels that those cars do not have actual drivers in them.
6. Roaming traffic cars are quite amazing, not only AI racers ram you like crazy, those roaming traffic cars also ram into you for no reason at all.
7. There's almost no balance between cars and missions. You can win by miles using Lotus Elise against some really slow Volkswagen, and at some other locatons you will face Audi R8, Gallardo, and many other cars that are way faster. BTW Lotus Elise is extremely overpowered.
8. I can't believe how bad the cops are. They seem to give up chasing you as long as you are 100 inches ahead of them. Sometimes it can be extremely hard to complete missions like cost-to-state challenge, because the cops do not chase you at all, even you are at heat level 5.
9. You can easily use the TAB key to fast travel to just jump right to the next race, so although there's a huge amazing open world, chances are that you don't even roam about at all.
10. Graphics are okay for a game this old, and it uses similar color scheme as the original NFS:MW. However it looks a lot less attractive than NFS:MW for some reason.
11. Road surface is modeled quite badly. Different road surface (asphalt, grass, dirt, etc) feels quite similar, and the only difference seems to be the smoothness.
12. Its compatibility with controllers has lots of problems. If I have my keyboard, XBOX360 controller, and my Logitech G27 all connected at the same time, the car will keep steering to the right, and the menu cursor keeps going down.
13. The cars' performace has little to do with their real-life version.
Conclusion:
If this game is on sale, and if you want some excitment road racing, and if you are not good at braking in racing games, pick this up. It can make you blood boil (Rush-time High Way Battle is the best mode in this game IMO), and it does not require too much skill.

I grew up during the days of arena shooters. It's all I played. Unreal 2K4 and Tribes. I had really high hopes for Toxikk to bring it back but they mismanaged that project so I kind of scoffed when I saw Cliffy B was back in action.

If you're new to arena shooters. Don't judge the game on the first hour. It's fast paced and it's not a feel good game. It doesn't have the Texas sized headshot hit boxes, it doesn't hold your hand to make it easier for you.  It's up to YOU to practice and raise your skill ceiling. The better you become, the better you'll do. While this is team orientated, you can stand on your own and do well without the need of a team/healer backing you up.
There's different modes to play through. Blitzball where you pick up a ball and try running it to your enemy's basket. Occypy which is basically King of the Hill but the zones switch and a few others.
You'll have different classes that have their own abilities to suit your play style.
So far balancing has been done very well.
The maps are fun, the fast paced in your face gameplay is something I've missed for the past decade, and overall the different classes are a blast to play.
At this price, GIVE IT A SHOT. If you're not hooked within your refund time, I doubt you'll care later.

NOT SOME OVERWATCH CLONE -
LawBreaks is awesome it is the cure for having played to much Overwatch.  Despite what you may have heard this game is no overwatch or team fortress 2 clone.  If you had to classify it I would say it is a mash up of old school quake and team fortress combined with the gun play of newer modern warfare type games.  The game consists of 5 player teams across a bunch of different maps.  The game types are a couple variations of capture the flag, king of the hill and capture the point.  Unlike a game like overwatch that is very dependent on a quality team make up in Lawbreakers you have still win with two players that don't know what to do and our playing the wrong character for the map. This is refreshing because you still have a chance to win even if you are down with half the objectives already claimed.  Game typically last for about 10 minutes but on occasion against equally matched teams they can go for the entire 20 minutes.  The gun play is very tight and the weapons feel weighty.  As far as I can tell the netcode is running really well and the hit boxes are accurate to the character models.  Right now I believe Wraith is a little OP given the range of his weapon and his speed but all characters are viable.
Pros:
1.  Great gun play
2.  Good net code
3.  Quickly match into games
4.  All heroes viable across different game types
5.  Quality graphics
6.  Unique IP from small studio that plays like a AAA title
7.  Great game for teamwork
8.  Multiple routes to victory not a rock paper shotgun type of game
9.  Not pay to win
10.  Highly addicting gameplay.
Cons:
1. Blitz ball team can be carried by one player that knows the map and is playing a quick character
2. Some heroes are less viable at higher levels of play
Questions:
1.  What is the post beta anti hack going to be. Hope it is battleye.
Overall this is a great game easy to learn but difficult to master even if your team is down you always feel like you can come back and possibly win.

Legacy of Kain: Defiance is the fifth game in a series of highly story-focused games that technically fall under the category of action.
In Defiance, control alternates between the series' two protagonists, Kain and Raziel in the world of Nosgoth.
The story to Defiance is extremely well done. It picks up shortly after the events of LoK: Soul Reaver 2. Raziel has managed to pospone his fate, and Kain still lurks around in the shadows, trying to discover ways to restore balance to the world of Nosgoth.
In a departure for the series, the game takes a more action-based approach to combat and gameplay. You no longer have to toss enemies into lakes or fire to kill them (though that’s still an option in many places), but instead what you get is more enemy variety and much tougher battles. Kain and Raziel’s skills are largely interchangeable, with both playing the same. Except Kain is stronger and Raziel is faster. Both, once fully experienced, can pull off insane combos.
As the other games of the series, Defiance has puzzles as well, some more grueling than others. But all rather cleverly designed.
The Legacy of Kain series has some of the highest quality voice acting around. The entire cast brings all of the characters to life, from the protagonists to the ever-embittered Vorador, melencholy Janos, devious Moebius, even the vampire hunters and undead.
The graphics in this game are the best in the series so far. The characters are all well designed and the use of Gothic backgrounds suits the game well.
Legacy of Kain: Defiance delivers what it promised, the continuation of the series that answers more questions then it proposes, a refined combat system and replay value. This game will be sure to twist and make that brain think through it's depth-full storyline.

LawBreaks is awesome it is the cure for having played to much Overwatch.  Despite what you may have heard this game is no overwatch or team fortress 2 clone.  If you had to classify it I would say it is a mash up of old school quake and team fortress combined with the gun play of newer modern warfare type games.  The game consists of 5 player teams across a bunch of different maps.  The game types are a couple variations of capture the flag, king of the hill and capture the point.  Unlike a game like overwatch that is very dependent on a quality team make up in Lawbreakers you have still win with two players that don't know what to do and our playing the wrong character for the map. This is refreshing because you still have a chance to win even if you are down with half the objectives already claimed.  Game typically last for about 10 minutes but on occasion against equally matched teams they can go for the entire 20 minutes.  The gun play is very tight and the weapons feel weighty.  As far as I can tell the netcode is running really well and the hit boxes are accurate to the character models.  Right now I believe Wraith is a little OP given the range of his weapon and his speed but all characters are viable.

Batman: Arkham Asylum is one of my favourite games of all time. I've played through this many times on PS3, which explains my low playtime as I already know what happens. Do I get bored of doing everything all over again? Nope. An interesting story, the best melee combat system in gaming, a stealth system with high variety, backtracking that dosen't feel boring and tons of lore and easter eggs are just some reasons why this game is amazing.
This is the game that began the "Freeflow" combat trend in many recent releases, but none of them have matched up to the original. It's smooth, requires skill and not button mashing, and rewards people who can get into those high hit streaks.
The stealth is great too. Multiple ways to take down and lure your enemies with some smart A.I to back it up. It may not seem hard at first, but it does get pretty challenging later on.
There are also challenge maps that require you to get a certain amount of points with the freeflow system or perform certain takedowns with the stealth system. Extreme versions of these maps offer an even harder challenge with some unique takedown requisites.
However, while the PC port is great, it is missing the Joker Challenge Maps which are exclusive to the PS3 and Mac versions of the game. If you have either of these, pick that version up instead as he is a very fun character to play as.
The original freeflow game that began one of the best franchises in gaming still holds up to this day. Play it whether you are a Batman superfan or you have no idea what he is. Overall: 10/10.

Batman: Arkham Asylum is a third person action-adventure game that puts you in control of the famous Caped Crusader.  Up until this game came out in 2009, there were very few, if any, good video games based on comic book super-heroes, but Rocksteady really nailed this one.
The game follows Batman as he delivers his arch-nemesis, the Joker, to Arkham Asylum, a facility for the criminally insane located on an island off the shores of Gotham City.  As you might imagine, all hell breaks loose and you square off against many of your well-known super-villains and their thugs as you try to restore order.
The island is quite large and you get to (eventually) access all the buildings situated there.  Loading times are magically kept to a bare minimum.  The game uses the checkpoint save system, but they are fairly generous with those saves and you are rarely faced with having to replay very much after an unfortunate failure.  There are three difficulty choices for the game and they do an excellent job of slowly introducing you to the moves and gadgets.
The storyline is well-written and gives great purpose to your actions.  There are many short cutscenes and the performances by the voice actors are superb throughout, especially fan favorite Mark Hamill’s Joker.  So many quotable lines and wonderful humor make this a joy to experience.  The graphics are also excellent including the animation of the action.  You really feel like you are Batman, whether brawling with goons or using your grapple to soar around the island.  The number of moves you can perform is staggering.
Since you are Batman, gadgets are an important part of the experience.  No shortage here as you have quite an array of items to choose from including batarangs, explosives, hacking devices, zip lines and more.  The Batmobile even makes a brief appearance.
This game is meant to be played with a controller although the traditional PC keyboard/mouse setup works just fine.  In fact, I played it without a controller against the advice of family and friends and felt completely in control, even with my abysmal gaming skills.
Collectors and achievement junkies will be in heaven as there is much to do, adding to the story’s gameplay.  The Riddler has planted puzzles galore for you to find and solve and much of it unlocks interesting facts about the story and the characters.  There are also challenges that are best tackled after the campaign is complete (so all gadgets are unlocked).  These involve rounds of combat and stealth challenges in different settings.  Depending on your gaming abilities, it could take over 30 hours to master all the challenges and collectibles in the game.
The GOTY Edition can usually be found on sale if you have patience and it is definitely a great value if you have any interest in the world of Batman.  Even after a few years, it holds up very well.

As far as the campaign goes, the map is not a 3D world, but more of a traditional paper looking map. It's more colorful than the first TW game, Shogun, and it's personally my favorite style.
The goal of the campaign is to start in a country, build your armies, and then INVADE! Invade other countries, but beware: as your army grows, and you have more to manage, some generals may rebel. (When my generals are about to rebel, I like to send them by themselves to figth a HUGE enemy army. It gets the job done well. )
Overall, I think this is a fun game, and well worth the few dollars.

Sorry, but this game is massively overrated.
The famous combat system is klunky, especially since combo systems have been implemented in much better ways in the past. I just don't get why this condescendingly simple, monotonous combat system is so revered by fans. It's just Assassin's Creed combat with a combo system crammed in and the counter attacks no longer instant kill.
The stealth isn't great, especially as enemies ave a tendency to group together in sections you are supposed to stealth past, meaning you have to wait for an extended period of time for them to organically split up before you can stealth attack them one by one.
As for the skill tree, all of the upgrades are either utterly redundant or you should have had them from the start. There is literally no reason for it to be there.
Also, the boss fights are utter BS.
Finally, there's the accursed Riddler puzzles. They are optional, but the game keeps reminding you of their existence to the point that it's better to do them to get all the irritating reminders off of your screen. However, "puzzles" is a generous term. Basically you scan every unique asset in case it happens to be the solution to the "puzzle". Often, I woud just stand in the middle of the room and slowly turn, scanning as I go, until it registered something.
Overall, not a terrible game, but hardly deserving of the overwhelming praise poured onto it by doting critics and the fans who have no doubt already downvoted this review. Batman fans probably get a kick out of it, as would people who seriously claim to like "Arkham style combat". This game truly encapsulates what it feels like to be Batman, a perfect balance of stealth and action. The stealth and action complement each other rather than juxtapose one another like in other games, you can go all out and dive into a crowd and take them out with sheer brawn if you want to most of the time but you can also take the sneaky approach.
I cannot describe how satisfying it to creep around a room, silently picking off goons one by one and listening to the others slowly begin to panic before you finally take them out as well.
The environments are wonderful, not only do they look great but they give you plenty of open areas to run, climb and swing across. Exploring is fun and intuitive, especially with the use of Detective Vision to help you find vents and tunnels to crawl about in.
One last touch that I as a Batman fan really loved was the voice cast, several characters, most notably Batman, Joker and Harley are all played by the same voice actors who played them in Batman the Animated Series! They have played them in many shows and films I know but BTAS is where it all started for this crew. It really helped the characters feel like ones I already knew, rather than re-meeting them all again in a new context.
If you love Batman, stealth, action, fun characters or good story telling in any sense, you will love this game.

This game is everything that was ever censored on TV.  It is an 80s horror fan's dream game.
I grew up with horror.  Its kept me sane.  The world has a kind of passive-aggressive horror about it that drives good people crazy.  Games like this are a great way to reconcile that with your subconscious -  that's right - Harvester spills it all out in the open - from closet BDSM house moms to the Illuminati.  Strangely - crazy games like this one remind you that you're NOT crazy.  Great way to relieve stress.  Harvester also has moments which send the player into fits of laughter.

The story is a whole heap of 80s tropes, icons, and catchphrases slapped together with a hint of modern spice that does something that I personally think is special: while the setting, dialogue, and weapons are wild, none of these things become overly ridiculous as the game progresses; no wildly out of place bonerfarts or buttstallions prodding you with a red-hot poker for a reaction here. What happens instead is that the story and setting are introduced immediately as parody, allowing the player to immediately suspend their disbelief and simply enjoy the ride.
Rex is a great extension of the player: he has small reactions to the world around him (including missions), the character is actually enjoying himself, and there’s no emotional turmoil for Rex outside of a very 80s twist at the end. This is in stark contrast to young Whiny Zoolander from Far Cry 3, who couldn’t decide if he was a hardened killer or a scared kid who just wanted to take his friends and family home and could somehow proficiently wield firearms with zero prior training (I’m not purposefully omitting the main character’s name, I actually do not remember him as anything else but Whiny Zoolander). Rex’s character is actually surprisingly important in this regard because if the main character is lively and likes what he’s doing, the player will be on the receiving end of those feelings as well.
In FC3, Whiny Zoolander is a know-nothing college student who has to slowly become lord of the game, but there isn’t any extreme challenge early on because FC3 forcibly railroads the player into what they should and shouldn’t go after early on with mandatory early missions, so this limitation does nothing to actually make the player truly feel as if they’re overcoming a challenge. Quite conversely, in combination with the elasticated XP gain, it simply makes the player wonder when they’ll finally be able to get into the thick of it as they click on lone guards and wild animals for the nth time and by the time they reach the second island, the game is already almost over. It also doesn’t help that in FC3, any weapon that actually looks fun is stashed behind a tech tree, quest, and/or XP wall.
The most important thing about Blood Dragon’s combat to me is that although there are fewer weapons to choose from altogether, none of the weapons suck. Instead, they start off good and just get better the more one plays and the more the player unlocks things. Weapons are accurate, reasonably powerful in regards to what each weapon does, and have plenty of ammunition. Players can carry 4 weapons right off the bat. Weapon upgrades merely enhance the versatility and further increase the power of the weapons they upgrade instead of being absolutely necessary to obtain reasonable firepower and accuracy. There is no weapon deprecation; instead, weapons fill different purposes and niches.
Another one of my absolute favorite parts of the game is the fact that there’s no overarching “best strat” of just assassinating everything in your path or taking high ground in one spot and picking the bots off as they predictably run to trigger the base alarm. You can choose to be a sneaky bugger and chain assassination kills if you want, or you can go right in guns blazing and break some backs. The bases were constructed in such a way that there’s more thought and freedom to what the player can actually do. There’s a lot more detail to each base in Blood Dragon than in FC3.
Another thing I’d like to bring up is that while Far Cry 3 will have people clocking in low double-digit hours if they want to hunt down everything in the game, Blood Dragon is an easy 7 or 8 hours of constant fun depending on how one plays it. The quests are much more active, but there are fewer of them. The immediate response to this is “Well that sucks! I want a game with content!” My response to that would be, “Would you like to jackass around the map just to stealth kill the same officer 60 times or would you rather a rescue mission take place in reasonably close proximity to a base you want to capture right after?” Essentially, it’s quality and uniqueness over quantity and repetitiveness.
Despite my lavish praise, Blood Dragon isn’t the perfect game I’ve made it out to be in the last few paragraphs. It has its fair share of shortcomings. For one, the world is pretty static. The AI doesn’t really do anything to step up unit spawns and patrols (more and bigger squads of enemies) once the player starts their conquest, it’s more of a world that’s simply yours to take from without consequence. The enemy types are pretty limited – human enemy types (the most common) are limited to 5. You fight lots of grunts and Molotov tossers with a scattering of heavy troopers and the odd sniper here and there, and that’s it. I had the following gripe for when I played Wolfenstein The New Order: with the setting provided and how wild and imaginative the game was, there wasn’t enough experimentation with unit types in relation to the trope. Cyberninjas that could digitize themselves to hide in computers? Enslaved Vietnam War II veterans encased in robotic suits? Luddite forces that fight against all the factions with old or even primitive weaponry?
The fact that the super weapon was highly encouraged until reaching “the” mount during the ending sequence was also not terribly fun, since it was a thoughtless “point and win” weapon. I would have loved if it was a plot device instead, with Rex going in guns blazing with a horde of angry nerd scientists jacking helicopters and vehicles and fighting to support Rex. There were so many explosive barrels and variances in height that it would have made sense for that entire first half of the ending sequence to be a clash between the two factions.
Overall, I really liked Far Cry 3 Blood Dragon, much more than the base game. I recommend it to anyone looking for a fun time, but if you’re someone who doesn’t like dropping $15 on 7 hours of content, grab it on sale.

Rob stores -> Heists -> Buy that one cheap garage -> Heists -> Even more heists -> Buy the cheapest company and warehouse -> Grind crates and hesists to unlock everything in the game -> Ignore motorcycle club because of telephone spam

I liked this game. I love my Jeep and  I love driving it on trails so naturally this game drew me in. I have played spintires and once this game works out a few physics issues I would say it is as good at capturing the offroad experiece as spintires. Spintires never really gave you the opportunity to do any real crawling and this game does.
Here's my main issue. The vehicles are far too bouncy. I wish there was a way to air down the tires or fine tune the suspension set up because you drive over a wooden bridge with any form of speed and your vehicle is bouncing off the trail. It's almost like the vehicle has no weight. When you go over a crack you bounce out instead of the tire going down in and requiring a bit of work to get out. When you approach a rock instead of hitting it nice and slow and crawling over it you bounce and bounce and hope you dont bounce off the trail.
The tires are another issue. I want to be able to lower my tire pressure to increase my grip on the rocks. These over inflated tires are like riding on balloons. They're jsut too bouncy! They also do not grip like real tires do. It's too easy to slide on obstacles that wouldn't slide on in real life.
Overall I really enjoy the game and will continue to play it despite my issues because it is fun and you can just group the bounce issues into part of the challenge. But at the end of the day, I would like it to feel a lot more real so I can experience the challenge of crawling when I can't take my own Jeep out on the trails.

Games can take on many different forms. Some are super complex, and feature a robust art style. Some go for a simpler approach, and may use realism as its drawing factor. Neither is superior to the other, it's all a matter of taste. The options are limitless for what form a game may take. Even, say... squares. Lots of squares.
The ♥♥♥♥ is going on in this game? That's a very good question. You see, there's squares. Cubes, rather. Because they're three-dimensional.
This is Edge. Original title, yes. They came up with it all by themselves.
Edge is a game about squares that must roll around other squares in order to collect squares and make it to the square at the end of all of the other squares.
It's easy to see where its simplistic roots come from. Edge originally launched on iOS, with ports later coming to many more platforms including the Wii U, 3DS, PC, and Android. A mobile game, of course. That explains everything.
Edging is a simple concept. Masturbate until you're right on the verge of climax, and then stop. Right at the edge. Wait for your body to settle down, and then do it again. Pushing slowly closer and closer to the edge, building up the tension in you as the sweet release of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ lies just out of reach. Sometimes it's a little kinkier, with a dom policing your edging. If you♥♥♥♥♥too soon, they beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you.
This game is kinda like that.
It's not really a puzzle game. Calling this a puzzle game is like calling a traffic light a puzzle game. Green means go, red means stop. I mean, I suppose that's kind of a puzzle. Especially if you're colorblind. Or completely blind, that usually makes things like crossing the street or driving kind of difficult. Especially if it's an ambulance, with a lady giving birth inside. She's all grunting and pushing and trying to get the baby out, and her husband is all "What the ♥♥♥♥ are you doing, who are you, stop please, you're gonna kill us all" and getting on your case for stealing an ambulance that just so happened to be parked outside someone's house. It might not even be an ambulance, it might just be a family's SUV. In labor, having a panic attack because you forced yourself into their car, same thing.
It's not really any kind of game. There's what could be called obstacles or puzzles all around each course, but they're always simplistic and easily maneuverable in a way that's only vaguely stimulating.
Edge is pretty good for a mobile game at least. It's relaxing to roll squares around while you're pooping. And the art style is extremely satisfying. Some very striking minimalism. It's very nice just to look at.
Don't know what the ♥♥♥♥ is happening in this game, but there's some damn fine lookin' squares. Mmm, mmm.
If you're looking for a game to really push you, challenge you, and get you riled up, Edge is not it. There's no climax to Edge, much like actual edging. There's just squares. Lots, and lots of ♥♥♥♥ing squares.
It's a perfect example of the great things designers are capable of on mobile. And, at the same time, the many drawbacks of mobile. It's designed with simplicity, accessibility, and ease of getting into in mind. It's easy to pick up a level, play it, and stop. It's not something that could realistically hold your attention for longer than an hour, but poops don't usually take that long anyway. Considering it's only a couple bucks, it's definitely worth it.
Short, sweet, and simple. But clever, smart, and stylish. By far some of the nicest squares I've ever seen. But still, this game is literally just ♥♥♥♥ing squares. That's all it is. All there is to it.
Like they always say. Every square has its edges. They usually say that about roses, actually. But a game about roses would be even stupider than a game about stupid ♥♥♥♥ing squares.

Always Sometimes Monsters is a game where you live the life of a broken adult, trying to reclaim their life but face many decisions that a normal human being would most likely never face. This is the story of your character, whom ever it may be, facing many everyday problems, from money to love. It is an amazing game that always managed to throw my emotions around and made me feel for the character. The one thing I would complain about this game is how the game handles money. Every "main quest" has some cash output for you to progress, but these "main quests" do not give enough money. After you are done with these "main quests", you are stuck to do an odd job at a employment agency to get the remaining cash to progress and these jobs are very tedious and boring, unlike the rest of the game. I would recommend this game to anyone willing to dish out 10 dollars and ~7-8 of their life for an amazing story and never ending music that WILL get stuck in your head.

So I don't usually write this sort of stuff but I felt like this game deserved an exception. So what I have to say about this game... Always Sometimes Monsters is simply engaging. Whitout giving away to much of it's stoyline, which frankly it is nearly imposible to spoil anything, this was one of the few games I've played lately that made made me actually care for my character and their outcome in the story. Maybe it's because you can be whomever you want and pick any choices you feel like, or maybe because this is a regular story about a regular person. Your character is not a hero, it's not a villian, they are just trying to get on with their lifes trying not too make any wrong choices, which is also kind of difficult because life is like that, at the end, you always have one or two wrong choices.
So, as a tl;dr, this game is one lil' neat indie game that explores so many issues, many of them feel wrong, some of them feel right. Just like life itself. I would recommend this to anyone wanting to expercience a different kind of story.

If I could have given this game a neutral rating I would have, but since I have to pick one I’ve gone with recommending it.
ASM certainly got me hooked at the start – the freedom of character choice was good, and it seemed like there was a lot to do. From Day 1, there are quite a few options available to you, and many choices you can make. The game claims to run on a system where every small choice affects you, but in the end that doesn’t really happen.
The games plot is linear – no matter which decisions you make, you always end up travelling between certain places to make your way towards your ex’s wedding, although there are a few options on how to do that dictated by what your do in the places you visit. A lot of short side missions never really do anything – the phrase “You’re a good friend” appears several times throughout the story, but these characters never really do anything else afterwards. One of the side missions even seems like it’s going to reappear near the end (when it turns out a big event happening at the same time as the wedding is one you can win a pass to for someone) but that doesn’t go anywhere, the kid you help out is completely missing from the last arc. No matter your actions, you’ll end up in the final situation where all that happens is you might have locked yourself out of the endings.
Speaking of the endings… my main gripe with this game is that they’re unsatisfying. Endings don’t necessarily need to be happy, but all of the outcomes for ASM leave a sour taste in one’s mouth. To start off with, the stamina system (which exists solely to keep you spending money on food or fishing) means that if you go to sleep when it’s too low, game over. It’s far too abrupt. Obviously it doesn’t need to be dramatic, but a little cutscene of what happens during the night would help rather than the screen flashing “YOU DIED IN YOUR SLEEP” and taking you back to the title screen. I presume something similar happens if you manage to waste enough time to miss the wedding – although there may be some event that forces you to get there anyway. As for the main endings, some of them flat out don’t work – such as you becoming a millionaire but inexplicably becoming a hobo, and others just see that characters don’t work together. Even the ‘perfect’ ending sees your love hint at being discontent with the situation, before leaving you in a pointless epilogue which seems to exist just so you can play the video games freely or try and hit up a high score in time spent in the shower, which could have been accomplished by adding an extra option to the title screen upon completion.
The moral of the game seems to be that you either have to screw people over or be a successful gambler to make any money. I disagree with it but I understand why the developers have done it.
However, for all its flaws, I did enjoy the game (sans the ending.) Of the 10 or so hours I put into it, I enjoyed most of them – the story is nothing spectacular, but it’s enjoyable. The graphics aren’t the best and the music choice is all over the place but I still liked playing it (even if most of the time was spent save scumming on scratch cards, races and casinos.) The developers insert themselves from time to time and there are other brief moments of humour which certainly help with the experience.
All in all, ASM claims that it presents a story which is heavily decided by the choices you make. As you’d expect, this isn’t the case because that would be a development nightmare. Despite that, the game is mostly enjoyable despite having a bitter aftertaste due to the unsatisfying endings. While I don’t think Vagabond Dog have hit it off with this game, it looks like there is a lot of potential so I’ll probably keep an eye out to see what else they’ve got in store in the future.

From Critical Miss' Best Games of 2012
In her 10/10 review for Destructoid, Holly Green described Mark of the Ninja as "the benchmark by which all stealth games are now measured." I can't say I disagree.
MOTN may not be the overall best game in the stealth genre - its cheesy, grindhouse-aping narrative prevents it from toppling either Thief 2 or Chaos Theory - but its gameplay is both a celebration and a distillation of everything that makes the genre great. There isn't one genre mechanic that MOTN doesn't somehow improve. It does away with clunky light and sound meters and instead tells you everything you need to know via series of organic visual cues. Objects in shadow are rendered as subtle outlines. Sound is represented by a series of concentric rings emanating from your feet. Leaning against a door allows you to peek into the room beyond, no button presses required. MOTN is the perfect example of streamlined game design. Your options are many and varied, but they're all accessed through an elegant, intuitive interface that never puts itself between you and the game.
This innate understanding of the genre extends to MOTN's campaign design. While most stealth games offer "gadgets" as a way to escape failure, MOTN actively encourages you to engage enemies in varied ways and with different tools. Kill them, toy with them, do anything but avoid them; the game rewards pretty much every approach, both lethal and non-lethal. Klei seems to understand that, at their core, stealth games are essentially a series of puzzles. MOTN funnels you into tight, complex arrangements of sentries that require increasingly elaborate strategies. The guards are just stupid enough to be manipulated into leaving themselves open, but are still smart enough to pose a threat.
MOTN actually shares a lot in common with #4, Dishonored. Both Corvo and the Marked One share a similar move set, right down to freezing time and teleporting. But while Dishonored dumped the player into a series of relatively open environments and left them to their own devices, MOTN provides tools and then problems to solve. If Dishonored is a playground, MOTN is an assault course.

Interestingly, the game offers you two different modes at the beginning, Story and Stealth. Although the core gameplay is the same, in Stealth mode the family can see you and you must remain hidden in order to be able to influence them. You accomplish this by hiding inside light bulbs, for some reason that is never explained. Unfortunately, both modes get tedious. In Story, the game has no challenge to it and it's basically just a mix of "walking simulator" and choose-your-own adventure gameplay. In Stealth mode, you end up spending a lot of time just hanging out in lightbulbs, waiting for family members to walk to another room.
The core gameplay consists of you reading notes and letters left by the family members to find out what they want. You can also read their thoughts and explore their memories. Ultimately, you find out what each person wants and then select who gets their want by touching the object associated with the want. Gameplay then shifts to nighttime mode where you read more notes left by the house's previous owners and can choose a compromise for another family member to at least partially get their want.
There are a lot of unique ideas present in this gameplay loop that I really like. The problem is, what I have just described is the whole game and you have to repeat it for nine chapters with very little variation. What feels very fresh and interesting at the start of the game feels way overplayed and boring by the end, even though the game takes only 2-3 hours to complete. In the end, I felt that the game only really had about 30 minutes worth of ideas and the game felt very stretched and empty as a result.
The game has a great cell-shaded aesthetic and the family members all move about and act in realistic ways. I found it immersive in this way where I really did feel like I was observing a real family go about their day. Unfortunately, the graphics suffer the same problem as the gameplay, as being confined to a single house with three characters for several hours means that you are looking at the same boring rooms over and over again.
The music does a good job setting the tone but isn't anything to write home about. On the other hand, the voice acting is great, which really carried the game since it's mostly about listening to the internal monologues of these characters. The actors were very convincing and were able to put a lot of emotion into their lines without hamming it up.
Essentially, the family has moved to a remote summer home so that the father/husband can focus on writing his novel. The mother/wife is unhappy in the marriage and an aspiring artist. Their son is struggling with bullying and schoolwork. It's not the most interesting story but it is very human and the characters feel like real people. It is interesting to see how decisions made in one chapter effect the rest and what ending you get. Also welcome is a "The story so far" feature when you load up the game.
Overall, I felt the game just got very stale by the end but it's still a unique experience that you may like if you want a non-violent, non-competitive game focused on family drama. If you like the "Aspirations" part of the Sims games, you may find something to like here. For most people, however, I think the experience may fall a bit flat.

This satirical game is about DLC. If that wasn't obvious from the title, well, this game may not be for you. Anyways, in this game, you play as, well, a character. Just a generic sprite in a empty world. That's right, it's completely empty besides a princess and an evil arch-villain. You have to buy DLC to do literally everything in this game, including walking left. This said, the DLC purchasing is what gives it its charm. It is made to mock all these other free-to-play games that, under the technicality of the term, are free to play, but cannot be played effectively without buying some DLC starter pack. Of course, in this game, you don't actually have to use real money to purchase any of the DLC. The currency you use is the in-game coins, so all you will pay for the game is the initial purchase price. It even comes with a DLC Expansion of the story: Live Freemium or DIE!. Overall, this game is worth the price, even if it is a little shorter than it could have been.

There is plenty of replay value here (it's worth beating at least twice) and even if you play it just once, it's very enjoyable from start to finish. I can't give this game enough praise, it's one of the best indie games I've played and well worth the asking price (on sale or not).

This game is one of the trickiest and cutest things in the puzzle genre. Getting stuck on a puzzle only to come back the day after and solve it in 5 seconds is VERY common, because the answers just require a different perspective to solve. The idea that the snakebirds keep their contorted shape after moving is novel and used to a satisfying degree to solve puzzles.
Basically:
YES: If you like really hard puzzles that actually feel incredibly rewarding to solve, buy! Then pump your fists in the air every single time you solve one and treat yourself to something really good (soda, beer, whatever floats your ice cream)!
NO: If you're the kind to tear your hair out in frustration over puzzle games, do NOT buy. Keep your hair where it belongs and feel smug about not throwing yourself into this deceptively cute puzzle hell.

I have no idea why this game has only 65% positive rating. Wait, actually I do, but more on that later.
For some reason I played DXMD just recently and totally skipped its release, also meaning I skipped all the hype about it. To be honest, I even barely remembered what Human Revolution was about, so I basically played this game unclouded without any memories about its predecessor and without any grand expectations.
And oh boy, I had a blast! To make this reading easier, I made this review using bulleted list.
Alright, so about this 65% rating. When the game was just released, fresh, I heard, vaguely, about microtransactions issue the game had, but I did not care enough at the time to understand what all the fuss was about. Well, now I do, I have seen the in-game shop, and yes, you can buy bullets, weapons, Praxis kits and other consumables there; but really, it looks like all the complainers haven't actually played the game at all. If you will play the game how it is meant to be played (meaning you will explore your surroundings and pick up all the stuff laying around), you will never be short of anything. In fact, when I finished the game, I had 20k credits, 20 multitools, 1k various bullets and 10 (!) spare Praxis kits I didn’t even spent because I already had everything for stealth-hacking playstyle I chose to play.
So, all the downvotes were just because of possibility to buy some in-game things for real money, and might I remind you, it's not even a multiplayer game! So I don’t really get what the heck this all was about; including microtransactions in the game probably was a bad desicion, but in-game shop availability doesn't eradicate all the amazing work that was put into making the game itself. Therefore, if you missed that game just because you heard of microtransactions - congratulations, you just spoiled yourself this great game for no real reason.
So, definitely
. If you want to play the game with rich story and fascinating world - it is a game for you. Do not be too sensitive to unfounded accusations that are irrelevant to the game in the first place.

Time Trap is one of those games that I enjoy but have a hard time putting my finger on exactly why.  The presentation has a lot to be desired, and the writing could certainly use some polishing up by an English speaking proof reader.  But the story isn't why I'm here.  Despite the abundance of HOPAs on Steam, there's a dearth of pure hidden object games on the platform.  And sometimes I just want to load up a game and shut my brain down while I search for objects on my screen.
And search for objects I did.  Actually, if you're working towards 100%-ing the game, you'll be playing each scene over and over until you've successfully collected all of the items and scored 3 stars.  While this admittedly can be a bit of a grind, I found it quite enjoyable.  Learning all of the objects' placements and quickly picking them out was satisfying in a way that's hard to describe.  Using the HINT button for those particularly difficult to find items doesn't feel like much of a penalty either, but it's actually nice to have a HOG that doesn't enforce no-hint playthroughs for achievements.  For those looking for even more challenge, there are leader boards for each HOS.  This was something I wasn't particularly interested in myself, but it adds replay for those who are so inclined.
Really, there's not much more I can say.  If you're looking for a HOG without the adventure-lite elements, you might want to check this one out.  Even at full price, I feel like I've gotten my money's worth.  It may not be the perfect game, but if you just want something to whittle away your time without having to put much thought into it, you can do much worse.

Time Trap – Hidden Objects:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
The Journalist John Doe has vanished unexpectedly. Would it be because he uncovered a distressing story and published his findings a few years ago? Don’t you remember, that experiment at the scientific centre that went sideways? The entire complex and it proximities (miles after miles) were put in quarantine. Deep in your stomach, you know he went back to investigate once more! Are you willing to follow his steps? Is it a Time Trap?
Time Trap is an adventure / Hidden Objects game where you retrace the steps of the journalist, John Doe.
This game has over fifty hidden objects and puzzles (recreate a picture) to go through. I did enjoy the fact that some of the objects are well-blended within pictures and can be easily missed. The story itself is very thin and as a player, you don’t have the ability to choose a path like other games of the same genre will enable you to.  In this game, you’ll be led towards it. The ability to zoom in and out is nice and can be helpful to spot objects. However, I am not a fan of having to move up and down the screen in order to find objects - it can be frustrating at times.

In terms of the gameplay, you’ll have a certain time limit within which to clear a stage. If you manage to clear a stage super-fast, you’ll be rewarded with three stars for that level and will receive a great numbers of points. If you find objects within a certain time limit (we are talking seconds here), points will multiply very quickly, which will give you a chance to show your name in the leader board section. So make sure to spot all the objects before you start your round.

Graphically, the game looks good and it is easy to play.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Nice Graphics
-	Stacks of levels
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No trading cards
-	Thin story line
-	Mechanisms could have been better
6/10

The game begins and the inner monologue suggests that you are to find a man of substance. It turns out it's substance as in 'substance abuse' not 'substantial character', because everyone in the room is a copy pasted background prop who's dialog only differs in the drink that they offer for a toast. After I make my arbitrary choice and accidentally become gay due to reckless plot advancement I'm confronted again by the inner monologue, or as I suspect simply a narrator stuck in a flimsy framing mechanism, and asked if these were to be the heroes of the story: I say no. Thought that was pretty clever since this game makes it immediately clear that it's a hella-indie pretentious mess with an emphasis on decisions™, but it just reset me to the time when I began my fruitless search for a character of substance. The sort of thing that happens when you exit the first dungeon of any other game in case you want to redo something; speaking of any other game, that's exactly what I'd rather be playing. That was my introduction to the game from the developers, and I think it's a great introduction from me as a reviewer to a potential player as well.
I'd better write a bit about the more mechanical side of the game. The level design allows no visible indication for the occasional stage left, right and bottom doorways so you just have to walk into the one-dimensional wall and see what happens. The art is a bad mix of stylings. The audio is comprised of free sound effects that I've heard before in other indie games accompanied by four note synth music, probably from a free trial of Fruity Loops.

I remember the FMV genre being an odd novelty in the video game industry which was both amazing and annoying at the same time. Seeing live actors fully interacting within a digital world was fascinating. Unfortunately, the concept was poorly implemented--resulting in all frills and no thrills gameplay. Corpse Killer immediately comes to mind; what a horrible game. Point-and-click adventure seemed best suited for this particular class, and Harvester is a fine example of that. I'm surprised at the level of violence in this game and how it managed to sneak under the radar of sensitive noses.
FMV may be dead, and will probably never return; but I salute the hardwork by programmers to preserve these lost artifacts for future generations.

It really feels this game is taking PC gaming to its limits, so if you have a solid rig to run it then you will find here one of the best looking and most technically impressive games for PC ever. Having a system capable of running this beast on ultra-settings will make you think that all your hardware is being put to the test and that your investment was totally worth it.
I’m very happy with this version, yes the PC version is awesome and everything is almost flawless.

Mark of the Ninja is a 2d stealth platformer that applies the stealth genre in unique ways and encourages a wide variety of approaches to tackle a problem. Being a game about ninja, the visual design employs some Japanese style in the levels. There are also other styles depending on the current level, ranging from a modern city, a castle, and the Middle East. This game uses a hand drawn and animated style for objects and people, which look nice visually and stand out from each other. The game's background graphics have intricate designs and distinct silhouettes. Most of the game is shown in a black silhouettes with some highlights. This is both an artistic and a gameplay choice, since lit areas will show the full color of things on screen, while in darkness black silhouettes are shown. The animated cutscenes help drive the story and stay consistent with the style of the game. The cutscene animation quality is great, as if it were an actual show, and has its unique Japanese inspired style like the game's graphics. Overall, the art style leans towards a great animated style with some Japanese influences along with a few other distinct designs.
The music in this game is both a mix of traditional Japanese and contemporary styles. There aren't that many tracks to this game, but the music tends to change dynamically based on actions in the game. There are a few special songs that play at certain parts of the game to heighten a certain mood. Still, the music sounds great here and helps drive the game's style along.
The story of Mark of the Ninja features an unnamed ninja under the control of Azai, his master, on a mission to assassinate the owner of a company called Hessian. Along the way the player meets up with Ora, a female ninja who guides the player along in the game and Dosan, an artist who gives the playable unnamed ninja special tattoos. These tattoos grant special powers to the bearer, but cause them delve into madness if they have the mark for too long.
There is obviously more to the plot without spoiling it, but the story for Mark of the Ninja is thought out well and has excellent twists and turns throughout the whole game. The animated cutscenes occur mainly between levels and help drive the story, along with special levels designed to advance the story further. The strong story will keep players on the game, along with its excellent gameplay.
This game takes the stealth genre and applies it to a 2d platformer with wildy amazing results. For starters, the player needs to take advantage of line of sight, lighting, and sound to slip by undetected. These three things each have their own visual cues, ranging from blurring, silhouettes, and circles to represent sound that others can hear. The player can kill enemies, but it usually has to be done using stealth. Going at an enemy head on where they can see you is a surefire way to get killed. Along the way, the player can use special tools or moves to help kill or sneak by enemies, and can be upgraded or unlocked with special tokens earned from playing the game. Enemies can be distracted, take notice of you, and can even be terrified. Knowing the best course of action when the enemy behavior changes is vital. Sometimes, a puzzle needs to be solved to advance, which is based on some special mechanics seen throughout the levels. The game does open up a wide amount of options to get through an area with complex tools to accomplish the task. Solving a puzzle or navigating a room of enemies successfully feels rewarding, and it's not just the assassination animations looking cool too. Taking the stealth genre and putting it in a 2d game is well done here, as you do have many options and tools to use for a very engaging experience.
Mark of the Ninja nails its 2d stealth platforming down, and it also has an animated visual style and a well written story. You will definitely enjoy all three of these parts of the game for the high quality demonstrated in this game as a whole.

This is one of my favorite total war games. I have been plying the series since the first one: Shogun Total War.
Those two games made a few things better then more recent total war games and that is why I still love playing them.
First one the strategic map played differently. It was not as visually appealing and it did not try to look like the actual terain you are conquerring. It looked just like a map but the way it worked allowed for much more depth in the strategic maneuvers that newer titles of the series do not allow.
Instead of marching your armies around the map similar to Heroes of Maith and Magic, you moved your amrmies only from one province to adjacent provine. If at the end of the turn there are two rival armies in the same provine, they fight an open battle. Sounds very simple and without much depth, but that approach allowes for one very inportant difference: all factions turns are played at the same time. In the Heroes style of starategic movement, when you march your army and meet another army, you can attack them and they can not escape because it is your turn. They can withdraw just once a couple of tiles away, but if you still have movement points and attack them again they are trapped. If they are in a city and you besiege them, they have to either sally our and defeat you, or just stay and stavre to death. They can not run away. You just have to create a strong army and march arount conquering everithing that stands before you. Any army you can reach withihn your turn you can destroy.
In Medival TW I and Shogun TW I, when you are attacked you have a choise: you can fight the battle, you can reatreat to your stronghold(if there is any in this province) or you can abbandon the province. This gives much more stratgic options. When you are attacked you can give ground to the enemy and regroup your troops. The further the enemy goes in your teritory the more troops they have to leave behind as a garrison to maintain order in the  conquerred terrytory and your retreating troops combine with more troops from other provinces, so your army is getting stronger and the invader is getting weakr. You can choose where to fight. You can avoud his main army and just attak weak provinces and so on. This also gives many options to the attacker. You may attack with overwhelming force some central provinces cutting the enemy empire to peaces, isolating his armies, and then attacking each pocket with concentrated strength. You can attack multiple provinces at once cutting the reatreat of any troops so they got captured at the border without a fight and outmaneuvre your opponent and destroy him without battle.
Sure this does not allow for other cool strategies like having more strategic mobility then your enemies by creating an entire army of cavlary like the steppe nomads. You can't do that because all armies move just one province at a time but the strategic depth is definitely supperior to the Heroes style total war games.
Another thing that I like abouth the first two total war games are the battles. At first glance they look very bad compared to more recent TW games. If however you don't look at the details but instead look at the action and the dynamics of the battle, they look and work much more like a real battle. The battle is much more chaotic. The terrain have much greater effect. The individual soldiers go back and forth, attacking, defending, trying to outmaneuvre each other, they take or give ground, they fight for their lives even when routing. The pace and movement speed of the units is very well made so the battle is not just one big click fest but it requires sound maneuvres and good judgment of timing.
I reccomend this game to every real strategy and war gamer.

The Novelist intends to reflect on the difficulty of juggling different aspects of life, but the way the story unfolds feels like nothing more than a basic decision tree, with a predictable structure that ultimately fails to deliver its point.

What is The Novelist?
Genre: first person exploration game for adults
Setting: family on vacation trying to solve problems
Difficulty: 3/10 --> basically easy
Length: 2 hours for a single playthrough
Mode: singleplayer campaign
First of all: The Novelist is a game for adults. It confronts you with interpersonal situations you will encounter in your adult life (or have encountered yet). It is about taking responsibility, making decisions and achieving a balance in a family's needs.
You play some sort of a poltergeist observing a family on vacation in a secluded house. The family consists of Dan, father and writer who is facing writer's block and has to finish his latest novel; there also is Linda, Dan's wife and former artist, trying to get a grip on her marriage with Dan and to start over her working career; and there is Tommy, their little boy struggling with grapho legasthenia and the need for playmates.
Now, in every chapter you read their thoughts, find out about each of their needs and have to decide which sounds the most important to you to have this character make a progress. At the same time, the other two will be disappointed. As you can choose another one for a compromise, you might soften negative aspects for one further character.
Eventually the player is absolutely free in his decisions; you can push forward only one character, letting both the other two drop badly; you can try to make them all happy; depending on what you choose the story developes further.
And that is why I would recommend the game: How would you decide? What is your priority? And, in the end, how would you rate your decisions made?
Really worth the price - and even more the experience!

Defiance is the unfortunate result of the mix of some of the worst aspects of the first two Soul Reaver games, namely the scarce story exposition from SR and SR2's linearity, with the latter being taken to the extreme.
Gone is the excellent world design of SR, replaced by evident linearity. You'll spend most of the game finding elemental reavers, navigating the same environments and solving boring puzzles. If at first you may find the battle system improved, you'll soon come to the realization of how basic it really is, thanks to the game's over-reliance on it. The way the game is segmented feels unnatural and pace-breaking. The fixed camera angles rarely work in the game's favor. Character interactions and plot progress feel rare, when compared to SR2's expertly distributed story exposition. The graphics feel, at times, worse than SR2's. I can only assume Crystal Dynamics had significant budget limitations when making this game.
So, what good is there here? Well, things get really interesting in the the final hours with a lot of exposition, confrontations and character interaction. The conclusion was satisfying to me, but I can see others not being completely content with it. But all the good the game has to offer is meaningless if you have to endure a considerable number of hours of boring gameplay to get to it.
If you play the first two SR games, odds are you'll want to see how it ends, and so you will play Defiance regardless of others' opinions, but unlike those two, this is a game you'll probably only play once. Disappointing.
