Pre-emptive warning: I haven't spoiled any major plot points, but there are some tonal spoilers for one of the game's endings.
I err on the side of recommending this game, but I can't claim that it isn't very deeply flawed. Its main failing is that the story is about a lot of things, but the ending is 100% reliant on whether or not you "win back" your love interest. Personally, I thought it would be most satisfying to play a character initially very deeply set on reconnecting with his ex, but gradually coming to terms with the breakup and, in the end, letting the ceremony go uninterrupted. In this playthough, I had been successful in almost every aspect of my life: religiously keeping a journal, participating only in activities I believed in, and treating everyone with kindness. My character's future was promising. So, what ending did I get?
The one where I'm suicidal, nihilistic and alone because I couldn't bear the pain of losing my ex-girlfriend, who I'd had every intention of getting over on the way to her wedding. This is the only ending possible if you fail to "win her back", regardless of your other achievements or the way you've roleplayed your character. The game as a whole could be massively improved by the removal of the framing device at the beginning and end, as, for many endings, it fundamentally doesn't make sense and stands contrary to the story's themes. There's a fine post-credits scene, but it didn't negate my confusion at my character's hysterical response to making a perfectly fair, mature decision that, in my mind, caused him no great pain. It was a very "Huh?" moment for me.
As for the rest of the story, it's pretty good. Extremely tonally uneven (I found myself going "Really?" probably a dozen times) but not at all bad when you look past that, and I genuinely enjoyed most of the campaign. The trip was gruelling but satisfying, with more than its share of close calls and poignant moments, and it felt like I was coming to the end of a long journey when I finally arrived at the ex's wedding location. It's not realistic, but there's a realness to it -- something humbling about the situations you're faced with, an earnestness in the way the game presents love, friendship, and hope. I guess that's why I felt degraded by the ending... I mean, how can my character be so nihilistic when the past month has probably been the most interesting in his life? He's learned so much, experienced so much, yet the game gives me a pitch-black failstate because I didn't adhere to the arbitrary goal. It's not only unsatisfying, but also troubling philosophically. I guess I would recommend this game with the cliche that you should focus on the journey, not the desitation... or play with the LI in mind. Either way.

Always Sometimes Monsters is frequently tedious and rife with things that shatter any suspension of disbelief. I had high hopes for this game, but it really fails to deliver on its promise of an open story of moral ambiguity in favor of a tedious romp through a poorly explained plot that looks like it was written by a 15-year-old going through their "edgy" stage. There is a lot to do, but none of it feels especially worth doing, and a lot of it affects nothing so far as I can tell. Maybe there's a point to buying crab rather than chicken apart from wasting money. Also, ideas like "Sandwich Furtures" traded at a terminal in a sandwich shop, banks that require a security question to make a deposit, and day care providers willing to overlook an allegation of terrorism on a criminal background check are all sufficiently stupid (and not actually funny) that they do nothing but detract from the story.
The characters are too close to being parodies of archetypes to feel truly endearing, and some of them are introduced to disappear completely from the game moments later. I stayed at a girl's house for nine days and saw her exactly once, despite the fact that the she seemed like she could be an interesting and dramatic character. Meanwhile, I have to deal with the Kurt Cobain / Courtney Love analogues far more than I want. Too often, the choices I wanted to make I could not, and the questions I wanted answered were not.
Production-wise, the graphics are bland and inconsistent Some characters look completely different in their close-up versions and their walking versions. The imagery is often too cartoony for how dark the subject matter is trying to be (although a lot of that "darkness" comes off as a ham-fisted attempt at shock value), but not cartoony enough to feel like more than a bland vaguely anime look. The sound effects are ear-bleedingly jarring at times, with obnoxious beeps and sudden bursts of animal noise contrasted by the near complete silence of the game world apart from the music (of which I have generally few complaints). Even when the sound effects are appropriate, the lack of other appropriate sound effects make them feel out of place. If that was a design decision, it was a terrible one, but judging by the overall production value, I suspect they just couldn't be bothered to put any serious work into them.

This game had a lot of promise as a DF-lite, but it's been abandoned by the dev. It's by no means a bad game, but it does have it's problems and is definitely not complete by any means.
Here are (IMO) the problems:
- Lack of end-game
Once you have things up and running, there just isn't that much to do. This was a problem I ran into in all of my playthroughs - I'd have a blast fending off the initial goblin raids and getting my basic setup, but after that it was just wave after wave of goblins, and the only real threat that they pose to you is lagging your game to death.
- Combat
Combat is pretty terrible, mostly due to enemies being able to stack endlessly on a single hex. What this means is that you'll have a hundred-goblin doomstack running around, one-shotting your soldiers because they're getting hit hundreds of times before they can do anything. Now there are ways to devise traps so that enemies will trickle more slowly into your forces or eliminate the need for a military entirely, but that doesn't detract from the fact that the core mechanic - combat, is lacking.
- Crashes/game breaking bugs
I've lost a few of my kingdoms due to this. Most of the time it seems like something specific is causing it because I'll get crashes at the exact same point when I reload the game.
- Performance
The game is pretty badly optimized, especially once you get to about the mid-game. Goblin raids are also pretty bad once they pick up in size.
- Communication
While this doesn't relate directly to the game, I thought it'd be worth mentioning. The developer, Robob0b, has disappeared off of the face of the earth, deleting his social media accounts. There was also a developer roadmap on his website listing promised features, but it's since been removed. Not a very professional attitude.

I have no idea why this game has only 65% positive rating. Wait, actually I do, but more on that later.
For some reason I played DXMD just recently and totally skipped its release, also meaning I skipped all the hype about it. To be honest, I even barely remembered what Human Revolution was about, so I basically played this game unclouded without any memories about its predecessor and without any grand expectations.
And oh boy, I had a blast! To make this reading easier, I made this review using bulleted list.
Alright, so about this 65% rating. When the game was just released, fresh, I heard, vaguely, about microtransactions issue the game had, but I did not care enough at the time to understand what all the fuss was about. Well, now I do, I have seen the in-game shop, and yes, you can buy bullets, weapons, Praxis kits and other consumables there; but really, it looks like all the complainers haven't actually played the game at all. If you will play the game how it is meant to be played (meaning you will explore your surroundings and pick up all the stuff laying around), you will never be short of anything. In fact, when I finished the game, I had 20k credits, 20 multitools, 1k various bullets and 10 (!) spare Praxis kits I didn’t even spent because I already had everything for stealth-hacking playstyle I chose to play.
So, all the downvotes were just because of possibility to buy some in-game things for real money, and might I remind you, it's not even a multiplayer game! So I don’t really get what the heck this all was about; including microtransactions in the game probably was a bad desicion, but in-game shop availability doesn't eradicate all the amazing work that was put into making the game itself. Therefore, if you missed that game just because you heard of microtransactions - congratulations, you just spoiled yourself this great game for no real reason.
So, definitely
. If you want to play the game with rich story and fascinating world - it is a game for you. Do not be too sensitive to unfounded accusations that are irrelevant to the game in the first place.

Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is an incredibly ambitious, expansive and exciting game, based in a realistic, living world, filled with NPC's who talk about the world you inhabit with other NPC's, occasionally giving you useful information on alternative infiltration methods or paths, and sometimes, information on areas you have yet to explore, or areas you didn't even know existed.
DEMD is very much a game for strategists, rewarding those who plan and utilise stealth, while punishing those who move in guns blazing. A method of game design that has unfortunately been in decline over the last 10 years or so.
As always DEMD is very much reflective of current first-world political landscapes, showing a very much exaggerated version of the current attitude to politics, and the NPC's reflect the general civilian opinions, that the oppressive government is controlling media and enforcing the law to an unnecessary but ultimately self-damaging extent in response to internal and external pressure in the form of terror attacks.
In DEMD you are provided with a series of rudimentary choices, whether to side with the augmented civilians, or the government backed militant forces, an interesting position, as throughout gameplay I was never sure whether I was doing the "right" thing, and that is where this game shines; As a stealth, narrative-driven semi open-world game, it's pretty basic, fun abilities to play with, but locked behind a gameplay wall, reminiscent of having abilities and equipment locked to levels in other games, but as a serious satire piece on the current political landscape, this is a brilliant game, blurring the lines between what is "right" and "wrong", forcing you into the position, of not really being sure whether what yo are doing is ever right, but pushing you on, following your initial choice which cannot be taken back.
This game shows the futility of both faction's actions, and that the conflict between the militants and augmented will simply amplify until one side is triumphant over the other, but destroying a large part of itself in the process.
The gameplay itself is almost identical to Human Revolution, with improved mouse smoothing to help prevent the jerkiness of the camera this time around, but from a gameplay perspective, very little has changed, with the exception of having some new abilities.
With RPG elements being part-and-parcel of a Deus Ex title, the inventory, collection and consumption systems are almost unchanged and fairly rudimentary, with nothing particularly special about them.
The inventory's context menu (right click on objects) has an issue of selection, forcing you to left-click away to cancel the menu before opening it on another object a lot of the time, leaving you frustrated when you finally manage to clear out 20 different pieces of junk from the inventory.
Although on my third playthrough now, I am still finding new secrets, new areas and new items to play with, explore and learn about, this game is filled to the brim with optional content that, unfortunately due to the style of game, many players will never see.
Many will shun this game for it's short narrative which can be beaten in a few hours, whereas myself, currently at 25 hours, and still finding new content in a world which is far larger than initially realised.
The game's main major fail is that it has all of this wonderful, interesting and sometimes funny (NPC dialogue) content which many players will never see, as it is not along the main narrative line, and is not seen unless you take to an extreme amount of exploring between missions, exploring the different areas using the transit and sewer systems.
I love exploring generally unseen areas, the first time I realized I could open a sewer manhole cover, I fell in love, escaping firefights which I started frequently in my first play through by walking around 50 feet below my enemies, allowing me to reposition, explore the backend of the city, gain access to areas generally far more difficult to explore, discover areas that aren't seen until later in the game along the narrative line, and finding useful equipment which can make the story and exploration far more interesting.
Many, many computer terminals and information devices are strewn across the game's map, which allow you to gather information from insight into the world you inhabit, to grocery lists. All of these make the world feel just a little bit more alive.
Related to the computer terminals, pretty much all the security doors can be opened by obtaining a security code from various places, instead of hacking it. You can get these from computer logs, audio logs, NPC chatter, sometimes from world elements and other places, all of this makes for a much more immersive experience, it's a wonderful feeling to casually sit next to 2 NPC guards and overhear the code to a door, casually wander off and completely circumvent their security due to the guards incompetence.
With all of this in mind, DEMD makes for an interesting, if not convoluted game when taking ALL elements into account.
DEMD succeeds in strides in its narrative, world building, open-world gameplay and freedom between missions, but fails on more basic elements such as controls, ability accessibility and voice acting (sometimes coming off very unbelievably, breaking immersion at times).
DEMD must be commended for its use of curfews and their programmed responses are wonderful, and really add to the illusion that this is indeed a real world.
In conclusion, DEMD is quite a good game, with clear passion and hard work put into the storyline, world-building, art, animation, world population (NPC's, items, computers, messages etc) open-world exploration, freedom and abundance of hidden areas, but falls short in others like controls, access to abilities, forcing you to toggle abilities at times to prevent overheating when you just want to be an unstoppable tank sometimes just for fun.
DEMD isn't a bad game, it's quite a good game, and it doesn't deserve the reception it has received, a game such as this not meeting or exceeding sales predictions casts an uncertain shadow over narrative-focussed games such as Deus Ex and Dishonored, the last refinance of a long-gone era of complex games that require forethought and planning to execute perfect missions, and I hope with all my heart that games like this continue to be made in this scope and attention to detail far into the future.

World-Building & Believability: 8 / 10
Controls and Player: 6 / 10
Graphics: 9.5 / 10
Animations: 9 / 10
Voice Acting: 6 / 10
Open-World Aspects: 9 / 10

I have played for just over an hour so far, using a controller and monitor, the graphics are good and on my system with a little over the minimum requirements will run smoothly on max settings.  The recommended settings may be more of a guide for VR use.
The core idea of the game is solid, and seems to play its best when aiming for the motor trials ideal.  The levels that task you with difficult turns or routes over complicated terrain I have found the most enjoyable, allowing the player to have a chance to get to grips with the vehicles and the games use of physics.  Unfortunately often the game faces you with levels that amount to no more than target shooting, firing the trucks at a part of the level geometry in the hope of landing somewhere near the finish.  In these cases the game can be frustrating and tedious, the bouncy, poorly damped nature of most vehicles handling combines poorly with the feel of low gravity that the game gives off in most levels, let alone the actual low gravity space based ones.
The music in the levels quickly grates and the vehicle sound effects are poor, there also appears to be issues with sound volume and camera position, meaning that quite often on the jumping levels you launch the truck into a distant rock to hear no sound from its collision with the ground, only for the camera and noise to catch up as the wreckage rolls into the sea.
I can see the core of a good, maybe even great, game here, but I feel the developers should look at spliting up the more technical levels from the zany and crazy ones and perhaps open the levels out in physical width, allowing for a more natural playstyle that gives the player a chance to devise routes and learn how to make the most of the game engine.  weighting the trucks in a more realistic way, modifying in game grip to give more actual usable power to the ground to better represent traction but at the same time reducing the trucks tendency to back or front flip would also improve the feel of the game.
The new 3rd person camera is a fantastic improvement, but I feel adding pitch adjustment would also help greatly, in a game focussing on careful movement through difficult terrain having a very adjustable and mobile camera will help the player in the long run.
I am happy with my purchase of the game, I understand its position as early access and am happy to see frequent updates from the developers and I am also interested to see what the community can produce with the in game editor, it is the next element of the game I am interested in trying.
Do I recommend this game?  at this time I think yes, I hope for good things in the future and am encouraged by the updates being produced.  Others may find more value when it is picked up on a sale but I have enjoyed my playtime overall.

1: Make a text file (right click on desktop -> new -> text document)
2: Name it
3: Type the following commands:
@ echo off
:loop
date month-day-year
echo Set Date 1
timeout /t 1
date month-day-year
echo Set Date 2
timeout /t 1
goto loop
4: Replace dates as necessary (first date current, second a few years in the future)
5: Rename file extension to .bat

I have been looking for a game even relatively like Carbon for ages. I'm not sure how I missed this, but I love it. And I want more. I want so much more.
Just... God, it's good. It's that perfect line between being arcade-styled racing, but not being so over-the-top arcadey that it forsakes all physics. Driving may not be realistic - as in, your tires have such insane grip that you won't spin out and crash after ripping on the handbrake for a turn - but god DAMN it's fun.
On top of that, the customization. Good LORD! The customization! Just... I can't describe how well it's done. Controls in the customization menu are a wee bit wonky, but, managable. Other than that, though, just, holy crap. At least half my game time is spent editing visuals, upgrading and tweaking cars, and I love it. Every second of it. Of course, there's also the option to not customize your car if that ain't your thing, but for those of you who love vinyls and paint jobs and all that jazz? You. Will. Be. Pleased.
It's fast, it's satisfying, it's got a feeling of personalization, it's almost everything I've wanted in a racing game.
Almost.
Where it lacks is two things. And both of them are the placement of difficulty.
Once a mission is done, you get a hefty chunk of change. Do it again? 10% of that change, at most. This is severely depressing if you manage to lose a car to the police by bad luck. Car gets impounded with less than $3000 or so in the bank? Kiss it goodbye. Customizations and all. This means that you'll likely be grinding a lot if you get unlucky and lose your favorite car at a horrble moment, or if you want to get all the cars. (Well... You can use cheat codes, but, nyeh.)
And, then there's the missions themselves. The only times I've lost is to cars that are a tier above mine - and those times were all just barely losses - or when I made, like, 5-10 mistakes in a race. I've made it a personal challenge to not use speedbreaker - which is basically bullet time for better turning - and it's still easy. Every race is more a time trial than a race, really, that's how far ahead of the pack I normally am. But god damn, it's a fun time trial, and it's only marginally less satisfying to play because of it.
Final verdict? Unless you're a diehard racing simulator type person, buy this. Buy it now. And then wonder why the hell there aren't more games like it.

There is no mouse support whatsoever, not even on menus.  You can rebind all the keys to any buttons on keyboards, joysticks, etc.  I highly recommend playing this with a controller or even a joystick.
As with most Lego games, you can play local co-op on a single computer, which is a great feature.  Supsequently, there is no online co-op.  However, co-op is nearly impossible with a keyboard.  Essentially, one player uses one half of the keyboard and the other player uses the second half.  This isn't the issue though.  The problem is that regular keyboards cannot register more than 4 keys being pressed at the same time, so sometimes one player won't be able to attack or jump.  If you have a mechanical keyboard, this isn't an issue.  Ideally both players should have controllers, but either player can bind their controls to any kind of input peripheral.

The Novelist is deceptive in its title. While the story is indeed primarily about a novel writer, the writer isn't who you think it actually is. What is more important, that your son gets the help and love he needs and deserves, or your career that your family might live a comfortable life?
I generally hate it when games make me cry, but good tears were made and for that I think the creator of The Novelist deeply. I've never had an experience like this before.

I thought it was a great game, it works on a very deep psychological level as you are faced with making some difficult and uncomfortable decisions and facing their consequences. I really haven't played anything else like this. The game is short and simple yes, but there is a lot of replay value as you try to find the best outcomes for all the characters. You may even find that it turns a mirror on you and makes you consider more deeply the effects that your own decisions have on those around you in real life.

If there's one thing I've learned in adulthood, it's that free time is the most precious limited resource we have. The decision to do anything in life is at the expense of countless other potential activities, which is the fundamental struggle I deal with while playing video games all the time. Where will you invest your free time? Your writer's block? Your broken marriage? Your needy son? You can't do it all.
The Novelist is a game about family, priorities, and compromise.
Perhaps the game's most brilliant coup is casting you in the role of a ghost. It would be easy and incorrect to assume that the player character is the novelist himself. You, the ghost, work behind the scenes as an observer of the experience and can only help to influence the thoughts of the novelist. You the Player decide where he invests his time, and that decision (made at the end of each chapter by whispering suggestions into his ear while he sleeps) affects his wife, his son, and his career.
Why is this so brilliant? It's a question of agency. If you controlled the novelist directly, you might get frustrated by the family's inability to communicate successfully. In fact, you might feel that frustration anyway, since each character begins the game with wildly different needs. "Aren't I working on my career for the sake of my family?" you might ask yourself as the novelist. "Can't my family accept that a few months to myself will pay off in the long term?" "Why can't I make compromises that please everybody?" "Why can't my wife and son spend time together without me?" These are all valid questions....but you are not the novelist. You are just a ghost. This is the rare game where your limitations as a player work within the context of your character, and your limited and indirect effect on the game world makes total sense.
In the end, while you can only set the stage and watch it unfold, the way the game makes you think remains powerfully human. How do I take care of my family? How do I balance my goals and their needs?
What will make me a happy person?

I'm really stuck on whether I can say I would recommend this game to someone else or not.
Brawlhalla is a fun game with an interesting concept, fun mechanics, and overall fun design. Balance is pretty easy to maintain in this game due to its weapon system, and throwing/(chase) dodge mechanics can result in the ability to create some amazing combos and counters.
Matches always have the
to be insanely fun, with fast-paced, hard-fought, and smart actions, which is even truer with the new dash feature that has been getting a lot of hate.
The problem is that the only thing this game has is potential.
Lots of games have potential. And most of those games waste the potential. This game is still really new, but the devs continue to disappoint me time after time, showing the community that they fail to understand how to improve their game.
When I first started playing, this game's balance was a mess. Certain weapons were far stronger than others, and the difference in weapon balance was easy to feel. I was new however, and so it did not bother me. The balance also gradually improved.
As my skill level increased, I learned about new issues with the game, as well as some really cool things such as how to properly utilize the versatile dodge feature for combos, which is to be expected.
Many people complain about "passive" this, "parry" that, and these were definitely a massive problem in the past. The community had been complaining about these things since before  I started playing, and it took the devs at least a year to begin to tackle this problem. On the other hand, it only took them a couple of months to fix it. The fact that it took so long to tackle the problem is rather ridiculous as the community had been making many, many suggestions on how to fix the game, including the new dash feature.
When the dash feature first arrived in test features, much of the community (especially higher level players) was happy about it. I was also included in the group that was happy about it. BMG then proceeded to immediately gut dash to the point of it being useless, which resulted in the problematic "parry" and "passive" play to become even stronger. At that point I uninstalled, and kept an eye on what happened in the game's following updates.
BMG proceeded to nerf dash multiple times following the initial nerf (as well as giving it some compensation buffs), and they kept doing so until they released that dash would become an actual mechanic in the game in the next two or three weeks. When I saw that dash was finally fixed, I reinstalled the game and tried it out. I loved the dash feature, and I was finally able to get back into the game.
Here's where the next problem shows up...
As it turns out, many  people had been experiencing lag in Brawlhalla since its release. Severe lag. And the lag is (mostly) not due to said users' internet connections, but rather the game itself.
To me, this wasn't really a problem, as I'd never experienced it myself, and I just continued to look forward to the official release of dash.
BMG, however, decided that they were going to couple the release of dash with a botched netcode change, albeit the lack of dash playtesting by the majority of the community.
It was with this patch in which Blue Mammoth Games (BMG) tampered with the netcode where the game became borderline unplayable for myself and many others.
The netcode changes were an attempt to fix the long-lasting lag that many players have been experiencing, which on its own, is fine.
The changes, however, caused far more lag than they resolved, with the majority of players I've played with and against in this game since this patch claiming that they are getting far more lag than they ever received before. The game has become so shoddy that even in BMG's official online tournaments, players are constantly failing to connect to their matches.
It doesn't really make sense to me how the community is supposed to adjust to dash when they're busy tampering with the netcode at the same time, causing many people to receive ridiculous lag.
The lag isn't just connection lag, either. Somehow, the lag (for me, at least) persists in single-player, resulting in teleporting bots that randomly kill me. That's only one type of lag, as well. Input lag is also really common, and I happen to have that input lag as well at times.
The devs never take the time to resolve a problem before trying to introduce something, they simply toss out skins left and right while hoping the community ignores all the problems that perpetually accumulate. Every single solution Blue Mammoth Games hurls out is bundled with another two rage-inducing faults.
While BMG
listen to the community and extensively interacts with the community, it's all for naught if they change the game too frequently with inadequate thought and testing before any of their solutions resolve any of the game's errors.

I'm happy with my purchase. It's a lot like DF, a lot more accessible, and somewhat less deep, so I will compare this game to DF. It does improve on DF here and there, like with automatons and mechanic limbs. I also found combat to be more game-y, since you regularly get varied opponents with specific strengths and weaknesses, depending on their race and equipment, so you need to balance your single/double handed swords, hammers, shields and crossbows, the materials and qualities they are made of, and how much training your gnomes have at them. All of this is also simulated in DF, but in Gnomoria it affects the strategic choices you have to make a lot more.
Core crafting is more interesting as well: for example, beds require a wooden sub-part to be made, and a cloth/wool mattress, each with their respective quality depending on the material used and the skill of the carpenter and tailor that made them. Metallic armor requires cloth padding and metallic weapons require wooden handles.
If what you want is gnomes that learn skills over time, crafting quality, material modifiers, digging for metals, training and equipping a varied army; getting it good at different weapons to beat the very distinct kinds of enemies you'll get; starting with wood and stone and then going through bronze and steel; traps, invasions, butchering orcs, smelting their drops, and then laughing at the combat log; trading and amassing wealth, legendary sandwiches and majestic dining rooms, then this game is for you.
Regarding the other reviews: There are (in my opinion) very few bugs and nothing game breaking. At least I never encountered a bug that broke my game or put me off from playing it. I paid about 9 bucks for the game a pretty long time ago, and I've personally considered my purchase worthy since version 0.8 or so. I'm not sure what some of the other players were expecting, but during development, the dev was always open about what might or might not make it into the game, what were the priorities and what (few) things might get dropped; and as far as I'm concerned, everything I realistically expected made it into the game, and more. Sure, he could have gone on working on it forever, but the same can be said about every other game.

A great story driven RPG game. However due to the limitation of RPG maker engine,the graphic and control is too simple. Moverover, the condition to get a happy ending for first time player is harsh, which makes the choice the player made in game oversimplified, insignificant and frustrated.

Instead of a hero saving the world, you are a regular down-and-out writer living in a cruel society. A year ago, you signed a deal with a publisher and foresaw a bright future with your significant other. What followed was a chain of events that would set your life downhill for the next year.
Now, you are alone. Your career is on the verge of collapse. Your wallet is empty, and so is your stomach. Your ex is getting married in a city across the country, and you are invited. You are homeless because you could not pay the rent.
Would you steal and lie, or work honestly?
Would you do everything you can to win back your love, or learn to let go?
Would you attend the wedding to voice your objection, or give your regards?
Would you leave your friend to die, or sacrifice yourself for their good?
These are some of the questions you will find in this game. The game is not a typical RPG game. You don't have weapons, you don't kill people unless you choose to.
In life, sometimes there is good choice and bad choice. But sometimes, there is no choice at all. What would you do? How far are you willing to go when your life, happiness or future is at stake?
This game has, in my opinion, one of the best stories I have ever seen. It makes you think about choices and consequences. If you are not into narrative games, this game may not appeal to you.

Off-Road Paradise: Trial 4X4:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

One of the greatest inventions of the 19th Century is without a doubt the automobile. Some are built to look good but surprisingly are lemons; some are built to go fast, but these days unless you are a professional racing driver you are pretty much going to do 110 KM/H at best on a motorway (Down Under, that is). However, some are built for discovering and passing the most difficult terrains. They are Off-Road vehicles. . . Oh, what about Off-Road in Paradise; let’s give it a trial!
Off-Road Paradise: Trial 4X4 is a car simulation where you have to successfully navigate your 4X4 vehicle to the checkered flag.
One aspect of this game I really liked straight away is the fact that you can choose to play it either as a VR experience or with your gamepad and current monitor. This way you get the best of both worlds!
At first, you will reach the main menu.  Here you can select to play in one of a few different modes: in the main game, consisting of 150 levels; on local multiplayer, where one person uses the VR setup and the other one uses the monitor; or as two players using the same PC. A level editor will be coming soon as well as an arena mode.
Let’s write about the scenery . . . you are in the middle of the ocean, with the sound of the waves crashing on the rocks and the birds flying by dropping free gifts as they pass through (just kidding)! The gameplay is splendid. It consists of short levels where you have to successfully reach the checkered flag. In terms of the terrain, you will be driving on rocks in the middle of the ocean with additional obstacles in your way, such as logs, wooden boats and more. In each level, you can collect a totem which will allow you to unlock new cars, paint, engines, tyres and steering wheels. I used the HTC VIVE and I must admit it was fun to use the right controller to steer the car. You will have plenty of options in regards to the camera angles, and depending on some levels, you will need to swap from one angle to another to clear the stage.
Graphically the game looks great and the soundtrack is fabulous too. Control-wise, I used a gamepad and the HTC controllers and I must admit I am very surprised at how responsive the controls are. You can use a steering wheel if you own one.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Great Graphics
-	150 Levels to clear (40 in Early Access)
-	Compatible with HTC Vive, Oculus and monitors
-	Trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Can bit frustrating at times
Off-Road Paradise: Trial 4X4 has short, entertaining progressive difficulty level. Just well done!
7/10

Medieval: Total War is a game I spent hundreds of hours on in my gaming youth. For the time, the graphics were amazing (and are still charming today), while the game-play was addicting. Up until a few months ago, I still had the disc version installed on my computer, and knew a number of tricks and hax to get the game to function without crashing every other turn. So when I saw that the game had been released on Steam with the promise of new patches and upgrades, I had to get it and see for myself if there were any improvements.
So how does the game run? Very well. Load times are massively reduced. Ten hours in, and not a single crash (auto-save is enabled). Wide-screen resolutions actually work; the game plays flawlessly in 1080p . A slight downside: the on-screen text gets REALLY small at higher resolutions; the game also ran flawlessly in 1440p, but the text was so tiny I was worried about eye-strain. Also strange: if you select “wide screen” in the options menu, the battles play out with black bars at the top and bottom of the screen. If you select “full screen”, the black bars are gone and the battlefield takes up the entire screen (which is what I wanted anyway).
The Medieval: Total War is one of the classic strategy titles for a reason. You'll build your armies and manage your economy, while trying to establish an empire – one faction to rule them all! There are a lot things Medieval: Total War does that the sequels (starting with the very next Total War game, the first Rome TW) simply don't have. Like faction respawning. Think you've wiped a faction from the map? Not likely; the next rebellion  may spawn several massive armies in your heartland with a message like “A long-lost heir from a faction presumed destroyed is trying to reclaim his throne.” Even better, if a rival destroyed a faction, send in spies and assassins to wreak havoc and cause a revolt, in the hopes of the faction respawning in your enemy's territory, giving you the perfect opportunity to strike. Other factions emerge at specific times, like the Burgundians and the Swiss; each field some new troop types that cause a variety of problems. Putting an effort into building trading routes pays dividends, awarding huge amounts of cash if you can protect your trading routes. Conserving money and investing in the right technologies at the right time can produce an unstoppable army; spending too much too soon may give you powerful troops, but no cash to pay them. Loyalty will decline, and the troops might even rebel. Failing a crusade or jihad, or your king dying will seriously impact army loyalty - at least until the new king shows himself to be a strong leader.
The battle AI is actually smart, trying to flank with cavalry, or keep you at a distance to pelt your army to death with arrows. Say you've struggled to beat most of an Egyptian army; there's just four more units located on the other side of that sand dune. Your now-exhausted troops trudge up to the ridge, ready to turn and run at the first surprise, and... those four units are all Ghulam Bodyguards. Well, you're screwed. Your own greed will defeat you time and again in battle. Balance your armies, choose good defensive positions, attack with careful timing, and send your troops in pursuit of a fleeing enemy with prudence. A sudden influx of enemy reinforcements could rout the units you sent in pursuit, which could turn the tide of the battle against you.
The Steam version of Medieval: Total War is exactly the game that I remember from before, now with faster load times and wide-screen resolutions. This might be my nostalgia talking, but the game stands as one of the greatest and best Total War titles, despite its age. Don't hesitate to grab this one.
